en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Section on Defeat in the Basket of Discipline (First Part)
The Introduction to the Composition:
He who, even after an immeasurable time of ten million eons,
while passing away, performs deeds that are exceedingly difficult to accomplish;
The Protector grew weary for the sake of the world’s welfare;
homage to him, the Greatly Compassionate One.
That which is unawakened yet frequented by the Buddhas—
The world of living beings goes from existence to existence;
homage to that excellent Dhamma which destroys the net of defilements beginning with ignorance.
He who is endowed with qualities such as virtue,
concentration, wisdom, and the knowledge of liberation,
is a field for people who seek what is wholesome.
I bow my head in homage to that Saṅgha of the Tamarisa.
Thus, paying homage to this Triple Gem, which is worthy of eternal veneration;
I obtained an abundant outflow of merit;
by its power, my obstacles were destroyed.
While he remained, the Dispensation remained; when he passed away, it too ceased.
It is well-established for one who is well-composed;
I shall describe that Vinaya, free from admixture,
relying upon the power of the ancient teachers.
And although [this work] was [composed] by those who were like the foremost of former teachers,
whose stains and impurities had been washed away by the water of knowledge,
and who possessed purified clear-knowledge and analytical insight;
By those skilled in the exposition of the true Dhamma,
who are difficult to equal even by those practicing effacement,
and who are like the banner of the Mahāvihāra.
This Vinaya has been expounded by means of methods that follow the excellent lineage of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s mind.
This commentary was composed by one from the Island of Siṃhala.
But because this [work] was composed by means of prose, it does not accomplish any purpose for the community of monks in other islands. This is why.
Therefore, I shall now begin this commentary in accordance with the method of the canonical text (pāḷi),
following the request of the one named Buddhaśrī.
Correctly recollecting that Elder,
and commencing this commentary upon him,
[I shall rely] upon the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*) as its body.
Having likewise composed the Mahāpaccarī,
as well as those renowned as the Kurundi and others,
the exposition stated in the commentaries has been set forth.
O friend, without abandoning even that which is most essential,
I shall properly begin this commentary,
which is included within the Theravāda.
May the elders, the newly ordained monks, and those of middle standing, with hearts full of faith, listen to this from me:
[the teaching] of the Tathāgata, the lamp of the Dhamma.
Honoring the Dhamma with reverence—
this Dhamma and Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha,
and it is known in exactly that same way by his sons.
Therefore, since those wise men of old composed commentaries,
whatever has been stated in those commentaries [is to be accepted].
Having set aside that writing on negligence,
for those who possess reverence for all the trainings,
it is the standard here for the wise.
Then, having set aside the different languages,
having condensed the detailed path,
and having omitted no part of the entire analysis;
Without deviating from even a single step of the sequence,
I shall elucidate the meaning of the words of the Suttas in accordance with the Suttas themselves.
"Since this commentary shall also exist,
therefore it should be studied with diligence.
Thus ends the introductory narrative of the external context.
In this context, since it is said, "I shall explain that Vinaya," the Vinaya must first be defined. Therefore, this is said:
"Here, 'Vinaya' refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. For the purpose of its commentary, however, this is the summary (mātikā):
By whom it was spoken, when, and for what reason; by whom it was preserved and brought [to this land];
Having stated the procedure [beginning with] "Wherein this mind is established," I shall provide a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya,
demonstrating in various ways the meaning of the passage beginning with the word "tena" (by that).
Regarding that, the statement "by whom, when, and for what reason" was made with reference to such passages as: "At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā.
For this [latter] passage is not a word spoken by the Buddha, the Blessed One, from his own direct experience;
therefore, it must be asked: "By whom was this statement spoken? When was it spoken? And for what reason was it spoken?"
This was stated by the Venerable Elder Upāli, and that was at the time of the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti).
Regarding the discourse on the First Great Council:

although this so-called "First Great Council" is mentioned in the section on the Council of Five Hundred (Pañcasatikasaṅgītikkhandhaka), it is [discussed here] for the sake of proficiency regarding the introductory narrative (nidāna).

However, here too it should be understood according to this same method. For when the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, had performed his Buddha-activities— beginning from the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma until the conversion of the wanderer Subhadda—

and having passed away into the element of Nibbāna without residue at the time of dawn on the full-moon day of the month of Visākha, between the twin Sāla trees in the Mallans’ Sal Grove at Upavattana in Kusinārā, [the following occurred] regarding the Blessed One...

When seven hundred thousand bhikkhus had assembled for the Parinibbāna, the Elder of the Saṅgha, the Venerable Mahākassapa—seven days after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna—[replied] to Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age, who said: "Enough, friends, do not grieve, do not lament!
We are well rid of that Great Ascetic; we were troubled by him [when he said]: 'This is permitted to you...'"
"This is not permitted for you!"— recalling these words, [he thought: "It is indeed possible that, thinking the Teacher has passed away and the dispensation is now merely a word,
wicked bhikkhus might find followers and before long cause the true Dhamma to disappear."
As long as the Dhamma and Vinaya endure, so long does the teaching remain with its Teacher as if he were not yet passed away. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya which have been taught and laid down by me shall be your teacher after my passing.
“What if I were now to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together, so that this Dispensation might endure for a long time and remain stable?”
And when the Blessed One said to me, “Kassapa, will you wear my worn-out hempen rag-robes? and shared with me the use of robes, saying:
“Bhikkhus, as long as I desire, secluded from sensual pleasures... [I enter and dwell] in the first jhāna.”
‘I dwell thus; Kassapa too, monks, as long as he wishes, secluded from sensual pleasures...

[and so on] ... enters and dwells in the first jhāna’—in this manner, by means of his own [attainment], [he declares] the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) distinguished by the nine successive dwellings and the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā).
“Having been favored by this bestowing of equality upon equals, what other debt of gratitude could there be for him?
Did not the Blessed One, like a king, favor me with this extraordinary favor—by granting me his own armor and sovereignty, regarding me as a son who establishes his own family lineage, thinking:
‘This one shall be the establisher of my lineage of the True Dhamma’? Thus he reflected.
He inspired the bhikkhus to undertake the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya. As it is said:
“Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus:
‘Friends, on one occasion I was traveling along the highway from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering about five hundred bhikkhus.’”
The entire Subhadda Chapter should be understood in detail.
Following that, he said:
"Come now, friends, let us recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya. Before long, non-Dhamma will shine forth, while the Dhamma..."
“Non-Discipline is being displayed, while Discipline is being rejected.

Those who speak what is contrary to the Dhamma are powerful, while those who speak according to the Dhamma are weak; those who speak contrary to the Vinaya are powerful, while those who speak according to the Vinaya are weak.

The monks said, “In that case, venerable sir, let the Elder select the monks. The Elder [selected] those who had mastered the entire scriptural tradition of the Teacher’s dispensation consisting of the ninefold division.
Excluding several hundreds and several thousands of bhikkhus— ranging from worldlings (*puthujjana*) to stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakadāgāmi*), non-returners (*anāgāmi*),

dry-insight practitioners (*sukkhavipassaka*), and those whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*)— there remained only four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus whose taints were destroyed, who were endowed with great majesty, had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*),

and were masters of the entire classification of the scriptures of the Three Baskets (*tipiṭaka-pariyatti*), most of whom had been designated by the Blessed One as "foremost" (*etadagga*) in various categories such as the "Three-Veda-knowers" (*tevijja*).
He selected them. It was with reference to these that it was said: "Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected four hundred and ninety-nine Arahants.
But why did the Elder leave one short? For the sake of making room for the Venerable Ānanda.
For it is impossible to hold the Dhamma Saṅgīti either together with or without that Venerable; for that Venerable is still a trainee (sekha) who has duties yet to perform.

Therefore, it was not possible for him even together [with others]; yet, because there was nothing whatsoever taught by the One of Ten Powers—such as the Suttas or Geyyas—that he had received from the Blessed One in the Blessed One’s absence, it was not possible for him even apart [from others].

If this were so, then being still a trainee (*sekha*), he ought to have been selected by the Elder for the Dhamma-council on account of his great assistance; why then was he not selected? Because he wished to avoid the censure of others.

For the Elder was exceedingly confident in the Venerable Ānanda; indeed, even when grey hairs had grown upon his head, he would exhort him with the word "boy," saying, "This boy does not know his measure.

Moreover, this Venerable One was born into the Sakyan clan, being the Tathāgata’s brother and the son of his younger paternal uncle. For among the monks there, [the Venerable Ānanda] was like one who went according to his own will.

Fearing that others might criticize him, saying, "Setting aside Ānanda, who has attained the analytical knowledges of one still in training (sekha), the Elder has selected only those monks who have attained the analytical knowledges of one beyond training (asekha)," he avoided such censure and did not select [anyone], thinking:
"The rehearsal cannot be performed without Ānanda; I shall include him with the consent of the monks themselves."
Then the monks themselves requested the Elder on behalf of Ānanda. As it is said:

“The monks said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa: ‘Venerable sir, although this Venerable Ānanda is still a trainee, he is incapable of going astray through desire, hatred, delusion, or fear; furthermore, much has been heard by him in the presence of the Blessed One.’”
“The Dhamma and the Vinaya have been mastered. Therefore, venerable sir, let the Elder choose the Venerable Ānanda as well.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa chose the Venerable Ānanda as well.
Thus, together with that Venerable who had been chosen with the consent of the monks, there were five hundred elders.
Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus: "Where indeed should we recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya?
Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus: "Rājagaha has a great alms-resort and abundant lodgings;
what if we were to spend the rains retreat at Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya there?"
“Let no other bhikkhus enter the rains residence at Rājagaha. But why did they think this? [They thought:
“This is our secure undertaking; lest some person of a different character should enter the midst of the Saṅgha and reopen the matter.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa announced it by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*); that should be understood in the same manner as described in the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka*.
Then, when seven days of celebratory rejoicing and seven days of relic worship following the Tathāgata’s parinibbāna had passed,
the Elder Mahākassapa— considering that "half a month has elapsed, now only one and a half months of the summer remain,
and the commencement of the rains retreat is approaching"— said, "Friends, let us go to Rājagaha," and took half of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha with him.
One [monk] set out on one path. The Elder Anuruddha also took the other half and set out on a different path.
However, the Elder Ānanda, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robe and surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, departed for Sāvatthī;
desiring to go to Rājagaha, he set out on a journey toward Sāvatthī. Wherever the Elder Ānanda went, there was great lamentation.
He asked, "Venerable Ānanda, where have you come from, having left the Teacher behind?
When the Thera had gradually arrived at Sāvatthī, there was a great lamentation as on the day of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna.
There, the Venerable Ānanda [comforted] that great multitude with a discourse on the Dhamma connected with impermanence and other such themes.
Having consoled him, he entered the Jeta Grove, opened the door of the Perfumed Chamber where the One of Ten Powers had dwelt,
removed the bed and chair, shook them out, swept the Perfumed Chamber, discarded the withered garland and refuse, brought the bed and chair back inside,
and placed them back in their original positions; thus he performed every duty and service that was to be done when the Blessed One was present.
Then, from the time of the Blessed One’s parinibbāna, because the elder had spent much time standing and sitting, his body was afflicted by an excess of humors;
on the following day, having drunk a milk-purgative to restore his health, he remained seated right there in the monastery.
It was with reference to this that he spoke to the young man whom the youth Subha had sent.
“It is not the right time, young man; I have just drunk my dose of medicine today. Perhaps we may come again tomorrow.
On the second day, having gone with the Elder Cetaka as his attendant monk, he was questioned by the young man Subha and spoke the tenth sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya, known as the Subha Sutta.
Then, after having the repairs of the dilapidated parts of the Jetavana Monastery carried out, as the time for the commencement of the rains retreat drew near—
He went to Rājagaha. Likewise, the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Anuruddha, taking the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus with them, also went to Rājagaha.
Now at that time, there were eighteen great monasteries in Rājagaha; all of these were abandoned, fallen into ruin, and dilapidated.
They were thus. For at the time of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, all the bhikkhus took their own bowls and robes and departed, leaving behind the monasteries and the cells.
Thereupon, the elders, in order to honor the word of the Blessed One and to refute the doctrines of the sectarians, said:
"Let us first carry out the restoration of what is broken and dilapidated for one month."
They reflected. For the heterodox teachers (titthiyā) might say: "The disciples of the ascetic Gotama tended to the dwellings only while the Teacher was still alive;
once he had attained final nibbāna, they abandoned them. It is said that they reflected for the purpose of refuting such a claim. For this has also been stated:
Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus: “Friends, the Blessed One has praised the repair of what is broken and dilapidated.
Come now, friends, let us perform the repair of what is broken and dilapidated during the first month;
having assembled during the middle month, we shall chant together the Dhamma and the Vinaya.”
On the second day, they went and stood at the king’s gate. King Ajātasattu came, paid homage, and asked, “Venerable sirs, for what purpose have you come?
He then inquired about the task he was to perform. The elders informed him that they required manual labor for the restoration of eighteen great monasteries.
“Very well, venerable sirs,” the king replied, and he provided the men who would perform the manual labor.
The Elders, having had the entire monastery renovated during the first month, informed the king: "Great King, the renovation of the monastery is finished.
Now let us perform the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya. "It is well, venerable sirs; proceed with confidence.
Let my wheel of authority be yours as the wheel of Dhamma. Command me, venerable sirs; what shall I do?"

“Great King, it is fitting for the monks who are compiling [the Dharma] to have their assembly place on the slope of Mount Vebhāra, at the entrance to the Sattapaṇṇi Cave. “Where shall I build it, venerable sir?
“It is suitable, Great King, to build it at the entrance to the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the side of Mount Vebhāra. “Very well, venerable sir,” said King Ajātasattu.
Then he had a hall constructed resembling what was fashioned by Vissakamma, with well-proportioned walls, pillars, and staircases, and variegated with various kinds of floral designs and vine-work.
Having caused a pavilion to be constructed— a dwelling of glory that seemed to surpass the splendor of royal palaces, to mock the majesty of celestial chariots,
a single landing-place for the birds of the eyes of gods and men, as if the very essence of worldly beauty were gathered together—
he adorned it with various flower garlands and hanging festoons from which beautiful canopies dangled down.
Having adorned that great pavilion so that it resembled a Brahma-palace— with its ground-work perfectly finished and variegated with various offerings of flowers,
like a floor paved with jewels and diverse gems— he spread out five hundred priceless, allowable rugs for five hundred bhikkhus,
and [he himself] sat down on the southern side, facing north.
Having prepared a seat for the Blessed Buddha worthy of his throne in the center of the pavilion, facing eastward,
and having placed there a fan inlaid with ivory, he announced to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus:
"Venerable sirs, my task is finished."
At that time, some monks, referring to the Venerable Ānanda, said:
"In this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, there is one bhikkhu who wanders about emitting a foul odor. When the Elder heard this, he thought:
"There is no other bhikkhu in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus who wanders about emitting a foul odor; surely these [monks]..."
“...are speaking with reference to me,” he thought, and he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Some monks said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Friend, there is a gathering tomorrow; since you are still a trainee (*sekkha*) who has work yet to do, it is not fitting for you to go to the assembly.
Be diligent. Then the Venerable Ānanda thought: “There is a gathering tomorrow, and it is not fitting for me, being a trainee...”

“May I go to the assembly while still in this state. Having spent most of the night in mindfulness directed to the body, at the time of dawn he descended from his walking path, entered the dwelling, and as he inclined his body with the thought, “I shall lie down,” his two feet left the ground and his head had not yet reached the pillow;
in that interval, without clinging, through the destruction of the taints—
His mind was liberated. For this venerable one, having spent much time outside walking to and fro, being unable to produce any further distinction, thought:
"Did not the Blessed One say this to me: 'You have performed merit, Ānanda; apply yourself to striving;
soon you shall be free from the taints'? There is no fault in the words of the Buddhas. It must be my own energy that was too over-exerted."
"Because of that, my mind tends toward agitation. Come now, I shall apply energy and tranquility.

Having descended from his walking path, he stood at the place for washing his feet; having washed his feet and entered the monastery, he sat down on the couch and, thinking, "I will rest for a little while," he leaned his body against the couch.
Both feet were released from the ground, and his head rested upon the pillow.
Before he had even reached [the seat], in that interval his mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging;

the Elder attained Arahantship devoid of the four postures. Therefore, when it is asked in this Dispensation, "Which bhikkhu has attained Arahantship?", it is fitting to say, "The Elder Ānanda," even though he was not lying down, sitting, standing, or walking.
Then, on the second day, after having finished their meal duties, the elder bhikkhus put away their bowls and robes and assembled in the Dhamma Hall.
However, the Elder Ānanda, desiring to make known his attainment of Arahatship, did not go with the bhikkhus.
As the bhikkhus were each sitting down in their respective seats according to seniority, they [reached] the seat of the Elder Ānanda.
They sat down after setting it aside. There, when someone asked, "Whose seat is this?", they replied, "It belongs to the Elder Ānanda.
When asked, "But where has Ānanda gone?", at that moment the Elder thought, "Now is the time for me to depart.
Then, displaying his own supernatural power, he sank into the earth and made himself appear right upon his own seat.
Some say that he arrived by way of the air and sat down.
When the Venerable One was thus seated, the Elder Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, which shall we recite first:
the Dhamma or the Vinaya? The bhikkhus replied: "Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya."
“The life-span of the Buddha’s teaching is the Vinaya; when the Vinaya stands, the teaching stands. Therefore, let us first recite the Vinaya.
“Upon whom shall we rely as our authority? “Upon the Venerable Upāli. “Is Ānanda not capable? “He is not incapable;
however, while the Perfectly Enlightened One was still living, he [Upāli] relied upon the mastery of the Vinaya.”
He placed the Venerable Upāli in the foremost position, saying: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus who are masters of the Vinaya, namely Upāli.
Therefore, “having questioned the Elder Upāli, let us recite the Vinaya.
Then the Elder, for the purpose of questioning on the Vinaya, appointed himself by himself. And the Elder Upāli, for the purpose of answering—
He was thus authorized. Herein is the canonical text:
"Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:
'Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, I would question Upāli on the Vinaya.'"
The Venerable Upāli also informed the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, when questioned by the Venerable Mahākassapa on the Vinaya, I shall provide an answer.
Having thus authorized himself by himself, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, and—
There, having paid homage to the monks, he sat upon the Dharma-seat, taking up a fan inlaid with ivory.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having sat down on the Elder’s seat, questioned the Venerable Upāli regarding the Vinaya:
"Friend Upāli, where was the first *pārājika* offense laid down? "At Vesālī, Bhante. "With reference to whom? "With reference to Sudinna."
“Concerning Kalandaputta. “In what matter? “In the matter of sexual intercourse.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Upāli about the matter of the first *pārājika*, he asked about the origin, he asked about the person, he asked about the formal rule, he asked about the subsequent rule, and he asked about the offense.
He asked about [the first offense], he asked even about the non-offense;

and as he did for the first, so for the second, so for the third, so for the fourth *pārājika*—he asked about the basis [of the offense]... pe ...and he asked even about the non-offense. Being asked each time, the Elder Upāli replied.
Then, having compiled these four *pārājikas* under the title "The Chapter on *Pārājikas*," he placed them into the collection.
They established thirteen rules as the "Thirteen" (terasa). They established two training rules as the "Undetermined" (aniyata).
They established thirty training rules as the "Forfeiture and Expiation" (nissaggiya-pācittiya). They established ninety-two training rules as the "Expiation" (pācittiya).
They established four training rules as the "Confession" (pāṭidesanīya). Seventy-five...
They established the training rules as "the Sekhiyas. They established the seven principles as "the Settling of Litigations.

Having thus compiled the Mahāvibhaṅga, they established eight training rules in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga as "this is called the Pārājika section," and they established seventeen training rules as "the Sattarasaka. [They established] thirty training rules...
They established the rules as "nissaggiya-pācittiya. They established one hundred and sixty-six training rules as "pācittiya.
They established eight training rules as "pāṭidesanīya. They established seventy-five training rules as "sekhiya.
They established seven principles as "adhikaraṇasamatha. Thus they compiled the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga.
Having thus established [the Sutta Piṭaka], by this very same method they also established the Khandhaka and Parivāra.

In this way, the entire Vinaya Piṭaka—including the Saṃghādisesa, Vibhaṅga, Khandhaka, and Parivāra—was brought into compilation. The Elder Mahākassapa questioned it all, and the Elder Upāli answered.
At the conclusion of the questioning and answering, five hundred Arahants performed a communal recitation (saṅgīti) according to the very method in which the collection had been established.
At the conclusion of the compilation of the Vinaya, the Elder Upāli set aside his ivory-inlaid fan, descended from the Dharma-seat, paid homage to the senior monks, and sat down on his own seat.
Having compiled the Vinaya, the Venerable Mahākassapa, desiring to compile the Dhamma, asked the monks: "The Dhamma..."
“Taking whom as the leader should the Dhamma be recited by those who chant it together? The bhikkhus replied, “Taking the Elder Ānanda as the leader.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa made a formal announcement to the Saṅgha:
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, friends: if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, I would ask Ānanda about the Dhamma.
Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Saṅgha:
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs: if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, being asked by the Venerable Mahākassapa about the Dhamma, I would answer.”

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, and sat down on the Dhamma-seat, taking up a fan inlaid with ivory. Then the Elder Mahākassapa asked the Elder Ānanda about the Dhamma:
"Friend Ānanda, where was the *Brahmajāla Sutta* spoken? "Between Rājagaha and..."
“Between Nāḷandā and Rājagaha, at Ambalaṭṭhikā. “Concerning whom?
“Concerning the wanderer Suppiya and the young Brahmin Brahmadatta. “On what subject? “On praise and dispraise.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda about the introduction to the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and also about the individuals involved.
He also asked about the setting: “But, friend Ānanda, where was the *Sāmaññaphala* (The Fruit of the Ascetic Life) spoken?
“At Rājagaha, venerable sir, in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. “With whom? “With Ajātasattu, the son of the Videhī.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda about the occasion for the *Sāmaññaphala* as well.
He also questioned the person. By this very method, he questioned [the contents of] the five Nikāyas. The five Nikāyas are:
the Dīghanikāya, the Majjhimanikāya, the Saṃyuttanikāya, the Aṅguttaranikāya, and the Khuddakanikāya.
Among these, the Khuddakanikāya refers to everything remaining after setting aside the four Nikāyas.

The word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*). Among these, the Vinaya was expounded by the Venerable Elder Upāli, while the remaining Minor Collection (*Khuddakanikāya*) and the four primary Collections (*Nikāya*) were expounded by the Elder Ānanda. All of this word of the Buddha is of one kind according to its flavor (*rasa*);
it is of two kinds according to the Dhamma and the Vinaya; it is of three kinds according to the first, middle, and last [teachings]; likewise, it is of three kinds according to the Pitakas.
It should be understood that [the Dhamma] is fivefold by way of the Nikāyas, ninefold by way of the Aṅgas, and eighty-four thousandfold by way of the Dhamma-aggregates (dhammakkhandha).

How is it singlefold by way of its flavor (rasa)? For, from the time the Blessed One fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until his final passing away (parinibbāna) into the Nibbāna-element without residue, throughout this interval of forty-five years—
Whether spoken by one instructing or reviewing [the teachings] for gods, humans, nāgas, yakkhas, and so forth, all of that has the single flavor of the flavor of liberation (vimuttirasa) alone.
Thus it is of one kind by way of flavor.
How is it of two kinds by way of Dhamma and Vinaya? All of this is reckoned as both Dhamma and Vinaya.
It proceeds. Therein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is the Vinaya, and the remainder of the Buddha’s word is the Dhamma; for this very reason it was said:
“What if we, friends, were to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together?
And: “I would question Upāli on the Vinaya, and Ānanda on the Dhamma. Thus, it is twofold by way of the Dhamma and the Vinaya.

How is it threefold by way of first, middle, and last? All this [Buddhist teaching] here is indeed divided into three types: the first word of the Buddha, the middle word of the Buddha, and the last word of the Buddha. In that regard:
“I have wandered through the cycle of many births, Seeking, but not finding, the builder of the house; For birth again and again is suffering.”
“House-builder, you have been seen; you shall build no house again.
All your rafters are broken, the ridge-pole is demolished;
the mind has reached the state of disintegration and attained the destruction of craving.”
This is the first word of the Buddha.
Some say that the verse from the Khandhaka, “When indeed phenomena become manifest,” is [the first word].
However, this [verse] arose on the day of his attainment of omniscience (sabbaññubhāva), when he was reflecting upon the mode of conditions (paccayākāra) with knowledge consisting of joy.
It should be understood as "inspired verses" (udānagāthā).

Furthermore, that which he spoke at the time of his final passing away—"Now, monks, I address you: all conditioned phenomena are subject to decay; strive with diligence"—this is the final word of the Buddha.
That which was spoken between these two is the intermediate word of the Buddha. Thus, it is threefold according to the categories of first, intermediate, and final.
How is it threefold by way of the Piṭakas? For all of this consists of exactly three divisions: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

Therein, having combined everything—both that which was recited and that which was not recited at the First Council—the two Pātimokkhas, the two Vibhaṅgas, the twenty-two Khandhakas, and the sixteen Parivāras: this is called the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Dīghanikāya is a collection of thirty-four suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla; the Majjhimanikāya is a collection of one hundred and fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya;
the Saṃyuttanikāya is a collection of seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa;
and [the Aṅguttaranikāya] is a collection of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna.

The Khuddakanikāya, which has fifteen divisions consisting of the Aṅguttaranikāya, Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidā, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, and Cariyāpiṭaka—this is called the Suttanta Piṭaka.
The Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna—this is called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therein—
Because it possesses various specific characteristics, because it disciplines both body and speech,
and because it is known by those who understand the meaning of discipline— this is declared as "Vinaya" (discipline) by the experts in the meaning of Vinaya.
For here, there are various [elements], namely the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha and the matrices of the seven classes of offenses beginning with the Pārājikas.

The methods (*naya*) such as the Vibhaṅga and others are its specific features; the methods of subsequent ordinances (*anupaññatti-naya*) have the purpose of strengthening what is already established or relaxing what is too strict.
Because it restrains misconduct of body and speech by prohibiting them, it disciplines both body and speech;

therefore, due to its various methods, its specific methods, and its disciplining of body and speech, it is called "Vinaya" (Discipline). Thus, this was said for the sake of skill in understanding the meaning of this term:
“Because it possesses various specific characteristics, and because it disciplines both body and speech,
this is declared as ‘Vinaya’ by those who know the meaning of Vinaya.
As for the other [definition]:

It is called *sutta* because it indicates meaning (*attha*), because it is well-spoken, because it is heard, because it causes to flow forth, because of its guidance, and because of its similarity to a thread (*suttāṇā*).

For it indicates meanings divided into those concerning one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth; and here, the meanings are well-spoken in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained.
Because it has been so stated. It "flows" (savati) in the sense that it produces fruit like a crop;
this is what is meant. It "oozes" (sūdati) like milk from a cow; this is what is meant. And it "well protects" (suṭṭhu tāyati) them; this is what is meant.
Furthermore, it shares the same nature as a measuring line (*sutta*); for just as a carpenter’s line provides a standard of measure, so too does this [Dhamma] for the wise.
And just as flowers gathered by a string are not scattered nor destroyed, so too are the meanings gathered by this [sutta].
Therefore, for the sake of skill in the meaning of its words, this was said:
“Because it indicates meanings, because it is well-spoken, because it is heard, and because it flows forth;”
"And because it shares the characteristics of a thread (*sutta*), it is called a 'discourse' (*sutta*).
But the other [teacher] says:
"That which herein possesses growth, is characterized by its own marks, is honored, and is well-defined;"
The Dhammas that have been spoken [in the Suttas] are in addition [to those]; therefore it is called Abhidhamma.
For this prefix *abhi-* is seen in the senses of increase (*vuḍḍhi*), characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), honored (*pūjita*), delimited (*paricchinna*), and additional (*adhika*).
Thus, it occurs in the sense of increase in such passages as: "Friends, my painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding. Likewise— "Yā... [and so forth].

In such passages as "those nights were well-known, well-characterized," it has the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). In "the king of kings, lord of men," it has the sense of being honored (*pūjita*).
In "capable of instructing in the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya," it has the sense of being delimited (*paricchitta*)—meaning in the Dhamma and Vinaya that are free from mutual confusion.
In "with surpassing beauty," it has the sense of being superior (*adhika*).

And herein, by way of such passages as, “He develops the path for rebirth in the form realm; he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,” there are also states that possess growth.

By way of such passages as, “Having a visible form as its object, or a sound as its object,” they are also characterized because they are to be defined by their objects and so forth. “States of the trainee, states of the adept...”
The intention is that they are worthy of honor even though they have been honored in such a manner as, “Dhammas, supramundane dhammas,” and so forth.
They are delimited because their individual essences are delimited in such a manner as, “There is contact, there is feeling,” and so forth.
Furthermore, dhammas that are superior have been stated in such a manner as, “Lofty dhammas, immeasurable dhammas, unsurpassed dhammas,” and so forth. Therefore, this [is the case] for him.
It was said for the sake of skill in the meaning of words:
“Those phenomena which herein possess growth, possess specific characteristics, are honored, are delimited,
and are stated as additional, are therefore called Abhidhamma.”
As for that which is not specifically distinguished here:
"Those who know the meaning of the Piṭakas say that 'Piṭaka' refers to the scriptures and the sense of a container;
having combined these meanings, all three—the Vinaya and so forth—should be understood as such."
For the word *piṭaka* is used to denote "learning" (*pariyatti*) in such passages as, "Do not [rely] on the acquisition of the Piṭakas," and so forth;

yet in such passages as, "Then a man might come carrying a hoe and a basket," it refers to any kind of container. Therefore, those who know the meaning of the word *piṭaka* have stated that it signifies both learning and a container.
Now, having combined these two meanings, the three—the Vinaya and the others—are to be understood as the *piṭakas*. Thus, by means of the word *piṭaka* in this twofold sense...

Having formed a compound, it is called the *Vinayapiṭaka* because it is both the Vinaya and a Piṭaka, since it is a Piṭaka by virtue of being a formal learning (*pariyatti*) and because it contains the various meanings [of the Vinaya].

Likewise, according to the same method, it is the *Suttantapiṭaka* because it is both the Suttanta and that Piṭaka, and the *Abhidhammapiṭaka* because it is both the Abhidhamma and that Piṭaka; thus these three, beginning with the Vinaya, are to be understood.
Having understood this, and furthermore, for the sake of proficiency in the various modes within those very Piṭakas:
One should elucidate the teaching, the dispensation, and the discourse; their classification as appropriate;
and the profound nature of training and abandonment.
One should also analyze in detail how a bhikkhu attains, in whatever way and wherever, the excellence of the divisions of the scriptures as well as their failure.
Herein, this is the exposition and the analysis: for these three Piṭakas are, respectively, the teaching of the command, the conventional, and the ultimate.

They are called the instructions according to the offense, according to conformity, and according to the Dhamma; and the discourse on restraint, non-restraint, the resolution of views, and the delimitation of name-and-form.
For herein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is an instruction by way of command (*āṇādesanā*), because it was taught by the Blessed One, who possesses authority, primarily by way of commands;

the Sutta Piṭaka is an instruction by way of conventional usage (*vohāradesanā*), because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in conventional usage, primarily by way of conventional usage; and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka...
It is called the "Teaching of Ultimate Meaning" because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in ultimate meaning, for the sake of the abundance of ultimate meaning.
Likewise, the first [classification] is the "Teaching according to Offense," because those beings who have committed frequent offenses are disciplined herein according to their offenses;

the second is the "Teaching according to Suitability," because beings with various inclinations, latent tendencies, conducts, and dispositions are disciplined herein according to what is suitable for them.
In the third [chapter], because beings who perceive "I" and "mine" in what is merely a heap of phenomena are herein disciplined according to the Dhamma,
it is called the "Teaching according to the Dhamma" (*yathādhammasāsana*).

Likewise, in the first [chapter], because restraint and non-restraint— which are the opposites of misconduct— are discussed therein, it is the "Discussion on Restraint and Non-restraint" (*saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā*).
The second is called the "Discourse on the Unraveling of Views" because here the unraveling of views—which serves as the antidote to the sixty-two views—is explained.
The third is called the "Discourse on the Delimitation of Name-and-Form" because here the delimitation of name-and-form—which serves as the antidote to lust and so forth—is explained.
Furthermore, in all three of these discourses, the three trainings, the three abandonments, and the fourfold profundity are to be understood.
For instance: in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is specifically taught; in the Sutta Piṭaka, the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā);
and in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā).
Furthermore, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of transgressions regarding the defilements (kilesa), because virtue is the antidote to transgression. In the Sutta Piṭaka...

In the Sutta Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), because concentration is the antidote to obsessions. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), because wisdom is the antidote to underlying tendencies.

Furthermore, in the first [Piṭaka], there is the abandoning of defilements by way of "partial abandonment" (*tadaṅga-pahāna*); in the others, there are the abandonings by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and eradication (*samuccheda*). Moreover, in the first, there is the abandoning of the corruption of misconduct; in the others, there is the abandoning of the corruptions of craving and views.
In this context, it should be understood that each one of these four—the profundity of the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and the penetration—is fourfold.
Therein, "Dhamma" refers to the Pāḷi (the text). "Meaning" refers to the meaning of that very text. "Teaching" refers to the teaching of that Pāḷi as it has been established by the mind.
"Penetration" refers to the realization of the Pāḷi and the meaning of the Pāḷi exactly as they are. And in all three of these—

These penetrations of the teaching on the nature of phenomena (dhamma) are profound because, like the great ocean with its sea-monsters, they are difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom and provide no foothold;
therefore, they are profound. Thus, in each case here, the fourfold profundity should be understood.
Another method: "Dhamma" means cause. For it has been said: "Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of dhamma."

"Meaning" (*attha*) refers to cause and fruit. For it has been said: "Knowledge regarding cause and fruit is the analytical knowledge of meaning" (*atthapaṭisambhidā*). "Teaching" (*desanā*) refers to designation;
the intended meaning is that it is the verbal expression of phenomena in accordance with their nature. "Penetration" (*paṭivedha*) refers to clear realization (*abhisamaya*);

and that is both mundane and supramundane, according to its object and its non-delusion, [applying] to phenomena in accordance with their meaning, to meanings in accordance with their phenomena, and to designations in accordance with the path of designation.
It is the comprehension of the designations.
Now, regarding these Piṭakas, whatever kind of Dhamma or matter there is,
and whatever meaning that is to be made known becomes manifest to the knowledge of the listeners— such is the teaching that illuminates that meaning.

Furthermore, this penetration—which consists of unerring realization—is difficult to plunge into and provides no foothold for those of poor wisdom who have not accumulated the requisites of merit, just as the great ocean is for crocodiles; therefore, it is profound.
In this way, each one of these [factors] should be understood to possess a fourfold profundity.
And to this extent:
“The discourse on the teaching and the dispensation, their respective divisions,
as well as the profundity of the training and its relinquishment, should be fully elucidated.”
This verse has its meaning already explained:
“In whatever way a bhikkhu attains excellence through the various divisions of the scriptures, as well as failure, let him discern all of that.”

In this context, however, the threefold classification of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) within the Three Pitakas should be understood. For there are three kinds of scripture: that which is like a water-snake (*alagaddūpamā*), that for the sake of deliverance (*nissaraṇatthā*), and the scriptural storehouse (*bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti*).
Among these, that which is wrongly grasped and mastered for the sake of criticism and so forth is "like a water-snake. With reference to this, it was said:
"Bhikkhus, just as if a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, wandering in search of a water-snake..."
While walking, he might see a large water-snake. He might catch it by its coils or by its tail.
That water-snake, turning back upon him, would bite his hand or his arm or some other limb.
Because of that, he would meet death or suffering amounting to death. Why is that?
What is the reason? It is because of their misapprehension of the *alagadda* (water-snake), monks.
In the same way, monks, here certain foolish persons master the Dhamma—the discourses... [and so on] ...the *vedallas*.
Having mastered that Dhamma, they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. As they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom, [they fall into ruin].
They do not find satisfaction in reflective contemplation. They master the Dhamma for the sake of finding fault and for the sake of escaping from debates.
They do not experience the purpose for which they master the Dhamma.
Those teachings, being wrongly grasped by them, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Why is that? Because of their wrong grasp.
“...of phenomena, monks.

However, that which is well-learned by one desiring only the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth, and is mastered not for the sake of criticism and the like, is for the purpose of escape (*nissaraṇatthā*).
With reference to this, it was said: “Those teachings, being well-learned by them, for a long time...”
“They lead to welfare and happiness. Why is that? Because, monks, the teachings have been well grasped.

However, when one who has fully understood the aggregates, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, penetrated the unshakable, realized cessation, and whose taints are exhausted, studies [the texts] solely for the purpose of preserving the tradition and for the sake of protecting the lineage, this is the stewardship of the storekeeper.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu who has practiced well in the Vinaya attains the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) by relying on the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampatti*), because it is precisely those [knowledges] that are explained there in detail.

One who has practiced well in the Sutta attains the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*) by relying on the perfection of concentration (*samādhisampadā*), because it is precisely those [knowledges] that are explained there in detail.
One who has practiced well in the Abhidhamma [attains] the perfection of wisdom (*paññāsampadā*).
By relying on this, one attains the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), because their detailed classification is explained right there.

Thus, one who practices correctly regarding these [three trainings] attains, in due order, this excellence consisting of the threefold clear knowledge (*vijjāttaya*), the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and the four analytical knowledges.

However, one who practices incorrectly regarding the Discipline (*vinaya*) [attains nothing], because of the commonality of tactile contact with permitted pleasant-to-touch items such as rugs and coverlets.
He perceives as blameless those things that have been rejected, such as grasping-contact and so forth. For it has been said:
“I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that these things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
Thereby he falls into a state of immorality. One who practices wrongly regarding the Sutta [says]: “Bhikkhus, there are these four...”
One who does not understand the intended meaning in such passages as "there are persons existing who are found" grasps it incorrectly.
With reference to this, it was said: "By his own misapprehension, he misrepresents us, injures himself, and produces much demerit";
from that, he falls into wrong view. One who practices wrongly regarding the Abhidhamma [misunderstands] the contemplation of phenomena (dhammacintā).
Those who overstep the bounds think even about things that are inconceivable; consequently, they fall into mental derangement. For it has been said:
"Monks, there are these four inconceivable things that should not be thought about; by thinking about them, one would partake of madness and distress.
Thus, one who practices wrongly with respect to these [four] successively incurs this breach consisting of immorality, wrong view, and mental derangement.
“He encounters misfortune.
And by this much:
“Whatever excellence or misfortune there may be, in whatever study-classification it belongs,”
“Just as a bhikkhu attains [the goal], so too one should analyze all of that.

This verse also has its meaning already explained. Thus, having understood the Piṭakas in their various aspects, it should be known that this word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) is threefold by way of them.
How is it fivefold by way of the Nikāyas? All of this is the Dīghanikāya, the Majjhimanikāya, the Saṃyuttanikāya, [the Aṅguttaranikāya, and the Khuddakanikāya].
The *Aṅguttara Nikāya* and the *Khuddaka Nikāya* constitute the fivefold division. Among these, what is the *Dīgha Nikāya*?
It consists of thirty-four discourses beginning with the *Brahmajāla*, comprised within three groups (*varga*).
There are exactly thirty-four discourses whose collection forms the three groups.
"This is the *Dīghanikāya*": this is the first [section] in accordance with the order.
But why is it called the *Dīghanikāya*? Because it is a collection (*samūha*) and an abode (*nivāsa*) of suttas of long extent;
for "collection" and "abode" are what is meant by the term *nikāya*. "Monks, I do not see even a single other *nikāya*..."

And so it is with the *Cittavagga*; for instance, monks, there are the "animals" (*tiracchānagatā pāṇā*), the "Poṇika group," the "Cikkhallika group," and so forth—these are the proofs for this from both the Teaching (*sāsana*) and common worldly usage (*loka*).
In this way, the meaning of the term for the status of a "group" (*nikāya*) should be understood for the remaining [vaggas] as well.
What is the *Majjhima Nikāya*? It consists of discourses of medium length, comprised of fifteen chapters (*vagga*), beginning with the *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*, totaling one hundred and fifty-two suttas.

One hundred and fifty suttantas, together with two additional suttantas, wherein it [the Buddha] appears, constitute the Majjhima Nikāya, which is comprised of fifteen chapters. What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya?
It consists of seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttantas, arranged according to the Devatāsaṃyutta and other such groupings, beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta.
Seven thousand suttas, seven hundred suttas, and sixty-two suttas—this is the Saṃyutta Saṅgaha. What is the Aṅguttara Nikāya?
It consists of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas, arranged according to the progressive increase of each successive factor (aṅga), beginning with the Cittapariyādāna and so forth.
Nine thousand suttas, five hundred suttas, and fifty-seven suttas: this is the enumeration in the Aṅguttara. What is the Khuddakanikāya?

It consists of the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and the fifteen divisions beginning with the Khuddakapāṭha previously indicated, excluding the four Nikāyas—the remainder of the Buddha’s word.
"Setting aside these four Nikāyas, beginning with the Dīgha,
any other word of the Buddha is considered the Khuddaka Nikāya.
Thus, it is fivefold by way of the Nikāyas.

How is it ninefold by way of its constituent parts (*aṅga*)? For this entire [Dhamma] consists of nine divisions: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla.
Among these, the two Vibhaṅgas, the Niddesa, the Khandhaka, and the Parivāra, as well as the Maṅgalasutta, Ratanasutta, Nālakasutta, and Tuvaṭṭakasutta in the Suttanipāta, [are Sutta].
Furthermore, other words of the Tathāgata called *sutta* should be understood as *sutta*.

All *sutta* that contains verses should be understood as *geyya*. Specifically, the entire Sagāthāvagga in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, the whole Abhidhamma Piṭaka, *sutta* that is devoid of verses, and whatever other word of the Buddha is not included within the [other] eight factors (*aṅga*), that is *veyyākaraṇa*.
It should be understood that the *Dhammapada*, the *Theragāthā*, the *Therīgāthā*, and the pure verses not titled as suttas within the *Suttanipāta* are "Verses" (*gāthā*).
It should be understood that the eighty-two suttantas associated with verses consisting of joy and knowledge are "Inspired Utterances" (*udāna*).
The one hundred and ten suttantas occurring in the manner beginning with "For this was said by the Blessed One" (*vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā*) are "Thus-Spoken" (*itivuttaka*).
It should be understood as follows: the more than five hundred Jātakas, beginning with the *Apaṇṇaka-jātaka*, are to be understood as the "Birth Stories" (*jātaka*).

All discourses (*suttanta*) connected with wonderful and marvelous qualities, such as those proceeding in the manner of the passage beginning, “Bhikkhus, there are these four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda,” are to be understood as the "Marvelous Qualities" (*abbhutadhamma*).
[These include] the *Cūḷavedalla*, *Mahāvedalla*, *Sammādiṭṭhi*, *Sakkapañha*, *Saṅkhārabhājaniya*, *Mahāpuṇṇama-sutta*, and others.
All those discourses that have been asked about and received with both knowledge and joy should be understood as *vedalla*.
Thus, it is ninefold by way of its constituent parts (*aṅga*).
How is it eighty-four thousandfold by way of the categories of Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*)? For all this is indeed the word of the Buddha:
“I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, two thousand from the bhikkhus;
thus, eighty-four thousand are the teachings that have been transmitted to me.
In this way, according to the categories of the aggregates of Dhamma thus elucidated, there are eighty-four thousand divisions. Among these, those consisting of a single connection...

In the Sutta, one discourse (*sutta*) constitutes one aggregate of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*). Where there are multiple sections (*anusandhi*), the counting of aggregates of the Dhamma is according to those sections.
In the verse compositions (*gāthābandha*), the posing of a question is one aggregate of the Dhamma, and the answer is one.

In the Abhidhamma, each individual treatment of the triplets (*tika*) and couplets (*duka*), as well as each individual treatment of the mental cycles (*cittavāra*), is one aggregate of the Dhamma. In the Vinaya, there exists...
There is the basis, there is the matrix, there is the word-commentary, there is the intermediate offense, there is the offense, there is the non-offense, and there is the delimitation;
therein, each single section should be understood as a single division of the Dhamma (dhammakkhandha).
Thus, by way of divisions of the Dhamma, it is of eighty-four thousand kinds.

Thus, this word of the Buddha is of one kind when considered without distinction according to its flavor; but when distinguished, it has various divisions such as the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and so forth.

By the assembly of masters headed by Mahākassapa, who were chanting [the scriptures], it was established: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya; this is the first word of the Buddha, this is the middle word of the Buddha, this is the final word of the Buddha."
Having established this classification—“this is the Vinaya Piṭaka, this is the Sutta Piṭaka, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this is the Dīgha Nikāya... [and so on]...
this is the Khuddaka Nikāya; these are the nine divisions beginning with the Suttas, and these are the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma”—it was thus chanted.

And not only this much, but also many other types of collections were established, such as the collection of summaries (uddāna), the collection by chapters (vagga), the collection by prose sequences (peyyāla), the collection by the single-stanza section (ekakanipāta), the collection by the two-stanza section (dukanipāta) and so forth, the collection by groups (saṃyutta), and the collection by fifties (paṇṇāsa).
Having established the classification and divisions as they appear within the three Piṭakas, the recitation was completed in seven months.

At the conclusion of the recitation, this great earth, filled with joy at the thought, "This teaching of the One of Ten Powers has been rendered by the Elder Mahākassapa capable of enduring for a period of five thousand years," gave forth a cry of approval, as it were.
Having made the ocean its boundary, it shook, trembled, quaked, and vibrated in many ways, and many wonders appeared;
this is called the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti). As for that which is said in the world:
"It was performed by five hundred [monks], therefore it is called 'The Five Hundred'."
"And because she performed that very act, she is called 'Therikā' (the Elder Nun).

Now, while this First Great Council was being held, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked about the Vinaya, saying, "Friend Upāli, where was the first *pārājika* offense laid down? and so forth, at the conclusion of such words, [he stated] regarding the matter (*vatthu*)...
Regarding the statement, "He asked about the source, he asked about the individual," when the source was asked,
the Venerable Elder Upāli— who wished to explain that source in detail from the beginning, including both by whom it was laid down and for what reason it was laid down—
said: "At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā."
Everything should be stated. Thus it was spoken by the Venerable Elder Upāli; furthermore, it should be understood that this was spoken "at the time of the First Great Council.
To this extent, the meaning of these phrases—"By whom was this statement spoken? When was it spoken?"—has been clarified.

Now, as to why it was spoken here, it is said: because this [question] was asked by the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa regarding the introduction (*nidāna*), it was therefore spoken by him in order to explain that introduction in detail from the very beginning.
Thus, it should be understood that when the Venerable Elder Upāli spoke this at the time of the First Great Council (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāla*), he did so for this reason.
Thus far, the meaning of these matrix headings—“by whom,” “when,” and “because of what”—has been elucidated.
Now, having stated “by whom it was borne” and “wherein it was established,” this is said for the purpose of elucidating the meaning of these [remaining headings]:
“and by whom it was brought,” and “the method thereof. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was at Verañjā...
By whom was the Vinaya Piṭaka, whose introduction is adorned with such words as “he dwells,” preserved? By whom was it brought down?
Where was it established? It is said: first of all, this was preserved by the venerable Elder Upāli in the presence of the Blessed One;
from his presence, while the Tathāgata had not yet attained final Nibbāna, it was [transmitted] by many thousands of bhikkhus distinguished by the six supernormal powers and other qualities.
When the Tathāgata had attained final Nibbāna, [the text] was brought down by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, headed by the Elder Mahākassapa.
By whom was it brought? First, in Jambudīpa, beginning with the Elder Upāli, it was brought down through the succession of teachers until the Third Council.
In this regard, the succession of teachers is as follows:
Upāli, Dāsaka, Soṇaka, and likewise Siggava;
Tissa Moggaliputta—these five were the victors.
Through this lineage, the Vinaya was transmitted on the island named Jambusiri.
They received it without interruption until the third council.

For the Venerable Upāli, having learned this lineage of the Vinaya, the tradition of the Vinaya, and the succession of the Vinaya directly from the Blessed One, established it in the hearts of many bhikkhus. From that Venerable one...

Among those who had mastered the Vinaya-vamsa and attained proficiency in the Vinaya, the number of worldlings (puthujjana), stream-enterers (sotāpanna), once-returners (sakadāgāmi), and non-returners (anāgāmi) exceeded all calculation;
there were one thousand arahants whose taints were exhausted (khīṇāsava). The Elder Dāsaka was also his co-resident (saddhivihārika);
having learned it from the presence of the Elder Upāli, he likewise taught the Vinaya. Of that venerable one as well—
Having learned [the Vinaya] in the presence [of their teachers], there were those beyond counting—beginning with worldlings (puthujjana)—who attained mastery of the Vinaya;
there were exactly one thousand of those whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava). The Elder Soṇaka was also a co-resident disciple (saddhivihārika) of the Elder Dāsaka;
he too, having learned it in the presence of his own preceptor, the Elder Dāsaka, taught the Vinaya in that same manner.
Having learned the Vinaya from that venerable one as well, ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and others who attained proficiency in the Vinaya became beyond counting;
there were exactly one thousand *khīṇāsava* (those whose taints were destroyed). The Elder Siggava was a co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*) of the Elder Soṇaka;
he too, having learned the Vinaya from his own preceptor, the Elder Soṇaka, [became the teacher] of one thousand *arahants*.

He took up the leadership. In his presence, having studied the Vinaya, there were those who attained proficiency—ranging from worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), to those whose taints were exhausted (*khīṇāsava*)—numbering in the hundreds or thousands, beyond all reckoning.
At that time, it is said, there was a truly vast assembly of bhikkhus in Jambudīpa. Such was the majestic power of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.

It will become manifest at the Third Council. Thus, it should be understood that this Vinaya Piṭaka was brought down into Jambudvīpa by means of this succession of teachers, from the beginning until the Third Council.
The account of the First Great Council is concluded.
The Account of the Second Council:
Furthermore, this sequence should be understood for the purpose of discerning the Second Council.
For when— Having chanted the True Dhamma together, and having illuminated it in every respect;
Remaining until the end of their lives, those five hundred elders,
Kassapa and the others, who were free from taints, radiant,
and like lamps whose oil was spent, attained Nibbāna, being without attachment.
Then, as days and nights passed in succession, one hundred years after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, the Vajjiputta monks of Vesālī declared at Vesālī:
"The practice of using rock salt is permissible; the practice of the two-fingerbreadth measure is permissible; the practice of traveling between villages is permissible;

the practice of residing within the same boundary is permissible; the practice of subsequent consent is permissible; the practice of customary behavior is permissible; the practice of consuming unchurned milk is permissible."
They proclaimed these ten points: "It is permissible to drink fermented grain-liquor; it is permissible to use a sitting mat without a fringe;
it is permissible [to accept] gold and silver. Of them, King Kālāsoka, the son of Susunāga, was a partisan.
Now at that time, the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta, while wandering on tour among the Vajjis, [arrived at] Vesāli...
Having heard that "the Vajjiputtaka bhikkhus in Vesālī are indeed proclaiming the ten points," he thought:
"It is not fitting that I, having heard of a failure in the teaching of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, should remain indifferent.
Come now, I shall refute those who speak what is contrary to the Dhamma and illuminate the Dhamma. Thinking thus, he arrived at Vesālī. There...
At that time, the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta was staying at Vesālī in the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest.
Now on that Uposatha day, the Vajjiputta monks of Vesālī filled a bronze bowl with water,
placed it in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, and spoke thus to the lay followers of Vesālī as they arrived:

—“Friends, there will be need for the Saṅgha to make use of even a single kahāpaṇa, or half a kahāpaṇa, or a quarter of one, or even a māṣaka coin as an article for the Saṅgha”; all this should be stated first, up until:
“In this recitation of the Vinaya, there were seven hundred bhikkhus, neither fewer nor more; therefore, this second council is called the ‘Seven Hundred’.”
Thus, at that assembly, twelve hundred thousand bhikkhus gathered, having been exhorted by the Venerable Yasa.
In their midst, when questioned by the Venerable Revata, the Elder Sabbakāmī answered regarding the Vinaya, and those ten matters were adjudicated;
the legal dispute was thus settled. Then the Elders [said]: "Once again, the Dhamma and..."
Thinking, "And we shall recite the Vinaya," they selected seven hundred bhikkhus who were masters of the Tipiṭaka and had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having assembled at the Vālikārāma in Vesālī, they purified all the defilements of the Dispensation exactly as it had been recited by the Elder Mahākassapa;
furthermore, they [reorganized it] according to the Piṭakas, the Nikāyas, the Aṅgas, and the Dhammakkhandhas.
And they recited the entire Dhamma and Vinaya. This council was completed in eight months. Regarding it, it is said in the world:
"Because it was performed by seven hundred [monks], it is called 'Seven Hundred';
and because it is based on what was done previously, it is called 'The Second'."
Now, as for this [council]:
The council is renowned among those elders by whom it was rehearsed—
Sabbakāmī, Sāḷha, Revata, and Khujjasobhita.
Yasa and Sāṇasambhūta—these were the co-residents;
the elders had previously seen the Tathāgata with the Elder Ānanda.
Sumana and Vāsabhagāmī are to be known as the co-residents.
"Anuruddha, these two [instances] have been seen by you before regarding the Tathāgata.
But the second is that which was chanted together by those elders who performed the compilation:
'All of them had laid down their burdens, they had done what was to be done, and were free from the taints.'"
This was the Second Council.
Having thus recited this Second Council, the Elders, looking forward to see whether such a corruption of the Dispensation would arise in the future as well, perceived this:
"One hundred years from now, in the eighteenth [reign]..."
In the rainy season, a king named Dhammāsoka will arise in Pāṭaliputta and rule over the whole of Jambudīpa.
Having gained faith in the Buddha’s dispensation, he will bestow great material gain and honor upon it.
Then, the heretics, desiring such gain and honor, will enter the dispensation and proclaim their respective views. Thus, within the dispensation, a great...
“An *abbuda* hell will arise. Then it occurred to them:
“When this *abbuda* hell has arisen, shall we be present before it, or shall we not?
Then, all of them, realizing their own absence from that place, thought, “Who indeed will be capable of settling that legal dispute? and [surveyed] the entire human world.

Looking toward the world of the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), they saw no one; however, in the Brahma-world, they beheld a Great Brahmā named Tissa, whose lifespan was short and who had cultivated the path for rebirth in a higher Brahma-world. Having seen him, this thought occurred to them:
"If we were to make an effort for this Brahmā to be reborn in the human world, surely..."
“This one will take rebirth in the house of the brahmin Moggallī; then, enticed by mantras, he will go forth and become a monk.

Having thus gone forth and mastered the entire word of the Buddha, and having attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), he will crush the heretics, adjudicate that legal dispute, and uphold the Dispensation.”
Having gone to the Brahma-world, they said this to the Great Brahmā Tissa: "One hundred years from now, in the eighteenth year, a great calamity will arise within the Dispensation.

While we were surveying the entire human world and the six celestial realms of the sense-sphere gods, we saw no one capable of upholding the Dispensation; thus, searching through the Brahma-world, we have come to you alone."
“We have seen you. Excellent, worthy man! Having been reborn in the world of humans, give us your promise to uphold the teaching of the One Possessed of Ten Powers.

When this was said, the Great Brahmā, thinking, “I shall indeed be able to purify the corruption arisen in the teaching and uphold the teaching,” became exceedingly joyful and overjoyed; saying “So be it,” he gave his promise.
He gave it. Having completed that task in the Brahma-world, the elders returned once more.

Now at that time, the two elders Siggava and Caṇḍavajjī were both newly ordained young bhikkhus who were masters of the Three Piṭakas, had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and were free from the outflows (khīṇāsava); they did not reach that legal dispute. The elders—
“Friends, you were not our allies in this legal dispute; therefore, let this be your disciplinary task:
the Brahmā named Tissa will take rebirth in the house of the brahmin Moggallī.
One of you must bring him forth and give him the going-forth, and another must have him master the word of the Buddha. Having said this, they all remained for the full span of their lives.
Those elders of great psychic power, beginning with Sabbakāmī,
having blazed like masses of fire throughout the world, have attained final nibbāna.
Having performed the second council and purified the Dispensation, they passed away.
Even in the future, having established the cause for the purification of the True Dhamma,
those elders— whose taints are destroyed, who have attained mastery, and whose analytical knowledges are fully blossomed—
even they shall indeed come under the sway of impermanence.
Thus, having understood that this wretched impermanence is difficult to overcome,
the wise person should strive to attain that which they call the permanent, deathless state.
With this much, the commentary on the Second Council is completed in every respect.
The Discourse on the Second Council is finished.
Now begins the Discourse on the Third Council:
The Great Brahmā Tissa, having passed away from the Brahma-world, took rebirth in the house of the Brahmin Moggali.
From the moment of his rebirth, the Elder Siggava entered the brahmin’s house for alms for seven years.
Yet, not on a single day did he receive even a bowlful of rice-gruel or a spoonful of cooked rice.
However, at the conclusion of those seven years, one day he received merely the words, "Pass on, venerable sir."

On that very day, the brahmin, having attended to some business outside, was returning when he saw the Elder on the path and said, "O renunciant, did you go to our house? "Yes, brahmin, we went," he replied.
"Did you receive anything? "Yes, brahmin, we received something. Having gone home, he asked [his wife]: "Of that..."
“Did you give anything at all to the one who has gone forth? “We gave nothing,” he replied.
On the second day, the brahmin sat right at the door of his house, thinking, “Today I will refute the one who has gone forth with a lie.
On the second day, the Elder arrived at the door of the brahmin’s house. As soon as the brahmin saw the Elder, he said this: “Yesterday you were in our house...”
“Without having received anything at all, you said, ‘We have received. Is this not a lie for you?
The Elder replied, “Brahmin, for seven years we did not receive even the mere words ‘Please stay’ in your house;
however, yesterday we did receive the mere words ‘Please stay,’ and it was with reference to that hospitality that we spoke thus.”
The brahmin thought: “Having received even a mere greeting, they praise themselves, saying, ‘We have received.
Why do they not praise themselves when they receive other kinds of food, both hard and soft?
Having thus gained confidence, he had them given a ladleful of alms-food and appropriate curry from the meal prepared for himself, and said: “This alms-food—”

“You shall receive [me] at all times,” he said. From the following day onward, seeing the elder’s tranquility as he approached, the king became even more deeply inspired with faith and requested that the elder always take his meal at his own house.
The elder consented; and going there every day after finishing his meal, he would walk a short distance each time.
Having spoken the word of the Buddha, he departed. That young brahmin boy, though only sixteen years of age, had already mastered the three Vedas.
When that pure being who had come from the Brahma-world went to his teacher’s house, there was no one else to sit or lie upon his seat or bed;
whenever he went to the teacher’s residence, his couch and chair [remained for him alone].
Having covered it with a white cloth, they hung it up and left it there. The Elder thought: "Now is the time to ordain the young man;
it has been a long time since I arrived here, yet no conversation has arisen with the young man.
Well then, by this means he will come near my seat. Having gone to the house, so that... [he arranged it] in his presence.
He resolved that no seat other than the young man’s couch was to be seen in the house.
When the brahmin’s household members saw the Elder and found no other seat, they spread out the young man’s couch and gave it to the Elder.
The Elder sat down upon the couch. At that very moment, the young man also [returned] from his teacher’s house.
Seeing the Elder seated upon his own couch, he became angry and displeased, saying, "Who has prepared my couch for this ascetic?
When the meal was finished and the young man's fury had subsided, the Elder spoke thus: "But why..."
“Young man, do you know any incantations? The young man replied, “O renunciant, if I do not know the incantations now, who else will know them?
He then asked the elder, “But do you know the incantations?
“Ask, young man; once you have asked, it is possible to know. Thereupon, the young man [recited] the three Vedas, together with the Nighaṇḍus and the Keṭubhas...

Regarding those various knotty points in the *Sakkharappabheda*—with its histories as the fifth—on which neither he himself nor his teacher had seen the method, he questioned the Elder on each of them. The Elder thought:
"He was already a master of the three Vedas by nature, but now he has attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*); therefore, he has no difficulty with these questions."
"An answer is a burden," he said. Having answered those questions immediately, he spoke to the young man:
"Young man, I have been asked many questions by you; now I shall ask you one question in return. Will you explain it to me?
"Yes, venerable renunciant, ask; I shall explain. The Elder then asked this question concerning the *Cittayamaka*:

“Is it the case that for one whose consciousness arises and does not cease, that consciousness will cease but will not arise; or conversely, for one whose consciousness will cease but will not arise, that consciousness arises and does not cease?
Unable to move either upward or downward, the young brahmin asked, “What is this, venerable renunciant?
“This, young brahmin, is called the ‘Buddha-spell. “Can you give this to me as well, venerable sir? “I can, young brahmin.”
“I shall give [this] to one who takes the going-forth that has been taken by us.
Then the young man approached his mother and father and said, “This renunciant knows what is called the Buddha-mantra, yet he does not give it to anyone who has not gone forth in his presence;
I will go forth in his presence and learn the mantra.”
Then his parents, thinking, "Even though he has gone forth, let our son learn the mantras;

having learned them, he will return again," gave their permission, saying, "Learn them, my son. The Elder ordained the boy and first explained to him the meditation subject of the thirty-two aspects of the body.
While performing the preliminary work on that, the boy was established in the fruit of stream-entry before long.
Then the Elder thought: "The novice has established himself in the fruit of stream-entry; he is now incapable of turning back from the Dispensation.
However, if I were to increase his meditation subject and teach it to him, he would reach Arahantship and would have no need to concern himself with learning the Buddha’s word.
Now is the time to send him into the presence of the Elder Caṇḍavajjī."
Then he said: “Come, novice, go into the presence of the Elder and learn the word of the Buddha.
In my name, inquire after his health and say this: ‘Venerable sir, my preceptor has sent me to you.
And when he asks, ‘What is your preceptor’s name? you should reply, ‘His name is the Elder Siggava, venerable sir.’”
“When he asks, ‘Who am I by name?’, you should say: ‘Venerable sir, my preceptor knows your name.

“Very well, venerable sir,” the novice Tissa replied. He paid homage to the elder, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and after traveling by stages, he approached the elder Caṇḍavajjī, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. The elder questioned the novice.
“From where have you come? “Venerable sir, my preceptor has sent me to you.
“What is the name of your preceptor? “He is named the Elder Siggava, venerable sir. “And what is my name?
“My preceptor, venerable sir, knows your name. “Then take back your bowl and robes. “Very well, venerable sir,” he replied.
The novice, having put away his bowl and robes, swept the courtyard again the following day and set out water and a tooth-stick.

The Elder swept the place he had already swept, discarded the water he had already set out and brought other water, and removed the tooth-stick he had already taken and took another. In this manner it continued for seven days.
On the seventh day, he asked him again. The novice spoke once more, exactly as he had said before.
