The Elder, recognizing him, thinking, "This must indeed be that Brahmin," asked, "For what purpose have you come?
"To learn the word of the Buddha, venerable sir," he replied. The Elder said, "Learn it now, novice," and from that day forward...
He established the word of the Buddha. While still a novice, Tissa mastered the entire word of the Buddha, together with its commentaries, with the exception of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
At the time of his full ordination, although he was not yet twenty years old, he became a bearer of the Three Piṭakas (Tipiṭakadhara).
Having placed the entirety of the Buddha’s word into the hands of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, his preceptor and teacher, [he departed].

Having remained for the full span of their lifespan, they attained final Nibbāna. Later, on another occasion, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, having expanded his meditation subject, attained Arahantship and taught the Dhamma and Vinaya to many.
Now at that time, King Bindusāra had one hundred sons; all of them [were under the care of] Asoka himself.
Having spared Prince Tissa, who was of the same maternal lineage as himself, he had the others executed.

While exercising rule for four years without being formally consecrated, at the end of those four years—in the eighteenth year after the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata—he attained the consecration of sole sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa. By the power of that consecration...
These royal powers came to him: his command prevailed for a distance of one *yojana* beneath the great earth;
likewise, in the sky above, from Lake Anotatta, deities brought sixteen water-jars in eight canisters every day.
Having conceived faith in the Teaching, he gave eight jars to the Saṅgha of monks and two [to himself].
He used sixty water-jars for the bhikkhus who were masters of the Tipiṭaka, two jars for the chief queen Asandhimittā, and four jars for his own use.
Indeed, in the Himavat there is a substance called *nāgalatādantakaṭṭha*, which is smooth, soft, and flavorful;
the deities bring this to him day after day for the sake of the king and the chief queen.
Daily, the task of preparing tooth-sticks for sixteen thousand female dancers and sixty thousand bhikkhus was accomplished.
Day by day, deities brought him *agada*-myrobalans, *agada*-yellow myrobalans, and mangoes of golden hue, endowed with exquisite fragrance and flavor.
Likewise, from the Chaddanta Lake, they brought five-colored lower garments and upper robes.
They brought a yellow-colored hand-towel and celestial drink.

Furthermore, every single day, the Naga kings from the Naga realm brought bathing perfumes, unguents for anointing, a fine cotton-free cloth made of jasmine flowers for wearing, and highly precious ointment.
Also, fresh rice grown on Lake Chaddanta...
Every day, thousands of carts bring in fine rice. The mice reduce it to huskless grains;
not even a single broken grain remains, and this very rice alone is consumed by the king in all his quarters. Honey-bees produce honey.
In the smithies, the bellows blow clearly. Cuckoo birds come and utter their sweet songs.
Crying out, they performed an offering for the king.
Possessed of these supernatural powers, one day the king sent a golden chain as a bond,
and having brought the Naga King named Kāḷa— who had attained the vision of the forms of the four Buddhas and possessed a lifespan of an eon— he placed him beneath the white parasol.
Having seated him upon a magnificent couch below, and having performed worship with hundreds of varieties of lotus flowers—
both aquatic and terrestrial— as well as golden flowers, and having surrounded him on all sides by sixteen thousand dancing girls adorned with every ornament,
[she thought: "May the form of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Wheel-Turner of the Excellent True Dhamma, whose wisdom is infinite, appear within these eyes of mine."

Having said, "Make yourself visible," [the Buddha appeared] like the surface of a body of water adorned with blossoming lotuses, blue lilies, and white lotuses—due to the majesty of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, which were produced by the radiance of merit scattered throughout his entire body;

or like the vault of heaven illuminated by the brilliant, shimmering splendor of the net of rays from the host of stars; or [like a jewel] through the beauty of the encircling halo of his fathom-wide radiance, interwoven with rays of various colors such as blue, yellow, and red.

Beholding the form of the Buddha—which, like the peak of the Golden Mountain, was encircled by the rainbow of Indra’s bow with its radiance and crimson hue; which possessed the beautiful splendor of its crown, brilliantly illuminated by a garland of pure banners of various colors;
and which was like a source of aesthetic delight for the eyes of the hosts of Brahmas, gods, humans, nāgas, and yakkhas—he performed what is known as the "eye-worship" for seven days.
It is said that after receiving his consecration, the king followed the non-Buddhist sects for exactly three years.
In the fourth year, he gained faith in the Buddha’s teaching. It is said that his father, Bindusāra, was devoted to the brahmins;
he supported about sixty thousand brahmins and those of the brahminical sects, such as the white-robed wanderers (paṇḍaraṅga-paribbājaka) and others.

He established a regular daily meal offering. Asoka, too, giving alms in his own palace just as his father had done, one day stood at the lion-window and saw them eating with a conduct devoid of tranquility, their senses unrestrained and their deportment undisciplined.
He thought: "Having examined such an act of giving, it should be bestowed upon a worthy recipient."

“It is appropriate,” he thought. Having reflected thus, he said to his ministers, “Go, sirs, and bring into the inner palace those ascetics and brahmins whom each of you regards as most excellent; we shall give alms.

The ministers replied to the king, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and having assented, they brought those various wanderers—such as the Pāṇḍaraṅgas, the Ājīvakas, the Nigaṇṭhas, and others—and said, “These, O Great King, are they.”
“They are Arahants for us,” they said.

Then the king, having prepared various high and low seats within his inner palace, said, “Let them come,” and to those who had arrived he said, “Sit each on a seat suitable for yourself. Among them, some sat on fine chairs, while others...
They sat upon wooden benches. Seeing them, the king realized, "There is no core within them," and after giving them food and drink appropriate for them, he dismissed them.
As time passed in this manner, one day the king, standing at the lion-window, saw the novice Nigrodha in the royal courtyard.
“He goes, tamed, guarded, with his faculties at peace, perfected in deportment. But who is this Nigrodha?
He is the son of Prince Sumanas, the eldest son of King Bindusāra.
Herein is the sequential account:

It is said that while King Bindusāra was still weak, Prince Aśoka abandoned the sovereignty of Ujjain which he had obtained, came [to Pāṭaliputta], brought the entire city under his own control, and seized Prince Sumanas.
On that very day, Queen Sumanā, the consort of Prince Sumanas, became pregnant. She, in an unknown guise—

Having gone out, while traveling toward a certain village of Caṇḍālas not far away, she heard the voice of a deity dwelling in a banyan tree near the house of the chief Caṇḍāla, who was saying, "Come this way, Sumanā.
Hearing this, she went into her presence. By her own supernatural power, the deity created a palace.
"Live here," she said, and gave it to her. She entered that sal tree and on that very day gave birth to a son.
Because he had been protected by the deity of the *nigrodha* tree, she gave him the name "Nigrodha.
From the day he was seen, the chief Caṇḍāla, regarding him as his own sister's son, established a constant routine of service for him.
The princess lived there for seven years. Prince Nigrodha also reached the age of seven.
At that time, a certain Arhat named Mahāvaruṇa Thera, seeing the prince’s perfection of causal conditions, remained there protecting him.
Thinking, "The boy is now seven years old; it is time to ordain him," he informed the princess and [took] Prince Nigrodha.
He ordained him. The youth attained Arahantship at the very edge of the razor.

One day, having attended to his body early in the morning and performed the duties toward his teacher and preceptor, he took his bowl and robe and set out, thinking, "I shall go to the door of my mother’s house as a lay devotee.
Having entered the city through the southern gate, he proceeded through the center of the city to his mother’s dwelling place.
Having gone out by the eastern gate, he had to proceed.
At that time, King Asoka, the Dhamma-king, was walking back and forth in the eastern window facing the eastern direction.
At that very moment, Nigrodha reached the royal courtyard with his faculties and mind calmed, looking only a yoke’s length ahead. By him—

It is said: “One day, while standing in the lion-window, the king saw the novice Nigrodha walking through the royal courtyard—tamed, guarded, with senses calmed, and perfect in his deportment. Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him:
“All these people have distracted minds, resembling agitated deer; but this boy has an undistracted mind.”
"His looking ahead and around, and his bending and stretching, are exceedingly graceful. Surely there must be some supramundane quality within him.
At the mere sight of the novice, the king’s mind became serene and affection was established. Why was this?
It is said that in the past, when he was performing meritorious deeds, this novice had been the king’s elder brother, a merchant. For it has been said:
“Whether through former association or through present benefit, love for you arises in this way, like a lotus in the water.
Then the king, having conceived affection and great respect, sent his ministers with the command: “Summon that novice monk. They—
Thinking, "He is taking too long," he sent two or three more messengers, saying, "Let him come quickly! The novice went by his own natural pace.
The king, having provided a suitable seat, said, "Please sit down.
The novice looked here and there and, seeing that there were no other monks present, approached the royal throne under the raised white parasol in order to receive the bowl.
He displayed his demeanor to the king. As soon as the king saw him approaching the couch, he thought, "This very day, this young monk shall become the master of this house.
The young monk placed the bowl in the king's hand, ascended the couch, and sat down. [The king offered] everything prepared for his own use—
He offered him various preparations of rice gruel, parched grain, and cooked rice. The novice accepted only as much as was necessary for his own sustenance.
At the conclusion of the meal, the king asked, "Do you know the instruction given to you by the Teacher? "I know it, Great King, though only in part," he replied.
"Dear son, tell it to me as well," said the king. "Very well, Great King," he said, and [recited] that which was appropriate for the king.
He recited the Chapter on Heedfulness from the *Dhammapada* for the sake of giving thanks.
But when the king heard the verse, "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path of death," he said, "I understand, dear one; please conclude [the recitation].
At the conclusion of the thanksgiving, the king said, "Dear one, I give you eight regular meals. The novice replied:
—“I give these to my preceptor, Great King. —“Who is this, dear son, called a ‘preceptor’?
—“One who, having seen what is right and wrong, exhorts and reminds, Great King. —“I will give you eight others as well, dear son.
—“I give these to my teacher, Great King. —“Who is this, dear son, called a ‘teacher’? “In this dispensation...”
“O Great King, he is one who establishes others in the things that ought to be trained in. “Excellent, my son! I shall give you eight more.
“I give these too to the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus, O Great King. “Who, my son, is this so-called Saṅgha of Bhikkhus?
“It is that, O Great King, by depending upon whom our teachers, preceptors, and I ourselves have gone forth.”
“...and full ordination. The king, his heart filled with even greater joy, said: “My dear son, I give you eight more as well.

The novice, accepting this with the words “Very well,” entered the royal palace the following day together with thirty-two monks and partook of the meal. The king [said]: “Thirty-two other monks besides yourselves...”
By this very means— saying, "Let them take alms together with me"— increasing [the number] day by day,

he cut off the food for sixty thousand brahmins, wanderers, and others, and established a permanent meal within his own residence for sixty thousand bhikkhus out of the very faith he had found in the Elder Nigrodha. And the Elder Nigrodha [regarded] the king...

Having established him and his assembly in the three refuges and the five precepts, he caused them to be established with an unshakable confidence in the Buddha’s teaching through a faith that transcends the worldly.
Furthermore, having constructed the great monastery named Asokārāma, the king provided permanent alms-food for sixty thousand bhikkhus.
Throughout the entire Jambudīpa, [he established... eighty-four thousand...
In eight thousand cities, he had eighty-four thousand monasteries constructed, adorned with eighty-four thousand cetiyas,
and this was done solely through righteousness,
not unrighteousness. It is said that one day, after the king had given a great almsgiving at the Asokārāma in the midst of the Saṅgha of sixty thousand bhikkhus—
Having sat down and invited the Saṅgha to partake of the four requisites, he asked this question: “Venerable sirs, how much of the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is there?
“In terms of its constituent parts, Great King, there are nine divisions; in terms of aggregates, there are eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma.
The king, having gained confidence in the Dhamma, thought, “I shall honor each single aggregate of Dhamma with a single monastery,” and on that very same day—
Having disbursed ninety-six crores of wealth, he commanded his ministers: “Come, sirs!
Having caused a monastery to be built in each city, cause eighty-four thousand monasteries to be built throughout the eighty-four thousand cities.
He himself began the construction of the Asoka Mahāvihāra within the Asoka Monastery. The Saṅgha [appointed] the Elder Indagutta...
He gave him [a pupil] named Mahiddhika, who was possessed of great psychic power and great majesty, whose taints were destroyed, and who was a supervisor of new construction work.
Whatever the Elder did not complete, he brought to completion through his own supernatural power. In this way, he finished the construction of the monastery in three years.
On a single day, letters arrived from all the cities.
The ministers informed the king: "Your Majesty, the eighty-four thousand monasteries are finished.
The king had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: "Seven days from now there will be a festival for the monasteries.
Let everyone, having undertaken the eight precepts, prepare for the monastery festival both within and outside the city."
Then, at the end of seven days, surrounded by a fourfold army numbering many hundreds of thousands and adorned with every ornament,

he was wandering through the city— which had been decorated and prepared by the great multitude of people who were filled with enthusiasm, desiring to make the capital Amarāvatī in the world of the gods even more resplendent than it already was in glory.
Having gone to the monastery, he stood in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
At that moment, there were eighty koṭis of bhikkhus assembled, and nine million six hundred thousand bhikkhunīs.
Among them, the number of bhikkhus who had destroyed the taints alone reached one hundred thousand. This thought occurred to them: "If the king..."
"One would see one’s own duty in its entirety and would have exceeding faith in the Buddha’s teaching.

Thereupon, they performed the miracle called the "Opening of the World. Standing in the Asokārāma, King [Asoka], looking toward the four quarters, beheld Jambudvīpa extending all around to the limits of the ocean, as well as the eighty-four thousand monasteries with magnificent offerings for the great festival of the monasteries.

They were shining brilliantly. Seeing that splendor, he was filled with sublime joy and gladness, and thinking, "Has such joy and gladness ever arisen in anyone else before? he asked the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus:
"Venerable sirs, who has made a great renunciation in the teaching of our Lord of the World, the One Possessed of the Ten Powers?"
"Whose renunciation is great? The Saṅgha of bhikkhus placed the burden upon the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.
The Elder said, "Great King, even while the Tathāgata was still living, there was no one equal to you as a donor of requisites for the Dispensation of the One of Ten Powers;
your renunciation alone is great. Having heard the Elder’s words, the king, with sublime...
With his body continuously suffused with rapture and joy, he thought: "It seems there is no donor of requisites equal to me;
it seems my renunciation is great; it seems I uphold the Dispensation through the things to be given.
But even so, am I a true heir to the Dispensation, or am I not? Then he questioned the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: "Am I..."
“Am I, venerable sir, indeed an heir to the Dispensation?
Then, having heard these words from the king, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, perceiving the excellence of Prince Mahinda’s spiritual potential, thought:
“If this prince goes forth into homelessness, there will be a great increase for the Dispensation.”
Having reflected, he said this to the king: "Great King, one does not become an heir to the Dispensation merely by this much;

rather, one is reckoned as a provider of requisites or an attendant. For even one who, Great King, were to give a heap of requisites equal in measure to the world-system from the earth up to the Brahma-world, he too would not be reckoned as 'an heir to the Dispensation.'"
“He goes,” [he said]. “Then, venerable sir, how indeed does one become an heir to the Teaching?
“Anyone at all, great king—whether rich or poor—who ordains his own legitimate son, this one, great king, is called an heir to the Teaching.”
When this was said, King Asoka thought, "It seems that even though I have made such a sacrifice, I have not attained the status of an heir to the Teaching.
Desiring to become an heir to the Teaching, he looked here and there and saw Prince Mahinda standing nearby.
Upon seeing him, it occurred to him: "Although I [gave] this prince to Prince Tissa..."
"From the time of his renunciation, I have desired to appoint him as viceroy; however, even compared to the position of viceroy, renunciation itself is supreme.
Then he said to the prince, "My son, will you be able to renounce the world?
Although the prince had already been desirous of renouncing from the very moment Prince Tissa had done so, upon hearing the king's words, he was filled with exceeding joy.
He said, “I shall go forth, O King; having ordained me, may you become the heirs to the Teaching.
At that time, the king’s daughter Saṅghamittā was also standing in that very place.
Her husband, the prince named Aggibrahmā, had already gone forth together with the crown prince Tissakumāra. The king [addressed] her—
Seeing this, he said, “Mother, will you also be able to go forth? “Very well, father, I can,” she replied.
Having gained his sons’ consent, the king, with a joyful heart, spoke thus to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: “Venerable sirs, please ordain these children and make them heirs to my teaching.
The Saṅgha, accepting the king’s request, [ordained] the prince...
He received the going-forth (pabbajjā) with the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa as his preceptor (upajjhāya) and the Elder Mahādeva as his teacher (ācariya).
He received full ordination (upasampadā) with the Elder Majjhantika as his teacher. At that time, it is said, the prince was exactly twenty years of age.
Within that very boundary-mandala of full ordination, he attained Arhatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). It was the same for the royal princess Saṅghamittā.
Her preceptor was the Elder Āyupālī by name, while her preceptor-ni was the Elder Dhammapālī by name.
At that time, Saṅghamittā was eighteen years old. Immediately after she had gone forth, they established her in the training within that very boundary-circle.
At the time both of them went forth, the King had been on the throne for six years.
Then, from the time of his full ordination, the Elder Mahinda, while mastering both the Dhamma and the Vinaya in the presence of his own preceptor,
learned the entire Theravāda— including the Tipiṭaka as compiled in the two councils together with its commentaries—
within three years; and [he taught it] to his preceptor’s pupils.
He was the leader of about a thousand bhikkhus. At that time, King Asoka had been consecrated for nine years.

However, at the very time the king had been consecrated for eight years, the Elder Kontaputta Tissa, while wandering on his alms-round for the purpose of treating an illness, failed to obtain even a *pasata* measure of ghee; consequently, through the force of that illness, the constituent of his life-span was exhausted.
Having exhorted the community of bhikkhus with diligence, he sat cross-legged in the air, entered the fire-element, and attained final nibbāna.
When the king heard this news, he paid honor to the elder and, thinking, "While I am ruling the kingdom,
such requisites for the bhikkhus are so difficult to obtain," he had lotus ponds constructed at the four gates of the city.
Having fulfilled the cost of the medicine, he had it given to him.
At that time, it is said, four hundred thousand [pieces of gold] were received daily at each of the four gates of Pāṭaliputta, and one hundred thousand at the assembly hall;
thus, five hundred thousand were produced for the king every day. From that, the king [gave] to the Elder Nigrodha...
Every day he disbursed one hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. One hundred thousand was for the purpose of worshipping the Buddha’s stupa with perfumes, garlands, and so forth;
one hundred thousand was for the Dhamma, which was presented to those who uphold the Dhamma and are of great learning for the sake of the four requisites;
one hundred thousand was for the Saṅgha; and one hundred thousand was for medicine at the four gates. Thus, there was a magnificent [offering] toward the Dispensation.
Gain and honor arose.

The sectarians, having lost their gain and honor—some not even receiving food or clothing—went forth in the Teaching out of a longing for gain and honor, and they proclaimed their respective views, saying, "This is the Dhamma; this is the Vinaya."
Even though they could not obtain ordination, they shaved their heads themselves, donned saffron robes, and wandered through the monasteries;
they participated in the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and both Saṅgha and Gaṇa formal acts. Yet, the bhikkhus did not perform the Uposatha together with them.
At that time, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa thought: "Now this legal dispute has arisen."
"Before long, that [conflict] will become harsh. It is not possible for one living among these people to bring it to peace.
Having thus led the community of Mahinda Thera away, and desiring to dwell in a comfortable residence for himself, he went to Mount Ahogaṅga.
Those sectarians, however, were [dealt with] by the Saṅgha of monks according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction.

Even while being exhorted toward a practice in conformity with the Dhamma and Vinaya, they failed to settle therein and gave rise to various kinds of swellings, stains, and thorns within the Dispensation. Some worshipped fire; some tormented themselves with the five fires;
some circumambulated the sun; and some said, "We shall split asunder both the Dhamma and the Vinaya."
They took them [into their own group]. At that time, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus did not perform the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā ceremony together with them.
For seven years, the Uposatha was suspended in the Asokārāma. They reported this matter to the king as well.
The king commanded a minister: “Go to the monastery, settle the legal dispute, and have the Uposatha performed.”
Unable to question the king himself, the minister approached other ministers and said, “The king has sent me with the instruction:
‘Go to the monastery, settle the legal dispute, and have the Uposatha performed.
How, then, is a legal dispute settled? They replied, “We observe it thus: ‘Just as when a border region...’”
“Just as they kill thieves while suppressing them, even so the king will become one who wishes to destroy those who do not observe the Uposatha.
Then that minister went to the monastery, assembled the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and said:
“I have been sent by the king with the command, ‘Cause the Uposatha to be performed. Now, venerable sirs, perform the Uposatha. The bhikkhus replied, “We will not [perform it] with the heretics...”
"Let us perform the Uposatha together," they said. Then the minister began to strike off their heads with a sword, starting from the seat of the Elder.
The Elder Tissa saw that minister acting in such a perverse manner. It was not just any Elder Tissa;
he was the king’s half-brother named Prince Tissa, whom the king, having been consecrated, had appointed to the position of viceroy.
One day, having gone out for a walk in the forest, he saw a great herd of deer sporting in a game of hide-and-seek.

Upon seeing this, it occurred to him: "If even these grass-eating deer can sport in such a way, what kind of games will these recluses not play, when they eat choice foods in royal households and lie upon soft beds?"
Having returned from there, he reported this thought of his to the king. The king thought, "The prince has fallen into groundless anxiety!

Come now, I shall convince him thus. One day, as if angry for some reason, he threatened him with the fear of death, saying, "Come, accept the kingdom for seven days; after that, I will have you executed," and [stated] that matter.
He made him understand. It is said that the prince, thinking, "They will kill me on the seventh day," did not bathe, eat, or sleep according to his pleasure;
he became exceedingly emaciated in body. Then the king asked him, "Why have you become like this?
"Out of fear of death, Your Majesty," he replied. "Hey! Do you really perceive your own death as something fixed?"
"Do you not play with confidence? How could the bhikkhus, who behold death as bound up with every inhalation and exhalation, play?
From that time forth, the prince gained faith in the Teaching.
On another day, having gone out for a hunt and wandering through the forest, he saw the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, a Yavana.
He saw [the Elder] sitting there being fanned with a *sāla* branch by a certain noble elephant. Seeing this, he was filled with joy and thought:
"When indeed shall I too go forth into homelessness like this great Elder? Might that day ever come?
The Elder, knowing his intention, leapt into the air even as he watched and alighted at the lotus pond in the Asoka Monastery.
Standing on the surface of the water, he hung his robe and upper garment in the air and began to bathe.
Seeing the Elder’s supernatural power, the prince was deeply inspired with faith and, thinking, "I shall go forth this very day," turned back and informed the king:
"Your Majesty, I shall go forth. Although the king entreated him in many ways to turn back, [he would not do so].
Being unable [to stop him], he had the road leading to the Asoka Monastery decorated, had the prince dressed in festive attire, and surrounded by an adorned army, led him to the monastery.
Hearing that "the crown prince is about to go forth," many monks prepared their bowls and robes.
The prince went to the meditation hall and [approached] the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita alone.
He went forth into homelessness in the presence [of the Buddha] together with one hundred thousand men; however, there was no limit to the number of those who followed the prince in his ordination.
The prince had gone forth at the time of the king’s fourth year of consecration.
Now, there was another prince named Aggibrahmā, the king’s nephew and the husband of Saṅghamittā. Saṅghamittā gave birth to an only son on account of him.
Hearing that the crown prince had gone forth, he too approached the king and requested, "Your Majesty, I too shall go forth.
Being granted permission by the king with the words, "Go forth, dear one," he went forth on that very day.
Thus was he followed in succession by a multitude of kshatriyas of great splendor.
The king’s younger brother should be understood as the Elder Tissa.
Seeing that minister acting so perversely, he thought: "The king would not have sent me to have the elders killed;
surely this must be a misunderstanding on the part of this very minister. Having gone there, he sat down himself on a seat close by.
He sat down. Recognizing the Elder, and unable to bring himself to strike the blow, he went and reported to the king:
"Your Majesty, I have struck off the heads of so many monks who were unwilling to observe the Uposatha;
now the turn of the noble Elder Tissa has arrived—what shall I do? Upon hearing this, the king cried out: "Hey!..."
"But why were you sent by me to have the bhikkhus killed? At that very moment, a fever arose in his body;
he went to the monastery and asked the elder bhikkhus, "Venerable sirs, this minister did this even though he was not commanded by me.
To whom, then, must this evil belong? Some elders said, "This was done at your word."
“‘This evil was done by you,’ they said. Some said, ‘This evil belongs to both of you.
Others said, ‘But what, Great King, was your intention when you sent him, thinking, “Let him go and have the monks killed”?
‘I had no such intention, venerable sirs; I sent him with a wholesome purpose, saying, “Let the Saṅgha of monks perform the Uposatha in concord.”’”
“If you intended it for what is wholesome, there is no evil for you; this evil belongs only to the minister.
The king, filled with doubt, said: “Venerable sir, is there any bhikkhu capable of cutting through this doubt of mine and upholding the Teaching?
“There is, Great King; there is an elder named Moggaliputtatissa. He will [cut through] this doubt of yours...”

“...is capable of upholding the Dispensation after it has been severed. On that very day, the king dispatched four preachers of the Dhamma, each with a retinue of one thousand bhikkhus, and four ministers, each with a retinue of one thousand men, saying, “Go, bring the Elder back.
They went and said, “The king summons you. The Elder did not come. A second time, the king sent eight preachers of the Dhamma...

He dispatched eight ministers, each with a retinue of a thousand men, saying: "Venerable sirs, tell them 'The king summons you,' and bring them back by force. They did exactly as instructed. Yet the Elder still did not come.
The king asked the Elder: "Venerable sir, I sent twice; why does the Elder not come? [The Elder replied: "'The king...'"
"Because it was said, 'He summons,' O Great King, he does not come. But if it were said thus:
'Venerable sir, the Teaching is declining; be our companions for the sake of upholding our Teaching,' then he might come.
Then the king, having spoken thus, dispatched sixteen preachers of the Dhamma and sixteen ministers, each with a retinue of a thousand followers. The monks—
And he asked: “Venerable sir, is the elder an old man, or is he young? “He is an old man, Great King.
“Will he mount a horse or a palanquin, venerable sir? “He will not mount them, Great King.
“Where does the elder dwell, venerable sir? “Upstream on the Ganges, Great King. The king said: “In that case, my man—”
“Having fastened the boat together, have the Elder sit right there, and having established a guard on both banks, bring the Elder here.
Then the monks and the ministers went to the Elder and delivered the king’s message.
Having heard it, the Elder thought: “I went forth because I intended to uphold the Dispensation from its very foundation. This—”
“Now that time has come for me,” he said, and rose up while still holding his piece of hide.
Then, during the night, the king saw a dream, thinking, “The Elder will reach Pāṭaliputta tomorrow. Such was the dream:
“A pure white royal elephant came and, having touched the king from the head down, took him by the right hand.”
On the following day, the king asked the dream-interpreters: "I have seen such a dream; what will happen to me?
One of them replied: "Great King, a noble ascetic (samaṇanāga) will seize you by your right hand.

Then the king, having heard at that very moment that "the Elder has arrived," went to the bank of the Ganges, descended into the river, and as he was emerging, he saw the Elder in the water up to his knees.
Having arrived, he gave his hand to the Elder as he was stepping down from the ship. The Elder took the king by the right hand.
Seeing this, the sword-bearers drew their swords from their scabbards, thinking, "We shall strike off the Elder’s head. Why?
For this is the custom in royal households: "Whoever takes hold of the king's hand, his head must be struck off with a sword."
“He must be cast down. But the king, seeing only the shadow, said: “Even before, when I failed to attend upon the monks, I found no satisfaction;
let me not fail the Elder now! Why, then, did the Elder take the king by the hand?
Because the king had summoned him for the purpose of asking a question, he took hold of him, thinking, “This man is my pupil.”
The king led the Elder to his own park, had it surrounded three times over from the outside, and established a guard;
then, having personally washed the Elder’s feet and anointed them with oil, he sat down beside him and thought:
"Is the Elder capable of cutting through my doubts, settling this arisen legal dispute, and upholding the Dispensation?"
In order to test him, he said, "Venerable sir, I wish to see a miracle.
"Which miracle do you wish to see, Great King? "The shaking of the earth, venerable sir. "Do you wish to see the shaking of the entire earth, Great King, or the shaking of a portion of the earth?
"And which of these, venerable sir, is more difficult to perform? "What—?"
"Now, Great King, is it difficult to cause all the water in a bronze bowl filled with water to tremble, or is it the half?
"The half, venerable sir. "In the same way, Great King, it is difficult to cause even a portion of the earth to tremble.
"In that case, venerable sir, let us see a portion of the earth tremble. "Very well, Great King."
Let the chariot stand in the eastern direction, having stepped across the boundary with one wheel;
let the horse stand in the southern direction, having stepped across the boundary with two feet; let the man stand in the western direction, having stepped across the boundary with one foot;
[let the elephant stand] in the northern direction, having stepped across the boundary with half its body.
“Let one water vessel remain,” the king commanded, and he had it done accordingly. The Elder, having entered the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge and emerging from it, resolved:
“Let the king see! He then performed a shaking of the earth extending for the distance of a league.

The wheel of the chariot stood within the boundary of the eastern direction; only that part [of the wheel] situated within the boundary shook, while the other did not. It was the same in the southern and western directions.
The feet of the horses and men standing within the boundary trembled, as did half of their bodies.
Even in the water-basin in the northern direction, only the portion of the water situated within the boundary moved, while the remainder remained motionless.
Having seen this miracle, the king reached the conclusion: "Now the Elder will indeed be able to uphold the Dispensation."
He asked himself about his own remorse: "Venerable sir, I sent a minister with the instruction:
'Go to the monastery, settle the legal dispute, and have the Uposatha performed. Having gone to the monastery, he took the lives of so many bhikkhus.
To whom does this evil belong?"
“But what, Great King, do you have such a thought as: ‘Having gone to the monastery, let me have the monks killed’?
“I do not, venerable sir. “If you, Great King, do not have such a thought, there is no evil for you.
Then the Elder made this matter clear to the king by means of this Sutta: “Intention, O bhikkhus, I declare to be karma...”
“I say: having willed, one performs an action—whether by body, speech, or mind.
To illustrate this very point, he related the Tittira Jātaka: “In the past, Your Majesty, a partridge from Dīpaka asked an ascetic:
‘A relative of ours is seated there; many people are coming.’”
“Dependent on [the birds], my mind touches upon karma; therefore, my mind is apprehensive regarding them.
The ascetic asked, “But do you have the thought: ‘May these birds, having come here because of my voice and my sight, be caught or killed’?
“No, venerable sir,” the partridge replied. Thereupon, the ascetic instructed him.
“If you have no intention, there is no evil; for it is only one who intends that evil touches, not one who does not intend.
‘Karma does not touch one who has no dependence [on the mind], provided the mind is not corrupted;
for the fortunate one who is free from concern, evil does not adhere.’”
Having thus instructed the king, the Elder stayed right there in the royal park for seven days and caused the king to master the *samaya* (the doctrinal points).
On the seventh day, the king convened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus at the Asokārāma,
had them enclosed by a screen-wall (*sāṇipākāra*), and sitting within that screen-wall, he [instructed] the bhikkhus who held the same view, grouping them together one by one.
Having had them built, he summoned each group of monks one by one and asked: "What does the Perfectly Enlightened One teach?

Thereupon, those who held the doctrine of eternalism said, "He is a proponent of eternalism. Those who held partial-eternalism... [and so on] ...those who held the doctrine of finitude and infinity... those who held the doctrine of endless equivocation... those who held the doctrine of fortuitous origination...

those who held the doctrine of conscious existence... those who held the doctrine of unconscious existence... those who held the doctrine of neither-conscious-nor-unconscious existence... those who held the doctrine of annihilation... and those who held the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life.
“They are proponents of Nibbāna in this very life,” they said. Because the king had already grasped the nature of the teaching, he realized, “These are not monks;
these are followers of other sects. Having given them white garments, he caused them to disrobe.
They numbered sixty thousand in all.
Then, having summoned other bhikkhus, he asked: "What is the doctrine of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, venerable sir?
"He is an analyst of doctrines, Great King. When this was said, the king asked the Elder: "Is the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, an analyst of doctrines, venerable sir?
"Yes, Great King. Thereupon the king said: "Now the Dispensation is pure, venerable sir; let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus perform [the Uposatha]."
Having assigned guards, he entered the city.
The Saṅgha, being in harmony, assembled and performed the Uposatha. In that assembly, there were six million monks.
At that gathering, the Elder Moggaliputtatissa, crushing the doctrines of others, [expounded] the Kathāvatthu treatise.
He spoke thus. Then, having selected from among the monks numbering six million, he took one thousand monks— those who had mastered the Pāḷi of the Tipiṭaka,

who possessed the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and who were distinguished as "possessors of the threefold knowledge" (tevijja) and so forth— and just as the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Yasa,
son of Kākaṇḍaka, had compiled the Dhamma and the Vinaya, in that very same manner [he compiled] the Dhamma...
Reciting the Vinaya and having purified all the impurities of the Dispensation, he held the Third Council.
At the conclusion of the Council, the earth trembled in many ways. This Council was completed in nine months.
It is known in the world as "The One Performed by a Thousand Monks," and therefore it is called the Sahassika.
"Taking the first two as a basis, it is called the third.
This is the Third Council.
And to this extent, regarding the answer to the question "By whom was it brought?", we have said: "In Jambudīpa..."
This was transmitted through a succession of teachers beginning with the Elder Upāli down to the Third Council. In this regard, the lineage of teachers is as follows:
"Upāli, Dāsaka, Soṇaka, and likewise Siggava;
Tissa Moggaliputta—these five were victors."
“In the island named Jambusiri, they maintained the Vinaya through successive lineage without interruption until the Third Council.
Its meaning has already been explained.
Furthermore, it should be understood that after the Third Council, this island was brought [the teaching] by Mahinda and others;
after receiving it from Mahinda, for some time it was brought by Arittha Thera and others;
and from then until the present day, it has been brought down by a succession of teachers consisting of a lineage of their own pupils. As the ancients have said:
“Then Mahinda, Iṭṭhiya, Uttiya, and likewise Sambala,
as well as the wise one named Bhadda—
these Nāgas of great wisdom came here from Jambudīpa.”
They caused him to recite the Vinaya, the Piṭaka of Tambapaṇṇi.
They taught him the five Nikāyas and the seven Pakaraṇas;
thereafter, the wise Ariṭṭha and the learned Tissa-datta [also studied them].
“Visārado Kāḷasumana, the Elder named Dīgha,
and the wise Dīghasumana.
Again, Kāḷasumana, the Elder Nāga, and Buddharakkhita.”
The wise elder Tissa and the learned elder Deva;
furthermore, the wise Sumana, confident in the Vinaya;
and Cūḷanāga, of great learning, who is as difficult to overcome as an elephant.
“One named Dhammapālita was highly honored in Rohaṇa;
his disciple, Khema by name, possessed great wisdom and was a master of the Tipiṭaka.
Like the king of stars in the sky, he shone pre-eminently in wisdom throughout the island.”
Upatissa was wise, and Phussadeva was a great speaker.
Furthermore, Sumana was wise, and the one named Puppha was learned;
Mahāsiva was a great speaker, skilled in all the Piṭakas.
“Furthermore, Upāli was wise and confident in the Vinaya;
he was a great nāga of vast wisdom, skilled in the lineage of the True Dhamma.
Furthermore, Abhaya was wise and proficient in all the Piṭakas.”
And the wise Elder Tissa was confident in the Vinaya.
His disciple, named Puppha, possessed great wisdom and was learned;
protecting the Dispensation, he was established in Jambudīpa.
“Cūḷābhaya was wise and confident in the Vinaya;
the elder Tissa was wise and skilled in the lineage of the True Dhamma.
Cūḷadeva was wise and confident in the Vinaya.”
And the wise Elder Siva was skilled in all aspects of the Vinaya.
These great beings of vast wisdom, knowers of the Vinaya and experts on the Path,
proclaimed the Vinaya Piṭaka on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.

In this regard, the following is the sequential account: It is said that after the Elder Moggaliputtatissa had performed this Third Council of the Dhamma, he thought to himself, "Where indeed will the Dispensation be well-established in the future?
Then, as he investigated, it occurred to him, "It will be well-established in the border regions."
Thus, assigning the responsibility to various bhikkhus, he dispatched them to their respective destinations.
He sent the Elder Majjhantika to the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra, saying: "Go to that kingdom and establish the Dispensation there.
Having spoken likewise to the Elder Mahādeva, he sent him to the Mahiṃsaka region. He sent the Elder Rakkhita to Vanavāsi.
[He sent] the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita to Aparanta; the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita to Mahāraṭṭha;
the Elder Mahārakkhita to the land of the Yonakas; the Elder Majjhima to the region of Himavanta; the Elders Soṇa and Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi;
and his own pupil, the Elder Mahinda, together with the Elders Iṭṭiya, Uttiya, and Sambala.
He sent [them] together with the Elder Bhaddasāla to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, saying: “Having gone to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, you must establish the Dispensation there.
As they all departed for their respective regions, they went accompanied by themselves as the fifth member, thinking:
“In border districts, a group of five is sufficient for the ritual of full ordination.”
Now at that time, in the kingdom of Kasmīra-Gandhāra during the harvest season,
a dragon king named Aravāḷa caused a rain called *karakavassa* to fall, and having had the crops harvested, he brought them to the great ocean. But the Elder Majjhantika,
having risen into the air from Pāṭaliputta, descended above Lake Aravāḷa in the Himalayas and [stood] upon the surface of Lake Aravāḷa.
He walked about, stood, sat down, and even lay down. When the young nāgas saw him, they informed the nāga king Aravāḷa:
"Great King, a certain man wearing tattered, torn clothes, shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes, is defiling our water.
At that very moment, the nāga king, overcome with anger, came out and, seeing the Elder, felt revulsion.
Unable to endure this, he manifested many terrifying portents in the sky. From here and there, violent winds blew;
trees were torn asunder; mountain peaks fell; clouds thundered; flashes of lightning issued forth; thunderbolts crashed;
and water poured down as if the vault of heaven had been split open. Frightful forms of young nāgas gathered together.
He himself emitted smoke, burst into flames, and discharged showers of weapons.
He terrified the Elder with harsh words such as, "Who is this shaveling wearing tattered, torn robes? He commanded his elephant-force, saying, "Come, seize him! Strike him! Drive this ascetic away!
The Elder, having warded off all those terrifying displays by the power of his own psychic potency (*iddhi*), spoke to the Naga king:
“Even if the entire world, including the gods, were to come and terrify me,
it would not be able to produce fear or dread within me.
Even if you [were to bring] the whole earth, together with its oceans and mountains...”
“O Great Naga, having picked me up, you might hurl me over yourself.
Yet you would not be able to produce any fear or terror in me;
on the contrary, O Lord of Serpents, it would be your own exhaustion.”
When this was said, the Naga king, his power destroyed and his efforts rendered fruitless, became pained and dejected. The Elder, having instructed, exhorted, inspired,
and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma appropriate for that moment,
established him, together with eighty-four thousand Nagas, in the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
Many other inhabitants of the Himalayas—yakkhas, gandhabbas, and kumbhaṇḍas—having heard the Elder’s discourse on the Dhamma, established themselves in the refuges and in the precepts.
The yakkha Pañcaka, together with his wife the yakkhinī and his five hundred sons, was established in the first fruit [of the path]. Then the Venerable Majjhantika Thera [addressed] all of them...
Having addressed the nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, he spoke thus:
“Do not now give way to anger as you did before;
do not destroy the crops, for living beings desire happiness.”
"Practice loving-kindness toward all beings; let humans dwell in happiness.
They all replied to the Elder, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and practiced according to his instructions.
On that very day, it was the time for the Naga king’s worship. Then the Naga king had his own jeweled throne brought forth.
He prepared a seat for the Elder. The Elder sat down cross-legged on the couch. The Nāga king also stood nearby, fanning the Elder.
At that moment, the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kaśmīra-Gandhāra arrived;

seeing the Elder, they thought, "The Elder is even more possessed of great psychic power than our own Nāga king," and having paid homage to the Elder, they sat down. The Elder [then taught them] the Āsīvisopama Sutta.

He preached the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse, there was a realization of the Truth (dhammābhisamaya) for eighty thousand beings, and one hundred thousand families went forth into homelessness.
From that time until the present day, Kasmīra-Gandhāra has indeed been illuminated by the saffron robes and fanned by the breezes of the seers.
Having gone to Kasmīra-Gandhāra at that time, the seer Majjhantika—
Having appeased a wicked elephant, he released many from their bonds.

The Elder Mahādeva also went to the Mahiṃsaka region and preached the Devadūta Sutta. At the conclusion of the discourse, forty thousand beings attained the Dhammacakkhu, and another forty thousand beings went forth into homelessness.
Having gone to the Mahiṃsa kingdom, the highly powerful Mahādeva—
Having summoned them by means of divine messengers, he released many from their bonds.
The Elder Rakkhita, however, went to Vanavāsi and, standing in the air, gladdened the people of Vanavāsi with a discourse on the "Exposition of the Beginningless Round of Existences.
At the conclusion of that discourse, there was a realization of the Dhamma for sixty thousand people; approximately seventy thousand attained [the fruits of the path].
They went forth, and five hundred monasteries were established. In this way, he established the teaching there.
Having gone to Vanavāsi, the elder Rakkhita, possessed of great psychic power, stood there in the air and taught the *Anamataggiya* [Sutta].

The Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita also went to Aparanta; after winning over the people of Aparanta with a discourse on the Sutta of the Simile of the Mass of Fire, he caused seventy thousand living beings to drink the nectar of the Dhamma.
A thousand men from a kṣatriya family went forth, as did more than six thousand women. In this way, he established the Dispensation there.
Having plunged into the western region,
the Yonaka Dhammarakkhita gladdened many people there with a simile of a mass of fire.
As for the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, having gone to the Great Kingdom (Mahāraṭṭha), he [gladdened] the people of the Great Kingdom with the discourse on the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka.
Having inspired confidence, he established eighty-four thousand living beings in the fruits of the Path. Thirteen thousand went forth into homelessness.
In this way, that seer, Mahādhammarakkhita, established the Dispensation there in the Great Kingdom.
"Having told a Jātaka, he inspired confidence in the great multitude.

The Elder Mahārakkhita also went to the Yona country; having inspired confidence among the Yona people by recounting the Kāḷakārāma Sutta, he bestowed the ornament of the Path and its Fruit upon one hundred and seventy thousand beings. And in his presence—
Ten thousand [people] went forth into homelessness. Thus he established the Dispensation there as well.
Having then gone to the Yona country, that great seer Mahārakkhita gladdened those Yonakas with the Kāḷakārāma Sutta.
The Elder Majjhima, however, went to a region of the Himalayas together with the Elder Kassapagotta, the Elder Aḷakadeva, the Elder Dundubhissara, and the Elder Mahādeva.
Having gladdened that region by preaching the discourse on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, he caused eighty million beings to attain the jewels of the paths and fruits. Thus, all five elders—
They brought faith to five kingdoms; in each one’s presence, about a hundred thousand people went forth.
Thus they established the Teaching there.
Having gone to the Himalayas, the Elder Majjhima brought them to faith.
Proclaiming the army of *yakkhas*, [he spoke of] "the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
The Elder Soṇa also went to Suvaṇṇabhūmi together with the Elder Uttara.
At that time, a certain female *rakkhasī* there would emerge from the ocean and devour every child born into the royal family. On that very day—

And in the royal palace, a single boy was born. When people saw the Elder, they thought, "This is a companion of the *rākṣasas*," and taking up weapons, they came intending to strike the Elder. The Elder asked, "Why do you come with weapons in hand?
They replied, "Whenever a boy is born in the royal palace, the *rākṣasas* devour them."
“Are you our companions? The Elder replied, “We are not companions of rākṣasīs; we are called recluses, abstaining from taking life... [and so on] ...
abstaining from drinking intoxicants, eating only one meal a day, virtuous, and possessed of wholesome qualities.
At that very moment, that rākṣasī, together with her retinue, emerged from the ocean, thinking, “A boy has been born in the royal palace; I shall devour him!”
When people saw her, they cried out in fear, saying, "Venerable sir, a female ogre is coming!
The Elder, having manifested bodies twice as large as those of the ogres, surrounded her and her retinue on both sides, placing them in the middle.
It occurred to that female ogre and her retinue: "Surely these [monks] have taken this place..."
"Something will surely be gained; we, however, shall become their food. All the *rākṣasa*s, terrified, fled in haste.
The Elder, too, having made them flee until they were out of sight, established a protective guard all around the island.
And at that time, having gladdened the great multitude of people who had assembled with a discourse on the *Brahmajāla Sutta*,...
He established them in the refuges and in the precepts. Therein, sixty thousand attained the realization of the Dhamma.
Three thousand five hundred sons of noble families went forth, as did one thousand five hundred daughters of noble families.
In this way, he firmly established the Dispensation there. From that time forward, they gave the name Soṇuttara to all children born into the royal family.
"Having gone to Suvaṇṇabhūmi, Soṇa and Uttara, possessed of great psychic power, having expelled the pisācas, taught the Brahmajāla Sutta.
But the Elder Mahinda [was told by his preceptor], "Go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and establish the Dispensation. And...
Being requested by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he reflected: "Is now the time for me to go to the island of Tambapaṇṇi?
Then, upon investigation, it occurred to him: "It is not yet the time. But what did he see that led him to this thought?
He saw the advanced age of King Muṭasiva. Thereupon he thought: "This king is old; it is not possible to establish the Dispensation by taking him [with us]."
“...to support [the Dispensation]. Now, however, his son Devānampiyatissa will rule the kingdom.
Having gained him, it will be possible to support the Sasana. Come now, let us wait for his kinsmen until that time arrives;
shall we return to this country again or not? Having thought thus, he [addressed] his preceptor and—

Having paid homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and departed from the Asoka monastery, he traveled together with those four elders beginning with Iṭṭiya, with the novice Sumanas—the son of Saṅghamittā—and with the lay follower Bhaṇḍuka, wandering on tour through the Dakkhiṇāgiri region around the city of Rājagaha.
While observing his kinsmen, he spent six months there. Then, by way of stages...
The mother’s place of residence, the city named Vedisa, was reached.

It is said that while Asoka, having received his provincial domain as a prince, was traveling toward Ujjeni, he arrived at the city of Vedisa and took the daughter of the merchant-chief of Vedisa as his wife.
On that very day, she conceived, and in Ujjeni she gave birth to Prince Mahinda. When the prince was fourteen years old...
The king received his consecration. At that time, his mother was living in her own family home. Therefore it is said:
"Then, in due course, he arrived at Veṭhadīpa, the city named Veṭhasanagara, which was his mother’s residence.
And when she saw the Elder had arrived, the queen, his mother, bowed her head at his feet, gave him alms-food, and—
He established for the Elder the great monastery named Vedisa-giri-mahāvihāra, which he had himself built. While sitting in that monastery, the Elder thought:
"Our duties here are finished; is now the time to go to the island of Laṅkā?
Then he thought: "Let Devānampiyatissa enjoy for a while the consecration sent by my father."
“Let him hear of the virtues of the Triple Gem, and let him leave the city for the festival and ascend Mount Missaka;
then we shall see him there. Thereafter, he remained dwelling in that very place for another month.
When the month had passed, on the Uposatha day of the full moon in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, they all assembled and said: “Is it now time for us?”
They deliberated: "Is it for the sake of going to Tambapaṇṇidīpa, or not? Regarding this, the ancients said:
"At that time there was a senior elder of the Saṅgha named Mahinda;
also the elders Iṭṭhiya, Uttiya, Bhaddasāla, and Sambala."
“The novice Sumana, possessed of the six direct knowledges and great psychic power,
and Bhaṇḍuka as the seventh among them— a lay follower who had seen the Truth—
these great Nāgas deliberated thus when they had gone into seclusion.”
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Elder Mahinda and said this: "Venerable sir, King Muṭasiva has passed away;
now the Great King Devānampiyatissa rules the kingdom. And you were prophesied by the Perfectly Enlightened One:
'In the future, a monk named Mahinda will bring faith to the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Therefore, in this matter—"
“Venerable sir, it is time for you to go to the excellent island; I too shall be your companion. But why did Sakka speak thus?

It is said that while the Blessed One was still at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and, seeing the future prosperity of this island, announced this matter: “At that time, you too should be my companion.”

He gave the command. Therefore, he spoke thus. The Elder, having accepted his words, rose into the air from Veṭṭhisaka Mountain with himself as the seventh person and alighted on Missaka Mountain to the east of Anurādhapura.
That which is nowadays known as "Cetiya Mountain" is this very place. Thus said the ancients:
“Having dwelt for thirty nights at Veṭṭhisagiri in Rājagaha, it is time to depart;
let us go to the supreme island.
Like swan-kings in the sky, we have grown weary of Jambudīpa.”
Thus having arisen, the elders descended upon the best of cities.
In front of the preeminent city, upon the mountain resembling a cloud,
they alighted on the Peak of Virtue like swans upon the summit of a mountain.

Thus, it should be understood that the Venerable Mahinda Thera, arriving together with Iṭṭiya and the others and establishing himself on this island, did so in the thirty-sixth year after the two hundred years following the Parinibbāna of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For the Perfectly Enlightened One passed away in the eighth year of Ajātasattu’s reign; in that very same [year]...
In the year of Vassa, Vijaya Kumāra—the son of Siha Kumāra and the first king of the island of Tambapaṇṇi—arrived at this island and established a human habitation.
In the fourteenth year of Udayabhadda in Jambudīpa, Vijaya passed away here.
In the fifteenth year of Udayabhadda, the one named Paṇḍuvāsudeva attained sovereignty over this island. Therein:
In the twentieth year of King Nāgadāsaka, Paṇḍuvāsudeva passed away here.
In that very same year, a prince named Abhaya attained the sovereignty over this island.
There, in the seventeenth year of King Susunāga, twenty years of King Abhaya’s reign were fulfilled. Then, in the twentieth year of Abhaya, Paṇḍukābhaya...
Nāgadāsa, the executioner, seized the kingdom. There, during the sixteenth year of Kālāsoka, seventeen years had been completed here under Paṇḍuka; including the preceding year, these total eighteen.
There, during the fourteenth year of Candagutta, Paṇḍukābhaya passed away here. King Muṭasiva attained the sovereignty.
Therein, in the seventeenth year of King Aśoka Dhamma, King Muṭasīva passed away here.
Devānampiyatissa attained the kingship. After the Perfectly Enlightened One had attained parinibbāna, Ajātasattu reigned for twenty-four years;
Udayabhadda for sixteen; Anuruddha and Muṇḍa for eight; Nāgadāsaka for twenty-four; and Susunāga—
For eighteen years; his son Kālāsoka ruled for twenty-eight. Then his ten sons, the brother-kings, reigned for twenty-two years.
Following them, the nine Nandas reigned for exactly twenty-two years;
Candagutta for twenty-four, and Bindusāra for twenty-eight. At the conclusion of his reign, Asoka attained the sovereignty. Prior to his consecration...
Mahinda Thera was established on this island in the eighteenth year from the consecration. Thus,
according to this royal chronology, it should be understood that he was established on this island in the thirty-sixth year after the Parinibbāna of the Sammasambuddha.
On that day, the constellation known as Jeṭṭhamūla was occurring on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Having caused the proclamation of the festival, the king commanded his ministers, “Celebrate the festival!
Then, surrounded by forty thousand men and desiring to sport in the hunt, he departed from the city and set out for Mount Missaka. Now, the deities residing on that mountain—
A certain deity, thinking, "I shall show the king the Elders," assumed the form of a red deer and wandered nearby as if grazing on grass and leaves.
When the king saw him, he thought, "It is no longer appropriate to shoot one who is so heedless," and he plucked his bowstring.
The deer began to flee by way of the Ambaṭṭha road. The king followed closely behind him.
“Ascend Ambatthala itself. The deer also vanished not far from the elders.
When the Elder Mahinda saw the king approaching nearby, he made a resolution: “Let the king see me alone, and not the others,” and said, “Tissa, Tissa, come this way!
Upon hearing this, the king thought: “One born on this island addresses me by the name ‘Tissa’—”
“There is no one capable of addressing me by name. Yet this shaven-headed man, wearing tattered and torn robes and clad in saffron garments, addresses me by my name.
Who could he be—is he a human or a non-human? The Elder said:
“We are recluses, O Great King, disciples of the Dhamma-King.”
“Out of compassion for you alone, they have come here from Jambudīpa.
At that time, King Devānampiyatissa and King Aśokadharma were friends who had not yet met.
And by the power of King Devānampiyatissa’s merit, there was one Tissathera in a bamboo grove at the foot of Mount Chāta.
Bamboo poles appeared, equal in size to chariot poles—namely, one called the creeper-pole (*latāyaṭṭhi*), one called the flower-pole (*pupphayaṭṭhi*), and one called the bird-pole (*sakuṇayaṭṭhi*).
Among these, the creeper-pole was silver-colored; when decorated with it, the creeper that had grown appeared golden in color.
On the flower-pole, however, there were flowers of blue, yellow, red, white, and black colors.
They appear with their stalks, petals, and filaments well-divided.
Upon the bird-staffs, various kinds of birds such as swans, chickens, and pheasants, as well as quadrupeds, appear as if they were alive. And this is also said in the *Dīpavaṃsa*:
“At the foot of Mount Chāta, there were three bamboo-staffs;”
“Like a white silver staff, the creeper resembles gold.
Whatever kind of flower there is—blue or otherwise—it is of that same color upon the flower-staff.
The birds, too, are established upon the bird-staffs in their very own forms.”
From the ocean, too, there arose for him many kinds of gems, such as pearls, jewels, and beryl.

On Tambapaṇṇi, however, eight kinds of pearls appeared: horse-pearls, elephant-pearls, chariot-pearls, *āmalaka*-pearls, bracelet-pearls, finger-ring-pearls, *kakudha*-fruit-pearls, and natural pearls. He [took] those rods and those pearls...
And he sent many other treasures as a gift to King Aśoka, the Dharma-king. Aśoka, being pleased,
dispatched to him the five insignia of royalty— the parasol, the fly-whisk, the sword, the crown, and the jeweled sandals—
as well as various other articles for his consecration, such as a conch shell and water from the Gaṅgā.
The *vaḍḍhamāna*, the *vaṭaṃsaka*, the *bhiṅgāra*, the *nandiyāvaṭṭa*, the *sivika*,
the maiden, the ladle, the pair of lower garments, the hand-towel, yellow sandalwood, reddish-brown clay, collyrium, myrobalan, and emblic myrobalan.
And this has also been said in the *Dīpavaṃsa*:
“A yak-tail fan, a turban, an umbrella, a sword, and sandals;
a head-wrap, a fine silk cloth, a water-pot, and a *nandivaṭṭaka* ornament.
A palanquin, a conch shell, an ear-ornament, a lower garment, and a corner of a cloth.”
A golden bowl, a ladle, a costly hand-towel;
water from Anotatta, a maiden, supreme yellow sandalwood;
clay the color of dawn, and collyrium brought by a Naga.
“Harītaka and āmalaka, precious and like the medicine of immortality;
six hundred cartloads of fragrant rice, brought by excellent carriers—
these were sent by the one called Asoka, produced through his meritorious deeds.”
Not only did he send this material gift, but it is said he also sent this gift of the Dhamma:
“I have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha;
I have declared myself a lay follower in the teaching of the Sakyan Son.”
“In these three matters, within the supreme teaching of the Conqueror;
you too, O Citta, should find confidence and go for refuge with faith.
On that very day, this king was consecrated with the royal inauguration sent by King Asoka, having been anointed for one month.
For on the full moon day of Visākha, they performed his consecration.

Not long after, recollecting that news of the proclamation of the Teaching he had not yet heard, and having heard the Elder’s words, "Great King, we are disciples of the Dhamma-King," he thought, "Has my noble lord arrived?
At that very moment, laying aside his weapons, he sat to one side, engaging in friendly conversation. As it is said:
“Having laid aside his weapon, he sat down to one side;
having sat down, the king exchanged greetings and spoke much that was meaningful.
While he was still engaged in this friendly conversation, those forty thousand men arrived and surrounded him.
Then the Elder showed the other six men as well. When the king saw them, he asked, "When did these people arrive?
"Along with me, Great King," he replied. "But are there now others like these ascetics in Jambudīpa? "There are, Great King;
at present, Jambudīpa is ablaze with the saffron robes and fanned by the wind of the seers. Regarding that—
“‘Possessors of the threefold knowledge, attained to supernormal powers, skilled in the penetration of others’ minds, Arhats with taints destroyed—many such disciples of the Buddha.
‘Venerable sir, by what means have you come? ‘Neither by water nor by land, O Great King,’ [replied the Elder]. ‘[Then] by the sky, O King.’”

He recognized that [the King] had arrived. Desiring to test whether the King possessed proficiency in wisdom, the Elder asked a question concerning a nearby mango tree: "What is the name of this tree, Great King?
"It is called a mango tree, Venerable Sir. "But apart from this mango tree, Great King, is there another mango tree or not?"

“There are, venerable sir, many other mango trees as well. “Setting aside this mango tree and those other mango trees, are there any other trees at all, great king? “There are, venerable sir, but they are not mango trees.
“Setting aside both the mango trees and the non-mango trees, is there any other tree at all? “This very one, venerable sir, is the mango tree.”
“Excellent, Great King! You are wise. But do you have any relatives, Great King?
“There are, Bhante; there are many people. “Having set those free, are there any others who are not your relatives, Great King?
“Those who are not my relatives, Bhante, are more numerous than my relatives. “Having set free both your relatives and those who are not your relatives, is there anyone else remaining, Great King?”

“I am indeed a stranger. Then the Elder, thinking, “The king is wise; he will be able to understand the Dhamma,” preached the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta (The Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint).
At the conclusion of the discourse, the king, together with forty thousand living beings, was established in the Three Refuges.
At that very moment, the king’s meal was brought. And while still listening to the sutta, the king attained realization.

“Food is not permitted for us at this time. Thinking, “But it is improper to eat without having asked permission,” he asked, “Will you eat, venerable sirs? “No, Great King, food is not permitted for us at this time.
“At what time, venerable sirs, is it permitted? “From the rising of the sun until the time of midday.”
“Great King,” [the Elder replied]. “Let us go to the city, Bhante. “Enough, Great King; we shall dwell right here.
“If you will stay, Bhante, let this boy come along. “Great King, this boy has already attained the fruit and understood the teaching;
he is seeking the going-forth and will go forth now. The king said, “In that case, Bhante, tomorrow [we shall go] by chariot.”
“I shall send it; having mounted it, you may come. Having said this and paid homage, he departed.
Not long after the king had left, the Elder addressed the novice Sumanas: “Come, Sumanas, announce the time for hearing the Dhamma.
“Venerable Sir, how far shall I make the proclamation heard? “Throughout the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi.”

“Very well, venerable sir,” the novice said. Having entered the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge, he emerged, made a resolution, and with a concentrated mind, while sounding it throughout the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi, he proclaimed the time for hearing the Dhamma three times.
When the king heard that sound, he sent messengers to the elders, saying: “Venerable sirs, what is this?”
“Is there some calamity? [They replied: “There is no calamity for us; we merely had the time announced for hearing the Dhamma, as we wished to speak the word of the Buddha.
Upon hearing that sound from the novice, the earth-dwelling deities raised their voices.
By this means, the sound ascended as far as the Brahma-world. Because of that sound, a great assembly of deities gathered.
It happened thus. Seeing the great assembly of deities, the Elder preached the *Samacitta Sutta*.
At the conclusion of the discourse, there was a penetration of the Dhamma by incalculable numbers of deities. Many *nāgas* and *supaṇṇas* established themselves in the refuges.
Such was the assembly of deities when the Elder Sāriputta preached this sutta.
Such a one was born to the Elder Mahinda as well. Then, at the end of that night, the king sent a chariot for the Elders.
The charioteer, having parked the chariot to one side, announced to the Elders: "Venerable sirs, the chariot has arrived;
please board it and we shall go. The Elders said, "We do not board a chariot; you go [on your own]."
Having said, "We shall come later," they rose up into the air and descended at the site of the First Stūpa in the eastern direction of Anurādhapura.
For that stūpa is called the "First Stūpa" precisely because it was built at the place where the Elders first descended.
The king, having dispatched his charioteer, commanded his ministers, "Prepare a pavilion within the palace grounds.
Immediately, everyone, joyful and delighted, prepared an exceedingly beautiful pavilion. Then the king thought:
"Yesterday, while the Elder was preaching on the aggregate of virtue, he said that 'high and luxurious beds and seats are not permitted. [They will sit...]"
“Will the noble ones not sit upon the seats? While he was thinking thus, the charioteer arrived at the city gate.
There he saw the elders who had arrived earlier, fastening their waist-bands and putting on their robes.
Seeing them, his heart became exceedingly serene, and having returned, he announced to the king: “They have come, Your Majesty.”
“Elders,” he said. The king asked, “Have they mounted the chariot? “They have not, Your Majesty;
rather, having departed after me, they arrived first and are standing at the eastern gate.

When the king heard that they had not even mounted the chariot, he thought, “Now these noble ones will not consent to high and luxurious beds and seats,” and said, “In that case, my man, [prepare for] the elders...”
Having said, "Prepare seats using a spread of earth as a covering," he set out on the opposite path.
The ministers prepared a mat of grass upon the ground and then laid out variegated rugs such as woolen blankets and the like.
When the diviners saw this, they prophesied: "Now the earth has been seized by these; they shall become the masters of the island of Tambapaṇṇi."
The king also went, paid homage to the elders, and taking the bowl from the hand of Mahinda Thera,
having caused the elders to enter the city with great worship and honor, he led them into his own palace. Seeing that a seat had been prepared, the elder thought,
"Our teaching shall be established throughout the entire island of Laṅkā, spreading like the earth and remaining immovable."

He sat reflecting. After the king had personally satisfied and served the elders with choice hard and soft foods, he summoned Queen Anulā and her five hundred women, saying, "Let them pay homage to the elders and offer them honor and respect," and then sat down to one side.
At the conclusion of the meal, the elder [addressed] the king together with his retinue.
Showering the rain of the jewel of the Dhamma, he preached the *Petavatthu*, the *Vimānavatthu*, and the *Saccasaṃyutta*.
Having heard that Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma, those five hundred women realized the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
And as for those people who had seen the Elder on the previous day at Missaka Mountain, they [were found] in their respective places.
They spoke of the virtues of the elders. Hearing this, a great multitude of people gathered in the royal courtyard and raised a great clamor.
The king asked, "What is this noise? "Your Majesty, the citizens are crying out, 'We do not get to see the elders!
The king thought, "If they enter here, there will be no room," and said, "Go!"

"Friend," he said, "having tended the elephant stable, having strewn sand, having scattered flowers of five colors, and having fastened a canopy of cloth, prepare seats for the elders in the place of the auspicious elephant. The ministers did exactly so.
The elder went there, sat down, and preached the Devadūta Sutta. At the conclusion of the discourse—
A thousand beings were established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then, thinking that the elephant stable was too cramped, they prepared a seat for him in the Nandana Grove at the southern gate.
The Elder sat there and preached the Āsīvisopama Sutta (The Simile of the Venomous Snake).
Having heard that as well, another thousand beings attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Thus, on the second day after his arrival, there was a realization of the Dhamma for two thousand five hundred people.
As the Elder was exchanging greetings with the women who had come from various noble families—wives, daughters-in-law, and young maidens—in the Nandana Grove, evening fell.
Perceiving that it was time, the Elder rose, saying, "We shall now go to Missaka Mountain."

The ministers asked, "Where are you going, venerable sir? "To our place of residence," he replied. Having informed the king, they said with the king's permission, "Venerable sir, it is not the right time to go there now;
let this very Nandana Grove be the dwelling place for the masters. "Enough, we shall go," he said. Again, at the king's word, they said, "The king..."
"Venerable sir," he said, "this park named Meghavana belongs to my father;
it is neither too far from nor too close to the city, and it is well-suited for coming and going. Let the elders dwell there. The elders dwelt in the Meghavana park.
Then, at the end of that night, the king went to the elder, inquired whether he had slept well, and—
“Venerable sir, is it permissible for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to have a monastery? he asked.
The Elder replied, “It is permissible, Great King,” and recited this Sutta: “I allow you, bhikkhus, a monastery.
Delighted, the king took a golden pitcher, poured water into the Elder’s hand, and gave him the Mahāmeghavana garden. With the pouring of the water—
The earth quaked. This was the first earthquake at the Mahāvihāra. Terrified, the king asked the Elder, “Venerable sir, why does the earth quake?
“Do not fear, Great King. The teaching of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers shall be established on this island;
this shall be the site of the first monastery, and this is its omen.”
The king became even more deeply inspired with faith. On the following day as well, the Elder ate at the royal palace itself and preached the *Anamatagga* discourses in the Nandana Grove.
On the next day, he preached the *Agnikhaṇḍhopama-sutta*.
In this same manner, he preached for seven days. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma by eight thousand five hundred beings.
From that time forth, Nandana Grove received the name "Jotivana" (The Forest of Light), as it was regarded as the place where the light of the Dispensation appeared.
On the seventh day, however, the elders, having preached the *Appamāda-sutta* (Discourse on Heedfulness) to the king in the inner palace, returned to Cetiyagiri.
Then the king asked his ministers: "The elder exhorts us with such earnest admonition; would he perhaps depart?"
The ministers said, "Your Majesty, the Elder came of his own accord without being asked by you; therefore, he may also depart without asking for permission.
Thereupon, the king mounted his chariot, had the two queens board as well, and went to Cetiyagiri with great royal splendor.
Having arrived, he had the queens move aside and [approached] himself.
As he approached the elders, he appeared extremely exhausted.
Then the elder said to him, "Great King, why have you come looking so weary?
"Venerable sir, it was in order to find out whether you intended to depart now after having given me such strict instruction. "Great King, we do not intend to depart."
"Moreover, Great King, this is the time for entering the rains-retreat; on that occasion, it is fitting for a recluse to know the place for entering the rains-retreat.
On that very day, a minister named Ariṭṭha, who was standing near the king together with fifty-five younger brothers, said: "Your Majesty, I wish to go forth in the presence of the Elders."
“Very well, my friend, go forth,” the king replied, granting permission, and he caused the Elder to receive him. The Elder ordained him that very day.
All of them attained Arahatship at the mere touch of the razor’s edge.
At that very moment, the king had the courtyard of the Kaṇṭaka Cetiya surrounded with a fence and began work on sixty-two caves.

Having established [the order], he went back to the city itself. Those elders, having won over the royal family which was filled with the ten brothers, spent the rains retreat on Mount Cetiyagiri while instructing the great multitude.
At that time, there were sixty-two arahants who had entered the first rains retreat on Mount Cetiyagiri.
