Then, when the venerable Mahāmahinda had completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, on the full moon day of the month of Kattika—
On the day of the Uposatha, he said this to the king: “Great King, we have not seen the Perfectly Enlightened One for a long time;
we have lived in a state of homelessness. We wish to go to Jambudīpa. The king said:
“Venerable sir, I provide you with the four requisites, and this great multitude of people has established itself in the three refuges by depending upon you. Why [do you wish to leave]?”

“Are you longing for him? “Long ago we saw the Perfectly Enlightened One, Great King. We have had no opportunity to pay homage, to rise up in greeting, to join our palms in salutation, or to perform the duties of respect;
it is for this reason that we are longing. “But did you not say, venerable sirs, ‘The Perfectly Enlightened One has attained final Nibbāna’?
“It is true, Great King, that he has attained final Nibbāna; nevertheless, his bodily relics remain. “I understand, venerable sir.”
“Venerable sir, do you desire the site for the stupa? “I do, venerable sir; I shall build the stupa. Now, please examine the ground.
However, venerable sir, from where shall we obtain the relics? “Consult with Sumanas, Great King.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the king said, and approaching Sumanas, he asked: “Venerable sir, from where shall we now obtain the relics?”
“Shall we be able? Sumana said, “Be at ease, Great King. Have the streets cleared, have them adorned with banners, flags, full water-jars, and the like;
together with your retinue, undertake the Uposatha vows; have all kinds of musical instruments prepared;
have the auspicious elephant decorated with every ornament; and having raised a white parasol over him, in the evening time...”
"Go toward the Mahānāga forest park; you will certainly obtain the relics at that place. The King accepted, saying, "Very well.
The Elders went to Cetiyagiri itself. There, the Venerable Mahinda Thera said to the novice Sumanas:
"Go, novice, approach your grandfather, King Aśoka the Dhamma-king, in Jambudīpa..."
"Speak thus in my name: 'Your friend, O Great King, Devānampiyatissa, is devoted to the Buddha’s teaching and desires to establish a stūpa;
it is said that you have relics in your possession—grant them to me.
Having taken them, approach Sakka, the king of the gods, and speak thus: 'It is said, O Great King, that you have two...'"
“There are two relics—the right canine tooth and the right collar bone. Therefore, you should worship the right canine tooth, but give the right collar bone to me. And speak thus to him:
“Why, Great King, having sent us to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, do you neglect us?”
“Very well, venerable sir,” Sumana replied, accepting the elder’s words.
He immediately took his bowl and robe, rose into the air, descended at the gate of Pāṭaliputta, went into the presence of the king, and reported this matter.
The king was delighted; he took the bowl from the novice’s hand, rubbed it with perfumes, and [filled it] with the finest pearls.
Having filled the reliquaries, he gave them [to him]. He took them and approached Sakka, the king of the gods.

As soon as Sakka, the king of the gods, saw the novice, he asked, "What is it, venerable Suman, that you are wandering about? "Great King, why do you neglect us after having sent us to the island of Tambapaṇṇi?
"I have not neglected you, venerable sir; tell me, what shall I do? "For you..."
“It seems there are two relics in his hand—the right canine tooth and the right collarbone.
Therefore, you should worship the right canine tooth, but give the right collarbone to me. “Very well, Bhante,” replied Sakka, Lord of the Devas.
Having opened a jeweled stupa one yojana in height, he extracted the relic of the right collarbone and gave it to Sumanas.
Thus, having taken it, he established it right there on Cetiyagiri.
Then all those Great Nāgas, headed by Mahinda, having established the relics given by King Aśoka Dhamma right on Cetiyagiri,
took the southern shoulder-bone and went to the Mahānāga forest park during the increasing shade.

The king, having performed the aforementioned acts of worship and honor by Suman, mounted the back of a noble elephant and, holding a white parasol over the head of that auspicious elephant, arrived at the Great Elephant Wood. Then this thought occurred to him:
"If this is the relic of the Perfectly Enlightened One, let the parasol incline; let the auspicious elephant kneel."
“May it be established upon the ground; may the reliquary casket be established upon my head.
With the arising of this thought in the king’s mind, the parasol tilted down, the elephant knelt on its forelegs, and the reliquary casket was established upon the king’s head.
The king, as if his body had been anointed with the Deathless, was endowed with supreme joy and gladness.
Having offered the oblation, he asked: "Venerable sir, what shall we do with the relic? "For now, Great King, place it right upon the elephant's forehead," he replied.
The king took the relic casket and placed it on the elephant's forehead. The delighted elephant let out a cry like a peacock.
A great cloud arose and rained down a shower of lotus blossoms. Then, reaching as far as the edge of the water, there was a great earthquake.
It came to pass. "The relics of the Perfectly Enlightened One will indeed be established even in a border region," they exclaimed, and gods and humans rejoiced.
Thus, generating joy among gods and humans through the glory of his supernormal power, the Great Hero [arrived] here on the full moon day of the fourth month.
"Having come from the world of the gods, he has alighted upon the elephant's frontal globe.
Then that noble elephant, surrounded by a retinue of many musical instruments and being honored with exceedingly magnificent offerings and respect,
turned toward the western direction and, withdrawing, proceeded as far as the eastern gate of the city.
Having entered the city through the eastern gate, while a magnificent worship was being performed by the entire city, he departed through the southern gate.
Having gone to the place known as Mahejavatthu, located in the western direction of the Thūpārāma, he turned back again toward the Thūpārāma itself. At that time, in the Thūpārāma—
This was the site of the *paribhoga-cetiya* (relic-shrine) of the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
It is said that in the past, this island was named Ojadīpa; the king was named Abhaya; the city was named Abhayapura;
the Cetiya Mountain was named Devakūṭapabbata; and the Thūpārāma was named Paṭiyārāma. Now, at that time...

The Blessed One Kakusandha appeared in the world. His disciple, the elder Mahādeva by name, established himself on Devakūṭa together with a thousand bhikkhus, just as the elder Mahinda did at Cetiyapabbata.
At that time, the beings on Ojadīpa were falling into ruin and calamity because of Pajjaraka. Then the Blessed One Kakusandha saw this.
Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, he saw those beings falling into ruin and calamity.
Having seen this, surrounded by forty thousand bhikkhus, he went there. Through his majestic power, the plague was immediately pacified.
When the disease had subsided, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma; there was a penetration of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand living beings.
The Blessed One gave him a water-vessel and departed. Having placed it inside, they constructed a shrine in Paṭiyārāma.
Mahādeva dwelt there, ruling over the island.
However, in the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, this island was named Varadīpa, and the king was named Sameṇḍī.
The city was named Vaḍḍhamāna, and the mountain was named Suvaṇṇakūṭa. Now at that time, there was a drought on Varadīpa;
there was famine, scarcity of grain, and lack of crops. Beings were falling into ruin and calamity due to the disease of starvation.
Then the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, saw those beings falling into ruin and calamity.

[The people] were falling into [distress]. Seeing this, [the Blessed One] went forth, surrounded by thirty thousand bhikkhus. Through the supernatural power of the Buddha, the rain-god poured down rain in proper measure.
There was an abundance of food. The Blessed One taught the Dhamma. There was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings.
The Blessed One, accompanied by a retinue of a thousand bhikkhus, [established] the Elder named Mahāsumana on the island.
Setting it aside and giving him his waist-band, he departed. They placed it inside and built a cetiya over it.
However, in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, this island was named Maṇḍadīpa;
the king was named Jayanta; the city was named Visāla; and the mountain was named Subhakūṭa. Now at that time, there was a great dispute on Maṇḍadīpa.

There were many beings who, having fallen into quarrels and disputes, met with ruin and disaster. As the Blessed One Kassapa surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye, he saw those beings meeting with ruin and disaster.

Having seen this, surrounded by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus, he arrived, quelled the dispute, and taught the Dhamma. There was a penetration of the Dhamma by eighty-four thousand living beings.
It came to pass that the Blessed One, having established the elder named Sabbakāmin—surrounded by a retinue of one thousand bhikkhus—on the island, gave him a bathing robe and departed.
They enclosed it within [the structure] and built a cetiya.
Thus, the cetiyas of the three previous Buddhas were established in the Thūpārāma. These will perish with the disappearance of the Dispensation; only their sites will remain.
It remains. Therefore it was said: “At that time, in the Thūpārāma, there was the site of the *paribhoga-cetiya* (shrines of use) of the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Since those shrines had fallen into ruin, this site remained surrounded by various shrubs with branches covered in thorns through the power of the deities, [thinking]:
“Let no one defile it with leftover food, impurities, filth, or rubbish.”
Then, the king’s men went ahead of the elephant, cleared away all the shrubs, leveled the ground, and made it as smooth as the palm of a hand.
The elephant went forward, placed that spot in front of him, and stood at its western side, where the site of the Bodhi tree was located. Then, in order to lower the relic from his head—
They began [to dig], but the nāga would not allow them to lower [the relic]. The king asked the Elder, “Venerable sir, why does the nāga not allow the relic to be lowered?
“It is not proper, Great King, to lower what has been mounted,” he replied. At that time, the water in the Abhaya tank had run dry;
the ground all around was cracked, and the lumps of clay were easy to extract. Then the great multitude...
Having very quickly brought clay, they fashioned a site the size of an elephant’s frontal globe.
At that very moment, they began preparing bricks for the purpose of building the stupa.

Until the bricks were finished, the elephant king stayed during the day at the site of the Bodhi tree or in the elephant stable, and at night he paced around the ground where the stupa was to be established.
Then, having had the site measured out, the king asked the Elder, "Of what kind, venerable sir, should the stupa be built? "Like a heap of rice, Great King," he replied.
"Very well, venerable sir," said the king; and having had a stupa built to the height of a man's leg, he made great preparations for the enshrining of the relics.
The entire city and the countryside gathered together for the purpose of beholding the great festival of the relics. When they had assembled—

Furthermore, from the elephant’s frontal globe, the relics of the One Possessing the Ten Powers rose into the air to the height of seventy palm trees and displayed the Twin Miracle. From those various parts of the relics,
streams of water and masses of fire issued forth, exactly like the miracle displayed by the Blessed One at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree in Sāvatthī.
A miracle occurred. And that was neither by the power of the elders nor by the power of the deities, but rather solely by the power of the Buddha.
It is said that while the Blessed One was still living, he made this resolve:

“When I have attained final Nibbāna, in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, in the southern direction from Anurādhapura, at the site of the Relic Shrine where the three previous Buddhas used to eat, my right collar-bone relic [shall remain].”
“Let the Twin Miracle take place on the day of the establishment [of the relic].
“Thus inconceivable are the Buddhas, inconceivable are the qualities of the Buddhas;
for those who have faith in what is inconceivable, the result is inconceivable.”
It is said that during his lifetime, the Sammasambuddha came to this island three times.

First, having come alone for the purpose of subduing the yakkhas and having subdued them, he thought, "After my parinibbāna, the Dispensation shall be established on this island," and thus he visited the island three times, providing protection for Tambapaṇṇadīpa. Second, [he came] for the sake of his maternal uncle and nephew...

He came alone for the purpose of subduing the nāga kings, and having subdued them, he departed. Thirdly— accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus— he came to the site of the Mahācetiya, the site of the Thūpārāma-cetiya,
the site where the Mahābodhi was established, the site of the Mahiyaṅgaṇa-cetiya, the site of the Mutiyaṅgaṇa-cetiya, the site of the Dīghavāpi-cetiya, and the site of the Kalyāṇiya-cetiya.
And having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), he sat down. This was his fourth arrival with the relic-body (*dhātusarīra*).
And from that relic-body, by the drops of water falling from it, there was not a single spot on the entire surface of the island of Tambapaṇṇi that was not touched.
Thus, by those drops of water from that relic-body, [he quenched] the fever of the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Having pacified the great multitude and displayed a miracle, he descended and alighted upon the head of the king.
The king, considering his attainment of human birth to have borne fruit, performed a great act of honor and enshrined the relic.
Simultaneously with the enshrinement of the relic, a great earthquake occurred. And during that miracle of the relic, [the people’s] minds...
Having inspired confidence, the king’s brother, the prince named Abhaya, went forth into homelessness together with a thousand men.
From the village of Cetaraṭṭha, five hundred boys went forth; likewise, from villages such as Dvāramaṇḍala, five hundred boys each went forth.
Thus, thirty thousand monks in total had gone forth, both from within the city and from outside the city.
When the stupa was completed, the king, his royal brothers, and the queens each performed individual acts of worship that inspired wonder even among the gods,
nāgas, and yakṣas. Once the relic-worship was concluded and the noble relic had been installed,
the Elder Mahinda went to the Meghavana monastery itself and took up residence there.
At that time, Queen Anulā, desiring to go forth into the religious life, informed the king.
Having heard her words, the king said this to the Elder: "Venerable sir, Queen Anulā desires to go forth; please let her go forth.
"Great King, it is not permitted for us to ordain women. However, in Pāṭaliputta, my sister, the Elder Saṅghamittā—"
“Summon him by name. Furthermore, Great King, on this island the Bodhi trees of the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were established.
Our Blessed One’s Bodhi tree must also be established here, emitting a network of rays from its essence;
therefore, send such a message that Saṅghamittā may take the Bodhi tree and come.”
“Excellent, venerable sir,” the king replied, accepting the elder’s words. Then, consulting with his ministers, he said to his own nephew named Ariṭṭha:
“Dear boy, will you be able to go to Pāṭaliputta and bring back the noble Saṅghamittā Therī together with the Great Bodhi tree? “I shall be able to do so, Your Majesty, if—”
“Grant me the going forth. “Go, dear one, bring the Elder and then go forth,” he said.
Taking the message of both the king and the Elder, and by means of the Elder’s supernormal power, he traveled in a single day to the port of Jambukola;
there he boarded a ship, crossed the ocean, and arrived at Pāṭaliputta itself. Meanwhile, Anulā—

The queen, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred women of the inner apartments, undertook the ten precepts, donned saffron robes, and having had a residence constructed in a certain part of the city, took up her abode there.
On that very same day, Ariṭṭha also sent a message to the king, saying: "Your son, O King, the Elder Mahinda..."
He spoke thus: “It is said that the queen named Anulā, the sister-in-law of King Devānampiyatissa, your ally, wishes to go forth;
therefore, dispatch the noble Elder Saṅghamittā to ordain her, and let the Great Bodhi tree come along with the noble lady.
Having delivered this message to the Elder, he approached the Elder Nun Saṅghamittā and spoke as follows.
“Noble lady, your brother, the Elder Mahinda, has sent me to you.
Queen Anulā, the sister-in-law of King Devānampiyatissa, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred women of the inner court, desires to go forth into the religious life.
It is said that she has come here; please grant her the going-forth. At that very moment, she [hurried] with great haste to the king...
Having approached him, he spoke thus: "Great King, my brother, the Elder Mahinda, has sent this message:

'It is said that the queen named Anulā, the sister of the king’s brother, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred women of the inner apartments, desires to go forth and awaits my arrival. Great King, I am going to the island of Tambapaṇṇi."
The king said: “Mother, my son Mahinda Thera and my grandson the novice Sumanas have gone to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, making me feel like one whose hands have been cut off.
The grief that arose in me because I could not see them is now pacified as I behold your face! Enough, mother; do not go. “It is a heavy burden for me, Great King.”
“Let my word be heard! Anulā, surrounded by a thousand kṣatriya women and intent on going forth, awaits me;
I shall go, O Great King. “In that case, dear mother, take the Mahābodhi and go,” [the king replied]. “Where is the Mahābodhi for the king? [She asked.
It is said that even before that, the king had already sent [messengers] to the island of Laṅkā for the purpose of obtaining relics when Sumana was yet to come.
Desiring to send forth the Great Bodhi, and seeing no means by which he might send the Great Bodhi—which is not subject to being struck by a weapon—he questioned his minister named Mahādeva.
The latter said, "Your Majesty, there are many wise bhikkhus.
Having heard this, the king prepared a meal for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; at the conclusion of the meal, he questioned the Saṅgha.
“Venerable sir, should the Great Bodhi tree go to the island of Laṅkā? The Saṅgha placed this burden upon the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.
The Elder said, “It must go, Great King, the Great Bodhi tree to the island of Laṅkā,” and he recounted to the Blessed One the five great resolutions.

What are these five? It is said that while the Blessed One was lying on his deathbed at the time of the Great Parinibbāna, for the purpose of establishing the Great Bodhi tree in the island of Laṅkā...

He made this resolution: “When King Aśoka goes for the purpose of taking the Great Bodhi tree, then let a southern branch of the Great Bodhi tree break off of its own accord and settle in a golden basin”—this was the first resolution.
And at the time of its settling there, he resolved: “Let the Great Bodhi enter the womb of a Himālayan cloud and settle there”—this was the second resolution.
“On the seventh day, descending from the womb of a cloud of snow and alighting upon a golden basin, may it emit six-colored rays through its leaves and fruits”—this was the third resolution.
“On the day of the enshrinement of the collar-bone relic at the Dakkhiṇakkhaka Cetiya in Thūpārāma, may it perform the Twin Miracle”—this was the fourth resolution.

“At the very moment the relics, measuring a *doṇa*, are established in the Mahācetiya on the island of Laṅkā, may they assume the form of a Buddha, ascend into the air, and perform the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*)”—thus he made this resolution; this is the fifth resolution.

Having heard these five great resolutions, the king, with a heart full of faith, had the road prepared from Pāṭaliputta as far as the Great Bodhi tree and caused much gold to be brought out for the golden bowl in his hand. At that very moment—
Then, having understood the king’s thought, Vissakamma, the son of the gods, assumed the form of a smith and stood before him.
When the king saw him, he said, “Dear son, take this gold and fashion a basin. “Do you know the dimensions, Your Majesty?
“You yourself, dear son, must determine them and make it. “Very well, Your Majesty, I shall do so,” he replied, and took the gold.
Having taken it, he fashioned a golden basin by his own supernatural power, rubbing it with his hand;
it was nine cubits in circumference, five cubits in height, three cubits in width, eight finger-breadths thick, and its rim was as large as an elephant’s trunk.
Then the king, departing from Pāṭaliputta with a great army seven yojanas long and three yojanas wide, set out.
Taking the Noble Saṅgha with him, he went into the presence of the Great Bodhi tree.

The army, with its banners and flags raised high, variegated with various jewels, adorned with many ornaments, strewn with diverse kinds of flowers, and resounding with the music of many instruments, surrounded the Great Bodhi.
The King, having taken with him a thousand leading Mahātheras who had received the consecration throughout the whole of Jambudīpa...
Having surrounded himself and the Great Bodhi Tree with a thousand kings, he stood at the foot of the Great Bodhi Tree and gazed up at it.
Leaving aside the trunk of the Great Bodhi Tree and a space measuring four cubits around its southern great branch,
the remainder vanished from sight.
Having witnessed that miracle, the king, filled with joy and gladness, said to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, “Venerable sirs, having seen this miracle, I am delighted;
I shall honor the Great Bodhi with the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa. Having spoken thus, he bestowed the ceremonial sprinkling (abhiseka).
Then, after honoring it with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, and circumambulating it three times, he [prostrated] at eight places.
Having paid homage, stood up, and remained with palms joined in reverence, desiring to take hold of the Bodhi tree by means of an act of truth (*saccavacana*),
he had a golden basin placed upon a throne made of all kinds of gems— which stood as high as the right branch of the Great Bodhi tree extending from the ground—
and having ascended the jeweled throne and taken a golden brush, [he wrote] with *manosilā*...
Having written a letter, he performed an act of truth, saying:

"If the Great Bodhi Tree is to be established on the island of Laṅkā, and if I am free from doubt regarding the Buddha’s teaching, may the Great Bodhi itself descend and be established within this golden vessel.
Simultaneously with that act of truth, at the spot where the branch of the Bodhi tree was severed by the emerald stone, it descended.
Having split open, it stood upon a golden basin filled with fragrant mud.
Its trunk was ten cubits in height, with four main branches and five great secondary branches adorned with fruits, while there were a thousand smaller branches.
Then the king cut another line above the original mark at a distance of three finger-breadths.
Then, at that very moment, they became buds and ten great roots emerged. Again, at intervals of three finger-breadths each, nine further lines were demarcated.
From those as well, ten buds each formed, and ninety roots emerged.
The first ten great roots had emerged to the extent of four finger-breadths; the others, too, were like a lattice-window.

They emerged, trailing behind one another. Having witnessed this miracle from his very position atop the jeweled throne, the king raised his joined palms and let out a great roar. Many thousands of monks shouted "Excellent!
The entire royal army broke into a tumultuous clamor, and hundreds of thousands of people waved their garments. Beginning with the earth-dwelling deities...
As far as the gods of the Brahma-world, they raised shouts of "Well done!
While the king stood with palms joined in reverence, his body continuously suffused with joy as he witnessed this miracle, the Great Bodhi tree was established in a golden vat by its hundred roots.
Ten of the great roots struck the bottom of the golden vat and remained there; the remaining ones...
The ninety minor roots, having gradually increased, descended and remained within the fragrant mud.
Thus, as soon as the Great Bodhi tree was established in the golden basin, the great earth shook; celestial drums resounded in the sky;
and there were the dances of the mountain deities, the shouts of "Well done! from the gods, the cries of "Hiṅ" from the *yakkhas*, and the hymns of praise from the *asuras*.
With the snapping of Brahmās, the thundering of clouds, the cries of quadrupeds, the songs of birds, and the individual improvisations of all musical instruments,
there arose from the surface of the earth up to the Brahma-world a single tumultuous roar,
a single resonance. From each fruit upon the five branches, six-colored rays issued forth, such that the entire Cakkavāḷa was covered as if with jeweled rafters.
As if performing a dance, they rose up as far as the Brahma-world.
From that very moment, however, for seven days the Great Bodhi remained within the womb of a great snow-cloud; no one could see the Great Bodhi.
The King descended from the jeweled throne and performed the Great Bodhi-pūjā for seven days. On the seventh day, from all directions...
The snow and the six-colored rays turned back and entered the Great Bodhi tree itself.

When the interior of the world-system was cleared of snow and clouds and became serene, the Great Bodhi appeared established as if in a golden basin, with its trunk, branches, and twigs fully developed, adorned with the five kinds of fruit.
Upon seeing the Great Bodhi and these miracles, the king was filled with joy and gladness.
Thinking, “I shall worship the young Great Bodhi tree with the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa,” he bestowed the consecration and remained at the site of the Great Bodhi for seven days.
On the evening of the full-moon day of the month of Kattika,
during the ceremony of the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), the Great Bodhi first settled within the golden basin.
Then, having passed the seven days of the "Womb of Snow" and the seven days of the consecration, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, the King entered Pāṭaliputta in a single day;
and on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kattika, he established the Great Bodhi tree at the foot of the Great Eastern Sāla tree.
On the seventeenth day from the day it was placed in the golden basin, [the Great Bodhi... of the Great Bodhi...

New sprouts appeared. Seeing them, the king was filled with faith; honoring the Great Bodhi tree once more with the sovereignty of his kingdom, he bestowed upon it the consecration of the entire Jambudīpa.
At that time, the novice Sumanas, having gone on the full-moon day of Kattika to receive the relics, witnessed the Kattika festival offerings for the Great Bodhi.
Thus, having brought [the Bodhi tree] from the Great Bodhimanda to Pāṭaliputta...
Referring to the Great Bodhi tree that had been set aside, he said, "In that case, mother, take the Great Bodhi and go.
She consented, saying, "Very well.
For the purpose of protecting the Great Bodhi, the king [appointed] eighteen families of deities, eight families of ministers, and eight families of brahmins.
Having given eight families of householders, eight families of cowherds, eight families of hyenas, and eight families of Kāliṅgas,
as well as eight golden jars and eight silver jars for the purpose of pouring water [for the consecration],
he placed the Great Bodhi tree upon a boat on the Gaṅgā with this retinue; then, departing from the city himself, he proceeded toward the Vijjhā forest.
Having passed through [the sea], he arrived at Tāmaliptī in seven days by traveling stage by stage.

Along the way, gods, nāgas, and humans performed a magnificent worship of the Great Bodhi tree. The king also, having placed the Great Bodhi on the seashore for seven days, bestowed the entire great sovereignty of Jambudīpa upon him.
This was his third gift of sovereignty over Jambudīpa.

Having thus honored [the Bodhi tree] with a great royal ceremony, on the first day of the month of Māgasira, King Aśoka raised up the Great Bodhi tree, descended into water reaching up to his neck, and established it upon a ship.
Having also caused the Elder Saṅghamittā and her retinue to board the ship, he spoke thus to the minister Ariṭṭha: "Dear son, I shall [bring] the Great Bodhi three times..."
"Having honored [the Bodhi tree] with sovereignty over the entire Jambudīpa, I descended into water reaching up to my neck and sent it to my friend, saying:

'May he likewise honor the Great Bodhi tree. Having thus given this message to his friend, and thinking, "The Great Bodhi tree is indeed departing, emitting a web of rays from the essence of the One of Ten Powers," he paid homage and raised his hands in añjali.
He stood there shedding tears. And that ship, having embarked upon the Great Enlightenment, sank into the depths of the great ocean as the Great King looked on.
In the great ocean, too, for a league all around, the waves were stilled; lotuses of five colors blossomed;
celestial musical instruments resounded in the sky; and from the sky, [sounds] issued forth from those dwelling in water-born, land-born, and tree-born [creatures].
An exceedingly magnificent worship was conducted by the deities.
The Elder Nun Saṅghamittā, moreover, in the form of a Supaṇṇa, terrified the families of Nāgas in the great ocean. Those Nāgas, being struck with fear, came forth;

having witnessed that splendor and entreated the Elder Nun, they escorted the Great Bodhi tree to the Nāga realm, where they worshipped it for seven days with the sovereignty of the Nāgas, and then...
They did not land the ship. On that very day, the ship reached Jambukola port.
King Asoka, distressed by the pain of separation from the Great Bodhi tree, wept and wailed; having gazed at it as long as it remained within the range of his vision, he turned back.
King Devānampiyatissa, however, following the words of the novice Sumanas, [began] from the first day of the month of Māgasira...
Starting from the northern gate and continuing as far as the port of Jambukola, he had the road cleared and decorated.

On the day of the departure from the city, while standing right at the site of the Ocean Hall near the northern gate, he saw the Great Bodhi tree approaching across the great ocean through the power of the Elder; his heart was filled with joy at that splendor.
Having departed, scattering five-colored flowers along the entire path and placing flower-offerings at intervals, he reached the port of Jambukola in a single day;
surrounded by all kinds of musical instruments and honoring him with flowers, incense, perfumes, and ointments, he entered water up to his neck and cried out:
"The Ten-Powered One, who emits a network of rays from his own essence, has indeed arrived!"
With a mind full of faith, he lifted the Great Bodhi tree, placed it upon his head as the highest limb,
and surrounded by sixteen clans of noble birth who had come to attend him, he disembarked from the ocean.
Having set the Great Bodhi tree upon the shore, he honored it for three days with the entirety of the sovereignty over the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
He administered the kingdom for sixteen noble families of high birth. Then, on the fourth day, taking the Mahābodhi tree and performing magnificent worship, he arrived in Anurādhapura by stages.

Having also rendered great honor in Anurādhapura, on the fourteenth day, when the shadow had increased [in length], he brought the Mahābodhi tree through the northern gate and into the center of the city.
Carrying it out, he exited through the southern gate and went to a place five hundred bow-lengths from the southern gate,

where our Perfectly Enlightened Buddha sat having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), as well as where the three previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas sat having entered that same attainment;
and where there was the Mahāsirisabodhi tree of the Blessed One Kakusandha, and [the *bodhi* tree] of Koṇāgamana...
The Bodhi tree of the Blessed One was an Udumbara, while that of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa was a Nigrodha;

he established the Great Bodhi at the gateway of the royal precincts, in a place where the ground had already been prepared following the words of the novice Sumanas, which served as the very ornament of the Mahāmeghavana garden.
How was it? It is said that those sixteen noble families of perfect birth, having arrived surrounding the Bodhi tree, assumed the guise of kings.
The King assumed the guise of a gatekeeper. The sixteen families took up the Great Bodhi tree and set it down.
Immediately upon being released from their hands, the Great Bodhi rose eighty cubits into the air.
He emitted six-colored rays of light. These rays spread across the entire island and remained fixed, reaching as far as the Brahma-world above.

Having beheld this Great Bodhi miracle, ten thousand men, filled with faith, established themselves in gradual insight (anupubbavipassanā), attained Arahatship, and went forth into homelessness. Until the setting of the sun, the Great Bodhi remained suspended in the sky.
He stood there. But when the sun had set, he descended to the earth under the constellation Rohiṇī.
Simultaneously with his descent upon the Bodhi tree, the great earth trembled as far as its ocean boundaries. Having descended, the Great Bodhi remained settled for seven days within a womb of frost;
it became invisible to the world. On the seventh day, the sky was free of clouds.
There was. Six-colored rays, blazing and flashing, issued forth. The trunk, branches, leaves, and five fruits of the Great Bodhi tree became visible.
The Elder Mahinda, the Elder Saṅghamittā, and the King with his retinue went to the very site of the Great Bodhi tree. And almost all the inhabitants of the island [did likewise].
They gathered together. Even as they were watching, a single fruit ripened from the northern branch and detached itself from the branch.
The Elder extended his hand; the fruit settled into the Elder’s hand. The Elder gave it to the King, saying, “Plant this, Great King.
The King took it, scattered sweet soil in a golden basin, filled it with fragrant mud, and...
Having planted it, he established it in a place near the Mahābodhi tree. While everyone was looking on, eight young Bodhi trees, each measuring four cubits in height, sprang up.
Seeing that marvel, the King honored the eight young Bodhi trees with white parasols and performed the consecration ceremony.
Then, one of those Bodhi trees [was the same as] the one with which the Mahābodhi tree had come at the time of its arrival.
They planted one at the site where he first set foot, in the town of Jambukola; one at the gate of the village of the Brahmin Tavakka;
one in the Thūpārāma; one in the Issaranimmāna Vihāra; one at the site of the First Cetiya; one on Cetiyapabbata;
one in Kājaragāma in the Rohaṇa province; and one in Candanagāma, also in the Rohaṇa province. As for the others...
They established thirty-two young Bodhi trees, grown from seeds of the four [original] fruits, in monasteries extending for a league.

Thus, through the succession of sons and grandsons, the Great Bodhi tree—which serves as the Dhamma-banner of the One Possessed of Ten Powers—was established for the welfare and happiness of the inhabitants of the entire island.
Then Queen Anulā, together with five hundred maidens and five hundred women of the inner court, [honored it].
Having gone forth in the presence of the Elder Nun Saṅghamittā together with a thousand women, she established herself in Arahantship before long along with her retinue.
Ariṭṭha, the king’s nephew, also went forth in the presence of the Elder together with five hundred men, and before long he too established himself in Arahantship along with his retinue.
Then one day, after the King had paid homage to the Mahābodhi, he went with the Elder to the Thūpārāma.
When he arrived at the site of the Lohapāsāda, men brought flowers to him.
The King gave the flowers to the Elder, and the Elder made an offering of them at the site of the Lohapāsāda. As soon as the flowers had fallen upon the ground, a great earthquake occurred.
It happened thus. The king asked, "Venerable sir, why has the earth trembled? "In this place, Great King, there will be a Uposatha hall for the Saṅgha in the future; this is its omen.
As the king was proceeding again with the Elder, he arrived at the site of the mango courtyard. There, [he saw] that which was endowed with color and fragrance...
A single mango fruit of exceedingly sweet flavor was brought forth. The king gave it to the Elder for his consumption.
The Elder, having eaten it right there, said, "Plant this very here. The king took the mango seed, planted it in that same spot, and poured water upon it.
Simultaneously with the planting of the mango seed, the earth shook. The king asked, "Why?"
“Venerable sir, why did the earth tremble? he asked. “Great King, in this very place there will be a meeting hall for the Saṅgha in the future called ‘Ambaṅgaṇa’; this was its omen.
The king scattered eight handfuls of flowers there, paid homage, and as he proceeded further with the Elder, he said:
He arrived at the site of the Great Cetiya. There, men brought him *campaka* flowers. The king gave them to the Elder.
Having worshipped the Great Cetiya with those flowers, the Elder paid homage to it.
At that very moment, the great earth quaked. The king asked, "Venerable sir, why did the earth quake? [The Elder replied: "In this place, Great King..."
“In the future, there will be an incomparable Great Stupa for the Buddha, the Blessed One; this is its omen.
“I myself shall build it, Bhante,” [the king replied]. “Enough, Great King; you have other many tasks to attend to.
However, your grandson named Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya shall cause it to be built. Then the king said, “If, Bhante, it is not for me...”
Thinking, "My grandson will build it; it is as good as built by me," he had a stone pillar twelve cubits long brought, had the inscription written upon it:

"Let the king Devānampiyatissa’s grandson, named Abhaya Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, build a stupa in this place," and having set it up and paid homage, he asked the Elder: "Venerable sir, has the Tambapaṇṇi island been established?"
“Is the Dispensation established? “It is established, Great King; however, its roots have not yet taken hold.
“But when, venerable sir, will the roots be said to have taken hold?
“When, Great King, a child born on the island of Tambapaṇṇi to parents from Tambapaṇṇi goes forth on the island of Tambapaṇṇi and [attains realization] right here on the island of Tambapaṇṇi...”
“Having mastered the Vinaya, he will teach it on the island of Tambapaṇṇi; then the roots of the Dispensation will truly have been established.
“But, Bhante, is there such a monk? “There is, Great King; the monk Mahā-Ariṭṭha is capable of this task.
“What must I do here, Bhante? “Great King, you must build a pavilion.”
“It is fitting,” he said. “Very well, venerable sir,” replied the king.

At the time of the Great Council, the king used his royal power to have a pavilion constructed at the site of the minister Meghavaṇṇābhaya’s dwelling, modeled after the kind of pavilion built by King Ajātasattu.
Having employed all the musicians in their respective arts, the king, surrounded by many thousands of men, thought, “I shall witness the roots of the Dispensation being established.”
He arrived at the Thūpārāma.
At that time, sixty-eight thousand bhikkhus had assembled in the Thūpārāma.
A seat for the Elder Mahāmahinda was prepared facing south, and the Dharma-seat for the Elder Mahāariṭṭha was facing north.
It was prepared. Then the Elder Mahā-Ariṭṭha, requested by the Elder Mahinda, sat upon the Dhamma-seat according to his own appropriate order of seniority.
The sixty-eight great elders, headed by the Elder Mahinda, sat surrounding the Dhamma-seat.
Also, the King’s younger brother, the Elder named Mattābhaya, sat down as the leader of the assembly.
Thinking, “I shall learn the Vinaya,” he sat down together with five hundred bhikkhus, surrounding the very Dhamma-seat of the Elder Mahā-Ariṭṭha.
The remaining bhikkhus and the assembly, including the king, each sat down on their own respective seats.
Then, at that time, the Venerable Elder Mahā-Ariṭṭha [recited]: “The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree.”
He spoke on the origin of discipline (*vinayanidāna*). When the Venerable Elder Ariṭṭha had spoken this account of the origin of discipline, the sky let out a great roar;
untimely flashes of lightning burst forth; the deities uttered cries of "Well done!"; and the great earth, bounded by the waters, trembled.
While these many miracles were thus occurring, the Venerable Elder Ariṭṭha—
Surrounded by sixty-eight great elders who were solitary leaders with taints destroyed, headed by Mahāmahinda, and by another eighty-six thousand bhikkhus,
on the day of the first Kattika Pavāraṇā, in the midst of the Thūpārāma monastery,
he [delivered] the instruction of the Blessed One which illuminates the qualities of the Teacher’s compassion and which restrains the fluctuations of bodily and verbal actions.

He proclaimed the Vinaya Piṭaka. Having proclaimed it, while remaining for the duration of his lifespan, he taught it to many and established it in the hearts of many, and then attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
And those present at that assembly, headed by Mahāmahinda—the sixty-eight great Theras who had taken up the burden—gathered together:
All those who were leaders of separate groups were disciples of the King of Dhamma.
Having destroyed the taints, attained mastery, possessing the threefold knowledge, and being skilled in supernormal powers,
they instructed the king after having realized the supreme goal through direct higher knowledge.
“Having shown forth light and illuminated this earth,
those great seers, having blazed like masses of fire,
passed into Nibbāna. After their Parinibbāna, there were other disciples of those elders as well, such as Tissadatta, Kālasumana, Dīghasumana, and others.

And the disciples of the Elder Mahā-Ariṭṭha, and the disciples of those disciples—in this manner, the lineage of teachers described above has transmitted this Vinaya Piṭaka down to the present day. Therefore it was said:
"From the Third Council onwards, this [Vinaya] was brought to this island by Mahinda and others; having learned it from Mahinda..."

"For some time it was brought down by the Elder Ariṭṭha and others; from then until the present day, it has been brought down by a succession of teachers who have formed a lineage of pupils among themselves.
Wherein is it established? It is established in those for whom it exists without deficiency, both in its textual wording and in its meaning, like oil poured into a jeweled vessel.

It does not leak even slightly; thus it should be understood that [the teaching] is established among persons who possess such extraordinary mindfulness, understanding, and fortitude, who are modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training.
Therefore, a monk who desires to train, having observed the benefits of the mastery of the Vinaya for the sake of establishing the discipline, should master the Vinaya.

In this regard, the benefit of mastery in the Vinaya is as follows: A person skilled in the mastery of the Vinaya serves as a mother and father to those sons of good family who have gained faith in the Dispensation;
for their going forth, their full ordination, their practice of the rules and secondary observances, and their skill in conduct and resort depend upon him.
Furthermore, by means of his mastery of the Vinaya, his own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded.
He is well-guarded; he is a refuge for monks who are overcome by remorse; he speaks with confidence in the midst of the Saṅgha;
he effectively refutes adversaries in accordance with the Dhamma;
and he is practicing for the endurance of the true Dhamma. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these five benefits for a person who is an expert in the Vinaya: his own..."
“The aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected... [and so on] ...he is practicing for the endurance of the true Dhamma.

Furthermore, those wholesome qualities rooted in restraint which were spoken of by the Blessed One—the person who is a bearer of the Vinaya is the heir to them, because those qualities are rooted in the Vinaya.
For this was said by the Blessed One: “The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint...”
Restraint is for the purpose of non-regret; non-regret is for the purpose of gladness; gladness is for the purpose of rapture;

rapture is for the purpose of tranquility; tranquility is for the purpose of happiness; happiness is for the purpose of concentration; concentration is for the purpose of knowing and seeing things as they really are;
knowing and seeing things as they really are is for the purpose of disenchantment; disenchantment is for the purpose of dispassion; dispassion is for the purpose of liberation.
"Liberation is for the sake of the knowledge and vision of liberation; the knowledge and vision of liberation is for the sake of final Nibbāna through non-clinging.

This is the purpose of discourse, this is the purpose of consultation, this is the purpose of the underlying cause, this is the purpose of lending an ear—that is to say, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging.
Therefore, application to the mastery of the Vinaya should be undertaken.
And at this point, regarding the matrix (mātikā) established for the purpose of explaining the Vinaya, it was said:
"Having stated by whom, when, and why it was spoken; by whom it was preserved and brought [here];
where it was established—having thus stated these and then the method..."
Thus the meaning of this verse has been clarified, and the commentary on the external introduction to the Vinaya has been explained according to its intended purpose.
The account of the Third Council is finished.
The account of the external introduction is finished.
The Commentary on the Verañjā Chapter 1. Now,
[I shall explain] the meaning of the passage beginning with "By that" in its various aspects:
"Showing [the way], I shall compose a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya.
Because it was stated thus, I shall provide a commentary on the meaning of the phrases beginning with "At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
To explain: *tena* is a term used as an indefinite demonstrative. Although its specific form is not explicitly stated, it is established by implication through the subsequent context.
The detailed explanation (*paṭiniddesa*) should be made by means of this word "yenā" (by which).
For later on, the reflection of the Venerable Sāriputta, which served as the cause for requesting the formulation of the Vinaya rules, was fulfilled.
Therefore, the connection here should be understood as follows: "At the time when that reflection arose, at that same time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā."

For this is the underlying logic (*yutti*) throughout the entire Vinaya: namely, wherever the word "by that" (*tena*) is used, there it must be supplemented by the expression "by which" (*yena*), whose meaning is established either previously or subsequently.
Here is a mere illustration of this principle: "Therefore, monks, I shall lay down a training rule for the monks."
"By whom Sudinna committed sexual intercourse; because he committed it, therefore I shall lay down the rule"—this is what was said.
Thus, first of all, the demonstrative pronoun *yena* (by whom), which is established by its prior meaning, is appropriately used as a correlative reference.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha; at that time, Dhaniya the potter’s son...
"He took the king's wood without it being given"—thus, by this word *yena*, which is established in its sense later on, the reference is appropriate;
such is the meaning of the expression *tena*. Now, regarding the word *samayena*:
first, the term *samaya* [is used] in the senses of collection, moment, time, assembly, cause, and view.
It is seen in the senses of acquisition, abandoning, and penetration.
For instance, in such passages as, "Perhaps tomorrow we might go, taking into account the time and the occasion," the meaning is "conjunction.
But in such passages as, "Monks, there is indeed only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life," [the meaning is "opportunity"].
“Moment”: in such passages as “the time of heat,” “the time of feverish distress,” and so forth, it means time. “In the great assembly in the forest”: in such passages, it means a multitude.
“Indeed, Bhaddāli, this was not penetrated by you: ‘The Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī;
the Blessed One will know me—the monk named Bhaddāli who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation’.”
In such passages as, "Bhaddāli, this opportunity of yours was indeed not penetrated," it refers to the cause (*hetu*). In such passages as, "Now at that time,
the wanderer Uggahamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was staying at Mallikā’s Park, in the single-hall Tindukācīra grove, which was a place for debating doctrines," it refers to a view (*diṭṭhi*).
“In the benefit pertaining to the present life, and the benefit pertaining to the future life—the wise person, through the realization of these benefits, is called ‘a sage’.
In such passages as these, it is acquisition. “Through the realization of conceit rightly, he made an end of suffering. In such passages as these, it is abandoning.

In such passages as, “The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, and the meaning of realization,” the meaning is penetration.

But here, its meaning is time. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as: “at that very time when the venerable Sāriputta’s reflection, which became the cause for his request for the formulation of the Vinaya, arose.”

Here it may be asked: "Now, why is it that, instead of making the description here by means of the instrumental case as 'at one time' (ekaṃ samayaṃ) in the Suttanta, or by means of the locative case as 'at whatever time [there is] pertaining to the sense-sphere' (yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ) in the Abhidhamma, the description is made here by means of the instrumental case as 'by that time' (tena samayena)?
To this, the answer is: because the meaning is possible in that way there, but in another way here.
How so? First, in the Suttanta, the sense of "absolute connection" (*accantasamyoga*) is possible.

For at whatever time the Blessed One taught such discourses as the *Brahmajāla*, at that very time he dwelt exclusively in the abiding of compassion; therefore, the accusative case is employed there for the purpose of indicating that meaning.
And in the Abhidhamma, the sense of "location" (*adhikaraṇa*) and the sense of "characterizing a state by means of another state" (*bhāvena-bhāvalakkhaṇa*) [are applicable].
And [the meaning] is possible. For "occasion" (*samaya*) has the sense of time and the sense of a collection;
the existence of those phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) mentioned therein is characterized by the state of that "occasion," which is reckoned as the coincidence of moments and the causal complex.
Therefore, the locative case was employed there for the purpose of indicating that meaning. But here, the sense of cause and the sense of instrument are possible.
For that time when the training rules were laid down was difficult to discern even for Sāriputta and others;

it was with that time as the cause and as the instrument that the Blessed One, laying down the training rules and taking into account the reason for laying down those training rules, dwelt here and there.
Therefore, for the purpose of illustrating that meaning, this is expressed here by means of the instrumental case.
It should be understood as "katā" (done).
And there is this [verse] here: "Depending on the respective meaning, it is stated elsewhere by means of the instrumental case or the locative case;
but here it is stated by means of the instrumental alone."
The Ancients, however, comment: “Whether it be ‘at one time,’ ‘at which time,’ or ‘at that time,’ this is merely a difference in expression;

in all cases, the meaning is simply the locative case. Therefore, according to their view, even when ‘at that time’ (tena samayena) is stated, the meaning should be understood as ‘at that moment’ (tasmiṃ samaye).
We shall explain the meaning of the words "Buddho bhagavā" hereafter. Regarding the phrase "viharati Verañjāyaṃ":
*Verañjā* is a designation for a certain city; *Verañjāyaṃ* is the locative case used in the sense of proximity (*samīpatthe*).

*Viharati* is a general indication that he is possessed of one or another of the dwellings (*vihāra*), whether they be those consisting of postures (*iriyāpatha*), divine (*dibba*), sublime (*brahma*), or noble (*ariya*).
Furthermore, among the postures distinguished as standing, walking, sitting, and lying down, this indicates association with one particular posture;
thus it should be understood that the Blessed One dwells even when standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.
For he, having interrupted the fatigue of one posture with another, maintains his person from falling.
It carries one along and causes one to proceed; therefore, it is called "dwells" (*viharati*).
Regarding the phrase "at the foot of the Naḷerupucimanda": here, *naḷeru* is the name of a *yakkha*, *pucimanda* is a *nimba* tree, and *mūla* means the vicinity.
For this word *mūla* is used in such passages as: "He should pull up the roots, even down to those as small as a blade of *usīra* grass."
It is seen in the sense of "at the very root" in such passages as "Greed is a root of unwholesomeness. It is used in the sense of "a non-common cause" in such passages as [the definition of roots].
It is used in the sense of "in the vicinity" in such passages as "As long as the shadow extends at midday, and leaves fall in a windless place, to that extent is the vicinity of the tree's root.
However, here it is intended in the sense of "in the vicinity"; therefore, it means "in the vicinity of the *pucimanda* tree possessed by the *naḷeru-yakkha*."

The meaning here should be understood in this way: it is said that this delightful and beautiful *pucimanda* tree, exercising a kind of sovereignty over many other trees, stood not far from that city in a place convenient for coming and going.
Then the Blessed One, having gone to Verañjā and dwelling in a suitable location, stayed near the lower part of that tree.
He dwelt there. Therefore it was said: “He was dwelling at Verañjā, at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree.
Herein, one might object: if the Blessed One was dwelling in Verañjā, it should not be said that he was “at the foot of the Naleru Pucimanda tree”;
and if he was dwelling there [at the tree], it should not be said that he was “in Verañjā,” for it is not possible for him to be in both places simultaneously.
"Is it that they dwell there simultaneously, neither before nor after? This, however, should not be viewed in that way.

Have we not said, "The locative case is used in the sense of proximity"? Therefore, just as herds of cattle grazing near the Ganges or the Yamunā are said to be "grazing on the Ganges" or "grazing on the Yamunā," so too here, in the vicinity of Verañjā...
While dwelling there at the foot of the Naḷeru pucimanda tree, he is said to be "dwelling at Verañjā,

at the foot of the Naḷeru pucimanda tree. The mention of Verañjā is for the purpose of indicating the village of his alms-round, while the mention of the foot of the Naḷeru pucimanda tree is for the purpose of indicating a place of residence suitable for one who has gone forth.
In this context, by the mention of Verañjā, the Venerable Elder Upāli shows the Blessed One’s favoring of householders;

by the mention of the foot of the Naḷeru Pucimanda tree, he shows his favoring of those who have gone forth. Likewise, by the former, through the acceptance of the four requisites, there is the avoidance of devotion to self-mortification;
by the latter, through the abandoning of sensual objects, there is the demonstration of the means for avoiding devotion to sensual pleasure.
By the former [verse], there is application to the teaching of the Dhamma; by the latter, a resolve for seclusion. By the former, there is the approach through compassion;
by the latter, the withdrawal through wisdom. By the former, there is the resolve to accomplish the welfare and happiness of beings;
by the latter, being untainted while performing the welfare and happiness of others. By the former, it is the cause for not abandoning righteous happiness.

The former [part] concerns dwelling in comfort, while the latter concerns the pursuit of superhuman states; the former concerns the great benefit to human beings, while the latter concerns that for deities;
the former concerns being born in the world and growing up in the world, while the latter concerns being unsullied by the world;
and the former refers to: "Monks, one person, appearing in the world, appears for the welfare of many."
"for the welfare of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
From this statement, [the first verse] refers to the fulfillment of the purpose for which the Blessed One appeared;
the latter [verse] refers to his dwelling in a manner appropriate to the place where he appeared. For the Blessed One [dwelt] first in the Lumbinī grove, and secondly...

Regarding the phrase "at the seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍe*): since he arose in the forest itself for the sake of both mundane and supramundane attainments, it shows that his dwelling was indeed in the forest;
the construction of the meaning here should be understood according to this method.

Regarding the phrase "together with a great community of monks" (*mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ*): here, "great" (*mahatā*) means great in terms of qualities (*guṇamahatta*), and also great in terms of number (*saṅkhyāmahatta*).

For that community of monks was great both in terms of its qualities, because even the last among them was a stream-enterer (sotāpanna), and it was great by number, consisting of five hundred members.
"By the community of monks" means by the *bhikkhusaṅgha*; the meaning is: by that group of ascetics designated as a "community" (*saṅgha*) due to their commonality of view and virtue.
"Together with" (*saddhim*) means on one side. "With about five hundred monks" means those of whom there are five as their measure.

"Fivefold" (*pañcamattāni*): "fold" (*matta*) refers to a measure (*pamāṇa*). Therefore, just as when it is said, "one who knows the measure in food" (*bhojane mattaññū*), the meaning is that one knows the measure, that is, one knows the limit;
so too here, the meaning should be understood as "five measures" or "five limits" for those hundred bhikkhus.
"Hundreds of bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusatāni*): [is a compound of] bhikkhus and hundreds. By them...

“With about five hundred bhikkhus. By this, the greatness of number of that great community of bhikkhus mentioned in the phrase “together with a great community of bhikkhus” is demonstrated. Furthermore, later on it says:
“For, Sāriputta, the community of bhikkhus is free from maggots, free from defects, rid of black elements, pure, and established in the essence.”
By the statement, “Sāriputta, among these five hundred bhikkhus, even the least one is a stream-enterer,” the greatness of their virtue will be made manifest.
“The brahmin of Verañjā heard” means he heard— that is, he perceived— by following the sound of the speech that had reached the door of his hearing.
He understood. *Kho* is a particle used merely for the purpose of completing the metrical line (*padapūraṇa*) or for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).

Therein, in the sense of emphasis, the meaning should be understood as: "He indeed heard; there was no obstacle whatsoever to his hearing. In the sense of completing the line, however, it serves merely to provide smoothness of expression (*byañjana-siliṭṭhatā*).
He was born in Verañjā, his existence was in Verañjā, or Verañjā was his residence; thus he is "Verañja. [This is] according to the name given by his mother and father.
Furthermore, this [process] is called "arising" (*udaya*). One who "breathes the *brahman*" (*aṇati*) is a *brāhmaṇa*; the meaning is that he recites the mantras.
For this indeed is the etymological definition of those who are *brāhmaṇas* by birth. However, the Noble Ones (*ariya*) are called "*brāhmaṇas*" because they have banished evil (*bāhita-pāpa*).
Now, in order to clarify the matter that the Brahmin of Verañjā heard, he said: "The ascetic Gotama, sir," and so forth.
In this context, he should be understood as a *samaṇa* because of having stilled evil.
For it has been said: "One who has banished evil is a *brāhmaṇa*; one who has stilled evil is called a *samaṇa*. And the Blessed One has stilled evil by means of the unsurpassed Noble Path;

therefore, this name—namely, "*samaṇa*"—is acquired by him through the attainment of qualities according to reality. The particle *khalu* is used in the sense of tradition. *Bho* is a form of address arising from birth for those belonging to the *brāhmaṇa* caste.
It is merely a form of address. For it has been said:
“He is one who addresses others as ‘bho,’ if he is one who possesses something. By saying “Gotama,” he describes the Blessed One by way of his clan;
therefore, in the phrase “the ascetic Gotama, sir,” the meaning should be understood as: “The ascetic, sir, belongs to the Gotama clan.”
"Sakyaputta" (Son of the Sakyans) is an indication of the Blessed One’s high birth. "One gone forth from the Sakyan clan" is an indication of his state of having gone forth out of faith;
it means that he did not abandon that family because of any loss or misfortune, but rather went forth out of faith while that family was still intact.
The rest has already been explained. "Taṃ kho pana" (And as for that... is used in the accusative case in the sense of describing a particular state of being.
"Of that venerable Gotama"—this is the meaning. "Kalyāṇa" means endowed with excellent qualities; "supreme" is what is meant.
"Kittisaddo" (fame-sound) means fame itself, or the sound of praise.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Itipi so Bhagavā," this is the construction: "That Blessed One is thus an Arahant, thus a Perfectly Enlightened One... [and so on]... thus a Blessed One" means "for this and this reason."

Now, for the sake of the experts in the Vinaya gaining skill in the method of the Suttantas, and for the purpose of gladdening the minds of these [monks] at the commencement of the Vinaya commentary by means of a Dhamma talk connected with the Buddha’s qualities, I shall provide a detailed explanation of these words.
Therefore, regarding what was said—“That Blessed One is indeed ‘Arahant’”—and so forth: therein, because of being remote (*ārakatta*), because of [having overcome] enemies (*arīnaṃ*)...

The Blessed One should be understood as "Arahant" for these reasons: because he has slain the enemies (arīnaṃ hatattā), because he is worthy of requisites and so forth (paccayādīnaṃ arahattā), and because there is an absence of secrecy (rahābhāva) regarding his evil deeds.
Indeed, he is far removed from all defilements, standing at a very great distance because the defilements along with their latent tendencies have been destroyed by the Path;
thus, because of being "far away" (ārakā), he is an Arahant. Furthermore, those enemies that are the defilements have been [destroyed] by him through the Path...

He is an *arahaṃ* because he has slain his enemies; and because he has slain [the spokes of] that wheel of saṃsāra—which has ignorance, existence, and craving for its hub, meritorious and other formative forces (*saṅkhāra*) for its spokes, old age and death for its rim, and which has been yoked to the chariot of the three realms of existence by piercing it with the axle consisting of the origin of the taints (*āsava*), and which has been revolving since beginningless time—he is an *arahaṃ*.
For at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), having established himself upon the earth of virtue with the feet of energy, and using the hand of faith...
Having taken up the wisdom-axe that brings about the destruction of karma, he has "slain all the spokes"; thus, because the spokes have been slain, he is an *arahaṃ*.
Alternatively, the "wheel of saṃsāra" refers to the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra-vatta*). Of this wheel, ignorance is the hub because it is the root;
aging-and-death is the rim because it is the end; and the remaining ten factors are the spokes, because they are rooted in ignorance and terminate in aging-and-death.

And therein, ignorance regarding suffering and the other truths is *avijjā*. Furthermore, ignorance in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is a condition for the volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) in sense-sphere existence;

ignorance in fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) is a condition for the volitional formations in fine-material existence; and ignorance in immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*) is a condition for the volitional formations in immaterial existence.
The volitional formations in sense-sphere existence are conditions for rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*) in sense-sphere existence.

This is the method for the others as well. In the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) is a condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in the sense-sphere existence;
likewise in the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*). In the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*), it is a condition for name alone.

In the sense-sphere existence, name-and-form is a condition for the sixfold base (*saḷāyatana*) in the sense-sphere existence. In the fine-material existence, name-and-form is a condition for three bases in the fine-material existence.
In the formless existence, name is a condition for one base in the formless existence.

In the sense-sphere existence, the six bases are a condition for the sixfold contact in the sense-sphere existence. In the fine-material existence, three bases are a condition for three types of contact in the fine-material existence;
in the formless existence, one base is a condition for one type of contact in the formless existence.

In the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), the six types of contact are conditions for the six types of feeling in that same sense-sphere existence. In the fine-material sphere existence (*rūpabhava*), three [types of contact] are conditions for three [types of feeling] right there;
in the immaterial sphere existence (*arūpabhava*), one [type of contact] is a condition for one type of feeling right there.

In the sense-sphere existence, the six types of feeling are conditions for the six groups of craving (*taṇhākāya*) in that same sense-sphere existence. In the fine-material sphere existence, three [types of feeling] are conditions for three [groups of craving] right there; in the immaterial sphere existence...

A single feeling is a condition for a single mass of craving in the formless existence (*arūpabhava*). In each respective case, that particular craving is a condition for its corresponding clinging (*upādāna*);
and from clinging onwards, there are the conditions for becoming (*bhava*) and so forth. How so?
Here, someone thinking, "I shall enjoy sensual pleasures," engages in misconduct with the body, conditioned by clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
One engages in misconduct by way of speech and mind; through the fulfillment of that misconduct, one is reborn in the woeful states.
Therein, the karma that serves as the cause for that rebirth is *kammabhava*; the aggregates produced by that karma are *upapattibhava*;
the arising of the aggregates is *jāti* (birth); their maturation is *jarā* (aging); and their dissolution is *maraṇa* (death).

Another person practices good conduct in the same way, thinking, "I shall experience the attainment of heaven"; through the fulfillment of that good conduct, he is reborn in heaven. Therein, the karma that serves as the cause for his rebirth is *kammabhava*; such is the method.

Yet another, thinking, "I shall experience the attainment of the Brahma-world," develops loving-kindness (*mettā*), compassion (*karuṇā*), appreciative joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*) precisely with the condition of clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmupādāna*); through the fulfillment of that development, he is reborn in the Brahma-world. Therein, his...
Kamma that serves as the cause for rebirth is "kamma-bhava"; this is the same principle.
Another person, thinking, "I shall experience the attainment of the formless realm," likewise develops the meditative attainments (samāpatti) of the base of infinite space and so forth;
through the perfection of that development, he is reborn there. The kamma that serves as the cause for his rebirth therein is [kamma-bhava].
Kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) is [volitional] action; the aggregates produced by that action are rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*);

the arising of the aggregates is birth (*jāti*); their maturation is aging (*jarā*); and their dissolution is death (*maraṇa*). This same method applies to the other analyses rooted in clinging (*upādāna*).
Thus, in the discernment of conditions: "This ignorance is the cause; the formations are arisen from a cause; both of these are arisen from a cause."
"Wisdom regarding the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is as follows: in the past time and in the future time, ignorance is the cause and formations are cause-born;
both of these are cause-born. Wisdom in the grasping of conditions is 'knowledge of the stability of phenomena'.

In this manner, all the terms should be expanded. Therein, ignorance and formations constitute one summary; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling [constitute another].
One [link] consists of craving, clinging, and becoming; one is birth; and one is aging-and-death. Herein, the first summary refers to the past period;
the two middle ones refer to the present; and birth, aging, and death refer to the future.

Furthermore, by the inclusion of ignorance and formations, craving, clinging, and becoming are already included. Thus, these five factors constitute the round of kamma in the past; while consciousness and the others [constitute the result in the present].

Five factors constitute the present round of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*). Since ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are already included by way of grasping (*upādāna*), craving (*taṇhā*), and becoming (*bhava*), these five factors constitute the present round of kamma (*kammavaṭṭa*).

Because consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and the other factors are indicated under the heading of birth, aging, and death (*jātijarāmaraṇa*), these five factors constitute the future round of result. These, in terms of their modes, are twentyfold.
Herein, there is one junction between formations and consciousness, one between feeling and craving, and one between existence and birth.
Thus the Blessed One knows, sees, understands, and penetrates dependent origination in its entirety—with its four summaries, three periods of time, twenty modes, and three junctions.
That is "knowledge" in the sense of knowing; it is "understanding" in the sense of understanding.
Wisdom. Therefore it is said: “Wisdom in the discernment of conditions is knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
Having known those phenomena as they really are through this knowledge of the stability of phenomena, the Blessed One became disenchanted with them, detached from them, and liberated from them;
he struck, shattered, and demolished the spokes of this wheel of saṃsāra described above. Thus, because his spokes have been destroyed, he is an Arahant.
Because he is the foremost among those worthy of offerings, he is entitled to the requisites such as robes and to special forms of worship;
for this very reason, whenever a Tathāgata has appeared, whatever gods and humans possess great influence do not offer their worship elsewhere.
Thus, for example, Brahmā Sahampati honored the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland as large as Mount Sineru, and other gods and humans likewise did so according to their respective power.

[There were] King Bimbisāra, King Kosala, and others. Even after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, the Great King Aśoka, having bestowed ninety-six koṭis of wealth for his sake, established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
What need is there to mention the various other offerings made by others? Thus, he is "Arahant" because he is worthy of such requisites and so forth. Just as...
Furthermore, there are some fools in the world who, imagining themselves to be wise, commit evil deeds in secret out of fear of ill-repute; he never does such a thing even when alone.
Thus, because he is devoid of secrecy in the commission of evil, he is an *Arahaṃ*.
And on this point it is said: “Because he has driven away and destroyed the enemies that are the defilements, that Sage is [an *Arahaṃ*].”
“Because he has destroyed the wheel of saṃsāra, because he is worthy of receiving requisites and so forth, and because he commits no secret evils, he is therefore called ‘Arahant.
Furthermore, he is the ‘Sammāsambuddha’ because he has awakened to all phenomena correctly and by himself. For in this way, he [has realized] all phenomena...”

The Buddha is awakened to correctly and personally; he is awakened to phenomena that are to be directly known as things to be directly known, to phenomena that are to be fully understood as things to be fully understood, to phenomena that are to be abandoned as things to be abandoned, to phenomena that are to be realized as things to be realized, and to phenomena that are to be developed as things to be developed.
And for this very reason it was said:
“That which was to be directly known has been directly known; that which was to be developed has been developed;
that which was to be abandoned has been abandoned by me. Therefore, O brahmins, I am a Buddha.
Furthermore, the eye is the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), and the prior craving that originates it by being its root cause is the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca).
The non-arising of both is the truth of cessation (nirodhasacca), and the practice that leads to the full understanding of cessation is the truth of the path (maggasacca).
Thus, by extracting each term individually, he has perfectly and independently awakened to all phenomena. This same method applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as well.

By this very method, one should understand the six bases (āyatana) beginning with form, the six groups of consciousness (viññāṇakāya) beginning with eye-consciousness, and the [six] contacts beginning with eye-contact.

The six contacts, beginning with eye-contact; the six feelings, beginning with those born of eye-contact; the six perceptions, beginning with perception of forms; the six volitions, beginning with volition regarding forms;

the six groups of craving, beginning with craving for forms; the six applied thoughts, beginning with applied thought regarding forms; the six sustained thoughts, beginning with sustained thought regarding forms;
the five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of form; the ten kasiṇas; the ten recollections; and by way of the perception of the bloated corpse, and so forth.
The ten perceptions, the thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements,
the nine existences beginning with sensual existence, the four jhānas beginning with the first, the four immeasurables beginning with the development of loving-kindness,
the four formless attainments, and the factors of dependent origination— beginning with aging-and-death in reverse order and beginning with ignorance in forward order— should also be applied.
In this regard, here is the construction of the single phrase: "Old age and death are the truth of suffering; birth is the truth of the origin;
the escape from both is the truth of cessation; and the practice for the full understanding of cessation is the truth of the path.
Thus, by extracting each individual term, he has rightly and personally awakened to, followed, and penetrated all phenomena. Therefore it is said: "rightly and personally."
Furthermore, he is called the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddho*) because of his awakening to all phenomena (*sabbadhammā*).
He is "perfect in knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*) because of his endowment with true knowledges (*vijjā*) and conduct (*caraṇa*).

In this context, "true knowledges" refers to either the three true knowledges or the eight true knowledges. The three true knowledges should be understood according to the method explained in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*; the eight...

"Vijjā" (clear knowledge) is [explained] in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. For there, having included the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) along with insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and mind-made psychic power (*manomaya-iddhi*), eight clear knowledges are stated.

"Caraṇa" (conduct) consists of these fifteen factors: restraint by virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven true qualities (*saddhamma*), and the four fine-material-sphere jhānas.
The qualities (dhammā) are to be understood. For it is these very fifteen qualities that the noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) practices and by which he goes toward the deathless state;
therefore, they are called "conduct" (caraṇa). As it is said in detail: "Here, Mahānāma, the noble disciple is virtuous...
The Blessed One is endowed with this knowledge (vijjā) and this conduct; for that reason, he is so called.

"Endowed with true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*). In this context, the Blessed One’s perfection of true knowledge stands having fulfilled omniscience, while his perfection of conduct stands as great compassion (*mahākāruṇikatā*).
