Having understood, through omniscience, what is beneficial and what is harmful for all beings, he—by means of his great compassion—avoids what is harmful and directs them toward what is beneficial, just as one who is endowed with true knowledge and conduct would do. Therefore, his disciples...

They are well-practiced, not ill-practiced; for unlike those disciples who have fallen away from true knowledge and conduct, such as the self-mortifiers and others, [the Buddha] is the Sugata because his gait is beautiful, because he has gone to a beautiful place, because he has gone rightly, and because he has spoken rightly.
For "gait" (*gamana*) is also called "going" (*gata*), and that of the Blessed One is beautiful, purified, and blameless. Why?

But what is that path? It is the Noble Path. For by means of that journey he has gone to the secure direction without being obstructed; thus, because his going is beautiful, he is the "Well-Gone One" (Sugata).
Furthermore, he has gone to that beautiful place, the deathless Nibbāna; thus, because he has gone to a beautiful place, he is also the "Well-Gone One.
And he has gone rightly, not returning again to the defilements abandoned by each respective path. And this has been said:
“Because he does not repeat, does not return to, and does not go back to those defilements which have been abandoned by the path of stream-entry, he is the Sugata...
[and so on] ...because he does not repeat, does not return to, and does not go back to those defilements which have been abandoned by the path of arhatship, he is the Sugata.
Or else, he has come rightly from the foot of Dīpaṅkara up until the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) through the fulfillment of the thirty perfections (pāramitā).

He is the Sugata because he has come rightly (*sammāgatatā*): he has arrived by practicing correctly, bringing about only the welfare and happiness of the entire world while avoiding these extremes—eternalism, annihilationism, sensual pleasure, and self-mortification.
Furthermore, he is the Sugata because he speaks rightly (*sammāgadattā*): he speaks only appropriate words on appropriate occasions.

In this regard, here is the Sādhaka-sutta: “Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and which is disagreeable and unpleasant to others—that speech the Tathāgata does not utter.
Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true and correct, yet unbeneficial, and which is disagreeable and unpleasant to others—that too the Tathāgata [does not utter].”

The Tathāgata does not utter speech. And as for that speech which the Tathāgata knows to be true, real, and beneficial, yet which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others—the Tathāgata knows the proper time for the explanation of such speech.
And as for that speech which the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, unreal, and unbeneficial, yet which is pleasant and agreeable to others—

The Tathāgata does not speak such speech. Even that speech which the Tathāgata knows to be true, factual, and pleasant to others, yet not conducive to their welfare—that speech the Tathāgata does not speak.
But as for that speech which the Tathāgata knows to be true, factual, and conducive to welfare, and which is also pleasant and agreeable to others—in that case, he speaks it, knowing the proper time.
“The Tathāgata is one who gives an explanation for that speech. Thus, he should be understood as the Sugata because he speaks rightly.

Furthermore, he is the Lokavidū (Knower of the World) because he has known the world in every way. For the Blessed One knew, understood, and penetrated the world in its entirety—by way of its intrinsic nature, its origin, its cessation, and the means to its cessation. As it was said: “In that case, friend, where...”
It is not born, it does not age, it does not die, it does not pass away, and it does not reappear.
I do not say that the end of the world can be known, seen, or reached by traveling.

To those who possess perception and are subject to the cycle of existence, I proclaim the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the practice leading to the cessation of the world.
“The end of the world can never be reached by traveling;
yet without reaching the end of the world, there is no release from suffering.”
“Therefore, indeed, the wise one who knows the world,
having reached the end of the world and lived the holy life,
being a sage who has known the end of the world— ”

“He would not desire this world and the next. Furthermore, there are three worlds: the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), the world of beings (*sattaloka*), and the world of space (*okāsaloka*). Among these, in the passage where it is said, “One world:

Four hundred thousand and eighty million—

The supreme mountain Sineru plunges eighty-four thousand [yojanas] into the great ocean and rises to exactly that same height above it. From there,

Sublime peaks rising deep within, variegated with diverse jewels:

He trains those who are to be tamed by men; thus he is a “charioteer of men to be tamed” (*purisadammasārathi*). It is said that he tames and disciplines them.
In this context, “men to be tamed” (*purisadamma*) refers to untamed beings fit to be tamed—whether they be animals, human beings, or non-human beings. For it is thus:
The Blessed One tamed even non-human beings such as the Naga kings Apalāla, Cūḷodara, Mahodara, Aggisikha, Dhūmasikha, and the elephant Dhanapālaka;
he rendered them free from venom and established them in the refuges and the precepts.
He likewise tamed human beings such as Saccaka the son of the Nigaṇṭhas, the young Brahmin Ambaṭṭha, Pokkharasāti, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, and others.
Non-human beings—such as the yakkhas Āḷavaka, Sūciloma, and Kharaloma, as well as Sakka, the king of the gods, and others—were also tamed and disciplined by various means of discipline.

In this regard, the following sutta should be cited in detail: “Kesi, I discipline a person to be tamed both gently, and I discipline him harshly, and I discipline him both gently and harshly. Alternatively, [this applies] to those whose virtue and other qualities are purified.

By teaching the first jhāna and so forth, as well as the progressive path of the higher maggas for those who have already entered the stream (sotāpanna) and others, he indeed tames even those already tamed.
Alternatively, "the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed" is a single phrase.

For the Blessed One guides those men to be tamed in such a way that, while sitting in a single cross-legged posture, they rush toward the eight directions without obstruction. Therefore, "unsurpassed..."

"He is called the charioteer of men to be tamed. In this context, the following sutta should be cited in detail: "Bhikkhus, when an elephant to be tamed is guided by an elephant-tamer, it runs in only one direction.
He is the Teacher (Satthā) because he instructs appropriately according to the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal. Furthermore, he is the Teacher...

The Teacher is the Blessed One, the Caravan Leader. "Just as a caravan leader leads a caravan across a wilderness—leading it across a wilderness of robbers, a wilderness of wild beasts, a wilderness of famine, and a wilderness of waterlessness;
leading it out, across, and through, and bringing it to a land of safety—in the very same way, the Blessed One is the Teacher, the Caravan Leader."
The meaning here should be understood according to the method of exposition [in the *Niddesa*] as follows: “He leads beings across the wilderness;

he leads them across the wilderness of birth,” and so forth. The phrase “of gods and humans” is stated by way of defining the highest limit and also by way of defining those individuals who are capable [of liberation].
Yet the Blessed One is indeed the Teacher even for animals, because he provides them with his instruction. For they too [are taught] by the Blessed One...

Having attained the perfection of the decisive support (*upanissaya-sampatti*) through hearing the Dhamma, they become partakers of the paths and fruits in that very same life or in the second or third existence, precisely because of that perfection of the decisive support. The frog-deva sons and others are examples in this regard.
It is said that while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the inhabitants of the city of Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond, a certain frog...
He took up a mental sign (nimitta) in the presence of the Blessed One. A certain cowherd, standing there leaning on his staff, pressed down upon his head and stood over him.
He died at that very moment and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in size.
And there, as if waking from sleep, he saw himself surrounded by a host of nymphs.
Having seen this, he thought, "Alas! I too have been reborn here! What deed must I have done?

As he reflected, he saw nothing else at all except for his having grasped the sign of the Blessed One’s voice. He came forth from that very place together with his celestial mansion and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, though already knowing, asked:
“Who is it that worships my feet, shining with supernatural power and glory,
illuminating all directions with a most excellent radiance?
“I was once a frog, living in the water, feeding on the water.”
"While you were listening to the Dhamma, the calf-herder met his death.

The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings attained penetration of the Dhamma. Having established himself in the fruit of stream-entry, the son of the devas smiled and departed.
Furthermore, because he has become a Buddha with respect to everything that is to be known, by means of the knowledge pertaining to liberation—
"Buddho. Or, because he himself awakened to the four truths and awakened other beings as well, for these and other such reasons he is "Buddho.
To make this meaning known, the entire method of exposition—or the method of the *Paṭisambhidā*—which proceeds thus: "He is 'Buddho' because he has awakened to the truths;
he is 'Buddho' because he has awakened the world," should be expanded in detail.
"Bhagavāti" is a designation for one who is distinguished by virtues and is revered as the supreme among beings. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"The word 'Bhagavā' is the best; the word 'Bhagavā' is the most excellent.
He is venerable and worthy of reverence; therefore he is called 'Bhagavā'."
Name is indeed fourfold: situational (*āvatthika*), indicative (*liṅgika*), causal (*nemittika*), and fortuitous (*adhiccasamuppanna*).
That which is called "fortuitous" is what is termed "at will" in worldly parlance. Among these, such terms as "calf," "ox," and "bull" are situational.

Such terms as "staff-bearer," "umbrella-bearer," "crest-wearer," and "elephant" are indicative. "One possessing the three knowledges" (*tevijjo*) and "one possessing the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñño*)... [are causal].

Such [names] as these are based on signs (*nemittika*). Expressions such as “Sirivaḍḍhaka” (Increaser of Fortune) or “Dhanavaḍḍhaka” (Increaser of Wealth) are adventitious (*adhiccasamuppanna*), occurring without regard for the actual meaning of the words. However, this name “Bhagavā” is based on signs;
it was not given by Mahāmāyā, nor by King Suddhodana, nor by the eighty thousand kinsmen, nor by distinguished deities such as Sakka or Santusita.
For this was said by the General of the Dhamma: “‘Bhagavā’—this name was not given by his mother...

[and so on] ...it is a designation based on realization, pertaining to the end of liberation, which the Blessed Buddhas acquired at the foot of the Bodhi tree together with the attainment of omniscience; that is to say, ‘the Blessed One’ (Bhagavā).
And in order to illustrate those qualities for the sake of which this name is used, they recite this verse:
“He is a possessor, a partaker, a sharer, a distributor;
he has broken [defilements], he is venerable, he is fortunate;
by many methods, his self is well-cultivated.”
“He is called the Blessed One because he has gone to the end of becoming.
Here, the meaning of these various terms should be understood according to the method explained in the *Niddesa*.
However, there is this other way as well:
“He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), he has destroyed (bhaggavā), he is endowed with (yutto), he is distinguished by excellences (bhagehi ca vibhattavā);
he has enjoyed (bhattavā) and has gone beyond (vantagamano) states of existence (bhavesu)—therefore he is the Blessed One (bhagavā).

In this regard, having taken the characteristics of etymology such as “the addition of a syllable” (vaṇṇāgamo) and “the substitution of a syllable” (vaṇṇavipariyayo), or according to the method of grammar through the application of the rule for *piśodara* and similar compounds—
Since he possesses the fortune that reaches the further shore of giving, virtue, and so forth— which brings about mundane and supramundane happiness— therefore,
while he should be called "possessing fortune" (*bhāgyavā*), it should be understood that he is called "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*).

Furthermore, because he has abandoned greed, hatred, delusion, distorted attention, lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), anger, enmity, disparagement, domineering, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, pride, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, craving, and ignorance...

The threefold unwholesome roots, misconduct, defilements, stains, perceptions of inequality, discursive thoughts, proliferations, the fourfold perversions, taints, fetters, floods, yokes, destinations, the arising of craving, clinging, the five mental stumps, bondages, hindrances, delighting, the six roots of dispute, the body of craving, the seven underlying tendencies,

the eight wrongnesses, the nine rooted in craving, the ten unwholesome actions, the speculative views, the hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering— all these hundreds of thousands of afflictions consisting of distress, fever, and defilements.
Or, in brief, he has shattered the five Māras—the Māra of defilements, the Māra of volitional formations, the Māra of the aggregates, the Māra of death, and the Māra of the son of a god.
Therefore, because these perils have been shattered (*bhagga*), he is to be called "Bhaggava," yet he is called "Bhagavā. And it is said in this regard:
"He whose lust is shattered, whose hatred is shattered, Whose delusion is shattered, and who is free from taints;..."
“Evil states have been destroyed (bhaggā) by him; therefore he is called the Blessed One (Bhagavā).

By his possession of good fortune, there is the manifestation of the perfection of the physical body, characterized by the hundred marks born of merit; by his destruction of faults, there is the perfection of the Dhamma-body.
Likewise, there is his state of being highly esteemed by worldly critics, as well as by householders and those who have gone forth.

It is shown that [the Buddha] is worthy of being approached; that he is capable of removing the physical and mental suffering of those who have approached him; that he is a benefactor through the giving of material gifts and the giving of the Dhamma;
and that he is able to provide for the attainment of both mundane and supramundane happiness.

Furthermore, because the word *bhaga* is used in the world for these six qualities: sovereignty (*issariya*), virtue (*dhamma*), fame (*yasa*), glory (*sirī*), desire (*kāma*), and effort (*payatta*).

He possesses supreme sovereignty over his own mind, as well as all the mundane powers esteemed by the world, such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and *laghimā* (lightness), in their entirety and perfection; likewise,
he possesses supramundane Dhamma pervading the three worlds, a most pure fame attained through qualities in accordance with reality,
and a splendor of every limb and member, complete in all aspects, capable of gladdening the eyes of people intent on beholding his physical form.
Whatever—for one's own benefit or for the benefit of others—has been desired or longed for by him, that very thing has been accomplished accordingly;

thus there is "icchit'-icchita" (the desired-at-will). Furthermore, there is "payatta" (exertion), which consists of right effort (*sammāvāyāma*) and serves as the cause for attaining the state of being honored by the whole world.
Therefore, because he is endowed with these "bhagas," he is called "Bhagavā" in the sense that "he possesses bhagas."

However, because all phenomena are classified by way of categories such as the wholesome and so forth; or because wholesome and other phenomena are categorized by way of aggregates, bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, and so on;
or because the Noble Truth of Suffering is defined in the sense of oppression, being conditioned, burning, and changeability;
the Origin [of Suffering] in the sense of accumulation, source, bondage, and obstruction; and [the Cessation of Suffering] in the sense of escape, seclusion, being unconditioned, and immortality—
Having analyzed, opened up, and taught the cessation [of suffering] in the sense of its predominance as the cause for deliverance, it is said that he "analyzed" (vibhattavā).
Therefore, although one should say "one who has analyzed" (vibhattavā), he is called the Blessed One (Bhagavā).
And because he [has mastered] the divine, brahma, and noble abidings; the seclusion of body, mind, and requisites; and the emptiness, wishless, and signless liberations—
Furthermore, he cultivated, frequented, and practiced extensively other mundane and supramundane qualities superior to those of ordinary men;
therefore, while he could be called "one who possesses" (*bhattavā*), he is called "Bhagavā.

Moreover, because he has vomited out (*vanta*) the going (*gamana*)—that is, craving (*taṇhā*)—within the three realms of existence (*bhava*), he is thus "one who has vomited out the going within existences" (*bhavesu vantagamo*).
It should be said that by taking the letter *bha* from the word *bhava*, the letter *ga* from the word *gamana*, and the letter *va* from the word *vanta*, making them long, one says "Bhagavā.
Just as in the world, when it should be said "a garland of the filth of excrement," one says "mekhalā" (a girdle).
"So imaṃ lokaṃ" means that Blessed One [knows] this world. Now he indicates what is to be said: "sadevakaṃ" (together with the devas).

"Together with the devas" means including the world of devas (*sadevaka*). Likewise, "together with Māra" means including Māra (*samāraka*); "together with Brahmā" means including Brahmā (*sabrahmaka*);

"together with recluses and brahmins" means including recluses and brahmins (*sassamaṇabrāhmaṇi*). Because it is born, it is a generation (*pajā*); that is the generation. "Together with devas and humans" means including devas and humans (*sadevamanussa*).
In this context, by the term "together with the devas," the inclusion of the five classes of sense-sphere devas (*pañcakāmāvacara-devagga*) should be understood; by the term "together with Māra,"...
The mention of the "six classes of sense-sphere devas" includes the Brahmakāyika and other such devas by the expression "together with the Brahmas";

the mention of "together with recluses and brahmins" includes those recluses and brahmins who are adversaries and enemies of the Teaching; it also includes those recluses and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil;
the mention of "the generation" includes the world of sentient beings; and the mention of "together with devas and humans" includes conventional devas and the remainder of the human race.
Thus, it should be understood that here the world of space is included by three terms, while the world of beings is included by two terms according to their generation.

According to another method: by the inclusion of "together with devas," the deva-world of the formless realm is included; by the inclusion of "together with Māras," the six deva-worlds of the sense-sphere are included;
by the inclusion of "together with Brahmas," the Brahma-world of the fine-material realm is included; and by the inclusion of "with recluses and brahmins, etc.," the four assemblies are included.
Either the world of humans together with the conventional gods, or the entire world of all remaining beings.

Furthermore, here, by the term "together with the devas," the fame of that Blessed One has spread forth, establishing that he has realized the entirety of the world through the highest possible limit. Therefore, for those who might think: "Māra is of great power..."
"Is even Vasavatti, the lord of the Cātumahārājika realm, one who has realized this?
Dispelling their doubt, he rose up [saying], "Together with Māra. However, for those who might think: "Brahmā is of great power;
with one finger he radiates light over one thousand world-systems, with two... [and so on] ...with ten fingers over ten thousand world-systems," [the Buddha says: "Together with Brahmā."
"He radiates light and experiences the unsurpassed bliss of meditative attainment; has he realized this too?
Dispelling their doubt, he declared, "Together with Brahmā. Then, for those who might think, "There are many ascetics and brahmins who are adversaries of the Teaching;
have they also been realized?"—dispelling their doubt, he declared, "Together with ascetics and brahmins."

"He has risen above" (*pajanti abbhuggato*). Having thus declared the state of having realized the most exalted [beings], he then, starting from the conventional gods (*sammutideva*) and the remaining humans, declares the state of having realized the rest of the world of beings by way of the limit of the exalted, saying "together with gods and humans" (*sadevamanussa*);
this is the sequence of connection here.
Regarding the phrase "having realized it through direct higher knowledge, he declares it": here, *sayam* means "by himself," that is, having become independent of others;

*abhiññā* means "through higher knowledge" (*abhiññāya*), the sense being "having known by means of superior wisdom. *Sacchikatvā* means "having made manifest to oneself," by which there is a rejection of inference and other such means.
*Pavedeti* means he awakens [others], makes them know, and proclaims it. He [proclaims] the Dhamma...
"He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... [and] good in the end"—out of compassion for beings, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma even while abandoning unsurpassed bliss of seclusion.
And whether he teaches it little or much, he teaches it in such a manner as to be good in the beginning and so forth.

How so? For even a single verse is good in the beginning because the Dhamma is all-pervadingly auspicious; it is good in the middle through its second and third lines, and good in the end through its final line.

A discourse with a single sequence of meaning is good in the beginning by way of its introduction (*nidāna*), good in the end by way of its conclusion (*nigamana*), and good in the middle by way of the remainder.
A discourse with multiple sequences of meaning is [good in the beginning] by way of its first sequence...
It is good in the beginning through the latter [portion], good in the end through the former, and good in the middle through the remaining [portions].

The entire Dhamma of the Dispensation is good in the beginning by virtue of morality, which constitutes its own purpose; it is good in the middle by means of serenity, insight, the path, and the fruit;
and it is good in the end by means of Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is good in the beginning through morality and concentration, and good in the middle through insight and the path.
It is beautiful in the end through the fruits of liberation (*nibbāna*). Alternatively, it is beautiful in the beginning because of the Buddha’s perfect awakening;

beautiful in the middle because of the Dhamma’s perfect nature; and beautiful in the end because of the Saṅgha’s perfect practice. Or, for one who has heard it and is practicing accordingly, it is beautiful in the beginning through the perfect awakening to be attained;
beautiful in the middle through the awakening of a Pacceka-buddha; and [beautiful in the end] through the awakening of a disciple (*sāvaka*).

It is "beautiful in the conclusion" (pariyosānakalyāṇa). While being heard, it brings about what is beautiful even through the hearing itself because it suppresses the hindrances; thus it is "beautiful in the beginning" (ādikalyāṇa).
When practiced, it brings about what is beautiful even through the practice because it brings the bliss of serenity and insight;

thus it is "beautiful in the middle" (majjhekalyāṇa). And for one who has practiced accordingly, once the fruit of the practice is accomplished, it brings about the state of suchness (tādibhāva); thus it is "beautiful in the conclusion."

It is "beautiful in the conclusion" because it brings about what is beautiful even through the fruit of practice. Furthermore, it is "beautiful in the beginning" due to the purity of its origin, as it originates from the Protector;
it is "beautiful in the middle" due to the purity of its meaning; and it is "beautiful in the conclusion" due to the purity of its function.
Therefore, it should be understood that whether he teaches little or much, this Blessed One teaches in a manner that is beautiful in the beginning and so forth.

Regarding the phrases "with meaning" (*sāttha*) and "with phrasing" (*sabyañjana*), and so forth: when teaching this Dhamma, he reveals both the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsanabrahmacariya*) and the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*), illustrating them through various methods.

And that [teaching] is "with meaning" due to its perfection of meaning (*atthasampatti*) and "with phrasing" due to its perfection of phrasing (*byañjanasampatti*), because it consists of the conjunction of words of meaning through the acts of making known, revealing, explaining, analyzing, clarifying, and defining.
It is "with meaning" (sāttha) because it is endowed with the perfection of syllables, phrases, phonemes, modes, etymologies, and explanations;

it is "with phrasing" (sabyañjana) because of its profundity of meaning and profundity of penetration, and its profundity of Dhamma and profundity of teaching. It is "with meaning" insofar as it is the domain of the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of inspired speech (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā);

it is "with phrasing" insofar as it is the domain of the analytical knowledge of Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of etymology (niruttipaṭisambhidā). Because it is to be experienced by the wise, it inspires confidence in those who investigate it.

It is "with meaning" because it inspires faith in worldly people; it is "with phrasing" because it is accompanied by appropriate expression. It is "with meaning" because its intention is profound; it is "with phrasing" because its words are clear.
It is "entirely complete" because it is perfect in every respect due to the absence of anything to be added;

it is "pure" because it is stainless due to the absence of anything to be removed; and it is [praised] by those who have become sublime (*brahmabhūta*) because it is encompassed by the three trainings.

It is called *brahmacariya* because it is to be practiced by the best of beings and because it constitutes their mode of conduct. Therefore, it is said: “He proclaims the *brahmacariya* that is meaningful in its essence and beautiful in its expression... [and so forth].

Furthermore, because he teaches with its source and its origin, he teaches what is good in the beginning; and because he teaches in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained, [he teaches what is good in the middle and at the end].
Because the meaning is unerring and because it is endowed with logical reasons and examples, he teaches what is "good in the middle";
and because the listeners gain faith and there is a conclusion, he teaches what is "good in the end. Teaching in this way, he reveals the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
And that [teaching] is "meaningful" (*sāttha*) due to the excellence of attainment through practice, and "well-phrased" (*sabyañjana*) due to the excellence of the tradition through study.

It is called "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*) because it is endowed with the five aggregates of virtue and so forth, and is thus entirely complete; because it is free from defilements and proceeds for the sake of crossing over [suffering];

and because it is independent of worldly gain, it is utterly pure; and because it is the conduct of those who have become sublime—namely, the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha—it is designated as such in the sense of being supreme.
Therefore, it is said: "He teaches the Dhamma... which is excellent in the beginning... the holy life."
"He proclaims" is what is said.
"It is good indeed" means it is excellent, bringing benefit and bringing happiness; this is what is stated.
"Of such Arahants" means of those like that Blessed Gotama, who, through the attainment of qualities exactly as they are, is known in the world as an Arahant.
“Of the Arahants who have attained renown. “There is a sight [of them]”:
having opened his eyes, which were serene and gentle with faith, and having formed the aspiration, “Even a mere sight is good,” the Brahmin of Verañjā then approached the Blessed One. 2. *Yena*:
this is the instrumental case used in the sense of the locative. Therefore, it means that he approached him where the Blessed One was; thus it is here.
The meaning should be understood as follows: or rather, by whatever reason the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans, it is by that very reason that he approached;
thus is the meaning to be understood here. And for what reason is the Blessed One to be approached?

It is with the intention of attaining various distinguished qualities, just as a great tree that constantly bears fruit is approached by flocks of birds with the intention of enjoying its sweet fruit.
"Upasaṅkami" means he went; this is what is expressed. "Upasaṅkamitvā" (having approached) indicates the completion of the act of approaching.
Alternatively, it is also said that having gone in this manner, he went to a place even closer than before, which is reckoned as the vicinity of the Blessed One.
"Sammodi with the Blessed One" means that just as the Blessed One was asking him about his health and so forth, so too did he [greet the Blessed One].
He shared in joy together with the Blessed One; like cold water meeting warm water, they were reconciled and attained unity.
And by means of that conversation beginning with, "I hope, Master Gotama, that you are bearing up; I hope you are getting along;
I hope that Master Gotama and his disciples are free from affliction, free from illness, and are enjoying lightness, strength, and comfort," [he conversed].
It is "conducive to amity" (*sammodanīya*) because it generates that amity known as joy and gladness, and because it is appropriate for such amity.

It is "conducive to recollection" (*sāraṇīya*) because, by virtue of its sweetness in both meaning and phrasing, it is worthy of being remembered and can be continuously maintained in the mind even for a very long time;
or alternatively, it is "conducive to amity" when being heard, and "conducive to recollection" when being recollected.
It is memorable. Thus, it is "pleasing" because of the purity of its phrasing, and "memorable" because of the purity of its meaning.

Having thus exchanged pleasantries and memorable words in many ways, and having concluded, finished, and brought the conversation to a close, he sat down to one side, desiring to ask about the purpose for which he had come.
“Ekamantaṃ” (to one side) is a neuter abstract designation, as in such expressions as “the moon and sun move unevenly.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: he sat in such a way that he was seated to one side.
Alternatively, this accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. “Nisīdi” means he sat down; for wise men [approach] one who is worthy of honor.
Having approached, they sit to one side with skill regarding seating. And this one among them [did so]; therefore, he sat to one side.
But how does one sit "to one side"? By avoiding the six faults of sitting. Namely:
too far away, too near, upwind, on high ground, directly in front, or directly behind. Too far away...
For if one sits down wishing to speak, one must speak in a loud voice. If one sits too close, one causes physical contact.
If one sits upwind, one is troubled by the odor of the body. If one sits on high ground, one displays a lack of respect.
If one sits directly in front, and if one wishes to look [at the teacher], one must gaze with eye meeting eye.
It must be seen. If one sits too far back and wishes to see, it must be seen by stretching out the neck.
Therefore, this [Verañja Brahmin] also sat down, avoiding these six faults of sitting. Hence it is said: "He sat down to one side.
As for the phrase, "While sitting to one side, the Verañja Brahmin said this to the Blessed One," the word "this" refers to the matter that is now to be spoken.

It indicates [this]. The syllable *da* serves as a phonetic euphonic junction (*padasandhi*). "He spoke" (*avoca*) means he said. "I have heard this" (*sutaṃ metaṃ*) means "this has been heard by me";
it indicates the matter that is now to be stated, namely, "this was heard by me. "O Gotama!"—he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name.
Now, showing what he had heard, he said: "The ascetic Gotama is not... and so forth. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not yet explained.
"Brāhmaṇa" refers to one who is a brāhmaṇa by birth. "Aged" (*jiṇṇa*) means one who has become decrepit, having reached a state of brokenness and so forth due to old age.
"Venerable" (*vuḍḍha*) means one who has reached the limit of growth in the limbs and members of the body. "Elderly" (*mahallaka*) means one endowed with seniority by birth;
it is said that he is one who has been born for a long time. "One who has gone the way" (*addhagata*) means one who has traversed the path, having passed through two or three royal successions.
The intended meaning is "past. "Having reached old age" means having arrived at the final stage of life; "final stage of life" refers to the last third of a hundred-year lifespan.

Furthermore, "aged" (*jiṇṇa*) means ancient; it is said to refer to one belonging to a lineage that has existed for a long time. "Venerable" (*vuḍḍha*) means endowed with the growth of virtues such as moral discipline and conduct.
"Mahallaka" means one endowed with greatness of wealth, possessing great riches and great enjoyments.

"Addhagata" means one who has set out on the path—that is, one who proceeds without transgressing the boundaries of the brahmins' practice of vows and so forth. "Vayo-anuppatta" means one who has reached the state of being aged by birth, having arrived at the final stage of life;
thus should the construction of the terms here be understood.

Now, regarding the phrases beginning with "he pays homage," they should be understood according to their meaning by applying them in the same manner as what was stated previously under the phrase "the ascetic Gotama is not [one who...]"—namely:
"He does not pay homage, nor does he rise from his seat, nor does he invite him to a seat by saying, 'May the venerable sirs sit here.
For in this context, the word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of emphasis (*vibhāvana*). "Form is permanent... [and so on].
...or impermanent," and so forth. Having spoken thus, he then saw that the Blessed One was not returning his salutation or other courtesies, and said:
"This is indeed so, Master Gotama. That which I have heard is exactly so;
my hearing and my seeing coincide and agree, and in meaning they come to a single unity. "For indeed, sir..."
“Gotama... [and so on] ...or invites him to a seat,” having thus refuted what he had heard by means of what he had seen, he spoke in reproach:
“This, Master Gotama, is indeed not proper. That failure to perform such acts as salutation was indeed not fitting.
Then the Blessed One, without falling into the fault of self-exaltation and disparagement of others, with a heart cooled by compassion, addressed him:
Desiring to dispel ignorance and demonstrate his state of being endowed with reason, he said: “I do not see anyone, O Brahmin... even my head would fall off for him.

Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: “O Brahmin, even when I look with the unimpeded eye of omniscience, I do not see such a person in this world comprising the realms of devas and so forth, whom I might pay homage to.”
Or I might rise to greet him, or invite him to a seat. It is not surprising that today, having attained omniscience, I do not see such a person worthy of such respectful service.
Moreover, when I was just born, I walked seven steps facing north and surveyed the entire ten-thousandfold world system.
Even then, in this world with its divisions of devas and so forth, I did not see any person whom I should pay homage to, or rise up for, or invite to a seat.
Rather, even the Great Brahmā Khīṇāsava, whose lifespan was sixteen thousand eons, raised his joined palms to me and said:
"You are a Great Man in the world; you are the foremost and the eldest in the world with its devas."
And being filled with joy, he replied, “There is none superior to you.
Even then, seeing no one superior to myself, I uttered this lion’s roar: “I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world.
Thus, even at the very moment of my birth, I was worthy of homage and the like.
"There is no person; now that I have attained omniscience, whom should I salute... or whom should I invite to a seat?
Therefore, brahmin, do not expect such personal honor from the Tathāgata.
For if the Tathāgata were to salute someone... or invite them to a seat, his head would [split asunder]."

"At the end of the night, the bonds of this person’s maturity having slackened, he would suddenly fall to the ground, severed from the neck like a palm fruit falling from its stalk when its stem has loosened.
Even when this was said, the brahmin, due to his lack of wisdom, failed to perceive the Tathāgata’s preeminence in the world.
Unable to endure those words alone, he said: "Master Gotama is devoid of flavor. This, it is said, was his intention:
"That which in the world is called the 'flavor of concord'—namely, salutation, rising from one's seat, joining of palms, and respectful homage—that does not exist for Master Gotama;
therefore, Master Gotama is devoid of flavor, one whose nature is flavorless, one whose very essence is flavorless."

Then, in order to produce softness in his mind and avoiding a state of direct opposition, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with, “There is indeed this way, brahmin,” demonstrating to him that the meaning of his statement was otherwise.
In this context, *pariyāya* means a reason; for this word *pariyāya* is used in the senses of teaching, section, and reason. “The Madhupiṇḍika-pariyāya... [and so on].

For this [term] occurs in the sense of "instruction" in such passages as, "Hold him fast," and so forth; in the sense of "opportunity" in such passages as, "Ānanda, whose turn is it today to exhort the bhikkhunīs?";

and in the sense of "reason" in such passages as, "It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would explain another method by which this Saṅgha of bhikkhus might be established in higher knowledge. Here, however, it occurs in the sense of "reason."
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood in this way: "There is indeed, brahmin, such a reason;
for by that reason, a person speaking of me as 'the venerable Gotama is devoid of flavors' would be speaking rightly and would be reckoned as one who speaks truthfully.
And who is he? Those, brahmin, which are the flavors of forms... [and so on] ...the flavors of tangibles—these are absent in the Tathāgata.

"Abandoned. What is meant by this? Those worldly pleasures reckoned as the relish of sensual desire—which arise for even those ordinary persons (puthujjana) esteemed as superior by birth or by rebirth, who relish, delight in, and are attached to visible objects and so forth—namely, the flavors of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles;
these [are abandoned] by one who has cut off this world by the neck.
They pull [the mind] as if binding it; they are called "harmonious" because they arise from the combination of factors such as the object and the sense base.

All of these have been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Although he could say, "They have been abandoned by me," he teaches the Dhamma without elevating himself through the use of the possessive pronoun "mine.
Or rather, this is simply the Blessed One’s skillful elegance in teaching.

In this context, "abandoned" (*pahīnā*) means departed from or relinquished from the continuum of consciousness. Furthermore, in this sense, the genitive case should be understood as having an instrumental force.
They are called "cut off at the root" (*ucchinnamūlā*) because they have had the root consisting of craving and ignorance cut away by the sword of the Noble Path.
Their basis has been made like the stump of a palmyra tree (*tālāvatthukatā*). For just as a palmyra tree, together with its roots—
Once that site has been cleared and that spot has been made into a mere stump, the further growth of that palm tree is no longer perceived;

likewise, when the Noble Path-sword has extracted the "saps" of form and so forth along with their roots, and the mental continuum has been reduced to a mere stump by virtue of those [defilements] having previously arisen there, all of them are said to be "made into stumps like palm trees. This is because they are subject to the nature of non-growth.
Or, it is called "made like a palm stump" because it is made like a palm tree with its head cut off.
Furthermore, because those who have been thus made like a palm stump are rendered non-existent—being made in such a way that no further existence remains for them—it is said: "rendered non-existent.
Herein, the word-division is as follows: *anu-abhāvaṃ katā* = *anabhāvaṃkatā*. "Rendered non-existent..."
The reading “gatā” is also found; its meaning is “gone to non-existence.

Therein, the word-division is “gone to non-existence (anubhāvaṃ gatā), gone to non-being (anabhāvaṃ gatā),” just as “not wonderful (anu-acchariyā)” becomes “not wonderful (anacchariyā). “Subject to non-arising in the future” means having a nature that does not arise again in the future.
For how could those who have gone to non-existence arise again? Therefore he said:
“Having gone to non-existence, they are of a nature not to arise again in the future.

This, brahmin, is the way; this, brahmin, is the reason why one speaking rightly might say of me, “The ascetic Gotama is devoid of taste,” yet it is not with reference to what you have said. And as for that which...
"You are speaking with an underlying intention (*sandhāya*), but that is not a valid method. Why, then, did the Blessed One say this?
Is it not the case that by saying this, the presence within oneself of that 'taste of harmony' (*sāmaggirasa*) mentioned by the brahmin is admitted? It is replied:
It is not so. For one who is capable of producing that taste of harmony but does not do so, is considered to be "lacking flavor" (*arasarūpa*) due to the absence of that [harmony].
It would have been something that could be said. However, the Blessed One is simply incapable of doing this; therefore, demonstrating his incapacity for such an act, he said:
"But it is not as you say with reference to that. Whatever method you intended when you called me "lacking in flavor," that [method] cannot be predicated of us.

4. Thus, being unable to impose upon himself the state of "tastelessness" (arasarūpatā) that he intended, the brahmin then said, "Furthermore, Master Gotama is one who has no enjoyment," and so forth.

In all these modes of expression, having understood the sequence of application according to the method already stated, it should be understood that this is merely what was spoken with a specific underlying intention (*sandhāya*).
The brahmin [referred to] that very act of salutation and so forth performed toward those who are young and old.
Thinking that in the world there is enjoyment through communal harmony, he said that the Blessed One was without enjoyment because of the absence of such [harmony].
However, the Blessed One, perceiving within himself the absence of that very thing which is the enjoyment of beings' desire and lust for forms and so forth,
authorized another method as well.

5. Furthermore, because the brahmin perceived the Blessed One’s non-performance of those worldly customary acts of family etiquette—such as saluting those who are senior by age—which people in the world perform, he called the Blessed One an “advocate of non-action” (*akiriyavāda*).

However, because the Blessed One speaks of the non-performance of bodily misconduct and so forth, the brahmin, perceiving that doctrine of non-action within himself, acknowledged another way of explaining it.
In this context, bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*) should be understood as the volition of killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.

Verbal misconduct (*vacīduccarita*) should be understood as the volition of false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. Mental misconduct (*manoduccarita*) should be understood as covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
Apart from those states, the remaining unwholesome states are "the various kinds of evil, unwholesome [states]."
...should be understood as "phenomena" (*dhammā*).

Furthermore, not seeing that same act of salutation and so forth performed toward the Blessed One, the brahmin—thinking, "By coming to this [Buddha], this lineage of the world and the tradition of the world is being cut off"—accused the Blessed One of being a proponent of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). The Blessed One...

However, because he declares the eradication of passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure—present in the eight greed-accompanied consciousnesses—and the eradication of hatred arising in the two unwholesome consciousnesses by means of the Non-returner path;

and because he declares the eradication, without remainder, of delusion—the source of all unwholesome states—by means of the Arahant path; [he speaks thus] with regard to those three, excluding the remaining [defilements].
He declares the eradication of evil, unwholesome states by means of the four paths according to their respective natures;
therefore, perceiving that [teaching] as annihilationism within himself, he acknowledges another method. 7.
Again, the brahmin thought: "I suppose the ascetic Gotama feels disgust toward this customary conduct of families, such as the salutation of elders and the like."
Thinking, "Therefore he does not do that," he said to the Blessed One, "You are loathsome.
But the Blessed One is indeed loathsome of bodily misconduct and so forth. What is meant?
Of the threefold bodily misconduct, the fourfold verbal misconduct, and the threefold mental misconduct—apart from those misdeeds, of the remainder...
In the sense of being base, and in the sense of being unwholesome because they arise from lack of skill, there is the attainment, the entering into, and the state of possessing unwholesome states;
all of that a person who is of a decorative nature loathes and feels shame for, as if it were excrement.
Therefore, perceiving that loathsomeness within himself, he allows another method [of explanation]. In this context, "by bodily misconduct" means:
The instrumental case should be understood here in the sense of utility (*upayoga*).
Furthermore, not seeing that very act of salutation and so forth being performed toward the Blessed One, the brahmin thought:
"This man leads away—that is, destroys—this duty which is the foremost in the world; or else, because he does not perform this customary service, he must be led away, that is, restrained."
Thinking thus, he addressed the Blessed One as "Venayika. Herein, this is the meaning of the words: it "removes" (vinayati), thus it is *vinaya*;
what is meant is that it "destroys. That which is *vinaya* itself is *venayika*; or, it "deserves" (*arahati*) *vinaya*, thus it is *venayika*;
what is meant is that it "deserves" restraint. However, because the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the removal and pacification of passion and the other defilements, therefore...
He is a disciplinarian (*venayiko*). This is precisely the meaning of the term here: he is a disciplinarian because he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of discipline (*vinaya*).
For the formation of derivative nouns (*taddhita-vutti*) is indeed manifold! And so, perceiving within himself that state of being a disciplinarian, he allows another explanation as well.
9. Furthermore, because a brahmin performs respectful services such as salutations toward those who are young and old, he pleases them and makes them joyful.
But those who do not [practice such austerities] instead cause pain, harass others, and give rise to mental distress in them; yet the Blessed One does not do these things.
Therefore, either thinking, "This man torments the elderly," because he is devoid of the conduct of a true noble one, or thinking, "This is a wretched man," he called the Blessed One a *tapassin*.
In this context, the word-meaning is as follows: *tapati* means "he torments" (*tapa*).
"He harasses" is what is meant; this is a name for the failure to perform respectful service (*sāmīcikamma*). One who possesses austerity (*tapa*) is an "austere one" (*tapassī*).
In the second interpretation of the meaning, without examining the literal words, a miserable person in the world is called "austere.
However, the Blessed One, because he has abandoned those unwholesome states (*akusala-dhammā*) which are called "tormenting" (*tapanīya*) since they torment the world—[is thus called *tapassī*].
Because he has attained the designation "ascetic" (*tapassin*), therefore, perceiving that state of asceticism within himself, he allows for another method of explanation as well.
Herein, this is the meaning of the words: they "burn," thus they are *tapā*; this is a designation for unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*).
For it has been said: "One burns here, one burns after passing away. Likewise, those *tapas* he has assailed, driven out, and abandoned.
"One who destroys [the womb] is an ascetic.
Furthermore, the brahmin, thinking that such acts as salutation lead to the attainment of the womb of the deva-world— that is, to obtaining rebirth in the deva-world—
and seeing that these were absent in the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as "one without a womb" (*apagabbha*).
Or, out of anger, even one who would point out a fault in the Blessed One’s taking of rebirth in his mother’s womb speaks thus.
Herein, this is the meaning of the words: "apagabbho" means one who has departed from the womb; the intention is that he is incapable of reaching rebirth in the world of the gods.
Or, "apagabbho" means one whose womb is inferior; because he is excluded from the womb of the world of the gods, he is destined to obtain an inferior womb in the future.
The intention is that his dwelling in the mother’s womb was inferior.

However, because the Blessed One has departed from lying in a womb for the future, he—perceiving within himself that state of being "one who has left the womb"—allows for another way of explaining it.
And therein [he says]: "In whomsoever, O Brahmin, the lying in a womb for the future and the production of renewed existence have been abandoned..."

The meaning of these terms should be understood as follows: O Brahmin, for that person whose lying in a womb and rebirth in a future existence have been abandoned because their causes have been destroyed by the unsurpassed Path—here, by the mention of "lying in a womb," the birth from a womb is included;
and by the mention of "rebirth in a future existence," the other three modes of birth are also included.
Furthermore, "lying in a womb" is *gabbhaseyyā*; "renewed becoming" itself is "the manifestation of renewed becoming," and this is how the meaning should be understood here.

And just as when "stations of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) is said, there is no station other than consciousness, so too here it should be understood that there is no lying down other than the womb.
And as for what is called "manifestation" (*abhinibbatti*): because...
There are those that have become renewed existence and those that have not become renewed existence; here, however, it is those that have become renewed existence which are intended.
Therefore it was said: "Renewed existence itself is the manifestation [of birth]; thus, 'the manifestation of renewed existence'. 11.
Thus, even when one reviles [another] with the eight grounds of abuse, such as being tasteless, ugly, and so forth, starting from the time of arrival...
The Blessed One— the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Master of Dhamma, the Tathāgata— out of compassion,

gazed upon the brahmin with his cool eye; and having thoroughly penetrated that element of Dhamma through which he attained mastery in the elegance of teaching, because of his perfect penetration of that element of Dhamma,
he was like the full moon risen high in a cloudless sky during the autumn season.
Like the sun, dispelling the darkness from the Brahmin’s heart,
he presented those very grounds for abuse in various ways and through different perspectives;
furthermore, he demonstrated his own expansion of compassion, his earth-like evenness of mind attained through being unshakable by the eight worldly conditions, and his state of imperturbability.
Explaining this, [the Blessed One said]: "This brahmin perceives his own state of old age merely through such things as grey hair, broken teeth, and wrinkled skin;

yet he does not truly know that he is followed by birth, pursued by aging, overcome by sickness, struck down by death, and become like a rotten stump—having died today, destined once again tomorrow to return to the state of a child lying on its back."
Thinking, "He has come into my presence with great resolve;

let his coming be fruitful," he expanded the Dhamma teaching for the brahmin by way of the passage beginning with "Just as, O brahmin," demonstrating his own peerless status in this world through the principle of priority in birth.
In this context, *seyyathā* is a particle used in the sense of comparison; *pīti* is used in the sense of esteem.

By both, he shows: "Just as, for example, O Brahmin. Regarding the phrase "eight, ten, or twelve eggs of a hen," although there may be eggs fewer or more than the stated number, it is nevertheless spoken thus for the sake of euphony in speech.
This is how it should be understood; for in this way, the expression is smooth in common usage. *Tānassa* means *tāni assu*, which is to say, "they would be.
"Properly incubated by a hen" means they were properly incubated by that mother hen as she lay upon them with her wings spread out over them.
"Properly brooded" means she caused them to receive warmth at the appropriate times.

"Thoroughly incubated on all sides" means they have been made warm. "Properly developed" means they have been properly and thoroughly developed from time to time; it is said that they have been made to take on the odor of a hen.
Now, because those eggs were thus protected by that hen in these three ways, they did not become putrid.
...come to be. Even their residual moisture comes to an end. The shell becomes thin, while the tips of the claws and the beak become hard;
the chicks reach maturity, and because the shell is thin, light from the outside is perceived within. Then those chicks [think]:
"Alas, for a long time we have had our hands and feet cramped..."
"We have been lying in a cramped space, yet this light is visible outside; now we shall dwell in comfort here.
Desiring to go out, they strike the shell with their feet and stretch out their necks.
Then that shell splits in two, and the chick-poults emerge, shaking their wings and crying out in a manner suited to that moment.
Thus, among those emerging, whoever emerges first is called "the eldest.
Therefore, wishing to establish his own status as the eldest by means of that simile, the Blessed One asked the brahmin:
"Now, regarding those chicks of the hen... [as before] ...how should he be addressed? In this context, "of those chicks of the hen" refers to—
"Of chicks. "How is he to be addressed? means: how should he be addressed, how should he be spoken to—as the elder or as the younger? The rest is self-evident.
Then the brahmin said: "He is to be addressed as the elder, Master Gotama. "Master Gotama, he is the elder."
He should be addressed [as such]. Why? Because he is their eldest; therefore, the meaning is that he is their senior.
Then, providing a simile for him, the Blessed One said: “Even so, O brahmins,” and so forth.
Just as that chick of a hen is reckoned as the eldest, even so am I among the generation immersed in ignorance (*avijjāgata*). “Immersed in ignorance” means...
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is said to be non-knowing; it is "gone" into that [ignorance]. "Pajā" is a designation for beings (*satta*).
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "among those beings who have entered within the egg-shell of ignorance.
"Aṇḍabhūtāya" means having become, been born, or arisen within an egg. For just as certain beings produced within an egg are called "egg-born," so too is this term used.
Thus, this entire generation is called "egg-born" because it is produced within the shell of ignorance (*avijja*).
"Enveloped" means completely covered, bound, and wrapped by that shell of ignorance. "Having burst the shell of ignorance" means having broken that egg-shell consisting of ignorance.
"I alone am the world" means that throughout the entire habitation of the world, I alone [am the world].
"Alone, without a second. "He has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho*).
*Anuttaraṃ* means "without superior," that which is most excellent. *Sammāsambodhiṃ* means "perfect and personal awakening"; or alternatively, "praised and beautiful awakening.
*Bodhi* refers to the Bodhi tree, the Path, omniscient knowledge, and also Nibbāna. "At the foot of the Bodhi tree..."
In the passages where it says, "the first fully enlightened one," and "between Gayā and Bodhi," the word *bodhi* refers to the tree.
In the passage where it says, "*Bodhi* is said to be the knowledge in the four paths," it refers to the path.
In the passage where it says, "The one of vast wisdom attains *bodhi*," it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). [And] having attained *bodhi*...
In passages where it is said "the deathless, the unconditioned," it refers to Nibbāna. Here, however, the knowledge of the path to Arahatship of the Blessed One is intended;
they also call it the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). Is the path to Arahatship of others the unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarā bodhi*)?
It is not. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities. For in their case, the path to Arahatship leads only to the fruit of Arahatship.

It bestows the three types of higher knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*) upon some, the six direct knowledges (*ṣaḍ abhijñāḥ*) upon others, the four analytical insights (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) upon others, and the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (*śrāvakapāramitājñānam*) upon others. It bestows the very knowledge of the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabodhijñānam*) even upon the *pratyekabuddhas*.

But for the Buddhas, it bestows the perfection of all qualities, just as an anointing confers upon a king the state of sovereignty over the entire world. Therefore, it is unsurpassed for anyone else whatsoever.
“Enlightenment does not exist. He realized and penetrated that he was fully awakened; what is meant is that he had reached and attained it.

Now, this application of the simile spoken by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with, “In the same way, O brahmins,” should be understood by correlating it with this meaning. For just as that hen, regarding her own eggs...

The performance of the threefold action beginning with incubation; likewise, for the Blessed One while he was still a Bodhisatta sitting at the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), the performance of the threefold contemplation (anupassanā) upon his own mental continuum as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Just as the eggs do not rot through the hen’s accomplishment of the threefold action, so too, through the Blessed One’s accomplishment of the threefold contemplation while he was a Bodhisatta—

The non-decline of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). Just as the moisture and grease within the eggs are exhausted by the hen’s performance of the threefold action, so too is the moisture of craving (*nikanti-sineha*) that follows along with the three realms of existence exhausted for the Blessed One while he was a Bodhisatta, through his accomplishment of the threefold contemplation (*tividhānupassanā*).
Just as the shells of the eggs become thin through the hen’s performance of the threefold action, so it was for the Blessed One while he was a Bodhisatta... [the text continues].
Through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation, the shell of the egg of ignorance is thinned. Just as the claws, talons,
and beak of a chick become firm and sharp through the hen performing her threefold duties, so too,
through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation by the Blessed One while he was a Bodhisatta, his knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) became keen, sharp, clear, and courageous.
Just as the time for the maturation of a chicken chick occurs through the hen performing the threefold act,
so too the time for the maturation and growth of the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) by the Blessed One while he was a Bodhisatta— through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation—
should be understood as the time of conception.
Then, just as a hen, by performing the threefold action, pierces the shell of her chick with the tip of her claw or her beak,
fans its wings, and [allows it] to emerge safely; so too,

for the Blessed One while he was a Bodhisatta, having caused the embryo of insight-knowledge to take conception through the accomplishment of the threefold contemplation, [it was brought forth] by means of gradual attainment.

It should be understood that by means of the path of arahantship, having split open the eggshell of ignorance and burst through the membrane of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), the time when all the qualities of a Buddha were realized in safety is to be known.
"Therefore, O Brahmin, I am the eldest, the best in the world"— O Brahmin, just as among those chicks of the hen,
the chick that first splits open the eggshell and emerges is the eldest, even so, for those who have entered into ignorance...
Having split open that eggshell of ignorance for the world, he attained the designation "the eldest" and "the most senior" because he was born first of all through noble birth;
and because he is peerless in all virtues, he is "the best.
Having thus revealed to the brahmin his own unsurpassed state as the eldest and the best, the Blessed One now—by means of which...
In order to show that path from its preliminary stage onwards—how he attained it by means of that path—the Blessed One said, "But, brahmins, exertion was undertaken by me," and so forth.
Alternatively, having heard of this unsurpassed state of being the eldest and best of the Blessed One, the brahmin’s mind arose thus:
"By what path, indeed, has he reached this? Having known his mind, [the Blessed One spoke].
He spoke thus, demonstrating: "By means of this practice, I have attained this unsurpassed state of being the eldest and most excellent.
In that regard, "But energy was aroused by me, brahmin," means:
O brahmin, this unsurpassed state of being the eldest and most excellent was not attained by me while being lazy, heedless, with a restless body, or with a distracted mind.

Moreover, for the sake of attaining that, energy was exerted by me; while seated at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), energy endowed with four factors was exerted by me—it is said to have been "aroused," meaning it proceeded without slackening.
And because it was indeed aroused, it was not sluggish. And it was not only energy, but mindfulness as well.
It became established for me by way of being directed toward its object. And because it was established, it was not forgotten.
"The body is tranquil and unagitated": through the tranquility of both body and mind, my body also became tranquil.
In this context, since the material body also becomes tranquil when the mental body is tranquil, [the text] speaks without making a distinction between the mental body and the material body.
"The body is tranquil" is said. "Unagitated" means that it is unagitated precisely because of its tranquility;
what is meant is that it is free from distress. "The mind is concentrated, one-pointed": my mind, too, was rightly placed, well-established, as if fixed;
and because of its concentration, it was one-pointed, unmoving, and unwavering. Up to this point, [the description] of jhāna...
The preliminary practice has been explained.
Now, beginning with the first jhāna attained by means of this practice, [the exposition] proceeds up to the conclusion of the threefold true knowledge.

Showing the distinction, he said, "So indeed I... and so forth. In that context, although regarding such passages as "quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states," [it might be asked]:
"Therein, what are sensual pleasures (*kāma*)? Desire is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, desire-and-lust is sensual pleasure;
intention is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, intention-and-lust is sensual pleasure—these are called sensual pleasures. Therein, what are..."
What are unwholesome states? Sensual desire … [and so on] … doubt—these are called unwholesome states.
Thus, he is secluded from these sensual pleasures and secluded from these unwholesome states; therefore it is said:
“Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states,” and so forth. The meaning has already been stated in the *Vibhaṅga* according to this method. Nevertheless, …
Since this matter is not clearly evident without the method of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), we shall explain it according to that very method.
That is to say: "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures" means having become secluded from, separated from, and withdrawn from sensual pleasures.

Furthermore, the particle *eva* (quite) used here should be understood as having the sense of restriction (*niyama*). And because it has the sense of restriction, therefore [only] in that [state] is there the first jhāna.

This indicates that even though sensual desires are not actually present at the time of entering and abiding [in the first jhāna], they constitute the antithesis of that first jhāna, and that its attainment occurs precisely through the relinquishing of those desires.
How so? By making the restriction "quite secluded from sensual desires," this becomes evident:
surely sensual desires must be the antithesis of this jhāna, for when they are present, this [jhāna] does not arise.
It does not proceed, just as a lamp [does not shine] when there is darkness;
its attainment occurs only through the relinquishing of those [unwholesome states], just as the further shore is reached only by relinquishing the near shore. Therefore, he establishes a restriction.
In this regard, it might be asked: "Why was this stated only in the first member [of the compound] and not in the second? What [is the purpose of excluding] unwholesome states?"
“Could one, even without having investigated, enter and dwell in jhāna? This, however, should not be viewed in that way.

For it was stated in the preceding phrase precisely because of its transcendence of that [realm]. Indeed, because it transcends the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) and because it is the antidote to sensual lust (kāmarāga), this jhāna is the very escape from sensual desires.
As it has been said: “This is the escape from sensual desires, namely, renunciation (nekkhamma).”

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent phrase, it should be stated by supplying the word *eva* (only), just as in the passage: "Right here, monks, is the first ascetic; right here is the second ascetic.

For it is not possible to enter and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from unwholesome states known as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Therefore, [it should be said]: "secluded indeed from sensual pleasures..."
“Having become quite secluded from unwholesome states”—thus this should be understood in both instances of the phrase.

And although in both cases all forms of seclusion, such as seclusion by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgaviveka*) and so forth, as well as physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) and so forth, are included under the general term “having become secluded,” nevertheless, there are only three:
physical seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion by suppression (*vikkhambhanaviveka*).

These are to be understood here. By the phrase "by means of sensual pleasures" (*kāmehi*), however, it should be understood that all are included—both the sensual objects (*vatthukāmā*) described in the *Niddesa* by way of the formula beginning, "What are sensual objects?

Agreeable forms," and so forth, and the sensual defilements (*kilesakāmā*) described in that same [text] and in the *Vibhaṅga* by way of the formula beginning, "Desire is sensual pleasure," and so forth. For this being the case, [the text says]: "Quite secluded..."
The meaning “secluded even from sense-pleasures (*vatthukāma*)” is appropriate for the phrase “from sense-pleasures. By this, physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) is expressed.

The meaning “secluded from unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*)” is appropriate for the phrase “secluded from unwholesome states,” whether it refers to the defilements of sense-pleasure (*kilesakāma*) or from all unwholesome states.
By this, mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*) is expressed. And here, by the very mention of seclusion from sense-pleasures in the former [phrase], [physical seclusion is indicated].

By the first [verse], through the renunciation of sensual pleasure, the embracing of the happiness of renunciation is manifested by virtue of the statement regarding seclusion from the defilements of sensuality (kilesakāma).

Thus, precisely because of these statements regarding seclusion from objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and the defilements of sensuality, the abandoning of the basis for defilement is shown by the first, and the abandoning of the defilement itself by the second;
by the first, there is the renunciation of the cause of greediness, and by the second, that of foolishness.
It should be understood that by the first [verse], purification of the means is revealed, and by the second, the nourishing of the underlying disposition (*āsaya*).
This is the method, first of all, regarding the "sensual pleasures" mentioned here in the sense of objects (*vatthu-kāma*).
However, in the sense of defilements (*kilesa-kāma*), it is simply sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) itself, which has many divisions such as "zeal" (*chanda*) and "lust" (*rāga*).

"Kāma" is intended here. Although it is included within the unwholesome (akusala), it is mentioned separately in the *Vibhaṅga* as the opposite of jhāna, according to the method beginning with: "In this context, what is sensual desire (kāmachanda)?
It is kāma. Alternatively, it is mentioned in the first phrase because it is a defilement-kāma (kilesakāma), and in the second phrase because it is included within the unwholesome.
Furthermore, rather than saying "by kāma" (kāmato) because of its manifold divisions, it is said "by means of kāmās" (kāmehi).

Although other states also exist that are unwholesome, they are mentioned specifically as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) in the Vibhaṅga by way of the passage beginning, "In this context, what are the unwholesome states?
They are sensual desire," and so forth. This is because it demonstrates that, among those [unwholesome states], the hindrances alone function as the opposites and adversaries to the factors of jhāna.
For the hindrances are the opposites of the jhāna-factors; indeed, the jhāna-factors themselves are their adversaries and destroyers.
This has been stated. For it is said in the *Peṭaka*: “Concentration is the antidote to sensual desire; rapture is the antidote to ill will;
applied thought is the antidote to sloth and torpor; pleasure is the antidote to restlessness and remorse; and sustained thought is the antidote to doubt.
Thus, in this context, by the phrase “quite secluded from sensual desires,” the seclusion consisting in suppression of sensual desire is expressed.
By the phrase “secluded from unwholesome states,” there is the abandoning of all five hindrances.
By way of inclusive inclusion, however, the first [phrase] refers to sensual desire, while the second refers to the remaining hindrances.

Likewise, among the three unwholesome roots, the first refers to greed whose object is the variety of the five strands of sense pleasure, while the second refers to hatred and delusion whose objects are the various bases for resentment and so forth.

Or, regarding the categories beginning with the floods (*ogha*): by the first [set], there is the abandoning of the flood of sensual desire, the yoke of sensual desire, the taint of sensual desire, the clinging of sensual desire, the bodily tie of covetousness, and the fetter of lust for sensual desire;
by the second, the remaining floods, yokes, taints, clingings, ties, and fetters. Furthermore, by the first, there is the abandoning of craving and those mental states associated with it;
by the second, ignorance and those mental states associated with it. Moreover, by the first, there is the abandoning of the eight types of consciousness arising in association with greed.
By the second [phrase], it should be understood that the seclusion by suppression of the remaining four unwholesome types of consciousness is stated.
This, first of all, is the exposition of the meaning of the passage: “quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states.
Having thus far shown the factor of abandoning for the first jhāna, he now shows the factor of association:
He said, "With applied thought (savitakka) and sustained thought (savicāra)," and so forth. In this context, *vitakka* is the act of applying the mind; it is said to mean "investigating.
It has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object (*ārammaṇa*). Its function is striking and repeatedly striking [the object]. For it is said:
"By means of that, the practitioner makes the object struck by applied thought, repeatedly struck by applied thought. Its manifestation is the leading of the mind toward the object.
Vicāra is sustained examination; it is said to be "moving along after. Its characteristic is the continued rubbing of the object;
its function is to keep associated states engaged with that object; its manifestation is the continuous binding of the mind [to the object].
And although these two are inseparable in some instances, by virtue of its grossness, vitakka is the mind's initial impact, like the sound produced by the striking of a bell.
Applied thought (*vitakka*) is the initial directing of the mind; sustained thought (*vicāra*) is the continuous following after, like a subtle resonance.

Herein, applied thought is expansive, being the state of mental movement, like the flapping of wings by a bird wishing to fly into the air, or like the bee’s descent toward a lotus when its mind is drawn by the fragrance.
Sustained thought has a peaceful course, being the state of not excessively moving about.

It is like the spreading of wings and the circling of a bird that has flown up into the sky, or like a bee falling toward a lotus hovering above the lotus; however, that distinction between these two becomes manifest in the first and second jhānas.
Thus, it proceeds together with this applied thought (*vitakka*) and this sustained thought (*vicāra*), just as a tree does with its flowers.
And because of its fruit, this jhāna is called "with applied thought and sustained thought.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, the teaching is given by way of reference to the person, in the manner beginning: "It is endowed with this applied thought and this sustained thought, fully endowed...
But the meaning there should also be understood in exactly the same way.

Regarding "born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*): here, *viveka* means seclusion, that is, withdrawal; the meaning is the disappearance of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Alternatively, *viveka* means that which is secluded;
the meaning is the mass of states associated with jhāna, being secluded from the hindrances. Therefore, it is "born of seclusion" because it arises from seclusion, or in that seclusion.
Regarding "rapture and pleasure" (*pītisukha*): here, *pīti* means it gladdens; its characteristic is endearment, its function is to refresh body and mind, and its function is pervading.
Alternatively, [joy] has gladness as its manifestation. Pleasure (*sukha*) is so called because it is pleasant, or because it thoroughly consumes and carves away bodily and mental afflictions;
thus, pleasure has gratification as its characteristic, the strengthening of associated states as its function, and assistance as its manifestation.
And although these two are sometimes inseparable, joy is the satisfaction at obtaining a desirable object, whereas pleasure is the experiencing of the flavor of what has been obtained.

Pleasure (*sukha*). Where there is rapture (*pīti*), there is pleasure; but where there is pleasure, there is not necessarily rapture. Rapture is included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*);
pleasure is included within the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*). Rapture is like seeing or hearing about water at the edge of a forest when one is exhausted by a desert journey;
pleasure is like entering the shade of that forest and enjoying the water. At each respective time:

And it should be understood that this is stated because of its manifest nature. Since this rapture (*pīti*) and this bliss (*sukha*) exist in this jhāna, or in this jhāna, this jhāna is called "rapture-and-bliss" (*pītisukha*).
Alternatively, "rapture-and-bliss" (*pītisukha*) refers to both rapture and bliss, just like the terms *dhamma-vinaya* and so forth. Rapture-and-bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja*) belongs to it.
Or, it is "born of seclusion" because this joy and happiness exist in this jhāna. For just as the jhāna itself, so too the joy and happiness herein are born of seclusion;
and since they belong to it, it is therefore appropriate to call it by the single phrase "joy and happiness born of seclusion.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, it says: "This happiness is accompanied by this joy," and so forth.
