This has been stated according to the method [of exposition]. However, the meaning there should also be understood in exactly this way.
It is "first" (*paṭhama*) because it is first in the numerical sequence; it is also "first" because this is the first one to be attained.

It is "meditation" (*jhāna*) because it burns up (*jhāpeti*) opposing states; it is also "meditation" because by means of it, yogis meditate (*jhāyanti*), burning up opposing states within their field of experience.
The meaning is that they contemplate it. Or, it is called *jhāna* because one contemplates (*jhāyati*) and closely contemplates (*upanijjhāyati*) it oneself;

for this very reason, it is said to have the characteristic of close contemplation. This [close contemplation] is twofold: close contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and close contemplation of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*).

Therein, "close contemplation of the object" refers to the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) together with access concentration. Why? Because they involve the close contemplation of objects such as the kasiṇas and so forth.
"Contemplation of characteristics" refers to insight, the path, and the fruit. Why?
Because of the contemplation of characteristics. For herein, insight contemplates the characteristics such as impermanence;
however, since the function of contemplating is accomplished by the path, the path is called "contemplation of characteristics. As for the fruit, it is [the realization] of cessation.
It is called "contemplation of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*) because it contemplates the characteristic of suchness.

However, in this context, what is intended by "jhāna" is specifically the contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*). Here one asks: "But what is that which is called jhāna, which is with applied thought and sustained thought... [and] accompanied by rapture and pleasure?"

"Does he thus deserve to be designated [by that name]? It is said: Just as in expressions such as "with wealth" or "with retinue," there is something else besides the wealth and the retinue that deserves to be so designated, so too, apart from the mental states such as applied thought (vitakka), there is nothing else that deserves to be so designated.
However, just as when it is said, "an army with its chariots" or "an army with its wives," the designation "army" applies specifically to the constituent parts of the army, so it is here.

The designation "jhāna" should be understood as applying only to five factors. Which five? Initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), pleasure (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā)—it is to these that the designation applies.
For it is precisely these that have been stated as constituent factors by way of the method beginning with "with initial application and sustained application.
If it is argued that one-pointedness is not a factor because it has not been so stated [in that specific formula], that is not so. Why? Because it has indeed been stated.

It is indeed so. For in the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated precisely thus: "Jhāna is applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittassekaggatā*).

Therefore, just as [jhāna] is described as "with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ*), so too—though not explicitly mentioned here—one-pointedness of mind must be understood as a factor by this statement from the *Vibhaṅga*. For it was with this very intention that the Blessed One [spoke].
The summary (uddesa) has been given; that very same [summary] is also explained in detail (vibhaṅga).
"Having attained" (upasampajja) means having approached, which is to say, having reached; or it means having brought about, having accomplished.
In the Vibhaṅga, however, it says: "Attaining (upasampajja) means the gaining, the obtaining, the reaching of the first jhāna."
"It is said: 'attainment, contact, touching, realization, and full admission. Its meaning should be understood in exactly this way.

'While dwelling' means: having become possessed of the aforementioned kind of jhāna through the mode of conduct known as sitting upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he brought about the movement, the activity, the protection, the maintenance, the sustenance, the course, and the dwelling of his own being."
This is the meaning. For it is said in the Vibhaṅga: “‘Dwells’ means he moves about, conducts himself, protects, maintains, sustains, goes about, dwells;
therefore it is called ‘dwells.
But having done what did the Blessed One enter upon and dwell in this jhāna? Having developed the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Which one?
The meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati-kammaṭṭhāna*). What should another person who desires it do?

Another person should also develop either this meditation subject or one of the others, such as the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*) and so forth. The method for developing these is to be understood according to the method already stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, if they were explained here, the introduction to the training would become too burdensome; therefore, we shall merely provide an exposition of the meaning of the text.
The Discourse on the First Jhāna is finished.
The Discourse on the Second Jhāna:
"With the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought" means with the subsiding of these two, namely, applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
"By surmounting"; this means that at the moment of the second jhāna, they are not manifest.

In this regard, although none of the factors of the first jhāna exist in the second jhāna—since the contact and other factors in the first jhāna are one thing and those here are another—it is nevertheless said "by surmounting each successive gross factor" because of the surmounting of the first jhāna for the sake of the subsequent states, such as the second jhāna.
It should be understood that the phrase "with the stilling of applied and sustained thought" was spoken for the purpose of illustrating that realization occurs.
Here, "internally" (ajjhatta) refers to one's own internal state (niyakajjhatta). In the Vibhaṅga, however, only this much is stated: "internally, personally" (ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ).
Since it is one's own internal state that is intended, therefore [it means] "born within oneself," belonging to oneself.
They arise in the mental continuum; this is the meaning here.

"Sampasādana" refers to faith (*saddhā*). Because it is associated with clarity, the jhāna itself is called "sampasādana," just as a garment is called "blue" because it is associated with the color blue.
Or rather, because that jhāna is endowed with clarity through the subsiding of the agitation caused by applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*), [it is so named].

It clarifies the mind; therefore it is called "tranquillity" (*sampasādana*). And in this interpretation of the meaning, the connection between the words should be understood as "tranquillity of the mind.
But in the previous interpretation of the meaning, the word "of the mind" (*cetaso*) should be joined with "singleness" (*ekodibhāvena*).
Therein, this is the construction of the meaning: that which arises alone is "single" (*ekodi*); [it is so called] because of [the absence of] applied thought and sustained thought.
The meaning is that, because it has not ascended [to higher levels], it arises as the foremost and best. For even in the world, one who is best is called "one" (*eka*).

Alternatively, it may be said that it is "one" in the sense of being alone, devoid of applied thought and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*). Or else, it is "arising" (*udi*) because it causes associated states to arise—that is, it causes them to stand up.
It is "one" in the sense of being preeminent, and it is "arising" (*udi*); thus it is "one-pointedness" (*ekodi*). This is a term for concentration (*samādhi*).
It is a designation. Thus, because one develops and increases this singleness (*ekodi*), this second jhāna is "singleness" (*ekodibhāva*).
Since this singleness belongs to the mind (*cetaso*) and not to a being (*satta*) or a soul (*jīva*), it is therefore called "the state of singleness of the mind" (*cetaso ekodibhāva*).

But surely this faith (*saddhā*) exists even in the first jhāna, and this concentration named "singleness" (*ekodi*) is present there too; so why is it only this [second jhāna] that is [so designated]?
Is it said that "tranquillity" (sampasādana) and "unification of mind" (cetaso ekodibhāva) are mentioned [only] here? It is replied:

For that first jhāna, being agitated by applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra), is not perfectly clear, like water troubled by ripples and waves; therefore, even though faith (saddhā) is present, "tranquillity" is not mentioned.
And because it is not perfectly clear, concentration (samādhi) is also not well-manifested therein; therefore, "unification of mind" is also [not mentioned].

It was not stated [there]. However, in this jhāna, because the hindrances of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are absent, faith (*saddhā*) gains its opportunity and becomes powerful;

and through the acquisition of such powerful faith as its companion, concentration (*samādhi*) also becomes manifest. Therefore, it should be understood that this [jhāna] alone is described in this way.
In the *Vibhaṅga*, however, it says: "Sampasādana means that which is faith, believing, conviction, and full confidence."
"Unification of the mind" refers to that stability of the mind... [as far as] "...right concentration. Only this much was stated.
However, this commentary on the meaning should be understood in such a way that it does not contradict what was thus stated, but rather accords with it and is entirely consistent.

"Without applied thought and without sustained thought": because it has been abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is no applied thought (*vitakka*) in this [state] or for this [state], thus it is "without applied thought.
By this same method, it is "without sustained thought" (*avicāra*). It is also said in the *Vibhaṅga*:
"Thus, this applied thought and this sustained thought have become stilled, calmed, subsided, passed away, vanished, dissolved, fully dissolved, dried up, and completely dried up."
“...having been brought to an end; therefore it is called ‘without applied thought and without sustained thought.
Here it may be asked: “Is this meaning not already established by the phrase ‘with the stilling of applied and sustained thought’?
Then why is it stated again as ‘without applied thought and without sustained thought’? It is replied: This is indeed so; this meaning is established, yet it is not [redundant].

That explains its meaning; for have we not already said: "The words 'the subsiding of applied and sustained thought' are spoken thus for the purpose of showing that the attainment of the second jhāna and those following it occurs through the surmounting of each successive gross factor of the first jhāna"?

Furthermore, this "tranquillity" (*sampasādana*) arises from the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā*), not from the removal of the turbidity of the defilements (*kilesakālusiyassa*). And from the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, there is "singleness" (*ekodibhāva*);

this is not like access concentration (*upacārajjhāna*), which results from the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇappahānā*), nor like the first jhāna, which results from the manifestation of its factors (*aṅgapātubhāvā*).
Thus, this statement illustrates the causes for both tranquillity and singleness. Likewise:

"With the subsiding of applied thought and sustained thought, this is without applied thought and without sustained thought" indicates the cause for the state of being without applied thought and sustained thought—meaning it is not that they are non-existent as in the third and fourth jhānas or as in eye-consciousness and so forth—and it does not merely indicate the absence of applied thought and sustained thought.
However, the expression "without applied thought, without sustained thought" does indeed merely indicate the absence of applied thought and sustained thought; therefore...
"Even though it was stated previously, it must be stated again.
The phrase "born of concentration" (samādhija) means born from the concentration of the first jhāna, or from the associated concentration.
In this regard, although the first [jhāna] is also born from associated concentration, nevertheless, only this [second jhāna] deserves to be called "concentration."
It is worthy [of the designation] because it is exceedingly immovable and perfectly serene due to its freedom from the agitation of applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*).
Therefore, for the purpose of praising this state, it is described as "born of concentration" (*samādhija*). "Rapture and happiness" (*pīti-sukha*) is exactly as previously explained.
"Second" (*dutiya*) means second in the numerical sequence; it is also called "second" because one attains this as the second [jhāna]. "Jhāna" (*jhāna*)...

In this context, however, just as the first jhāna possesses five factors such as applied thought (vitakka) and so forth, so too should this be understood as "four-factored" by way of serenity (sampasāda) and the rest.
As it is said: "Jhāna is serenity, rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind. This is indeed a figurative expression;
for if one sets aside the act of serenifying itself, then in its primary sense (nippariyāya), this jhāna consists of only three factors.
As it is said: "What at that time is the three-factored jhāna? Rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind.
The rest is exactly as described by the method already stated.
The discussion of the second jhāna is finished.
Regarding the discussion of the third jhāna:
"With the fading away of rapture" (*pītiyā ca virāgā*); here, *pīti* has the meaning already explained. *Virāga* means either a sense of disgust toward it or its transcendence.

Between these two, the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction; for it either joins [the phrase] with tranquility, or it joins [it] with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicāra*).

Alternatively: when one groups [the factors] together as "only tranquility," then the construction should be understood as follows: "due to the fading away of rapture (*pīti*) and, moreover, due to tranquility (*vūpasama*).
In this construction, "fading away" (*virāga*) has the sense of disgust.

Therefore, the meaning should be seen as: "due to disgust for rapture and due to tranquility. However, when [one groups them] as "the subsiding of applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicāra-vūpasama*),...

When one combines [the phrases], the construction should be understood as follows: "and with the fading away of rapture (pīti), moreover, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought (vitakkavicāraṇaṃ).
In this construction, "fading away" (virāga) has the sense of "surmounting. Therefore, the meaning should be seen as:
"from the surmounting of rapture, and from the stilling of applied and sustained thought."

Granted that these applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) have already been stilled in the second jhāna itself, this [phrase] is nevertheless stated for the purpose of illustrating the path of this jhāna and for the purpose of praising it.
For when it is said, "With the stilling of applied and sustained thought," this is understood:
"Surely the stilling of applied and sustained thought is the path to this jhāna. And just as in the case of the third noble path...
Even in the case of personality view and the other fetters that have not yet been abandoned,
when their "abandoning" is spoken of as "the abandoning of the five lower fetters," it constitutes a praise that generates enthusiasm in those striving for their attainment.
In the same way, even though applied and sustained thought have not yet subsided here, the "subsiding" of them is spoken of as a praise.
Therefore, this meaning was stated: “With the surmounting of rapture and with the stilling of applied and sustained thought.
Regarding the phrase “and he dwelt equanimous”: here, it is called *upekkhā* because one views (*ikkhati*) by way of arising;

the meaning is that one sees evenly, seeing while remaining without partiality. Because he is endowed with that [equanimity] which is clear, expansive, and firmly established, he is a possessor of the third jhāna.
“One who is equanimous” is what is said. Equanimity, however, is tenfold:

equanimity with the six factors, equanimity as a divine abiding, equanimity as a factor of enlightenment, equanimity of energy, equanimity regarding formations, equanimity regarding feeling, equanimity of insight, equanimity as specific neutrality, equanimity of jhāna, and equanimity of purification.
Thus, this tenfold equanimity—according to the method presented in various places—is classified by way of plane, person, consciousness, and object.

It should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā* (the *Aṭṭhasālinī*) by way of the compendium of aggregates, the single-moment wholesome triad, and the summary;
however, it is not mentioned here because doing so would make the introduction to the Vinaya too burdensome.
As for its characteristics and so forth, the equanimity intended here has the characteristic of neutrality (*majjhatta*), the function of non-exertion, and the manifestation of non-activity.
"Having rapture as its proximate cause.
Here it is asked: Is this not, in meaning, simply equanimity as specific neutrality?
And since that exists in the first and second jhānas as well, should it not therefore be said of those too, "And he dwelt in equanimity"? Why is it not so stated there?
Why is it said [to be "present"]? Because its function is not fully manifest. For its function there is unmanifest due to being overwhelmed by applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other factors.
But here, because it is not overwhelmed by applied thought, sustained thought, and rapture (*pīti*), it has become one whose function is fully manifest, as if with its head held high;
therefore, it is said [to be "present"].
The complete commentary on the meaning of the phrase “and he dwelt with equanimity” is finished.
Now, regarding the phrase “mindful and clearly comprehending”: one who remembers is “mindful” (*sato*); one who clearly understands is “clearly comprehending” (*sampajāno*).

Thus, mindfulness and clear comprehension are stated by way of the person. In this context, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering, the function of non-forgetfulness, and the manifestation of protection.
Clear comprehension has non-delusion as its characteristic, investigation as its function, and discrimination as its manifestation.
Although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist even in the preceding jhānas— for one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension does not even achieve access concentration,
let alone absorption— nevertheless, because those jhānas are gross, it is like a man on the ground [who cannot see what is above].
The movement of the mind is pleasant, yet therein the task of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*) is not evident.

However, because this jhāna is subtle due to the abandoning of gross factors, the movement of the mind must be maintained as being embraced by the task of mindfulness and clear comprehension—just as for a man on the edge of a razor’s blade;
therefore, it is stated right here [in this context]. Furthermore, it is like a calf that follows its mother.
Just as a calf that has been taken away from its mother cow, if left unguarded, returns to the cow once more;

so too, this bliss of the third jhāna, even though it has been removed from rapture (*pīti*), if left unguarded by the protection of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), might return to rapture and become associated with rapture once again.
Furthermore, beings are attached to pleasure, and this is an exceedingly sweet pleasure; therefore—

It is because of the absence of supreme happiness [in the lower jhānas]. However, it should be understood that this was stated specifically here in order to show this particular distinction: that in this state, there is no attachment to pleasure by virtue of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), whereas this is not the case otherwise.

Now, regarding the phrase "he experiences pleasure with the body" (*sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti*): although for one possessing the third jhāna there is an application of mind toward the experience of pleasure...

It does not exist; nevertheless, because there is pleasure associated with his mental body (*nāmakāya*), or because his material body (*rūpakāya*) is suffused by an exceedingly refined matter produced by that pleasure associated with the mental body—by virtue of which suffusion he would experience pleasure even after emerging from meditative absorption—it is for the purpose of showing this meaning that it says: "and [he experiences] pleasure with the body."
He said, "he experienced. Now,
regarding that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous," it is on account of this jhāna,
for the sake of this jhāna, that the Noble Ones— the Buddhas and others— describe and teach that person who possesses the third jhāna.
They describe it, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it plain, and elucidate it; the intention is that they praise it.
How so? By saying, "Equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness. Thus, the construction here should be understood as: "Having attained and dwelt in that third jhāna."
But why do they praise him in this way? Because he is worthy of praise.
For he is equanimous even toward the third jhāna, which possesses exceedingly sweet bliss and has reached the perfection of happiness;

he is not drawn there by attachment to that bliss, and just as rapture (pīti) does not arise, so too he is mindful through the presence of established mindfulness. And because he [possesses] what is beloved by the Noble Ones...
And he experiences with his mental body a happiness that is untainted and practiced only by noble persons; therefore, he is worthy of praise.

Thus, it should be understood that because he is worthy of praise, the Noble Ones—manifesting those very qualities that serve as the grounds for praise—praise him in this way: "He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous."
"Third": it is the third in the numerical sequence; it is also called "third" because one attains this as the third [meditative attainment]. Regarding "jhāna":
just as the second jhāna possesses four factors beginning with serenity (*sampasāda*), so too this [third jhāna] possesses five factors beginning with equanimity (*upekkhā*).
As it is said: "Jhāna is equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), bliss, and one-pointedness of mind. This is merely a synonym.
This is so. However, excluding equanimity and mindfulness-and-clear-comprehension, this [jhāna] consists of only two factors in the direct sense (nippariyāya).
As it is said: "What at that time is the two-factored jhāna? It is bliss and one-pointedness of mind.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The discussion on the third jhāna is concluded.
The discussion on the fourth jhāna:
“With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain” means with the abandoning of bodily pleasure and bodily pain.
"He has already abandoned" means that he has done so previously, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna.
"With the disappearance of mental pleasure and mental pain" means that these two—namely, mental happiness and mental suffering—have already disappeared and been abandoned;
this is what is meant. When, then, does their abandonment occur? At the moment of the access concentration (upacāra) of the four jhānas.
For mental joy (*somanassa*) is abandoned at the very moment of the access concentration (*upacārakkhaṇa*) of the fourth jhāna;
while pain (*dukkha*), mental grief (*domanassa*), and pleasure (*sukha*) are abandoned at the moments of access for the first, second, and third jhānas respectively.

Thus, although the order of their abandonment has not been stated here, the abandonment of pleasure, pain, mental joy, and mental grief should be understood according to the order in which these faculties (*indriya*) are enumerated in the *Indriyavibhaṅga*.
But if these are abandoned at the very moment of access concentration (*upacārakkhaṇa*) for each respective jhāna, then why [is it said]:
"And where does the arisen faculty of pain cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...
attains and dwells in the first jhāna; it is here that the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder"?
"It ceases. And where does the arisen faculty of mental grief... the faculty of pleasure... the faculty of mental joy cease without remainder?
Here, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure... [etc. ...a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna;
herein the arisen faculty of mental joy ceases without remainder. Thus it is said regarding the jhānas themselves.

Is it said that there is cessation? Because it is a cessation of excellence (*atisayanirodha*). For in the first jhāna and so forth, there is indeed a cessation of excellence for these [factors], but not a total cessation;
however, at the moment of access (*upacāra*), there is only cessation, not a cessation of excellence.

For instance, even when the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*) has ceased during the access to the first jhāna through the application of various objects, it may still arise due to contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or from the affliction of an uneven seat.
Or there may be its arising in access, but not within absorption. In access, even though this [pain] has ceased, it is not thoroughly ceased because it has not been struck down by its opposite.
But within absorption, the entire body becomes suffused with happiness through the pervasion of rapture;
and for one whose body is suffused with happiness, the faculty of pain is thoroughly ceased because it has been struck down by its opposite.
Furthermore, regarding the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*) which was abandoned in the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna among various faults:

since this arises when there is physical fatigue and mental affliction even though applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are its conditions, it does not arise in the absence of applied and sustained thought.
However, wherever it does arise, there applied and sustained thought are present. And these [two] have indeed not yet been abandoned in the preliminary stage of the second jhāna.
"Applied thought and sustained thought": their arising might occur there [in the first jhāna] because their conditions have not been abandoned.

But this is not so in the second jhāna, because their conditions have been abandoned. Likewise, in the preliminary stage of the third jhāna, although the faculty of pleasure has been abandoned, its arising might still occur for the body touched by the sublime matter produced by rapture;
but this is not so in the actual third jhāna. For in the third jhāna, rapture—which is the condition for pleasure—has ceased entirely.

"Ceased": likewise, although the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) has been abandoned in the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) of the fourth jhāna, its arising might still occur because it is proximate and because the state has not yet fully transcended it due to the absence of equanimity (*upekkhā*) that has reached absorption (*appanā*).
However, this is not the case in the fourth jhāna itself. And for this very reason, it is said: "Here, the arisen faculty of bodily pain ceases without remainder."
In each of those instances, the term "without remainder" (aparisesa) has been employed.
Here it may be asked: "If these feelings have already been abandoned in the access (upacāra) stage of each respective jhāna, why are they included here?
It is for the purpose of grasping the pleasure (sukha). For that feeling which was described as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (adukkhamasukha) in this context is indeed pleasure.
It is subtle and extremely difficult to discern; it cannot be grasped with ease.

Therefore, just as a cowherd, for the sake of catching a bull that is stubborn and impossible to catch by approaching it in any ordinary way, gathers all the cattle together into one pen and then, driving them out one by one, says of the one that comes along in order: "This is it! Catch it!"...
He causes one to grasp even that [neutral feeling] by means of these; in the same way, the Blessed One has collected all these for the sake of easy comprehension.

For when they are thus collected and shown, it is possible to cause one to grasp this: "That which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither mental joy nor mental grief, is this neither-pain-nor-pleasure feeling."
Furthermore, it should be understood that these [factors] are taught for the purpose of showing the conditions for the deliverance of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
For the abandoning of pleasure and so forth are its conditions. As it is said: "There are, friends, four conditions for the attainment of the deliverance of mind that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...enters upon and dwells in the fourth jhāna."
“...having attained, he dwells. These, friends, are the four conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind.

Alternatively, it should be understood that just as elsewhere the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth—though already abandoned—are said to be “abandoned there” for the purpose of praising the third path, so too these [fetters] are mentioned here for the purpose of praising this jhāna.
Alternatively, it should be understood that these [feelings] are mentioned here to show the extreme remoteness of lust and hatred by way of the destruction of their conditions.
For among these, pleasure is the condition for joy, joy for lust; pain is the condition for grief, and grief for hatred.
And by the destruction of pleasure and the rest, those lust and hatred, together with their conditions, are destroyed and thus become extremely remote.

"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant" means it is not painful due to the absence of pain, and not pleasant due to the absence of pleasure. By this, he indicates here a third feeling that is the opposite of both pain and pleasure, rather than merely the absence of pain and pleasure.
This third feeling is called "neither-painful-nor-pleasant," and it is also termed "equanimity" (*upekkhā*).
Its characteristic is the experience of what is neither desirable nor undesirable; its function is neutrality; its manifestation is non-manifestation.
They should be understood as the footing for the cessation of pleasure. "Purity of mindfulness through equanimity" means the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity.
For in this jhāna, mindfulness is perfectly pure. And that purity of mindfulness is effected by equanimity and not by anything else;
therefore, it is called "purity of mindfulness through equanimity. This is also stated in the *Vibhaṅga*: "This..."
By means of this equanimity, mindfulness becomes clear, purified, and bright; therefore it is called "purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
And as for that equanimity by which there is purity of mindfulness here, it should be understood in its actual sense as "onlooking-equanimity" (*tatramajjhattatā*).
Not only is mindfulness itself purified by this, but all associated mental states are as well; however, the teaching is expressed under the heading of mindfulness.
In this regard, although this equanimity exists even in the three lower jhānas, it is nevertheless like the crescent moon that, though present by day,
is neither pure nor bright because it is overwhelmed by the sun’s radiance during the day and because it lacks the night which is similar to it in its gentle nature or in its helpfulness;
so too is this crescent moon of equanimity consisting in balance (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).

Because it is overwhelmed by the fires of opposing states such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and because it fails to obtain the corresponding delight of equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā-rati*), this [concentration] remains impure even though it exists within the various stages of the first jhāna and so forth.
And because it is impure, its co-nascent factors such as mindfulness (*sati*) and the rest are likewise impure, like the light of an impure crescent moon during the day; therefore—
Among those [other jhānas], not even one is described as "purity of mindfulness through equanimity" (*upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi*).

Here, however, because there is no overpowering by the heat of opposing states such as applied thought (*vitakka*), and because it has attained a corresponding delight in the feeling of equanimity, this crescent moon of equanimity toward the middle (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) is exceedingly pure.
Due to its purity, like the radiance of a pure crescent moon, the co-nascent factors such as mindfulness (*sati*) and the rest are also purified.
They are completely pure and bright; therefore, it should be understood that this alone is called "the purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
It is the "fourth" because it is fourth in the sequence of counting. It is also called the "fourth" because one attains this as the fourth [jhāna].
Regarding "jhāna": just as the third jhāna possesses five factors beginning with equanimity, so too this [fourth] possesses three factors beginning with equanimity.
As it is said: “Jhāna consists of equanimity, mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind. This is indeed a figurative explanation (pariyāya).
However, setting aside mindfulness and taking only equanimity and one-pointedness, it becomes two-factored (duvaṅgika) in its literal sense (nippariyāya).
As it is said: “What, at that time, is the two-factored jhāna? Equanimity and one-pointedness of mind. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The Discussion of the Fourth Jhāna is finished.
Regarding the Discussion of Past Lives (Pubbenivāsakathā):
Thus, these four jhānas serve as a basis for one-pointedness of mind for some, while for others they serve as a foundation for insight (vipassanā).
For some, they are the basis for direct knowledge; for some, the basis for cessation; and for some, for the purpose of transcending existence.
Among these, for those whose taints are destroyed, they serve the purpose of one-pointedness of mind;

for, having entered them with the thought, "With one-pointed minds we shall dwell happily throughout the day," they perform the preliminary work of the kasiṇas and thus produce the eight attainments. For trainees and worldlings...
For those who, having emerged from attainment, develop insight with a concentrated mind, thinking, "We shall practice insight," these [attainments] serve as the basis for insight.
However, for those who, having produced the eight attainments, enter the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and then, having emerged from attainment,
produce them while aspiring to the direct knowledges described in the method beginning with, "Being one, he becomes many," [these attainments serve as the basis for direct knowledge].
For those [who develop them for this purpose], they serve as the basis for the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).

However, for those who, having produced the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), think, "Having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and remained mindless for seven days, we shall dwell in happiness, having attained Nibbāna—cessation—in this very life," they serve as the basis for cessation. Furthermore, for those who [develop] the eight attainments...
Having produced it, they produce it thinking, "May we arise in the Brahma-world without falling away from our jhāna";
for them, it serves the purpose of ascending to a new existence (bhava).
However, this fourth jhāna was produced by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree; it served both as the basis for his insight (vipassanā) and—

It should be understood that [this concentration] is the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), the basis for the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*), the accomplisher of all tasks, and the bestower of all mundane and supramundane qualities.
To show a portion of those qualities it bestows, he said: "When his mind was thus concentrated" (*so evaṃ samāhite citte*), and so forth.
Therein, "he" (*so*) refers to "I. "Thus" (*evaṃ*) is an indication of the sequence of the fourth jhāna. By this sequence, the fourth jhāna...
"Having obtained" is what is meant. "Concentrated" means concentrated by means of this fourth-jhāna concentration.
Regarding "purified" and so forth: it is "purified" by way of the purity of equanimity and mindfulness; because of that very purity, it is "bright" and "radiant," as it were.
Because the stains of lust and so forth have been destroyed by the removal of conditions such as pleasure, it is "unblemished. Because of that very lack of blemish—
And it is free from defilement; for by means of blemish the mind becomes defiled. Because it is well-developed, it has become pliant; what is meant is that it has reached mastery.
For a mind that functions under control is called "pliant. And because of its very pliancy, it is "workable";
what is meant is that it is capable of work and fit for work. For a pliant mind is workable, like well-refined gold; both of these— [pliancy and workability]—are...

And it is precisely because of its being well-developed. As it is said: "Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that, when developed and cultivated in this way, becomes so supple and wieldy as the mind, monks.
Because of its stability in these qualities such as complete purity, it is "steadied" (*ṭhita*). Precisely because of its steadiness, it has reached imperturbability; it is immovable and unwavering.
This is what is meant. Or else, it is "steadfast" because it stands under its own control by virtue of being pliant and workable;
it has "reached imperturbability" because it is embraced by faith and the other [faculties]. For a mind embraced by faith is not shaken by lack of faith;
one embraced by energy is not shaken by laziness; one embraced by mindfulness is not shaken by negligence; and one embraced by concentration is not shaken by restlessness.
It does not waver: being embraced by wisdom, it does not waver through ignorance; having reached illumination, it does not waver through the darkness of the defilements.
A mind embraced by these six qualities has attained imperturbability.
Thus, a mind endowed with these eight factors is capable of being directed toward the direct realization, through direct knowledge, of those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.
Another method: [the mind] is concentrated by means of the concentration of the fourth jhāna; purified by the removal of the hindrances; cleansed by the surmounting of applied thought and so forth;
free from blemish through the absence of evil states belonging to the sphere of desire that would be conditions for the non-attainment of jhāna;

and free from defilement through the disappearance of mental corruptions such as covetousness and the like. Both of these [terms, "free from blemish" and "free from defilement"], moreover, are according to the *Anaṅgaṇa-vatthu-sutta*.
It should be understood as follows: when it has become supple through the attainment of mastery; when it has become wieldy through the development of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*);

and when it is established and has reached imperturbability through the excellence attained by the perfection of cultivation. "Established" means that it is established in such a way as to have reached imperturbability.
In this way, a mind endowed with these eight factors is capable of being directed toward those things to be realized through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
The meaning is that it is the basis and the foundation for the direct realization through higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) of phenomena.

"For the knowledge of recollection of past lives" means: when this consciousness, which serves as the basis for higher knowledge, has thus arisen, it is for the sake of that knowledge regarding the recollection of past lives.
In this context, "past lives" (*pubbenivāsa*) refers to the aggregates (*khandha*) in which one dwelt in previous, past births. "Dwelt" (*nivutta*) means...
*Dhammas* that have been dwelt upon (*ajjhāvutthā*)— having arisen and ceased within one’s own continuum— and experienced (*anubhūtā*), or those that have been inhabited (*nivutthā*),

meaning they have been inhabited by way of being an object of experience (*gocaranivāsena*) or discerned (*viññātā*) and delimited by one’s own consciousness, or even discerned by the consciousness of another,
as in the recollection of past lives (*chinnavaṭumakānussaraṇa*) and so forth. *Pubbenivāsānussati* is that mindfulness (*sati*) by which one recollects a previous dwelling (*pubbenivāsa*).
That is the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati*). "Knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) refers to the knowledge associated with that recollection.
Thus, it is said: "for the sake of this knowledge of the recollection of past lives," which means for the attainment and acquisition of this knowledge of the recollection of past lives.
"He directed his mind toward" (*abhininnāmesi*) means he extended it.
*So* means *I*. *Anekavihitam* means manifold; the meaning is that it has been set forth or described in many ways.
*Pubbenivāsam* refers to the continuum of existence dwelling here and there, beginning from the immediately preceding past life.
*Anussarāmi* means that I recollect by following along the succession of births, saying, "one birth, two births," and so forth.

"I remember," "I remember following after," or "I remember as soon as the mind is directed"—this shows that for Great Beings who have fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*), there is no need for preliminary preparation (*parikamma*); therefore, they remember simply by directing their minds.
However, sons of good family who are beginners remember only after performing preliminary preparation; thus, in their case, the preparation must be explained. That [preparation]...
However, if it were explained in detail, it would result in an excessively burdensome account of the origins of discipline; therefore, we shall not speak of it here.
Those who desire [further detail] should take it up according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*. Here, however, we shall explain only the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
The phrase "namely" (*seyyathidaṃ*) is a particle used in the sense of showing the manner in which something has begun. For this very reason, this past life (*pubbenivāsa*) has been undertaken.
Showing its specific divisions, he said, "even one birth," and so forth.

Therein, "even one birth" refers to a single continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna) comprised within a single existence (ekabhava), beginning with rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and ending with death (cuti). This same method applies to "two births" and so on.
However, in the phrase "many eons of dissolution" (saṃvaṭṭakappa) and so forth, an eon that is contracting is a "dissolution eon" (saṃvaṭṭakappa).

It should be understood that "increasing" refers to the period of evolution (*vivatta-kappa*). In this context, by means of the contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa*), the period of subsistence during contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa-ṭṭhāyī*) is included because it is rooted in that;
and by means of the evolution, the period of subsistence during evolution (*vivaṭṭa-ṭṭhāyī*) is included. For it is said:

"Bhikkhus, there are these four incalculable periods of a kappa. Which four? The period of contraction, the period of subsistence during contraction, the period of evolution, and the period of subsistence during evolution."
All those [points] have been stated and fully encompassed.
In this regard, there are three kinds of contractions: contraction by fire, contraction by water, and contraction by air. There are three boundaries of contraction:
the Ābhassara, the Subhakiṇha, and the Vehapphala realms. When the aeon contracts by fire, from the Ābhassara realm...
Below, it is consumed by fire. When the world-system dissolves by water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water.
When it dissolves by wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is destroyed by wind.
As for its extent, however, one entire Buddha-field is always destroyed.
The Buddha-field is threefold: the field of birth (*jātikkhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇākkhetta*), and the field of range (*visayakkhetta*).
Among these, the field of birth extends as far as ten thousand world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), which tremble at the Tathāgata’s conception and other such events.
The field of authority extends as far as one hundred thousand million world-systems, within which the *Ratana-paritta* [is effective].
The power of these protective charms—the Khandha-paritta, the Dhajagga-paritta, the Āṭānāṭiya-paritta, and the Mora-paritta—comes forth.
As for their range, however, it is infinite and immeasurable;
as it is said, "as far as he might wish," wherever and whatever one wishes, that very thing one recollects. Thus, within these three Buddha-fields...
One field of authority perishes. When that perishes, the field of birth also necessarily perishes; it perishes all at once, and when it re-forms, it re-forms all at once.
Its destruction and its re-formation have been described in the *Visuddhimagga*; those who desire this information should consult that work.

Regarding these contractions and expansions that have been mentioned, while sitting at the seat of enlightenment for the purpose of awakening to perfect self-enlightenment, the Blessed One recollected many aeons of contraction, many aeons of expansion, and many aeons of both contraction and expansion. How?
By way of the method beginning with, "In such a place I was. Therein, "In such a place I was" means: in such a contraction aeon, I was in such a place...
In such a state of existence, or birth, or destiny, or station of consciousness, or abode of beings, or class of beings, I existed.
"Of such a name" means Vessantara or Jotipāla. "Of such a clan" means Bhaggava or Gotama.
"Of such a complexion" means fair-skinned or dark-skinned. "Having such food" means eating rice with meat or subsisting on wild fruits. "Experiencing such pleasure and pain":
He is an experiencer of various kinds of bodily and mental pleasure and pain, distinguished as worldly (*sāmisa*) or unworldly (*nirāmisa*), and so forth.
"Thus having the limit of his lifespan" means thus having the limit of a maximum lifespan of one hundred years, or the limit of a maximum lifespan of eighty-four thousand eons.
"Passing away from there, he arose elsewhere" means that I, passing away from that state of existence, from that womb, from that destination, and from that station of consciousness...

"Passed away from such-and-such an abode of beings or such-and-such a class of beings, I was reborn again in such-and-such a state of existence, womb, destiny, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or class of beings.
There too I was," and so forth; "thus named," etc., is exactly as previously explained.
Alternatively, "because they dwell there" refers to the refuge taken at will by one ascending step by step;
"he passed away from there" refers to the reviewing [of that state] by one returning.

Therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "reborn here" follows immediately after that rebirth here, and the statement "arose there in the Tusita abode" is said with reference to the Tusita heaven. "There I was, such-and-such a name."
There too, in the Tusita heaven, I was a son of the gods named Setaketu. "Of such a clan" means I was of the same clan as those deities.
"Of such a complexion" means of golden complexion. "Of such food" means having divine ambrosia (*sudhā*) as food.

"Experiencing such pleasure and pain" means experiencing such divine pleasure; as for pain, it was merely the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*). "With such a limit to my lifespan" [means...].
Thus, his lifespan was limited to seventy-five million times one hundred thousand years.
"He passed away from there" means that I, having passed away from that Tusita heaven, was reborn here in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.
"Thus" means in this way. "With its aspects and particulars" means with its particulars by way of name and clan, and with its aspects by way of complexion and so forth.
For a being is designated by way of name and clan as "Datta," "Tissa," or "Gotama"; by way of complexion and so forth, he is known through his diversity as "fair" or "dark.
Therefore, name and clan constitute the enumeration (uddesa), while the others are the modes (ākāra). But do only Buddhas recollect past lives? It is said:
not only Buddhas, but also Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Buddha, and even followers of other sects (titthiya); yet [not all of them].
This applies without distinction. For the followers of other sects (*titthiya*) remember back only forty eons, and not beyond that.

Why? Because their wisdom is weak. Indeed, due to their lack of discernment regarding name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), their wisdom is feeble. Among the disciples (*sāvaka*), however, the eighty great disciples (*mahāsāvaka*) remember a hundred thousand eons;
the two chief disciples (*aggasāvaka*) remember one incalculable period (*asaṅkhyeya*) and a hundred thousand eons. As for the paccekabuddhas...
Two incalculable eons and one hundred thousand: such is the extent of their recollection. For the Buddhas, however, there is no limit; they remember as long as they wish.
The followers of other sects (titthiyā) remember only by way of the succession of aggregates (khandha-paṭipāṭi).

Having abandoned the succession, they are unable to recollect by way of death and rebirth-linking (cuti-paṭisandhi). For them, like blind men, there is no reaching of the desired place [of recollection].
[The ordinary person] does not. Disciples remember in both ways; likewise do Paccekabuddhas.

But Buddhas remember everything—whether below or above, across many millions of eons—whichever state they desire, whether by way of the sequence of aggregates, by way of death and rebirth-linking, or by way of the lion’s leap.
In the passage beginning with "This, O brahmin, is mine," the word *me* means "by me. *Vijjā* (clear vision) is so called in the sense of making something known.
What does it make known? One's former abodes (*pubbenivāsa*). *Avijjā* (ignorance) refers to the delusion that conceals those very former abodes, in the sense of making them unknown.
That same delusion is called "darkness" (*tamo*) in the sense of being a concealer. *Āloka* (light) is that very clear vision (*vijjā*).
It is called "light" in the sense of making illumination. Here, the meaning is "knowledge has been attained," while the remainder is words of praise.
As for the construction here: "This knowledge indeed has been attained by me;
for me, who has attained knowledge, ignorance is destroyed"—this is the meaning. Why? Because knowledge has arisen. This same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
"Yathā tanti": here, *yathā* has the sense of "as," while *tan* is a particle. "Of one who is heedful" means by not being separated from mindfulness;
"of one who is ardent" means by the exertion of energy; "of one who is resolute" means by having no regard for body or life—the meaning is that his mind is directed [toward liberation].
This is what is meant: as ignorance [is abandoned] in one who dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute...
Ignorance would be dispelled and true knowledge would arise; darkness would be dispelled and light would arise.

Even so, my ignorance has been dispelled and true knowledge has arisen; darkness has been dispelled and light has arisen. "I have obtained a fruit exactly corresponding to this application of striving.
This, brahmin, was my first breaking forth, like that of a chick from its eggshell.

"O Brahmin, this was my first breaking forth, my first emergence, my first noble birth, after I had split open the eggshell of ignorance that concealed the aggregates of former existences with the beak-tip of the knowledge of recollecting past lives—
just as a chick splits open its eggshell with its beak-tip or the tip of its claw."
"Having burst forth from that eggshell, he emerges and is reborn among the fowl.
The Discourse on Past Lives is concluded.
Now follows the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye.
13. Thus... [as before] ... "for the knowledge of passing away and rebirth" means for the knowledge of both death and rebirth;

what is meant is that it is for the purpose of that knowledge by which the death and rebirth of beings are known. "He directed his mind" means he brought forth the preliminary-work consciousness (*parikamma-citta*).
As for the passage, "With the divine [eye]... [as before] ... I see," here the preliminary work is performed by Great Beings who have fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*).

There is none. For those [beings] see beings with the divine eye as soon as their minds are directed toward it, whereas the sons of good family who are beginners must perform preliminary work (*parikamma*).
Therefore, the preliminary work ought to be explained according to their case. However, if that were to be stated, it would make the introduction to the training excessively burdensome;
therefore, we do not speak of it here. Those who desire it may find it in the *Visuddhimagga*.
It should be understood in the manner already stated. Here, however, we shall explain the Pāḷi itself.
Regarding the phrase "He... by the divine," etc.: it is called "divine" (dibba) because it resembles the divine.

For that which is produced by the kamma of good conduct performed by deities is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth; and because it is free from such defilements, it is capable of receiving objects even at a distance.
There is the divine eye of clarity (*pasādacakkhu*). And this eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*), produced by the power of the development of energy (*vīriyabhāvanābala*), is exactly like that;
thus, it is "divine" because it resembles the divine. It is "divine" because it is obtained through divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*) and because it is itself supported by divine abiding.
It is "divine" because it possesses great brilliance due to its mastery over light. It is also "divine" because it has a vast range due to seeing forms situated beyond walls and other such obstacles.
It is divine. All of that should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). It is "eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing.

It is also called "eye" because it performs the function of the eye, as if it were an eye. It is "purified" (*visuddha*) because it is a cause for the purification of view through the seeing of death and rebirth.
For he who sees only death takes hold of the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*); he who sees only rebirth...
One who sees neither passing away nor reappearance adopts the view of the manifestation of new beings.
But one who sees both of these, because he transcends both those types of views, his vision becomes a cause for purification of view.
And the Blessed One saw both of these; therefore it was said: "It is 'purified' because it is a cause for the purification of view through the seeing of passing away and reappearance."
Or it is pure because it is free from the eleven imperfections. For the Blessed One’s divine eye is devoid of the eleven imperfections.
As it is said: “Anuruddha, having understood that ‘doubt is an imperfection of the mind,’ I abandoned doubt as an imperfection of the mind.
[I abandoned] lack of attention... lethargy and drowsiness... trepidation... and so forth.
Exhilaration... coarseness... over-exertion of energy... slackness of energy... longing... perceptions of diversity...
"excessive preoccupation with forms is an affliction of the mind"—having understood this, I abandoned excessive preoccupation with forms as an affliction of the mind.
Then, Anuruddha, dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, I...
"I perceive light, yet I do not see forms; indeed, I see forms, yet I do not perceive light," and so forth.
Thus it is purified by being free from these eleven defilements.
It is "beyond the human" because it sees forms after having transcended the human sphere; or else, it is beyond the human fleshly eye (*māṃsacakkhu*).

Because it has transcended [the human state], it should be understood as "transcending the human" (*atikkantamānusa*). By means of that divine eye, purified and transcending the human—“I see beings” means that I see, behold, and survey beings just as one would with the eye of human flesh.

Regarding the phrase “passing away and being reborn,” it is not possible to see by means of the divine eye either at the very moment of death (*cutikkhaṇa*) or at the very moment of rebirth (*upapattikkhaṇa*).

However, those who are near death and will pass away now are "passing away" (*cavamānā*). Those who have already taken rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) or have just been reborn are intended by the term "being reborn" (*upapajjamānā*).
He shows that he sees them passing away and being reborn in such a manner.
"Inferior" (*hīna*) means despised, reviled, and held in contempt because of inferior birth, family, wealth, and so forth, due to their association with the outflow of delusion (*moha-nissanda*).
"Despised. "Exquisite": because it is associated with the outflow (*nissanda*) of non-delusion (*amoha*), it is the opposite of that [despised state]. "Beautiful":

because it is associated with the outflow of non-hatred (*adosa*), it is endowed with a color that is desirable, lovely, and pleasing. "Ugly": because it is associated with the outflow of hatred (*dosa*), it is endowed with a color that is undesirable, unlovely, and displeasing;

the meaning is also "handsome" or "deformed. "Well-gone" (*sugata*): having gone to a good destination, or because it is associated with the outflow of non-greed (*alobha*), it means "wealthy" or "of great riches."
“Duggate” means those who have gone to an unhappy destination (duggati-gate), or those who are poor and lack food and drink because they are subject to the outflow of greed (lobha-nissanda-yuttattā).

“Yathākammūpage” means those who have arrived at whatever state corresponds to the specific karma they have accumulated. In this context, the function of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) is described by the preceding terms such as “passing away,” while the function of the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) is expressed by this term.
And this is the sequence for the arising of that knowledge: having extended the light downward toward the hells, he sees the beings in hell undergoing great suffering;
that seeing is indeed the function of the divine eye. He then attends to it thus:
"What kind of kamma have these beings performed to undergo this suffering? Then, for him—
Having formed the thought, “This is its name,” knowledge arises with that kamma as its object.
Likewise, by extending the light further toward the celestial worlds, he sees beings in the Nandana Grove, Missaka Grove, Phārusaka Grove, and so forth, experiencing great prosperity.
That seeing, too, is precisely the function of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). He then reflects thus: “What indeed...?”
"Did these beings perform such-and-such karma that they now experience this success? Then, the knowledge arises for him: "Having performed this very thing.
This is called the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*). There is no separate preliminary exercise (*parikamma*) for this.
Just as with this, so it is with the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*); for both of these have the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) as their basis.
They succeed simultaneously with the divine eye.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccarita*): it is called misconduct (*duccarita*) because it is a bad conduct, or because it is a corrupt conduct due to being rotten with defilements (*kilesa*).
Bodily misconduct is that which is misconduct by means of the body, or misconduct arising from the body. The same applies to verbal and mental misconduct.

They are to be seen. "Endowed with" means possessed of. "Revilers of the noble ones" means being desirous of harm toward the noble ones—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha—even down to householders who have attained the stream-entry fruit; they revile them either by means of the ten grounds for censure or by disparaging their virtues.
They are abusers and reproachers; this is what is meant. In that regard: "These possess no ascetic quality..."
By saying, "These are not ascetics," one reviles them by means of the final ground.
By saying, "They have no jhāna, nor liberation, nor the path, nor the fruit," one should be understood as reviling them by disparaging their qualities.
Whether one reviles knowing [the truth] or unknowing, in either case it is indeed a reviling of the Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda). It is a heavy deed that obstructs rebirth in heaven.
And it is an obstruction to the path, yet it is curable. To clarify this, they cite the following instance:
"It is said that in a certain village, an elder and a young bhikkhu were walking for alms.
In the very first house, they received a bowlful of warm gruel. The elder had a stomach ailment, and he thought: 'This..."
“Gruel is suitable for me; I shall drink it as long as it has not yet cooled.

Sitting upon a log of wood brought by people for the purpose of threshing, he drank it. The other [monk] felt disgusted, thinking, “This old man is indeed too greedy; he has done something that makes us ashamed.
After the elder had wandered through the village and returned to the monastery, he [approached] the young bhikkhu...
He said, “Friend, do you have a firm footing in this Teaching? “Yes, venerable sir, I am a stream-enterer.
“In that case, friend, do not exert yourself for the sake of the higher paths; you have slandered one whose taints are exhausted.
He asked his forgiveness, and because of that, he was restored to his former state. Therefore, whoever else slanders a noble one should likewise [seek forgiveness].
Having gone there, if he is senior to the other, he should ask for forgiveness, saying: "Venerable sir, I said this and that to you; please forgive me for that.
If he is junior, he should pay homage, sit in the kneeling position, raise his joined palms, and ask for forgiveness, saying:
"Venerable sir, I said this and that to you; please forgive me for that. If he does not grant forgiveness...
Or if he has gone abroad, he should go to those bhikkhus who are staying in that monastery;
if he is senior to them, he should do so while standing, but if he is junior, he should sit down on his heels, raise his joined palms, and say:
"Venerable sirs, I said such and such to the Venerable so-and-so; may that Venerable one forgive me."

He should ask for forgiveness by speaking thus. If he has attained final Nibbāna, one should ask for forgiveness by going to the place where his parinibbāna occurred, and even as far as the charnel ground. When this is done, there is no obstruction to heaven or obstruction to the path;
it becomes as it was before.

"Those of wrong view" means those with perverted vision. "Those who undertake actions based on wrong view" refers to those who, by way of wrong view, have undertaken various kinds of kamma, as well as those who encourage others in bodily kamma and so forth rooted in wrong view.
In this context, by the inclusion of verbal misconduct, slander of the Noble Ones is already covered; and by the inclusion of mental misconduct, wrong view is also included.
It should be understood that although these two have already been included [in the previous list], they are mentioned again for the purpose of showing their extreme gravity.
For reviling the Noble Ones is extremely grave, being similar to an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense. As it is said:

"Sāriputta, just as a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom might attain final knowledge (*aññā*) in this very life—even so, Sāriputta, is this [reviling the Noble Ones]."
"Sāriputta, I say that one who has not abandoned that speech, not abandoned that mind, and not relinquished that view is deposited in hell just as he was brought there.
And there is nothing more blameworthy than wrong view. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, I do not..."
“I do not see even a single other thing that is so greatly blameworthy as wrong view.
Monks, wrong views are the supreme offenses. “With the breaking up of the body” means the relinquishing of the aggregates that have been clung to.
“After death” means immediately thereafter, at the grasping of the newly produced aggregates.
Alternatively, "with the breaking up of the body" means the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "After death" means after the moment of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).

"The state of deprivation" (*apāya*) and so forth—all these are synonyms for hell (*niraya*). For hell is called *apāya* because it is devoid of the "gain" (*āya*) of merit that serves as the cause for heaven and liberation, or because it lacks the "gain" of happiness.
It is called a "bad destination" (*duggati*) because it is the resort and refuge of suffering.
It is a "bad destination" (*duggati*) because it is a state of existence produced by defiled action due to an abundance of hatred.
It is a "fall" (*vinipāta*) because those who have committed evil deeds fall there helplessly; or, it is a "fall" because they fall there while perishing, their limbs and members being shattered.
It is a "hell" (*niraya*) because there is no pleasure (*āyasa*) perceived therein.
Alternatively, by the mention of "the states of loss" (*apāya*), he indicates the animal realm. For the animal realm is a state of loss because it is removed from the happy destinies (*sugati*);

yet it is not a miserable destiny (*duggati*), because highly powerful beings such as the Nāga kings can be born there. By the mention of "the miserable destiny," he indicates the sphere of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*).
For that is both a state of loss and a miserable destiny, because it is removed from the happy destinies and because it has become a destination of suffering.

But there is no "falling away" (vinipāta) [into the state] similar to that of the asuras, because they have not fallen away from their status. For even celestial mansions (vimāna) are produced for hungry ghosts (peta) who possess great psychic power (mahiddhika).

By the inclusion of the term "falling away," he indicates the host of asuras. For that [state], in the sense already mentioned, is called a "falling away" (vinipāta) because it is a state of loss (apāya), a miserable destination (duggati), and because one has fallen away from all superior forms of existence (samussaya). By the inclusion of the term "hell" (niraya), [he indicates] the many varieties such as Avīci and so forth.

It illuminates only hell. "Reborn" means having approached; the intention is that they have been produced there. The bright side (the positive case) should be understood by reversing what was stated above.
However, this is the distinction: here, by the inclusion of a "happy destination," the human destination is also included. By the inclusion of a "heavenly realm,"...

It is simply the divine realm (*devagati*). In that context, a beautiful destination is a "good destination" (*sugati*). Because it is a supreme state (*agga*) with respect to sense objects such as forms, it is a "heaven" (*sagga*).
Since all of that is subject to breaking up and disintegration, it is called a "world" (*loka*); this is the etymological meaning. "Knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the knowledge of the divine eye.
"Ignorance" (*avijjā*) is the ignorance that conceals the death and rebirth-linking of sentient beings. The rest is exactly as previously stated. This very same...
Herein is the distinction: just as it was stated in the discourse on the recollection of past lives,

"having split open the eggshell of ignorance that conceals the aggregates lived in the past by means of the beak and tip of the knowledge of the recollection of past lives," so too here it should be said,
"having split open the eggshell of ignorance that conceals death and rebirth by means of the beak and tip of the knowledge of death and rebirth."
The discourse on the knowledge of the divine eye is finished. Regarding the discourse on the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa):
"When his mind is thus concentrated"—here, it should be understood as the fourth jhāna consciousness that serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā).

"For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints" means for the sake of the knowledge of the path of arahantship. For the path of arahantship is called "the destruction of the taints" because it destroys the taints;
and this knowledge is included therein. "They directed their minds" means they extended their insight-minds.
In such passages as "This is suffering," [it is understood that] "this much is suffering, not more than this..."
"Furthermore": through the penetration of its intrinsic characteristic, I fully understood, knew, and realized the entire truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) as it truly is.
And I understood that craving which produces that suffering as "this is the origin of suffering" (dukkhasamudaya);
and I understood that state where both of these cease and do not arise—that Nirvana—as "this is the cessation of suffering" (dukkhanirodha).

And regarding the Noble Path that leads to its attainment, one should understand the meaning as follows: "I have directly known, understood, and penetrated it as it truly is, through the penetration of its essential characteristic, thinking: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

Having thus shown the Truths according to their specific nature, he now speaks the words beginning with "These are the taints" (ime āsavā) in order to show them by way of their synonyms based on the defilements (kilesa).
"Of me who thus knew and thus saw": this refers to me who was knowing and seeing in this way;

it explains that the path, having reached its culmination, arises together with insight (*vipassanā*). "From the taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*): from the outflow of sensual desire. "Was liberated":
by this phrase he shows the moment of fruition (*phalakkhaṇa*). For at the moment of the path, the mind is being liberated; at the moment of fruition, it is liberated.
"Released," "there is the knowledge 'it is released'"—by this he shows the reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). By the words "birth is exhausted" and so forth, he shows its plane.
For it was by means of that knowledge that the Blessed One, while reviewing, directly knew: "Birth is exhausted," and so on.
But what is the birth exhausted for the Blessed One, and how did he directly know it? It is said: first of all, his...

Past birth is exhausted because it was already exhausted in the past; future [birth] is not [exhausted] because there is no effort regarding the future; present [birth] is not [exhausted] because it exists.

However, that birth—which, due to the non-cultivation of the Path, would arise in the various one-, four-, or five-aggregate existences as distinguished by the one-, four-, or five-aggregates—is exhausted through the attainment of the state of non-arising by means of the cultivation of the Path; that [he exhausts] by means of the cultivation of the Path.
Having reviewed the defilements that have been abandoned, I directly knew: "In the absence of defilements, even though karma exists, it will not lead to rebirth in the future.
"Vusitaṃ" means lived, fully lived, accomplished, practiced, and brought to completion; this is the meaning. "Brahmacariyaṃ" refers to the holy life of the Path.

Indeed, together with the virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), the seven types of trainees (*sekkha*) are said to dwell in the holy life (*brahmacariya*); one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) has completed that dwelling.
Therefore, when the Blessed One reflected upon his own dwelling in the holy life, he directly knew: "The holy life has been lived.

"What was to be done has been done" refers to the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) through the four paths regarding the four truths, by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing.

The meaning is that the sixteenfold duty has been brought to completion. For while those such as the "virtuous worldlings" (puthujjanakalyāṇaka) perform this duty, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) has already accomplished what was to be done.
Therefore, the Blessed One, reviewing his own task, directly knew: "What was to be done has been done.
"There is nothing further for this state of being"—this means that there is now no more returning to this very condition, namely, to the state of these sixteen duties.
"I realized: 'I have no further task to perform regarding the cultivation of the path for the destruction of the defilements.
Now, showing to the brahmin that attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa) which is embraced by such reviewing-knowledge, he said:
'This, O brahmin, is my true knowledge,' and so forth. In this context, *vijjā* refers to the knowledge of the path of Arahantship; *avijjā* refers to..."
Ignorance is that which conceals the Four Noble Truths. The rest is exactly as previously stated. However, this is the distinction:

regarding the phrase "This, O Brahmin, was my third breaking forth," it means: "O Brahmin, having split open the eggshell of ignorance—which conceals the Four Noble Truths—with the beak and snout of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—this was my third breaking forth, my third emergence."

The third type of noble birth was that of one who, like a chick, having broken the eggshell with its beak or the tip of its claw, emerged from that eggshell and was reborn within the flock of chickens.
What does this demonstrate? It shows, O Brahmin, that very chick... the eggshell.
Having burst it open and emerging from it, one is born all at once; however,
I first became born through the knowledge and vision of the recollection of past lives by breaking the eggshell of ignorance that shrouds the aggregates of former existences, and then,
by bursting the eggshell of ignorance that shrouds the passing away and rebirth of beings, I was born secondly through the knowledge and vision of the divine eye.

Furthermore, having burst asunder the eggshell of ignorance that conceals the Four Noble Truths, he was born through the third kind of knowledge, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
Thus, he was born three times by means of the three knowledges (*vijjā*). By saying, "And this birth of mine is noble and perfectly pure," he demonstrated this.

And in demonstrating it thus, he showed the knowledge of the past through the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa*), and the knowledge of the present and future through the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
"By the destruction of the taints, all mundane and supramundane qualities [are perfected]"— thus, having manifested all the qualities of omniscience through these three knowledges (*vijjā*),
he showed the Brahmin the preeminent seniority of his own noble birth.
The Discussion on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints is concluded.

The Discourse on the Expression of Gratitude for the Teaching (Desanānumodanakathā) 15. When this was said, the brahmin of Verañja— though the Blessed One, out of compassion for the world and out of compassion for that brahmin,
had concealed his own noble birth and preeminence— [listened] to the teaching of the Dhamma which illuminates the threefold knowledge.
When this was said, the brahmin of Verañjā, his body and mind filled with the expansion of rapture, realized that the Blessed One was the eldest and most excellent by noble birth;

and knowing this, he thought: "Alas, what ignorance it was of mine to say, 'He does not perform such acts as salutation toward others,' regarding one who is indeed the eldest and most excellent in all the world, endowed with every virtue, and omniscient! Thus he lamented: "Fie upon that ignorance of mine!"

Having reproached himself and reached the conclusion, “Now this one is the eldest in the world by virtue of being born first into the noble lineage, and the most excellent by virtue of being peerless in all qualities,” he said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Gotama is the eldest;
Venerable Gotama is the most excellent. And having spoken thus, he [requested] that Dhamma teaching from the Blessed One once more.
Expressing his appreciation, he said, "Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! and so forth.
In this context, the word *abhikkanta* is seen to be used in the senses of destruction, beautiful, handsome, and expressing appreciation.

For instance, in such passages as, "Venerable sir, the night has passed; the first watch has ended; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time," it is used in the sense of destruction (*khaya*).
It is seen [in the sense of] "beautiful," as in such passages as: "This person is pleasing to me; he is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons," and so forth.
Also: "Who is saluting my feet, shining with the glory of supernormal power, illuminating all directions with most excellent beauty?"—

In such contexts as these, it means "beautiful. In expressions such as "Excellent, venerable sir" (*abhikkantaṃ, bhante*), it signifies approval (*abbhanumodana*). Here too, it is used specifically for approval. And because it is used for approval, it should be understood that the words "Well said, well said, Master Gotama!

(*sādhu sādhu, bho gotamā*) have been spoken. As it is said: "A wise person should employ repetition (*āmeḍita*) in cases of fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, distress, laughter, sorrow, and faith."
It should be understood that this characteristic is stated twice here: once by way of serene confidence (*pasāda*) and once by way of praise (*pasamsā*).
Alternatively, "excellent" (*abhikkanta*) means exceedingly desirable, exceedingly agreeable, and exceedingly beautiful.
In this regard, he praises the teaching with one instance of the word "excellent," and his own confidence with the other. For this is the intended meaning here:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! This teaching of the Dhamma by Master Gotama is excellent; it is excellent that through this teaching of the Dhamma by Master Gotama, confidence has arisen in me.
