Or rather, he praises the very words of the Blessed One with reference to two pairs of meanings: the word of Master Gotama is excellent because it destroys the defilements (dosa), and it is excellent because it leads to the removal of them.

By way of the attainment of qualities; likewise, by way of generating faith and generating wisdom; by way of being meaningful and possessing elegant phrasing; by way of having clear words and profound meaning;
by way of being pleasant to the ear and reaching the heart; by way of not exalting oneself and not disparaging others; by way of being cooled by compassion and purified by wisdom;
by way of being delightful when heard and capable of withstanding scrutiny; and by way of being pleasant while being heard and beneficial while being investigated.
It should be applied with these and similar [phrases].
Beyond that, he further praises the teaching itself by means of four similes. Therein, "upturned" (*nikkujjita*) means placed face down, or having its opening facing downward.
"He would turn it up" (*ukkujjeyya*) means he would make it face upward. "Concealed" (*paṭicchanna*) means covered over with grass, leaves, and so forth.

"Should open" means he should unlock. "Of one who is lost" means of one who is confused about the directions. "Should point out the way" means he should take him by the hand and say, "This is the way.

"In the darkness" refers to the fourfold darkness: the darkness of the dark fortnight on the fourteenth day, the darkness of midnight, the darkness of a dense forest thicket, and the darkness of a mass of clouds.
This, first of all, is the literal meaning of the words. This, however, is the application of the underlying intention—just as someone...
He would turn upright what had been overturned—thus, by raising me up from unrighteousness, having turned me away from the true Dhamma and established me in it;

he would reveal what was concealed—thus, by revealing the teaching that had been concealed by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation; he would show the path to one who was lost...
Thus, by one who points out to me—who has entered upon a wrong path and a false path—the path to heaven and liberation;

and just as one would hold up an oil lamp in the dark, so too by one who holds up the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion obscuring it for me, who am submerged in the darkness of delusion and do not see the forms of the Three Jewels beginning with the Buddha. For my sake...
Because the Blessed Gotama has made it manifest through these methods, the Dhamma has been made manifest in many ways.
The discourse on rejoicing in the teaching is finished. Now follows the discourse on the manner of showing confidence.
Having thus praised the teaching, and manifesting his confidence by means of this teaching with a mind clear toward the Triple Gem, he said, "Esāhaṃ," and so forth.
Therein, "esāhaṃ" means "this I. "Bhavantaṃ Gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī" means "I go for refuge to the venerable Gotama";
the venerable Gotama is my refuge, my final resort, [the protector] from suffering.
"O dear one, with the intention of being a provider of welfare, I go to, associate with, serve, and attend upon the venerable Gotama;
or rather, I know and I understand thus. For those verbal roots whose meaning is "going," "understanding" is also their meaning;
therefore, for this word "I go," the meanings "I know" and "I understand" are also stated. And the Dhamma...

Regarding the phrase "and the community of bhikkhus": herein, it is called *dhamma* because it sustains those who have attained the path, realized cessation, and are practicing according to the instructions, preventing them from falling into the four states of misery (*apāya*). In its essential meaning, that *dhamma* is both the Noble Eightfold Path and Nibbāna.
For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, as far as there are conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*), the Noble Eightfold Path is the foremost among them..."
“It is declared the foremost,” and so on in detail. And it is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the Dhamma of the scriptures together with the Noble Fruits.
For this has been said in the *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna*:
“The Dhamma free from lust, unshaken, sorrowless, unconditioned, and non-repulsive;”
"Come to this Dhamma—sweet, skillful, and well-expounded—for the sake of refuge.
Herein, "fading away from passion" refers to the Path; "unshakable and sorrowless" refers to the Fruit; and "the unconditioned Dhamma" refers to Nibbāna.
"Sweet, skillful, and well-expounded, not repulsive" refers to all the aggregates of the Dhamma as analyzed within the Three Piṭakas.

It is called the *saṅgha* because it is united by the combination of right view and virtue. In its actual meaning, it is a collection of the eight noble persons (*ariyapuggala*). For this has been said in that very same *Vimānavatthu*:
“Where they say a gift yields great fruit—among the four pure pairs of persons;
those eight individuals who are seers of the Dhamma—to this Saṅgha go for refuge.”
The community of monks is the *bhikkhu-saṅgha*. At this point, the brahmin has declared the three goings for refuge.
The discussion on the manner of his serene confidence is concluded. This concludes the discourse on going for refuge.
Now, for the sake of proficiency regarding those very three goings for refuge, this method should be understood:
refuge, the act of going for refuge, he who goes for refuge, the classification of the going for refuge, the fruit of the going for refuge, the defilement, and the analysis.
However, since explaining that here would result in an excessively burdensome introduction to the Vinaya, it has not been stated; yet it should be sought by those who require it.
This should be taken from the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, specifically from the commentary on the *Bhayabherava Sutta*,
or from the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīgha Nikāya*, specifically from the commentary on the *Saraṇa Sutta*.
The Discourse on Going for Refuge is concluded.
The Discourse on the Declaration of Lay-Follower Status:
"May Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower" means that Master Gotama should remember me thus: "This one is a lay follower.
Furthermore, for the sake of proficiency regarding the rules for a lay follower, it should be understood here: who is a lay follower? Why is he called a lay follower? What is his...

Regarding virtue (*sīla*), one should understand this miscellaneous matter: what is right livelihood (*ājīva*), what is its failure, and what is its success. It has not been analyzed here because it would be too burdensome;
however, those who desire to know it should understand it according to the method explained in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.
As for the phrase "from this day forward" (*ajjatagge*), here the word *agga* is seen to mean "beginning," "limit," "portion," and "best. "From this day forward... [and so forth].
In such passages as, "O gatekeeper, I shut the door against the Nigaṇṭhas and the Nigaṇṭhīs," it is seen at the beginning.
In such passages as, "He might touch that fingertip with this fingertip; the tip of a sugarcane, the tip of a bamboo," it is seen at the end.
In such passages as, "Monks, I allow [fruit] that is sour at the tip, sweet at the tip, or bitter at the tip, or [the use of] a dwelling at the tip... it is seen at the middle.
In such passages as "or let him divide it by the courtyard," it refers to a portion. In such passages as, "Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings—whether footless or two-footed...
the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them," it refers to the best. But here, this [word] should be understood as referring to the beginning.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: *ajjatagge* means "making today the beginning. *Ajjatan* means "the state of being today" (*ajjabhāva*).
This is what is meant. Alternatively, the reading is *ajjadagge*, where the letter *da* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikaro*); thus it means "making today the beginning.

*Pāṇupetaṃ* means "endowed with life" (*pāṇehi upetaṃ*); that is to say, for as long as my life continues, may the Blessed Gotama accept and know me as one who has gone for refuge through the three goings-for-refuge, endowed [with this practice] and having no other teacher. For even if I...
"Even if they were to cut off one's head with a sharp sword, one would not say of the Buddha, 'He is not the Buddha,' nor of the Dhamma,
'It is not the Dhamma,' nor of the Saṅgha, 'It is not the Saṅgha. And here, it should be understood that when the brahmin speaks of going for refuge for as long as life lasts,
by stating this going for refuge once again, he makes known his total self-surrender.
Having thus offered himself, and desiring to attend upon the Blessed One together with his assembly, he said:
“May the venerable Gotama accept from me a residence for the rains at Verañjā, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. What is meant by this?
“May the venerable Gotama recognize me as a lay follower (upāsaka), and may he accept from me a residence for the rains at Verañjā—these three [points].”
"May he accept residence for one month depending on Verañjā out of favor toward me. Having heard his words, the Blessed One consented by silence.
This means that after hearing his speech, the Blessed One—without moving either a limb of the body or a limb of speech, but rather expressing his acceptance within himself—consented through silence;
it is said that he accepted with his mind alone for the sake of favoring the brahmin.
Then the brahmin of Verañjā, having understood the Blessed One’s acceptance— thinking,
"If the ascetic Gotama had not accepted my invitation, he would have rejected it either by body or by speech;
but since he did not reject it and instead maintained his forbearance within, he has accepted it through his mind alone"— thus, through his skill in discerning such signs, [he knew].
Having understood the Blessed One’s acceptance, he rose from his own seat, paid respectful homage to the Blessed One in the four directions,
and circumambulated him three times. Then, having reproached himself for not having performed salutations and other marks of respect toward the elderly brahmins since the time of his arrival,
he now— having come to know the qualities of the Buddha through body, speech, and mind— [proceeded].
And even though he had paid homage many times, still feeling as if he were insufficiently satisfied, he raised his hands in a brilliant añjali with the ten nails joined together,
placed it upon his head, and withdrew while facing him as long as he remained within the range of vision;
then, at the point where he passed out of sight, he prostrated himself once more and departed.
The Discourse on the Declaration of Lay-Follower Status is finished.
16. The Discourse on Famine:
Now at that time, Verañjā was suffering from a famine—at which time, by the brahmin of Verañjā...
The Blessed One was requested to observe the rains retreat in dependence on Verañjā; at that time, Verañjā was suffering from a famine.

"Famine" means that alms-food is difficult to obtain. Furthermore, such scarcity of alms occurs even during times of good harvests and when prices are very low in places where people are faithless and lack confidence. But in Verañjā...

Because it was not so [as previously stated], but rather occurred due to the fault of drought caused by a failure of rain, he spoke the passage beginning with "dvīhitikā" (twofold exertion) in order to demonstrate that matter.
Therein, "dvīhitikā" means twofold exertion (*īhitikā*). Exertion (*īhita*) refers to activity (*iriyā*); it is twofold:
mental activity (*cittairiyā*) and mental exertion (*cittaīhā*). [This is the thought: "Will we obtain something here by begging, or will we not obtain anything?"
“Will we be able to live or not?”—this is the intended meaning here.
Alternatively, *dvīhitikā* means a difficult livelihood (*dujjīvikā*). The words *īhitaṃ*, *īhā*, *iriyanaṃ*, *pavattanaṃ*, and *jīvitaṃ* are synonymous.
Therefore, the meaning of the term here is: “that which is lived with difficulty (*dukkhena*) proceeds (*pavattati*) here; thus it is *dvīhitikā*.”
*Setaṭṭhikā*: It is called *setaṭṭhikā* because there are white bones (*setakāni aṭṭhīni*) here.
What is meant is that it is strewn here and there with the bones, the color of mushrooms, of wretched people who died after begging for something even during the day but receiving nothing.
There is also the reading *setaṭṭikā*. Its meaning is: it is called *setaṭṭikā* because there is white distress (*setā aṭṭi*) here. *Aṭṭī* means affliction.

Disease is illness. In that regard, at the time when the crops take root, they are indeed afflicted by the "white disease" (*setaka-roga*), whereby the milk [of the plants] is cut off and the heads of the rice, barley, or wheat emerge completely white and devoid of grain;
therefore, it is called "the white-bone disease" (*setaṭṭikā*).
Because even when the grain was sown very well during the planting season, only stalks (*salākā*) were produced there, they are called *salākāvuttā*.
Or, because they subsist there by means of stalks, they are called *salākāvuttā*. What is meant?
It is said that there, when buyers went to those who sell grain, the strong men would overpower the weak men.
Having purchased grain, they depart. Weak people, unable to obtain it, raise a great outcry.

The grain-sellers, thinking, "We shall provide for everyone," have a grain-measurer sit at the place where the grain is prepared and station a color-inspector on one side. Those seeking grain go to the inspector. He—
Having taken the principal amount according to the order of arrival and having written a tally-stick (*salāka*) stating, "So-and-so must be given this much," he hands it over.
They take that stick and go to the grain-measurer, receiving grain according to the order in which they were given their sticks.
Thus, because they maintain their livelihood there by means of a tally-stick, they are called "those who live by the tally" (*salākāvuttā*).
"It is not easy to subsist on gleanings and alms" means that it is not easy to subsist by means of those gleanings which are obtained through alms.
What is meant is that it is not easy to subsist by means of those gleanings which the Noble Ones perform when they take their bowls and go on alms-round.
At that time, it is said, even after wandering for alms through seven or eight villages there, one could not sustain oneself for even a single day.
They did not receive even enough to sustain themselves.
Now at that time, horse-dealers from the Northern Road... [the text continues] ...the Blessed One heard the sound of the mortar.
"At that time" means: at the time when the Blessed One had entered upon the rains retreat in dependence on Verañjā, at that time.
Horse-dealers from the Northern Country— or so called because they had come from the Northern Country—
having taken five hundred horses from the breeding grounds in the North, were traveling to another region hoping for a double or triple profit;
with those five hundred horses which were their own merchandise for sale, they [arrived] at Verañjā.
They entered upon the rains residence. Why? Because it was not possible to travel on a journey during those four months of the rainy season in that region.

And as they entered, they had dwelling-places built for themselves and stables for their horses in a place outside the city that was not inundated by water, and they surrounded them with a fence. Those were their places of residence.
“Huts for the non-monastics” was how they were designated. Therefore he said: “In those huts for the non-monastics, a layer of straw sufficient for each monk had been prepared.
“A layer of straw sufficient for each” means a layer of straw measuring one *pattha* for each individual monk.
A *pattha* is the measure of a single *nāḷi*, which is enough to sustain one man. For it has also been said:
—“A measure of porridge is not enough for two. What is called *pulaka* refers to barley grains that have been winnowed to remove the husks and then parched.
For if they were still moist, insects would infest them and they would not endure the journey.
Therefore, those merchants took parched barley grains that were fit for travel and set out on their way, [thinking], “Wherever there are horses...”
“Hard fodder will become scarce, and this will serve as the horses’ food.
But why did they provide that for the monks? It is said: “For those people of the Southern Region were not faithless or lacking in confidence like those of the Middle Country;
rather, they were faithful and confident, devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha.”

While entering the city on some business in the morning, they saw two or three days ago seven or eight bhikkhus—well-robed, well-clad, and perfect in deportment—who, having wandered for alms throughout the entire city, had received nothing.
Having seen them, it occurred to them: "These venerable ones are dependent upon this city..."
The rains have begun, and a drought prevails; they receive nothing and are suffering greatly.
We, moreover, are newcomers and are unable to prepare daily rice-gruel and meals for them.
However, our horses receive their meal twice a day, both morning and evening. What if we were to provide [food] for each horse...
“Let us give each monk a handful of husked rice for his morning meal. In this way, the masters will not be exhausted, and the horses will be sustained.
Having gone to the monks and announced this matter, they said, “Venerable sirs, please accept the handfuls of husked rice and consume it by whatever means necessary.”
Having requested it, they prepared rice-porridge with every morning’s fresh grain. Therefore it is said:
“In the monks’ quarters, rice-porridge with every morning’s fresh grain had been prepared for the bhikkhus.
“Prepared” means set aside by way of a regular meal provision. Now, regarding the passage beginning with “Then the bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning,” etc.:
*Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ* means the period of the early part of the day; the sense is *pubbaṇhasamaye*.
Alternatively, *pubbaṇhe samayaṃ* is *pubbaṇhasamayaṃ*, meaning "at one moment in the forenoon. Thus, the accusative case is employed in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
*Nivāsetvā* means having put on [the lower robe]; this refers to the manner of wearing the robe for dwelling in the monastery (*vihāra-nivāsana-parivattana-vasena*).

This should be understood. For they were not unclad prior to that. "Taking bowl and robe" means having taken the bowl with the hands and the robe with the body, having accepted them, and having put them on; this is the meaning.
Indeed, those who take [anything] by whatever manner are said simply to have "taken," just as in the expression, "having taken up, he departs. "Not obtaining alms-food":
"Having wandered through the entire district of Verañjā, let alone receiving almsfood, they did not even obtain the words 'please accept'.
"Bringing back handfuls after handfuls of grain to the monastery" means that wherever they went, they took whatever single handful of grain they obtained and brought it to the monastery.
"Pounding it repeatedly in a mortar and eating it" refers to a certain attendant (kappiyakāraka) belonging to the Elders.
There was no one among them who could take that [grain] and cook gruel or a meal. Cooking for oneself is neither suitable for a recluse nor permissible.

Thinking, "In this way, we shall have a very simple livelihood and be freed from the task of cooking," eight or ten people would gather together, pound [the grain] repeatedly in a mortar, and then... their own [food].
They moisten their own portions with water and consume them. Having consumed them in this way, they perform the duties of a recluse with little exertion.
But those horse-dealers give the Blessed One fine rice-powder and the appropriate accompaniments of ghee, honey, and sugar.
Venerable Ānanda brings these and grinds them upon a stone slab. What is prepared by a meritorious and wise person is indeed pleasing.
Then, having ground it and properly mixed it with ghee and other ingredients, he offered it to the Blessed One. Thereupon, deities added divine nourishment to it.
The Blessed One consumed it; having consumed it, he spent his time in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
From that point on, he no longer went out for alms.
But was the Elder Ānanda then the personal attendant of the Blessed One? He was; yet he had not yet attained the formal position of attendant.
Indeed, during the twenty years following the Blessed One’s first enlightenment, there was no one appointed as a permanent attendant.
At times the Elder Nāgasamāla attended upon the Blessed One, at times the Elder Nāgita, and at times the Elder Meghiya.
Sometimes it was the Elder Upavāṇa, sometimes the Elder Sāgata, and sometimes Sunakkhatta the Licchavi-son.
Having attended upon him according to their own preference, they would depart whenever they wished. While those various individuals were attending upon him, the Elder Ānanda remained unconcerned;
but when they had departed, he himself performed the duties of service. The Blessed One also thought: "Even though I..."
The foremost kinsman did not yet receive a place among the attendants; however, thinking that in such matters this very person was the most suitable, he consented.
Therefore it is said: "Venerable Ānanda, having ground fresh rice-porridge on a stone, offered it to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One partook of it."
But surely, at a time of famine, people become exceedingly zealous and perform meritorious deeds;
they even think that what should be given to the monks must be given, even if they themselves have not eaten. Why, then, did they not give even a spoonful of alms-food at that time?
And why did this Brahmin of Verañjā, having requested the Blessed One with great zeal for the rains-residence, [not provide it]?
"Does he not even know of their existence? It is said: because of Māra’s enticement.

For as soon as the brahmin of Verañjā had departed from the Blessed One's presence, Māra—having enticed and deluded everyone throughout the entire city and for a distance of one league all around, within which it was possible to return after walking for alms before the meal—[took control] of them all.
Having made his departure without even taking notice [of the Buddha], no one—even down to the very least—thought that any act of hospitality should be performed.
But did the Blessed One also enter the rains retreat there without knowing it was Māra’s haunt? No, he did not do so unknowingly.
Then why did he not enter the rains retreat in one of the other places, such as Campā, Sāvatthī, or Rājagaha? Let alone Campā, Sāvatthī, and Rājagaha.
Even if the Blessed One were to go to Uttarakuru or the city of the Thirty-three and enter the rains retreat there for that year, Māra would still have enticed him.
It is said that during that year, his mind was exceedingly obsessed with resentment.
But here, the Blessed One saw this further reason: "The horse-dealers will provide support for the monks..."
“They will do so. Therefore, he entered the rains retreat right there at Verañjā.
But was it that Māra was unable to entice the merchants? No, he was not unable; rather, they returned after having been enticed.
Why did he not entice them on their way back? Because of his inability; for he could not overcome the Tathāgata.
It is able to create an obstacle for alms brought [to him], for regular giving, or for a practice that has been undertaken;
however, it is not possible to create an obstacle for four things. Which four?
It is not possible to create an obstacle for the four requisites that have been relinquished, whether by way of alms brought to the Tathāgata or by way of regular giving or a practiced routine.
It is impossible for anyone to create an obstacle. It is impossible for anyone to create an obstacle to the life of the Buddhas.
Nor is it possible for anyone to create an obstacle to the eighty minor marks or to the fathom-wide aura;

for even the radiance of the moon, the sun, the gods, and the Brahmās, upon reaching the region of the Tathāgata’s minor marks and fathom-wide aura, have their power destroyed. [This applies to] the Buddhas.
"No one can create an obstacle for the knowledge of omniscience"—thus, no one can create an obstacle for these four.
Therefore, it should be understood that at that time the Blessed One, together with the community of disciples, partook of the alms-food for which no obstacle had been created by Māra.
While partaking in this manner, on one day the Blessed One heard the sound of a mortar; the Blessed One [saw] the *patthapattha* rice-porridge...
He heard the sound of the mortar produced by the clashing of pestles from the monks who were pounding [grain].
Thereafter, the passage beginning with "The Tathāgatas, though knowing... was spoken for the purpose of showing the answer to what he later asked: "Ānanda, what indeed is that sound of the mortar?
Herein, this is the brief commentary: the Tathāgatas, though they know...
If there is such a reason for questioning, they ask; but if there is no such reason for questioning, even though they know [the answer], they do not ask.
However, because there is no such thing as ignorance on the part of the Buddhas, it is not said that "even though they do not know.
Having understood the proper time, they ask: if that is the right time for such a question, then at that time...
Having understood this, they ask; and if it is not so, even then, having understood the time, they do not ask.
And when they do ask, the Tathāgatas ask what is connected with the goal—that which is based on the goal and based on the reason—and they do not ask what is not connected with the goal. Why?
Because for the Tathāgatas there is a demolition of the bridge regarding what is not connected with the goal. "Bridge" is said to mean...
The path; by the path itself there is the destruction of such speech—this is what is meant by "complete eradication.
Now, regarding the phrase "conducive to the goal" (*atthasaṃhita*), in order to show that the Tathāgatas ask about whatever speech is dependent on the goal, he says, "in two ways," and so forth.
Therein, "ways" (*ākārehi*) means reasons (*kāraṇehi*). "Or I shall teach the Dhamma"—thus it is said.
"Either we shall relate a discourse connected with a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), or a birth story (*jātaka*) connected with a past life; or else,
thinking 'we shall lay down a training rule for the disciples,' we shall— having made manifest through that question by the disciples any transgression,
whether grave or light— lay down a training rule and establish an injunction."
Regarding the phrase, "Then the Blessed One... [as before] ...reported this matter," there is nothing further to be said.

For it is precisely while reporting to the monks the successive harvests of rice stalks they had obtained, their very light livelihood, and their release from having to cook for themselves that he is said to have "reported this matter.
As for the words, "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda," the Blessed One—
He spoke, gladdening the Venerable Ānanda. Having given his approval, and selecting one of two aspects, he taught the Dhamma, saying:
"By you, Ānanda, who are true men, has victory been won; future generations will hold rice and meat in contempt.
Herein, this is the intended meaning: by you, Ānanda, who are true men, even in such a time of famine...
By this light mode of living and by this austerity, even a time of scarcity has been conquered.
What has been conquered? A famine has been conquered; greed has been conquered; the pursuit of desires has been conquered. How so?

"This Verañjā is a place of famine, but all around it, the neighboring villages and market towns have crops bent down with the weight of fruit; they are places of plenty where alms are easily obtained."
"Even so, the Blessed One remains right here, having subdued us," not even a single bhikkhu had such a thought or any distress.
Thus, first of all, the famine was conquered, overcome, brought under his own control, and subjugated.
How was greed conquered? "This Verañjā is a place of famine, but on all sides there are neighboring villages and market towns."
"The crops are bent down by the weight of their fruit; there will be plenty of food and alms will be easily obtained. Come, let us go there and enjoy ourselves.
Driven by greed, not even a single bhikkhu broke his night-vow, nor did anyone break the rains-retreat by saying, "Let us enter the rains-retreat there for the later period.
In this way, greed was conquered.
How was conduct according to one's wishes overcome? This Verañjā is suffering from famine, and these people do not think of us at all even though we have been staying here for two or three months.
Suppose we were to engage in the "trade of virtues," announcing to one another among the people, "Such-and-such a bhikkhu is an attainer of the first jhāna...
[and so on] ...such-and-such a one possesses the six supernormal powers," and thus fill our bellies?
“Having first looked after [the monastery], we shall afterwards resolve upon the precepts”—not even a single bhikkhu conceived such a desire.
Thus was the conduct of longing conquered, overcome, and brought under one's own control.
But in the future, the later generation, sitting in the monastery, will easily obtain [food] and yet ask, "What is this? Is it unhusked rice?"
Thinking, "It is overcooked, unsalted, too salty, not sour enough, or too sour; what is the use of this?
one would despise the rice and meat meal in such a manner, treating it with contempt and disdain. Alternatively, a country is not always short of food;
sometimes it is short of food, and sometimes there is an abundance of food. This [country]...
When there is an abundance of food, people who have gained confidence in you, O good men, through this practice,
will think that various kinds of rice preparations and meat-rice, such as rice-gruel and solid food, should be given to the monks. Your fellow practitioners,
known as your companions in the holy life, will [receive] the honor arising from that which depends upon you.
The people, sitting among you and experiencing [the food], will look down upon it; on that account, they will harbor both conceit and self-deprecation.
How so? "Why has this much been cooked? Do you have no vessels in which you might put your own portion and set it aside? Thus they will speak.
The Discussion on Famine is finished.
Regarding the "Lion’s Roar of Mahāmoggallāna" (Discourse 17):
now, in the passage beginning with "Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna," the word *āyasmā* is a term of endearment; it is a designation for one who is respected, revered, and held in high esteem.
“Mahāmoggallāna”: he is called Mahāmoggallāna because he is great (*mahā*) due to the greatness of his virtues, and Moggallāna by clan (*gotta*).
“He said this” (*etadavoca*): this indicates the words that are now to be stated, beginning with “At present, venerable sir.
Why did he say it? It is said that on the seventh day after going forth, the Elder reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*).
The Teacher, too, on account of his great psychic power, placed him in the foremost position among those possessing such power. Relying upon that great psychic power of his own, he thought:
"This Verañjā is suffering from famine, and the monks are weary; what if I were to overturn the earth and feed the monks with the juice of the *pappaṭaka* fungus?
Then this thought occurred to him: "If I were to do so in the presence of the Blessed One..."
"If I were to do this without having asked the Blessed One while he was dwelling here, it would not be fitting for me;
it would be as if I were competing with the Blessed One. Therefore, desiring to ask, he approached the Blessed One and said this.
"The lower surface is complete": it is said that on the lower surface of the earth there is the essence of the earth, the sap of the earth, the crust of the earth.
It exists; it is with reference to this that he speaks. In this context, "well-ripened" (*sampanna*) means sweet;

the meaning is "of excellent flavor. For just as in the passage, "There is a tree there with well-ripened fruit and fully developed fruit," the meaning is "having sweet fruit," so too here "well-ripened" should be understood as sweet and of excellent flavor.
It is like pure honey (*khuddamadu*) that is free from beeswax.
This, however, is stated for the purpose of providing an illustration by way of its sweetness.
"Honey from small bees" means honey made by small bees. "Without a hive" means free from bees, free from bee-stings, and perfectly pure.
It is said that this honey is the foremost, the best, the most flavorful, and the most nutritious of all honeys. Therefore he said: "Just as if it were honey from small bees..."
"...would have such a lack of stability and such a lack of enjoyment.
"Excellent, venerable sir," [he said]. "Excellent, venerable sir" (*sādhu*) is here a word of entreaty.
For the Elder, entreating the Blessed One to turn the earth over, spoke thus: "I would turn it over" (*parivatteyyan*); that is, I would overturn it, [placing] the lower surface...
“I would make it on top. Why? Because if it were made thus, the monks would be able to eat the earth-essence and the *pappaṭaka* fungus with ease.
Then the Blessed One, although not wishing to grant permission, asked the Elder to let him utter a lion’s roar:
“But as for those living beings, Moggallāna, who depend upon the earth—how will you deal with them? “Those who depend upon the earth...”
"Regarding the living beings in villages, market towns, and so forth—since they would be unable to remain in the air when the earth is turned over, what will you do?

Where will you place them? Then the Elder, demonstrating his own power of psychic potency (iddhi) in accordance with the status he had been assigned by the Blessed One as foremost among those possessing such powers, said: "One day, Bhante," and so on. Its meaning is: "For one day, Bhante..."
"Just as this great earth is, so shall I create [another]; I shall make it identical to the earth.
Having done so, those living beings who depend upon the earth, I shall transfer them from one palm of my hand to the other, as if moving living beings already situated on a single palm."
Then the Blessed One, rejecting his request, said, "Enough, Moggallāna," and so forth. In this context, *alam* is a word of rejection.
"Beings might even obtain a perversion" means that beings might arrive at a distorted grasp. How so? "Is this earth, or is it not? Or alternatively, "Is this village ours, or is it not?"
"Of others. Thus it is with regard to villages, market towns, fields, monasteries, and so forth. Or rather, this is not a distortion;
for the range of psychic power (*iddhi*) of one possessing psychic power is inconceivable. However, they might perceive such a distortion as follows:
"This thing called famine does not occur only now, but will also occur in the future. At that time, monks [will find] a fellow practitioner possessing such psychic power..."

How will they obtain [alms]? Although they are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, practitioners of dry-insight, attainers of jhāna, possessors of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and those whose taints are destroyed, they will approach other families for alms because they lack the power of psychic potency (iddhibala). There, people will think:
"In the time of the Buddha, the monks were fulfillers of the training; having produced such qualities..."
"In times of famine, they turned over the earth and ate the *pappaṭaka* fungus. But now, there are none who fulfill the training.
If there were, they would act just as they did before; they would not give us anything at all to eat, whether cooked or raw.
Thus, regarding those very noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), [he says]: "There are no noble persons."
They might fall into this perversion; and by way of such perversion, reviling and disparaging the Noble One, they would go to the states of misery.
Therefore, let it not please you to overturn the earth.
Then, not obtaining this request, the Elder made another request, saying, “It is well, Bhante,” and so forth. And for him too—
The Blessed One, declining [the offer], said, "Enough, Moggallāna," and so forth.

Although it is not explicitly stated there that "sentient beings might also obtain a perversion [of perception]," nevertheless, it should be understood according to the method previously explained; its meaning should also be known as being exactly like what was said.
But if the Blessed One had permitted it, what would the Elder have done? [He would have] [dried up] the great ocean with a single...
Having resolved upon the mere outline of the path that must be traversed by stepping along the footprints,
he should lead the way from Naḷeru-pucimanda toward Uttarakuru, and having established it at a place where going to and coming from Uttarakuru is convenient,
he should show it so that the monks may enter and leave for alms as they please, just as one would do for a village of resort.
The Discourse on the Lion’s Roar of Mahāmoggallāna is finished.
18. Commentary on the Discourse Requesting the Formulation of the Vinaya:
Now, the Venerable Upāli, in order to show the origin (*nidāna*) of the formulation of the Vinaya from its very root, [addressed] the Elder Sāriputta...
Showing the arising of a thought connected with the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), he said: “Then, to the Venerable Sāriputta,” and so forth.
Therein, “having gone into seclusion” means having gone to a private place. “Being in retreat” means being secluded, having attained a state of solitude.
“Of which ones? means of which among the past Buddhas, such as Vipassī and the others. “His stability would be long” or “for a long time...”
"Of its stability" means having long duration. The rest here has a meaning that is plain on the surface.
But is it that the Elder was unable to determine this reflection of his own? It is said:
he both can and cannot. For he [can] know that the teaching of these Buddhas does not have long duration.
He was able to determine only this much: "This [teaching] will endure for a long time" or "This will endure for such a length of time.
However, he was not able to determine by what cause it would not endure for a long time, or by what cause it would endure for a long time. But the Elder Mahāpaduma said:
"Even this was not difficult for the Chief Disciple, who had reached the pinnacle of the sixteenfold wisdom; yet by the Fully Enlightened One..."
"But for one living in the same place as [the Buddha], making a decision oneself is like weighing with the hand after having discarded the scale;
therefore, he approached the Blessed One himself and asked. Then, answering him, the Blessed One said:
"And of the Blessed One, Sāriputta, and Vipassi," and so forth. That has an obvious meaning.
19. Again, the Elder, asking for the reason, said, "What, venerable sir, is the cause? and so forth. In that context, "What, venerable sir?
is a question regarding the reason; its meaning is, "Which one, venerable sir, is it? Both "cause" (*hetu*) and "condition" (*paccaya*) are designations for a reason (*kāraṇa*);
for it is called a "cause" because by means of it, its fruit is brought about (*hinoti*) or made to proceed.
It is called "condition" (*paccaya*) because it comes toward and proceeds in dependence upon that; therefore, it is called a condition.
Thus, although in meaning they are one and the same, both terms are used here and there according to conventional usage and for the sake of euphony in speech. The rest here is of plain meaning.
Now, in order to show that cause (*hetu*) and condition (*paccaya*), he said: "The Blessed One, Sāriputta, Vipassī," and so forth. Therein:
"Free from lassitude" means they are not lazy or sluggish; for there is no laziness or slackness of energy in the Buddhas.
Indeed, whether teaching the Dhamma to one person, to two, or to the entire world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), the Buddhas teach the Dhamma with equal enthusiasm.
They do not become slack in their energy upon seeing the smallness of the assembly, nor do they become over-exerted upon seeing its greatness.

Having seen this, they exerted intense energy. For just as Sīha, the king of beasts, having departed for his range after seven days have passed, runs with a speed exactly the same toward small or large creatures alike—for what reason?
“Lest my speed should diminish”—even so do the Buddhas, whether toward a small or a great assembly, [proceed] with equal [speed].
They teach the Dhamma with enthusiasm. For what reason? "Lest our reverence for the Dhamma should decline.
For the Buddhas are those who revere the Dhamma and cherish the Dhamma.
Just as our Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail, as if filling the great ocean, so too [do they].
Thus they did not teach [the Dhamma] in detail. Why? Because of the small amount of dust on the eyes of beings (*sattānam apparajakkhatāya*).
It is said that at that time, beings were long-lived and possessed little dust on their eyes; having heard even a single verse connected with the Four Noble Truths, they realized the Dhamma.
Therefore, they did not teach the Dhamma in detail. For that very reason, their discourses (*sutta*) were few... [and so forth].
"Vedalla. In this context, the diversity of the Sutta and other categories has already been explained in the commentary on the First Council.

"A training rule not laid down for the disciples" means that because the disciples were faultless, no formal command as a training rule had been laid down according to their faults, by way of the seven classes of offenses.
"The Pātimokkha not recited" refers to [the half-monthly recitation].
The Pātimokkha of the formal recitation was not recited. They recited only the Pātimokkha of the exhortation, and even that only once every half-month.
For the Blessed One Vipassī recited the Pātimokkha of the exhortation only once every six years, and he did so personally.
His disciples, however, did not recite it in their own respective dwelling places throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
In one place alone—in the Khema Deer Park at the royal capital of Bandhumatī, at the dwelling place of the Blessed One Vipassī—the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus observed the Uposatha.
And that was indeed the Saṅgha Uposatha; it was not the Gaṇa Uposatha, nor the Puggala Uposatha, nor the Pārisuddhi Uposatha, nor the Adhiṭṭhāna Uposatha.
At that time, it is said, there were eighty-four thousand monasteries in Jambudīpa.
In each monastery, ten or twenty thousand bhikkhus lived without interruption, and even more lived there.
Deities who announce the Uposatha went here and there and proclaimed: "Venerable sirs, one year has passed; two, three, four..."

"Five years have passed; this is the sixth year. On the coming full moon day, you must go for the purpose of seeing the Buddha and for the purpose of observing the Uposatha. The time for your assembly has arrived.
Then the powerful bhikkhus went by their own respective power, while the others went by the power of the deities. How so? It is said that those bhikkhus...

Whether they were staying at the edge of the eastern ocean, or at the edge of the western, northern, or southern oceans, having fulfilled their duties toward those departing, they took up their bowls and robes and resolved, "Let us go. With the mere arising of that thought, they were as good as having gone to the Uposatha hall.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened Vipassī, they sat down. And the Blessed One, seeing that they were seated...
He recites this Pātimokkha of exhortation to the assembly:
“Patience is the supreme austerity; endurance is the supreme austerity;
the Buddhas declare that Nibbāna is the supreme.”
For one who harms others is not a renunciant;
one who oppresses another is not a śramaṇa.
"To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome,"
The purification of one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas:
non-reproach, non-harming, restraint according to the Pātimokkha,
moderation in food, and dwelling in secluded lodgings.
"And application to higher consciousness—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
By this very method, the recitation of the Pātimokkha for the other Buddhas should also be understood.
For all Buddhas have these same three verses of the Pātimokkha as their exhortation. These [verses] remain for Buddhas of long life until the end of their dispensations.

They come for recitation during the first enlightenment of Buddhas of short lifespan. However, from the time of the formal proclamation of the training rules (sikkhāpada) onwards, only the *āṇā-pātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha of the command) is recited. And that is recited by the monks alone, not by the Buddhas.
Therefore, for us as well, our Blessed One recited this *ovāda-pātimokkha* (Pātimokkha of exhortation) for only about twenty years during his first enlightenment.
Having recited [the Pātimokkha], one day, while sitting in the Migāramātā’s Palace in the Eastern Park, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, from this time forward I shall no longer perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha;
you yourselves, bhikkhus, should henceforth perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha. This is impossible, bhikkhus—”
"It is impossible that a Tathāgata would perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha in an assembly that is not pure.
From that time forth, the monks recited the Pātimokkha by command. This was the "Pātimokkha by command" which had not been formally recited for them.
Therefore it is said: "the unrecited Pātimokkha."
"Of those Buddhas" means of those three Buddhas beginning with Vipassī. "By their disappearance" means by the disappearance of the aggregates (*khandha*);

it is synonymous with their *parinibbāna*. "Those who awakened after the Buddhas" refers to those who were the direct disciples (*sammukhasāvaka*) of those Buddhas, and [their disappearance] is by the disappearance of their aggregates.
"Those who were the final disciples" refers to those who were in the presence of those direct disciples.
The last disciples who went forth [were as follows]: "Of various names" means they had diverse names by way of their personal names, such as "Buddharakkhita," "Dhammarakkhita," and so on.
"Of various clans" means they were of diverse lineages by way of their clan names, such as "Gotama," "Moggallāna," and so on.

"Of various births" means they were of diverse castes by way of their birth-status, such as "Khattiya," "Brāhmaṇa," and so on. "They went forth from various families" refers to those from Kṣatriya families and others.
Nor did they go forth from various families by way of high or low, noble or ignoble, or great or small enjoyments and so forth.
"They [practice] that holy life"— those later disciples, because they have gone forth from one name, one clan, one birth, and one family,
take it upon themselves as their own burden, thinking, "This is our teaching, our tradition, our lineage," and thus they guard the holy life.
They preserve the Dhamma of the scriptures for a long time. But these [monks] were not like that.
Therefore, harassing one another and taking up opposing views, saying, "This elder will know;
that elder will know," they acted laxly and caused that holy life to disappear very quickly; they did not protect it by committing it to a formal compilation. "Just as if... [and so forth].
This is the illustration by way of a simile for that meaning. "Scatters" means it disperses. "Dissipates" means it leads to another place.
"Destroys" means it removes from its original location. "Just as because it is not held together by a thread":

just as, because it is not held together by a thread—because it is not knotted and not bound—it scatters, so too do those things which are not held together by a thread scatter when they are dispersed.
"Thus he scattered it"—this is what is meant. "In this very way" is the application of the simile.

"They caused it to disappear" means that, failing to collect it into sections (*vagga*) or fifties (*paṇṇāsa*), they took only whatever suited their own preferences and destroyed the rest, leading it to non-appearance.
And those Blessed Ones, Sāriputta, were untiring in exhorting their disciples by encompassing their minds with their own minds;
that is to say, Sāriputta, those Buddhas were untiring in exhorting their disciples after having encompassed and delimited their minds with their own minds.
Having known the minds of others, they did not regard the instruction as a burden or as a tedious task. Once upon a time...
“Sāriputta,” and so forth, was spoken for the purpose of demonstrating their state of being untiring. “In the terrifying” means in that which is fearful, that which generates fear.
“Reflect thus” means reflect upon the three types of reflection, beginning with renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*).
“Do not reflect thus” means do not reflect upon the three unwholesome reflections, beginning with sensual desire (*kāma-vitakka*). “Attend to the mind thus” [means attend to it as] “impermanent”...
“Meditate thus: ‘It is suffering, non-self, and unattractive. Do not meditate thus:
‘It is permanent, pleasant, self, and attractive. Abandon this: abandon what is unwholesome.
Having entered upon and attained this, dwell having accomplished it: enter upon and dwell in what is wholesome.”
“Without clinging, their minds were liberated from the taints” means they were liberated without grasping.
For as to those taints from which their minds were liberated, they were not liberated by grasping them; rather, ceasing through non-arising and cessation, they were liberated without grasping.
Therefore it was said: “Without clinging, their minds were liberated from the taints. All [of them].

Having attained arahantship, their minds blossomed like a bed of lotuses touched by the rays of the sun. In this context, "there" (*tattha*) refers back to the previous statement regarding the terrifying nature of the Bhiṃsanaka forest grove;

"sudaṃ" is a particle used merely to fill out the meter; and "Sāriputta" is a form of address. This, then, is the construction of the meaning here: [They] attained arahantship and became those whose hearts were fully blossomed, like a cluster of lotuses struck by the rays of the sun. In that very place, Sāriputta, there was indeed a state of terror within the terrifying forest grove;

thus, the word "there" (*tattha*) depends upon the preceding statement. "Sudaṃ" is a mere expletive particle (*nipāta*). "Sāriputta" is an address. Furthermore, this is the interpretation of the sense in this passage: [and so forth].
Regarding what was said there, “in a certain terrifying forest thicket,” that which was called the “terrifying forest thicket”:
it occurs in the state of being terrifying of that terrifying forest thicket; the meaning is that it occurs by way of the act of terrifying.
What occurs? This occurs: anyone who is not free from lust... [and so on] ...their hair stands on end.

Alternatively, *tatra* here is in the locative case used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmi-atthe*). *Su* is a particle, as in such expressions as “What indeed, O venerable recluses and brahmins? (*kiṃ su nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā*). *Idaṃ* is a term of demonstration that presents the intended meaning as if it were directly perceived before one’s eyes.
*Suidaṃ* is *sudaṃ*; the elision of the vowel *i* should be understood as occurring by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
“The faculty of the eye, the faculty of femininity, the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown’... (*cakkhundriyaṃ, itthindriyaṃ, anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ*)... [and so forth].
It is as in such passages as “What is wealth, indeed? Herein, this is the construction of the meaning:
regarding the terrifying nature of that terrifying forest grove, Sāriputta, this occurred to him. “In the terrifyingness” (*bhiṃsanakatasmim*) means in the state of being terrifying;

one *t*-sound is to be understood as elided. Or rather, the reading is simply “in the state of being terrifying” (*bhiṃsanakattasmim*). [The commentary says: “By way of terrifyingness” (*bhiṃsanakatāya*).
Although it should have been stated thus, a change of gender has been made. Furthermore, this locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*);
therefore, the connection should be understood as follows: "In the state of being terrifying, they become afraid";

that is, on account of the state of being terrifying, by reason of the state of being terrifying, through the condition of the state of being terrifying, they become afraid. Whoever, not being free from lust, enters that grove, for the most part...
"The hairs bristle" means that the majority of the hairs bristle; they remain standing with their tips turned upward, resembling needles and thorns, while only a few do not bristle.
Alternatively, it means they bristle in most beings, but do not bristle in a few individuals who are exceedingly courageous.
Now, "This, Sāriputta, is the cause," and so forth, is the conclusion. Whatever has not been stated here in between is of plain meaning;

therefore, it should be understood according to the sequence of the text itself. As for what was said—that [the teaching] did not endure for long—that should be understood as being stated by way of the succession of pairs of persons. For, by the calculation of years, [it lasted] of the Blessed One Vipassī...
The lifespan was eighty thousand years, and his immediate disciples lived for exactly that same duration.
Thus, including even the very last disciple, the holy life (brahmacariya) endured for one hundred and sixty thousand years.
However, when calculated by way of successive pairs of men, it endured for only two such pairs.

Therefore, it is said that [his dispensation] did not endure for long. However, the lifespan of the Blessed One Sikhī was seventy thousand years, and the lifespan of his immediate disciples was exactly the same.
The lifespan of the Blessed One Vessabhū was sixty thousand years, and the lifespan of his immediate disciples was exactly the same as well.
Thus, even including those who were the very last of his disciples, together with them—
Having calculated from one hundred thousand years upwards, he remained in the holy life for forty thousand and twenty thousand years.
However, according to the succession of human pairs, it lasted for only two pairs of men.
Therefore, it is said that his duration was not long.

20. Thus, having heard the reason why the holy life of three Buddhas did not endure for long, the Venerable Sāriputta, desiring to hear the reason why the holy lives of the other three did endure for long, again questioned the Blessed One in the same manner, beginning with the words, "But what, venerable sir, is the cause?
The Blessed One answered him as well; all of that is to be understood by way of the opposite of what was previously stated.

This should be understood. Furthermore, regarding their long endurance, it should be understood that they endure for a long time in two ways: by the measure of their lifespan and by the number of generations of men.
For the Blessed One Kakusandha’s lifespan was forty thousand years, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana’s was thirty thousand years, and the Blessed One Kassapa’s was twenty thousand years.
For their face-to-face disciples as well, it was exactly that much. And many pairs of disciples maintained the holy life (brahmacariya) through successive lineage.
Thus, both by way of the measure of their lifespan and by way of the pairs of disciples, the holy life remained long-lasting for them.
However, for our Blessed One [Gautama], at a time when the lifespan was ten thousand years—half the measure of the lifespan of the Blessed One Kassapa—...

It might have arisen [at other times]. Failing to achieve that, it might have arisen during a time when the lifespan was five thousand years, or a time when the lifespan was one thousand years, or even a time when the lifespan was five hundred years.

However, because he sought, searched for, matured his knowledge, and took conception while pursuing the qualities that constitute Buddhahood, it arose during a time when the lifespan was five hundred years.
His knowledge reached full maturity. Therefore, he appeared during a time when the lifespan was exceedingly short.

Consequently, it is appropriate to say that while his holy life (*brahmacariya*) endured for a long time by way of the succession of disciples, it did not endure for long in terms of the calculation of years due to the limit of the lifespan.
21. Now, as for "Then the Venerable Sāriputta": what is the connection? It is the connection regarding the holy life of these three Buddhas.

Having heard the reason for long endurance, and having reached the conclusion that the very laying down of training rules is the cause for the state of long endurance, the Venerable Sāriputta—desiring the long endurance of the Blessed One’s holy life—requested the Blessed One to lay down training rules.
This was said in order to show the manner of that request: "Then the Venerable... [and so forth].
Sāriputta rose from his seat... [as before] ... "for long endurance. Therein, "enduring" means capable of withstanding a journey;
it is said to be for a long period of time. The rest is plain in meaning.
Then the Blessed One, making it clear that "this is not yet the time for the laying down of a training rule," said to him, "Wait, Sāriputta," and so forth.
In this context, "āgamehi tvan" means "wait, you"; it is said as "endure, you" for the time being.

It is stated twice here for the sake of emphasis. By this, the Blessed One, having set aside the possibility of disciples being the scope for the promulgation of training rules (*sikkhāpada*), spoke the words beginning with "or the Tathāgata," thereby revealing that "the promulgation of training rules is the domain of a Buddha alone. And herein—
*“Therein”* (*tattha*) is a locative expression referring to the request for the laying down of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The construction here is as follows:
regarding what was said, “He shall lay down a training rule,” it is that the Tathāgata alone will know the proper time for that laying down of the training rule.
Having said this, he spoke the words beginning with “Not yet, Sāriputta” in order to show that it was not yet the right time.
In this context, "bases for the taints" (*āsavaṭṭhānīya*) means that the taints abide within them.

This refers to those things subject to transgression in which the taints of suffering pertaining to the present life and the future life, as well as the taints of the defilements—namely, the reproach of others, remorse, execution, imprisonment, and so forth, including the specific sufferings of the states of deprivation—indeed abide;
for they are the causes of these [taints]. These are the things subject to transgression which serve as bases for the taints.
The construction here is as follows: "As long as [the offenses] do not manifest within the Saṅgha, so long does the Teacher not lay down a training rule for his disciples.
For if he were to lay them down [prematurely], he would not be freed from the reproach, attacks, and the fault of censure by others. How so?
Because by one who lays them down, the entire rule beginning with "Whosoever, monk, should engage in sexual intercourse... and so forth [would have been established].
It would have had to be prescribed. Had they seen no fault in transgression, yet having understood this prescription, others might have raised such criticism, objection, and reproach as:

"How is it that the ascetic Gotama, whose monastic community follows him and obeys his word, will enclose them with training rules to such an extent that he will prescribe an offense entailing expulsion?"
"Surely these sons of good family have gone forth, having abandoned a great mass of wealth, a vast circle of kinsmen, and even kingdoms held in their own hands;

they dwell content with mere food and clothing, possessing intense reverence for the training, and remaining indifferent toward both body and life. Among them, who indeed would indulge in sexual intercourse, which is but a bait of worldly things?"
"He might steal another's property, or he might cut off the life of another who is dear, beloved, and very sweet to them, or he might make his living by speaking of non-existent qualities!
Even before the *pārājika* rules were laid down, was this not made evident by the mere fact of his going forth?
[If not,] beings would not know the power and strength of the Tathāgata. Even when they have been laid down...
The training rule would be violated; it would not remain in its proper place.

It is just as if an unskilled physician, having summoned a man who has no tumor, were to say: "Come, sir, a great tumor will arise in this part of your body and bring about your ruin and misfortune; have it treated beforehand. To which [the man] replies: "Very well, teacher."

When told, "You yourself must treat him," he would cut open the diseased part of his body, drain out the blood, and having restored that area to its natural state through ointments, bandaging, washing, and so forth, he would say to the man: "I have treated your great disease;
give me what is to be given. The other would ask: "What is this foolish physician saying? Which..."

"Has this disease of mine been cured by him? Does it not rather produce suffering for me and lead me to the loss of blood?"—thus one would revile, find fault with, and censure [the physician], and would not recognize his merit.
In the same way, if the Teacher were to lay down a training rule for his disciples when the fault of transgression had not yet arisen, because of the reproach of others and so forth...
Furthermore, [the Teacher] would not be fully liberated, nor would beings know his steadfastness or power;
even a formulated training rule (*sikkhāpada*) would become invalid and fail to remain in its proper place. Therefore it was said: "Sāriputta, so long as the Teacher has not yet appeared...
[etc. ...among his disciples. Having thus shown the improper time, he spoke the passage beginning with "But when, Sāriputta... in order to show the proper time. Therein:
*Yato* means "when"; that is to say, "at which time. The rest should be understood according to what has already been stated.

This, then, is the summarized meaning here: at whatever time the faults of transgression, designated as "states conducive to the taints" (*āsava-ṭṭhānīyā dhammā*), become manifest in the Saṅgha, at that time the Teacher proclaims a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) for his disciples and recites the Pātimokkha.
Why? For the purpose of warding off the faults of transgression against those very things designated as "states conducive to the taints.

When prescribing thus, it is just as a skilled physician, treating an arisen boil with incision, ointment, bandaging, washing, and so forth, might suppress the disease and restore the skin, yet would not thereby be free from blame or the like; rather, he remains [responsible] for his own...
Having become one whose power is known within the teacher's circle, he receives honor;
thus he is not subject to censure and the like, and having become one whose power is known within his own domain of omniscience, he receives honor.
And that training rule of his becomes unshakable, remaining in its proper place.

Having thus stated that the non-arising of states conducive to the taints (*āsava*) is the improper time for the formulation of training rules (*sikkhāpada*), while their arising is the proper time, he now spoke the passage beginning with “Not yet, Sāriputta, here some...
in order to show the time of non-arising and the time of arising of those states.
Therein, the words whose meaning is obvious should be understood according to the text itself.
Now, for this non-obvious commentary on the words: *rattaññū* means "knowing the nights";
they know many nights starting from the day of their own going forth—thus it is said they are "long-ordained. *Rattaññumahattaṃ* means "greatness by those who know the nights";
the meaning is the state of greatness among those long-ordained. In that regard, having attained greatness by those who know the nights...
It should be understood that this training rule was formulated concerning Upasena Vaṅgantaputta in the Saṅgha.

Having seen monks granting full ordination when they were less than ten years [of standing], that venerable one—being himself only one year [of standing]—granted full ordination to his own resident pupil.
Then the Blessed One laid down the training rule: "Monks, one who is less than ten years [of standing] must not grant full ordination. Whoever..."

“If one should confer full ordination [on such a person], there is an offense of wrong-doing. When this training rule had been thus laid down, monks who were foolish and incompetent conferred full ordination [thinking], “We have ten years of seniority; we have ten years of seniority. Then the Blessed One laid down another training rule:
“Monks, one who is foolish and incompetent must not confer full ordination. Whoever should confer it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
“I allow you, monks, a learned and competent monk—whether ten years senior or more than ten years senior—to confer full ordination.
Thus, at the time when the greatness of long-standing seniority was reached, two training rules were laid down.
Greatness by way of abundance means greatness through its vast extent; for as long as the Saṅgha [consists of] elders, novices, and those of middle standing...

When [the Saṅgha] has reached a state of abundance and greatness, then the lodgings suffice. While certain conditions conducive to the arising of taints (*āsava*) do not arise in the Dispensation as long as it has not yet reached that state of abundance and greatness, they do arise once it has reached that state.
Then the Teacher lays down a training rule for his disciples. In that regard, when the Saṅgha has reached a state of abundance and greatness, the training rules laid down are: "Whoever..."
“Furthermore, if a monk should lie down in the same sleeping place as one who is not fully ordained for more than two or three nights, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

“Furthermore, if a nun should give the full admission every year, it is an offense of expiation. “Furthermore, if a nun should give the full admission twice in a single year, it is an offense of expiation”—these [rules] are to be understood according to this method.
"Lābhaggamahattaṃ" means the preeminence and greatness of gain. The meaning is that he has attained that which is the foremost, the highest, and the vast state of gain.
Alternatively, the meaning is that by means of gain he has attained both preeminence and greatness.
For as long as the Saṅgha has not attained the preeminence and greatness of gain, it does not, on account of that gain, [attain its full status].
Conditions conducive to the taints arise. But when they have attained [the highest gain], then the Teacher lays down a training rule for his disciples:

“Whosoever, however, should with his own hand give hard food or soft food to a naked ascetic, or to a male wanderer, or to a female wanderer, there is an offense of expiation. For this is the attainment of the pinnacle of gain and greatness.
A training rule was laid down for the Saṅgha.
"The greatness of great learning" refers to the magnitude of great learning.

For as long as the Saṅgha has not attained the greatness of great learning, the states that are the basis for the taints do not arise; but when it has attained the greatness of great learning, [they do].
Because individuals who, having mastered even one Nikāya, or two...

[or] even all five Nikāyas, emerge with improper reflection and—blending essence with essence—proclaim what is contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, and outside the Teacher’s instruction; therefore, the Teacher said:
"Whosoever, O Bhikkhus, should speak thus: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One... [and so on]... even a novice..."
“He who should speak thus,” and so forth, in this manner the Blessed One laid down the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

Having thus shown both the time when the conditions for the arising of the taints (*āsava*) do not occur and the time when they do occur, the Blessed One, at that moment, demonstrating the total absence of them all, said: “For it is free from worms, Sāriputta,” and so on.
In this context, *nirabbuda* means "devoid of *abbudas*"; *abbudas* are called thieves (*corā*), so the meaning is "free from thieves.
And in this sense, it is the immoral ones who are intended by the term "thieves," for they, while not being true recluses, steal the requisites of others under the pretense of being recluses.
Therefore, *nirabbuda* means "free from thieves," which is to say, "free from the immoral. *Nirādīnava* means...

It is free from affliction and free from calamity; what is meant is that it is indeed devoid of the disadvantage of immorality and so forth. "Devoid of black" (*apagatakāḷaka*): "black" refers specifically to those who are immoral.
For even though they may possess a golden complexion, because they are joined with the nature of blackness, they should be understood as being truly black.
Due to the absence of such persons, it is "devoid of black. There is also a reading *apahatakāḷaka*. It is "pure" (*suddha*) precisely because it is devoid of blackness.

"Pure, cleansed, and luminous. "Established in the essence": the essence refers to the qualities of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana). Because he is established in that essence, he is said to be "established in the essence.
Having thus stated the state of being established in the essence, it should further be understood how that state of being established in the essence is to be known.
He said, "Sāriputta, showing these [qualities]," and so forth. Herein, this is the brief commentary:

Of these five hundred bhikkhus who entered the rains retreat at Verañjā, even the bhikkhu who was the least in terms of qualities, possessing the most meager virtues, was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
"Stream-enterer" means one who has entered the stream; and "stream" is a designation for the Path (*magga*).
“Stream-enterer” refers to a person endowed with that [stream]. As it is said:
“‘Stream, stream,’ this is what is said here, Sāriputta. What, Sāriputta, is the stream?
It is precisely this noble eightfold path, namely: right view... right concentration.”
“‘Stream-enterer, stream-enterer,’ this is said, Sāriputta. But who, Sāriputta, is a stream-enterer?
“Venerable sir, whoever is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path, he is called a stream-enterer. This venerable one, of such a name and such a clan, is one.
In this case, however, the name of the fruit has been given by means of the path. Therefore—
One who stands at the stage of the fruit should be understood as a "stream-enterer" (sotāpanna).

Regarding the term *avinipātadhamma*: that which causes one to fall into the states of ruin (*vinipāta*) is called *vinipāta*; one whose nature is not such as to cause falling into ruin is *avinipātadhamma*.
What is meant is that his nature does not consist in casting himself into the states of misery (*apāya*). Why is this? Because those qualities which lead to going to the states of misery—
Through the complete exhaustion of those [defilements]. *Vinipāta* means falling into ruin; one whose nature (*dhamma*) is not such ruin is *avinipātadhamma*;

what is meant is that he lacks the inherent tendency to fall into the states of misery (*apāya*). Because he is made certain by the path through the fixedness of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*), he is *niyata*.
One for whom full enlightenment (*sambodhi*) is the supreme goal (*para-ayana*) or ultimate destination (*parā-gati*) is *sambodhiparāyaṇa*. [This refers to] the three higher paths.
The meaning is "one who will certainly reach [the goal]. Why? Because he has attained the first path.
The discussion on the request for the formulation of the Vinaya is finished. Now, the discussion on the practices customary among the Buddhas.

22. Having thus persuaded the General of the Dhamma and having spent the rains retreat at Verañjā, the Blessed One—having completed the rains and performed the Great Invitation (mahāpavāraṇā)—then addressed the Venerable Ānanda.
"Addressed" means he spoke to him, conversed with him, and awakened him. With what? With the words beginning, "It is indeed the custom... "Custom" means habitual practice.

This is the proper conduct (*vatta*) and accordance with the Dhamma (*anudhammatā*). Furthermore, that customary practice (*āciṇṇa*) is of two kinds: the practice of the Buddhas and the practice of the disciples.

What is the practice of the Buddhas? First of all, this is one: those by whom [the Buddha] has been invited to spend the rains retreat do not set out on a tour of the countryside without having taken leave of or informed them.
But the disciples, whether they have taken leave or not, [may do so].
They set out at their own pleasure.

Furthermore, this is another practice customary for Buddhas: having completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, they set out on a journey through the countryside for the purpose of gathering people.

And while wandering on that journey through the countryside, [they travel] through these: the Great Circle (*mahāmaṇḍala*), the Middle Circle (*majjhimamaṇḍala*), and the Outer Circle (*antimamaṇḍala*).
They move about within one of three circles. Therein, the great circle is eight hundred yojanas, the middle circle is six hundred yojanas, and the final circle is three hundred yojanas.

When they desire to wander in the great circle, then, having performed the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā), on the first day of the lunar fortnight (Pāṭipada), accompanied by a great community of monks, they set out.

Having gone forth, they benefit the great masses of people in villages, market towns, and other places by accepting material gifts, and by means of the gift of the Dhamma, they increase the wholesome merit conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭupanissita*).
After nine months, they conclude their journey through the countryside.
However, if during the rains retreat the monks’ serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) are still immature, they do not perform the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*).

Having granted the invitation for the *pavāraṇā* ceremony and performed the *pavāraṇā* on the full moon day of the month of Kattika, they set out on the first day of the month of Māgasira accompanied by a great assembly of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.
Following the aforementioned method, they completed their alms-tour within the Middle Region over the course of eight months.
However, if there were beings to be converted whose faculties had not yet matured after they had spent the rains retreat, [the Buddha would remain] until those faculties reached maturity.
Having stayed right there until the full moon of the month of Māgasira, on the first day of the month of Phussa, they set out surrounded by a great community of bhikkhus.
Following the same method as described before, they completed their wandering for seven months within the final circuit.
While wandering anywhere within those circuits, they liberated various beings from their defilements through the fruits of stream-entry and the rest.
They act by employing various colors of flowers, as if gathering them according to the needs of those to be converted (*veneyya*).
Furthermore, it is the custom of the Buddhas to daily enter the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) at the time of dawn, taking peaceful bliss with *nibbāna* as its object;
and having emerged from that attainment of fruition, they daily enter the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Entering [the meditative attainments], and after emerging from them, surveying the beings in the ten thousandfold world-system who are ready to be enlightened.

Furthermore, another custom of the Buddhas is: exchanging greetings first with those who have arrived as guests, giving a teaching on the Dhamma by way of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), and laying down a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) when a fault has occurred—this is the custom of the Buddhas.
What is the custom of the disciples? At the time of the Blessed Buddha, there were two assemblies prior to the commencement of the rains retreat.

[This was said] for the purpose of taking up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), for the purpose of announcing the qualities attained by those who have completed the rains-retreat (*vassa*), and for the purpose of taking up a further meditation subject.
This is the practice of the disciples. But here, showing the practice of the Buddhas, he said: "Now this, Ānanda, is the custom of the Tathāgatas. "Āyāma" means "come, let us go.
"Apalokessāma" means "we shall take leave [to set out on] a walking tour. "Evaṃ" is used in the sense of acceptance.
*Nipāto* (the particle). *Bhante* is a term of respect; it may also be understood as the giving of a reply to the Teacher.
*Paṭissosi bhagavato* means he listened to the word of the Blessed One; having turned toward him, he heard and accepted it.
By the word *evaṃ*, it is said that he accepted it.
Now, regarding the phrase "Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself," it is not specified here whether it was at the time of forenoon or at the time of evening.
Nevertheless, having finished his meal and passed the midday, the Blessed One made the Venerable Ānanda his attendant monk and,
starting from the city gate, [illuminated] the city streets with rays of light tawny like liquid gold.
Illuminating [the world], he approached the residence of the brahmin Verañja.
As soon as the Blessed One was seen standing at the door of the house, the attendants announced his arrival.

Regaining his senses and overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency, the brahmin rose up suddenly, prepared a magnificent seat, and went out to meet the Blessed One, saying, "Come this way, Blessed One."
"Let him approach," he said. The Blessed One approached and sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the brahmin of Verañjā, desiring to sit near the Blessed One, moved from his own standing place toward where the Blessed One was.
From this point onward, the meaning is self-evident.
As for what the brahmin said— “Furthermore, that gift which was to be given has not been given”— the intention here is this:
for you who were invited by me and have resided for the three-month rains retreat, there was daily in the morning rice-gruel and solid food,
at midday various kinds of fresh and cooked foods, and in the evening many varieties of drinks, along with honor and worship consisting of perfumes, flowers, and so forth.

"Whatever gift of such a kind ought to have been given has not been given"—here, however, a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*) is to be understood. The meaning here is: "And that gift of ours is not [actually] existing.
