Alternatively, the meaning should be understood thus: "Whatever object for giving we might give to you, even that is not existing [for us]."
"Nor is there a lack of desire to give": even the wish not to give is absent, as it is for the miserly who possess abundant wealth and requisites.
"How could that be found here, for household life has many duties"—the application of this is as follows:
because household life has many duties, therefore, even though there is property to be given, how could that [desire to give] be found here? How is it possible to obtain it?
He spoke thus while censuring the household life, thinking, "What gift could we possibly give you? It is said that he did not realize he had been ensnared by Māra;
rather, he thought, "My mindfulness has become clouded due to the shackles of domestic life," and therefore he spoke in this way.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "Where could such a thing be found here?": within these three months, what could I possibly give to you?
"How could that be obtained? For household life is full of many duties"—thus the application of the words here should be understood.
Then the brahmin, thinking, "What if I were to give all that ought to be given by me over three months on this very single day?
said, "May the venerable Gotama consent," and so forth. In that context, *svātanāya* means "for tomorrow."
"If I were to show you honor, tomorrow there would be merit for me as well as joy and gladness; it is for that purpose.
Then the Tathāgata thought: "If I do not consent, they might think, 'He has received nothing during these three months and is surely angry;
that is why, though entreated by us, he does not accept even a single meal. He lacks the patience to grant his consent.'"
“Thinking ‘this one is not omniscient,’ the brahmin and the inhabitants of Verañjā might censure him and generate much demerit;
let that not happen to them. Out of compassion for them, the Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Having consented, the Blessed One then said to the brahmin of Verañjā, “Enough with this concern regarding the hindrance of household life.”
Having instructed him with a discourse on the Dhamma appropriate for that occasion,
having shown him the benefit pertaining to both the present life and the future life, having encouraged and established him in wholesome states, having inspired him therein and made him zealous,
and having gladdened him by that zeal and by other existing virtues, he rained down the rain of the jewel of the Dhamma.
Having risen from his seat, he departed. But after the Blessed One had left, the brahmin of Verañjā addressed his wife and children:
"Friends, we have invited the Blessed One for three months, yet we have not given him even a single meal during that time.
Come now, prepare such a gift that the entire offering intended for three months may be presented in a single day."

“...it is possible to give. Then, having had an exquisite gift prepared, on the day the Blessed One was invited, at the end of that night, he had the seating area decorated, arranged costly seats, and prepared a great offering variegated with perfumes, incense, scents, and flowers;
then he informed the Blessed One that it was time. Thus it is said: “Then the brahmin of Verañjā...”
When that night had passed... [as before] ... "the meal was finished.
Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, went there. Therefore it is said: "Then the Blessed One... [as before] ...
sat down together with the community of monks. Then the brahmin of Verañjā [approached] the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
“With the Buddha at its head” means having the Buddha as its leader; it is said that they sat down having placed the Buddha as the senior member of the Saṅgha.
“With excellent” means with the most superior. “With one’s own hand” means by means of one’s own hand.

“Having satisfied” means having thoroughly satisfied, having made them full, well-fed, and as much as they required. “Having invited to eat” means having properly invited them to eat, [signaling] with a hand gesture, saying “Enough.”
Having caused [him] to refuse by means of a verbal signal and through a vocal expression. "One who has eaten" (*bhuttāvi*) means one who has finished eating.

"One who has removed the hand from the bowl" (*onītapattapāṇi*) means one whose hand has been taken away from the bowl; it is said to mean "one who has withdrawn the hand. "He clothed him with the three robes" (*ticīvarena acchādesi*) means he gave the three robes to the Blessed One. However, this expression "he clothed him with the three robes" is merely a conventional mode of speech; and in that regard—

Each single robe in the triple set was worth a thousand [pieces of gold]. Thus the brahmin gave the Blessed One a triple set of robes worth three thousand, made of the finest cloth similar to Kāsī fabric.
And to each individual monk he gave a pair of cloths—one pair of cloths for each.
There, one single cloth was worth five hundred [pieces of gold]. In this way, for the five hundred monks...
He gave cloths worth five hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Even after giving this much, the brahmin was not satisfied;

he further cut up many woolen blankets and fine cotton cloths worth seven or eight thousand [pieces of gold] and gave them for the purpose of making waist-bands, shoulder-straps, girdles, water-strainers, and so forth.
He also filled jars with medicinal oils that had been processed a hundred times and a thousand times, and for each [monk], he gave...
She gave oil worth a thousand [pieces of money] for the purpose of anointing the bhikkhu.
What need is there to say more? Among the four requisites, there was no article used by a recluse that had not been given. However, in the Pāli text, only the robe is mentioned.
Having thus performed the great sacrifice, and while he sat having paid homage with his wife and children, the Blessed One then [addressed] the brahmin of Verañjā.

Having spent three months deprived of the enjoyment of the nectar of the Dhamma due to Māra’s interference, [the Blessed One] rained down the rain of the nectar of the Dhamma in a single day, fulfilling his intention.
After instructing him with a discourse on the Dhamma... [and so forth]... he rose from his seat and departed.
The brahmin, together with his sons and wife, paid homage to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, saying, "Once again..."
Saying such things as, “Venerable Sir, please show us favor,” he followed after [the Buddha] and turned back while shedding tears.
Then the Blessed One, having dwelt at Verañjā for as long as he desired—meaning having stayed there according to his inclination or preference—departed from Verañjā.
At the time of setting out on a journey toward Mahāmaṇḍala, the path to be traveled by a Buddha was as follows:

Leaving behind the Saṅgha of bhikkhus who were exhausted by the calamity of famine, and desiring to proceed by the direct route, he did not go via Soreyya and other places, but went to the Payāga landing-place; having crossed the river Gaṅgā there, he arrived at Bārāṇasī.
He arrived there. Having stayed there according to his inclination, he [proceeded] to Vesālī.
He arrived. Therefore it was said: “Without approaching Soreyya... [and so forth] ...he dwelt at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Gabled Hall.
The account of the Buddha’s customary practice is concluded.
From the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the Verañja Chapter is finished.
Herein, regarding its being "all-around beautiful" (*samantapāsādikā*) in every respect:
because it is [derived] from the succession of teachers, and because it illuminates the distinctions of the introductory narratives and the subject matter;
Because of the avoidance of other systems, and because of the purification of one’s own system;
because of the clarification of the phrasing, the meaning of the words, and the sequence of the textual connection;
because of the determination of the training rules, and the demonstration of the divisions of the method of the analysis (vibhaṅga).
To those who perceive clearly, nothing unpleasing is seen herein;
therefore, this is called the *Samantapāsādikā* (The All-Pleasing) for the wise.
This commentary on the Vinaya has been composed by one skilled in training those to be tamed.
"Spoken by the Lord of the World, out of compassion for the world.
The commentary on the Verañjā Chapter is finished. 1.
The Chapter on Defeats (Pārājika-khaṇḍa).
1. The First Pārājika:
Commentary on the Section on Sudinna. 24.
From here onwards, the passage beginning with "At that time, not far from Vesālī," etc., is for the most part clear in meaning.
Therefore, setting aside a word-by-word commentary, we shall explain only those points that require further elaboration wherever they occur.
"Kalandagāma" means a village so named after the *kalandakas*—that is, blackbirds (*kāḷaka*)—who lived there.

"Kalandaputta" refers to the son of the merchant Kalandaka, who was appointed as a royal official and possessed a fortune of four hundred million, and who had received his name from the village itself.
However, because there were other people in that village who also had the name Kalandaka, he was called "the son of Kalandaka," and then further specified as "the merchant’s son.
*Sambahulehi* means by many. *Sahāyakehi*: they are called *sahāyā* (companions) because they come together (*sa-hāyanti*) or approach one another in times of pleasure and pain;
those very companions are *sahāyakā*, and it is with them, the companions, that he is meant. *Saddhim* means together.
"By some business or other" means by some task such as the preparation of goods, the collection of debts, or the recovery of property;
they also say it refers to the festival of the Kattika full moon. For the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī during the bright fortnight of the month of Kattika.
And the festival of the Kattika full moon was a grand occasion there. It should be understood that he went for that purpose.

“He saw”: how did he see? It is said that having seen a great multitude of people leaving the city—having already eaten their morning meal, with their upper robes tucked in, and carrying garlands, perfumes, and ointments in their hands for the purpose of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dhamma—he asked, “Where are you going?
They replied, “To see the Buddha and to hear the Dhamma. He then said, “In that case, I shall go too,” and having gone there...
He saw the Blessed One surrounded by the fourfold assembly, teaching the Dhamma with a Brahma-voice.
Therefore it is said: "He saw... teaching. "Having seen him" means: having seen him. "This thought occurred to him":
this occurred to that son of good family who was being urged on by his past merit. What occurred? "What if I too..."
“May they hear the Dhamma. In this context, “What if... is an expression indicating reflection. Indeed, such a reflection had arisen in him:
“This assembly listens to the Dhamma with one-pointed minds; oh, that I too might hear it!

Now, as for why [the text] says here, “where that assembly was,” instead of saying “where the Blessed One was”: *Note: This passage appears to be a commentary on a specific textual variant or editorial choice regarding the phrasing used when Sudinna Kalandaputta approaches the assembly.*
If it is asked, "By which [way] did he go to that assembly?"—for indeed, a great assembly of most excellent people was seated surrounding the Blessed One;
in that situation, it would not have been possible for him, having arrived later, to approach the Blessed One and sit down.
However, since it was possible in one part of the assembly, he approached that very assembly. Therefore it was said.
—“Then Sudinna Kalandaputta went to where that assembly was. Regarding the statement, “It occurred to Sudinna Kalandaputta as he was sitting to one side”:
it did not occur to him merely by the act of sitting down; rather, it occurred to him after he had heard a brief discourse on the Dhamma connected with the Blessed One’s smile.
However, because it occurred to him while he was already sitting to one side, it is said: “as he was sitting to one side.”
—“As Sudinna Kalandaputta was sitting to one side, this thought occurred to him. What thought occurred?
“In whatever way...,” and so forth.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: “In whatever manner I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One...”
As I investigated this from various perspectives, it occurred to me:

"This holy life, which has been sprinkled with water, must be lived entirely fulfilled so that it may reach its final consummation in the last moment of consciousness by being kept unbroken for even a single day;

and it must be lived entirely purified so that it may reach its final consummation in the last moment of consciousness by being kept unstained by the defilements' impurities for even a single day. It is polished smooth as a conch shell."
One should conduct oneself like a polished conch shell, resembling a clean conch shell.
It is not easy for one living at home, dwelling in the midst of a household, to conduct oneself in this way—perfectly complete... [and so on]...
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, and, having donned saffron robes that are dyed with an astringent taste and suitable for those leading the holy life, [go forth]?
"Having clothed themselves and put on [robes], they would go forth from the household life into homelessness.

And here, since the work such as farming and trade that is beneficial to the household is called "the state of the householder" (*agāriya*), and that does not exist for one who has gone forth, therefore going forth should be known as "the state of the homeless" (*anagāriyā*). That is the going forth into that state of homelessness. "They would go forth" means they would wander forth.
25. "When the assembly had not yet risen, he approached the Blessed One"—this means that Sudinna did not request the Blessed One for the going-forth while the assembly was still seated.

Why? Because there were many kinsmen, blood-relations, friends, and colleagues there who, saying, "You are the only son of your mother and father; you must not go forth," would even have seized him by the arm.

“They might drag me away, and that would become an obstacle to my going forth. Thinking thus, he rose together with the assembly, walked a short distance, and then, on some pretext of attending to his body, turned back, approached the Blessed One, and requested the going forth.
Thus it is said: “Then Sudinna Kalandaputta, when the assembly had not long risen... ‘May the Blessed One let me go forth.’”

But because the Blessed One, from the time Prince Rāhula went forth, did not allow the going forth of a son who had not been permitted by his parents, he asked him: "Have you, Sudinna, been permitted by your mother and father...
for the going forth? 26. From here onwards, following the text itself, one should understand the meaning of the phrase "having completed that duty" as follows:
having brought that duty to completion by laying down the burden; for [the Buddha] does not [grant the going forth] to one who lacks an intense desire for the going forth.
Or his mind inclines toward the employment, restoration, or repair of goods, or toward the sport of astrology. Regarding the words "Mother, Father":
here, "Mother" is an address to the mother, and "Father" is an address to the father. "Tvaṃ khosi" means "you indeed are. "Ekaputtako" means "only one son";
you have no other elder or younger brother. And here, although it should be said "ekaputto," [the form used is "ekaputtako"].
It is said to be “like an only son” by way of compassion. “Beloved” means one who generates joy. “Dear” means one who increases mental esteem.
“Brought up in comfort” means nourished by comfort; the sense is that he was raised in happiness. “Rested in comfort” means nurtured by comfort;
from the time of birth, being carried from lap to lap by nurses and entertained with such children’s toys as horse-carts and the like.
"Playing and being fed delicious food, you have been brought up in comfort.
You, dear Sudinna, know nothing of suffering"—that is to say, dear Sudinna, you do not know even the slightest fraction of suffering;
or rather, the meaning is that you do not experience any suffering at all. [The instrumental sense is used here.]

The genitive case (*sāmivacana*) [is used] in the sense of experiencing, and "knowing" (*jānanā*) is in the sense of remembering. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Do you not remember even some suffering?

Here, the genitive case is in the sense of the object (*upayogatthe*), and "knowing" is in the sense of remembering (*saraṇatthe*). In both alternatives, one should understand that the case-ending of the first word is elided because it is identical to the case-ending of the subsequent word.
All of this should be understood according to the rules of grammar (*saddasattha*). Even by death, we shall be separated from you against our will.

"‘We shall be’ means: even if death should come to you while we are still living, by that death of yours—even though we are unwilling, undesirous, and not by our own choice—we shall exist without [you]; or rather, we shall reach separation from you.
This is the meaning. ‘But what of us?’—this being so, what indeed is that reason by which we [should act]?"

"We shall permit him while he is still living"; or alternatively, "But why [should we], and for what reason should we permit him while he is living?"—this is how the meaning should be understood here. 27.
*Tattheva* (right there) means in that very place where his parents did not grant him permission. *Anantarahitāya* means because it has not been covered by any kind of rug or covering.

28. "Paricārehi" means: having had musicians, actors, dancers, and so forth presented before you, there, together with your companions, move and direct your sense-faculties as you please; that is to say, lead them here and there. Alternatively, "paricārehi" means:
having had musicians, actors, dancers, and so forth presented before you, sport there together with your companions.
"Enjoy yourself, take your pleasure, play!"—this is what is meant. "Enjoying sensual pleasures" means enjoying wealth together with one's own children and wife.
"Performing meritorious deeds" means performing wholesome actions such as giving gifts and so forth, dedicated to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, which clear the path to a happy rebirth.
"He became silent" was for the purpose of interrupting the continuity of the conversation.

There was no conversation or discourse. Then his parents, having spoken to him three times and receiving no reply, summoned his companions and said, "This companion of yours wishes to go forth; restrain him.
They too approached him and spoke to him three times, but he remained silent. Thus it is said: "Then..."
“...the companions of Sudinna Kalandaputta... [and so on]... he remained silent. 29.
Then it occurred to his companions: “If he dies without obtaining the going-forth, it will be of no benefit at all.
But if he has gone forth, even his mother and father will see him from time to time.”
"We too shall see. This going forth is indeed a heavy burden: day after day one must take an earthen bowl and wander for alms.
Sleeping alone, eating but one meal a day, and living the holy life are exceedingly difficult.
Moreover, he is delicate and of a refined urban birth; being unable to practice this, he will surely return here again. Come now, let us speak to his parents."
“We will get permission for him. They did so. His parents also gave him their consent. Therefore it is said:
“Then Sudinna Kalandaputta’s friends went to Sudinna Kalandaputta’s parents...
‘You have been permitted by your parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness.’”
30. *Haṭṭho* means joyful. *Udaggo* means with body and mind uplifted by way of rapture (*pīti*).
*Katipāhaṃ* means for several days. *Balaṃ gāhetvā* means having generated physical strength by eating suitable food and maintaining the body through anointing, bathing, and so forth;
then, having paid homage to his parents and abandoned his circle of relatives who were weeping with tearful faces.
He approached the Blessed One... [and said: "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One let me go forth.
The Blessed One addressed a certain alms-collecting bhikkhu standing nearby: "In that case, bhikkhu, let Sudinna go forth and ordain him.
"Very well, venerable sir," that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One, and he [led] Sudinna...
Having obtained Jinadattiya Kalandaputta as his attendant (saddhivihārika), he both granted him the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the full admission (upasampadā).
Therefore it is said: “Sudinna Kalandaputta received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received the full admission.
Standing upon this point, the going-forth and the full admission are explained in all the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā). However, we—
We shall explain it according to the sequence of the Pāḷi as it stands in the Khandhaka.

Not only this, but whatever else is to be explained in the Khandhaka or the Parivāra that has been discussed by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā in the Vibhaṅga, all of that we shall explain in those very places.
For when it is explained in this way, the commentary is made in accordance with the sequence of the Pāḷi itself. Therefore, by that—
By means of that legal decision, for those who desire it, this commentary on the Vinaya will become easy to understand once they have examined it according to the sequence of the Canon (pāḷi).
"Not long after his full admission" (acirūpasampanno) means having been fully admitted not long ago; that is to say, very shortly after the time of his full admission.
"Such as this" means of such a kind, of such a nature. "Ascetic qualities" (*dhutaguṇa*) refers to qualities that shake off the defilements.
"Having undertaken, he practices" means having formally adopted and taken up [the practice], he conducts himself, acts, and dwells.

"He is a forest-dweller" means that, having rejected a dwelling within a village, he lives in the forest by virtue of the forest-dwelling ascetic practice (*āraññika-dhutanga*). "An alms-food eater" means [one who practices] by rejecting extra acquisitions.
Having rejected fourteen meals, he is an alms-food eater by virtue of the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of eating only alms-food.
He is a rag-robe wearer because, having rejected robes given by householders, he is a rag-robe wearer by virtue of the ascetic practice of wearing rag-robes.

He is one who goes on a continuous round of alms because, having rejected wandering for the sake of greed, he is one who goes on a continuous round of alms by virtue of the ascetic practice of going on a continuous round, visiting houses in regular order.
He enters for alms. "Vajjigāma" means a village of the Vajjis, or a village among the Vajjis.
Regarding the phrase "wealthy, possessing great riches," and so forth: they are called "wealthy" because of the greatness of their enjoyments, usages, and requisites;
what is meant is that whatever enjoyments and requisites they have are great, abundant, and substantial. Having stored away...

They are "of great wealth" (*mahaddhana*) because of the vastness of their deposited riches. They are "of great possessions" (*mahābhoga*) because of the vastness of their daily expenditures, which constitute their enjoyment.
They are "possessing abundant gold and silver" (*pahūtajātarūparajata*) because of the abundance of gold and silver compared to other articles of use.
They are "possessing abundant goods and utensils" (*pahūtavittūpakaraṇa*) because of the abundance of those articles of wealth that serve as ornaments and produce joy and gladness.
"By way of common usage," it should be understood that they are called "those with abundant wealth and grain" because of the abundance of their money and rice as it circulates [in trade].
"Having put away the lodgings" means having arranged the lodgings; the meaning is that he placed them well so that they would not be lost.
"About sixty *thālipāka* offerings" refers to the numerical limit of sixty *thālipāka* offerings. Each one...
And here, the *thālipāka* (rice-pot meal) provides food for ten bhikkhus; all of that becomes food for six hundred bhikkhus.
Regarding the phrase "they brought forth an offering of food" (*bhattābhihāraṃ abhihariṃsu*): here, "offering" (*abhihāra*) means that which is brought forward (*abhiharīyati*).

What is it that is brought forward? Food. The food itself is the offering, thus "an offering of food" (*bhattābhihāra*); they brought forth that offering of food. "They brought forth" (*abhihariṃsu*) means they brought it forward.
"They took [it] away" means they returned after taking it from him. "What was the measure of this? It was sixty *thālipākas*.
Therefore it is said: "They brought a gift of food consisting of about sixty *thālipākas*.

"Having distributed among the bhikkhus" means that, because he himself was a strict alms-collector (*ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātika*) wishing to go on his regular alms-round, he did so for the sake of the bhikkhus' consumption.
Having completely renounced it and given it away. For this venerable one had come for this very purpose: "May the monks receive their gains, and may I not suffer from lack of almsfood.
Therefore, acting in accordance with his own arrival, he assigned [the goods] to the monks and entered for alms himself.
31. “A slave of kinsmen” means a female slave belonging to relatives. “Stale” (*ābhidosika*) means that which has been kept overnight, having passed one night and become putrid.
Herein, this is the word-meaning: it is called *abhidoso* because it is overcome by the fault of putrefaction; what is *abhidoso* is *ābhidosiko*.
Alternatively, this is a designation for that which has passed one night, namely *ābhidosiko*; that which is such is *ābhidosikaṃ*. “Rice-gruel” (*kummāsaṃ*).
Barley gruel. "She wishes to discard it" means that because it is unfit for consumption even by slaves, laborers, or cattle, she wishes to throw it outside like refuse.
"If this" (*sacetaṃ*) means if this. "Sister" (*bhagini*) is a term of noble address used for a female slave.
"Of a nature to be discarded" (*chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ*) means having the inherent quality of being something to be thrown away. This is what is meant: "Sister..."
“If this is something that ought to be discarded and is free from ownership, then pour it here into my bowl.
But is it permissible to speak in such a way? Is it not an act of requesting (*viññatti*) or a directed speech (*payuttavācā*)? It is not. Why?
Because it is free from ownership (*nissaṭṭhapariggaha*). For in the case of something that ought to be discarded and is free from ownership, where there are no owners—
They are without attachment; it is permissible to say of all such things, "Give it, bring it here, pour it into this.
For even the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, a follower of the foremost lineage of the Noble Ones, said: "Pour the gruel, which is of a nature to be discarded, into my bowl here.
Therefore, regarding such things as refuse-remnants, or other unowned items such as forest roots, fruits, and medicines—
Having had all that brought according to one’s pleasure, it should be consumed; one should not feel remorse.
“From the hands” means from the wrist upwards of both hands when they are extended to offer a bowl for the purpose of receiving alms.
“From the feet” means from the edge of the lower garment upwards of both feet. “From the body” means “if this, sister.”
"She grasped the sign" means she grasped, recognized, and observed the physical appearance previously noted during his time as a householder.

For Sudinna had gone forth in the twelfth year after the Blessed One’s own renunciation, and in his twentieth year he entered his kinsmen’s home for alms; thus, at the age of eight years since his own going-forth, she [perceived him].
Having seen him, the slave-girl did not recognize him, yet she took note of his physical characteristics.
She said this to Sudinna’s mother: "Being unable to speak such words as 'Venerable sir, are you perhaps my noble master’s son Sudinna?
to her husband—who had gone forth into homelessness and was exceedingly venerable—she hurriedly entered the house."
He said this to Sudinna’s mother. *Yaggha* is a particle used in the sense of making a request.
Regarding the phrase *sace je saccam*: here *je* is a particle used for addressing; for in that region, they address female slaves in this way.
Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: "O lady, O slave, if you speak the truth."

32. "At the base of a certain wall": it is said that in that region there were halls belonging to the houses of donors, where seats were prepared and water and gruel were set out. There, renunciants, having wandered for alms, would sit and eat.
If they so desired, they would also take what belonged to the donors. Therefore, that too—
It should be understood that this refers to a certain wall-base in such a hall belonging to a certain family.
For renunciants do not sit and eat in unsuitable places like miserable people.

Regarding the phrase "There is indeed, dear one": here *atthi* is used in the sense of existence (*vijjamānatthe*); *nāma* is used in the sense of questioning (*pucchanatthe*) and in the sense of supposition (*maññanatthe*).

This is a particle. For this is what is meant: "Is there indeed, dear Sudinna, any wealth of ours such that we should not be called destitute, for you, sitting in such a place as this, will eat last night's sour gruel?
Likewise: "Is there indeed, dear Sudinna, any life of ours such that we should not be called dead, for [you]..."
“Sitting in such a place as this, you will not eat yesterday’s sour gruel”;
likewise, “I suppose, dear Sudinna, that within you there is a quality of a recluse acquired by means of the Teaching,
since even though you were raised on the flavors of fine food, you will eat this loathsome, yesterday’s sour gruel without hesitation, as if it were the Deathless.”
But that householder, being overwhelmed by suffering, was unable to state this matter in its full detail;
he said only this much: "Is there, dear Sudinna, such a thing as yesterday’s sour gruel that you might eat?
Regarding this, grammarians state the following characteristic: the word *atthi* (is) is used here in the sense of non-acceptance and non-deliberation.
In the phrase "will you eat," a future tense has been employed as a periphrasis.
Its meaning is this: "There is indeed... [etc. ...you will eat; even though this is before my very eyes, I do not believe it, nor do I trust it.
In that regard, "ābhidosiko" means: "this *kummāsa* (fermented rice gruel) obtained from your house last night. There is also the reading "tato yaṃ," and likewise "tadā yaṃ."
They recite [it differently], but that is not correct. "Where the dwelling of his own father is" means where the dwelling of his own father—his biological father—is.
The Elder went there having become well-spoken out of sheer affection for his father. "He consented":
although the Elder was a strict alms-collector (*ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātiko*), he thought, "If I do not accept even a single meal, their distress will be excessive."
Thinking, “It will be so,” he consented out of compassion for his kinsmen.
33. *Opuñjāpetvā* means having had it plastered. *Ekaṃ hiraññassa*: here, *hirañña* should be understood as a *kahāpaṇa* coin. *Puriso*:
a man who is neither too tall nor too short, but of medium stature, should be understood. *Tirokaraṇiyaṃ*: in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*).
*Bhummaṃ*; the meaning is "having enclosed it with a screen-wall. Alternatively, *tirokaraṇiyaṃ* means that by which they make something hidden;
[the phrase] means "having enclosed that," i.e., having made it on all sides. *Tena hi*: because Sudinna will come today—for that reason.
*Hi* is a particle used merely to fill out the metrical line (*padapūraṇa*). *Tenāpi* is likewise a particle used in the sense of dismissal or urging.

34. Regarding "at the time of the morning": although the announcement of the time is not mentioned here in the text, it should nevertheless be understood that he went there only after the time had been announced.
"This for you, dear one"—saying this, he presented two heaps. "From mother" means from the biological mother.
"Clay" means what has come from the mother; this is the wealth given to your maternal grandmother when she came to this house.
"Meaning. He spoke thus in derision, saying, "The woman’s property for a woman.
How much indeed could the wealth obtained for the sake of a woman's personal requisites, such as bath-powder and the like, amount to?
Behold its measure! Or rather: "This, dear Sudinna, is your mother’s wealth; and that too is merely clay, not given by me."
The meaning is that they belong to your mother alone. Furthermore, this was not acquired through agriculture or trade;

rather, it is a woman’s property (*itthidhana*). One should understand the sense here as follows: "To what extent does that woman’s property consist of the bath-powders and such things which are to be obtained from her own family when she goes from her natal home to her husband’s family? It is simply that much.
"Another belonging to the father, another belonging to the grandfather"—that which belonged to his father and his grandfather was indeed different.
"Deposited and employed, and exceedingly much"—here, it should be understood that the word *pitāmaha* has undergone the elision of the *taddhita* suffix.
Alternatively, the reading is *petāmaha*. "It is possible, dear Sudinna, to turn back to the lower life"—"Dear," [he said].

"Sudinna, having abandoned the supreme banner of the Noble Ones—the mark of one who has gone forth—and having returned to the low state of a householder, it would be possible for you to enjoy wealth, but it would not be possible [to maintain the life of a monk]. You did not go forth out of fear of the king, nor were you bound by creditors.
"Dear father, I cannot bring myself to do so. Here, the word "father" (*tāta*) was spoken out of affection rooted in the household life.
“Not by the power of a recluse. “I am not able” means I cannot; “I am not capable” means I am not competent, I am not strong enough.
“We might indeed say that to you, householder”—this statement, however, was spoken by the power of a recluse.
“You should not drag [me] too much” means that the affection established in you toward me, you should not drag it too far by way of anger; that is, if you do not become angry.
Thus it was said. Then the merchant, thinking, "My son wishes to show me favor," spoke with a joyful heart:
"Speak, dear Sudinna. *Tenahi* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation, functioning as a substitute for a case ending. Regarding *tatonidānaṃ*:

it should be understood that the substitution of *to* for the nominative singular ending occurs in the sense of "having that as its source" (*taṃnidānaṃ*) or "having that as its cause" (*taṃhetukaṃ*); furthermore, there is no elision of the suffix in this compound.
Fear (*bhaya*) refers to the fear of kings and so forth, described by such modes as, "How might kings not seize my wealth?"—the meaning is mental terror.

Trembling (*chambhitatta*) is the physical agitation, the quivering of the body, and the throbbing of the flesh of the heart, in one who is being subjected to torture by kings or thieves with the command, "Give the wealth!
Horripilation (*lomahaṃsa*) occurs when fear has arisen.
The plucking out of body hair is its state of being pulled upward. "Guarding" (ārakkha) means protecting both internally and externally, by night and by day.
35. Therefore, the householder Seṭṭhi, having displayed wealth, was unable to entice his son away from the life of a householder;
thinking instead, "Now there is no bond for men like that of a woman," he—

He addressed his former wife: "In that case, my bride. "Former wife" (*purāṇadutiyikā*) means a former companion, one who was a companion in the past during the time of household life, a partner in the enjoyment of domestic pleasures, and a former wife—this is the meaning.
"In that case" (*tena hi*) refers to the reason that there is no bond like that of a woman. "Having grasped by the feet" (*pādesu gahetvā*) means having taken hold of her feet.
The locative case is used in the sense of "utility" (*upayoga*), or it is used by taking it [the word *pāda*] as referring to the feet.

Why did he say, "Of what sort, O noble son, are those celestial nymphs"? It is said that at that time, seeing many young kṣatriyas, brahmins, and sons of merchants going forth into homelessness after abandoning great prosperity, those who did not understand the virtues of the renunciant life raised this question.
—“Why have these gone forth? Others said, “It was for the sake of the celestial nymphs and the divine dancers.
That talk spread widely. Taking that [rumor], they said this. The Elder, rejecting it, said, “No, sister.
“Samudācarati” means he addresses or speaks to her. There she fell down, fainting.
Seeing him address her by the name "sister," she thought, "Now he has no need for me, since he regards me—who am his wife—as if I were a girl lying in the same mother's womb as himself.
With intense grief arising within her, she fainted and fell right there in that spot; "fell" is the meaning.
"Do not harass us" means: "Do not harass us by showing wealth and sending away our womenfolk; for such harassment is [unfitting] for those who have gone forth.
"In that case, dear Sudinna, give even a seed,"—here, "in that case" (tena hi) encourages him toward delight.
"If you practice the holy life with delight, having practiced it, sit in the sky..."
"Enter final Nibbāna, but grant us one son to be the seed of our family lineage.
Do not let the Licchavis seize our property, for we live under the rule of the Licchavi oligarchs;
after your father’s passing, they might otherwise take this vast estate and our wealth, as it would be left without an heir to protect the family property."
“‘They might have my own royal palace removed from its foundations,’ thinking thus, ‘let them not remove it, let them not remove it.
Why did he say, ‘This, mother, is something I can do’? It is said that he thought:
‘I alone am the master of their property; there is no one else. They will constantly follow after me for the sake of guarding that property.’”
Thinking, "Therefore, I shall not be able to practice the duty of a recluse with ease;
however, once they have obtained a son, they will desist, and then I shall practice the duty of a recluse as I please," he spoke thus, perceiving this course of events.
36. *Puppha* is the name for the blood that appears during the fertile period (*utu-kāla*). For at the time of the fertile period, in the place where conception occurs in a woman—
A red-colored pustule forms and, having increased for seven days, bursts open; from that, blood flows out.
This is its name: "flower" (*puppha*). As long as that [blood] remains powerful and flows profusely, even if rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is bestowed, it does not remain;
it flows out together with the bile (*dosa*). But when the bile has flowed out and [the body] is pure—
When the basis is given, rebirth-linking quickly becomes established. "A flower arose for her" means a flower arose for her (*assā*);

the elision of the vowel *a* is a grammatical contraction (*sandhi*). "Having taken hold of the arm of the former wife" means: that which is the arm of the former wife, having taken hold of it there—this is the meaning.
"Before the training rule was laid down" means before the first *pārājika* training rule had been established.
It is said that during the twenty years following the Blessed One’s first enlightenment, the monks pleased his mind; they did not commit such transgressions.
With reference to this very fact, the Sutta says: "Monks, on one occasion the monks indeed pleased my mind."
Then the Blessed One, seeing no transgression [of the kind], did not prescribe a *pārājika* or a *saṅghādisesa*.
However, in each of those cases, he prescribed only the remaining five groups of minor offenses (*khuddakāpattikkhandha*). Therefore it was said:
"when the training rule had not yet been laid down."
"One who does not see the danger" means: not seeing that danger which the Blessed One will now demonstrate when laying down this training rule, he perceives it as blameless.

For if he were to know, "This should not be done," or "This leads to the cutting off of the root [of the lineage]," then even if a clansman who has gone forth out of faith should meet his death on that account, [he would still refrain].
He would not have done so. However, seeing no danger therein, he perceived it as faultless. Therefore it is said: “one who sees no danger.

The term *purāṇadutiyikāya* is in the locative case. *Abhiviññāpesi* means he caused [her] to act; for even the instigation of action is called “making known” (*viññāpanā*) because it involves bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).
It should be understood that this threefold making known was performed by him for the purpose of determining the stabilization of the embryo.
"She conceived a fetus by him" means that she conceived a fetus through that very transgression, and not otherwise. But is there conception of a fetus in other ways as well?

Yes, there is. How so? Through physical contact, through grasping at clothing, through drinking impure fluids, through touching the navel, through seeing a form, through sound, and through smell. For some women, during their fertile period...
Women who, being stained by desire and lust, consent to men grasping their hands, grasping their private parts, or touching their limbs and members, also conceive a fetus.
Thus, conception occurs through physical contact.
However, in the case of the Elder Udāyī, his former wife, a bhikkhunī, took that semen with her mouth in part.
She placed a portion [of his seed] into her private parts along with a cloth, and she conceived a child by means of that.
Thus, conception occurs through the taking of a cloth.

The mother of the ascetic Migasiṅga was a doe; during her fertile season, she went to the place where the ascetic relieved himself and drank his urine together with its seminal essence. Having conceived a child by that, she gave birth to Migasiṅga. Thus, conception occurs through the drinking of impurity.
But when Sakka learned that the Bodhisatta Sāma’s parents were suffering from failing sight, he wished to give them a son and said to the wise Dukūla:
“Is sexual intercourse permissible for you? “We have no need for it;
we have gone forth into the ascetic life. “In that case, during her fertile period, you should touch her navel with your thumb.”
So she did accordingly. Having conceived a child by him, she herself gave birth to a young ascetic. Thus, conception occurs through the stroking of the navel.
In this same manner, the accounts of Maṇḍabya and Caṇḍapajjota are to be understood. How does it occur through the sight of a form?
Here, a certain woman, not obtaining sexual intercourse with a man during her fertile period, [conceives] through the power of desire and lust.
Just as royal courtesans gaze intently at a man who has entered their house, she conceives a child through him;
thus, conception occurs by the sight of a form.
In the case of cranes, however, there is no such thing as a man; they conceive upon hearing the sound of thunder during the mating season.
Even among hens, sometimes many conceive upon hearing the sound of a single cock;
likewise, a cow [conceives] from a bull. Thus, conception occurs through sound.
Furthermore, a cow sometimes conceives through the scent of a bull. Thus, conception occurs through smell.
But here, she conceived a child through misconduct. With reference to this it was said:
“When mother and father come together, and the mother is in her season, and the *gandhabba* is present—thus, through the coming together of these three, there is the descent of the embryo.”
The earth-dwelling deities raised a cry: "For there is no such thing as a secret evil deed for one who commits it in this world.
First of all, that evil is known by oneself; then by the protective deities; and then by other deities who possess knowledge of the minds of others.
Therefore, the earth-dwelling deities residing throughout the entire forest grove, being knowers of the minds of others, [perceived] that transgression of his.
Having seen [this], they raised a cry. They uttered it so that other gods might hear as well. What was it? "O, indeed, the world is free from cankers...
[as before] ...a danger has been brought about. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as explained in the Verañjakaṇḍa.
Having heard the cry of the earth-dwelling gods, the Cātumahārājika gods... here, regarding the cry of the earth-dwelling gods:
The deities dwelling in space heard it; from those in space, the sequence should be understood to extend to the Cātumahārājika gods.
"The Brahmakāyika gods" means that all Brahmas—excluding those in the realm of non-percipient beings and those in the formless sphere—heard it, and having heard it, they let out a shout;
this is how it should be understood. "Thus at that moment" means thus at the moment of Sudinna’s transgression. "At that instant."
"In an instant, he transgressed [the bounds]. As far as the Brahmā-world" means as far as the Akaniṭṭha Brahmā-world.
"He rose up" means he ascended, he emerged; there was a great tumult all at once.
"She gave birth to a son" means she brought forth a being in his final existence who resembled a golden image. "They gave him the name Bījaka."
They did not give him another name; because it was well known that his grandmother had said, "Give him even a seed," they gave him the name "Bījaka," saying, "Let his name be Bījaka.
And by means of the son's name, they also gave a name to his parents. At a later time, [they took] both Bījaka and Bījakamātā...
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). It is said that when Bījakā was seven or eight years old, his mother went forth among the bhikkhunīs and he himself went forth among the bhikkhus;
by relying on spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitta*), they both established themselves in arahantship. Therefore it was said:
"Having both gone forth from the household life into homelessness, they realized arahantship."
37. Thus the going forth of mother and son was fruitful. But the father remained overcome by remorse. Therefore it is said:
“Then, indeed, remorse arose in the Venerable Sudinna,” and so forth. In this context, *ahu deva* means *ahu eva*;
the letter *da* is used for metrical conjunction (*padasandhi*). The meaning is “it simply was. *Kukkucca* refers to the subsequent regret caused by a transgression of conduct.
"Remorse" (*vippaṭisāra*) is also a name for that very same state. For it is called "worry" (*kukkucca*) because it is a despicable action that should not be done by the wise.
It is called "remorse" (*vippaṭisāra*) because, being unable to turn back the transgression already committed, one has a distorted recollection (*saraṇabhāva*) based upon it.
"Alābhā vata me" means: "Alas, what a loss for me! [I have lost] those qualities such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*)."

"Losses indeed are mine, not gains"—this is the intended meaning. "Truly, these are not gains for me": even those qualities I have acquired—namely, going forth, taking refuge, and undertaking the training—they are not gains for me because they are defiled by transgression.
"Alas, it is poorly gained by me": although this Dispensation has been obtained by me, it is poorly gained. "Truly, it is not well-gained by me."
"Just as it is for other sons of good family, so indeed it has not been well-gained by me. Why?

Because I [have failed] to live the holy life under such a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya... "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the path of the holy life comprised within the three trainings.
"He became emaciated" means that being unable to eat or consume food, he became thin, with little flesh and blood. "He became pale and jaundiced" means...

"Having become pale and yellowish" means having the appearance of withered leaves. "With limbs covered by veins" means that because the flesh and blood have been consumed, the limbs are as if covered by a network of veins.
"With mind within" means that due to constant sorrow, the consciousness remains fixed inside;
however, all [beings] are "with mind within" insofar as their minds proceed in dependence upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). "With sluggish mind" refers to the summary...

"Līnamano" (one with a sluggish mind) means one whose mind is sluggish—contracted and not expanded—due to being devoted solely to indolence, having failed to apply himself to thorough inquiry regarding the meditation subject, to higher virtue, higher consciousness, and higher wisdom, and to the fulfillment of duties and practices.

"Dukkhī" (suffering) means suffering through mental pain. "Dummano" (dejected) means one whose mind is corrupted by hatred, or whose mind is disfigured by being overwhelmed by mental distress (*domanassa*).
"Pajjhāyi" means he brooded over this and that, like a donkey whose nose-string has been cut, due to remorse.

"The monks who were his companions": seeing him thus spending his time in the elaborations of socializing with the group, those monks with whom he had confidential and easy conversation spoke to him as follows. "Pīṇindriyo" means one whose faculties are refreshed by the opportunity for establishing serene confidence.
“Because of being complete,” he means one whose faculties, such as the eye, are fully perfected. Regarding the phrase “so dāni tvaṃ” (you, now):
here *dāni* is a particle, and it is equivalent to saying *tvaṃ* (you). “Kacci no tvaṃ” means “I hope that you [are not]. “Anabhirato” means disenchanted;
the meaning is that you are longing for the state of a householder. Therefore, in order to reject that very disenchantment, he said: “Indeed, I am not...”
"Friend, I am not delighted. However, I am indeed delighted by the cultivation of superior wholesome states.
"There is a wicked deed committed by me": there exists, is found, and is present a single wicked deed committed by me;
it stands before me as if at all times. Then, making that known, he said, "By my former wife," and so forth.

"Enough for you, friend Sudinna, of remorse"—this means, "Friend Sudinna, this evil deed of yours is sufficient, capable, and competent to produce remorse. Regarding the phrase beginning with "Whatever [evil]":
the connection is that whatever evil you will not be able to practice the holy life because of, that evil of yours is sufficient for remorse.
It is to be understood. Then, instructing him, they said, "Is it not so, friend, by the Blessed One...
and so forth. Therein, *nanu* is a particle used in the sense of seeking agreement. *Anekapariyāyena* means by way of many reasons. *Virāgāya* means for the sake of dispassion.
*No sarāgāya* means not for the sake of being colored by passion. For the Blessed One [taught] that "having heard this Dhamma of mine, beings..."
The intended meaning is that the Dhamma is taught for this purpose: that they shall become dispassionate toward all states of existence and enjoyments, and not be attached to them.

This same method applies to all the following terms. Furthermore, here these are merely synonymous expressions: “for the sake of dissociation” means for the sake of being dissociated from defilements;
“not for the sake of conjunction” means not for the sake of being conjoined; “for the sake of non-clinging” means for the sake of non-grasping.
"‘Not for the sake of grasping’ means not for the sake of taking hold.

‘In that regard, indeed, you’ means ‘in that very matter, you. ‘You will intend it with lust’ means you will intend, arrange, or plan sexual intercourse while it is occurring together with lust; the meaning is that you will exert yourself for this purpose."

This method applies everywhere. Furthermore, the nine terms beginning with "fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāga*) are spoken specifically with reference to the supramundane *nibbāna* that has been realized.
Therefore, even when it is said "for the fading away of lust" or "for the sobering of intoxication," the meaning should be understood exactly as "for the sake of *nibbāna*.
For it is by coming to, aiming at, and depending upon that *nibbāna* that lust fades away.

It does not exist; therefore it is called "the fading away of lust. Furthermore, because by resorting to it, intoxications such as the pride of conceit (*māna-mada*) and the pride of manhood (*purisa-mada*) become devoid of intoxication, free from intoxication, and perish, it is therefore called "the crushing of intoxication" (*madanimaddana*).
And because by resorting to it, all thirst for sensual pleasures (*kāma-pipāsā*) reaches its subduing and comes to an end, it is therefore called "the subduing of thirst" (*pipāsavinaya*).
Because, by depending upon it, the five bases of attachment to the strands of sensual pleasure are eradicated, it is therefore called "the eradication of the bases" (*ālayasamugghāta*).
And because, by depending upon it, the round of existence in the three realms is cut off, it is therefore called "the cutting off of the round" (*vaṭṭupaccheda*).
Furthermore, because, by depending upon it, craving goes to its utter exhaustion, fades away, and ceases, [it is so called].
And therefore, the destruction of craving is called dispassion and cessation. Furthermore, because it has emerged from, escaped from, and become dissociated from that craving—

which is designated as "binding" (vāna) because it causes beings to be known (vinana), bound (ābandhana), and sewn together (saṃsibbana) in successive states of existence within the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings— therefore [it is called nibbāna].
"It is called Nibbāna.
By "the abandoning of sensual pleasures" is meant the abandoning of both object-sensualities (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensualities (*kilesakāma*).

By "the full understanding of perceptions of sensual pleasure" is meant that the threefold full understanding—by way of knowing, investigating, and abandoning—is declared for all perceptions of sensual pleasure.

"Of thirst for sensual pleasures" means of those things that are to be drunk among sensual pleasures, or of the desires to drink sensual pleasures. "Of thoughts of sensual pleasure" means of thoughts associated with sensual pleasure.
"Of fevers of sensual pleasure" means of the internal burnings, the fevers arisen by way of lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
In these five instances, only the supramundane path that brings about the destruction of the defilements is spoken of. However, in the first three [instances], all [paths] are included.
It should be understood that the path, being a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane, has been described in these instances.
"Netaṃ āvuso" means "not this, friend"; your evil deed does not lead to the inspiring of those who lack faith, nor for the sake of such confidence.
"Atha khvetam" means "but rather this. "Atha kho" is also a reading found in the text. "Aññathattāya" means for the sake of the alteration of that confidence.
It leads to remorse. For those whose faith has not yet entered the Path, it causes them remorse, thinking:
"We have placed our confidence even in such a Dhamma and Discipline, wherein monks are so ill-behaved!
But for those whose faith has entered the Path, their confidence—unshakable by winds like Mount Sineru—is not moved by such instances or even more dreadful ones. Therefore...
It is said: "for the sake of the alteration of some.
39. *Bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesun* means they explained and reported this matter to the Blessed One.
And in reporting it, they did so neither out of a desire for favor, nor with a view toward causing division, nor for the purpose of proclaiming dispraise of that venerable one.

They did not report it for the purpose of casting blame on the Teaching, nor did they report it thinking, "Having heard this, the Blessed One will not provide support for this person's teaching; he will have him expelled.
Rather, they reported it thinking, "Knowing that this tumor has arisen within the Teaching, the Blessed One will lay down a training rule; he will establish a time, a limit, and an injunction."

Regarding the phrase "in this cause, in this context": here, Sudinna’s transgression of improper conduct should be understood as being called both the "cause" (*nidāna*) and the "context" (*pakaraṇa*), because it is the reason for the formulation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

For a cause (*kāraṇa*) is so called because it brings forth its own fruit (*nideti*), as if presenting it by saying, "Take this!"; and it "prepares" (*pakaroti*) it, meaning it begins to produce it, and indeed brings it about.

Or rather, it is called the "source" (*nidāna*) and the "treatment" (*pakaraṇa*). "The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked" means that the Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked and censured them—just as the Supreme Person does when people speak praise or blame regarding those who deserve either praise or blame.
For indeed, upon seeing a person who has transgressed the precepts, the Blessed One [does not think], "This one is [lowly] by birth, or by clan, or by being a son of a respectable family..."
Nor does the thought arise, “It is fitting to protect such a person who is renowned and famous for his mastery of the scriptures or for his ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).
Nor, upon seeing one who is amiable and virtuous, does the thought arise to conceal that person’s virtue.
Rather, he censures only what is censurable and praises only what is praiseworthy; and this [person] is indeed censurable.
Therefore, standing firm in the characteristic of suchness (tādilakkhaṇa), the Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him with an unshakable mind using such words as "inappropriate" (*ananucchavika*).

Herein is the commentary on the meaning: that deed which has been done by you, O vain man, O empty person—that is inappropriate for the qualities that make one a recluse, or for the teachings of the Path, the Fruits, and Nibbāna; it does not suit their outward appearance (*chavi*).
It does not follow nor does it conform to that beautiful state; rather, it stands far removed from those qualities.
And because it is unsuitable, it is "inappropriate" (*ananulomika*), meaning it does not accord with them; rather, it is contrary and stands in opposition.
And because it is inappropriate, it is "unbecoming" (*appatirūpa*); it is not suitable, similar, or corresponding, but rather the opposite. And because it is inappropriate...
It is indeed incomparable and without peer. Precisely because it is unsuitable, it is un-monkly (*assāmaṇaka*);
it is not the work of monks. Because it is un-monkly, it is improper (*akappiya*). For that which is not the work of a monk is not allowable for them.
Because it is improper, it is not to be done. Indeed, monks do not do what is not allowable. And since this has been done by you, therefore—
“O foolish man, what you have done is unbecoming... it is not to be done.

How so? By what reason? It is said: “What reason indeed do you see? Then, demonstrating the absence of such a reason, he says later, “Have I not [said], ‘O foolish men’,” and so forth. All of that has already been explained.
Now, because the evil deed he had committed was ripening as an extremely painful result,
his compassionate parents— like those feeling pity for an offending son— spoke these words beginning with "Better for you,
O foolish man," censuring Sudinna with a heart of mercy in order to show him that ripening result. In this context, *āsu* means quickly.
It is called a *āsīvisa* because its venom (*visa*) comes forth. It is a *ghoravisa* because its venom is terrible and fierce;
[the phrase] "of that *āsīvisa* with terrible venom" refers to this. The word "thrown" (*pakkhatta*) is connected with the word "better" (*vara*).
The male organ would be better if it were thrown into the mouth of such a *āsīvisa* with terrible venom; if it were so thrown, it would be better.

The meaning is: "It would be beautiful, excellent, and very good. "But not even that" (*na tveva*) means: not indeed better, not indeed more beautiful, not indeed more excellent, not indeed more very good.
This method applies everywhere. "Of the black snake" (*kaṇhasappassa*) means: of the dark snake. "In a pit of embers" (*aṅgārakāsuyā*) means: in a well filled with embers, or in a heap of embers.
"Blazing" (*ādittāya*) means: burning, having taken on the color of fire. "Flaming up" (*sampajjalitāya*) means: ... [flaming up].
"Blazing on all sides" means that flames are being released; "become incandescent" means possessing radiance.
What is meant is that it has become a single mass of light due to the crests of flame rising up on every side.
"For what reason?"—if one asks, "For what reason did I say 'excellent,' and by what cause?"—it is for this reason.
"He might meet death" means that whoever should insert his organ there would meet death or experience suffering amounting to death. "And on account of this...
he might be reborn" means that because of this—namely, the insertion of the organ into the female organ—the person who performs that act might be reborn in hell.
Thus, seeing the great blameworthiness of that action, he censured it, not because he wished for him to experience suffering.
In that context, *nāma tvam* means "even though such an action was indeed so greatly blameworthy.
Here, *yam* is a particle used in the sense of contempt (*hīḷanatthe*). *Tvam* is a synonym for the word *tam*; both [particles] are used as such.
"Or that which is despised and held in contempt"—this is what is meant. "Asaddhamma" means the dhamma of the wicked, of base persons;
the sense is: that which is to be practiced by them. "Gāmadhamma" means the dhamma of villages;
it is said to be the dhamma of the people living in the village. "Vasaladhamma": they are called *vasalā* because they dwell (*vasanti*) and flow with evil dhammas; [it refers] to those *vasalā*.
The teaching of base persons, or the teaching of the outcaste that drips with defilements.
"Dutthulla" means both wicked—being corrupted by defilements—and gross—not subtle; it is said to be unrefined.
"Odakantika" means one for whom the water-rite is near—that is, the end or conclusion—thus he is an *odakantika*; that is the *odakantika* rite. "Rahassa" means seclusion, in a hidden place.
It is that which arises in a secluded place. For this phenomenon, because it is loathsome, cannot be made manifest within the range of sight of others;
therefore it is called "secret. Regarding the phrase *dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti*: it is that which must be entered by two [partners] together.
There is also a reading, *dvayaṃ dvayaṃ samāpattiṃ*. Some read *dayaṃ dayaṃ samāpattiṃ*, but that is not good.

"You will attain" (*samāpajjissasi*) should be construed with the word "name" (*nāma*) mentioned in the phrase "there indeed you," as "you will indeed attain. Regarding the passage "You are the originator...
the forerunner of many," he speaks with reference to the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
In this Dispensation, you are the originator of unwholesome states for many persons, because you were the very first to perform them; thus, you are the forerunner.
Because he was the very first to enter upon this path—it is said that he is "the giver of the door" and "the one who shows the means.

For the underlying intention here is this: "Having obtained this hint and following your example, many individuals will commit various kinds of unwholesome deeds, such as engaging in sexual intercourse with female monkeys."
"In many ways" means by these numerous reasons stated in the manner beginning with "inappropriate.

"Having spoken in dispraise of being difficult to support... up to... of indolence" means having spoken in dispraise—that is, censure and reproach—of the lack of restraint (*asaṃvara*) which is the basis for being difficult to support and so forth. For the self of a person who stands in a state of lack of restraint—
Because one falls into being difficult to support and difficult to satisfy, non-restraint is therefore called "difficult to support" and "difficult to satisfy.

Furthermore, because one who stands in non-restraint falls into great greed for the four requisites and dissatisfaction even when obtaining requisites equal in size to Mount Sineru, non-restraint is therefore called "great greed" and "dissatisfaction."

And it is said [thus]: because for one who stands in non-restraint, the self leads to both the company of crowds and the company of defilements, and he follows after sloth, which leads to the fulfillment of the eight bases of laziness;
therefore, non-restraint is called "both company and sloth."

"Having spoken in praise of being easy to support... [and] of the arousal of energy": the meaning is, having spoken in praise of the restraint that constitutes the basis for being easy to support and so forth.
For when one has abandoned non-restraint and is established in restraint, one becomes easy to support and easy to satisfy;
one attains a state of fewness of wishes and lack of craving regarding the four requisites, and in each and every one of them—
Because restraint leads to threefold contentment— according to what is obtained, according to one's strength,
and according to what is appropriate— it is therefore called "being easy to support, easy to satisfy, of few wishes, and content. Furthermore,

because for one who has abandoned non-restraint and stands firm in restraint, the self is led toward the refinement and shaking off of the defilements, it is therefore called "refinement" (*sallekha*) and "ascetic purification" (*dhuta*).
And because one who has abandoned non-restraint and stands in restraint does not approach bodily and verbal misconduct— which is unpleasing,
uninspiring, non-existent, and unsuitable— nor the mental unpleasingness and uninspiring state consisting of the three unwholesome types of thought which are non-existent and unsuitable,
but rather [approaches] their opposite: bodily and verbal good conduct and the three wholesome types of thought.
And because it leads to the fulfillment of that which is serene, inspiring confidence, peaceful, and appropriate, restraint is therefore called "serene. Furthermore,

for one who has abandoned non-restraint and stands firm in restraint, the self— by means of the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*), which consists in the exhaustion of all defilements— [is purified].
And it leads to the fulfillment of the eight bases for the arousal of energy; therefore, restraint is said to be "both a reduction [of defilements] and an arousal of energy.
"Suitable and conformable to the bhikkhus" means that this training rule which he will now prescribe is both suitable and conformable to the bhikkhus assembled there.
Or, by such terms as "easy to support," etc., [it is meant that it is...]

The restraint has been stated; the meaning is that he gave a "sudden" (okkantika) teaching on the Dhamma—connected with the abandoning of that restraint, appropriate and conformable to it, yet not bound by the suttas and released from the formal Canon (pāḷi).
It is said that in such instances, the Blessed One acts like one weaving a garland of five-colored flowers or stringing a jewel necklace for those who intend to reject [the teaching].

To those who delight in non-restraint, he—urging them by means of the fear of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) in the future life and demonstrating the manifold disadvantages—establishs some who desire training in restraint in Arhatship;
others, even those lacking the necessary conditions (upanissaya), he establishes on the path to heaven. [He speaks] in the measure of the Dīgha Nikāya and the measure of the Majjhima Nikāya.
He gives a teaching on the Dhamma. With reference to this, it was said: “Having given a talk on the Dhamma that was appropriate and suitable for the bhikkhus.
“By that” means by that transgression of Sudinna, which served as the cause. “Training rule” (sikkhāpada): herein, it is that which should be trained in.
“Training” (*sikkhā*) is the term [derived from] “one trains by means of this”; thus, “the training’s term” is *sikkhāpada*.
The meaning is: “the means for attaining the training. Alternatively, it is said that “root,” “support,” and “foundation” are its synonyms.

This is a designation for the abstention from sexual intercourse, the restraint from sexual intercourse. For the restraint from sexual intercourse is the foundation for all other qualities comprised within the training—namely, virtue, insight, meditative absorption, and the path.
Because it possesses the meaning of what has been stated, the term "training precept" (*sikkhāpada*) is intended here in the sense of a word (*pada*).

This meaning should be understood according to the method explained in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*. Furthermore, the statement that elucidates that meaning should also be understood as a "training precept.

For it has also been said: "A training precept is the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the collection of words (*padakāya*), the collection of phrases (*niruttikāya*), and the collection of phonemes (*byañjanakāya*) therein."
Alternatively, just as when it is said, “Non-covetousness is a footprint of the Dhamma,” the meaning is that non-covetousness is a single constituent part of the Dhamma,
so too here the meaning of “training rule” (*sikkhāpada*) should be understood as a constituent part of training, or a single portion of the training.
“Depending on ten purposes” means depending on ten reasons, for the sake of the specific benefit to be attained through the proclamation of the training rules.
"Depending upon, having come to, and taking as a basis"—this means "perceiving the accomplishment of ten specific benefits.
Now, showing those ten purposes, he said, "for the well-being of the Saṅgha," and so forth.

Therein, "well-being of the Saṅgha" (saṅghasuṭṭhutā) means the state of the Saṅgha being well; it is like the sense of "well done, O King" in the passage where it occurs, or the manner of accepting a statement by saying, "Well, venerable sir."
And whoever accepts the word of the Tathāgata, that leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time;
therefore, for the sake of the Saṅgha’s acceptance of my words, saying "Very well, Bhante," I shall set forth [this matter],
having shown the danger in non-acceptance and the benefit in acceptance, and not by force or by overpowering them— this is the meaning.
Explaining it, he said: "For the well-being of the Saṅgha. "For the comfort of the Saṅgha" means for the state of ease of the Saṅgha;
the meaning is: for the sake of their livelihood and for their dwelling in happiness.
"For the restraint of difficult persons": "difficult persons" refers to individuals of immoral conduct; those who, even when being made to feel shame...
It is for the purpose of restraining those who commit an offense through suffering, or who feel no shame after having committed one;
for if there were no training rule, they would harass the Saṅgha, saying: "What have you seen? What have you heard?
What have we done? On what basis and for what offense do you charge us and restrain us?"—[this being said] regarding the training rule.
But if you are mindful, the Saṅgha, having shown you the training rule, will restrain you in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
Therefore it was said: “For the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct.
“For the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus” means for the sake of the comfortable dwelling of those bhikkhus who are well-behaved and of amiable character.
For monks who are fond of their own habits, not knowing what should and should not be done, what is blameworthy and blameless, and the proper time and limits,
they weary themselves while striving for the fulfillment of the three trainings, and when confronted with criticism, they become distressed. But those who know what should and should not be done,
what is blameworthy and blameless, and the proper time and limits, do not weary themselves while striving for the fulfillment of the three trainings, and when confronted with criticism...
They are not oppressed. Therefore, the laying down of these training rules leads to their comfortable dwelling.
Or rather, the restraint of persons who are difficult to manage is itself their comfortable dwelling.
For, by relying on a person of immoral conduct, the Uposatha does not stand, the Pavāraṇā does not stand, the formal acts of the Saṅgha do not proceed, and there is no harmony.
When there are no [restrained] monks, those who are distracted are unable to devote themselves to recitation, interrogation, meditation subjects, and so forth.
But when the immoral have been restrained, this entire affliction ceases to exist. Consequently, the well-behaved monks dwell in comfort.
Thus, in the phrase "for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved monks," the meaning should be understood in two ways.
"For the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya*):

"Taints pertaining to the present life" refers to various kinds of suffering—such as being struck by hands, struck by sticks, having one's hands cut off, having one's feet cut off, ill-repute, and remorse—which are to be experienced in that very same personal existence by one who stands in non-restraint.
Thus, the meaning is: for the restraint, the closing off, and the blocking of the path of arrival of these taints pertaining to the present life.

"For the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives" means: the taints pertaining to future lives are the specific kinds of suffering to be experienced in the hells and other realms in a future existence, rooted in the evil deeds committed by one who stands in non-restraint;
it is said "for their warding off," for their subsiding, and for their pacification.

"For the purpose of inspiring confidence in those who lack it": for when a training rule has been laid down, whether by learning of the laying down of that rule or by seeing monks practicing according to what was prescribed, even those wise people who were previously lacking in confidence [think]:
"Indeed, regarding those things in the world which are grounds for the passion, aversion, and delusion of the masses, these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, [have abandoned them]."

They dwell far removed and abstinent; "they perform what is indeed difficult, they perform what is indeed burdensome"—thus they develop confidence, like the brahmin with wrong views who, upon seeing a book in the Vinaya Piṭaka, became a triple-knower. Therefore it was said: "for the sake of inspiring confidence in those without confidence.

And "for the increase of those already confident" means that even those sons of good family who are already confident in the Teaching [are further strengthened] by the laying down of the training rules.
Having understood this, or seeing monks practicing according to what has been prescribed, they become increasingly confident, thinking: "Oh, these venerable ones perform difficult deeds;
they maintain the holy life, the restraint of the Vinaya, by taking only one meal a day for as long as life lasts.
Therefore it is said: "For the increase of those who are already confident."

"For the endurance of the true Dhamma" means that the true Dhamma is threefold: the true Dhamma as the teaching (*pariyatti-saddhamma*), the true Dhamma as practice (*paṭipatti-saddhamma*), and the true Dhamma as realization (*adhigama-saddhamma*).
Among these, all the word of the Buddha included within the Three Pitakas is called "the true Dhamma as the teaching.
[It consists of] the thirteen ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*), the fourteen rules of conduct for the Khandhakas, the eighty-two major rules, and virtue, concentration, and insight.

This is called the "True Dhamma of Practice" (*paṭipatti-saddhamma*). The four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—this is called the "True Dhamma of Realization" (*adhigama-saddhamma*).

All of this, moreover, exists because, when the formulation of training rules (*sikkhāpada-paññatti*) is present, monks master the training rules, their detailed analysis (*vibhaṅga*), and other words of the Buddha for the purpose of explaining their meaning.
And by practicing exactly as it has been prescribed, they fulfill that practice and attain the supramundane Dhamma which is to be attained through practice;
therefore, there is long-term stability for the proclamation of the training rules. Hence it is said: "for the endurance of the true Dhamma.

"For the assistance of the Vinaya" means that when the proclamation of the training rules exists, there is the Vinaya of restraint (*saṃvara-vinaya*), the Vinaya of abandoning (*pahāna-vinaya*), and the Vinaya of settling disputes (*samatha-vinaya*).
And since both the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) and the formulated discipline (*paññattivinaya*), these fourfold aspects of the discipline (*vinaya*) are thus assisted, supported, and well-supported.
Therefore it was said: "for the assistance of the discipline.
Furthermore, all these terms should be construed together with this statement: "I shall prescribe a training rule."
In this regard, the application of the first and last phrases is as follows: “I shall lay down a training rule for the well-being of the Saṅgha;
I shall lay down a training rule for the support of the Vinaya.
Furthermore, herein, that which is for the well-being of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha; and that which is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is [for the restraint] of difficult persons.
"For the sake of restraint" means: "That which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha;

that which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of difficult persons"—having thus applied this method of linked phrasing ten times, based on each individual word, as it is stated in the Parivāra:
“Eight hundred on the Dhamma, eight hundred on the etymological definitions, four hundred on knowledge—these are the eight purposes in this treatise.
All of that should be understood. However, since all of this will be made clear in the Parivāra itself, it has not been explained here.

Having thus shown the benefit of the formulation of the training rule, he said, "And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule in this way," pointing out the duty to be performed by the monks regarding that training rule. What is meant?
Monks, this training rule, whose benefits have been demonstrated by me in this manner, [should be recited] in the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
"You should recite it, master it, retain it, and teach it to others. For here the word *ca* has the sense of "bringing over" (addition);
thus, this meaning is brought in.
Now, in order to show what was stated as "this training rule," [the text says]: "Whatever monk [engages in] sexual intercourse..."
"should he consume it, he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, one who is no longer in communion," so he said.
