Thus, having established the first *pārājika* rule firmly by way of cutting off the root, another supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) arose concerning the story of the female monkey.
This was stated for the purpose of illustrating its origin: "In this way, this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks. Its meaning is as follows:
This training rule was thus laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus, and this other matter arose as well.
The discussion on the first laying down is finished.
The section on Sudinna is finished.
The Story of the Female Monkey (Makkaṭīvatthukathā). 40.
Now, in order to show that another incident had arisen, he said, "At that time," and so forth.

Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [already] explained: "With meat-offerings for the female monkey" means by the power of the qualities of patience, loving-kindness, and so on, belonging to the monks in the Great Forest.
Many animals—such as deer, antelopes, chickens, and monkeys—roam about in the places where the meditation hall is located with minds free from fear.
There, having enticed one female monkey with food—namely, with gruel, rice, snacks, and so forth—the meaning is that he has won her over.
"Of her" is a locative expression. "He frequents" means he is constantly frequenting; for the present tense is used here in the sense of frequency.
"So bhikkhu" refers to that bhikkhu who was practicing sexual intercourse. "Wandering about visiting lodgings":

those incoming bhikkhus, having come to see the Buddha and having received the morning meals for guests and finished their meal duties, wandered about thinking, "We shall look at the dwelling places of the bhikkhus.
Therefore it is said: "wandering about visiting lodgings."

“While wandering about,” [he said]. “He approached those bhikkhus”: having established a bond of trust with one bhikkhu, the animals known as *tiracchānagata* (beasts) likewise arouse such a thought toward others as well. Therefore, that female monkey approached those bhikkhus;
and having approached, she displayed that same gesture to them as she had done to her own trusted bhikkhu.
*Cheppanti naṅguṭṭhaṃ*: "The tail" means the penis. *Oḍḍīti abhimukhaṃ ṭhapesi*: "He set it up" means he placed it facing [her]. *Nimittampi akāsīti*:
"He even made a sign" means he performed that particular manner or action by which they would know his intention for sexual intercourse; this is the meaning. *So bhikkhūti*:
"That monk" refers to the one whose monastery this is. *Ekamantaṃ nilīyiṃsūti*: "They hid in a corner" means they remained concealed in a certain place.
41. "It is true, friend," he said. Like a thief caught in the act, because he had been confronted with the evidence before his eyes, he was unable to say, "What have I done?
or similar things, and so he replied, "It is true, friend. "Is it not, friend, exactly the same in that case?
"Friend, just as it is for a human female, is it not exactly the same for a female animal as well regarding that training rule?"
[It] exists. For even the seeing, grasping, touching, stroking, or rubbing of a human woman is indeed a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*).
Even with a female animal, all of that is indeed a grave offense. What is the distinction here? You have attributed a stain (*lesa*) to a place that is stainless. 42.
"Even with a female animal, one is defeated (*pārājika*) and no longer in communion" means that through sexual intercourse even with a female animal—
Having engaged in the act, one becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; thus he made the training rule even more stringent. For there are two kinds of training rules:

those that are offenses by nature (*lokavajja*) and those that are offenses by formal precept (*paṇṇattivajja*). Among these, that for which the mind is exclusively unwholesome on the side of intentional action is called an offense by nature.
The remainder are offenses by formal precept. Regarding offenses by nature, when a supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) arises—
It arises obstructing the door, closing the stream, cutting it off, and making it tighter—except in the case of overestimation (*adhimāna*) and except in a dream;
this, however, is stated because there is no transgression and because it is not subject to formal designation (*abbhohārika*).

When arising in the absence of a transgression regarding what is prohibited by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), it makes [the restraint] loose, releases it, opens the door, and even [occurs] from one to another.
It arises when one is performing what is not an offense, similar to the subsequent rules (*anupaññatti*) regarding eating in a group or eating in succession.
However, because it arises even when such a transgression has been committed—as in the phrase "even for a momentary lapse"—it follows the category of a formal rule (*paññatti*).
Since this first training rule is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*) and not an offense by formal precept (*paṇṇattivajja*), this [subsequent rule] is an *anupaññatti*.
It arose obstructing the door, closing the stream, cutting it off, and making it more firm.

Thus, having combined both instances and made them firmer by way of cutting off at the root, when the first *pārājika* rule had been laid down, another case—the story of the Vajjiputtakas—arose for the purpose of a subsequent supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*). This [text] is for the purpose of showing its origin.
It is said: “In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus. Its meaning is:
“This training rule was thus laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus, and this other matter also arose.
The Discussion on the Story of the Female Monkey is finished.
The Section on the Recitation of the Settlement;
Explanation of the Case of the Vajjiputtakas (43–44).
Now, in order to show another case that had arisen, he said, "At that time," and so forth.
Herein, this is the explanation of the non-obvious terms: *Vesālikā* means those who dwell in Vesālī.

*Vajjiputtakā* means the sons of families in Vesālī within the Vajjī territory. It is said that whatever calamity, disadvantage, or internal strife (*abbuda*) arose in the Dispensation, all of it occurred in dependence upon the Vajjiputtakas.
For instance, even Devadatta, having gained a faction among the Vajjiputtakas, [sought to split] the Saṅgha...

They broke [the unity]. And it was the Vajjiputtakas themselves who, a hundred years after the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna, proclaimed what was contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya, deviating from the Teacher’s instruction.
Even these [monks], though the training rules had been laid down for them in this very way, ate as much as they desired...
and so forth... and practiced sexual intercourse.
"Even through the loss of kinsmen": here, *asana*, *byasana*, *vikkhepa*, *viddhaṃsana*, and *vināsa* are all synonymous.
The "loss of kinsmen" (*ñātibyasana*) means the destruction of kinsmen; the meaning is: through that destruction of kinsmen caused by royal punishment, disease, death, or separation.
This same method applies to the second phrase as well. In the third phrase, however, it is a disease that destroys health.
Thus is the calamity of disease. For it is called a *byasana* because it ruins (*byasati*), distracts, and destroys health. Disease itself is the calamity;
thus, "the calamity of disease. "Afflicted" means seized, overcome, or possessed by that calamity of disease.
"Venerable Ānanda, we are not revilers of the Buddha" means, Venerable Ānanda, we do not revile the Buddha.
We do not blame the Buddha; we do not revile the Dhamma, nor do we revile the Saṅgha.
We revile ourselves, saying "we are to be blamed," and we assign the fault to ourselves. "Lacking fortune" means devoid of splendor.
"Of little merit" means having limited merit. "Insightful regarding wholesome states" refers to those wholesome states analyzed among the thirty-eight meditation objects.
“Phenomena” (dhammā) refers to those things which are objects of insight; the meaning is that having emerged from this or that object, they practice insight into those very same phenomena.
“In the first watch and the last watch of the night”: the beginning of the night is the “first watch,” and the end of the night is the “last watch”;
what is meant is the first watch and the final watch. “Of the factors of enlightenment” (bodhipakkhikānaṃ): of the side of enlightenment.
"Bhavānaṃ" means those things that are conducive to the knowledge of the path to arahantship. "Bhāvanānuyogaṃ" means application to development.

"Anuyuttā vihareyyāma" means that, having abandoned the impediments of household life and the impediments of dwelling, we would dwell in secluded resting places, diligently engaged, with no other duties.

“‘So be it, friends,’ said the Elder. Not knowing their intention, and thinking upon hearing this great roar of theirs, ‘If they will become such as this, that would be well,’ he accepted it, saying, ‘So be it, friends.
‘This is impossible, there is no occasion’—both of these are expressions of a negation of reason. For a reason is so called because, in that context, [the outcome] exists in dependence upon it.”
The fruit remains. And because there is room for it, in the sense that its existence is dependent upon that, it is called "a possibility and a scope.
Rejecting that, he said: "This, Ānanda, is impossible; this has no scope.
There is neither such a possibility nor such a scope that the Tathāgata—whether among the Vajjīs... [etc. ...should utterly eradicate [the defilements].

The meaning is that there is no such reason. For if the Blessed One were to grant the full ordination to these who are requesting it, saying, "May we receive the full ordination," then, that being the case, he would be subverting the rule established as: "He is one who has committed a pārājika offense; he is no longer in communion.
But since he does not subvert this, he therefore said, "This is impossible," and so forth.

“Such a person who has come should not be ordained. [The Blessed One said this] because he understood: “If one who has come in such a manner were to receive ordination, he would have no respect for the Teaching.
However, if he remains on the level of a novice, he will be respectful and will work for his own welfare.
Out of compassion, the Blessed One said: “Such a person who has come should not be ordained. [On the other hand,] “such a person who has come should be ordained.”

"Knowing that one who has come in this way, having remained in the state of a bhikkhu and possessing unimpaired virtue, will be respectful toward the Teaching, and that— provided there is a supporting cause—
he will before long attain the supreme goal, he should be ordained," it is said. Thus,
regarding those who have returned after having engaged in sexual intercourse, there are both those who should not be ordained and those who should be ordained.

Having shown these three cases and having brought them together to complete [the context], desiring to lay down the training rule, he said, "And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule," and then laid down the complete training rule: "Whosoever monk... [as before] ...is not in communion."
The commentary on the case of the Vajjiputtakas is finished. 45.
Now, analyzing its meaning, he said: "But whoever," "whoever of such a kind," and so forth. Regarding that training rule:
And by one who desires skill in the analysis of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga*) and in the entire determination of the Vinaya, the fourfold Vinaya must be known:
"For the great elders of great psychic power, the compilers of the Dhamma in the past,
having extracted it, proclaimed the fourfold Vinaya."
What is the fourfold [method]? It is: the discourse (sutta), that which is in conformity with the discourse (suttānuloma), the teacher’s tradition (ācariyavāda), and one’s own opinion (attanomati).
With reference to this it was said: “By the direct word, by the flavor, by the lineage of teachers, and by the intention.

For here, “the direct word” intends the discourse; “the flavor” intends that which is in conformity with the discourse; “the lineage of teachers” intends the teacher’s tradition; and “the intention” intends one’s own opinion.
In this context, "Sutta" refers to the Pāḷi of the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.
"Suttānuloma" refers to the four Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*), which were spoken by the Blessed One as follows:
"Monks, whatever has not been prohibited by me saying, 'This is not allowable,' if it conforms to what is unallowable and contradicts what is allowable..."

That is not allowable for you. Monks, whatever I have not prohibited by saying, "This is not allowable," if it conforms with what is allowable and excludes what is unallowable, that is allowable for you.
Monks, whatever I have not authorized by saying, "This is allowable," if it conforms with what is unallowable and excludes what is allowable, that is not allowable for you.
“It is allowable, monks. Whatever has not been permitted by me as ‘this is allowable,’ if it conforms to what is allowable and excludes what is unallowable, that is allowable for you.

The so-called *ācariyavāda* (the teachers’ doctrine) is the tradition of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) established by the five hundred arahants who compiled the Dhamma; it is independent of the canonical texts (*pāḷi*) and functions as an exposition of the principles underlying them.

*Attanomati* (one’s own opinion) refers to the statement of a presented mode [of thought] based on one’s own realization through inference and by grasping the method, setting aside the discourses (*sutta*), the works conforming to the discourses (*suttānuloma*), and the teachers’ doctrines (*ācariyavāda*).
Furthermore, all the Theravāda tradition found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the Suttanta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya is also called *attanomati*.
However, when speaking while adopting such *attanomati*, one should not speak by holding a rigid or dogmatic grasp. The reason for this is as follows:
Having discerned the meaning by means of the text, and having reconciled the text with the meaning, one should speak. One’s own opinion should be compared with the teacher’s doctrine.
If it enters into and accords with that, it should be accepted; if it neither enters into nor accords with it, it should not be accepted.
For this so-called "one's own opinion" is the weakest of all. From one's own opinion...
The teacher’s statement is more authoritative.

Even the teacher’s statement must be brought into conformity with the Sutta. In that regard, only what is consistent when brought into conformity should be accepted; the other should not be accepted. For the conformity with the Sutta is more authoritative than the teacher’s statement.
Even the conformity with the Sutta must be brought into the Sutta itself. In that regard, only what is consistent when brought into it should be accepted; the other...

It should not be accepted. For, in accordance with the Suttas, the Sutta itself is more authoritative. Indeed, the Sutta is unalterable, like a formal assembly of those who enact the law, and like the established era of the Buddhas.

Therefore, when two monks debate, if the proponent speaks by taking up the Sutta and the opponent speaks in accordance with the Sutta, they should neither disparage nor revile one another, but [uphold] what is in accordance with the Sutta.
It should be compared with the Sutta. If it fits and accords, it should be accepted;

if not, it should not be accepted, and one should remain solely by the Sutta. Now, if this person speaks having taken up the Sutta, and the other [speaks] according to the teacher’s tradition (*ācariyavāda*), they should—without mutual derision or reproach—compare that teacher’s tradition with the Sutta. If it fits and accords, it should be accepted.
While taking notes, one should not breathe a sigh of relief upon hearing the words of a reproachable teacher; rather, one must remain steadfast by the Sutta itself.

If this person speaks having grasped the Sutta, while another speaks according to his own opinion, both should refrain from mutual derision or censure and instead test their own opinions against the Sutta.
If it fits and accords with the Sutta, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be.
It should be accepted. One must remain strictly within the Sutta itself.
However, if this person speaks by taking what conforms to the Sutta, while the other cites the Sutta, then that Sutta should be compared against the Sutta-conformity.
If it fits and agrees—if it is found to have been included in the three councils and has appeared in the Canon—it should be accepted. If not...
If it appears thus but does not descend [into the teaching] or does not accord with it— whether it be a non-Buddhist sutta, a verse,
or any other censurable sutta originating from one of the *guḷha*, *vessantara*, *guḷhavinaya*, *vedalla*, and so forth— it should not be accepted.
One must remain strictly within what is in conformity with the Suttas.

Now, if this person speaks by taking up what is in conformity with the Sutta, while the other speaks according to the Teacher’s tradition (ācariyavāda), then the Teacher’s tradition must be compared with what is in conformity with the Sutta. If it fits and agrees, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted. One should remain solely with what is in conformity with the Sutta.

Furthermore, if this person speaks by taking up what is in conformity with the Sutta, while the other speaks according to his own opinion (attanomati), then that personal opinion must be compared with what is in conformity with the Sutta. If it fits and agrees, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted. One should remain solely with what is in conformity with the Sutta.
Now, if this person speaks having taken up the teacher’s doctrine (ācariyavāda), while the other speaks according to the Discourse (sutta), the Discourse must be compared with the teacher’s doctrine.
If it fits and accords, it should be accepted; otherwise, that which contradicts the Discourse should not be accepted, and one should remain solely by the teacher’s doctrine.

Furthermore, if this person speaks having taken up the teacher’s doctrine, while the other speaks in accordance with the Discourse (suttānuloma), the "in accordance with the Discourse" must be compared with the teacher’s doctrine. Only that which fits and accords should be accepted; the other should not be accepted. One should remain solely by the teacher’s doctrine.

Now, if this person speaks having taken up the teacher’s doctrine while the other speaks according to his own opinion, one’s own opinion should be compared with the teacher’s doctrine. If it fits and accords with it, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted, and one should remain solely by the teacher’s doctrine.
But if this person speaks having taken up his own opinion while the other speaks according to the Sutta, the Sutta should be compared with one’s own opinion.
If it fits and accords with it, it should be accepted; otherwise, that contrary Sutta which is to be censured should not be accepted, and one should remain solely by one’s own opinion.

Now, if this person speaks having taken their own opinion as the basis, while the other speaks in accordance with the Sutta, the opinion in accordance with the Sutta should be compared with one's own opinion. If it fits and is consistent, it should be accepted; otherwise, it should not be accepted. One should simply abide by one's own opinion.

Furthermore, if this person speaks having taken their own opinion as the basis, while the other speaks according to the Teacher’s doctrine (ācariyavāda), the Teacher’s doctrine should be compared with one's own opinion.
If it fits and is consistent, it should be accepted; otherwise, that censurable teacher’s doctrine should not be accepted.
One should stand firm in one's own judgment alone; one's own apprehension alone should be made authoritative.
In all instances, neither rejection nor censure should be directed toward others.

However, if this person speaks having taken something as "allowable" (*kappiya*) while another takes it as "unallowable" (*akappiya*), it must be tested against the Sutta and that which is in conformity with the Sutta (*suttānuloma*). If it is allowable, one should stand by what is allowable; if it is unallowable, one should stand by what is unallowable.
Then, if this person presents many scriptural reasons and legal determinations from the Suttas to establish its suitability (*kappiya*),
and the other finds no reason [to oppose it], one must remain on the side of what is suitable. Then,

if the other person presents many scriptural reasons and legal determinations from the Suttas to establish its unsuitability (*akappiya*), taking this as an occasion for his own grasping, he becomes firm.
One should not stand up [to accept] after having taken it. Having accepted with "Very well," one should indeed stand in an improper place.
Now, if the shadow of the two reasons is seen, it is better that the refusal itself occurs; one should stand in an improper place.
For once the Vinaya has been reached, through the investigation of what is allowable and what is unallowable, one must restrain oneself, act firmly, and cut off the stream [of transgression].
One should remain firm in what is indeed venerable.

Now, if this person speaks while taking it to be "unallowable" (akappiya), but the other takes it to be "allowable" (kappiya), it must be tested against the Sutta and that which is in accordance with the Sutta. If it is allowable, one should stand by what is allowable; if it is unallowable, one should stand by what is unallowable.
Then, if this person demonstrates its unallowable nature through many reasons for determining the Sutta, and the other finds no such reason—

One should remain firm regarding what is improper (*akappiya*). Then, if another person demonstrates its proper nature (*kappiyabhāva*) through many reasons and legal determinations (*suttavinicchaya*), one should not find fault with those reasons; rather, one should remain firm regarding what is proper.

If, however, the shadow of reason is seen in both cases, one should not relinquish one's own position. And such is the determination regarding what is proper and improper, as well as what is improper and proper.
Thus, the analysis should be understood for the discussion of non-offenses versus offenses, as well as for the discussion of light versus heavy offenses and heavy versus light offenses.
For here there is only a difference in terminology; there is no difference in the method of application.
Therefore, it has not been elaborated upon.

Thus, when a determination regarding what is allowable (*kappiya*) and what is unallowable (*akappiya*), and so forth, has arisen, one should stand by the position of whoever obtains a superior reason among the following:

the Sutta, that which is in conformity with the Sutta (*suttānuloma*), the teacher’s tradition (*ācariyavāda*), or one’s own reasoning (*attanomatī*). However, one who finds no reason for a determination whatsoever must not abandon the Sutta;
rather, one should stand by the Sutta alone. Thus it is with respect to that training rule (*sikkhāpada*) and the analysis of the training rule (*sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*).
Furthermore, by one who desires skill in the entire determination of the Vinaya, these fourfold aspects of the Vinaya must be understood.
Moreover, even after knowing this fourfold Vinaya, the person who upholds the Vinaya must be endowed with three characteristics.
For three characteristics are required of a Vinaya-dhara. Which three? "His Sutta..."
“‘Welcome’ is well-spoken, well-delivered, and well-determined according to the suttas and their phrasing”—this is the first characteristic.
“Furthermore, he stands firm in the Vinaya and is unshakable”—this is the second.
“Furthermore, his lineage of teachers has been well-learned, well-attended to, and well-retained by him”—this is the third.
In this context, "the Sutta" refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. "It has come down well to him" means it has been properly transmitted.
"Well-recited" means it is well-practiced, mastered through recitation, and thoroughly analyzed.

"Thoroughly analyzed according to the Sutta and according to the phrasing" means it is well-determined by way of the canonical text (*pāḷi*), by way of formal inquiry (*paripucchā*), and by way of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*); it has been learned after resolving all doubts.
"But he stands firm in the Vinaya" means he is established in the Vinaya through a sense of shame (*lajjībhāva*).

For one who lacks shame, even if he is very learned, might—out of greed for gain and honor—contradict the tradition, proclaim what is contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya as the Teacher’s instruction, and thereby cause great harm to the Dispensation;
he may even bring about a schism in the Saṅgha or a rebellion against the Saṅgha. But one who possesses shame...
One who is conscientious and desirous of training does not deceive the tradition even for the sake of life;
he illuminates only the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and, holding the Teacher’s instruction in high esteem, he establishes it. For thus in the past, the great elders uttered these words three times:
“In the future, one possessed of shame will protect [the teaching]; one possessed of shame will protect it; one possessed of shame will protect it.”
Thus, one who possesses a sense of shame (lajjī), not abandoning nor deviating from the Vinaya, stands well-established in the Vinaya by virtue of that sense of shame.

"Irreproachable" (asaṃhīra): one who is "reproachable" (saṃhīra) is one who, when questioned regarding the Canon (pāḷi) or the Commentary (aṭṭhakathā)—whether from below or above, or according to the sequence of words—evades, flinches, and is unable to stand firm; whatever is said to him by another...
He grants permission for this and that; having abandoned his own position, he adopts the position of another.

But when questioned according to the text, or the commentary, or from bottom to top, or by the sequence of the words, he does not waver nor struggle, but like one grasping a single hair with tweezers, says: "This is what we say; this is what our teachers say."

He expounds [the teaching]; and since in him both the scripture (*pāḷi*) and the analysis of the scripture (*pāḷivinicchaya*) remain without being exhausted or depleted—like lion’s fat poured into a golden vessel—he is called "unshakable" (*asaṃhīra*).
Furthermore, his succession of teachers has been well-learned; thus, there is for him a succession of elders (*theraparamparā*) and a succession of lineages (*vaṃsaparamparā*).
"Su-gahitā" means well-grasped. "Sumanasikatā" means well-attended-to; it becomes like a lamp that has flared up the very moment it is brought to mind.
"Sūpadhāritā" means well-retained; it is retained through the connection of what precedes and what follows, and by way of its meaning and its underlying reason.
Having abandoned one's own opinion, one speaks according to the purity of the teacher, saying: "My teacher [learned this] from such-and-such a teacher..."

He learned it from such-and-such a person. In this way, having brought forward the entire lineage of teachers—the constituent part of the Theravāda—down to the point where it concludes with the Elder Upāli learning it in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One, he establishes it.

Having brought it down even further than that, [he shows that] the Elder Upāli learned it in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Elder Dāsaka learned it from his own preceptor, the Elder Upāli.
Thera Soṇaka [transmitted it] to his own preceptor, Thera Dāsaka; Thera Siggava to his own preceptor, Thera Soṇaka;
and Thera Moggaliputtatissa to his own preceptors, Theras Siggava and Caṇḍavajjī.
Thus, having brought forward the entire lineage of teachers as a constituent part of the Theravāda and having reached his own teacher, [he spoke].
He establishes it. For when learned thus, the lineage of teachers is properly grasped.
However, for one who is unable to do so, two or three rounds must certainly be mastered.
At the very least, according to the final method, it is necessary to understand how both the teacher and the teacher’s teacher state the text and the interrogation.

Furthermore, when a Saṅgha has assembled for the purpose of deciding upon a legal matter (*vatthu*) by means of a Vinaya expert endowed with these three characteristics, and the matter has been introduced, and what is to be said has been spoken by both the accuser and the accused, that expert must—without making a hasty decision—examine six points.
What are the six? The legal matter (*vatthu*) must be examined; the summary (*mātikā*) must be examined; the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*) must be examined...
The section on the threefold delimitation should be examined; the offense in between [the offenses] should be examined; and the non-offense should be examined.

For even while examining the basis of the rule, one sees a certain offense thus: "One should come having covered oneself with grass or leaves; one must not come naked; whoever should come [naked], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). He...
Having brought forward that sutta, he will settle that legal issue.

Even while looking at the *mātikā*, if he sees one of the five offenses according to the method beginning with, “In the case of intentional lying, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*),” he will bring forward that sutta and settle that legal issue. Even while looking at the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājanīya*), [he sees]:
“If one engages in sexual intercourse while the body has not yet decayed, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).”
When he perceives one of the seven offenses according to the method beginning with, “If he engages in sexual intercourse when the body is mostly consumed,
it is an offense of thullaccaya,” he will resolve that legal issue by bringing the Sutta from the word-by-word commentary (padabhājanīya).

Even when examining the section on triads (*tikapariccheda*), if he sees within that section on triads any offense—whether it be a triad of *saṅghādisesas*, a triad of *pācittiyas*, a triad of *dukkaṭas*, or any other—he will settle that legal issue by bringing forward the relevant rule (*sutta*).

Even when examining the intermediate offenses (*antarāpatti*), if he sees an intermediate offense among the intervals between the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) such as, "If one ejects [a monk] who has already been ejected, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*," he will settle that legal issue by bringing forward that rule.
Even while looking for a non-offense, he sees the non-offense specified in each respective training rule (sikkhāpada) thus:

"There is no offense, monk, for one who does not consent, who has no intent to steal, who does not intend death, who does not intend to misrepresent, who does not intend emission, unless it was done intentionally, or through lack of mindfulness, or unknowingly. Having brought that discourse (sutta) forward, he...
He will settle that legal case.

For whatever monk, skilled in the fourfold Vinaya, endowed with the three characteristics, having surveyed these six points, settles a legal case, his judgment is irrefutable; it is as if the Buddha himself were sitting there.

He becomes like a judge. When a monk who has committed a transgression of the training rules approaches such a monk who is skilled in adjudication and asks about his own remorse, the latter, having carefully examined the matter, should say, "It is no offense," if it is indeed no offense;
but if it is an offense, he should say, "It is an offense."
If it leads to confession, it should be called "leading to confession. If it leads to emergence [from the offense], it should be called "leading to emergence.
Now, if the shadow of a *pārājika* offense is seen, one should not yet say, "It is a *pārājika* offense. Why?

Because the transgression of sexual intercourse and the transgression of a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) are coarse; whereas the transgression of taking what is not given and the transgression involving a human being [as an object]—[are less so].
However, they are subtle and light of mind; they enter [into an offense] only subtly and guard themselves only subtly.

Therefore, when specifically asked about remorse regarding that very basis, if he does not say "it is an offense" but his teacher maintains [the view], then that monk should be sent by him with the words, "Ask our teacher. If he returns again and says, "Your..."
If he says, "The teacher, having examined it from the perspective of the suttas and the underlying principles, told me it is curable," then he should be told by him: "Excellent!

You must do exactly as the teacher says. But if he has no teacher, yet there is an elder with whom he studied together, he should be sent to that elder, saying: "The elder with whom we studied together..."
"Go and ask the leader of the community. If he too has determined that "it is curable," one should say: "Very well, you must act according to his word.
Then, if there is no elder who has mastered the texts, but there is a wise pupil, he should be sent with the instruction: "Go to such-and-such a young monk and ask him. If he too—
When it has been determined that he is "one who can still be cured," one should say: "It is good; you must act well and properly upon his word.
Even if the shadow of a *pārājika* offense appears even for a junior monk, he should not be told, "You are a *pārājika*.
For the arising of a Buddha is rare, and the going forth and full ordination are rarer still. However, he should be told thus: "Go to a secluded place..."
“Having swept [the area], sat down for the day’s abiding, and purified your virtue, first bring to mind the thirty-two aspects.

If his virtuous conduct is healthy and accords with the meditation subject, then conditioned phenomena appear clearly, his mind becomes one-pointed as if it had reached access or absorption, and he does not even notice when the day has passed. He—
When he has come for attendance after the day has passed, he should be asked: "What is the state of your mind?
Once the state of his mind has been reported, he should be told: "Going forth is indeed for the sake of purifying the mind; therefore, be diligent in the practice of the ascetic’s duty.
However, for one whose virtue is broken, the meditation subject does not succeed, just like a horse struck by a goad.
The mind wavers and is consumed by the fire of remorse; like one sitting on a red-hot stone, it recoils at that very moment.
When he has returned, he should be asked: "What was the movement of your mind? Once the movement of his mind has been reported, [he should be told]:
"For one who commits an evil deed, there is no such thing as secrecy in the world. For when first committing an evil act, one does it oneself..."
If he knows, then his guardian deities, recluses and brahmins who know the minds of others, and other deities will know;
you yourself must now seek your own safety. Thus it should be said.
The fourfold discussion on discipline is concluded.
The Discussion on the Characteristics, etc., of the Vinaya-holder.
Commentary on the Analysis of the Terms for the Bhikkhus.
Now we shall explain the meaning of the analysis of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga*). As for what was stated—"But who [is it]?"—this means "whoever of such a kind," and so forth.
In this context, "but as for who" (*ettha yo pana*) is the term to be analyzed; "who, of such a kind," and so forth, are the terms that analyze it.

Furthermore, since *pana* here is merely a particle, and *yo* is the substantive term—which indicates a person without restriction—it is for the purpose of showing its meaning that the word *yo* itself is stated as indicating a person without restriction. Therefore, the meaning here is as follows:
It should be understood: "whoever" means whoever at all; this is what is stated.

However, since anyone who is called "somebody" must necessarily be known by way of one or another mode among gender, connection, birth, name, clan, virtue, abode, resort, and age, therefore, in order to make that known, he spoke the passage beginning with "of such a kind" while explaining those distinctions. Therein, "of such a kind" refers to gender.
"Of such a kind or of that kind" means: whether tall or short, dark or fair, smooth-skinned or thin or fat.
"According to what is appropriate" means: by way of application, let him be engaged in whatever [task] is suitable; the meaning is:
whether engaged in building work, engaged in recitation, or engaged in the duties of residence. "According to birth" means: by way of caste, whatever caste he may be.
"Of such a caste" means whether he be a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, or a sudda.
"By whatever name" means by way of name, let him be known by whatever name—that is, whether he be named Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, or Saṅgharakkhita.
"By whatever clan" means by way of clan, let him be of whatever clan or of whichever [clan] it may be.
"By clan" means: let him be a Kaccāyana, a Vāsiṭṭha, or a Kosiya—this is the meaning. "According to his virtue" means: let him be of such virtue or of that virtue regarding the precepts;

let him be one whose virtue consists in building works, or one whose virtue consists in recitation, or one whose virtue consists in the duty of residence—this is the meaning. "According to his dwelling" means:
let him be of such a dwelling or of that dwelling even regarding the monasteries; let him be one who dwells in building works, or one who dwells in recitation... [and so forth].
The meaning is that he dwells in the duty of residing (*vāsadhura*). "According to his range" (*yathāgocara*) means:

whether it be according to his range or otherwise, whether his range be the site of new construction (*navakamma*), the site of recitation (*uddesa*), or the site of residence (*vāsadhura*); such is the meaning. Regarding "an elder" (*thero*) and so forth:
among those who are young, old, and so on, let him be anyone at all; or he may be an elder by virtue of having completed ten years [of seniority], or one with less than five years [of seniority].
The meaning is: either a novice (*navaka*) or one who has exceeded five years of seniority is a "middle" (*majjhima*).
However, in this context, everyone is referred to as "anyone who" (*yo pana*).
In the description of a monk (*bhikkhu-niddesa*), he is a "mendicant" (*bhikkhaka*) because he begs; whether obtaining or not obtaining, he begs by means of noble solicitation.
The meaning is as follows: Because he has undertaken the life of wandering for alms as accepted by the Buddha and others, he is called "one who has undertaken the life of wandering for alms.

For anyone who, having abandoned a small or large mass of wealth, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, abandons the means of livelihood such as plowing and cattle-tending, and by the mere acceptance of the [monastic] marks, has undertaken the life of wandering for alms.
A bhikkhu: he is called a bhikkhu because he has entered upon the life of wandering for alms even while eating solid food in the midst of a monastery due to his livelihood being dependent on others;

or he is called a bhikkhu because he has entered upon the life of wandering for alms due to having conceived the aspiration for the going-forth by relying on the practice of eating morsels of alms-food.
One who wears a tattered robe is so called because he wears a robe that is torn apart according to its value, touch, color, and type.
In this context, the destruction of value should be understood through the cutting with a knife.
For even a cloth worth a thousand [pieces] becomes one of destroyed value when cut into pieces by a knife; it is not worth even half its former price.
The destruction of touch should be understood through the weaving together of threads. For even a cloth that is pleasant to the touch becomes one of destroyed touch when woven with threads.
It reaches a state of rough contact. The distinction in color should be understood through the needle-holes and so forth.

For even a perfectly pure cloth, from the time of the needlework onwards, becomes of variegated color due to the needle-holes, the dirt and stains from handling, and finally due to the dyeing process;
it abandons its original color. Thus, because he wears a cloth that has been altered in these three ways, he is called a "wearer of an altered cloth" (*bhinnapaṭadhara*).
A *bhikkhu*. He is called a *bhikkhu* simply by virtue of wearing the saffron robes, which are distinct from the clothing of householders, for he wears "torn garments" (*bhinna-paṭa*).
"By designation" (*samaññāya*) means by way of a concept or conventional usage. For it is by designation alone that a certain person is known as a "bhikkhu.
Thus, when bhikkhus are being counted during an invitation ceremony (*nimantana*) and so forth, even a novice (*sāmaṇera*) is included, and they say, "There are one hundred bhikkhus."
They say, "A thousand bhikkhus. Regarding "by admission": by one's own admission, some indeed become known as "bhikkhus.
Its occurrence should be seen in such instances as, "Who is here? and "I am, friend, a bhikkhu," and so forth.
However, this is a legitimate admission spoken by the Venerable Ānanda; whereas at night, even those who are immoral...
As they were coming along the path, when asked, "Who is here?", they replied, "We are bhikkhus," making an unrighteous and false claim. Regarding the term *ehibhikkhu*:
one who has attained the status of a bhikkhu through the mere words of the Blessed One, "Come, bhikkhu," has received the *ehibhikkhu-upasampadā*.
For the Blessed One [recognizes] a person endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) for the state of being an *ehibhikkhu*.
Having seen him, he drew forth his gold-colored right hand from within his red rag-robe and, emitting a Brahma-voice, said:
"Come, monk; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
At the very moment of the Blessed One’s words, his layman's marks vanished, and he was ordained and received full admission.

And he grew up. Bhaṇḍu was dressed in saffron robes. Having put on one robe, wrapped another around himself, and placed a third over his shoulder—with a clay bowl, the color of a blue lotus, resting upon his left shoulder—he [recited]:
“The three robes and the bowl, the razor, the needle, and the belt;”
“These eight [items] belong to a bhikkhu who is devoted to yoga by means of the water-strainer.
When these eight requisites had been thus fastened to his body, he— possessed of the four postures like a sixty-year-old elder,
following the Teacher’s way of life and having the Buddha as his preceptor— paid homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
He remains. For at the time of his first enlightenment, the Blessed One conferred the full ordination by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-upasampadā*) on one occasion.
Those thus ordained numbered three thousand four hundred and one monks;
namely, the five elders of the group of five, Yasa the son of a good family, and his forty-four companions.

The companions were the thirty members of the Bhaddavaggiya group, the thousand former matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila), two hundred and fifty wandering mendicants (paribbājaka) together with the two chief disciples, and the Elder Aṅgulimāla. For this is said in the Commentary:
"Three hundred and one thousand, and another forty;”
"And one elder who is wise—all of them were ordained by the 'Come, bhikkhu' formula.
Not only these, but there are many others as well. Namely: the brahmin Sela with a retinue of three hundred;
Mahākappina with a retinue of a thousand; ten thousand clansmen from Kapilavatthu; and sixteen thousand...
The *Pārāyanika-brāhmaṇas* and others such as these [are included]. However, because they are not specified in the text of the Vinaya Piṭaka, they were not mentioned there.
These [others] were mentioned because they are specified therein.
"Twenty-seven thousand and three hundred;"
“All these who have been ordained are indeed ‘come-hither’ monks.

One who is ordained by the three goings for refuge means one who is ordained by the three goings for refuge spoken three times by breaking the silence in the manner beginning with, “I go for refuge to the Buddha. For this ordination is eightfold.

—Full admission by the "Come, monk" formula; full admission by going for refuge; full admission by receiving instruction; full admission by answering questions; full admission by accepting the heavy rules;
full admission by means of a messenger; full admission by the eight declarations; and full admission by the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations.
Among these, full admission by the "Come, monk" formula and full admission by going for refuge have already been explained.
The admission by receiving instruction is as follows: “Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus:
‘Intense moral shame and moral dread shall be established in me toward elders, juniors, and those of middle standing.
Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: ‘Whatever [is to be done]...’”
‘I shall listen to the Dhamma connected with the wholesome; applying my whole mind, attending to it, and focusing with all my heart, I shall listen to the Dhamma with an attentive ear.
In this way, Kassapa, you should train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: ‘May mindfulness directed to the body, accompanied by pleasure, not be abandoned by me.’”
"Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself"—by this acceptance of advice, the Elder Mahākassapa received the consent for his full ordination (*upasampadā*).

The so-called "ordination by answering questions" refers to the consent for Sopāka’s full ordination. It is said that while the Blessed One was walking back and forth in the Eastern Monastery, he addressed the novice Sopāka:
"'The perception of a bloated corpse,' Sopāka, or 'the perception of form'..."

"Are these phenomena different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they identical in meaning and only different in phrasing? Thus he asked ten questions concerning the ten kinds of foulness (*asubha*).
He answered them. The Blessed One, having given him his approval, asked: "How many years have you been ordained, Sopāka?
"Seven years, Blessed One. "Sopāka, you [have answered] with my own omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*)."
Having synthesized the questions, he answered them; thus, with a mind resolved, he authorized full ordination (*upasampadā*). This is ordination through the answering of questions.
Ordination through the acceptance of the eight weighty rules (*garudhamma*) refers to the authorization of ordination for Mahāpajāpatī by her acceptance of the eight weighty rules.
Ordination through a messenger refers to the authorization of ordination for the courtesan Aḍḍhakāsī.

The ordination by means of the eight declarations (*aṭṭhavācikūpasampadā*) refers to the ordination of a bhikkhunī through two formal acts (*kamma*): one consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations from the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, and one consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations from the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.
The ordination by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā*) is the ordination of bhikkhus at the present time.
Regarding these eight types of ordination, [the Blessed One said]: "Monks, that ordination by means of the three goings for refuge which was permitted by me, from this day forward I revoke it."
“I allow you, monks, to confer full ordination by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations.
Thus, when this method of ordination has been authorized, one is said to be “fully ordained.
“Bhadra” means “blameless. For from the virtuous worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) up to the Arhat, [they are endowed] with blameless virtue and concentration.
Because they are endowed with wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they are reckoned as "noble bhikkhus.

Because they are endowed with those very essentials such as the essence of virtue (sīla-sāra) and so forth—just as a cloth is called "blue" due to its possession of the quality blue—they should be understood as "essential bhikkhus" (sāra-bhikkhu).
Alternatively, because the state of being like the pith (pheggu) of defilements has been removed, only one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) is the "essence."
[This] is to be understood. A *sekha* (trainee) refers to the seven noble ones together with the virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), for they train in the three trainings;
thus they are called *sekhā*. Among them, anyone may be understood as a "monk who is a trainee" (*sekho bhikkhu*). One who does not train is an *asekha*.

Having transcended the states of a trainee and being established in the supreme fruit, one whose taints are exhausted is called an "adept" (*asekha*), because there is nothing further beyond that to be trained in.

"By a unanimous Saṅgha" means: in the case of a formal act (kamma) to be performed by a quorum of five, having reached unanimity in that single act through the arrival of as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the act, the bringing of the consent (*chanda*) of those who are entitled to give it, and the absence of any protest from those present;
[it is done] by means of three proclamations (*anussāvana*) following one motion (*ñatti*).
And by means of what must be done with a single motion (*ñatti*). "By a legal act" (*kammena*) means by a legal act that is in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya.

"Irreversible" (*akuppena*) means having attained a state that cannot be overturned or refuted because it is complete in its basis, motion, proclamation, boundary, and assembly. "Worthy of the occasion" (*ṭhānāraheṇa*) means worthy of the reason and worthy of the Teacher’s instruction.
One who is "ordained" (*upasampanna*) has reached a higher state; the meaning is "one who has attained. For the state of a bhikkhu is indeed a higher state.

Because he has entered into that very procedure as described, he is called "fully ordained" (*upasampanna*). And here, only the formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (*ñatticatutthakamma*) is mentioned.
However, it is stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that, standing at this point, one should extract and explain in detail the four types of formal acts of the Saṅgha.

These are: the formal act of mere notification (*apalokanakamma*), the formal act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*), and the formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).

Regarding the phrase “a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations,” having set it aside for the moment, the Pāḷi has been brought forward in detail from the Khandhaka and at the end of the Parivāra from the Kammavibhaṅga. We shall explain those very matters at the end of the Parivāra, in the Kammavibhaṅga itself.
For if this is done, the commentary on the first Pārājika will not be overly burdensome, as it stands [in its proper place].
And the commentary on the text will thus be easy to understand. Those points will not be left empty;
therefore, we shall provide a word-by-word commentary.
"Therein" means among those monks spoken of by way of the method beginning with "the beggar" (*bhikkhaka*). "This monk" means this one who...

A bhikkhu. One who has been ordained by a united Saṅgha... [as described] ...is one ordained by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*) among the eight types of ordination. This is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context;

that is, in this sense of "having committed sexual intercourse, he becomes one defeated (*pārājika*)," it is this person who is intended as a "bhikkhu. As for the others, they are "alms-seekers" (*bhikkhaka*).
These and others are stated by way of extracting the meanings. Among them, "alms-seeker" (*bhikkhaka*) and so forth are stated by way of etymological derivation (*nirutti*);
"a monk by convention" (*samaññāya bhikkhu*) and "a monk by profession" (*paṭiññāya bhikkhu*)—these two—are stated by way of verbal expression; "Come, monk!

(*ehi bhikkhu*) is stated by way of the full ordination (*upasampadā*) received from the Buddha as preceptor. A monk by going for refuge is one prior to the recitation of the formal ritual (*kammavācā*).

It should be understood that [the terms] such as "noble" (*bhadra*) are stated by way of their qualities, whereas [the term] "full ordination" (*upasampadā*) is stated by way of the formal act itself.
The analysis of the terms for the bhikkhu is finished.
This concludes the commentary on the analysis of the terms for training and communal living (*sikkhāsājīva*).

Now, without analyzing the word "of the bhikkhus" because there is no specific meaning [to be distinguished], he spoke the passage beginning with "the training" (*sikkhā*) in order to show that one who has entered upon both the training and the mode of livelihood is "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood of the bhikkhus.
In that context, "training" (*sikkhā*) means that which is to be trained in. "Three" (*tisso*) is a numerical delimitation. "Higher training in virtue" (*adhisīlasikkhā*) means superior or supreme.
"Virtue" (*sīla*) means higher virtue (*adhisīla*); and because it is to be trained in, it is also "training" (*sikkhā*), thus "training in higher virtue" (*adhisīlasikkhā*).
This same method applies to the trainings in higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*). But here, what is virtue? What is higher virtue? What is mind? What is higher mind? What is...
Regarding wisdom (*paññā*), what is "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*)? It is said: First, the virtue consisting of the fivefold and tenfold precepts is simply virtue (*sīla*).
For that indeed exists in the world whether a Buddha has arisen or not. When a Buddha has arisen, both Buddhas and their disciples exhort the great masses toward that virtue.
When a Buddha has not arisen, it is the Paccekabuddhas and those who profess the efficacy of karma (*kammavādino*) who [exhort others].
Ascetics and brahmins, universal monarchs, great kings, and great bodhisattvas encourage others [to undertake it].
Wise ascetics and brahmins also undertake it themselves. Having fulfilled that wholesome quality, they experience prosperity among gods and humans.
Furthermore, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is called "higher virtue" (adhisīla), for...
Like the sun among lights and like Sineru among mountains, it is superior to and the most excellent of all mundane virtues;
it occurs only when a Buddha has arisen, and not without the arising of a Buddha.
For no other being is able to establish that designation after having extracted it, but only Buddhas [can do so] by completely cutting off the stream of misconduct at the doors of body and speech.
Having eliminated each respective transgression, they prescribe that corresponding restraint of virtue.
Furthermore, while virtue associated with the path and its fruit is indeed "higher virtue" (*adhisisa*) even beyond the restraint of the Pātimokkha, that is not what is intended here.
For a monk who has attained such [higher virtue] does not engage in sexual intercourse.

Furthermore, the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and the eight mundane attainment-consciousnesses (*lokīya-aṭṭhasamāpatti-citta*), taken together, should be understood as "consciousness" (*citta*) alone.
Its occurrence whether a Buddha has arisen or not, its instigation, and its undertaking should be understood in the same manner as described for virtue (*sīla*).
However, the eight attainment-consciousnesses that serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanā-pādaka*) are called "higher consciousness" (*adhi-citta*).
It is so called because, like "higher virtue" (adhisisīla), it is both superior and supreme among all mundane states of consciousness;
moreover, it occurs only when a Buddha has appeared, not without the appearance of a Buddha.

Even more so than that, "higher consciousness" (adhicitta) refers specifically to the consciousness of the paths and fruits, yet that is not intended here. For a bhikkhu who has attained that [state] does not engage in sexual intercourse.
However, the knowledge of the ownership of kamma, which proceeds in such a manner as "there is what is given, there is what is sacrificed," is wisdom (*paññā*).
For that wisdom exists in the world whether a Buddha has arisen or not.

When a Buddha has arisen, both the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha exhort the great masses of people in that wisdom. When no Buddha has arisen, the Paccekabuddhas [exhort them] as proponents of kamma.
And righteous ascetics and brahmins, universal monarchs, and great bodhisattvas encourage [others] to do so;
wise beings also undertake it themselves. For instance, Aṅkura gave a great gift for ten thousand years;
Velāma, Vessantara, and many other wise men gave great gifts. They [performed] that wholesome deed...
Having fulfilled the Dhamma, they experienced prosperity among both gods and humans.
However, the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that discerns the three characteristics is called "higher wisdom" (adhipaññā).

For this is both superior and more excellent than the mundane wisdom of all those who possess virtue and concentration—just as higher virtue and higher concentration are superior to virtue and concentration—and it does not arise in the world without the appearance of a Buddha.
Furthermore, it is specifically the wisdom of the path and its fruition that constitutes higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*), yet that is not what is intended here.
For a monk who has attained that [wisdom] does not engage in sexual intercourse.
"Therein" refers to among those three trainings. "That which is the training in higher virtue" refers to that which is designated as the *pātimokkha* virtue.
The training in higher virtue (*adhisīlasikkhā*). "This is called the common livelihood" (*sājīva*):

all these training rules (*sikkhāpada*) established by the Blessed One in the Vinaya are called "common livelihood" because, herein, monks who are otherwise divided by various differences of country, birth, clan, and so forth, live together—sharing one life, sharing a common life, and living in common conduct;
therefore, it is called "common livelihood. One trains in that [set of rules], thus it is "that training rule" (*taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ*).
Making the mind the basis, he trains while examining with the mind: "Am I training according to the training rule (sikkhāpada), or am I not?
Not only does he train in this training rule known as the "mode of livelihood" (sājīva), but he also trains in the training itself;
for by way of the immediately following phrase, "This is indeed called the mode of livelihood," [he trains].
“It trains in that” is what was said. Although it is stated thus, this is how the meaning should be understood here:
he trains while fulfilling the training in that training, and he trains by not transgressing that training rule.
Therefore it is said, “he has entered upon that way of life”; this too is according to the immediately preceding term, “way of life.”
It has been stated. However, because he has also undertaken the training (*sikkhā*), he should be understood in terms of meaning as "one who has undertaken the training" (*sikkhāsamāpanna*).
For this being the case, the word-analysis (*padabhājana*) for the phrase "one who has undertaken the training and the livelihood" (*sikkhāsājīvasamāpanna*) becomes complete.
The word-analysis of the terms "training" and "livelihood" is finished.

Commentary on the Analysis of the Renunciation of Training (*Sikkhāpaccakkhāna-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā*): "Without renouncing the training and without manifesting weakness" means without rejecting the training and without declaring one's own frailty.
For even when weakness is manifested, the training has not yet been renounced; however, as for the training...
When [the offense] has been confessed, the weakness [of one's position] is already made manifest. Therefore, no specific meaning is obtained by the phrase "without having manifested the weakness.

Just as when it is said, "one might share a sleeping place for two or three nights," no specific meaning is obtained by the mention of "two nights," but it is used merely for the sake of worldly convention and the elegance of expression.

This was said because it has "ascended to the mouth" (mukhārūḷhatāya). Likewise, this too should be understood as having been said because it has ascended to the mouth, due to its verbal smoothness and by way of conventional usage.
Or, because the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma with both meaning and phrasing, therefore [it is said]: "without renouncing the training."
Having established the meaning with this [phrase], one establishes the phrasing with the words "without disclosing weakness.

For a single meaningful phrase being spoken, if devoid of its surrounding context, does not shine—just like a king without his retinue, or a man without clothes and ornaments; but when it is accompanied by the auxiliary words that follow the sense, it shines together with them.

Alternatively, since the non-disclosure of one’s weakness constitutes a partial renunciation of the training, it was with reference to this that he said, "without disclosing his weakness," while explaining the meaning of the phrase "without renouncing the training.

Herein, it might be argued: since not every disclosure of weakness constitutes a renunciation of the training, one should first say "without disclosing his weakness" and then say "without renouncing the training" in order to define its specific meaning.

And that is not so; why? Because there is no sequential order of meaning. For since it was said, "one who has undertaken the training and the mode of livelihood," when it is stated, "without having renounced that training which he has undertaken," the meaning is expressed precisely in its proper sequence and not otherwise.
Therefore, this alone is what was stated first.

Furthermore, the meaning here should also be understood according to the sequence. How so? In the phrase "one who has undertaken the training and the mode of livelihood," it means that one has not renounced the training one has undertaken, nor has one revealed weakness regarding the mode of livelihood one has undertaken.

Now, demonstrating the distinction and non-distinction between the renunciation of the training and the revelation of weakness, as well as the characteristic of the renunciation of the training, he says:
"There is, monks... and so forth. In this context, "There is, monks... and so on constitute two summary headings (*mātikāpada*).
Analyzing those [terms], he said, beginning with, "And how, monks... Herein, this is the commentary on the obscure words: *Kathaṃ* means "in what manner" (*kena ākārena*).
*Dubbalyāvikammañca* means "and the disclosure of weakness. *Idha* means "in this teaching" (*imasmiṃ sāsane*).
*Ukkaṇṭhito* means one who, through dissatisfaction, has reached a state of difficult livelihood in this teaching; or alternatively, "I go today, tomorrow..."
"I go," "I go from here," "I go there"—dwelling thus with his throat constricted, he is said to be distracted and lacking one-pointedness of mind.
"Discontented" means devoid of delight in the Teaching.
"Desiring to fall away from the state of a recluse" means wishing to depart from the condition of being a *samaṇa*. "The state of a monk" means by way of the status of a *bhikkhu*.

The dative case is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*). However, in such passages as “one would be distressed by [something] clinging to the throat,” it is expressed by the instrumental case according to the grammatical rule.
“Being distressed” (*aṭṭīyamāno*) means acting as if one’s self were afflicted, oppressed, or suffering;
or the meaning is that one is being distressed or oppressed by that state of being a monk. “Being ashamed” (*harāyamāno*) means feeling shame.
“Feeling disgust” means feeling revulsion toward him as if he were impure. “Longing for the state of a householder,” and so forth, have their meanings already explained.
“What if I were to renounce the Buddha?”—here, *yaṃ nūna* is a particle used to indicate a reflection.
This is what is meant: “If I were to renounce the Buddha, it would indeed be well for me. He speaks; he makes himself understood.
Having made a vocal utterance through these or other words, he speaks this meaning and makes it known and understood to the one to whom he speaks.
The particle “evam-pi” (even thus) serves to include the subsequent meaning. Thus, there is both a disclosure of weakness and a non-renunciation of the training; and so too in other ways.
Now, demonstrating that disclosure of weakness can also occur in other ways and that there may be no renunciation of the training, he says, “Or alternatively,” and so forth.
All of this is clear in meaning; however, as for the words, from the beginning here:
“One might renounce the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, the Vinaya, the Pātimokkha, the recitation, the preceptor...”

“[One might] renounce the teacher, the co-resident student, the pupil, the fellow-student under the same preceptor, the fellow-student under the same teacher, or the fellow-celibate”—these fourteen phrases are stated in the manner of renunciation. “One might be a householder,” and so forth, refers to:

a householder, a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*), a novice (*sāmaṇera*), a member of another sect (*titthiya*), a follower of another sect (*titthiyasāvaka*), or one who is not a monastic (*assamaṇa*).
The eight phrases beginning with “*assan* ti” (may he be) are expressed in this way by means of the verbal mood (*bhāvavikappa*) “*assan*.
Likewise, there are twenty-two phrases associated with “*yaṃ nūnāhan* ti” (what if now I...).

And just as these are, so too there are twenty-two phrases associated respectively with each of the following: “*yadi panāhan*,” “*apāhan*,” “*handāhan*,” and “*hoti me*. Thus, all together there are one hundred and ten phrases.
47. Following that, there are seventeen phrases beginning with "I remember my mother," which proceed by way of showing the objects to be remembered.
Therein, "field" (khette) refers to a rice field and so forth. "Ground" (vatthu) refers to a place where grass, leaves, vegetables, fruits, or crops grow.
"Craft" (sippa) refers to crafts such as those of the potter or the weaver.

48. Following that, there are nine phrases beginning with "I have a mother, she must be supported by me," which function to demonstrate the state of possessing worldly possessions (*sakiñcana*) and obstacles (*sapalibodha*). 49.
Following that, there are sixteen phrases beginning with "I have a mother, she will support me," which function to demonstrate the state of having a basis (*sanissaya*) and a support (*sappatiṭṭha*).

50. Following that, there are eight phrases beginning with "It is difficult to do" (*dukkara*), which function to demonstrate the difficulty of practicing eating once a day (*ekabhatta*), sleeping alone (*ekaseyya*), and the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
In this context, "difficult to do" (*dukkara*) shows the difficulty in performing [practices] such as eating only one meal a day.
"Not easy to do" (*na sukara*) rejects the state of being easy. Similarly, "difficult to practice" (*duccara*) and "not easy to practice" (*na sucara*) apply here.

"I am not able" (*na ussahāmi*) shows a lack of effort and an inability [to perform it]. "I am not capable" (*na visahāmi*) shows that it is beyond one's power. "I do not delight" (*na ramāmi*) shows the absence of pleasure.
It shows [this]. "I do not delight" shows the absence of delight.
Thus, it should be understood that these fifty and the previous one hundred and ten—making one hundred and sixty words—are spoken in the section on the manifestation of weakness. 51.
In the section on the renunciation of the training as well, everything beginning with "And how, monks," etc., is clear in meaning.
Furthermore, here too, these fourteen phrases— “I renounce the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, the Vinaya, the Pātimokkha, the recitation,
the preceptor, the teacher, the co-resident, the pupil, one who has the same preceptor, one who has the same teacher, and my fellow celibate”—
are connected with the statement of renouncing the training.
[The words] have been explained. And in all instances, the meaning of the expression “he speaks, he makes known” is this: having made a vocal utterance, he speaks;
and to whomsoever he speaks, by that very vocal utterance he makes known, proclaims, and causes to be understood:
“This person desires to abandon the Dispensation, desires to be released from the Dispensation, desires to relinquish the state of a bhikkhu, and thus he makes this vocal utterance.”

But if, wishing to say "I renounce the Buddha," one were to omit the word order and say "I renounce the Buddha," or if one were to express that same meaning in one of the non-Aryan languages (milakkhabhāsā), or if,
wishing to say "I renounce the Buddha," one were to say it out of sequence as "I renounce the Dhamma" or "I renounce my fellow-celibates"— [in these cases, the renunciation is not valid].

Or if one were to speak thus: just as in the analysis of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), one who wishes to say "I am attaining the first jhāna" but says "the second jhāna"—if the person to whom he speaks recognizes even this much, namely, "This monk wishes to abandon his status as a bhikkhu and speaks for this purpose," then there is no offense;
it is simply that he has entered the wrong field.
The training is indeed renounced. Or, like a being who has passed away from the state of a Sakka or a Brahmā, he has indeed fallen away from the Dispensation.

However, if he speaks using expressions of past, future, or hypothetical construction—such as "I have renounced the Buddha," "I shall renounce the Buddha," or "I might renounce the Buddha"—or if he sends a messenger or dispatches a message, [the offense is incurred] through the syllable...
Whether one cuts it off verbally, or communicates that meaning by means of a hand gesture, the training (sikkhā) remains unrenounced.
However, the proclamation of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) is included even when done by hand gesture.

The renunciation of the training is included only when one makes a vocal utterance associated with consciousness in the presence of a being of human birth. Even one who makes a vocal utterance and makes it understood [is considered to have renounced].
And if, having restricted it to one person by saying, "Let this very person know," he makes the announcement, and that person alone knows it, the training is renounced.
But if he does not know, and another standing nearby knows it, the training is not renounced.
Then, if in the presence of two people he specifies both, saying, "I announce it to these two," and among them—
Even when two people know [of his offense], or even when many know, the training is indeed renounced. This should be understood in the same way regarding many as well.
However, if one who is oppressed by dissatisfaction and fearing his fellow monks makes a loud noise, saying, "Let anyone who knows hear me!
I renounce the Buddha," while a novice worker or someone else stands nearby—
A person who understands the occasion, having heard [the words], knows: "This ascetic is dissatisfied and longs for the state of a householder; he has fallen away from the Dispensation.
Thus the training is indeed renounced. However, that very moment is difficult to discern as being neither before nor after;
if one knows it at the moment of adverting [to the object], then just as people in the world normally know by hearing a statement, [it is known that] the training has been renounced.
The training remains intact. Later, however, if one wonders, "What was said by this person? and only after a long time comes to know it, the training has not been renounced.

For this renunciation of the training and the subsequent rules concerning false accusation (*abhūtārocanā*), speaking of a grave offense (*duṭṭhullavācā*), and speaking of a real fault with malicious intent (*attakāma-duṭṭhadosa-bhūtārocanā*) share the same legal definition.
They are included under the same heading only when the matter is known at the moment of reflection, for one who wonders, "What is this person saying? [is not yet certain].

When [the offense] is known after a long time, they do not incur [the penalty for] the head. And just as this is stated in the analysis of the phrase "I renounce the Buddha," so it should be understood for all phrases.
Furthermore, because when the training has been renounced, [thoughts such as] "What if I were now to renounce the Buddha," and so forth, [arise].
Even by speaking [thus], one’s weakness is indeed made manifest; therefore, it is stated at the end of all the phrases:
"In this way too, monks, there is both a manifestation of weakness and a renunciation of the training.
Following that, regarding the phrase "regard me as a householder," even if one says, "I shall become a householder" or "I am a householder"—
Or if she says, “I am born as a householder,” or “I am a householder,” the training has not been renounced.
But if she says, “From today onwards, consider me a householder,” or “Know me [as such],” or “Recognize me [as such],” or “Keep this in mind”—
whether she speaks in an Aryan tongue or a non-Aryan tongue— when this meaning has been stated to whomever she speaks, [the training is renounced].
If he knows [this], the training has been renounced. This same method applies to the remaining seven instances, beginning with "lay follower" (*upāsaka*).
Thus, these eight and the previous fourteen make twenty-two phrases.
52. Hereafter, there are only the previous fourteen phrases: "Enough for me," "What need have I? "I have no need," and "I am well-liberated."
By combining these four [sets], fifty-six [verses] are stated. Therein, *alaṃ* means "let it be"; *pariyattaṃ* means "sufficient.
*Kiṃ nu me* means "what is my duty, what is to be done, what is to be accomplished? *Na mamattho* means "there is no purpose for me.
*Sumuttāhaṃ* means "I am well-liberated. The rest here is exactly according to the method already explained. Thus, these...
Thus, seventy-eight words—fifty-six preceding ones and twenty-two following—are stated in their own forms.
However, since the renunciation of the training occurs even through synonyms for those [words], he said, "or whatever others," and so forth.
Therein, "or whatever others" refers to those other words besides the terms such as "Buddha" that appear in the Pāḷi.
There are synonyms for "Buddha," that is, alternative names for the Buddha... [and so on] ...or for one who is not a follower of the Sakyan son.

In this regard, the thousand names found in the *Vaṇṇappakaraṇa* (Section on Praise), the hundred names in the *Upāli-gāthā*, and other names obtained by way of their qualities should be understood as "synonyms for Buddha. All of these are also names for the Dhamma.
These should be understood as synonyms for *dhamma*. This method applies everywhere.
Here, however, is the construction: "I renounce the Buddha" is not a renunciation by means of a synonym; it is exactly according to the literal expression.
"I renounce the Perfectly Enlightened One, the one of infinite wisdom, the one of peerless wisdom, the knowledge of enlightenment, the steadfast one..."

"I renounce the Buddha who is free from delusion, who has shattered the stakes, and who is the victor over all victors"—this is the renunciation of the training by means of such synonyms for the Buddha.
"I renounce the Dhamma" is not a renunciation by means of a synonym; it is exactly according to the literal expression:
"I renounce the well-expounded Dhamma, which is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be realized individually."
I renounce the Dhamma for the wise. I renounce the unconditioned Dhamma; I renounce dispassion, cessation, and the deathless Dhamma.

I renounce the *Dīghanikāya*, the *Brahmajāla* of the *Majjhimanikāya*, the *Mūlapariyāya*, the *Saṃyuttanikāya*, the *Oghataraṇa*, the *Aṅguttaranikāya*, the *Cittapariyādāna*, and the *Khuddakanikāya*.
“Jātaka, Abhidhamma, wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, indeterminate phenomena,
the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna— I renounce them. Thus,
among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma, even the name of a single aggregate of Dhamma is merely a synonym for the Dhamma.
Thus, there is a renunciation of the training by means of synonyms for the Dhamma.
"I renounce the Saṅgha" is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. [It is as when one says:

"I renounce the Saṅgha that has entered upon the good way, the Saṅgha that has entered upon the straight way, the Saṅgha that has entered upon the proper way, the Saṅgha that has entered upon the correct way, the Saṅgha of the four pairs of persons..."

“I renounce the Saṅgha—the community of the eight types of persons, the Saṅgha worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world”—thus there is a renunciation of the training by means of synonyms for the Saṅgha.
“I renounce the training” is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. “I renounce the training of a bhikkhu, the training of a bhikkhunī...”
“I renounce the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom”—thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by means of a synonym for the training.
“I renounce the Vinaya” is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. “I renounce the Bhikkhu-vinaya, the Bhikkhunī-vinaya...”
"I renounce the first *pārājika*, the second, third, and fourth *pārājikas*, the *saṅghādisesas*, the *thullaccayas*, the *pācittiyas*,
the *pāṭidesanīyas*, the *dukkaṭas*, and the *dubbhāsitas*. In this way,
there is a renunciation of the training through such synonyms for the Vinaya.

“I renounce the Pātimokkha”: this is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. “I renounce the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha, the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha”—in this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of a synonym for the Pātimokkha.
“I renounce the recitation”: this is not a renunciation by means of a synonym.

“The Bhikkhu-pātimokkha recitation, the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha recitation, the first Pātimokkha recitation, the second, third, fourth, and fifth Pātimokkha recitations, the recitation of the Fully Enlightened One.”
