“I renounce the one described as possessing infinite intelligence, the one described as possessing incomparable intelligence, the one described as possessing the wisdom of enlightenment, the one described as wise, the one described as free from delusion, the one described as having shattered the stakes, and the one described as victorious over victory”—through such synonyms of description, there is a renunciation of the training.
“I renounce my preceptor” is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. “He who ordained me, he who conferred full ordination upon me... [and so forth].
"By whose root I went forth, by whose root I received full ordination; that which is the root of my going forth, that which is the root of my full ordination—to him I renounce.
In this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of a synonym for the preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
"I renounce the teacher" (*ācariya*) is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. "He who ordained me, he who intoned the proclamation for me..."
“I renounce her whom I rely upon for living, whom I instruct, and whom I question;
and I renounce him who instructs me and him who causes me to question”—in this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of synonyms for "teacher.
"I renounce my co-resident" is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. "Her whom I ordained... [and so forth].
"I have ordained him; he who has gone forth under me, he who has received full ordination under me, his going-forth is rooted in me, his full ordination is rooted in me—this I renounce.
In this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of synonyms for the co-resident disciple (*saddhivihārika*).
“I renounce the resident pupil” is not a renunciation by means of synonyms. Rather, renunciation of the training occurs by using synonyms for the resident pupil as follows:
“I renounce him whom I ordained, him whom I made to recite, he who lives depending on me, he who makes me recite, he who questions me, him to whom I recite, and him whom I cause to question.
In this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of synonyms for the resident pupil.
"I renounce one who has the same preceptor" is not a renunciation by means of synonyms. Rather, it is by means of synonyms for "one who has the same preceptor," such as:

"I renounce him who ordained me, who gave me full ordination; who was ordained under him, who received full ordination under him; whose ordination is rooted in him, whose full ordination is rooted in him.
It is in this way that [the renunciation occurs] through synonyms for "one who has the same preceptor."
There is the renunciation of the training.
Renouncing by means of a synonym, such as saying, "I renounce my fellow-student," is not [a valid] renunciation.
[Thinking: "My teacher—who ordained me, who gave me the instruction, who dwells depending on him, who causes me to recite and question him, and for whom my teacher..."
"I renounce that which he recites and that which he causes me to inquire about"—thus there is a renunciation of the training by means of a synonym for "co-student" (*samānācariyaka*).
"I renounce my fellow-celibate" (*sabrahmacārī*) is not a renunciation by means of a synonym.
"I renounce him with whom I train in higher virtue, and in higher mind and higher wisdom"—thus [it is] by means of a synonym for "fellow-celibate."
There is a renunciation of the training.
To say, "Regard me as a householder," is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. Likewise, to say, "Regard me as a householder;
regard me as a farmer, a merchant, a cattle-herder, a hunter, one who wears a topknot, or one devoted to the strands of sensual pleasure"—in this way, it is by means of a synonym for a householder.
There is the renunciation of the training.
Saying, "Regard me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*)," is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. [The forms include:

"Regard me as a lay follower by two utterances," "a lay follower by three utterances," "one who has gone for refuge to the Buddha," "one who has gone for refuge to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha," and "one who observes the five precepts."
“Regard me as a lay follower observing the ten precepts”—in this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of a synonym for "lay follower.
"Regard me as a monastery attendant"—this is not a renunciation by means of a synonym.
“Regard me as a kitchen assistant, a servant, a grass-cutter, a distributor of rice-gruel, a distributor of fruits, or a distributor of snacks”—regard me...
"Consider me an attendant (*ārāmika*). In this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of a synonym for "attendant.
"Consider me a novice (*sāmaṇera*)"—this is not a renunciation by means of a synonym.

"Consider me a youth (*kumāraka*), a servant (*cellaka*), a slave (*ceṭaka*), one with matted hair (*moḷigalla*), or a novice monk (*samaṇuddesa*)"—in this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of synonyms for "novice."
“Regard me as a *titthiya*”—this is not a renunciation by means of a synonym.

“Regard me as a Nigaṇṭha, as an Ājīvaka, as an ascetic (*tāpasa*), as a wanderer (*paribbājaka*), or regard me as one clad in white (*paṇḍaraṅga*)”—in this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of a synonym for a *titthiya*.
“Regard me as a disciple of a *titthiya*”—this is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. “Regard me as a disciple of a Nigaṇṭha... [and so forth].

"Remember me as a follower of the Ājīvaka, the ascetic, the wanderer, or the white-robed one"—in this way, there is a renunciation of the training by means of synonyms for a follower of another sect (*titthiya*).
"Remember me as a non-recluse (*assamaṇo*)"—this is not a renunciation by means of a synonym. "Remember me as immoral, one of evil character..."
"Remember me as one who is impure, of suspicious conduct, whose actions are concealed, who is not an ascetic though claiming to be an ascetic,
who does not live the holy life though claiming to live the holy life, who is internally rotten, leaking, putrid, and a eunuch"— in this way,
there is a renunciation of the training by means of synonyms for "non-ascetic."
“Do not hold me to be ‘a son of the Sakyan’”— this is a renunciation by means of a synonym.
“Do not hold me to be ‘the son of the Perfectly Enlightened One,’ nor the son of Infinite Intelligence, nor the son of Peerless Intelligence, nor the son of Awakening-Wisdom, nor the son of the Wise,
nor the son of One Free from Delusion, nor the son of One Who Has Shattered the Fetters, nor the son of the Conqueror of Victory.”
“Hold [it]!”—by such synonyms for a follower of the Sakyan (Sakyaputtiya), there is a renunciation of the training.
“By those modes, by those characteristics, by those signs” means by those synonyms of the Buddha and so forth, stated in the manner beginning with “or synonyms of the Buddha.
For these synonyms are called “modes” because they serve as the causes for the renunciation of the training.
The "marks" (*liṅga*) are so called because they illustrate the appearance of the Buddha and others, or because they constitute the very appearance of the renunciation of the training;
they are called "signs" (*nimitta*) because they are the causes for recognizing the renunciation of the training, just as moles and such are for humans.
"In this way indeed, O monks"—he said this from here on to restrict [the matter], since there is no other cause for the renunciation of the training. This is the meaning here:
In the same way, there is both the disclosure of weakness and the renunciation of the training; beyond this, there is no further cause.

(54) Having thus shown the characteristic of the renunciation of the training, [the Buddha spoke] for the sake of non-confusion regarding non-renunciation, and for the sake of showing the failure of that very characteristic of the renunciation of the training by way of the person and so forth: "And how, monks..."
He said, “Not renounced,” and so forth. Therein, “by whatever modes” and so on is according to the method already stated.
“A madman” means one who is mad with spirits (*yakkha*), or mad with bile (*pitta*), or anyone whose perception is perverted; if such a person renounces [the training], the training is not renounced.
“Of a madman” refers to one who is exactly like that—mad; for if a regular monk (*pakatatta*) [renounces] in the presence of such a person...
If one renounces the training, or if one is insane and does not know [what is being said], the training has not been renounced.

"One with a deranged mind" refers to one who is possessed by a *yakkha*. However, in the first phrase, it was stated generally as "insane" that "one who is possessed by a *yakkha* or one who is insane from bile.
The distinction between these two will be made clear in the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*). Thus, one with a deranged mind...
One renounces the training, yet it remains as if not renounced. Even if one has renounced it in his presence, if he is unaware of it, it remains as if not renounced.

"Overwhelmed by pain" means being struck by powerful painful sensations and overcome by fainting; even if one renounces it while thus lamenting, it remains as if not renounced. Even if one has renounced it in his presence, if he is unaware of it, it remains as if not renounced.
"In the presence of a deity" means that even if one has made a confession in the presence of any deity, starting from a terrestrial deity up to a deity of the Akaniṭṭha heaven,

it is as if it were not confessed. "In the presence of an animal" means that even if one has made a confession in the presence of anyone at all— whether a young *nāga*, a young *supaṇṇa*, a *kinnara*, an elephant, a monkey, or any other— it is as if it were not confessed.

It exists. In that regard, it is said that [the offense] is not confessed because those such as the insane do not understand in its presence. It is because of the excessively rapid understanding in the presence of a deity.
Deities—being of great wisdom, possessing a rebirth-linking with three roots—understand very quickly, and this mind is indeed swift in its revolutions.
Therefore, for a person whose mind is light, by the power of the mind alone, [one should say]: "Do not..."
"His destruction came too soon," [he said], and thus he rejected the renunciation of the training in the presence of the deity.

However, among humans there is no such restriction; for anyone—whether of the same class or a different class, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, provided they are a person of understanding—the renunciation is indeed valid once it has been made. But if that...
He does not know; it is because he has not personally witnessed [it]—showing this meaning, he said, "By one who is noble," and so forth.
In that context, "Ariyaka" means the noble mode of expression, the Māgadhī language. "Milakkhaka" refers to anyone who is non-Ariyan, such as the Andhras, the Damilas, and others.
And "he does not understand" is either due to unfamiliarity with another language or due to a lack of proficiency in the Buddha’s teaching.
“He does not understand: ‘This person is saying this particular meaning. *Davāya* means:
wishing to say something else impulsively, one impulsively says, “I renounce the Buddha. *Ravāya* means: by means of a confused utterance, saying one thing while intending to say another.
If it is asked, “What is the distinction from the former?”—the former refers to the speaking of something else impulsively even by a wise person.
But this "speaking otherwise" refers to one who, due to dullness, delusion, or lack of understanding, falters and intends to say one thing but says another.

Regarding the phrase "one who does not wish to announce yet announces": this refers to reciting the text of this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), questioning about it, learning it, rehearsing it, or praising it;
this is called "one who does not wish to announce yet announces. Regarding "one who wishes to announce but does not announce": this refers to [failing to announce] due to weakness.
One who renounces the training without making it known does not utter the verbal expression; this is called "one who wishes to make it known but does not make it known.

"He makes it known to one who lacks understanding" means he makes it known to an elderly person resembling a painted figure, or to one who is dull-witted and unskilled in the proper occasion, or to village children who have reached a state of lack of understanding.
"He does not make it known to one who understands" means [he does not make it known] to a wise person.

One does not announce it to someone capable of understanding. Or, "in every way" means that by whatever manner the training is renounced—as in "I renounce the Buddha," and so forth—one does not utter even a single such verbal expression.
"In this way" defines the characteristic of non-renunciation. For this is the meaning here: "In this very manner, the training has not been renounced."
“It exists, and not for any other reason.
The analysis of the renunciation of the training is finished.
Commentary on the Original Formulation.
55. Now, in order to show the meaning of the phrases beginning with “should engage in sexual intercourse,” he said, “What is called sexual intercourse,” and so forth.
Therein, “what is called sexual intercourse” is the statement of the subject for that which is to be defined.
“An unrighteous practice” (asaddhamma) means the practice of the wicked, of lowly people. “A village practice” (gāmadhamma) means the practice of those who dwell in villages.
“Vasaladhammo” means the dhamma of outcasts (vasala); or, because it rains down defilements, it is itself the dhamma of an outcast, thus “vasaladhammo.
“Duṭṭhullaṃ”: it is “duṭṭhu” because it is corrupted by defilements, and it is “thūla” because of its lack of subtlety;
thus it is “duṭṭhullaṃ. From this point onward, regarding the three locations, one should transpose the phrase “yo so” and apply it as “yaṃ taṃ.”
—“That which is lewd, that which is ‘at the water’s edge,’ and that which is ‘in secret.
And herein, because even the seeing, the grasping, the touching, the stroking, or the rubbing—which are the preliminary acts (parivāra) of that deed—are lewd, therefore that deed is also lewd.
That which is lewd is the act of sexual intercourse (*methuna-dhamma*). Water is at its end (*ante*).
It is taken for the sake of purification, thus it is "to the water's edge" (*udakanta*); that which is "to the water's edge" is *odakantika*.
That which is *odakantika* is the act of sexual intercourse. Because it is to be performed in a secluded, hidden place, it is "secret" (*rahassa*).
That which is secret is the act of sexual intercourse—this is how the construction should be understood.

Because it is to be entered into by means of two pairs, it is called "the attainment of the two pairs. Herein, the application is as follows: "That which is the attainment of the two pairs is what is called the practice of sexual intercourse.
But here, concluding all of that together, he says: "This is what is called the practice of sexual intercourse.
For what reason is it called the practice of sexual intercourse? Because it belongs to both who are lustful, infatuated, and impassioned.
“The practice of sexual intercourse” (*methunadhamma*) is said because it is the common characteristic (*sadisa-dhamma*) of both who are possessed by lust.
The phrase “he engages in” (*paṭisevati*) is a summary heading (*mātikāpada*) intended to show the manner in which one should engage, as expressed in the rule “he should engage.
In the passage beginning with “whoever, by means of a sign,” the word “whoever” refers to the monk. By means of a woman’s sign... [and so forth].
If one inserts even as much as a single sesame seed into one’s own organ by means of a woman’s organ—even if not touched by wind and in a non-public place—one is said to “indulge.
By this much, one incurs a breach of virtue and becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
In this context, five locations are possible in the female organ: the four sides and the middle. In the male organ...
There are four sides, the middle, and the upper part—thus six [parts]. Therefore, even if one inserts [the organ] below the female sex organ, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
Even if one inserts it from above, or from both sides, or inserts it through the middle while avoiding the four parts, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
However, even if one inserts it so that it touches the male sex organ only by its lower portion...

He becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. Even if he inserts it while touching it with the upper part, or inserting it while touching it on both sides, or inserting it while touching it only in the middle;

or even if, having contracted it like a finger with its joints bent at the middle phalanges, he inserts it while touching it with the upper part—he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. In that regard, this applies even to one who inserts it like the beam of a scale.

There are four sides and the middle, making five places; likewise for one who inserts [the organ] by contracting [the anus], there are the four sides and the upper-middle part, making five places—thus, in the case of a male organ, there are ten places in total.
If one inserts a growth that has arisen on the organ, such as a piece of skin or a wart, which is not one of the eight types of bodily tissue, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika).
If one inserts a dead skin, a dried-up tumor, or the like into that which has lost its bodily sensitivity, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even for one who inserts body hair, a finger, a thumb, seeds, and so forth, out of a desire for sexual intercourse, there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing.
And because this so-called "talk of sexual intercourse" is indecent talk and improper talk, therefore, whether it be this or another such matter in the Vinaya—
When speaking, one should speak having established mindfulness of repulsiveness, the perception of being a recluse, and moral shame and dread;
having generated reverence for the Perfectly Enlightened One and having reflected upon the quality of compassion of the Peerless Compassionate Lord of the World—
for indeed, that Blessed One, though his mind was entirely turned away from sensual pleasures, [acted] out of concern for beings and out of pity for the world.
He spoke such words for the purpose of establishing the training rules out of compassion for sentient beings.
One should speak while reflecting upon the quality of the Protector of the World’s compassion, thinking, “Oh, how great is the quality of the Teacher’s compassion!
Furthermore, if the Blessed One had not spoken such words in every respect, who would have known [of these] among so many?
"In these cases it is a *pārājika* offense; in so many cases it is a *thullaccaya*; in so many cases it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Therefore, neither the listener nor the speaker should sit with their mouth covered or laughing with their teeth bared.
Rather, reflecting that "even the Perfectly Enlightened One spoke in such a manner," one should remain grave, endowed with shame and moral dread.
"It should be spoken by acting as a substitute for the Teacher.
The section on the original formulation (*mūlapaññatti*) is finished.

In the section on subsequent formulations (*anupaññatti*): "At the very least" (*antamaso*) means by the most minimal limit. "Even to one who is an animal" (*tiracchānagatāya pi*) refers to by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Even among animals": all the more so for a human woman. Here, "human woman" refers specifically to one of human birth.

Furthermore, regarding the female animals that constitute the basis for an offense of defeat (pārājika), only those belonging to the animal realm are to be understood as "animals," not every [female].
In this regard, the following is the delimitation:
For those without feet, it is a snake; for fish, [a snake]; for two-footed beings, a hen;
for four-footed beings, a cat—this is the basis for a *pārājika* offense.
Therein, by the mention of "snake," all species of long-bodied creatures, such as pythons, vipers, and so forth, are included. Therefore, among long-bodied creatures...
Where it is possible to insert even as much as a sesame seed into one of the three [openings], that constitutes an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
The remainder should be understood as matters of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). By the term "catching fish," all aquatic species—including fish, turtles, frogs, and so forth—are included.
In that regard as well, according to the method already stated for long-bodied creatures, there are both matters of defeat and matters of wrong-doing.

And this should be understood. However, there is this distinction: there are those called "cricket-faced frogs" whose mouth-shape is large and the opening is small, so that entry [of a finger] is not possible;

yet the mouth-shape is reckoned as a wound, and therefore that should be understood as the basis for a *thullaccaya* offense. By the mention of "cocks," all varieties such as crows, pigeons, and so forth are included.
The class of birds is included. In that case as well, the basis for a *pārājika* offense and the basis for a *dukkaṭa* offense are to be understood according to the method already stated.
By the inclusion of "beasts with hooves," all four-footed species—such as dogs, mongooses, monitor lizards, and so forth—are included.
In that case as well, the basis for a *pārājika* offense and the basis for a *dukkaṭa* offense are to be understood according to the method already stated.
“Pārājika” means defeated; one who has fallen into defeat. For this term *pārājika* applies to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), the offense (*āpatti*), and the person (*puggala*).

Among these, regarding the training rule, it is said: “It is impossible, Ānanda, it is out of the question that a Tathāgata would abolish a training rule on a matter of defeat (*pārājika*) that has been laid down for his disciples, on account of the Vajjians or the Vajjiputtakas. Thus, [it refers to] the training rule.
It should be understood as occurring with respect to the offense: "Bhikkhu, you have fallen into an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
It should be understood as occurring with respect to the person: "We are not defeated; he who was carried off is the one who is defeated.
However, in such passages as "one should accuse another of an offense entailing defeat," they say it occurs with respect to the *dhamma* (the rule). For in that context, "dhamma" refers to...
In some instances it is an offense (*āpatti*), while in others it is the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) itself that is intended; therefore, it should not be spoken of separately from the latter.
In this context, the training rule "defeats" (*parājeti*) whoever transgresses it, and for that reason it is called a "defeat" (*pārājika*).
An offense, however, "defeats" whoever commits it, and for that reason it is called "defeating" (*pārājika*). [The term refers to] the person.
Because he has been defeated and has fallen into defeat, he is therefore called "one who has committed a pārājika offense. It is with reference to this very meaning that it is said in the Parivāra:
"Listen to the truth regarding what is called 'pārājika':
He has fallen away, he has failed, he has been cast out, for he has been excluded from the True Dhamma."
“Even co-residence there no longer exists; therefore this is said.
This is the meaning here: “One who transgresses that training rule and incurs an offense is fallen—this entire [passage] should be applied accordingly.
‘Therefore it is said’ means: for the reason that he is no longer a *samaṇa*, no longer a son of the Sakyans, and has fallen away.”
"He is cut off and defeated from the Teaching; therefore it is so called. How so? "He becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
"Co-residence" (*saṃvāsa*) means dwelling together therein; in order to demonstrate that, he said, "Co-residence is," and then stated "the same formal act" (*ekakamma*), and so forth.
Herein, this is the commentary with the word-connections: even the fourfold formal act of the Saṅgha [is performed] by those delimited by the boundary (*sīmā*).

It is called a "single legal act" (*ekakamma*) because it is to be performed together with regular monks. Likewise, even the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha is called a "single recitation" (*ekuddesa*) because it is to be recited together.

Furthermore, a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) that has been laid down is called "equal training" (*samasikkhatā*) because it must be trained in equally by all modest individuals. In this context, since all modest ones [are included] in these acts and so forth...
They dwell together, and not even one of them is seen outside [the community];

therefore, taking all of them together, he said, "This is what is called 'living in communion' (saṃvāsa). And since that aforementioned kind of communion does not exist with that person, for that reason, that person who has committed a defeat (pārājika) is called "one who does not live in communion" (asaṃvāsa).

56. Having thus analyzed the training rule (sikkhāpada) according to the sequence of its words, now, for the purpose of showing the manner in which one “should consume” as it is said in the phrase “paṭiseveyya,” the text sets down this summary heading (mātikāpada):
“paṭisevati nāma. Then it states: “with a sign, a sign; with the sexual organ, the sexual organ. Therein:
Since the characteristic mark (*nimitta*) is not the basis for a *pārājika* offense only in the case of a woman,
nor only in the case of a human woman— the mark of even women made of gold, silver, and so forth does not constitute the basis— it is therefore said,

by way of the method beginning with "three kinds of women," that after stating those beings whose marks constitute the basis, [the text specifies] "of a human woman... [to show] whatever constitutes the basis.
He stated those bases by way of the method beginning with "three paths," and so forth.

In that context, there are twelve beings who serve as the supports for the signs of the *pārājika* offenses: three women, three hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), three eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*), and three men.
Among them, women and men are indeed well known. As for the distinction between eunuchs and hermaphrodites:
This will become clear in the commentary on the Pabbajjā-khandhaka.
Regarding the phrase "for one who practices the sexual act with a human woman in the three ways":
here, the meaning should be understood as "in the three ways with a human woman. This applies everywhere. All of these [offenses] involve a human woman in the three ways.
There are nine paths for a female non-human being and three for a female animal, making nine; nine for a human hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) and so forth;
six, by taking two each for a human paṇḍaka and so forth; and likewise six for a human male and so forth—thus there are thirty paths.
In any one of these, which are reckoned as "signs" (*nimitta*), even if one’s own sexual organ is the size of a sesame seed...
Having entered [the dwelling], one commits a *pārājika* offense by engaging in sexual intercourse.
Regarding the commentary on the first tetrad (57):
since one commits the offense only with the intention of engaging in the act, and not without it, that is the defining characteristic.
The Blessed One, intending to explain this, said: “When a mind of sexual intercourse has arisen in a bhikkhu,” and so forth.
Therein, “of a bhikkhu” refers to a bhikkhu who is engaging in sexual intercourse. “When a mind of intercourse has arisen” is a nominative case used in the sense of a locative;
the meaning is “when a mind of intercourse is present. “Of one inserting the male organ into the anus” refers to that passage by which—
When one inserts even as much as a sesame seed into the male organ—the male characteristic—into that path from which feces emerge, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).
The meaning is: "there is an offense of defeat" for him; or alternatively, *āpatti* means "the act of falling into [an offense]," and *pārājikassa* refers to the offense of defeat.
This same method applies everywhere.

58. Having thus shown the offense for one who enters with the intention of consuming, [the text] now explains that this so-called "entering" occurs not only through one's own effort but also through the effort of another.
Furthermore, in that case as well, the offense belongs only to one who consents—that is, to one endowed with the intention of consumption—and not to the other.
Therefore, regarding those sons of noble family who have gone forth out of faith...
Those who have entered the right practice do not consent even when entry occurs through the agency of another;
for the sake of protecting them, [the Buddha] said, "enemies of the bhikkhus, a human woman," and so forth.

In this context, "enemies" (paccatthikā) refers to those who seek or desire what is contrary (paṭipakkha); "enemies of the bhikkhus" (bhikkhu-paccatthikā) means those who are enemies specifically toward the bhikkhus.
This is a designation for hostile monks who are dissimilar [to him]. "Having brought a human woman into the presence of the monk" means that those [monks],
overcome by envy and desiring to ruin that monk, either by enticing him with material gifts or through the intimacy of friendship,
say, "Do this service for us," and then bring some human woman to the monk's dwelling place during the night.

"Having brought [it]": they cause the male organ to enter through the female organ. This means that, having firmly grasped the monk by his hands, feet, head, or other parts so that he is motionless, they cause the monk's male organ to enter through the woman's anus;
that is, they insert it.

Regarding the phrase "so ceti" and so forth: if that bhikkhu consents to and tolerates the insertion of his own sexual organ into the interior of the anus, at that moment he arouses a mind of lustful intent;
if he consents to and tolerates it once it has been inserted, he arouses a mind of lustful intent at the time it has entered;
if he consents to and tolerates it while it remains there, [he arouses such a mind] at the time it has reached its position.
At the moment of emission, he arouses the intention of enjoyment; he consents to and accepts the extraction, and at the time of withdrawal, he arouses the intention of relishing.
Thus, by consenting in these four instances, he cannot say, "This was done to me by hostile monks," but incurs an offense of defeat (pārājika) itself. And just as one who consents to these four—

...one incurs [the offense]. Thus, even if one does not consent to the first [act] but consents to three, or does not consent to two but consents to two, or does not consent to three but consents to one, one still incurs [the offense].

However, one who does not consent at all—regarding the sexual organ as having entered a viper’s mouth or a pit of glowing embers—does not incur [the offense]. Therefore it was said: "The insertion..."
“He does not consent… he does not consent to being pulled out; there is no offense.

For it was protecting such a person—one who has begun insight meditation, who is indifferent toward both body and life, who sees all the sense bases as ablaze with the eleven fires, and who views the five strands of sensual pleasure as murderers with drawn swords—that the Blessed One guarded him against his adversaries.
Frustrating his desire, [the deity] brought forth and established this tetrad beginning with, "He does not consent to this entry," and so on.
The discussion of the first tetrad is concluded.
Now begins the discussion of the two hundred and sixty-nine tetrads.

59–60. Having thus shown the first tetrad, [the author now explains that] because enemies of monks do not only cause a woman to sit upon them through the anus, but also through the urinary passage and even through the mouth;
and furthermore, having brought a woman, some bring one who is awake, some one who is asleep, some one who is intoxicated, and some one who is insane—
"Negligent" means one who is distracted or whose mind is scattered. Some say "dead" means that which has been devoured;
the meaning is that it is a sign of having been devoured by dogs, jackals, and so forth. Some say "dead" means mostly devoured;
"mostly devoured" refers to a corpse where, among the signs, the majority of the area—whether the anus, the urinary tract, or the mouth—is devoured.
Some [women] are mostly devoured; "mostly devoured" means that in her bodily marks, such as the anus and so forth, much has been devoured and little remains undevoured.
And they do not bring only human women, but also non-human women and even animals. Nor do they bring only women of the aforementioned type.
They bring both hermaphrodites, eunuchs, and men [as well]. Therefore, showing other tetrads by way of those [categories], he said:
"The enemies of the bhikkhus lie in wait for a human woman," and so forth.
Therein, for the sake of clarity regarding the text, the tetrads mentioned should be understood according to this enumeration: of a human woman...
By way of the three paths, there are twenty-seven [sets]: three pure tetrad-groups (*suddhika-catuṣka*), three "watching" tetrad-groups (*jāgaranta-catuṣka*),

three "asleep" tetrad-groups (*sutta-catuṣka*), three "intoxicated" tetrad-groups (*matta-catuṣka*), three "insane" tetrad-groups (*ummatta-catuṣka*), three "negligent" tetrad-groups (*pamatta-catuṣka*),

three "described as dead" tetrad-groups (*mata-akkhāyita-catuṣka*), three "mostly described" tetrad-groups (*yebhuyyena akkhāyita-catuṣka*), and three "mostly described as dead" tetrad-groups (*yebhuyyena khāyita-catuṣka*).
There are sets of four. Likewise for a female non-human being; likewise for a female animal—thus there are eighty-one sets of four in the section on women.

And just as in the section on women, so it is in the section on hermaphrodites. In the sections on eunuchs and men, however, there are fifty-four sets of four each, based on the two paths. Thus, all together, there are two hundred and seventy-four sets of four.
These [passages] have their meaning already explained.
However, in all instances here, regarding the phrase "the dead body is for the most part ungnawed and gnawed," this is the analysis:
it is said that in the island of Tambapaṇṇi there were two elder masters of the Vinaya who were fellow disciples—the Elder Upatissa and... [the Elder Sumana].
...and the Elder Phussadeva. When a great danger arose, they preserved the Vinaya Piṭaka by memorizing it.
Among them, the Elder Upatissa was more proficient. He also had two pupils: the Elder Mahāpaduma and the Elder Mahāsiva.
Of these, the Elder Mahāsiva heard the Vinaya Piṭaka during the festival of the constellations, while the Elder Mahāpaduma—
He heard it nine times together with him, and another nine times alone by himself—thus he heard it eighteen times in total;
he was the most proficient among them. After hearing the Vinaya Piṭaka nine times, the Elder Mahāsumma left his teacher and went to Aparagaṅgā.
Then the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "Alas, this master of the Vinaya is truly a hero!"
"He who, while his teacher is still living, thinks he may dwell elsewhere— does he not realize that as long as the teacher is alive,
even after having mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka and the Aṭṭhakathā many times, they must not be abandoned;
they must be heard at all times and recited every year?"

Thus, on one occasion, while the Elder Upatissa was seated expounding this section of the first *pārājika* training rule to five hundred resident pupils headed by the Elder Mahāpaduma—monks who held the Vinaya in high esteem—the pupils asked him:
"Venerable sir, for the most part, a *pārājika* offense is declared when it has been manifested; for the most part..."
“If it has been chewed, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; when it is half-chewed, what should it be? The Elder said:

“Friend, when the Buddhas prescribe an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), they do not prescribe it leaving a remainder; rather, prescribing it without remainder, exhausting it entirely, and cutting off the stream [of the offense], they prescribe precisely an offense involving defeat for the basis of an offense involving defeat. For this—”
“The training rule is a *lokavajja* (an offense by its very nature), not a *paṇṇattivajja* (an offense by formal precept).

Therefore, if it were a *pārājika* when half [of the body] was exposed, the Perfectly Enlightened One would have prescribed it as such. However, here no shadow of a *pārājika* is seen; only a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) is seen.
Furthermore, when prescribing a *pārājika* for a dead body, the Blessed One generally established it in relation to what is not yet exposed: “From that...”
This is to show that there is no offense beyond a *pārājika*. When prescribing a *thullaccaya*, he established it at the point where the body is mostly devoured;
this should also be understood as showing that there is no offense beyond that, namely a *thullaccaya*.

Furthermore, this distinction between what is devoured and what is not devoured is to be understood only in the case of a dead body, not while it is still living. For in a living being, even if the skin and flesh are [consumed] down to the size of a fingernail or the back of a nail...

Or, if there is even a sinew, it is indeed a *pārājika*. Even if the mark has been completely gnawed away such that the skin and hide are gone, yet the shape of the mark is still discernible and penetration occurs, it is indeed a *pārājika*.
However, when the mark has not been left intact, but the entire mark has been cut off and scraped away on all sides until it is torn up, then by way of the mere presence of a wound—
A grave offense (thullaccaya). For one who makes an effort toward a piece of flesh that has fallen from its source, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

However, in the case of a dead body, even if the entire body has been devoured, or even if it has not been devoured at all—provided three passages remain undevoured—if one makes an effort toward those [passages], it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If the majority has been devoured, it is likewise an offense entailing defeat. If half has been devoured...
And when it is mostly eaten away, there is a thullaccaya offense.

In the case of a living human body, if one—with lust for sexual intercourse—inserts even as much as a sesame seed into the eye, nose, ear, orifice, or the sheath of the organ where a wound has been made by a knife or similar instrument, there is likewise a thullaccaya offense. In the case of the remaining parts of the body...
In the case of the armpits and so forth, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). When the entire body is dead, in a place where a Pārājika offense would apply, it is a Pārājika;
in a place where a Thullaccaya offense would apply, it is a Thullaccaya; and in a place where a Dukkaṭa offense would apply, it is a Dukkaṭa.
However, when the body has become bloated, putrefied, covered with blue flies, infested with swarms of worms, and oozing from nine orifices due to the nature of the festering corpse—
When it is impossible even to approach [the organ], one then relinquishes both the basis for a *pārājika* offense and the basis for a *thullaccaya* offense;

in such a body, any attempt made against any part results in only *dukkaṭa*. For animals—such as elephants, horses, oxen, donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and so forth—there is a *thullaccaya* for the nose.
There is likewise a *thullaccaya* for the vaginal opening (*vatthikosa*). For all animals, there is a *thullaccaya* for the eyes, ears, and wounds.
It is a *dukkaṭa*; even for the rest of the body, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. Regarding the fresh corpses of those who have died, in a zone where a *pārājika* offense occurs, it is a *pārājika*;
in a zone where a *thullaccaya* occurs, it is a *thullaccaya*; and in a zone where a *dukkaṭa* occurs, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
However, regarding putrefied corpses, in every case it is a *dukkaṭa*, according to the method previously stated. Or, [if it is done] out of lust for physical contact...
If, out of lust for sexual intercourse, one inserts [the organ] into the vaginal sheath of a living man without causing penetration, but touches organ to organ, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If, out of lust for sexual intercourse, one touches organ to organ with a woman without causing penetration, it is a *thullaccaya*.
However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "If one touches a female organ with the mouth out of lust for sexual intercourse, it is a *thullaccaya*."

It was stated in the *Cammakkhandhaka*: “The group-of-six monks, while cows were crossing the river Aciravatī, seized them by their horns, seized them by their ears, seized them by their necks, seized them by their tails, climbed onto their backs, and—with lustful minds—even touched their private parts.
This is the origin (aṭṭhuppatti) [of the rule], stated without distinction.
It is said: “Monks, one should not touch the private parts with a lustful mind; whoever should so touch them, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
All of this must be understood in such a way that it does not contradict one another. And how is it that there is no contradiction?
First, as for what was stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*: “With the passion for sexual intercourse, by means of the mouth...”
"‘Touched’—here, it is said, ‘the face of the sign’ (*nimittamukha*) is intended by the word ‘face.
Furthermore, because it is stated [in the rule] ‘by lust for sexual intercourse,’ this alone should be understood as the intended meaning there.

For there is no approach to sexual intercourse by means of the natural mouth in the case of a female sign. Also, in the *Khandhaka*, regarding those who, mounting on the back, touched organ with organ through lust for sexual intercourse..."
It should be understood that, with reference to those [cases], a *thullaccaya* offense was stated; otherwise, it would have been a *dukkaṭa*. However, some say:
"Even in the *Khandhaka*, with reference to touching with the mouth alone, a *thullaccaya* was stated because of the gravity of the act.
And in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, it is spoken with reference to that very same case: 'If one touches with the mouth out of lust for sexual intercourse, it is a *thullaccaya*.'"
...so it was said. Therefore, having carefully examined both legal determinations (*vinicchaya*), that which is more appropriate should be adopted.
However, those who are experts in the Vinaya praise the former.

But for one who, out of lust for bodily contact, touches the female sign (*itthinimitta*)—either by way of the natural opening or by way of the [genital] sign—it is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*). [This applies even] to a female animal, by way of the sign, [if one touches] the urinary passage.
For one who touches [in this manner], there is a thullaccaya offense according to the method already stated. For [touching] out of lust for bodily contact, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
The discussion on the two hundred and sixty-nine sets of four is concluded. Now begins the discussion on the classification of the fourfold group concerning the prepared bedding (santhatacatukka).
61–62. Thus the Blessed One, having extracted two hundred and seventy-four tetrads for the protection of the bhikkhu who practices accordingly, said:
"Now, those wicked bhikkhus in the future who will intentionally cast a slur, saying, 'This spread [santhata] is not anything clung-to;
it does not come into contact with what is clung-to; what fault is there here?'—for them, there shall be no establishment at all in the Teaching."

Having seen this, thinking, "It will be so," he explained each one of those seventy-two hundred tetrads by dividing them according to the fourfold distinctions such as "with a spread" (*santhatā*) and so forth,
saying: "The enemies of the bhikkhus bring a woman to the presence of a bhikkhu and sit upon his organ with their anus,
their vagina, or their mouth— [this refers to] 'with a spread' for one who is without a spread," and so on.

In this context, regarding the phrases "by one who is covered" (*santhatāya*) and "by one who is not covered" (*asanthatassa*), and so forth, the application of the rule should be understood according to this method: "While a woman is covered, she causes the male organ of a monk who is not covered to enter her by way of the anus, the urinary tract, or the mouth.
In that regard, "covered" (*santhatā*) refers to a woman whose [organ] has been wrapped around or inserted into any one of the three passages.
It is covered by some kind of cloth, leaf, cotton-patch, skin, or a strip of tin, lead, and so forth.
"Covered" (santhata) means that his private organ is concealed by any one of those aforementioned cloths or items.
In this regard, either the appropriated [organ] may touch the unappropriated [cloth], or the unappropriated may touch the appropriated, or the unappropriated may [touch] the unappropriated...

Whether it be what is not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*) or what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*), or whether what is clung-to is [entered] by means of what is clung-to—if it is said that a *pārājika* offense occurs when a certain amount has been entered, and one enters that much, then for one who consents in every case: in the sphere of a *pārājika*, there is a *pārājika*;

in the sphere of a grave offense (*thullaccaya*), there is a grave offense; and in the sphere of an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing. If a woman’s sign has been made into a post and spread over with grass, [the same applies].
If one rubs against a stump, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If a spread has been made using a stump as the male organ, there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who inserts the stump.
If both have been made into stumps and a spread has been made, there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who rubs stump against stump.
If something such as bamboo, reed, or wood has been inserted into the female organ, [there is an offense] for its lower part...

Even if, while touching [the opening], he inserts it only the size of a sesame seed, it is a *pārājika*. Even if he inserts it while touching the upper part, both sides, or even one side, it is a *pārājika*.
If, after inserting it without touching any of the four sides, he touches its base, it is a *pārājika*.
However, if he does not touch the sides or the base, but it remains entirely in the air—

Having made [the seat] and having inserted it, if he removes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If it touches a stump outside [the boundary], there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
And just as it was stated regarding the female sex organ, so too should the characteristic be understood in all cases.
The discussion on the fourfold classification of the spread (santhatā) is finished.
Commentary on the Fourfold Set of Offenses Concerning an Enemy of a Bhikkhu (Bhikkhupaccatthikacatukka), §§63–64.

Having thus explained the fourfold set concerning the spread of grass (*santhata*), [the author] now shows its subdivisions, because it is not only women and others who bring [the offense] to a bhikkhu’s presence;
rather, they also bring a bhikkhu into their presence. Therefore, he demonstrates those subdivisions:
“An enemy of monks [approaches] a monk in the presence of a human woman,” and so on—in this manner, he again brought forth and showed all those tetrads.
The analysis of these should be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the classification of the tetrads by way of enemies of monks is finished.
The Discourse on the Fourfold Classification beginning with Royal Enemies (Rājapaccatthikādicatukkabhedakathā). 65.

However, since it is not only those who oppose monks (*bhikkhu-paccatthika*) who act in this way, but also those who oppose kings (*rāja-paccatthika*) and others as well, he spoke the passage beginning with "royal enemies" (*rājapaccatthikā*) in order to show that classification as well. In that context, "royal enemies" refers to kings themselves who are adversaries.
"Royal enemies": it should be understood that these bring [trouble] themselves or cause others to bring it.

"Thieves who are enemies" means thieves themselves who are enemies. "Scoundrels" refers to city-dwellers addicted to the sport of sexual intercourse, or scoundrels such as those addicted to women or liquor;
"scoundrels who are enemies" means scoundrels themselves who are enemies. "Fragrance" means...

"Heart" (*hadaya*) is what is meant; they "pluck it out," thus they are "lotus-scented" (*uppalagandhā*). Enemies who are themselves lotus-scented are "lotus-scented enemies" (*uppalagandhapaccatthikā*).
It is said that these people do not live by agriculture, trade, or similar means; rather, by committing highway robberies, village raids, and the like, they support their wives and children.
Desiring success in their undertakings, they entreat the deities and [take] the hearts of humans for the purpose of making offerings (*balikamma*) to them.
They tear them out. Furthermore, humans are difficult to find at all times, whereas monks dwelling in the forest are easy to find.

Thinking, "The killing of one who possesses virtue is a grave matter," they bring women and other such persons there to destroy that monk's virtue, or they lead him away to those places. This is the distinction here.

The remainder should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. And just as in the section concerning the adversaries of the bhikkhu, the tetrads in these four sections are to be understood in that same manner;
however, they have been stated in brief in the Pāḷi.
The exposition on the analysis of the tetrads in all its aspects is concluded.
Commentary on the Section on Offenses and Non-offenses (Āpattānāpattivāra-vaṇṇanā) 66.

Now, regarding what was stated previously—"for one who engages in sexual intercourse with a human woman in three ways," and so forth—it is said here, "way by way," etc., for the sake of avoiding confusion.
In that context, "way by way" refers to [the penis] in relation to the three [orifices] of a woman.

One inserts one's own genitals into one of the [two] passages; or, when the two passages have become mixed, one inserts the urinary passage into the fecal passage, or the fecal passage into the urinary passage. "By way of the passage, not by way of the non-passage" means:

having inserted it by way of the urinary passage or another such passage, one extracts it through a wound in its vicinity. "By way of the non-passage, into the passage" means: from the vicinity of the passage...
Having inserted [the object] through a wound, one removes it through the anus. "Through what is not a path" means:

when there are two mixed wounds, having inserted it through one wound, one removes it through the second. In accordance with this sutta, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is to be understood in all cases involving the category of wounds.

Now, regarding what will be said later—"there is no offense for one who does not know and does not consent"—it is said here, "the monk [thinks] 'the other monk is asleep,'" and so forth, for the purpose of avoiding confusion. The intended meaning therein is this:
he who wakes up and consents is not released by thinking, "He has misbehaved while I was asleep; I did not know. And in this context, both must be expelled.
Both [types of persons] are to be expelled by means of the act of suspension (*liṅganāsanena*). In that regard, there is no formal admission for the one who defiles;
having questioned the one who has been defiled, he is to be expelled upon his admission. If he does not consent, he is not to be expelled.

This same method applies to the section concerning novices (*sāmaṇera*) as well. Having thus shown, in various instances, both what constitutes an offense and what does not, [the author] now shows only those cases where there is no offense:

He said, “There is no offense for one who does not know,” and so forth. In this context, “one who does not know” refers to someone who has fallen into a deep sleep and is unaware even of an assault committed by another, such as the bhikkhu who had gone to the Great Forest at Vesālī for his midday rest. For such a person, there is no offense.
And this has been stated: “‘I do not know, Blessed One. ‘There is no offense, bhikkhu, for one who does not know.’”
"One who does not consent" means one who, even though he knows [the offense], does not consent, like the bhikkhu who rose up suddenly at that very moment. And this has been said:
"‘I did not consent, Blessed One. ‘There is no offense, bhikkhu, for one who does not consent.
One who is "insane" means one insane from bile (pitta). For bile is of two kinds: bound bile and unbound bile.
Therein, the unbound bile (*abaddhapitta*) pervades all the limbs like blood;

when it is disturbed, beings suffer from itching, scabs, bodily tremors, and so forth, which are pacified by the application of medicine. The bound bile (*baddhapitta*), however, resides in the gall-bladder (*pittakosaka*).
When that is disturbed, beings become insane, their perceptions are perverted, and having abandoned shame and moral dread (*hirottappa*), they engage in improper conduct.
They wander about; even while trampling upon the light and heavy training rules, they do not realize it. Even when engaged in medical treatment, they remain incurable.
For one who is thus insane, there is no offense.
One whose mind is deranged (*khittacitta*) is said to have a distracted mind (*vissaṭṭhacitta*), meaning one who is crazed by a *yakkha*. It is said that *yakkhas* [inflict] terrifying things...

Having shown objects and thrusting their hands into the mouth, they crush the heart-organ (hadayarūpa) and render beings deranged in mind and perverted in perception. There is no offense for one whose mind is thus distracted. However, there is this distinction between these two types: one intoxicated by bile is perpetually insane and does not regain his natural state of consciousness; whereas one intoxicated by a spirit (yakkha)— [The text continues: ...is intoxicated only at certain times and regains his natural state of consciousness at other times. Regarding the one intoxicated by bile: if he commits an act while insane, there is no offense; but if he commits an act when his insanity has subsided, there is an offense.
