However, this bhikkhu, having desisted from sexual intercourse, consented to bodily contact; thus it should be understood. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"There is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*."
74. In the case of Bhaddiya, that city is named Bhaddiya. The "Jāti Grove" (Jātiyavana) received its name because of the abundance of clusters of jasmine flowers;
it was a grove situated on the outskirts of that city. Having lain down there, he fell into a deep sleep due to that support of wind.
Only the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), which has a single flavor, proceeded. It was moistened...
"Having seen" means having seen it soiled with impurity. 75.
The four items following this that relate to consenting, together with the item regarding ignorance—these five have meanings that are self-evident. 76.
Regarding the two items concerning not consenting: "He emerged suddenly" means like one bitten by a venomous snake or scorched by fire.

And he rose up quickly as if startled. "Having stepped on it, he set it rolling" means that the diligent bhikkhu, having begun insight meditation and established mindfulness, while rising quickly, stepped upon it and, rolling and turning it about on the ground, crushed and brought it down.
For in such situations, the mind must be guarded by a virtuous worldling (puthujjanakalyāṇaka). And this was for them...
A certain monk who had been a warrior at the head of a battle.
77. Regarding the account of lying down after opening the door: "retreating in solitude during the day" means lying down during the day.
"Retreating in solitude after securing the door" means lying down after closing the door. And here, although...

In the Pāḷi, it is not stated that "this is an offense. However, because it was said—"I allow you, monks, when lying down to meditate during the day, to meditate having closed the door"—when the matter arises due to the fault of lying down without opening [the door], an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is stated for one who meditates without closing it.
For [the rule] was formulated by one who understood the Blessed One’s intention.
The commentaries were established by the Elder Upāli and others. This is also proven by the statement: "There is an offense committed during the day, but not at night.
Now, what kind of door should be secured, and what kind should not?
Having made a door-panel from anything such as wood, bamboo, reeds, or leaves, it should be constructed by inserting it below into a mortar and above into a crossbar.
Only the revolving door should be secured. Others include: a door with wooden spikes and thorns like the pens for cattle;
a door with wheels at the village gate; a revolving shutter-door made by attaching two or three wheels to wooden planks or small huts;
and a sliding shutter-door made like those found in market stalls—these two [types].
Having inserted bamboo slips in three places, a door made of leaf-huts with a hand-held tally, or a cloth-screened door—such a door must not be opened.
However, when one has a bowl in hand, opening only a single cloth-screened door is non-offensive;
for all others, there is an offense for one who opens them. But for one who is in seclusion during the day, only a revolving door [is permitted].
Regarding that which causes an offense: for one who lies down having restrained the remaining [faculties], there is no offense;
however, one should lie down having restrained them—this is the proper conduct (*vatta*).
As for the "door of turning over," by how much is it restrained? It is indeed restrained when the needle, the bolt, and so forth have been applied.
Furthermore, it is permissible even if [the door] is opened by the measure of a needle; it is permissible even if opened by the measure of a water-clock (ghaṭikā);
it is permissible even when merely touched by the door-post and closed; it is permissible even when slightly untouched.
By the most minimal method, it is permissible as long as the head does not enter, even if it is slightly untouched. If it is a place used by many, [then...]
It is permissible to lie down even after saying to a bhikkhu or a sāmaṇera, "Friend, look after the door.
Furthermore, if bhikkhus are sitting engaged in robe-making or some other task, it is permissible to lie down even after forming the intention, "They will look after the door.
However, in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that one must also ask permission from a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Or, it is permissible to lie down after making the mental resolve, “He will watch over me.
However, it is not permissible to simply ask a bhikkhunī or a woman [to do so].
Furthermore, if the door’s bolt or upper crossbar is broken or not fixed, such that one is unable to secure it, or if there is a heap of bricks for the sake of construction...

If a heap of clay or other materials has been placed at the inner door, or if they are building a wall such that one cannot restrain oneself, then when such an obstacle exists, it is permissible to lie down even without restraining oneself. However, if there is no door-panel, it is indeed allowable.
One lying above must lie down after having ascended by means of a ladder. If [the ladder] is at the top...

It must be bolted; having bolted it, one may lie down. When lying down in a room, it is permissible to lie down after securing either the door of the room, the front door, or whatever other opening there may be.
If a house with a single wall has doors opening on two sides that are used for access, both doors must be secured.
Even in a three-storied palace, the door must certainly be looked after.
If, having returned from almsround, many bhikkhus enter a palace— such as one resembling the Lohapāsāda— to dwell for the day’s rest,
the senior of the Saṅgha should either tell the doorkeeper, “Look after the door,” or, having given the instruction, “Looking after the door is his responsibility,” he may enter and lie down.
It should be done in exactly the same way by the most junior member of the Saṅgha.
When entering [the dwelling], it is even permissible to take heed, thinking, "The maintenance of the door is the responsibility of those who come later.

However, there is an offense for those who lie down inside a room, at an unsecured door, or outside, either without having asked permission or without taking such heed. This applies even at the time they are lying down, whether inside or outside.
“Guarding the door” means that it is indeed permissible to lie down after making the resolve: “It is the duty of the gatekeeper at the main gate.
Even when lying on the open roof-terrace of the Lohapāsāda or similar structures, one must certainly secure the door.
This, in brief, is the method for daytime seclusion: [it applies] in any place that is enclosed and provided with a secured door.

This has been stated in the appropriate place. Therefore, when lying down anywhere—whether in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in a pavilion—one who lies down with the door closed must lie down having first secured the door.

If it is a large courtyard, like the courtyard of the Mahābodhi or the Lohapāsāda, which is a gathering place for many, and where the door does not remain secure even when shut, [one should secure] the door.
If they cannot find the wall, they wander about even after climbing over it; in that case, there is no need for restraint.
If one lies down after opening the door at night and rises when the dawn has broken, there is no offense. If, however, having woken up, one goes back to sleep again, there is an offense.
But if one has already delimited [the time], thinking, "I shall rise when the dawn has broken," yet leaves the door unsecured—
If one lies down at night and does not rise even until the appointed time has passed, there is indeed an offense for him.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "One who lies down in this manner is not exempt from the *dukkaṭa* of disrespect.
But as for one who, having stayed awake for most of the night or having traveled a long distance, sits upon a couch during the day appearing exhausted;
If one lies down due to drowsiness without having lifted one's feet from the ground, there is no offense for him.

If, while overcome by sleep, one places one's feet on a bed even without being aware of it, there is indeed an offense. There is no offense for one who falls asleep while sitting and leaning against something.
And if one who is walking with the thought, "I shall dispel my drowsiness," should fall and immediately wake up, for him too there is no offense.
However, for one who falls and lies right there, not rising up, there is an offense.
Who is released and who is not? First, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "Only one who remains lying down with a single bend [of the body] is released.
But one who lies down having lifted his feet from the ground—even if he is possessed by a spirit or has lost consciousness—is not released."
In the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "He is released only after having been bound and laid down. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, on the other hand, it says:
"If one who is walking is released and falls, and then sleeps right there, no offense is seen for him either, because that [case] is not within the scope [of the rule].
But the teachers do not speak thus. Therefore, it is an offense indeed; so it was said by the Elder Mahāpaduma."
"However, two persons are indeed released from the offense: he who was possessed by a *yakkha*, and he who was laid down after being bound. 78.

Regarding the case of Bhārukacchaka, "there is no offense on account of a dream": because this occurs precisely due to the fact that [the act] is outside the scope of reality within a dream, the Elder Upāli, by means of logical reasoning (*nayaggāhena*), determined this case even though it had not previously been adjudicated by the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, having heard this, said, "Well spoken, monks, by Upāli!
As if placing a foot where there was none, as if showing a footprint in the sky, Upāli has answered this question. Having said this, he established the Elder in the foremost position:
"Monks, among my disciples who are bhikkhus, this is the foremost of those who are masters of the Vinaya: namely, Upāli."
The subsequent cases beginning with Supabbā are of plain meaning. 80. Regarding the instigation by the bhikkhunī and so forth:
those Licchavi youths, preoccupied with play, acted in this way through their own misconduct. From that time on, the very destruction of the Licchavis arose.
82. In the case of the Elder Who Had Gone Forth, he went to see him out of compassion, thinking, "I shall see him," and approached his home.
He arrived. Then she described to him, in various ways, her own state of being without a protector as well as that of her children.
Knowing him to be indifferent, she became angry and, saying, "Come, let us leave the order," she seized him by force.
As he retreated in an attempt to free himself, he fell prostrate due to his weakness from old age. Thereupon, she did as she pleased.
However, that bhikkhu was a non-returner (anāgāmī) whose sensual desire had been utterly severed; therefore, he did not consent.
83. The Migapotaka-vatthu is of plain meaning.
The section on legal cases (vinītavatthu) is concluded.
The commentary on the first *pārājika* in the *Samantapāsādikā*,
the commentary on the Vinaya, is finished. Herein,
this is [the explanation] regarding the state of being "all-round illuminating" (*samantapāsādika*) of the *Samantapāsādikā*:
From the lineage of teachers, from the illumination of the origins, the bases, and the classifications;
from the avoidance of other systems, and from the purification of one's own system.
From the clarification of the phrasing, from the meaning of the words, and from the sequence of the connection to the canonical texts.
Because it provides a definitive determination of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), because it demonstrates the various methods of analysis (*vibhaṅga*),
and because nothing unpleasing is seen therein by those who perceive clearly,
this work is therefore called the *Samantapāsādikā* ("Completely Pleasing").
The commentary on the Vinaya, which was spoken by the Lord of the World out of compassion for the world, has been set forth by one skilled in training those to be tamed.
Thus ends the commentary on the first *pārājika*.
2. The Second Pārājika:
This second [offense], proclaimed by the Conqueror as being without a second, is now reached in its turn for detailed exposition.
Therefore, having set aside everything that was previously explained and is easy to understand,
this commentary is now provided. The Commentary on the Story of Dhaniya.
84. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha on the Vulture Peak Mountain (*Gijjhakūṭa-pabbata*).
Therein, "Rājagaha" refers to the city of that name; for it is called "Rājagaha" because it was occupied by Mandhātā, Mahāgovinda, and others.
Others describe various other etymologies here, but what need is there for them? This is simply the name of that city. Furthermore, this [name] was used during the time of the Buddha...
And during the time of a wheel-turning monarch, there was a city. At other times, it was empty and possessed by *yakkhas*, remaining as their forest dwelling.
Having thus shown the village for his alms-round, he stated the place of residence: "on Vulture Peak Mountain. Vultures dwelt on its peaks, or its peaks were like those of vultures; therefore—
It should be understood that it is called Gijjhakūṭa.
Regarding "a number" (sambahula): according to the Vinaya method, three persons are called "a number," and beyond that, it is a Saṅgha;
according to the Sutta method, only three are [counted as] such, and from four onwards they are "a number. Here, however, they are "a number" according to the Sutta method.
They should be understood as follows: "Sandiṭṭhā" (those seen) refers to those who are not overly intimate nor firm friends;
for they are called "sandiṭṭhā" because they have merely been seen meeting here and there. "Sambhattā" (those associated) refers to those who are very intimate and firm friends;
for they are called "sambhattā" because they are well-cherished associates, sharing both enjoyment and consumption together. "Isigilipasse" means on the slope of Isigili.

...on the side of that mountain. It is said that formerly about five hundred paccekabuddhas, having wandered for alms in the districts of Kāsī, Kosala, and so forth, would gather on that mountain after their meal and spend their time in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
People saw them only as they entered, but not as they departed. Thereupon, they said: "This..."
“This mountain swallows these seers,” he said. From that time on, the name “Isigili” (Swallower of Seers) arose for it.
At its side, at the foot of the mountain, they built grass huts—that is, having constructed huts with thatched roofs and fitted with door-fastenings.
For one who enters the rains retreat—even one practicing the Nālaka method—must indeed dwell in a hut with a thatched roof from among the five types of roofing and provided with door-fastenings.
One must enter upon the rains residence in a lodging. For this has been said: "Monks, one should not enter upon the rains residence without a lodging.
Whoever should do so incurs an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore, during the rainy season, if one obtains a lodging, that is well;
if one does not obtain one, one should even seek manual labor [to build one] and have it constructed. By one who cannot obtain manual labor...
A conciliation should also be performed. However, one who does not possess a dwelling should not enter the rains residence.

This is the natural course of things. Therefore, those monks, having built grass huts, having demarcated their night-quarters, day-quarters, and so forth, and having undertaken the formal agreements and the Khandhaka observances while training in the three trainings, entered the rains residence.
“Venerable Dhaniya too”—it is not only those elders who were the first offenders of this training rule, but Venerable Dhaniya as well.
“Son of a potter” means the son of a potter; for his name was Dhaniya and his father was a potter, which is why it is said: “Dhaniya, the son of a potter.
“He entered the rains retreat” means that he [entered] in exactly the same place as those elders.

Having constructed a grass hut, he entered upon the rains residence. Those who have completed the rains residence—meaning those who entered during the earlier period and were invited at the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā)—are called "those who have completed the rains" from the first day of the month onward. Having thus completed the rains residence, [he] broke the grass huts;
that is, not by crushing them to pieces with sticks, mallets, or the like, but rather by way of the proper formal procedure (vattasīsa).
The meaning is: having removed the grass, wood, creepers, and so forth.

For one by whom a hut has been built on the outskirts of a monastery, if there are resident monks there, they should be informed: "If anyone is able to maintain this hut and live here, give it to them.
Having said this, he may depart. This applies also to one by whom [a hut] has been built in the forest; [he should inform] the person who maintains it.
Or if he does not obtain [anyone], he should put it away with the thought, "It will be for the use of others as well," and then depart.
As for those monks who, having built huts in the forest, find no one to maintain them, they should put away and preserve the grass and wood;
that is the meaning. And so that what has been stored is not eaten by termites and remains protected from the rain—

Likewise, having set aside [the thought], "This will be for the benefit of my fellow celibates who wish to come and dwell in this place," and having fulfilled the duties of one departing on a journey, they set out on a tour of the countryside;
that is, they went to the various regions according to their own inclinations. The Venerable...
But Dhaniya, the potter’s son, spent the rains retreat right there; such passages have their meaning already explained.
*Yāvatatiyakaṃ* means "up to the third time. *Anavayo* is *anu-avayo*; the vowel *u* is elided by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
*Anu anu avayo* means that whatever is to be done by potters, he is not deficient (*anūna*) in any of it; the meaning is that his craft is complete. *Sake*...
"Belonging to oneself. "Teacher’s craft" means a teacher’s work. "Potter’s craft" means the work of potters;
the meaning is "the work to be performed by potters. By this, one’s own teacher’s craft is shown according to its specific form.
"One of purified craft" means one whose craft is completely pure; it is said that even when there is no deficiency, it is a craft unlike those of others.

"Made entirely of clay" means that, with the exception of the door-panels, door-latches, bolts, and window-shutters, all other building materials for the house—such as the walls, roof, tiles, pillars, and so forth—are made exclusively of clay.
Having gathered grass, wood, and cow-dung, one bakes that hut; thus, it is "made entirely of clay."

Having fashioned it by hand, rubbed it, dried it, and polished it with oil-red clay, she filled it inside and out with grass and other materials, and baked it until it was well-baked. And thus that hut was baked.
"Abhirūpā" means beautiful; "pāsādikā" means inspiring confidence; "lohitiyā" means red-colored; "kiṅkaṇikasaddo" refers to the sound of a small bell.

"The sound of a network of tinkling bells. Just as there is a sound from a network of tinkling bells made of various gems, so too was there a sound from that hut when struck by the wind entering through the openings of the windows and so forth.
By this, its state of being well-baked both inside and out is demonstrated. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it says "tinkling bells" (*kiṅkaṇikā*).
"A bronze vessel; therefore, just as the sound of a struck bronze vessel occurs, so too was the sound of this [earth] when it was struck by the wind," it was said. 85.
"What is this, monks?"—here, although the Blessed One already knew, he asked for the purpose of initiating the discussion.
"They reported this matter to the Blessed One" means they reported to the Blessed One, from the beginning, the fact that he was building a hut made entirely of clay.
"How indeed, monks, could he... build a hut?"—this is a future tense used in the sense of the past;
it means "he built. The grammatical rule for this should be sought from the treatises on grammar (*saddasattha*).
"Indeed, monks, that foolish man will have no compassion, no pity, and no harmlessness toward living beings. Here, "compassion" (*anuddayā*) means protection;
by this, he shows the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (*mettā*). "Pity" (*anukampā*) means the agitation of the mind at the suffering of others.
"Harmlessness" (*avihesā*) means non-injury; by these, he shows the preliminary stage of compassion (*karuṇā*). This is what was said.
“It occurs, monks: ‘When that foolish man, while digging the earth,
trampling the mud, and setting fires, harms and destroys many small and minute living beings,
there will surely not be even a mere preliminary degree of loving-kindness or compassion toward those beings, nor even a slight sense of sympathy, pity, or non-violence.’”

"Let it not be so. [The phrase] "lest the later generation fall into the habit of drinking blood" means that the final assembly of people should not fall into the state of drinking the blood of living beings.
Thinking, "Even during the time of the Buddha, the monks did this;
there is no fault in those who commit the taking of life in such circumstances," and thus following in his footsteps, the later generation...
It means that people might think, "They are being struck or crushed with living beings.
Having thus censured Dhaniya, [the Buddha] prohibited the construction of such huts in the future, saying, "Monks, a hut made entirely of clay must not be built";
and having prohibited it, he declared, "Whoever should build one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

He established an offense for the construction of a hut made entirely of clay. Therefore, even one who constructs such a hut without falling into the destruction of living beings by digging the earth and so forth incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
However, for one who falls into the destruction of living beings through digging the earth and so forth, whatever specific rule (*vatthu*) they transgress, the offense therein is exactly as stated.
One incurs an offense. Because the Elder Dhaniya was a beginner, there is no offense for him.
For the others, even those who build by transgressing the training rule, and even those who dwell in such a place after it has been built, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, if it is made of a mixture of building materials—whether mixed in this way or that—it is permissible. It is not permissible [if] it consists solely of pure clay. That too...
It is permissible if it is constructed using bricks, abbreviated as *giñjakāvasatha*. "Very well, venerable sir," they replied...
[and so on]... "They broke up that hut. Having accepted the Blessed One’s words, they broke up that little hut, scattering it with wood and stones.
Now, as for the passage beginning with "Then the Venerable Dhaniya," this is the summary of the meaning: Dhaniya was sitting at one side during his daytime rest when he heard that noise.
Having approached those monks and asked, "Friends, why are you breaking down my hut?
and having heard, "The Blessed One is having it broken down," he accepted it because of his easy nature.
But why did the Blessed One have this hut—which he had built for his own residence with such great effort—demolished? Was there not even the work of construction for it here?
Although there was, the Blessed One nevertheless had it demolished because it was *akappiya* (unallowable) and because it was a banner of the sectarians (*titthiyadhaja*).
This is the analysis (*vinicchaya*) in this matter. However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it says:
Other reasons have also been stated: out of compassion for sentient beings, for the purpose of protecting the bowl and robes, and for the sake of preventing an abundance of lodgings, and so forth.

Therefore, even now, if a learned monk who is knowledgeable in the Vinaya sees another monk wandering about having taken up an unallowable requisite, and he causes it to be cut or caused to be broken, he is without offense; he is not to be reproached at all.
He is not to be made to pay it back; it is not permissible to say to him, "My requisites were lost by you; give them back to me.
Herein, this is the decision on what is allowable and what is unallowable regarding requisites, independent of the canonical text—some [say] that a palm-leaf umbrella...
If they sew either on the inside or the outside with a five-colored thread to make it glossy and beautiful, that is not permitted.

However, it is permissible to sew either on the inside or the outside with a single-colored thread—whether blue, yellow, or any other—or to bind a handle for the umbrella-staff or a lattice-work frame; this is, moreover, for the purpose of making it durable.
Not for the sake of making it glossy. It is not permitted to carve makara-teeth or half-moons on the ribs of a sunshade.
On the handle of the sunshade, like on house pillars, neither a knob nor a beast-figure is permitted.
Even if a line has been drawn all over with a needle, that too is not permitted. Neither a knob nor a beast-figure [is allowed].
It should be worn after breaking [the bamboo]. The markings may be removed by rubbing them away, or the staff may be wrapped with a cord.
However, for the bundle of staffs, the shape of an *ahicchattaka* (snake’s-head) mushroom is permitted.
To prevent it from moving due to the force of the wind, they tie a circular umbrella to the staff using ropes; at that point of attachment, one should carve a ring-like mark like a bangle.
They place [ornaments] there; that is permissible.

For the purpose of adorning the robe, they sew it with various threads so that it resembles a centipede, they place an incoming patch, or perform any other kind of needlework transformation, such as a braid or a chain-pattern at the edge of the patch or along the border.
All such things as these are not permitted; only a plain needle-case is permitted.
They make cases with eight corners or sixteen corners, and therein they depict the *agghiya*, the *gaya*, the mallet, and so forth, or carve out the eyes of crabs—all this is not permitted;
only a four-cornered case is permitted. And when the robe is dyed, the corner-seams and the folds...
Forms that are perceptible by two [senses] are permissible. It is not permissible to place a robe in sour gruel, flour paste, dregs, and so forth.
However, it is permissible to do so during the time of making robes for the purpose of washing hand-dirt, fine dust, and the like, or when it is soiled for the purpose of washing.
It is not permissible to put perfume, lac, or oil into the dye.
Having dyed the robe-cloth, one must not strike it with a conch shell, a gem, or anything whatsoever.
One must not even rub it against a wooden trough while kneeling on the ground and holding it with the hands.
However, it is permissible to place it in a trough or on a board, grasp the edge, and strike it with the hands; yet even that must not be done with the fist. Thus say the ancient elders.
But they did not even place it in a bowl. One person took it and stood there; another, having taken it in his hand, struck it with his hand.
A thread for the corner of the robe is not permitted; when it is being dyed, it must be cut off.
However, that which was thus authorized by the rule, "Monks, I allow a corner-thread," should be tied after making a loop on the windward side.
For the purpose of dyeing at the time of coloring. Even on a knot, lines or pimples made for the sake of ornamentation are not permitted;
having removed them, it may be used.
Whether in a bowl or a dish, they draw lines with a needle; this is not permitted either inside or outside. [One should] polish the bowl.
Having mounted [the clay] and mixed it, they cook it thinking, "We shall make it the color of a gem"—this is not permitted;
however, the color of oil is permitted. Wall-painting on the rim of a bowl is not permitted, but the *makaradantaka* (tooth-design of a sea monster) is permitted.
Neither above nor below, nor within the interior of a water vessel or a sunshade, is a line permitted; however, a line on the curved edge of the opening of that sunshade is permitted.
It is not permissible to twist the thread double at various points for the sake of making the waistband look beautiful, nor is it permissible to attach crocodile eyes.
However, it is permissible to twist the thread double at both ends for the sake of securing the end of the fringe.
As for the fringe itself, one may fashion any decorative form, such as a jar, a crocodile’s mouth, or a water-snake’s head.
It is not permissible to do so. It is also not permissible to make it by showing the eyes here and there, or by making designs such as flower garlands or creepers;

even a body-belt that has been carved in such a manner is not allowed. However, it is permissible to carve it by making it straight, like a fish’s spine, or like a date-palm leaf, or like a smooth board.
Only one fringe for the body-belt is permitted; two are not.
Three or even four [strands] are permissible; beyond that, they are not. A waistband made of a single cord is permitted.
However, even a single one in the shape of a *pāmaṅga* (a braided ornament) is not permitted. But a fringe (*dasā*) in the shape of a *pāmaṅga* is permitted.
When many cords are joined together and woven continuously as one, it should not be called "many-corded"; that is permitted.

Regarding the waistband (*kāyabandhana*), no decorative form whatsoever—such as the eight auspicious symbols (*aṭṭhamangala*) and so forth—is permitted; however, a mere outline demarcating its boundaries is allowed. If a loop is made at both ends of the cord for the purpose of securing it firmly, that too is permitted.

Regarding the ointment box (*añjanī*), no decorative form in the shape of a woman, a man, a quadruped, or a bird is permitted, nor any such as floral designs, scrollwork, makara teeth, cow-urine patterns, or half-moons.
It must be made by grinding or cutting in such a way that [the prohibited forms] are not discernible.
It should be used after wrapping it with thread. However, an ointment box that is perfectly straight and has four, eight, or sixteen sides is permissible.
On its underside, two or three circular lines are allowed.
A single circular line is also permitted on the neck for the purpose of securing the lid.
It is not permissible to perform decorative coloring with an ointment-stick.
It is also not permissible to perform decorative coloring on an ointment-box with thread of any various colors. The same rule applies to a key-case.
It is not permissible to perform decorative coloring on a key, nor likewise on a casket. However, it is permissible here to sew anything with thread of a single color.
Even on the neck, it is not permitted to have a round jewel or anything else that is smooth and polished. However, a boundary line is permitted on the neck.
On the knob as well, it is not permitted to have a jewel, a protuberance, or anything at all raised up.
But a boundary line is permitted on the handle. As for the nail-cutter, they make it only curved, therefore that is permitted.

It is not permitted to apply any kind of colored polish for beauty, such as floral designs and the like, to the upper fire-stick (*uttarāraṇī*), the lower fire-stick (*adharāraṇī*), the fire-drill base (*araṇidhanuka*), or the pressing rod (*uparipellanadaṇḍaka*). However, there is a circular mark at the middle of the pressing rod;
a mere boundary line there is permitted. They also make needle-pincers, by which one may pick up a needle.
They polish it; in that regard, any kind of polished coloration, such as that of a makara’s mouth and so forth, is not permitted.
However, a mere opening for the purpose of inserting a needle is allowed, and that is permissible.
As for the adze used for cutting tooth-sticks, any kind of polished coloration is not permitted; it must be made straight from allowable metal.
It is permissible to bind [the handle] on both sides in either a four-sided or an eight-sided shape.

Regarding the walking stick (*kattaradaṇḍa*) as well, any kind of polished decoration is not permitted; however, one or two circular lines at the bottom and a knob at the top the size of an *ahicchattaka* mushroom are allowed.
In the case of oil vessels—whether made of horn, bamboo, gourd, or wood—the female and male figures must be excluded, but all other forms of polished decoration are permitted.
On beds and chairs, mattresses and cushions, floor coverings, foot-wipers, meditation mats for walking,
brooms, dustbins, dye-vats, water-scoops, water-jars, foot-stools, wooden benches, arm-rests, staff-stands,
bowl-covers, palm-leaf fans, and fans— in all these, any work involving floral designs or other decorative coloring and polishing is prohibited.
It is permissible. Furthermore, regarding dwellings, even if they are made of all kinds of gems, it is permissible to apply a smooth, colored finish to the door panels, window shutters, and so forth.
There is nothing whatsoever prohibited in a dwelling, except for a "conflicting dwelling" (*viruddha-senāsana*).
A "conflicting dwelling" is said to be a dwelling built by royal favorites within the boundary (*sīmā*) of others; therefore, those [who occupy] such a dwelling—
They do so; they should be told: "Do not construct a dwelling within our boundary.
If they nevertheless continue to construct it, they should be told again: "Do not do this! Do not create an obstacle for our Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies!
Do not break the harmony! Even though you have constructed your dwelling, it will not remain in the place where you built it. If...
Even while they are acting by force, when their assembly of modest people has become numerous and it is possible to obtain a righteous decision, then one should send word to them:
"Take [the requisites] to your own residence. If they take them upon being sent for up to three times, that is well;
if they do not take them, then—with the exception of the Bodhi tree and the shrine—the remaining lodgings [should be taken].
They should be dismantled, but not by those who would leave them unusable; rather, having removed the roof, rafters, bricks, and so forth in due order, they should send word to them:
"Take away your building materials. If they take them, that is well;
if they do not take them, then when those building materials have become rotten through frost, rain, wind, heat, and the like, or have been stolen by thieves...
If the buildings are swept away by water or consumed by fire, the monks who are the owners of the boundary are blameless;

it is not permissible to reproach them by saying, "You have destroyed our building materials," or "The liability for this falls upon you. Whatever has been done by the monks who are the owners of the boundary is indeed well-done.
The *Pāḷimuttakavinicchaya* is concluded. 86.
Now, in order to show Dhaniya’s reflection upon the hut having been destroyed, as well as his renewed effort to build another hut, the passage beginning with “Then, to the Venerable One...
was spoken. In that context, the term “accountant in the timber storehouse” refers to one in the king’s storehouse for timber.
*Dārugopaka* (guardian of timber): "Timber taken by the king" means timber that has been accepted by the monarch;

it refers to timber intended for the repair of the city. "Set aside for times of distress" means [timber] kept for the purpose of repairing the city gates, watchtowers, royal palaces, elephant stables, and so forth, in the event of fire, decay due to age, or siege by an enemy king.
"Calamity" (*vipatti*) is what is meant by "misfortune" (*āpadā*). "Laid down for that purpose" is what is intended.
"Having had it cut into pieces" means that, having observed the dimensions of his own hut, he had it cut into small fragments—some at the top, some in the middle, and some at the base. 87.
*Vassakāra* is the name of that brahmin. *Magadhamahāmatta* means a high official in the kingdom of Magadha.
He was endowed with great lordship, being a high minister of the King of Magadha; that is to say, a *mahāmatta*.
"Reflecting" means reviewing [the matter] by going here and there. "Addressing" refers to the speaking of lords to men in a subordinate position.
"Ordered his binding" means that the brahmin was already habitually envious of him; thus, at the king’s words, "Order [his binding]," he acted.
Because he did not say to the king, "Please summon him," [the king] ordered his binding, thinking, "I shall have him bound hand and foot and then give him my orders.
The Venerable Dhaniya saw him—how did he see him?
It is said that having learned through a hint that wood had been taken by himself, [he thought], "Without a doubt, this man is coming from the royal palace for the sake of the wood..."
“Whether he shall suffer execution or imprisonment, I myself will set him free.
Thus he wandered about, constantly listening to news of him. Therefore, going at that very moment, he saw him. Hence it is said: “The Venerable Dhaniya saw.
“For the sake of wood” means for the purpose of wood. “Before I am slain” means before I am killed.
“I am being killed; come while I have not yet been killed”—this is the meaning. 88.
Regarding the phrase “Come, venerable sir, please remember [your promise]”: here *iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation.
“The first consecrated” means having been consecrated, for the first time. “He spoke such words” refers to: “It has indeed been given to the recluses and brahmins...”

"Let them enjoy grass, wood, and water"—having uttered such words as you did immediately after being consecrated, you have now remembered what you yourself said; it is said that you do not remember it.
It is reported that as soon as kings are consecrated, they cause the drum of Dhamma to be beaten, proclaiming: "Grass, wood, and water are indeed given to the recluses and brahmins."
"He says this with reference to those who would enjoy it. "It was said by me with reference to them" means:

"It was said by me with reference to those recluses and brahmins who are scrupulous even regarding trifles and who have stilled and cast out evil, and for whom the taking of grass, wood, and water [is forbidden];
the intention is that it was not said of people like you. And furthermore, "in the forest, unappropriated."
He explains: "I said this with reference to that grass, wood, and water which is unowned in the forest.
Regarding the phrase "you are released by the hair" (*lomena*), here "hair" (*loma*) means like hair; what, then, is it? It is the mark of the renunciant. What is meant?
Just as rogues, thinking "we shall eat meat," might seize a sheep of great value for its wool. To that one—
If another discerning person were to see this and, thinking, "The meat of this sheep is worth only a single kahāpaṇa,
but its wool is worth many kahāpaṇas for each handful," were to give him two woolless sheep in exchange and take [the sheep with wool],
then that sheep, by encountering the discerning person, would be released because of its wool. In the same way, you, because of having performed this deed...
"You deserve execution or imprisonment. However, because the banner of the Arahants is beyond reproach by the virtuous, and because you, having gone forth in the Dispensation,
bear that banner of the Arahants which is the very mark of the renunciant life, you have been released like a goat upon encountering a wise man,
by virtue of this hair that serves as the mark of the renunciant life."

"People grumble" means that having heard [him] speaking both in the presence and in the absence of the king’s assembly, people here and there grumble, murmur, and—being contemptuous—they brood over him;
the meaning is that they look upon him with disdain or think of him as inferior. "They revile" means they speak ill of him and proclaim it. "They complain" means...
They cause it to spread widely; they propagate it everywhere. And this meaning is to be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
Here, however, the application (*yojanā*) is as follows: they grumble (*ujjhāyanti*), thinking such things as, "These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, are shameless.

They revile (*khīyanti*), saying such things as, "There is no asceticism (*sāmañña*) in these people. They disparage (*vambhenti*), saying such things as, "These people have fallen away from asceticism."

"Expanding upon this here and there, they explain it. By this method, the application of these terms beyond this point should be understood according to the corresponding terms found in those respective places. "Brahmacārino" means those of excellent conduct.
"Sāmaññaṃ" means the state of being an ascetic (*samaṇa*). "Brahmaññaṃ" means the state of being excellent (*brahma*). The rest is self-evident.
In the passage beginning with "The king’s timber," the phrase "he will take what is not given" has the sense of reproaching [the king].

However, in order to show that which he took when it was not given, it is said, "the king’s timber. Thus, the meaning should be understood by those who do not become confused by the difference in wording.

"An official experienced in ancient legal practice" refers to one who, in his former life as a householder prior to his becoming a monk, was experienced in the legal proceedings of judicial administration.
Because he was appointed to that office, the Great Minister became known as "Vohārika.

Then the Blessed One said this to that bhikkhu: the Blessed One himself knows even worldly convention, and he also knows the formal prescriptions of past Buddhas—“In the past, too, Buddhas prescribed a *pārājika* offense by means of just this much.”
“By this much there is a grave offense (thullaccaya); by this much there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Even so, if he were to prescribe a defeat (pārājika) for merely a foot [of meat] without consulting others who understand worldly conventions, there would be those who would say:
“The restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara) is immeasurable and incalculable even for a single bhikkhu; it is exceedingly vast, like the great earth, the ocean, and space.”
"How indeed could the Blessed One have destroyed [the tree] with a mere foot!

Thinking thus, those who do not understand the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge might find fault with the training rule; even a training rule that has been laid down would not remain in its proper place.
However, when the rule is laid down in consultation with those who understand worldly conventions, such criticism does not arise. On the contrary, people speak in this way:

—“If even householders, for a mere trifle, kill or bind a thief and yet still ordain him, why would the Blessed One not allow one who has gone forth to be expelled? For he must not take even so much as a blade of grass or a stick belonging to another!
In this way they will come to know the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, and the training rule that has been laid down will become unshakable.

"He will stand in the proper place. Therefore, desiring to explain [the matter] after reconciling it with those who understand worldly conventions, the Blessed One surveyed the entire assembly. Then, seeing that monk sitting not far away, he said to him:
"To what extent, monk, does King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having apprehended a thief, put him to death, imprison him, or banish him?"
In this context, *Māgadha* means the lord of the Magadhas; *Seniya* means one endowed with an army; *Bimbisāra* is his name.
*Pabbājeyya vā* means he would expel from the kingdom. The rest here is of plain meaning. "A quarter [of a kahāpaṇa] is five māsakas":
at that time, a *kahāpaṇa* was worth twenty *māsakas* in Rājagaha; therefore, a quarter is five *māsakas*. By this characteristic...
In all countries, one-fourth of a kahāpaṇa should be understood as a "quarter" (pāda).
This, moreover, is according to the ancient blue kahāpaṇa, and not according to others such as the Rudradāmaka and so forth.

For by that quarter, even the past Buddhas prescribed a *pārājika* offense, and the future ones will also prescribe it. For in the matter of the grounds for a *pārājika* offense, there is no difference among all Buddhas.
There is no difference between [the offenses] in the Pārājika section. These alone are the four bases for the Pārājikas; these alone are the four Pārājikas.
There is nothing less than this, nor anything more. Therefore, having rebuked Dhaniya, the Blessed One himself, while enacting the second Pārājika, said:
"Whatever monk, by means of theft, should take what has not been given," and so forth.

Thus, having made it firm by way of cutting off the root when the second *pārājika* was laid down, another case arose for the purpose of a subsequent laying down (*anupaññatti*), namely the story of the dyer’s bundle.
To illustrate its origin, this was said: “In this way, this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Its meaning and its connection with the subsequent laying down are [explained] in the commentary on the first *pārājika*.
It is to be understood in the very same manner as previously stated. And just as here, so it is with all the training rules (sikkhāpada) that follow this.
Having omitted everything that has already been said before, we shall explain only what is new in each successive section.
For if we were to explain again every point already explained, when would the commentary ever reach its end?
Therefore, having carefully observed everything that has been stated previously, the meaning and the application should be understood in each respective instance.
However, whatever is new or contains an unexplained point, all of that we ourselves shall explain.
The commentary on the story of Dhaniya is finished.
90. "Having gone to the washermen’s spreading-ground" means having gone to the washermen’s bathing-place (tittha).
For it is called the washermen’s spreading-ground because the washermen spread out clothes there. "The washermen’s bundle" means a bundle belonging to the washermen;
when the washermen enter the city in the evening, they tie up many clothes into a single bundle.
Then, having stolen—that is, having taken away—one bundle while they were not looking due to their negligence.
Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis (Padabhājanīya): 92.
Regarding "a village," etc., this refers to the village and the forest mentioned in the passage "from a village or from a forest."

And this is stated for the purpose of showing the various classifications. In that context, a village in which there is only one hut and one house—such as, for example, in the Malaya province—is called a "single-hut village. By this same method, the others should also be understood.
A "non-human" (*amanussa*) is one who, either through the total absence of humans, has come under the possession of a *yakkha*, or from whom humans have [departed] for some reason.
For some reason, they departed while still desiring to return. "Enclosed" means surrounded by a wall of bricks and so forth, down to even being surrounded by thorny branches.

"Situated for cows to sit" means not arranged according to the layout of streets and such, but rather like a place where two or three cows can sit here and there; thus, it is situated with two or three [cows] here and there.
"Having built houses, he has settled there. "Caravan" (*sattha*) refers to any caravan, whether on foot, by cart, or otherwise.
It should be understood that in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), both a market town (*nigama*) and a city (*nagara*) are included by the very mention of a "village" (*gāma*).

The phrase beginning with "the vicinity of the village" (*gāmūpacāra*) is stated for the purpose of defining the limits of the wilderness (*arañña*). "Standing at the threshold stone" (*indakhīle ṭhitassa*) refers to whichever village...

In the case of Anurādhapura itself, there are two gateposts (*indakhīla*); for one standing within its inner gatepost, its outer gatepost is considered "forest" according to the method of the Abhidhamma. But for one who has only a single gatepost, it is for one standing midway between the two door-posts of the village gate.
For even where no gatepost exists, it is [the same] regarding the two door-posts of the village gate.
The very middle is called the "city-gate bolt" (*indakhīla*). Therefore it is said: "standing in the middle of the two doorposts of the village gate.
"Of one who is middling" means of one who is middling in strength, not middling in size—neither of little strength nor of great strength;
what is meant is "of middling strength. "The range of a clod" (*leḍḍupāta*) refers to [the distance] as when a woman, scaring away crows, throws straight ahead...
One should not take the place where a clod of earth falls after being thrown by raising the hand, nor the place where water is thrown during a water-splash;

rather, one should take the place where a clod is thrown like young men who, displaying their strength, extend their arms and throw it—specifically, the spot where the thrown clod lands and rolls once it has fallen.
One must not take the place where it eventually comes to rest after rolling.
Regarding the phrase "the range of a stone’s throw for a man of medium height standing in the vicinity of the houses of an unenclosed village":
here, the "vicinity of the houses" (*gharūpacāra*) refers to the distance reached by the throw of a winnowing-fan or a pestle by a man of medium height standing at the edge of the water-trough.
The "vicinity of the village" (*gāmūpacāra*) is the range of a stone’s throw for a man of medium height standing within that vicinity of the houses; so it is stated in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*.

It has been stated [thus]. The *Mahāpaccarī* is likewise. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, having established the headings: “What is called a house, what is called the vicinity of a house, what is called a village, and what is called the vicinity of a village,” it says: “The interior of the space where water falls from a water-pot is called a ‘house.
Furthermore, the place where water falling from a vessel is discarded by a woman standing at the door, and the place where that [water] falls—”
The entire vicinity of the house (*gharūpacāra*) consists of: the place where a broom or a winnowing fan, normally kept outside, falls when dropped by a woman standing inside the house;

and the enclosure constructed in front of the house, connected at two corners and having a gate with wooden posts in the middle, for the purpose of preventing cattle from entering. All this constitutes the vicinity of the house.
The term *nāma* [is used]. For a man of medium height standing within that vicinity of a house (*gharūpacāra*), the range of a stone’s throw is called a village (*gāma*).
The space within another stone’s throw from there is called the vicinity of a village (*gāmūpacāra*); so it has been said. This is the measure here.
And just as it is in this case, so it is everywhere: whichever statement of the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) or of the Elders (*thera*) is stated later [should be understood accordingly].
Thus it should be understood by way of measurement.
Furthermore, that which is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* appears to be in contradiction with the *pāḷi*. For in the *pāḷi*, it is stated only thus:
"the distance of a stone’s throw for a man of middle stature standing within the vicinity of a house. But in the *aṭṭhakathā*, however—
Is it the case that, having made the range of a thrown clod the village precinct (*gāmasaṅkhepa*), what follows that is called the village vicinity (*gāmūpacāra*)? It is replied:

It is indeed true that this is stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*), but the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) here must be understood; and that [intention] is known only to the teachers of the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*).

Therefore, just as in the phrase "of one standing in the vicinity of a house" (*gharūpacāre ṭhitassa*), the definition of the vicinity of a house, though not stated in the Canon, [is to be understood].
This has been taken according to what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. The remainder should be understood in the same way.
Herein, this is the method: here, a village is of two kinds—enclosed and unenclosed.
Of these, for the enclosed one, the enclosure itself is the boundary. Therefore, without stating a separate boundary for it, [the text says] "the vicinity of the village."
"In the case of an enclosed village, it is stated in the Pāḷi: 'the range of a clod thrown by a middle-sized man standing at the gate-pillar (indakhīla).
However, for an unenclosed village, the boundary of the village must be described. Therefore, in order to show that boundary of such a village:
'In the case of an unenclosed village, [it is the range of a clod thrown by a middle-sized man] standing within the vicinity of the houses...'"

It is said: "the range of a clod thrown by a man. Since the boundaries of the village have already been shown, the definition of the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*) can be understood through the method previously explained; therefore, it is not stated again as "the range of a clod thrown by a man of medium size standing there. However, for one who asserts that the precinct of the village is merely the range of a clod thrown by someone standing within the precinct of a house— [The text continues: ...for him [that would be incorrect]. If one were to say that the precinct of a village is the range of a clod thrown by a person standing at the edge of a house, then even a single house would become a village, and the entire earth would become a village. Furthermore, if one were to say that the precinct of a village is the range of a clod thrown by a person standing at the edge of a field, then even a single field would become a village, and the entire earth would become a village. Moreover, if one were to say that the precinct of a village is the range of a clod thrown by a person standing at the edge of a threshing floor, then even a single threshing floor would become a village, and the entire earth would become a village. Therefore, this is not the definition of the precinct of a village. But if one were to say that the precinct of a village is the range of a clod thrown by a person standing at the edge of the village itself, then the definition of the village precinct is established. Thus, the definition of the village precinct should be understood according to the method previously explained. Regarding the phrase "the range of a clod thrown by a man": the word "man" (*purisa*) here refers to a human being (*manussa*), not a male (*puruṣa*). For it is said: "A man is a human being, not a male. The term "clod" (*leḍḍu*) refers to a lump of clay (*mattikāpiṇḍa*). "Thrown" (*pāta*) means cast or hurled. "Range" (*pāta*) means the distance reached by that which is thrown. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the word "man" is used here to indicate a person of medium stature. Why? Because the Blessed One has said: "I do not prescribe the eating of food after midday for one who is short, nor for one who is tall. Therefore, it is said: "the range of a clod thrown by a man of medium size. If one were to say that the range of a clod thrown by a man of medium size standing at the edge of a house is the precinct of the village, then even a single house would become a village, and the entire earth would become a village. If one were to say that the range of a clod thrown by a man of medium size standing at the edge of a field is the precinct of the village, then even a single field would become a village, and the entire earth would become a village. If one were to say that the range of a clod thrown by a man of medium size standing at the edge of a threshing floor is the precinct of the village, then even a single threshing floor would become a village, and the entire earth would become a village. Therefore, this is not the definition of the precinct of the village. But if one were to say that the range of a clod thrown by a man of medium size standing at the edge of the village itself is the precinct of the village, then the definition of the village precinct is established. Thus, the definition of the village precinct should be understood according to the method previously explained. In this context, the phrase "the range of a clod thrown by a man of medium size standing there" is used to indicate the limit of the village precinct. It is not intended to define the precinct of a village by the range of a clod thrown from within a house, a field, or a threshing floor. Rather, it is intended to show that the precinct of the village extends as far as the range of a clod thrown by a man of medium size standing at the very edge of the village. Thus, the definition of the village precinct is established. Therefore, the definition of the village precinct should be understood according to the method previously explained. As for the statement: "If one were to say that the precinct of a village is the range of a clod thrown by a person standing at the edge of a house," and so forth—the fault in such a position is that it would lead to the absurd conclusion that a single house, a single field, or a single threshing floor constitutes a village, and ultimately that the entire earth is a village. Consequently, these are not the definitions of the village precinct. Only when one says that the precinct of a village is the range of a clod thrown by a person of medium size standing at the edge of the village itself is the definition of the village precinct correctly established. Thus, the definition of the village precinct should be understood according to the method previously explained. Finally, regarding the term "man": the word "man" (*purisa*) here denotes a human being (*manussa*), not a male (*puruṣa*). For it is said: "A man is a human being, not a male. The term "clod" (*leḍḍu*) refers to a lump of clay (*mattikāpiṇḍa*). "Thrown" (*pāta*) means cast or hurled. "Range" (*pāta*) means the distance reached by that which is thrown. This is the meaning. Therefore, the definition of the village precinct should be understood according to the method previously explained. It is not the case that the precinct of a village is defined by the range of a clod thrown from within a house, a field, or a threshing floor; rather, it is the range of a clod thrown by a man of medium size standing at the edge of the village itself. Thus, the definition of the village precinct is established. Therefore, the definition of the village precinct should be understood according to the method previously explained. “A house,” “the vicinity of a house,” and “a village” are [distinct categories]. From that, the distinction between “a house,” “the vicinity of a house,” “a village,” and “the vicinity of a village” becomes confused.
Therefore, the analysis here—regarding such matters as entering a village at an improper time—should be understood without confusion.

Consequently, by correlating the canonical text (Pāḷi) with the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), the village and the vicinity of the village should be understood exactly according to the method stated herein.
Furthermore, even a village that was formerly large but later becomes small because its families have perished must be delimited by the range of a stone’s throw from the dwellings.
However, its previous boundary—whether it was enclosed or unenclosed—is simply irrelevant.

As for what is called "forest" (arañña), it is defined as excluding both the village and the vicinity of the village according to the characteristics already described. And as for the village and the vicinity of the village...
Except for this training rule on taking what is not given, the remainder should be understood as "forest.
In the Abhidhamma, however, it is said: "Forest means that which is outside the threshold post after having gone out; all this is forest. In the training rule concerning forest-dwellers, it is said:
"A forest dwelling is one that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant from the threshold post. That [distance] is from the threshold post...
It should be understood that [the distance] measured by a teacher’s bow, starting from its tip, is five hundred bow-lengths (*pañcadhanusatappamāṇa*).

Thus, while analyzing the meaning of the phrase “from a village or from a forest,” the Blessed One presented five categories—“a house, the vicinity of a house, a village, the vicinity of a village, and a forest”—for the purpose of closing off any pretext for evil monks. Therefore, regarding a house...

Whether in a village or its precincts, or in a forest, for one who steals property belonging to an owner starting from a value of one *pāda*, it should be understood that this is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
Now, in order to demonstrate the meaning of the phrases beginning with “should take what is not given, characterized as theft,” he said: “What is called ‘not given’,” and so forth.

In this context, "what is not given" (*adatta*) refers, in the training rule on tooth-sticks, to anything edible that is permissible even if it belongs to oneself, provided it has not been formally accepted.
Here, however, it refers to any kind of property belonging to another and under their ownership;
it is called "not given" because it has not been bestowed by those owners either by body or by speech. [It is taken] from one's own hand or from its place where it stands...

Or, it is "not relinquished" (*anissaṭṭha*) because it has not been let go. It is "not abandoned" (*apariccatta*) because, even while remaining in its original place, it has not been surrendered due to a lack of concern.
It is "guarded" (*rakkhita*) because it is protected by the provision of security. It is "concealed" (*gopita*) because it is hidden by being placed inside a chest or similar container.
It is "cherished" (*mamāyita*) because it is treated as "mine" through the conceit of craving (*taṇhāmama*). By means of those [actions]—non-relinquishment, guarding, and concealment—...
"Appropriated by others" means it is taken possession of by others who are the owners of the goods; this is what is called "not given. "Designated as theft": here, *theno* means a thief;
*theyya* is the state of being a thief; this is a designation for the mind intent on taking away.
"Designation (*saṅkhā*) and designated (*saṅkhāta*)" are one in meaning; this is a designation for a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*), [as in the phrase] "perception is the source..."

As in such passages as “for it is indeed conceptual proliferation (papañca-saṅkhā). It is both theft and a concept; thus, it is “conceptualized as theft” (theyyasaṅkhātaṃ), meaning a single mental factor (cittakoṭṭhāsa) consisting of a mind of theft.
This nominative case is used here in the sense of the instrumental; therefore, it should be understood in meaning as “by that which is conceptualized as theft.
And since he who takes by means of what is conceptualized as theft possesses a mind of theft, therefore—

It should be understood that the word-commentary was stated thus— "one with a thieving mind, one with a mind intent on taking"— in order to show the meaning alone, without adhering to the literal phrasing.
"Should take," "should carry off," "should steal," "should disturb his posture," "should move him from his place," "should pass the signal."
Here, however, the first phrase is stated by way of persistent effort; the second phrase, by way of one who goes taking the goods of others;
the third, by way of goods deposited as a pledge; the fourth, by way of animate beings;
the fifth, by way of goods placed on dry land and so forth; and the sixth, by way of conjecture or by way of evading customs duties.
It should be understood that this has been stated. Furthermore, the application here occurs both by way of a single article and by way of various articles.

By way of a single article, it applies only to that which possesses consciousness; by way of various articles, it applies to a mixture of those possessing consciousness and those lacking consciousness.
In this regard, first, by way of various articles, it should be understood thus: "should take" means he lays claim to a monastery; there is an offense.
Regarding a *dukkaṭa* offense: if one causes the owner to have doubt, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
If the owner, thinking “it will not be mine,” abandons the burden, there is an offense of *pārājika*.

“Should carry away”: while carrying another’s goods, if one touches the load on the head with a thieving intent, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. If one makes it move, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*. If one lowers it from the shoulder, there is an offense of *pārājika*.
"Should steal": when goods have been deposited as a trust and, being told "Give me the goods," one says "I will not take them," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one causes doubt to arise in the owner's mind, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*).
If the owner, thinking "He will not give it back to me," gives up the burden [of ownership], there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).

"Should disturb his posture": if, thinking "I will take him along with the goods," he moves his first foot, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*. If he moves his second foot, there is an offense of *pārājika*. "Should move it from its place":
if, with a mind of theft, he touches goods situated on dry land, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. If he makes them tremble, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
If he moves them from their place, there is an offense of *pārājika*. "Should pass beyond the signal": if he passes his first foot beyond the designated spot, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.

If he steps across with the second foot, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika). Alternatively, if he steps across the customs barrier with the first foot, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya);
if he steps across with the second foot, there is an offense entailing defeat—this is the application of the rule here according to the case of various goods.
Regarding a single article, however, if one takes, carries off, or steals a slave with an owner or an animal by the method already described—
namely, through force and so forth— or disrupts its posture, moves it from its place,
or causes it to cross a boundary: this is the application here in terms of a single article.
The Discourse on the Twenty-five Modes of Taking What Is Not Given:
Furthermore, by one describing these six terms, twenty-five modes of taking what is not given should be demonstrated by combining five sets of five.
For when it is described in this way, this Pārājika offense of taking what is not given becomes well-expounded. And in this regard—
In this matter, all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) are confused, muddled, and difficult to discern in their analysis. For indeed, among all the commentaries,

even those factors of theft (*avahāraṅga*) which are stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*) according to the method beginning with, "There is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) for one who takes what is not given in five ways,
provided it is the property of another," have been taken and presented in some places as a single set of five.
In some places, two sets of five [factors] are shown together with those that arrive under the heading "in six ways. However, these are not [true] sets of five.
For where the removal (avahāra) is accomplished by each individual term, that is called a "set of five" (pañcaka).
But here, there is only one single removal by all the terms combined. And as for those sets of five that are obtainable therein—
Although these have been shown, the meaning has not been clarified for all of them.
Thus, in this place, all the commentaries are confused, muddled, and their determinations are difficult to understand.
Therefore, having brought together the five sets of five, these twenty-five forms of theft should be carefully observed.

There are five groups of five, namely: the group of five diverse articles, the group of five single articles, the group of five by means of one's own hand, the group of five involving prior preparation, and the group of five consisting of theft.
Among these, the group of five diverse articles and the group of five single articles relate to the following phrases:
"should take up," "should carry away," "should steal," "should disrupt the posture," and "should move from its place."
They are obtained according to their respective modes. These should be understood by the same method already set forth and demonstrated previously.
As for this sixth phrase, "should spend the day," it is common to both the application of hypothetical usage (*parikappāvahāra*) and the application of forfeiture (*nissaggiyāvahāra*).
Therefore, it should be applied according to the phrases found in the third and fifth pentads. And the pentad of various articles has been stated.
And the pentad of single articles.
What is the pentad of taking by one’s own hand? There are five modes of theft: taking by one’s own hand, commanding, causing to be relinquished, accomplishing a purpose, and abandoning the burden.
Among these, "taking by one’s own hand" means that one steals another's goods with one’s own hand. "Commanding" [means...]
"Bring such-and-such a person's goods," he commands another. "Nissaggiya" means: standing within a customs barrier, one causes [goods] to fall outside the customs barrier;
there is an offense of *pārājika*. This, together with the phrase "he should let the appointment pass," receives its syntactical connection.
"One who accomplishes the purpose" means: "When you are able, then [bring] such-and-such a commodity..."

"Take it away," he commands. In that case, if the other person takes it away without any obstacle, the one who gave the command becomes guilty of a *pārājika* offense at the very moment of the command, whereas the taker becomes guilty at the time of the taking.
This is the "one who accomplishes the purpose. However, the laying down of the burden should be understood by way of the goods deposited.
This is the pentad of direct manual action (*sāhatthika-pañcaka*).
What is the pentad of preliminary effort? There are another five kinds of theft: preliminary effort, simultaneous effort, theft by appointment, making a sign, and making a gesture.
Herein, "preliminary effort" is to be understood by way of giving an order; "simultaneous effort" is by way of causing displacement from its place.
The other three, however, are to be understood according to the method set forth in the Canon. This is...
The fivefold preliminary effort.
What is the fivefold taking by theft? There are another five ways of taking: taking by theft, taking by force, taking by scheming, taking by concealment, and taking by trickery.
These five are as follows: "A certain monk [stole] from the Saṅgha..."

"When the robes were being distributed, with a thieving mind he diverted the *kusa* grass and took the robe"—this we shall explain in the context of that case concerning the diversion of the *kusa* grass.
This is the pentad of theft by taking away. Thus, having combined these five pentads, these twenty-five modes of taking away are to be understood.

Furthermore, when a case has been brought before these five groups of five, a skilled Vinaya expert, rather than deciding it hastily, should examine five points. With reference to these, the ancients said:
"The matter, the time, and the place, The value, and fifthly, the use;
Having weighed these five points, A wise man should uphold the meaning."

In this context, "the object" (*vatthu*) refers to the goods. For even if the thief says, "I have stolen such-and-such," one must not yet charge him with an offense, but must instead investigate whether those goods have an owner or are ownerless.

Even if they have an owner, one must investigate whether the owners still have a sense of attachment (*sālayabhāva*) toward them or are without attachment (*nirālayabhāva*). If, at the time when they still have attachment...
Having had the value of the stolen goods assessed, an offense should be determined. If it was during a time when there was no owner present, one should not be charged with a *pārājika* offense.
However, when the owners of the goods come to have their property returned, the goods must be given back; this is the proper procedure (*sāmīci*) in this matter.
To illustrate this point, there is the following account: it is said that during the time of King Bhātikarāja, at the festival for the Mahācetiya...
From the southern direction, a certain monk entered the courtyard of the cetiya carrying a yellowish-pale robe over his shoulder;
at that very moment, the king also arrived for the purpose of worshipping the cetiya. While the clearing of the way was taking place there, a great crush of the crowd occurred.
Then, that monk, being pressed by the throng of people, departed without even noticing that the robe was slipping from his shoulder.
Having departed and not seeing the saffron robe, he thought, "Who will obtain a saffron robe in such a crowd of people?
It is no longer mine," and having thus abandoned his effort, he went away. Then another monk, arriving later, saw that saffron robe;
taking it with a thieving mind, he subsequently became remorseful and thought, "I am no longer a recluse now; I shall disrobe."
Even though such thoughts had arisen in his mind, he thought, "I shall find out after questioning one who holds the Vinaya.
At that time, there lived in the Mahāvihāra a monk named the Elder Cūḷasumana, a master of the entire Piṭaka and a preeminent teacher of the Vinaya.
That monk approached the Elder, paid homage, requested an opportunity to speak, and [disclosed] his own remorse.

He asked. The Elder, having arrived after the crowd had dispersed and realizing he had been caught, thought, "Now there is an opportunity here," and said, "If you could bring a monk who owns these saffron robes, it would be possible for me to establish your innocence.
"But how, venerable sir, shall I find him? "Go here and there..."
“Look at the world! Having looked at all five great monasteries, he did not see anyone.
Then the Elder asked him, “From which direction are many bhikkhus coming? “From the southern direction, venerable sir.
“In that case, measure out a robe-cloth (kāsāva) both in length and breadth and set it down. Having set it down, [walk] in the sequence of the monasteries in the southern direction.”
“Search for that monk and bring him here. Having done so, he saw the monk and brought him into the presence of the Elder.
The Elder asked, “Is this your saffron robe? “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. “Where did you drop it? He related everything.
But the Elder, having heard of the burden-laying [the confession of defeat] committed by the other, asked the second one: “By you—”
“Where did you see this, and why was it taken? He too related everything. Then the Elder said to him:
“If you had taken it with a pure mind, there would have been no offense for you. But because you took it with a thieving mind, you have committed a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
Confess that, and you shall be free from offense. And as for this saffron robe, having made it your own property, [give it] to this very bhikkhu.”
"Give it back! That bhikkhu, as if sprinkled with the Deathless, attained supreme consolation. Thus should the case be examined.
As for "time," it refers to the time of the theft; for that same article may at one time be of little value and at another time of great value.
Therefore, whatever the value of that article was at the very time it was stolen, by that value [the offense is determined].
The offense must be adjudicated. This is how the time is to be considered.

As for the "place," it refers to the place of theft. For that stolen property, the offense must be adjudicated according to its value at the very place where it was stolen; for indeed, the property is worth more at the place where it originated.
It is of great value elsewhere.
And to illustrate this point, there is this story: it is said that in the middle of the ocean, a certain bhikkhu obtained a coconut of excellent shape;
having hollowed it out, he fashioned it into a charming drinking bowl resembling a conch-shell vessel.
Having done so and placed it right there, he went to Cetiyagiri.
Then another monk, having gone across the intermediate ocean and residing in that monastery, saw that bowl; taking it with a mind of theft, he returned to Cetiyagiri itself.
While that monk was drinking his gruel there, the owner of the bowl saw it and said:
—“From where did you obtain this? —“It was brought to me from the middle of the ocean. He dragged him into the midst of the Saṅgha, saying, “This is not yours;
it was taken by you through theft. Not obtaining a decision there, they went to the Mahāvihāra.
There, having had the drum beaten and assembled a gathering near the Mahācetiya, they reached a decision.
They began [the dispute]. The elders who were experts in the Vinaya pointed out the misappropriation.
Now, at that assembly, there was an elder named Ābhidhammika Godatta, who was skilled in the Vinaya.
He asked: "Where was this bowl taken away by him? "It was taken away into the middle of the ocean. "In that case, what is this here?"
“Is it worth anything? “It is not worth anything at all. For there, having broken open the coconut and eaten the kernel, they discard the shell;
however, it serves for the purpose of firewood. “What is this monk’s labor here worth?
“A māsaka coin, or perhaps less than a māsaka. “But is there anywhere where a Perfectly Enlightened One has accepted even a māsaka or less than a māsaka?”
“Or has a *pārājika* offense been prescribed? When this was said, there was a single cry of “Excellent! Excellent! Well-spoken! Well-judged!
At that time, King Bhātika, while departing from the city to pay homage at the cetiya, heard that sound;
having asked, “What is this? and having heard everything in sequence, he caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city.
—“While I am present, any legal dispute (adhikaraṇa) concerning bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, or laypeople shall be adjudicated by the Elder Ābhidhammika Godatta as a well-adjudicated matter.
I decree that anyone who does not abide by his adjudication shall be punished by royal command. In this way, the place should be examined.
As for value, it refers to the value of the goods. For whatever the value of a new good may be, it subsequently depreciates, just as [the luster of] freshly washed [cloth fades].
A bowl that was worth eight or ten [coins] later becomes of little value when it is broken, cracked, or damaged by the binding cord;
therefore, the value of an article must not always be determined solely by its original price. Thus should the value be assessed.
"Use" refers to the use of the article; for even through use, the value of articles such as axes and the like diminishes.
