Therefore, it should be investigated in this way: if someone takes away a hatchet worth a quarter [of a kahāpaṇa] belonging to another, the owner of the hatchet should be asked:
"For how much did you buy this hatchet? "For a quarter, venerable sir.
"But did you set it aside after buying it, or did you use it? If he says, "One day I used it as a tooth-stick..."
Or if she has cut, sharpened, or whetted a dye-stone, a cloth for boiling dye, or a piece of wood;
then it should be understood that her original value is lost.
And just as it is with an adze, so it is with a collyrium box, a collyrium stick, a key, straw, husks, or brick-dust—even by merely washing them after using them once.
It is of great value. Even by the mere polishing of the three circles with a shark-tooth scraper, or by the mere wearing of the water-strainer once as an undergarment or upper robe,
or by placing it on the shoulder or the head as part of its ritual use, or by the mere shaking off of rice and so forth from it,
or even by removing just one or two grains, or even by picking out a single pebble or stone— [it is of great value].
The value is forfeited even by merely discarding it; even by turning over the container of ghee, oil, or similar substances;
even by merely removing a fly or an ant from it before discarding it;
or even by scratching with a fingernail and taking a mere atom-sized portion for the purpose of testing the sweetness of a lump of sugar. Therefore, anything worth even one *pāda*—
In the manner already described, the property has been depleted through use by the owners; the monk who took it away should not be dealt with according to a *pārājika* offense.

Thus should the use be examined. Having thus weighed these five points, a wise person should maintain them for the sake of the goal, and should place an offense or a non-offense, whether grave or light, in its proper place.
The explanation of these terms, beginning with “should take up… should spend the appointment,” is now concluded.
Now, as for the passage beginning with “in what kind of taking of what is not given,” which was stated by one who analyzes [the rule], it begins with the words “what kind of thing is called.”
In that context, "of such a kind" means of such a sort. Since that [value] begins from a quarter (pāda), he said: "a quarter, or what is worth a quarter, or more than a quarter.
Therein, by "quarter," he indicates an unallowable article (akappiyabhaṇḍa) worth exactly one-fourth of a kahāpaṇa.
By "what is worth a quarter," he indicates an allowable article (kappiyabhaṇḍa) worth one-quarter of a kahāpaṇa. By "more than a quarter,"...
Both [cases]. Up to this point, the basis for the occurrence of the second *pārājika* offense has been shown in its entirety.
"King of the earth" (*pathabyā rājā*) refers to a king of the entire earth, such as a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*) like Aśoka, or any other king over a single island, such as a Sinhalese king.
"Local king" (*padesarājā*) refers to one who is the lord of a portion of a single island, such as Bimbisāra, Pasenadi, and others.
"Maṇḍalika" refers to those who enjoy even a single district as their own domain.
"Antarabhogika" refers to those who are the owners of a few villages situated between two kings. "Akkhadassa" means judges;

they sit in the hall of justice and, according to the nature of the offense, prescribe punishments for thieves such as the cutting off of hands or feet. As for those who have attained high positions...
When ministers or princes have committed an offense, they report it to the king, for they do not decide such serious matters themselves.
"High officials" (*mahāmatta*) refers to great ministers who have attained high positions;
they too carry out the king's business by sitting in various villages or market towns. "Or whoever else" refers to others as well who are dependent upon the royal family.
Whether they rely on a single sovereignty or rule over a divided territory, he shows that all of them are "kings" in this context.
"They might kill" means they would beat and cut [them]. "They might banish" means they would expel [them]. Having said such things as "You are a thief," they would revile them;
for that very reason he says, "This is a reproach. "With reference to the former" refers to sexual intercourse.
This refers to a person who, having practiced the Dhamma, has fallen into an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
The remainder is clear because it follows the method previously explained and because the meaning of the words is obvious. 93.
Having thus analyzed the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) according to the sequence of its terms, [the text now addresses] that which begins with "if he should take," and so forth.
Having shown the taking [of goods] in brief by means of six points, the goods to be taken—"whether it be a pāda, or what is worth a pāda, or more than a pāda"—are indicated in brief.

In order to show them in detail, exactly as they are situated wherever they may be and according to the manner in which their taking occurs, so as to block any opening for the pretext of future wicked bhikkhus, [the text says]: "That which is on the ground..."

Having established the matrix (mātikā) by way of the method beginning with "situated on land" and so forth, he stated its detailed analysis (vibhaṅga) by way of the method beginning with "goods situated on ground (bhūmaṭṭha) means goods placed upon the earth," and so forth.
The discussion on the twenty-five modes of taking [what is not given] is finished.
*Bhūmaṭṭhakathā* 94.
Herein follows the exposition of the legal decision together with an explanation of the obscure terms. "Buried" means placed after digging it into the ground.
"Concealed" means covered over with dust, bricks, and so forth. Regarding "property buried in the ground"... [as before] ...it goes.
"Or, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means: when a monk, having discovered by some means that a commodity has been placed in the ground after being buried or concealed,

and with a thieving mind thinking "I shall take it," rises and goes during the night— even before he reaches the place where the commodity is— he incurs an offense of wrong-doing for all his bodily and verbal movements.
He incurs [an offense]. How so? For as he exerts himself for the purpose of bringing it out, whatever limb or member he moves, in every case there is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
When he adjusts his lower garment and upper robe, for each movement of the hand there is a *dukkaṭa*.
Thinking, "This great treasure cannot be brought out by one person alone; I shall seek a second companion," he [seeks] a friend...
If one wishes to go into his presence and opens the door, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every step and for every hand-movement.
However, there is no offense if the door is closed or if it is something else that does not assist in the act of going.

Having gone to the place where he is lying down, if one calls out, "So-and-so," and after announcing the matter says, "Come, let us go," there is an offense of wrong-doing for every word spoken. He...
If she rises at his word, she incurs a *dukkaṭa*. Having risen and wishing to go to him, she adjusts her lower garment and upper robe;
when she opens the door and approaches him, there is a *dukkaṭa* for every hand-movement, gesture, or step.
He asks her, "Where are so-and-so and so-and-so? Summon so-and-so and so-and-so."
For every utterance, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Having seen that all have assembled, he says, "I have discovered such a treasure in such-and-such a place;
let us go and take it, and we shall perform meritorious deeds and live in happiness.
For every such utterance, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
Having thus obtained a companion, he searches for a spade.

However, if he already possesses his own spade, then while going with the thought, "I shall fetch it," and while taking it up and carrying it, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense in every instance—whether by hand, by arm, or by foot.
If he has none, he goes to another monk or a householder and asks for one; and while asking, if [he says] "a spade..."
If one requests without speaking falsely, saying, "Give me [something]; I have need of a hoe; there is something that must be done;
having done it, I will bring it back," then for every such statement there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If, however, one speaks falsely, saying, "There is a drainage ditch to be cleared" or "There is floor-work to be done in the monastery," then for each and every false statement, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated that there is only *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) for both truth and falsehood; this should be understood as a clerical error.
For there is no such thing as *dukkaṭa* in place of a *pācittiya* (offense requiring expiation) regarding the preliminary stage of taking what is not given.
But if there is no handle for the spade, and one sets down an axe or a hatchet, thinking, "I will make a handle," and goes for that purpose—
Having gone there, he cuts dry wood, hews it, and beats it; for all these actions involving the hand and the foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he cuts a living tree, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Beyond that, for all subsequent applications, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
However, in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* and the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that even for those seeking an axe or a hatchet for the purpose of cutting trees, creepers, or shrubs growing there...
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) has been stated. However, if they think, "If we ask for axes, adzes, and hoes, we will be suspected;

let us produce iron ourselves," and then go to the forest and dig up earth for the sake of iron seed—then for those digging unallowable earth, there are offenses of wrong-doing together with offenses of expiation (pācittiya); so it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī.
And just as it is here, so in all cases where there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya), one is not exempt from the offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For those digging on allowable ground, there are only offenses of wrong-doing. But having taken up seed, thereafter for every action, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each individual act.

Even in the search for a basket, there is an offense of wrong-doing according to the method already stated regarding hand-movements and foot-movements. In the case of lying, there is an offense of expiation.
The entire matter regarding the offense of *pācittiya* for cutting creepers out of a desire to make a basket should be understood exactly as in the previous method.

Regarding the phrase "or there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* while going": if one goes toward the place where the treasure is located with a companion and a spade-basket thus sought, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* for every step taken.
However, if, while going, [one thinks], "Having obtained this treasure, I shall perform an offering to the Buddha..."
If one generates a wholesome thought, thinking, "I will perform an offering of Dhamma or provide a meal for the Saṅgha," there is no offense in going with a wholesome mind.
Why? Because it is said: "If one goes with a thieving mind, or [if one goes] a second time... [etc.]... there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
And just as in this case, so in all instances there is no offense for one who has no thieving mind. Having stepped off the path to a place where treasure is stored...
If one cuts vegetation while preparing a path for the purpose of walking, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). If one cuts dry wood, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Grown there" refers to that which has grown upon a jar buried for a long time. "Wood or creeper" means not only wood and creepers;
for anyone who cuts grass, trees, creepers, or the like—whether wet or dry—it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing because of the concurrent application of the act.
The Elders have presented this eightfold *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) by bringing it together in this place:

the *dukkaṭa* of preliminary action, the *dukkaṭa* of simultaneous action, the *dukkaṭa* of touching what is not permitted, the *dukkaṭa* of improper conduct, the *dukkaṭa* of the Vinaya, the *dukkaṭa* of what is known, the *dukkaṭa* of a motion, and the *dukkaṭa* of promising.
In that regard: "With a thieving mind, [taking] a second hoe or a basket..."
“Or seeks [it], or goes [for it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This is called the preliminary wrong-doing (*pubbapayoga-dukkata*).
For here, where there would be a wrong-doing, there is a wrong-doing; where there would be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), there is indeed an offense of expiation.
“If one cuts wood or a creeper grown there, there is an offense of wrong-doing. This is called the concurrent wrong-doing (*sahapayoga-dukkata*). But here, however—

The matter of a *pācittiya* offense and the matter of a *dukkaṭa* offense both remain within the category of *dukkaṭa*. Why? Because they constitute a concurrent preliminary effort (*sahapayoga*) toward theft.

Furthermore, regarding the *dukkaṭa* stated for one who touches the ten kinds of gems, the seven kinds of grain, and all items such as weapons and implements—this is called the "offense of touching what should not be touched" (*anāmāsa-dukkaṭa*). As for the fruits produced thereon from plantains, coconuts, and so forth...
The *dukkaṭa* mentioned for one who touches [food] is called the *durupaciṇṇa-dukkata*.
However, the *dukkaṭa* mentioned for one walking for alms who takes food from a bowl where dust has fallen, without having first received it or washed it, is called the *vinaya-dukkata*.
"If, having heard [the admonition], they do not speak, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*."
This is called *ñātadukkaṭa*. That which is stated among the eleven formal admonitions (*samanubhāsanā*) as “an offense of wrong-doing for the motion” (*ñattiyā dukkaṭaṃ*) is called *ñattidukkaṭa*.
“Monks, for that monk neither the first rains-residence (*purimikā*) is recognized nor is there an offense of wrong-doing for the promise (*paṭissave*)”—this is called *paṭissavadukkaṭa*.
This, however, is *sahapayogadukkaṭa* (wrong-doing by simultaneous application).

Therefore it was said: "For anyone who cuts grass, trees, creepers, and so forth—whether wet or dry—there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) because of the simultaneous application [of the action].
However, if, even when grass, trees, creepers, and so forth growing there are cut, a sense of shame (lajjā-dhamma) descends upon him, there is restraint (saṃvara).
When [the offense] arises, one is freed by confessing the *dukkaṭa* for cutting.
However, if he does not abandon the task and continues to dig the soil with persistence, the *dukkaṭa* for cutting is suspended, and he incurs the *dukkaṭa* for digging.
For even one who digs unallowable earth incurs only a *dukkaṭa* here, because it is a simultaneous action. But if he has dug in all directions...
Even for one who has reached the base of the water-pot, the quality of shame arises; having confessed the *dukkaṭa* offense caused by digging, he is released.

"Or he arranges it": if, however, with persistent effort he arranges the soil and makes a heap on one side, the *dukkaṭa* for digging is quelled, and he stands guilty of the *dukkaṭa* for arranging. And while making that soil into heaps here and there—

For every act of preparation, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, if after making a heap one abandons the task, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing for violating the sense of shame;
having confessed the *dukkaṭa* for the act of shifting, one is released. "Or he removes it":
if, however, with persistence, he digs up the soil and throws it outside, the *dukkaṭa* for shifting subsides, and he stands guilty of the *dukkaṭa* for removing.
However, if one scatters dust here and there with a spade, with the hands, or with a basket, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each such action.
But if, after having removed all the dust and placed the jar on dry land, one still incurs the nature of shamelessness, one is released after confessing the dukkaṭa of the removal.
Yet, if he touches the jar while still possessing the intention [to steal], [he incurs a heavier offense].
The offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for lifting ceases, and he stands guilty of the offense of wrong-doing for touching.
Even after touching, one who incurs a state of shame is freed by confessing the offense of wrong-doing for touching.

But if, still with the same intention, he makes the pot shake, the offense of wrong-doing for touching ceases, and he stands guilty of the grave offense (thullaccaya) as stated in the rule: "If he makes it shake, there is an offense of thullaccaya."
In this context, here is the etymological explanation for both *dukkaṭa* and *thullaccaya*:

first, regarding *dukkaṭa*, it is "badly done" (*duṭṭhu kataṃ*) because it was performed by failing the duty prescribed by the Teacher. Alternatively, it is "badly done" in the sense that the action is deformed;
it does not shine among the actions of a monk—thus it is *dukkaṭa*. And this has been said:
“Listen to what is truly meant by ‘dukkaṭa’:
that which is transgressed, missed, stumbled over, and what is ill-done.
Whatever evil a person commits, whether openly or in secret...”
They declare it to be a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing); therefore, this is so called.

But the other is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) because of its grossness (*thūla*) and its transgression (*accaya*). Furthermore, in this context, the sense of a compound should be understood as in such passages as "in the future life, a bad destination" and "that which has a bitter fruit. Among those [offenses] that are to be confessed in the presence of one person...
Indeed, among transgressions, there is no transgression as grave as this. Therefore it is said: "Because of its gravity and because of its being a transgression, it is a *thullaccaya*.
And this has been said: "Listen to the truth regarding what is called a *thullaccaya*:
that which one confesses in the presence of another, and that which the other accepts."
“There is no transgression equal to this; therefore it is so called.

For each instance of causing to quiver, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). Even after causing it to quiver, one who has fallen into a state of shame is released from the offense after confessing a *thullaccaya*.
And in this case, starting from the very first instance of the preparatory effort (*payoga*), each preceding act constitutes an offense.

It subsides. However, for one who has descended into the state of shamefulness without having performed the preliminary effort (*payoga*), all those offenses—whether *dukkaṭa* or *pācittiya*—incurred during the preliminary effort must be confessed.
And in the case of performing the preliminary effort together [with others], even many *dukkaṭas* arising from cutting [the grass] there subside upon reaching the act of digging;
there is only a single *dukkaṭa* for the digging itself. Even if there are many [offenses] regarding the digging...
In the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* it is stated that when the act of spreading out occurs, even many instances of lifting are included;
when lifting occurs, even many instances of touching are included; and when touching occurs, even many instances of moving [the object] reach a state of subsidence.

Furthermore, regarding the digging of soil and so forth, even if many offenses arise when a factor involving shame (*lajjidhamma*) has occurred, one is released by confessing only a single one. This is the subsidence of the preceding offense.
Furthermore, this statement—“The *dukkaṭa* for the motion (*ñatti*) and the *thullaccaya*s for the two proclamations (*kammavācā*) are extinguished”—is found only in the *Anusāvana-sutta*s.
However, in this case [regarding the second *pārājika*], it must be accepted according to the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*-masters.

Regarding the phrase "he causes to move from his place, there is an offense of *pārājika*": this refers to one who, even after causing [the organ] to quiver, does not yet descend upon the part characterized by modesty (*lajjidhamma*).
The meaning is that if one causes that pot to move even by the measure of a hair’s breadth from its place, one incurs an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).
Furthermore, the displacement from its place here should be understood through six modes. How so?
While holding the pot at its rim and pulling it toward oneself, [if] even a space the measure of a hair’s breadth touched by this end [is moved] by the opposite end...

If he causes it to pass beyond [the boundary], it is a *pārājika*. Likewise, having grasped it, while pushing it further, if he causes it to pass even by the breadth of a hair’s tip from the point touched by this side to the opposite side, it is a *pārājika*.

Or, while moving it to the left or to the right, if he causes it to pass even by the breadth of a hair’s tip from the point touched by the left side to the right side, it is a *pārājika*. Or, by the right side...
If, with the left hand, one causes it to pass even by the breadth of a hair’s tip over the space touched [by the other], it is a *pārājika*.
If, lifting it upwards, one frees it from the ground even by the breadth of a hair’s tip, it is a *pārājika*.

If, having dug [underneath] and pushing it down, one causes even the space touched by the base to pass over the rim of the mouth even by the breadth of a hair’s tip, it is a *pārājika*—thus regarding a jar standing in one place. But if, regarding the rim of the jar’s mouth...
Having made a tethering post—either of iron or of heartwood such as *khadira*—and having driven it into the earth, they fasten it there with a chain;
when bound by a single chain in one direction, two places are possible;
when bound by four chains in two, three, or four directions, five places are possible.
In that case, regarding a pot tied to a single post: if he first pulls up the post or cuts the chain, it is a *thullaccaya*.
If he then moves the pot even by the breadth of a hair from its place in the manner previously described, it is a *pārājika*.
Alternatively, if he first pulls up the pot, it is a *thullaccaya*; if he then [moves] the post even by the breadth of a hair from its place...

If he causes [the animal] to move away, or cuts the chain, it is a *pārājika*. By this same method, even in the case of a jar tied to two, three, or four stakes, it is a *pārājika* at the final movement from its place. In the other instances, a *thullaccaya* should be understood.
If there is no stake, and having made a ring at the end of the chain, it is inserted into the root growing there—
Having first lifted the pot and subsequently cut the root, he removes the ring: it is a *pārājika*.
If, however, without cutting the root, he moves the ring here and there, he is protected [from the offense].
But if, even without removing it from the root, he grasps it with his hand and makes it go into the air, it is a *pārājika*. This is the distinction here; the rest is exactly as previously stated.
However, some plant banyan trees and the like on the rim of a water-jar for the sake of a sign; the roots grow so as to encircle the jar.
For one who cuts them with the intention, "I will take the jar by cutting the roots," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every stroke of the cut.
Once they have been cut and the space cleared, if he displaces the jar from its place even by the width of a hair, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
While cutting the roots, the pot rolls and goes to a low place; he still guards it. When he lifts it from that place, it is a *pārājika*.

If, after the roots have been cut, the pot remains standing on even a single root, and he cuts it thinking, "It will fall when this root is cut," then at the mere moment of cutting, it is a *pārājika*. But if...
She stands like a pig tied by a snare with a single root; there is nothing else attached.

As soon as that root is cut, it is a *pārājika* offense. If a large stone has been placed on top of a water-jar (*kumbhi*), and wishing to lift it away with a staff, she cuts the tree growing on top of the jar, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. Near it...
If one cuts off a stalk and takes it, because that stalk was not intended for one's own use, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for cutting it.

Regarding "one's own vessel": if, being unable to lift the pot, one inserts one's own vessel into the interior of the pot in order to take the goods contained within it, [and if the value therein is] five māsakas or more than five māsakas...

If one touches [an object] with a thieving mind, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Furthermore, the definition [of "value"] is stated here for the purpose of determining the *pārājika* offense.
However, even one who touches an object worth less than five *māsaka* coins with a thieving mind incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
Regarding the term "makes it move": as long as one makes it move by joining it together and inserting it into one's own vessel, to that extent one is said to "make it move."
It is said. Moreover, even if one merely stirs [the contents] here and there, he indeed causes them to quiver; he incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.

But when the state of being a single connected whole is severed—such that what is in the pot remains in the pot alone, and what is in a vessel remains in the vessel alone—then it is said to have "gone into its own vessel.
Having done this, even if [the contents] are not removed from the pot, one incurs a *pārājika* offense regarding the vessel.
"Or cuts a fist": here, just as coins passing through the gaps between fingers do not touch the coins already inside a jar, so too one is said to "cut a fist" when making a fist [in such a way];
he also incurs a *pārājika* offense. "Mounted on thread" (*suttārūḷha*) means mounted upon thread; this is a designation for both that which is woven with thread and that which is made of thread.
For *pāmaṅga* (necklaces) and the like may be made of gold, made of silver, or made of thread; and there are also pearl necklaces and so forth.
These are included right here. "A turban" refers to a cloth for wrapping the head. If one touches any of these with a thieving mind, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one makes them move, it is a *thullaccaya*. If one raises anklets and so forth by grasping them at the end without letting them hang in the air, it is a *thullaccaya*.

Regarding the phrase "removing while rubbing": here, for one who removes [the contents] by rubbing—whether the pot has been placed on top of another full pot so that they are level with the rim, or placed with one end at the base and the other end at the mouth-rim—there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
For one who releases [the contents] from the mouth of the pot, there is a *pārājika* (defeat). However, regarding that which is in a half-filled pot...
Or if it is placed in an empty jar, its "place" is only the space touched by itself, not the entire jar;
therefore, even for one who rubs it out or removes it, when even a hair’s breadth has been released from the settled space, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
However, for one who lifts straight up a jar that is either full or less than full, [the offense occurs] at the bottom edge of the settled space.

If it has been released, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika). For one who moves any article capable of constituting an offense entailing defeat that was placed inside a pot—whether moving it throughout the entire pot or pulling it out by rubbing against the rim—the offense is a serious transgression (thullaccaya) as long as it does not pass beyond the mouth-rim of the pot.
For, according to the *Saṅkhepa-Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, the entire pot constitutes the "place" for that object.
It has been stated [thus]. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "The 'place' (ṭhāna) refers only to the specific spot where [the bowl] was set down, not the entire pot.
Therefore, for one who releases [the bowl] even by the breadth of a hair from its original position, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense. That is the authoritative standard.
As for the other case, regarding one who does not let it go into the air, it is explained according to the method of the cloth-covering placed on a clothes-stand (*cīvaravaṃsa*).
That should not be accepted. For when a heavy matter has been brought forward in the adjudication of the Vinaya, one must stand firm;
this is the nature of the Vinaya. Furthermore, this should be understood from the statement: "He makes it enter his own vessel, or he cuts off a handful.
Just as when something is inside a pot, the entire pot is not the locus [of that thing].
Regarding the drinking of any of the [four] substances beginning with ghee, the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* states that if one drinks even a single mouthful in a single act, it is a *pārājika* offense.

However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries, this distinction is shown: "If one drinks while drawing [the liquid] in without withdrawing the mouth, and the value of what has entered the throat does not reach a *pāda*, then together with what remains in the mouth, it reaches [the required value];
[in such a case], one is still protected [from the full offense]."
However, it becomes a *pārājika* offense only at the very moment the throat is delimited. Even if one closes the lips while delimiting them with the lips, it is indeed a *pārājika*.
For one drinking through lotus stalks, bamboo tubes, reed pipes, and so forth, if the value of the drink is reached once it has entered the throat, it is a *pārājika*.
If the value is reached together with what is still in the mouth, it is not yet a *pārājika*.
If, having formed a single continuous connection with the lotus stalk and so forth, it is merely enclosed by the lips, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If it is valued together with the lotus stalk and so forth, then even when the stalk and so forth are merely covered by a finger at their base, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Even if it is worth more than one-quarter [of a kahāpaṇa], provided that it has not entered the throat and is still on the lotus stalks and so forth or in the mouth.
“Having become joined as one, it remains; indeed, it protects.
Since all of this follows the method of “making it enter its own vessel” or “cutting it with the fist,” it is clearly demonstrated. This, then, is the method regarding what is joined as one.
However, if one drinks by taking [the water] with the hand, or with a bowl, or with a dish or some other vessel, [the same principle applies].
When the value of the object reaches one *pāda* during that single act of taking, the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) is incurred once that [act] is completed.
Now, if the object is of great value, even if it is possible to take the value of one *pāda* in a single act by means of a small tool, the offense of defeat occurs at the very first lifting.
However, for one who takes a vessel by submerging it, it remains protected as long as it remains a single connected whole. This is determined by the boundary of its rim.

Or it is a *pārājika* offense by way of removal. However, when one draws ghee, oil, or honey-syrup—which is clear and just like oil—into a jar and pours it into one's own vessel, because of their clarity there is no state of being a single connected mass;
thus, as soon as [the liquid] has fallen from the rim of the mouth when the value is one *pāda*, it is a *pārājika*.
But honey and molasses that have been boiled and set aside become as sticky as glue; they are capable of being drawn out and pulled back.
When remorse arises, one is able to withdraw them while they remain still joined together.
Even if this [food] has passed from the rim of the mouth and entered the bowl, it is protected because it remains connected with the exterior; [this applies] from the rim of the mouth...
But when it has been cut, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika). Furthermore, if one, with a thieving mind, puts into another's pot—
whether it be ghee or oil sufficient for a quarter-measure, or anything from a linen garment down to a piece of hide or similar items—
that which must be drunk, there is an offense entailing defeat the very moment it leaves the hand.
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that if a person with the intention to steal, knowing that oil will now be poured into an empty oil-jar, puts anything into it,
and if that object is worth five māsakas when the oil has been poured in and he drinks it, he commits a *pārājika* offense at the very moment of drinking. However,
that [statement] is contradicted by the decision regarding the straightening of a dried-up irrigation channel in that very same place.
In this case, the characteristic of "taking away" (*avahāra*) is not discernible; therefore, it should not be accepted [as an offense].
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, a *pārājika* offense is stated for its removal; that is appropriate.
Having placed goods there for the purpose of guarding another's empty jar, when oil has spilled therein, [if one thinks]: "If this..."
Thinking, “He will find out; he will catch me,” one who, being afraid, lifts up merchandise for which a foot’s worth of oil was drunk with the intent to steal, commits a *pārājika* offense.
If one lifts it up with a pure mind, but others cause it to be brought back, it is a *bhaṇḍadeyya*.
The meaning of *bhaṇḍadeyya* is that the price of what was lost by another, or that very same merchandise, must be given. If not... [text ends]

If he gives [the substance] when the owner has relinquished his responsibility, it is a *pārājika* offense. If another person pours ghee or oil into someone else’s pot, and he then places a vessel for drinking oil there with a thieving mind, it is a *pārājika* offense according to the method already stated.
Having learned that ghee or oil is being poured into another’s empty pot, if he acts with a thieving mind—
If he deposits the goods, then according to the method previously stated, there is a *pārājika* offense upon their recovery.

If, having deposited them with a pure mind, he later recovers them with a thieving mind, there is likewise a *pārājika*. If he recovers them with a purely [innocent] mind, there is neither theft nor liability for the debt;
however, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that there is merely no offense. [As in the case of: "Why is there oil in my pot?"
"‘You pour it out!’—being angry, he takes up his own goods and throws them away; this is not ‘giving the goods’," so it is stated in the *Kurundi*.
If, with a mind of theft, desiring to drain the oil, he pulls a jar by its rim, there is a *pārājika* offense when the value of one *pāda* has been drained.
With that same mind of theft, he makes it leaky, thinking, "It will dry up and go away," [and there is an offense] when the value of one *pāda* [has been lost].

When the owner has departed, it is a *pārājika* offense. If one makes a breach with the intention of stealing—whether by cutting downwards (*omaṭṭha*), upwards (*ummaṭṭha*), or obliquely (*vemaṭṭha*)—this is a point of confusion;
therefore, it must be thoroughly examined. This is the analysis here:
"cut downwards" means a downward-facing breach; "cut upwards" means an upward-facing breach; "cut obliquely" means...

It is like a hole cut straight through a gourd. In that case, for one who has inserted [the organ], even if the oil—measuring a foot in depth—has flowed out from the inner end after it was applied starting from the outside, but has not yet exited the exterior, there is a *pārājika* offense. Why? Because as soon as it has flowed out from there, it is considered "having gone outside";
it does not receive the designation of being "inside the vessel. [This applies] to that which was applied starting from the inside and [flowed out] from the outer end.

When it has flowed out to the value of a quarter (pāda), there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika). For one who has had his hair shaved, whether it was done in such a way or otherwise, when it has flowed out from the outer edge to the value of a quarter, there is an offense entailing expulsion.
For as long as it has not flowed out from the outer edge, it remains merely within the vessel.

It is stated in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā): "In the case of one whose head is shaven, he should be dealt with according to the flow [of the substance] from the middle of the skull. Furthermore, that which is inside...
If [the breach] is made starting from the outside and placed in the middle, it is equalized by breaking the embankment of the pond.

However, if it is made starting from the inside, it must be carried out along the outer edge; if made starting from the outside, it must be carried out along the inner edge—this is what is appropriate here.
But as for one who, with a thieving mind, thinking "it will go around," [removes] the stand of a water-pot...
If she removes either the support or the stopper, once the oil has flowed out, there is a *pārājika* offense.

However, having recognized that it was in the state of being poured with oil, if the empty jar is worn out or holes have been made in it, then subsequently the value of the goods to be paid is determined by the amount of oil that actually flowed out.
In some commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is also written that this constitutes a *pārājika*, but that is a scribal error.
If, with a mind of theft, thinking, "A pebble or a stone will fall onto the full jar and break it,
and then the oil will pour out," he makes it difficult to fasten or places it poorly, then for one who acts so that it is bound to fall inevitably,
there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) at the mere act of doing so. If he does this over an empty jar, and later [the jar becomes] full...

Having fallen [into the water], it breaks; this is "value of the goods" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). For in such cases, because the effort was made at a time when the goods were not yet lost, there is no *pārājika* offense from the very beginning.
However, because the means for the destruction of the goods has been performed, there is "value of the goods.
When those who are making him retrieve it do not give [the goods back], there is a *pārājika* offense due to the owner's relinquishing of responsibility.
With a thieving mind, one straightens a watercourse, thinking, "It will flow in a curve," or "It will overflow its banks.
Whether it flows in a curve or overflows its banks, at the moment of straightening it, there is a *pārājika* offense.
For such applications are included within the category of "taking by prior application. This refers to the case where, after the dry watercourse has been straightened, water subsequently arrives.
Whether it goes after turning around or crosses the boundary, it is an offense involving the forfeiture of the goods. Why? Because there was no effort to move it from its place.
Its characteristic will become clear in the section on the boat.
Regarding the phrases "breaks right there" and so forth, it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "‘Breaks’ means with a mallet..."
Having struck it, he breaks it. He discards it, or having poured water or sand over it, he causes it to be swept away.
He burns it, or having brought firewood, he burns it. Or he makes it unusable: he makes it something that should not be eaten or drunk;
or he throws excrement, urine, poison, leavings, or a corpse upon it—there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Because there is no displacement from one's position, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); this indeed is the domain of the Buddha.
Although it is a *dukkaṭa*, when causing [the bowl] to be brought back, there is the restitution of the object (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). In that regard, the first two do not agree;
for they share the same characteristic as making a pot cracked or making the rim straight. However, the latter two apply even to one who does not displace it from its position.
It is possible [to do so]. Therefore, regarding this matter, they state the following determination:
"In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said that 'there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because there is no displacement from one's place. This refers to the latter two cases.
For even without displacing [the object] from its place, one might burn it with a thieving mind or with the desire to destroy it, or render it unusable. Regarding the former two..."
However, for one who breaks it or discards it in the manner already described, there is displacement from its place;

therefore, for one acting thus with the intention of destroying it, there is *bhaṇḍadeyya* (the value of the goods), and with a thieving mind, it is a *pārājika*. If it is argued that this is incorrect because the word "dukkaṭa" is stated in the *Pāḷi*, we say no;
for the meaning must be understood otherwise. For in the *Pāḷi*, under the heading of the thieving mind, it says: "He breaks..."
"Some say: 'It blows, it mixes with water, it is discarded, or it vomits there, or it discards urine.
But this is the essential point here: just as one who burns grass does not wish to move it from its place, [the wind] merely breaks [the body];
yet because of that breaking, the oil and other fluids flow out, or whatever is solid therein remains as a single connected whole."
It remains. One who does not wish to discard [the oil] merely pours water, sand, and so forth upon it;
however, because of being covered by these, the oil is discarded. Therefore, it is said figuratively that "one breaks it" or "one discards it.
In this way, the meaning of these words should be understood. On the other hand, in the sense of wishing to destroy, it is also appropriate in another way. For thus:
As it is being explained, both the Pāli and the commentary are presented in a way that reconciles what precedes and what follows.
Furthermore, one should not be satisfied with this much alone, but rather, having attended upon the teachers, the definitive analysis (vinicchaya) should be understood.
The *Bhūmaṭṭhakathā* is concluded.
*Thalaṭṭhakathā* 95.

"Placed on dry land" (*thalaṭṭhe thale nikkhittaṃ*) should be understood as that which has been set down anywhere—whether on the surface of the earth or on rocky surfaces, mountain tops, and so forth—in either a concealed or unconcealed place; that is what is meant by "placed on dry land. If that...
It is considered *rāsika* (a heap); it must be determined by the decision regarding whether it has been placed inside a pot or within a vessel, and by the decision regarding the breaking of the seal.
If it is a single mass, such as resin or exudate, it must be determined by the decision regarding cooked honey or molasses.
If it is heavy and bound in a load, such as a lump of iron, a ball of sugar, or jars of oil, honey, and so forth, [it is determined] by the decision regarding its removal from its place in the pot.
It must be judged. Furthermore, the displacement of the place where a chain-locked object is situated must be observed.

However, if one pulls straight toward oneself a woolen rug, a cloth, or similar item that has been laid out spread, the offense of *pārājika* occurs when the edge on this side passes beyond the point of contact with the edge on the opposite side.
This should be observed in all directions. If one lifts it by wrapping it around, [the offense occurs] at the mere breadth of a hair.
For one who makes it go into the air, there is a *pārājika* offense. The remainder is exactly as stated in the method [already] explained.
The commentary on what stands on dry land is finished.
Now begins the commentary on what stands in the air.
96. The delimitation of the space occupied by a peacock in the sky should be understood in six ways:
in front by its beak, behind by its tail feathers, on both sides by the edges of its wings, below by the tips of its claws, and above by the tip of its crest.
A bhikkhu, thinking, "I will catch a peacock in the sky that has an owner," might stand in front of it.
If he stretches out his hand, or if the peacock flaps its wings in the air, or if it stops its flight by catching the wind, that bhikkhu incurs a dukkaṭa offense.
If he touches it with his hand while it is not moving, it is likewise a dukkaṭa.
If he causes it to move without displacing it from its place, it is a thullaccaya. Whether he seizes it with his hand or not, if [he does so] with his beak—
If he causes the snout to pass beyond the space touched by the tip of the tail-feather, or the space touched by the tip of the tail-feather [to pass beyond] the snout, it is a *pārājika*.

Likewise, if he causes the right wing-tip to pass beyond the space touched by the left wing-tip, or the left wing-tip to pass beyond the space touched by the right wing-tip, it is a *pārājika*. Likewise, [if he does so] with the tip of a claw...
If he causes the tip of the crest to pass beyond the space touched by the tip of the crest, or the tip of the toenail to pass beyond the space touched by the tip of the crest, it is a *pārājika*.
When a peacock traveling through the air alights upon any limb such as the head, that is its "place.
Therefore, even if one moves it here and there while it is perched on the hand, one is indeed causing it to quiver; however, if one were to seize it with the other hand...
If he causes it to move from its place, it is a *pārājika*. If he brings his other hand near, and the peacock, of its own accord, flies up and settles there, there is no offense.
If, having recognized that it has settled on a limb, he moves even one step with the intention to steal, it is a *thullaccaya*; at the second step, it is a *pārājika*.
A peacock standing on the ground occupies three positions: two feet and the body-tuft. Regarding that—
For one who is lifting [the animal], as long as even a single spot touches the ground, it is a *thullaccaya*.
As soon as even the tip of a hair is released from the ground, it is a *pārājika*. If it is standing in a cage, he lifts it together with the cage; it is a *pārājika*.
However, if the foot does not [touch the ground], it must be determined in all cases according to its value. [This applies to] one walking within the enclosure.
If one, with a thieving mind, carries an object outside on foot and passes beyond the boundary of the door, it is a *pārājika*.
For the place where a bullock stands within a pen is like the pen itself;

likewise, for one who, having grasped it with the hand, moves it into the air even while still within the compound, it is indeed a *pārājika*. Even when moving it within the village, [if it passes] the village enclosure...
For one who causes [the bird] to pass beyond [that boundary], it is a *pārājika* offense.

However, if he himself goes out and, with a thieving mind, frightens with a stick or a stone a bird that is wandering either in the vicinity of a village or in the vicinity of its dwelling, and thus drives it toward the forest;
and if the peacock flies up and perches on the roof of a house within the village, or on the roof of its own dwelling—then he protects [it]. But if, at the entrance to the forest...

Whether it flies up or moves away, if there is no intention such as "I will catch it after leading it into the forest," then at the mere moment it has flown up even a hair's breadth from the ground, or at the second step [of the pursuer], it is an offense involving defeat (pārājika).
Why? Because for one who has departed from a village, the very place where he stands is considered his "place. This same legal analysis applies to the kapiñjala bird and others as well.
A *sāṭaka*—a garment tossed by the force of the wind, moving through the air as if spread out upon the ground—is a garment fastened with a buckle that comes toward one;

one takes hold of one end of it with the hand. If, without disturbing its position from side to side, one causes it to move or shake during the interruption of its motion, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one causes it to move without displacing it from its place, it is an offense of wrong-doing for making it quiver.

[If he moves it slightly,] there is a *thullaccaya* offense. If he causes it to fall from its place, it is a *pārājika* offense. The delimitation of its "place" should be understood through six modes, just as in the case of a peacock.
However, when a garment that is not tied falls, as soon as one end is grasped, it falls with the second end and lands on the ground;
thus, it has two places: the hand and the ground. That [garment], while still being held, [is moved] from the first space-point where it was grasped...
If he moves it, it is a *thullaccaya*. If he subsequently lifts it from the ground with his second hand or with his foot, it is a *pārājika*.
Or if he first raises it from the ground, it is a *thullaccaya*; if he subsequently displaces it from the place where it was grasped, it is a *pārājika*.
Or, without releasing the grasp, having simply lowered the hand straight down so that it reaches the ground, with that very same hand...
If she picks it up, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This same legal analysis applies even to head-dresses. Regarding "gold or silver being cut":
when people are adorning themselves with necklaces and other ornaments, or when goldsmiths are cutting gold pins or fragments of gold, and [the item] falls while being cut;
If a monk, with intent to steal, seizes with his hand one who is coming through the air, the very act of seizing is the offense.
If he moves his hand away from the place where it was seized, it is a *pārājika*. If he picks up with his hand what has fallen upon his robe, it is a *pārājika*.
If he goes away without picking it up, it is a *pārājika* at the second step. The same rule applies even if the bowl has fallen. Or [if it falls] on the head...
If he takes with his hand something that has fallen upon his face or his foot, it is a *pārājika*. If he goes away without having taken it, it becomes a *pārājika* at the second step.
Wherever it falls, that place of falling alone is the "location";
it does not include all the limbs, minor parts, the bowl, or the robes.
The commentary on "in the air" is finished.
Regarding "in the air":
when goods placed on beds, chairs, and so forth are stolen with the intent to steal—whether those goods are allowable (*āmāsa*) or unallowable (*anāmāsa*)—[the offense is incurred].

If one touches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Regarding goods placed upon beds and chairs, the legal determination here should be understood according to the method explained for items situated on dry land. However, this is the distinction:

if a robe tied with a string is spread out on a bed or a chair and does not touch the surface of the bed with its middle part, but only touches the bed-legs, then the location is determined by those [legs].
This should be understood. For in this case, a *pārājika* offense occurs merely by crossing over the space touched by the feet [of the bed].
However, for one who carries [the robe] together with the bed and chair, the location should be understood according to the area where the legs of the bed and chair are established.
"On a clothes-rod" means on a bamboo pole or wooden staff that has been set up and bound for the purpose of hanging robes.
In this context, "place" refers only to the space touched by the area where the robe has been set down after gathering it from the far end and making the near end the limit;

it does not include the entire robe-pole. Therefore, for one who, with a thieving mind, seizes it at the limit and pulls it toward the pole, [the offense occurs when] the area touched by the robe on the pole reaches the space established at the far end of the pole.
For one who exceeds [the limit], a *pārājika* offense occurs by the mere pulling of even a single or two finger-breadths. The same principle applies to one who pulls it after grasping the end.

However, for one who shifts it merely to the left or right on that very same robe-peg—whether shifting the left end to the place of the right end, or the right end to the place of the left end—even by shifting it only ten or twelve finger-breadths, [the offense is incurred].
It is a *pārājika*. For one who lifts [the robe] upwards, it is a *pārājika* by the mere lifting of a hair’s breadth.
For one who releases a robe that has been tied with a rope—whether touching the robe-pole or not—it is a *thullaccaya*;
once released, it is a *pārājika*. For as soon as it is released, it is reckoned as "fallen from its place. Having wound it around the pole...
For one who unfastens what has been set aside, there is a *thullaccaya*; as soon as it is unfastened, there is a *pārājika*.
If, after making a loop and setting it aside, one cuts the loop or releases it, or if one releases a single end of the bamboo pole and pulls it out, there is a *thullaccaya*.
As soon as it is cut, released, and pulled out, there is a *pārājika*. Likewise, without having done so, [if one moves it] here and there on the robe-pole...
And as long as he rolls it up and guards it, it remains [within its place]. For the entire bamboo pole of the robe is the "place" for the ring. Why? Because of its nature to move about there.
But when he takes hold of it with his hand and moves it into the air, it is a *pārājika* offense.
When it is placed after being extended, the "place" is only the area touched by the space where it is set down. In that case, when it is placed having been rolled up...

The determination should be understood according to the method already stated. However, in the case of that which stands touching the ground with only one end, there are two locations by way of the area established upon the robe-pole and the area established upon the ground.

Regarding that which is standing on the ground with one end, the determination for an unfastened robe should be understood by the very same method as stated above. This same determination applies to the robe-string as well.
However, regarding goods placed after being hooked with a hook— such as a medicinal jar or a medicine bag— if it was placed without touching either the wall or the floor,
then for one who is rubbing the hook and withdrawing it, the offense of *pārājika* occurs the very moment it has slipped from the tip of the hook.
If the hook is fastened and one lifts it by its base, making it go into the air, [the offense occurs] when it leaves the tip of the hook...
Even if [the object] has not yet been removed, it is a *pārājika* offense. If it is leaning against a wall, when one first pulls it out from the tip of the hook, it is a *thullaccaya*.
When one subsequently releases it from the wall, it is a *pārājika*. The same rule applies to one who first releases it from the wall and subsequently pulls it out from the hook.
However, if, being unable to carry away heavy goods, one leaves them leaning against the wall oneself...
He removes it by means of a hook; even without having detached it from the wall, as soon as it has been removed by means of the hook, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).
For that which was made by oneself is not considered "the place. However, for that which stands touching the ground, there are only two places;
the determination regarding these has already been stated. Furthermore, regarding that which was hung after being placed in a sling, even for one who is removing it from the sling—
There is a *pārājika* offense even for one who removes [the object] from a hook together with its carrying-sling (*sikkā*).

Furthermore, in this context, the distinction of locations should also be understood by way of whether it is supported by a wall or the ground. A "wall-nail" (*bhittikhīla*) is either one driven straight into a wall or one that has grown there naturally; whereas a "tooth of a Naga" (*nāgadanta*)...
A curved [spear] is likewise struck. Having hung it upon those [hooks], the determination should be understood in the same manner as stated for the hook (aṅkusaka).

However, when two or three are standing in succession, if one has lifted and placed a spear (kunta) or a javelin (bhindivāla), and then pulls it by grasping either the tip or the butt, there is a *pārājika* offense once it has passed through even the measure of the space touched by each individual [hook]. It is precisely the measure of the space touched...
For it is not the case that all of them—whether stakes or pegs—are in such a position. Standing facing the wall and grasping [the object] in the middle, he pulls it;
as soon as the space touched by one side has passed beyond the opposite side, there is a *pārājika* offense.
The same principle applies to one who pushes it from the other side. Grasping it with the hand and lifting it straight up, even by the measure of a hair’s breadth...

If he makes it go into the air, it is a *pārājika*. If he pulls back against a wall by rubbing a [part of the] garment placed leaning against the wall, it is a *pārājika* for one who causes the tip to pass beyond the space touched by the base, or the base to pass beyond the space touched by the tip.
If, standing facing the wall, he pulls it so that the space touched on one side passes beyond the other side, it is a *pārājika*.
Lifting it straight up, he makes it reach even the tip of a hair in the air; this is a *pārājika*.

Regarding "or fastened to a tree": having climbed trees such as the palmyra tree and so forth, the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) should be understood according to the method explained for hooks and the like.
However, for one who shakes a cluster of palmyra fruit growing there, it is a *thullaccaya*. As for the fruit in which the basis for a *pārājika* offense lies...
It fills [the bowl]; at the mere moment of being freed from its bond, it is a *pārājika*. If one cuts the stalk, it is a *pārājika*.
Having placed the tip against the leaf-vein, it gains two positions: the position where it was placed and the position of the stalk;
therein the analysis should be understood according to the method already stated. However, as for one who thinks, "If it were cut, it would make a sound as it falls..."
Out of fear, one himself attaches a leaf-slip to the top and cuts it; as soon as it is cut, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).
For that which has been made by oneself is not considered "the place" [of the tree]. By this method, the determination regarding the flowers and fruits of all trees should be understood.
Regarding "even in the case of a leaf-receptacle": here, whether it be a tree-receptacle, a ring-receptacle, or a staff-receptacle—it refers to whatever it may be.
Let there be both a bowl-rest and a bag; however, it is reckoned simply as a "bowl-stand.
In that case, the place for a bowl set down upon it is precisely the area touched by the bowl. Regarding a tree-stand, the delimitation of the place occurs in five ways.
When the bowl is placed there, one should grasp it by its rim and pull it from whichever of the four directions one likes.

If one causes the other end to pass beyond the space touched by one end, it is a *pārājika*. For one who lifts [the robe] even by the measure of a hair’s breadth above [the ground], it is a *pārājika*.
This same principle applies even for one who carries [it] together with its support.
The commentary on the section concerning the air is finished.

98. Discussion on "In Water" (*udakaṭṭha*): Regarding "placed in water"—it means placed in non-flowing water such as ponds and the like, having been well concealed in copper vessels and so forth, which by their nature do not decay when submerged in water, by those who are afraid of kings and other dangers.
For him, only that portion which is firm is the "place," not the entire body of water. "Or goes:
an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)" means that for one who goes on foot in shallow water, there is a *dukkaṭa* for every step.
In deep water, for one who makes an effort with hands or feet, there is a *dukkaṭa* for every effort, whether by hand-movements or by step-movements.
The same method applies to diving in and out for the purpose of seizing a water-jar.
However, if he sees a water-snake or a predatory fish in between and flees in fear, there is no offense.

Regarding touching and so forth, the determination should be understood by the same method as that stated for a jar situated on the ground. This, however, is the distinction: in that case, one drags it after digging into the earth.
Here, one deposits it in the mud. Thus, there is a delimitation of the location in six ways.

Regarding the blue lotus and other flowers, when the substance [of the stalk] is filled within whichever flower, at the mere moment of cutting that, there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).

Among those belonging to the species of blue lotus, one remains protected as long as even a single leaf (vāka) has not been severed on any side. However, for those belonging to the species of red lotus, it is with respect to the stalk...
When the internal thread is cut, even if it is not severed [at the stalk], it does not protect [the offense from being incurred].
If lotuses and such have been cut and set aside by their owners, when the portion that fills the *vatthu* (the required measure) is removed, there is a *pārājika*.
If they are tied together by the hand, when the portion that fills the *vatthu* within that hand is removed, there is a *pārājika*. If they are tied as a bundle, when that bundle...

If one causes anything among the six concealed things to move from its place in any manner whatsoever, it is a *pārājika* offense according to the method explained regarding the jar buried in the ground.

There are lotuses and other flowers with long stalks; having made a braid of the flowers or the stalks, they are placed or tied on the surface of the water after spreading grass over ropes. Of these, [the measurement] is by the tip of the flower in length.
By means of the six modes— the limits at the edge of the rim, the limits across, the space established below, and the back of that which stands above and on top—
one should understand the delimitation of displacement from its place.
Even when one moves a cluster of flowers placed on the surface of the water, causing the water to ripple and waves to arise, [one does not displace them] even by the measure of a hair-tip.
If one displaces it from its natural place, it is a *pārājika* offense. However, if one intends, "I will take it once it has gone there," one is still protected [from the offense] for that duration;
but when one removes it from the place where it has gone, it is a *pārājika* offense. For a flower that has risen entirely out of the water, the entire body of water is its "place";
if one pulls it up straight after uprooting it, even if the tip of its stalk is only a hair’s breadth above the water—
When [the water] has passed [its boundary], it is a *pārājika*. Having grasped a flower and moved it aside, if one pulls it out and uproots it, the water is no longer its place;

at the mere moment of uprooting, it is a *pārājika*. If flowers bound in clusters are placed tied to a place in the water, or to a tree, or to a shrub, for one who moves them here and there without untying the binding, it is a *thullaccaya*; [if he unties] the binding...
If it is released, it is a *pārājika*. Having first loosened the bond and then carrying it away—here, "the delimitation of the place" by way of the six modes;
both of these have been stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts.
For one who wishes to take the flowers from a lotus plant together with the plant itself, [the delimitation] is upwards by way of the water touched by the flower-stalks and the leaf-stalks.

And the horizontal boundary of the location must be understood. For one who pulls up a lotus plant without uprooting it, drawing the flowers or leaves toward oneself, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). As soon as it is uprooted, there is a *pārājika* (defeat).
Even if one does not move the flower, petal, or stalk from its place, for one who first uproots the lotus plant itself, there is a *thullaccaya*.
If the flower and the stalk are subsequently displaced from their place, it is a *pārājika* offense.

However, one who plucks a lotus and takes its flower must be dealt with according to the value of the property. The same principle applies to flowers that are placed outside, whether they are in heaps, bundles, or tied into loads.
Whether it be a lotus root (*bhisa*) or a lotus stalk (*muḷāla*), for one who plucks that which constitutes the substance [of the flower], it is a *pārājika* offense.
And here, the location must be delimited by the area touched by mud.
Even if one uproots them, as long as not even a fine root is severed, it is still protected.

It is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* itself that if there is a leaf or a flower growing on a lotus stalk, that too is protected. However, there is a thorn on the lotus bulb for those who have reached puberty.
Like a pimple on the face, this [offense] does not protect because it is not long.
The rest is exactly as described regarding the lotus and other flowers. For fish and turtles, the entire water in tanks and such places where they have owners constitutes their "place.
Therefore, for one who catches a fish belonging to another in its place of care—whether by hook, net, snare, or hand—by whatever [means...]
The object is fulfilled by means of a fish; when even a hair’s breadth of it has been lifted out of the water, there is an offense of defeat (pārājika).

If a certain fish, while being seized, runs here and there, leaps into the air, or falls onto the bank—even if one seizes it while it is still in the air or after it has fallen on the bank—there is likewise an offense of defeat.
This applies even to a tortoise that has gone out for the sake of grazing.
The same principle applies to one who takes [water]. However, for one who releases water that has reached the water-level [of a reservoir], it is a *pārājika* offense.

Furthermore, in various regions, people dig channels similar to small streams that serve as water-conveyors for the common use of all, based on the drainage outlet of a large, universally shared reservoir.
From there, they bring out smaller irrigation ditches (*mātikā*).
At the source of each stream, they dig pits for their own use. When they have need of water, they clear the small channels and the water-conduits within those pits and lift up the stopper.
Then, along with the water, fish emerge and gradually enter the pits to dwell there.
In that regard, they do not prevent people from catching fish in ponds or in water-channels.
However, they do not allow and they prevent [others] from catching fish that have entered their own small irrigation channels (*mātikā*) or water-pools (*udakāvāṭa*);
in such cases, whoever catches fish in a pond, in a drainage pipe (*niddhamana*), or in a water-channel, he is not to be prosecuted for theft.
In the *Khuddakamātikā*, however, one who catches a fish that has entered pits or holes is to be dealt with according to the value of what was caught.

If, while being caught from there, the fish leaps into the air or falls onto the bank, there is no offense of theft for one who catches it while it is situated in the air or on the bank and separated from the water.
Why? Because it is only when the fish remains within its own domain of possession (*pariggahaṭṭhāna*) that [theft occurs].
They are the owners. For such is the agreement made there. The same principle applies to a tortoise as well.
However, if a fish being caught climbs from a pit into a small stream, there is still theft for one who seizes it there;
but for one who seizes it after it has climbed from the small stream into a watercourse, and from there into a pond, [the same applies].
There is no theft. If one entices [fish] with grains of food from a pit, lures them out, and captures them, that is indeed theft.
However, for one who entices them and then captures them by leading them toward a water-channel, there is no theft.
Some, however, bring fish from some common location and cast them into a water-pool on the western side of the site.
Having fed them, they kill two or three every day for the sake of additional food.
For one who seizes such a fish—whether it is situated in the water, in the air, on the bank, or anywhere else—it is indeed theft (*avahāra*).
The same principle applies to turtles as well. Furthermore, during the hot season, when the flow of a river has been cut off, water remains in some low-lying place; therein—
People go there having thrown in substances such as the juice of the *madanaphala* fruit for the destruction of the fish;

the fish, eating those, die and remain floating belly-up on the water. If someone goes there and, thinking, "I will catch these fish before their owners return," catches them, he is to be dealt with according to the value [of the fish].
[But] for one who catches them with the perception that they are refuse-rags (*paṃsukūla*), [there is no offense].
There is no forfeiture; however, if they cause [the fish] to be brought back, there is the obligation to pay for the goods.

When people who have gone out after putting poison in the fish return, fill their vessels, and depart while still having the desire [to return], thinking, "We shall come again," then those fish belong to their owners.
But when they depart, saying, "That is enough for us," and are thus free from desire, then—

From the moment [the resolve] is established, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who takes with a thieving mind. There is no offense for one who perceives it as a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*).
And just as it is with fish and crabs, so too should the determination for all types of aquatic creatures be understood.
The Discussion on Water is finished.
Nāvaṭṭhakathā 99.
Regarding the boat: first, showing what a boat is, he says, "A boat is that by which one crosses.
Therefore, in this context, even a dye-vat or a bundle of bamboo should be understood as a "boat. [In the delimitation of the boundary...]
However, a permanent boat—whether dug out or constructed by lashing together planks—is permissible only as a vessel for three people at the very least.
In this context, even a vessel for just one person is called a "boat.
"Placed on a boat" refers to anything, whether bound to a sense organ or not bound to a sense organ; its characteristic is the act of taking it away.

This should be understood in the same manner as explained regarding [stealing] from dry land. In the passage beginning with "I shall steal the boat," the acts of going on a second search, seizing, and moving it are also to be understood according to the method already stated.

Regarding the phrase "she releases the bond": here, for one who does not move from her place as soon as she is released from the bond, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense as long as the bond has not been released; however, once released, there is both a *thullaccaya* and a *pārājika* offense.
That [matter] will be clarified later. The remainder is exactly as stated in the method already explained. This, then, is the commentary on the canonical text (*pāḷivaṇṇanā*).

However, here is the analysis independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimuttakavinicchaya*): In the case of a ship that has been tied up and left at a certain spot in a violent current, there is only the state of being bound;
as soon as it is released from that, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*). The reasoning for this has already been stated previously. Regarding those that have gone astray...
As for a boat, however, whatever portion of water it covers while standing is its "place.
Therefore, for one who causes it to move upward, or downward, or causes it to pass beyond the area touched in the four directions, there is a *pārājika* offense at the very moment it has passed.
[In the case of] a boat that is stationary in still water and remains by its own nature without being moored, [if one moves it] forward...

Or, while pulling [the boat] from behind, or from the left or right side, as soon as one end has passed over the area touched by it and the other end has settled in the water, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).

If [the boat] is released even by the breadth of a hair’s tip above the water, and the rim of the opening passes over the area touched by the bottom of the boat below, as soon as it has passed, there is an offense entailing defeat. Having moored it on the bank...
There are two locations: the mooring of a boat placed in still water and the place where it stands.

If one first releases it from its mooring, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). Afterwards, if one causes it to move from that location by any of the six modes of movement, there is a *pārājika* (defeat).
The same principle applies if one first causes it to move from its location and afterwards releases it from its mooring. [This applies also] when it has been hauled onto dry land and turned upright.
The "place" is simply the area touched by a boat that has been set down [on dry land]. The delimitation of that place should be understood in five ways.
However, in the case of a boat set down with its bow downward, the "place" is only the area touched by the rim of its mouth;
having understood the delimitation of that place also in five ways, as soon as one crosses even a hair’s breadth upward from whichever area was touched—

It should be understood as a *pārājika* offense. On dry land, however, the "place" (*ṭhāna*) is defined as the area touched by the wooden pegs of a boat placed upon two wooden pegs after it has been hauled up;

therefore, in that case, the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) should be understood according to the method already stated regarding a robe spread out and tied over the tops of bed-legs and a *bhindivāla* (a type of container) placed on wall-peg hooks.
However, when a boat fastened by a rope— having pulled it in without untying the rope measuring sixty or seventy fathoms in length,
and having brought it so that it touches the earth— is placed on dry land together with the rope, there is not merely a spot where it has touched; rather,
[the distance] extends from the end of the rope all the way to the rear limit of the space where the boat has come to rest upon the ground.
In length it is that much; but in width, it should be understood as the extent of the space occupied by the boat, the rope, and the portion of ground where they rest.

When one pulls it either in length or in width, as soon as the space touched by one end has passed beyond the point where the other end rests upon the ground—even if only by the breadth of a hair-tip, including the rope—[the kamma-path is completed].

If [a boat] is released from the land, it is a *pārājika* offense. Furthermore, if one boards a boat standing at a landing place and, with a thieving mind, propels it by means of a rudder or a sail, it is a *pārājika* offense.

However, if one tilts a sunshade, or steps on a robe with the feet and lifts it up with the hands, making it like a sail, and causes the wind to catch it—and if the wind is strong—[then there is no offense].
If one takes [the goods] by means of a boat, it is as if they have been carried away by the wind; there is no theft on the part of the person.

There is an effort, but that is not an effort to move [the goods] from their place. However, if one leads that boat—which was moving in its natural course—by cutting off its path and directing it toward another direction, it is a *pārājika* offense. [This applies even if] it has itself reached any village landing place.
If one sells [an item] without displacing it from its place and then departs, there is no offense of theft; however, it is an offense of "value of goods" (bhaṇḍadeyya).
The commentary on the boat is finished.
The commentary on the vehicle.
100. Regarding the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*): first, showing what a vehicle is, he said, "A vehicle is called a *vayha*," and so forth.
Therein, a *vayha* is one constructed by covering it entirely with a roof like a pavilion above, covered with planks.
A *sandamānikā* is one made in the manner of a Garuda's wings, with crossbeams made of gold, silver, and so forth, provided on both sides. A chariot (*ratha*) and a cart (*sakaṭa*) are well known.

In those cases, wherever there is property—whether animate or inanimate—placed in a heap or otherwise, for one who moves it from its place with the intent to steal, a *pārājika* offense is to be understood according to the method already stated for both items situated on water and items situated on land.

However, this is the distinction: when one takes rice or other goods placed in a vehicle by means of a basket, even if the basket has not yet been lifted [from the vehicle], [the offense is incurred].
If one steals a basket and thus disrupts the unified state of the rice and other contents, it is a *pārājika* offense. This same principle applies to items situated on dry land and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "I shall steal the vehicle," the search for a second [animal] and so on follows the method already explained.
As for the expression "removes from its place," in the case of a two-yoked vehicle, there are eight feet belonging to the two oxen and two...
"Wheels" refers to ten places. For one who sits on the yoke with the intent to steal and drives the oxen away, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) when the oxen lift their feet.
However, for the wheels, once they have moved even the breadth of a hair's tip beyond the spot where they were established upon the earth, it is a *pārājika* (defeat).
But if the oxen, realizing "this is not our master," abandon the yoke and pull [the cart] back...
Whether they stand still or move about, it remains protected for the time being.

Furthermore, when one has straightened the oxen, yoked them to the pole, firmly fastened the harness, and is driving them by piercing them with a goad, then according to the same method already described, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) upon lifting their feet;
upon the wheels passing over [the boundary], there is a *pārājika* (defeat).
Even if one wheel has become stuck in the mud on a muddy path, while the oxen turn and move the second wheel, there is as yet no offense because of the presence of that one [wheel].

However, for one who again aligns the oxen straight and drives them forward, once the space touched by even a hair’s breadth of the stationary wheel has been passed, it is a *pārājika* offense. This applies to a four-yoked cart.

Furthermore, there are eighteen positions for a properly harnessed carriage, and thirty-four for one that is improperly harnessed; by this method, the various positions of a harnessed vehicle should be understood.

As for the improperly harnessed one, which is set with a single prop at the front and two props at the rear, it has five positions by way of those three props and the wheels. If there is a prop at the front...

At the lower part, it is fashioned with a rim; there are six positions. Furthermore, by way of a support for that which is supported at the yoke-end without being propped from behind, there are three or four positions.
