There are three positions for that which is placed upon a plank or a wooden beam by means of the yoke-end. Likewise for that which is placed on the ground. Or, having pulled that yoke-end toward oneself...
If he lifts it up or moves it from its place forward or backward, there is a *thullaccaya* offense.
When even a hair’s breadth has passed the point where the wheels were established, there is a *pārājika* offense.

If the wheels have been removed and it is placed upon two wooden axle-heads, there are two points [of contact]. While dragging or lifting it, if he causes it to pass beyond the touched area, there is a *pārājika* offense.
There are five points regarding an ox placed on the ground: by way of its yoke and four feet being firmly established.
For one who pulls it by seizing the yoke, there is a *pārājika* offense when the front end of the yoke passes beyond the rear ends of the feet.
For one who pulls it by seizing the feet, there is a *pārājika* offense when the rear end of the feet passes beyond the front ends of the yoke. On the flanks...
If one takes hold [of the axle] and drags it, there is a *pārājika* offense upon exceeding the point where the axles were originally fixed horizontally.
If one lifts it by taking hold of the middle, there is a *pārājika* offense when even a hair’s breadth of it is released from the earth.
Now, if there are no upright stakes, but having made the arms level and pierced through the middle, the ends of the axles have been inserted, then [the offense occurs] regarding that lower surface.

It stands touching the entire earth on all sides. In this regard, an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) should be understood as occurring when it exceeds the point of contact in the four directions and upwards.
On the ground, there is only one location for the wheel placed upon its hub (*nābhi*); its delimitation is fivefold.
For that which stands touching both the side of the rim (*nemipassa*) and the hub, there are two locations. [The third is] the portion of the rim that has risen up.

When one has stepped on it with the foot and caused it to touch the ground, or having grasped it by the spokes or the rim, lifts it up, there is no "place" (ṭhāna) that constitutes the act committed by oneself;
therefore, even while it remains [in contact], once it has merely crossed over the remaining space, it is a *pārājika*.
There are also two places for a wheel placed leaning against a wall. Of these, for one who is releasing it from the wall—
[If he moves it] from the ground, there is a *thullaccaya*. Later, when even a hair’s breadth has been lifted from the earth, it is a *pārājika*.
However, for one who first releases it from the ground, if the spot where it was resting against the wall does not shift, the same principle applies.
Then, if one seizes it by the spokes and pulls it downward, once the upper edge of the space that was touching the wall passes below, [it is a *pārājika*].
This is a *pārājika* offense. When a carriage is traveling on a road, the owner of the carriage has dismounted for some business and stepped off the path;
then another monk, coming along the opposite way, sees that it is unguarded and climbs onto it with the intention, "I will steal this carriage.
If the oxen seize the carriage and depart even without his effort, there is no theft. The rest is similar to what was stated regarding the boat.
The Exposition of the Bases of Deliverance is finished.
The Exposition of the Burden (Bhāraṭṭhakathā). 101.
Hereafter, the burden itself is the "eight bases of the burden. It is shown in four ways by way of the burden on the head and so forth. Therein:

The boundaries of the head and so forth should be understood for the purpose of avoiding confusion regarding the "lump of lead" and other such objects. Therein, first, the lower boundary of the head is as follows:
from the front of the neck down to the nape, and at the back of the neck, there is a curve at the ends of the hair;
on both sides of the neck itself, the hair grows downwards, which is called the "ear-lobes," and the portion below these constitutes the lower boundary.
Above that is the head. The burden situated within this interval is called the "head-burden.
On both sides, starting from the ears and the occipital protuberance below, and starting from the temples above;
and starting from the hollow of the neck and the pit of the throat below, and from the curve of the spine and the middle of the chest above.
From the heart-base upwards to the shoulders is the section called the "shoulder-load" (*khandha-bhāra*); it is the weight situated within this interval.

From the middle of the spine downwards from the heart-base as far as the tips of the toenails is the section called the "waist-boundary" (*kaṭi-pariccheda*); it is the weight situated all around the body within this interval.

From the collarbone downwards as far as the tips of the fingernails is the section called the "pendant-boundary" (*olambaka-pariccheda*); it is the weight situated within this interval that is called the "pendant" (*olambaka*).
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "the burden on the head," this is the unprecedented analysis:
if a monk, unbidden by the owners who have said, "Take this and go there," but of his own accord says, "Give me such-and-such;

I will carry your goods," and while going along having taken their goods upon his head, touches that goods with a thieving mind, it is a *dukkaṭa*. [This applies] up to the aforementioned limit of the head.
If he does not let go of the load but rubs it here and there, causing it to shift back and forth, it is a *thullaccaya*.
As soon as the load is lowered from the shoulder—even if the owners have the intention that "let it carry on"—it is a *pārājika* because they did not give permission.

Furthermore, even without lowering the load from the shoulder, for one who releases it from the head by even the measure of a hair’s breadth, it is a *pārājika*. This applies to a double load (*yamakabhāra*).
However, one burden rests on the head and another on the back; in that case, the analysis should be understood by way of these two locations.

This teaching, moreover, was commenced specifically with reference to the pure "head-burden" and so forth. And whatever analysis has been stated regarding the head-burden applies equally to the shoulder-burden and the others as well.
Regarding the phrase "a burden on the hand": here, because it is held by the hand, the hanging object is called "a burden on the hand.
Whether it was first taken from the ground, or taken from the head or elsewhere with a pure mind, it is nonetheless reckoned as "a burden on the hand.
If one sees such an object in a place where it has been taken and, with a thieving mind, [takes it] from the ground...
Or, for one depositing [goods] in places such as a road, it is a *pārājika* offense at the mere moment they are released from the hand. Regarding the phrase "takes them from the ground":

here, if one has deposited any of those loads on the ground with a pure mind for the sake of a morning meal or similar purpose, and then later, with a thieving mind, lifts even a hair’s breadth of them, it is a *pārājika*.
The commentary on the burden is finished.
The commentary on the monastery (ārāma): Regarding the meaning of "monastery," in order to show what a monastery is, he said: "A monastery is a flower garden or a fruit garden."
Among these, a flower garden is one where jasmine and other such flowers bloom; a fruit garden is one where mangoes and other such fruits grow.
The method for determining what has been placed in a garden from four locations is exactly as described in the section on "ground-placed" items and so forth.
However, regarding what grows there: "root" refers to any root whatsoever, such as *usīra* (vetiveria) or *hiri-vera*, which has either been uprooted or is being uprooted.
Or, for one who takes [it], when the value of the object is fulfilled by the price at which it was acquired, there is a *pārājika* offense upon its taking. Even the bulb is included under the "root.
And for one who is digging it up, even if only a small portion has been severed, there is a *thullaccaya* offense.

The detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*) therein should be understood according to the method explained regarding the lotus root (*bisa*). "Bark" refers to that which is fit for use as medicine or for dyeing.
Any tree bark whatsoever: for one who tears it off or takes what has already been torn off, there is a *pārājika* offense according to the method explained in the section on roots.
Any flower whatsoever, such as jasmine (*vassika*) or Arabian jasmine (*mallikā*):

for one who plucks it or takes what has already been plucked, there is a *pārājika* offense according to the method explained in the section on blue and red lotuses. For even among flowers, the stalk or the binding [must be severed].
Or, one protects what has not been severed. However, in the case of some [fruits] where there is a stalk (*vaṇṭa*) inside, that [stalk] does not protect [the fruit].
Regarding "fruit"—such as mango fruit, palm fruit, or whatever else—the determination for one taking it from the tree has been stated in the discourse on "what is attached to the tree.
That which has been removed and placed [elsewhere] is included among things such as those lying on the ground (*bhūmattha*).
“He makes a claim against the monastery” means that he makes a false claim, saying of what belongs to another, “This is mine”;

it is an *dukkaṭa* because it is an application of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). “He arouses doubt in the owner” means that, through his skill in legal deliberation or by virtue of being supported by powerful persons and so forth, he generates uncertainty in the owner of the monastery. How so? For he is one who is thus habituated to such deliberation.
Having seen [this], the owner thinks: "Will I be able to make this monastery my own, or will I not?
Thus, as that doubt arises, it is produced by him; therefore, he incurs a thullaccaya offense.
"He abandons the task" means when the owner [thinks]: "This man is stubborn and harsh; even if there is an obstacle to his life or to the holy life..."
If he thinks, "I shall do it myself; now I have had enough of this monastery," and thus relinquishes his responsibility (*dhura*), the accuser commits an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).

If he himself has already relinquished his responsibility, yet even after the owner has relinquished his responsibility, the accuser does not relinquish his own responsibility and instead thinks, "Having pressed him hard, I shall demonstrate my authority over him..."
Thinking, "I will give it once I have established him as one who promises to do whatever he is told," he remains zealous in the matter of what must be given; thus, for the time being, he protects it.

But then, if the claimant—thinking, "Having seized it, I shall no longer give it to him"—abandons the effort, while the owner does not abandon the effort, but seeks allies, awaits the right time, and [approaches] an assembly of the modest...
Thinking, "I shall receive it now; I will know later," he remains intent on taking it once more and continues to guard it.
But when both he [the defendant] thinks, "I will not give it," and the owner thinks, "I will not get it"—when both thus lay down their burden—then the accuser incurs a *pārājika* offense.
However, if, after having brought the charge, while conducting the legal inquiry before the decision has been finalized...

In a legal dispute, even if the owner has not relinquished his responsibility and he knows that the item is no longer his own, if he nevertheless takes any flower or fruit from it, he must be made to pay the value of the goods.
"Practicing the Dhamma" means making a legal decision within the Saṅgha of monks or in the royal court. "Defeats the owner" means...
The meaning is that by giving a bribe to the judges and inducing them to give false testimony, one defeats the owner of the monastery. Regarding the offense of *pārājika*:
it is not only for the [monk] himself; for all those who intentionally act to achieve that purpose—including the fraudulent judges and the fraudulent witnesses—it is a *pārājika*.
And in this case, the defeat occurs solely through the relinquishment of responsibility by the owner.
This must be understood. For one who does not abandon their duty is indeed undefeated.

"While practicing the Dhamma, he is defeated" means that even if he himself incurs defeat because the decision was carried out according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, he nevertheless commits a grave offense (thullaccaya) on account of causing distress to the owners through his false speech.
The exposition on the meaning of *ārāma* is finished.
The exposition on the meaning of *vihāra*: 103.

Regarding the meaning of *vihāra*, it is set forth by way of four points, exactly as described in the method already stated. Furthermore, in this context, there is also application (*abhiyoga*) in the four directions.
If one makes a claim against a monastery, a courtyard, or a dwelling given to the monks for the sake of the Saṅgha—whether large or small—that claim does not succeed.
One cannot even take it back by force. Why? Because there is no relinquishing of responsibility by all [the monks].
For in this case, it is not that all the monks from the four quarters have relinquished their responsibility.
However, one who seizes property belonging to a group—such as those distinguished as Dīgha-reciters and so forth—or to a single individual, is able to make them relinquish their responsibility.
Therefore, the legal decision in that case should be understood according to the method explained for the monastery.
The Discussion on Monasteries is finished.
104. Discussion on the Field (Khettaṭṭhakathā).
Regarding the meaning of "field" as well—first showing what a field is—it is said: "A field is that wherein the primary crop or the secondary crop grows.
In this context, "primary crop" refers to the seven kinds of grain beginning with rice; "secondary crop" refers to things such as mung beans and black gram.
The sugar-cane fields and so forth are also included right here. In this case as well, it is set forth by way of four points, exactly according to the method already stated.

However, regarding that which grows there [in the field], for one who takes the rice-ears and so forth—whether by tying them up, or cutting each one individually with the hand, or pulling them with the mouth, or uprooting many at once—the offense occurs in whichever seed, ear, or handful [is taken].
Or, if the substance is filled with fruits such as mung beans or black gram, there is a *pārājika* offense as soon as it is released from its binding.
However, even a small portion—whether a stalk, a husk, or a skin—that remains unseparated protects [the object].
A rice stalk may be long; as long as the grain-head or the stalk-handle has not emerged from within the husk, it continues to protect [the object].
If even a hair’s breadth [of the stalk] has emerged from the bottom surface of the stalk, one must be dealt with according to the value of the goods.

However, for one who takes it after cutting it with a sickle, even if the parts below have been severed and are within the grasp of the hand, as long as the tips remain entangled, it is still protected.
But once they are disentangled, if one lifts up even a hair’s breadth and the value of the object is fulfilled, it is a *pārājika* offense.

However, for one who takes what has been gathered and set aside by the owners—whether it has been made into a bundle (*sabhusa*) or not—if the value of the object reaches the required amount, there is a *pārājika* offense once that [value] is reached.

If he intends, "I will take only the salt after crushing and shaking this," he is protected for as long as he does so. Even for one who moves it from its place during the crushing and shaking, there is no *pārājika*; [the offense occurs] later when it has entered the vessel.
What constitutes a *pārājika* offense? In this case, the method of application is exactly as previously stated.
Regarding the "crossing over a threshold" and so forth, earth is said to be of incalculable value.
Therefore, if by means of even a single threshold one makes even a portion of earth the size of a hair-tip one's own property—whether the owners see it or not—it is a *pārājika*.
As soon as the name has been transferred to that stake—whether it has been cut or not cut—there is a *pārājika* offense for him and for all those who are of one mind with him.

However, if it is to be taken by means of two stakes, there is a *thullaccaya* for the first stake and a *pārājika* for the second. If it is to be taken by means of three, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the first.

In the second [act], there is a grave offense (thullaccaya); in the third, a defeat (pārājika). Likewise, even in the case of many [acts], one should understand that—excluding the final two—the preceding ones constitute an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), while for the final two, by one there is a grave offense and by the other a defeat.
And this occurs through the owners' relinquishing of their responsibility. Thus it is in all cases.
Regarding "or a fence": wishing to make it known, "This belongs to me," he either stretches out a rope or lays down a staff;

there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Thinking, "Now, by two applications of effort, I shall make this my own," there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) in the first [action] and a defeat (*pārājika*) in the second.
Regarding "or a boundary": wishing to make another's field his own by means of an enclosure, he plants wooden stakes; in the application of effort...

For the preliminary effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). When one [person] has not yet arrived, it is a serious offense (thullaccaya); when that person has arrived, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If, being unable to do so with just that much, he is able to make it his own by encircling it with branches, the same principle applies even to the felling of the branches.
Thus, for whatever means he uses to encircle it and make it his own, for each of those initial efforts, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
At the conclusion, it should be understood that for one [of the two] there is a *thullaccaya*, and for the other, a *pārājika*.

"Or a boundary" means: desiring to make another's field known as "this is mine," one shifts the boundary of one's own field—the field embankment—in such a way that it oversteps the other's field; or by means of soil, clay, and so forth.
If one expands [the area] and makes it wide, or establishes what has not yet been built, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the preceding applications.
For the two subsequent ones, by one there is a grave offense (thullaccaya), and by the other there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
The Discussion on the Field is finished.
Vatthuṭṭhakathā 105.
Regarding the eightfold basis—first, showing what is meant by "basis," he says: "Basis means 'monastery grounds' or 'vihāra grounds.
In that context, it refers to a site where, having cleared the ground alone without yet sowing seeds or planting saplings, three walls [have been built].
Any portion of land set aside for the purpose of a flower garden and so forth, whether enclosed by a fence or not, is called *ārāmavatthu* (monastery grounds).
By this same principle, any portion of land set aside for the purpose of a single dwelling (*vihāra*), a courtyard (*pariveṇa*), or a residence (*āvāsa*) is called *vihāravatthu* (dwelling grounds).
Furthermore, even that which was formerly a monastery and a dwelling, but later fell into ruin and remains as mere ground...
One who remains stationary does not perform the duties of the monastery or the dwelling; he too is included by way of the inclusion of the monastery and dwelling grounds.
Furthermore, the analysis here is exactly the same as what was stated regarding the sense of "field.
The Discussion of the Grounds is finished.
106. That which ought to be said regarding one who dwells in a village has already been stated.
107. Regarding one who dwells in the forest (*arañña*): first, showing what constitutes a forest: "A forest (*arañña*) is that which is not claimed as property by people... [and so forth].

"...that is the forest," he said. In this context, since there are forests that are claimed by people as well as those that are not, what is intended here is that which is claimed and guarded by them—where one cannot take wood, creepers, and so forth without payment.
Therefore, having stated, "that which is claimed by people..."
Again, it is said: "The forest" (*arañña*). By this, he shows the following meaning:

"The state of being unenclosed is not the defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of the forest. Rather, that which is a forest by its own natural characteristic of being a forest, yet has been enclosed by people—that is 'forest' in this context.
The detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*) therein is similar to what was stated regarding the meaning of "monastery grounds" (*ārāmaṭṭha*) and so forth.
Regarding the plants growing there, however, if even a single large and valuable tree is cut down, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
As for the phrase "or a creeper," here both bamboo and creepers are indeed considered "creepers.

In this context, whatever is long—whether bamboo or creeper—that has grown by piercing through or entwining around a large tree or a shrub, does not constitute an act of theft (*avahāra*) even if it is cut at its root.
Even when cut at the tip, it does not constitute theft; however, when it is cut both at the tip and at the root, then it constitutes theft.
But if it has been wrapped around [the tree], as soon as it is released from the tree while still wrapped, it constitutes theft.
Regarding the phrase "or grass," whether it be grass or leaves, everything is included by the term "grass"; that is for the purpose of roofing houses and so forth.
One who takes [grass or leaves] either cut by others or having cut them oneself must be made to pay the value of the goods.
Not only grass and leaves, but whatever else—such as bark of reeds or the like—if the owners have an attachment to it, one who takes it must be made to pay the value of the goods.
A tree that has been felled and left standing, even if one has traveled a long way, must not be taken. However, whoever...
If it is cut at both the top and the root, and its branches have become rotten, and its bark has fallen away, it is permissible to take it, thinking, "This has been discarded by its owners.
Even in the case of one cut for a mark, when the mark is covered by the bark, it is then permissible to take it.
When trees have been cut down for the purpose of houses and such, and those [structures] have been built and inhabited...
There are also pieces of wood in the forest that have been destroyed by rain and sun; having seen such things, it is permissible to take them thinking, "They have been discarded.
Why? Because the owners of the forest have no authority over these things.

Those by whom they were cut down after giving the forest-owners their due share are the ones who have authority; and those [pieces] have been discarded by them, for the trees grow there without any sense of possession.
If a bhikkhu first gives a gift to the forest guards, enters the forest, and has them take him to whichever tree he prefers,
it is permissible for him to go by whichever path he wishes, even without going to their place of watch. Furthermore,
if he enters without giving anything, thinking, "I will give when I leave," and has them take him to a tree, then upon leaving—
If one goes after having given what was to be given to them, it is indeed permissible.
Furthermore, if one goes with the intention [to give], and when told "Give! says "I shall give," then upon being told "Give!", it must indeed be given.
If someone gives their own wealth and says, "Let the bhikkhu go," it is considered permissible to receive; it is allowable for him to go. However, if someone who is of a domineering nature...
If he prevents [the distribution] by saying, "Do not take a portion for the bhikkhus," without having given any wealth at all;
or if the forest guards say, "How shall we receive anything if we do not take a portion for the bhikkhus and the ascetics? Give it, Venerable Sir," then it must certainly be given.
However, if [the donor] comes while the forest guards are sleeping, or are intoxicated from play, or have departed elsewhere—
If he calls out, “Where are the forest guards? and they do not appear before he goes on, it is an offense requiring restitution (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
If, having reached the place of watch, he passes by through lack of mindfulness—either while attending to his meditation subject or being distracted—it is likewise an offense requiring restitution.
Furthermore, if for one who has reached that place a thief, an elephant, a wild beast, or a heavy rainstorm arises, [it is an offense requiring restitution].
If, out of a desire to be freed from that danger, he passes through that place hastily, he is protected for the time being, but it becomes a case of "goods to be paid for" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
However, this so-called "place of protection" in the forest is even more serious than a customs house.
For regarding a customs house, one who avoids it by keeping far away without crossing its boundary incurs only a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Furthermore, for one who carries it away with a thieving mind, even if traveling through the air, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
Therefore, one must be heedful in this matter.
The Commentary on the Forest-Dweller is finished.
108. Regarding water:
"placed in a vessel" means that at a time when water is scarce, it has been stored and kept in vessels such as water-jars;
having either pulled out or broken the vessel in which it was placed, [one may drink].
Or, in the case of one who inserts his own vessel into lotus ponds or reservoirs there and takes [the water],
the legal determination should be understood according to the method explained regarding ghee and oil.

However, in the case of breaking a boundary, for one who breaks a boundary together with a grove of living beings (*bhūtagāma*) grown there, it constitutes the preliminary act (*payoga*) of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Furthermore, it constitutes an offense for every single blow.
One who cuts from the inside outwards must be dealt with according to the outer edge; one who cuts from the outside inwards must be dealt with according to the inner edge;
one who cuts both from the inside and the outside, leaving the middle intact, must be dealt with according to the middle. Having made the boundary weak...
He calls the cows himself, or has them called by village boys; when they have come, they cut through the boundary with their hooves, and thus it is broken.
Having made the boundary weak, he lets the cows enter the water, or has them entered by village boys;
the waves raised by them break the boundary and flow away. Or [he tells] the village boys, "In the water..."
If one says, "Play," or frightens those who are playing, the waves raised by them also break through the boundary as they go;

if one cuts down a tree growing in the water, or has another cut it down, the waves raised by its falling also break through the boundary as they go—it is thus destroyed by that very act. If the boundary is weak...
Having done so, for the purpose of protecting the pond, he closes the water outlet from the pond or the drain-pipe;
or he builds a dam so that water flowing from elsewhere enters therein, or he straightens the channel;
or he breaks his own pond situated on the upper side [of the other], [causing] the overflowing water—
If he goes having taken up a boundary, it is severed by that very act. In all cases, the offense must be determined according to the value of the water that has flowed out.
The same principle applies to one who removes [the water] after opening a drain-pipe. However, if by him... [regarding the boundary]...
When a boundary has been established by one who is weak, cattle— either coming of their own accord or being driven in by village boys who have not been restrained—
break through the boundary with their hooves; or, when they are made to enter the water by their own nature or by unrestrained village boys,
they create waves, or the village boys themselves, having entered and playing, create them.
Or, when a tree in a reservoir is being cut down by someone else, it falls and displaces [the water];
the displaced waves break through the embankment.
Even if one makes the embankment weak and closes the outlet for the water of a dry pond or the drain-pipe, or builds a dam on a path leading elsewhere, or [blocks] a dry channel—
Or if he straightens it, and afterwards, when the rain has fallen, the water comes and breaks the boundary, the value of the goods must be paid in every case.

But if, during the heat of summer, one cuts the boundary of a dry irrigation channel down to its base, and afterwards, when the rain has fallen, the water that arrives escapes, the value of the goods must be paid.
From whatever amount of crop arises on account of that [damage], from that...
By failing to give even a value of a single foot-measure to one's owners and thereby abandoning one's responsibility, one ceases to be a *samaṇa*.
However, in the case of a reservoir that is common to all, all people have mastery over the water in that reservoir.
Yet, below it, they cultivate crops; for the purpose of protecting those crops, large irrigation channels (*mahāmātikā*) emerge from the reservoir and pass through the middle of the fields.
That [river] too is always common to all at the time of its flowing. However, after drawing out the small channels (*khuddakamātikā*), they cause the water to enter their own respective fields.
They do not allow others to take that water. Only during the summer season, when the water has diminished, they give it out by turn.
Whoever does not receive the water when his turn arrives finds his crops wither away.
Therefore, when it is another’s turn, no one else may take [the water]. In this regard, if a monk, with a thieving mind,
causes water from another’s small irrigation channel or field to enter his own channel or field,
or causes it to flow toward the forest entrance, there is an offense of theft for him.

If someone, thinking, "It will be a long time before my turn for water comes, and this crop is withering," blocks the channel through which water enters another's field and diverts it into his own field, it is indeed theft (*avahāra*). However,
if [he does so] while the water has not yet emerged from the reservoir and has not even reached the mouth of another's irrigation channel, [it is theft] only when the channel is dry.
Just as water coming along does not enter the fields of others but enters only its own field, so it is bound here and there.
If the water has not yet departed when it was bound, it is well-bound; if it has already departed, it is merely bound, and one must pay the value of the goods.
Even for one who goes to the reservoir and, having personally opened the outlet channel, causes the water to enter his own field—[the same rule applies].
There is no offense. Why? Because the field was constructed in dependence upon the pond. However, in the *Kurundi* and other commentaries, it is stated that there is an "offense.
That does not accord with the defining characteristic given by the phrase "the site, the time, and the location. Therefore, what is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* alone is correct.
The discussion on water is finished.
109. The Story of the Tooth-stick Cleaner.
The tooth-stick cleaner is to be adjudicated according to the decision regarding the eight items belonging to the monastery. However, this is the distinction:
if one who is paid as a wage-earner for the Saṅgha brings a tooth-stick daily, or on a fortnightly or monthly basis, he, having brought it—
Even after cutting it, as long as one has not caused it to be accepted by the Saṅgha of monks, it remains the property of that [original owner] alone.
Therefore, one who takes it with a thieving mind must be dealt with according to the value of the goods.

However, if it is a valuable item produced there, even taking that which is protected and guarded by the Saṅgha of monks, one must be dealt with according to the value of the goods. This same principle applies to items belonging to a group, an individual, or a lay person.

[There are two kinds: those that have been cut and those that have not been cut. When novices bring tooth-sticks grown on the grounds of monasteries or parks for the Saṅgha by turn, they also bring them for their teachers and preceptors. As long as they have not yet cut them and offered them to the Saṅgha, everything belongs to those [teachers and preceptors] alone.
Therefore, one who takes even such [tooth-sticks] with a thieving mind is [liable] according to the value of the goods.

[The offender] must be made to pay compensation. However, once they have cut [the tooth-sticks], offered them to the Saṅgha, and placed them in the tooth-stick storehouse with the thought, "May the community of monks enjoy them as they please," from that point on there is no offense of theft;
yet the proper procedure (*vatta*) must be known. For whoever enters into the midst of the Saṅgha every day, by him—day after day—only one [stick] should be taken.

A tooth-stick should be taken. However, for one who does not go out every day, but is seen in the meditation hall, at a Dhamma discourse, or at the Uposatha assembly after having stayed there, he should observe the proper measure, place four or five tooth-sticks in his own dwelling, and use them.
When those are exhausted, if there are many more in the tooth-stick storehouse—
They should indeed remain, and may be brought back and eaten again.
However, if one brings them without observing the proper measure, they may be exhausted in the storeroom even before those already taken have been consumed.

Consequently, some elders might say, "Let those who took them bring them back," while others might say, "Let them eat them; the novices will bring more. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding such disputes:
The measure should be observed; however, there is no fault in taking [more than that]. Even when traveling on a journey, one may go after having placed one or two [tooth-sticks] in a bag.
The discussion on tooth-sticks is finished.
The Discourse on the Forest-Tree (Vanappatikathā) 110. "Forest-tree" (*vanappati*) means the lord of the forest; this is a designation for the preeminent tree of the forest.

Here, however, every tree that has been taken possession of by humans is intended, such as the mango, breadfruit, and jackfruit trees. Or else, it refers to places where pepper vines and the like [grow].
They hang it up; while it is being cut, if it falls to the ground even while still connected by a single creeper, a piece of bark, a splinter, or the soft inner wood, it is still protected.
But that which, though cut, remains connected by creepers or by the branches of neighboring trees and, because it is supported, remains perfectly upright—[it is protected].
It remains standing, or even as it falls, it does not reach the ground; there is no exemption from liability in that case—it is indeed theft.
Even when a tree, though cut by a saw, stands exactly as it was as if it were uncut, the same principle applies.
However, if one makes a tree weak, and subsequently shakes it so that it falls, or causes another to shake it, or [causes] something else to...
If, having cut down a tree nearby, one covers it over, or causes another to cover it over;
or having caused a monkey to fall upon it, one places it there, or causes another to place it there;
or if bats cause that tree to fall, it is the theft of that [person].
But if, after he has made the tree weak, another person— without being commanded— shakes it and causes it to fall, or if the tree falls upon him,
or if monkeys or bats climb up by their own nature, or if another person climbs it without being commanded,
or if he himself cleanses the opening of a wind-channel, and a strong wind comes and [strikes] the tree...
He causes it to fall; in all such cases, the value of the goods must be paid. Furthermore, regarding the clearing of a wind-channel:
if the wind has not yet arrived, this is rectified by straightening the dried-up bed and so forth, and not otherwise.

If he shakes a tree and strikes it with a weapon, or sets fire to it, or strikes it with a frog-spine or poison—by whatever means he causes it to die—in all such cases, the value of the goods must indeed be paid.
The Discussion on the Forest-Dweller is finished. 111.
Regarding the Discussion on Stealing: "If one, with a thieving mind, touches another person’s stolen goods, such as a head-load [of goods]..."
Seeing him going along carrying the goods, [the thief] thinks, "I will take this," and goes quickly to touch it; up to this point, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for him.
"He makes it tremble" means he pulls it back and forth; if the owner does not let go, there is a *thullaccaya* offense for him because of that.
"He moves it from its place" means having pulled it, he releases it from the owner's hand; because of that, there is a *pārājika* offense for him.
But if the owner of that goods rises up, strikes him, and then causes that goods to be released and takes them back, the monk becomes one defeated (*pārājika*) by that very first act of taking.

For one who takes an ornament after cutting it from the head, the ear, the neck, or the hand, or after releasing it, there is defeat as soon as it is released from the head or other such parts. However, in the case of a bracelet on the hand—
Or, if one moves it back and forth as if rubbing the forearms together without having removed the bracelet, or holds it up toward the sky, it is still protected.
It does not produce a *pārājika* offense, being like a ring upon the bamboo poles used for robes at the foot of a tree. Why?
Because it possesses consciousness (*saviññāṇakatā*). For that which has reached the state of being possessed of consciousness remains right there until it is removed from that place.
The same principle applies to finger-rings, anklets, bracelets, and other ornaments worn on the body.

However, if one steals another’s lower garment (*sāṭaka*) and the owner, out of shame, does not immediately let go, and while the thief pulls it from one side, the owner holds it from the other, it is still protected. Only when it has slipped from the owner’s hand [is it considered stolen].
It is a *pārājika*. Furthermore, if while he is dragging it away, it breaks and a portion falls into his hand, and that portion is worth one *pāda*, it is likewise a *pārājika*.
Regarding "one who carries off goods together": having thought, "I will take the goods along with the carrier," he urges the carrier on, saying, "Go from here!
Being frightened, the carrier turns toward the direction intended by the thief and [proceeds] one...
If he causes it to be moved to another place, there is a *thullaccaya* for the thief; on the second [act], it is a *pārājika*. Regarding "he causes it to be dropped":

furthermore, if the thief, having seen a weapon in the hand of the one carrying the goods, becomes apprehensive and—desiring to seize it after having it dropped—steps aside and causes it to be dropped while threatening him, it is a *pārājika* at the very moment it is released from the other's hand.
"But 'if he causes it to fall, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*),' and so forth, is stated by way of hypothetical supposition (*parikappa*).

For if one, having caused an object to fall, makes the supposition, 'I shall take whatever pleases me,' and then causes it to fall, there is an offense of wrong-doing for both causing it to fall and touching it;
there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for making it move; and there is a defeat (*pārājika*) for moving it from its place when it is worth a quarter of a *pāda* coin. This...
Furthermore, for one who releases [the goods] while they are being carried back in succession, there is likewise no status as a monastic (samaṇa).
Also, if someone, seeing a thief passing by, pursues him and says, "Stop, stop! Drop the goods!
and causes them to be dropped, for that person too, there is a defeat (pārājika) the very moment they are released from the thief's hand.

However, if one says, "Stop! Stop! but does not say, "Throw it down," and the other person, having looked at him and thinking with attachment, "If he reaches me, he might even kill me," places that object in a place where it can be seized and departs with the thought, "I will take it back again later," there is no offense of defeat (pārājika) on account of causing it to fall. Upon returning...
However, for one who takes with the intent to steal, there is a *pārājika* offense upon the lifting [of the object].

But if it occurs to him, "By my very causing this to be thrown down, it has been made mine," and he then takes it with the perception that it is his own, he is protected from the *pārājika* at the moment of taking;

however, it becomes an offense requiring restitution (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). When told, "Give it back," if he does not give it because the owners have relinquished their responsibility, there is a *pārājika*. [The Buddha said: "He, having discarded this..."
The same principle applies even when one takes it with the perception that it is a *paṃsukūla* (rag-robe), thinking, "It has been left behind; now this is not inhabited.

However, if the owner, upon merely being told "Wait, wait," looks back, sees it, and then—having relinquished his responsibility by thinking "This is no longer mine"—deserts it and flees without attachment, then for one who takes it with a thieving mind, there is an offense of *uddhāra* (theft).
It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). When someone is having it brought back, it must be given [to him]; for one who does not give it, there is a pārājika offense. Why?
Because it was discarded through his action—so it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. In other cases, however, there is no further deliberation required.
Even when one takes it with the perception that it is one's own or with the perception that it is a rag-robe (paṃsukūla), this same rule of decision applies.
The Story of Haraṇaka is finished.
112. Regarding the story of deposits:
even in the case of a deliberate lie, such as saying "I will not take it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), because it constitutes an application toward taking what is not given.
“Even for one who says, ‘What are you saying? This is not suitable for me, nor is it for you,’ there is indeed a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the husband, having placed [the gift] in his hand in secret, gives rise to doubt, thinking, ‘No one else knows;
will he give it to me or not?’—there is a *thullaccaya* offense for the monk. Having seen his harshness and so forth, the husband...”
If he gives up the effort, thinking, "He will not give it to me," then if that bhikkhu is still intent on giving, thinking, "I will give it after making him weary," he still protects it.
Even if he is no longer intent on giving, if the owner of the goods is still intent on taking them, he still protects it.
But if he is no longer intent on giving and the owner of the goods also thinks, "He will not give it to me," [then he does not protect it].
He renounces his responsibility; thus, through the renunciation of responsibility by both parties, there is a *pārājika* offense for the monk.
Even if he says with his mouth, "I will give it," but in his mind he does not wish to give, there is still a *pārājika* offense upon the owner's renunciation of responsibility.
That, however, is called a "deposit" (*upanidhi*), which is goods placed in one's own hand by others for the purpose of safekeeping, from a place that is not guarded.
There is no offense for one who moves [an object] from its place in order to place it in a protected location.
Even for one who moves it from its place with a thieving mind, there is no theft. Why? Because it was placed in his own hand; however, it is subject to restitution (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).

The same principle applies even when using [an object] with a thieving mind. It is likewise in the case of taking [an object] on a temporary basis. "Practicing the Dhamma," and so forth, is exactly as previously stated.
This, first of all, is the commentary on the text.
As for the analysis independent of the text, it is stated here by way of the "fourfold bowl" and so forth:
it is said that once a certain bhikkhu, having conceived greed for another’s very costly bowl and desiring to take it away, [examined] the place where it was kept very thoroughly...
Having observed this, he placed his own bowl near that of the other as well.
At dawn, having returned and recited the Dhamma, he said to the Mahāthera who was sleeping, "I pay homage to you, venerable sir. "Who is this? "Venerable sir, I am the visiting monk;
I wish to depart at this early hour, and at such-and-such a place, with a shoulder-strap of such-and-such a kind..."
“The bowl was placed in such a leaf-woven bag. Venerable sir, may I receive it. The Elder entered and took it.
At the very moment of lifting it, the thief committed a *pārājika* offense. If, having arrived and being asked, “Who are you that has come at an improper time?
he flees in fear, he flees after having already incurred a *pārājika*. But because of the Elder’s pure intention, there is no offense for him.

The Elder, thinking, "I shall take that," took another; the same principle applies here. However, this [case] is appropriate when one takes another of a similar kind, as in the case where the offense is similar to an order regarding a human form.
In the *Kurundi*, however, it is stated, "He should be dealt with according to the number of steps," which is appropriate when one takes something that is not of a similar kind.

Thinking it was that [other bowl], he took his own bowl and gave it; because it was given by the owner to the thief, there is no *pārājika* offense, but because it was taken with an impure mind, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Thinking it was that [other bowl], he took the thief’s own bowl and gave it;
here too, because the thief’s own property was involved, there is no *pārājika*, but because it was taken with an impure mind...
It is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). In all cases, there is no offense for the elder.
Another [person], thinking, "I shall steal the bowl," paid homage to the elder who was sleeping in that very same manner. When asked, "Who is this?", he replied, "Venerable sir, I am a sick monk;
first give me one bowl, so that having gone to the village gate, I may obtain medicine."
“I shall take it. The elder, perceiving, “There is no sick person here;

this must be a thief,” thought, “Let him take this,” and having brought out his own bowl, gave it to the monk who was his enemy. For both of them, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) at the very moment of taking it up.
The same principle applies even if one takes up another’s bowl with the perception that it is “the enemy monk’s bowl. However, if...

Regarding the phrase “for the sake of an enemy”: if, perceiving [the recipient] as an enemy, he removes the bowl from the thief and gives it, then according to the method already stated, there is a *pārājika* offense for the elder and a *dukkaṭa* offense for the thief.
Alternatively, if, thinking “for the sake of an enemy,” he gives his own bowl, then according to the method already stated, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for both.
A certain great elder said to his attendant junior bhikkhu, "Take the bowl and robes; let us go to such-and-such a village to wander for alms.
The junior bhikkhu took them and followed behind the elder. While following him, he conceived a thieving intention.
If he shifts a load from his head onto his shoulder, there is no *pārājika* offense. Why? Because it was taken by way of an instruction.
If, however, he leaves the path and enters the forest, he must be dealt with according to the number of steps taken.
Then, if he turns back, flees toward the monastery, and having entered the monastery, departs; at the moment he crosses the boundary of the precincts (*upacāra*), it is a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, if he flees from the place where the Elder’s lower robe was changed toward the village, at the moment he crosses the boundary of the village precincts, [the same offense applies].
It is a *pārājika* offense. However, if both of them go out after having wandered for alms, having eaten, or having taken [the requisites], and the elder says again, “Take the bowl and robes;

we shall go to the monastery,” and there he, with the same previous intent to steal, shifts the load from his head to his shoulder—he is still protected for the time being. [This applies while in] the forest...
He enters; he must be made to proceed step by step. If he turns back and flees directly toward the village, there is a *pārājika* offense upon crossing the village boundary.

If he flees forward toward the monastery, yet does not stop or sit down within the monastery, but continues on with an unpacified intent to steal, there is a *pārājika* offense upon crossing the boundary.
However, as for one who takes [the goods] without being commanded, for him—
If one places a burden on the head or on the shoulder, it is a *pārājika* offense, as in the previous cases. The rest is exactly the same as before.

However, if someone who has been told, "Go to such-and-such monastery, wash and dye the robe, and then come back," accepts this saying "Very well" and goes there, and while on the way, he gives rise to a thieving mind and [places] the burden on his head or shoulder...
In the case of [using] implements and so forth, there is no offense of defeat (pārājika). When descending from a path, one should be made to pay by the number of steps.
If, having gone to that monastery and staying right there, one consumes [the goods] with a thieving mind and thus wears them out, or if thieves steal them from him, there is no theft;
however, there is an obligation to pay for the value of the goods. The same rule applies even if he leaves and returns from there.

However, if one who has not been instructed by the elder takes a robe—either when signs have been made known, or when he himself perceives it to be soiled—and saying, "Venerable sir, give me the robe;
I will go to such-and-such a village, dye it, and bring it back," he goes away;
and if, on the way, he conceives a thought of theft and shifts the load from his head to his shoulder or otherwise moves it, he commits a *pārājika* offense.

Why? Because it was taken as not being a formal instruction (*anāṇatti*). Even for one who departs from the path, or turns back and returns to that very monastery, or even for one who crosses the monastery boundary, there is a *pārājika* offense according to the method already stated. The same rule applies to one who goes there, dyes [the robe], and returns;
likewise when a thought of theft (*theyyacitta*) has arisen. However, if he goes to where he intended, or to a monastery along the way—
Or, having returned to that very monastery, while living on one side of it without overstepping the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*),
if he uses [the property] with a thieving mind and causes it to be worn out, or thieves carry it away from him, or it is lost in some way or another,
it is an offense requiring restitution (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). However, for one who oversteps the precinct boundary, it is a *pārājika* offense.
However, when the Elder is making a sign and [the messenger] says, "Venerable sir, give it to me;
I will dye it and bring it back," and asks, "Where shall I go to dye it, venerable sir?

and the Elder says to him, "Go wherever you wish and dye it," this is called a "messenger sent with full authority. Even one who flees with a thieving mind [is not [considered a messenger in this sense]].

He must be made to undergo forfeiture. However, even if one flees with the intention to steal, or destroys the goods by means of consumption or otherwise, it remains a case where the value of the goods must be paid.
Suppose a bhikkhu sends some requisite to another bhikkhu’s hand, saying, "Give this to such-and-such a bhikkhu in such-and-such a monastery";
when the thought of theft arises in him regarding all those locations, [he thinks], "To such-and-such a monastery..."
The legal analysis here is similar to what was stated regarding the instruction: "Go, wash the robe, dye it, and then come back.
Another monk, wishing to send a monk away, makes a sign, thinking, "Who indeed will take this and go?
If one there says, "Give it to me, venerable sir, I will take it and go," and having taken it, he goes with a mind of theft—[the offense is as previously described].

In all instances where [cloth] has arisen, the legal decision is similar to what was stated here: “Venerable sir, please give the robe-cloth; we shall go to such-and-such a village, dye it, and bring it back.
When the Elder had obtained cloth for the purpose of a robe, it was placed with a family of supporters.
Then his pupil, wishing to take that cloth, went there and said, “That cloth, they say...”
He speaks as if sent by the elder, saying, "Give it.

If, believing his words, a layman gives what was set aside by another layman, or a laywoman gives what was set aside by a laywoman, or someone else takes it out and gives it, there is an offense of defeat (pārājika) for the one who took it.
However, if the elder’s attendants say, "We will give this to the elder," and [the other] gives his own cloth...
It has been set aside. Then, a pupil of his, wishing to take it away, goes there and says, "They say you wish to give a robe to the Elder;
please give it to him. Believing him, they say, "Venerable sir, we set this aside thinking, 'We will give it after feeding him';
here, take it. Since it was given by the owners, there is no offense of defeat (pārājika), though it was with an impure mind.
However, because it was accepted, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) and the object must be given back.
A bhikkhu says to another bhikkhu while going to a village: "So-and-so will give me my rainy-season robe;
having received it, you should set it aside. Saying "Very well," that bhikkhu [accepts] a costly robe given by him along with what he himself had received.

Having set it down together with a cheap garment, whether he knew or did not know that his own expensive garment had been obtained by the person who arrived with it, he says when told, "Give me my rainy-season robe," "Your coarse garment was found, but my garment is expensive;
both have been placed in such-and-such a spot; enter and take them."
When he has entered and taken one thick cloth while the other person takes the other, there is a *pārājika* offense upon the lifting [of the second].
Furthermore, if he writes his own name on the other’s cloth and the other’s name on his own cloth, saying, "Go, read the names and take them," the same principle applies there as well.
However, if both he and the other person have obtained their cloths and place them together—
Setting those aside, he says this: "Both you and I have obtained robes; we have placed them both inside the inner chamber.

Go, search for whichever you wish and take it. If, out of modesty, he should take only the coarse robe obtained by the resident monk, there is no offense for the other person who takes the remainder after the resident monk has searched and taken his portion. [This applies to] the visiting monk (*āgantuka*).

If a monk, having placed his bowl and robe near resident monks who are engaged in making robes, thinking "they will look after these," goes to bathe or elsewhere; if the residents look after them, that is well.
If they do not, he is not liable for the loss when they are lost. Even if he goes after saying, "Venerable sirs, please keep this," [the same applies].
And the others, being preoccupied with their own duties, do not know [of this]; the same principle applies.

Furthermore, even if they are told, "Venerable sirs, please set this aside," they decline, saying, "We are busy," and the other person, thinking "They will certainly set it aside," goes on without taking it;
the same principle applies. But if, whether requested or unrequested by him, they say, "We shall set it aside, you..."
They say, "Go! That [property] must be guarded. If they do not guard it, he is liable for the loss if it is lost.

Why? Because he accepted the responsibility. A monk who, having served as the storekeeper, at the time of dawn takes down the bowls and robes of the monks from the lower story of the palace, closes the door, and goes on his alms-round far away without even informing them—those [items...]
If thieves carry these off, the responsibility falls upon that very person. However, if a monk is told by other monks, "Venerable sir, please set aside your bowl and robes;
it is time to take the voting sticks," and after asking, "Have you all assembled?
and being told, "Yes, we have assembled," he takes out his bowl and robes, sets them aside, locks the storehouse door, and [says], "You [should keep] your bowls and robes..."
"Take this, guard the lower palace gate, and then go," he said, and departed.
Thereupon, a certain lazy monk, after the other monks had left, rose up later while rubbing his eyes and went to the water source to wash his face.
Seeing that moment, the thieves carried off his bowl and robes; it was well-robbed.
The treasurer is not liable for the loss.
Even if someone, without informing the treasurer, places his own requisites in the storehouse, if they are lost, the treasurer is still not liable.
However, if the treasurer sees them and [thinks], "They have been placed in an improper spot,"...
Having taken it, he sets it aside; if it is lost, he is liable for its value. Even if the monk who set it aside says, "Venerable sir, such an article was placed by me;
please look after it," and [the other] accepts, saying, "Very well," yet—either thinking it was poorly placed or placing it in another spot—he loses it;
the liability for that belongs to the former alone. As for one who refuses, saying, "I do not know [where it is]," [the responsibility remains with the one who deposited it].

But there is no liability for loss. Even if someone places it down while he is looking on, and does not have the storekeeper accept it, if it is lost, it is indeed lost [to the owner]. If the storekeeper places it elsewhere, he is liable for the loss.
If the storehouse is well-guarded, and all the requisites of the Saṅgha and the Cetiya are kept right there, the storekeeper—
If a fool who is incompetent opens the door and goes elsewhere— whether to listen to a discourse on the Dhamma or to do something else—
and at that moment thieves take whatever they can, he is liable for all of it.
This applies whether he has gone out from the storehouse and is pacing outside, or whether he has opened the door and is letting his body take in the air right there.
Whether he is sitting engaged in the practice of the ascetic’s duty, or sitting right there occupied with some task,
or even when oppressed by the need for excrement or urine; or if, while remaining within the precincts, he goes outside, or otherwise becomes negligent,
[the thief] opens the door or enters through one already open, and breaks into the wall.
Or, having cut it down, whatever thieves take away due to his negligence, all that is his liability.
However, they say that it is permissible to lie down with the window open during the heat of the day.

But for one who is oppressed by the urge to defecate, if there is no space within that vicinity and he goes elsewhere, it does not fall under the category of illness; therefore, there is no liability.
But if one who is oppressed by heat inside goes out while keeping the door well-guarded, and thieves seize him and say,
"Open the door," it should not be opened even up to the third time. However, if those thieves [threaten], "If you do not open it,
we shall kill you and break down the door to carry off the belongings," and they brandish axes and other weapons—
They throw [the door] open. [One may think: "When I am dead and the Sangha’s lodgings have been ruined, there is no benefit [in keeping it closed]";
thus, it is permissible to open it. Here too, they say that because it is not one's domain, there is no liability for loss.
If some visitor gives the key or opens the door, whatever the thieves steal, all of it is his liability. [This applies] when the Sangha [entrusts the key] for the purpose of guarding the storehouse.
If the needle-case and the key have been locked together and given [to the keeper], and the storekeeper, having given only a small amount [of goods], goes to sleep,
and thieves open [the door] and carry off the requisites, the responsibility for that falls upon him alone. However,
if he has locked the needle-case and the key together and gone to sleep, and thieves come and say, "Open it," then in that case, it is according to the previous method.

One should proceed in this manner. Having thus secured [the storehouse] and lying down, if they break through the wall or the roof, or enter by a side passage and carry it off, there is no liability for him.
If other elders also reside in the storehouse and, while the door is open, take their own requisites and depart, once they have gone, the storekeeper [should act accordingly].
If he does not guard the door and something is stolen there, the responsibility falls on the storekeeper alone because of his authority;
however, they must be companions with the resident monks. This is the proper conduct in that regard.
If the storekeeper says, "Stay outside and take your requisites; do not enter," [one should comply].
He speaks thus: "Among them, if one greedy *mahāthera* enters the storehouse together with novices and attendants and sits or lies down there, whatever goods are lost shall be his liability.
However, the storekeeper must be on friendly terms with the remaining elders. Then the storekeeper himself—
If he takes a restless novice or an attendant and sits or lies down in the storehouse, whatever is lost there is his responsibility.
Therefore, only the storekeeper himself should live there;
the rest should live at the foot of a tree, and certainly not in the storehouse.

Furthermore, if one places requisites in the living quarters of fellow monks who belong to the same community, then in the event that those requisites are lost, the liability for them falls upon those very individuals by whom they were placed there; however, the others must act as companions.
But if the Saṅgha causes the storekeeper to receive rice gruel and alms-food right in the monastery itself, and he [the storekeeper] goes to the village for the purpose of wandering for alms...
If it goes [and is lost], the loss is the responsibility of that very person.

Even for a vihāra steward appointed to guard extra robes when monks enter upon alms-round—who receives either rice gruel or food as his own portion—if anything is lost there while he has gone on the alms-round, all of it is his responsibility.
And not only this much; like a storekeeper, whatever...
If it is lost through his negligence, he must pay for the whole.
However, if the monastery is large and he goes to guard another area, and someone steals what was placed in a different spot, there is no liability because it was outside his jurisdiction.
But in a monastery such as this, which is of medium size and serves as a common meeting place for everyone—
One should sit down after setting aside the requisites. Or, two or three monastery attendants (*vihāravārika*) should be stationed there.
If, while they are guarding [the items] here and there with diligence, something is lost, there is no liability for compensation.

Even if the monastery attendants have been bound and the stolen goods have been carried off, or if the stolen goods have been carried off by another path when the thieves have gone on a different route—[in such cases, there is no liability].

It is not their responsibility. If there is no rice gruel or meal to be given in the monastery for those on duty (*vihāravārika*), it is permissible for them to set aside two or three extra gruel-slips from what they themselves are entitled to receive, as well as enough rice-slips for a full meal;
however, these should not be set aside as a fixed rule, for people may become resentful.
“Only the one on duty in the monastery is eating our meal. Therefore, it should be exchanged and set aside.
If they bring and give tickets for meals that are common to all, that is well; if they do not give them, the tickets should be obtained by taking turns and then brought out.
If the one on duty [receives] two or three tickets for rice-gruel, or four or five...
Even while receiving tickets for meals, he still goes out on almsround; it is as if everything were lost and he were liable for the debt, like a storekeeper.

If there is no meal or fodder to be given to the Saṅgha or to the monastery guards, the monks take turns at the duty of guarding the monastery and look after their own respective dependents, rather than failing to accept the turn that has come to them.

They do not obtain [it]; it must be done exactly as other bhikkhus do. However, for a bhikkhu who is without companions or has only himself as a second, and for whom there is no fellow bhikkhu to bring and give him food, such a person’s turn should not be assigned.
Furthermore, whatever is set aside in the monastery for the purpose of cooked provisions, one who lives by taking that should remain [there]. Whoever...
One who does not subsist [on the produce] should not be made to take his turn. Monks are also stationed in a monastery for the sake of fruits;
having tended and guarded them, they divide the fruit according to the turn and eat it. Whoever eats those fruits must remain [in the monastery].
One who does not subsist on them should not be made to take his turn. They may also station monks for the sake of guarding the lodgings, beds, chairs, and bedding.
One dwelling in a monastery residence must remain there. However, one who lives in the open air or at the foot of a tree need not take up a residence.

Suppose there is a single junior monk who is well-learned; he recites the Dhamma for many, provides answers to their questions, explains the Canon, delivers discourses on the Dhamma, and carries out the burdens of the Saṅgha—even such a person, while enjoying gains, may remain in the residence.
Even during the spring season, one should not enter [the village] on certain days. They say, "The distinction of the person must be known.

However, for the one who tends the Uposatha hall and the image house, double the daily portion of rice-gruel and boiled rice should be given, along with a nāḷi of husked rice every day, the three robes at the end of the year, and articles of allowable use (kappiyabhaṇḍa) worth ten or twenty [coins]. But if, for him...
If something belonging to that [monastery] is lost there due to negligence while one is actually receiving it, all of it must be made good.

However, what is forcibly taken away after having been bound is not to be made good. In this regard, it is permissible to have property belonging to a cetiya guarded by means of property belonging to the Saṅgha;
it is not permissible to have property belonging to the Saṅgha guarded by means of property belonging to a cetiya.
However, if something belonging to the Saṅgha has been set aside together with what belongs to a cetiya, it is considered protected as long as it is protected within the property of the cetiya;

thus, this is permissible. Even for one who guards the Uposatha hall and other such places by turns during the fortnight, if anything is lost through negligence, the responsibility for it falls upon that person alone.
The Discourse on the Deposit is finished.
The Discourse on the Customs House (Suṅkaghātakathā) 113:
They take the tax from there, thus it is called a "customs house" (suṅkaghāta); this is a designation for a place where taxes are collected. For that reason...
Then, those who carry out goods subject to duty without paying the tax strike down and destroy the king’s revenue; therefore, it is called "a place for destroying the tax" (*suṅkaghāta*).

Having entered there means having entered that place for collecting taxes (*suṅkaṭṭhāna*) established by the king within the boundaries of mountain ranges and so forth. "Goods fit for a king" (*rājaggaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ*) means goods worthy of a king; from [the part] of the king...
The meaning is that the goods worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas must be paid as a toll (*suṅka*).
"Pleasant to the king" (*rājakanti*) is also a reading; it has this same meaning. "With a thieving mind":

having generated the thought, "I will not give the king a toll from this," if one touches those goods, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Having taken them from the place where they were set down, [placing them] in a bag...
Or if she inserts it, or ties it together with her thigh in a concealed place, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

Because the location is delimited by the customs station (*suṅkaṭṭhāna*), there is no "shifting from one place" (*ṭhānācāvana*). If she causes the second foot to cross the boundary of the customs station, it is a *pārājika* (defeat).
Regarding "she causes [the goods] to fall outside the customs station": having seen that the king’s officers are otherwise occupied, while still standing inside, she [causes them] to go outside.
He throws it for the purpose of making it fall. If it was bound to fall inevitably, then at the mere moment of being released from the hand, there is a *pārājika* offense.
If, however, it strikes against a tree or a stump, or is carried back inside again by the force of a strong wind, he is protected [from the offense].
If he takes it up again and throws it, there is a *pārājika* offense according to the method previously stated. After it has fallen to the ground...
If it enters while turning again inside, it is indeed a *pārājika*. However, in the *Kurundi* and *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"If, having fallen outside, it enters while standing still and turning, it is a *pārājika*; if it enters after having turned without standing still at all, it is protected."
Standing inside, one turns it with the hand, the foot, or a staff, or causes another to turn it;

if, while not standing inside, it goes as it is being turned, it is a *pārājika*. If it remains inside while protecting that which is going outside—whether because one thinks, "It will go after being turned," or "Another will turn it"—or if that which was placed inside later turns by itself; [in these cases, there is no offense].
Or if it has been rolled up by another and goes outside, it is still protected.
However, when it is placed by a person with a pure mind and goes out in that manner, there is nothing at all to be said.

If one joins two packets together and places them within the boundary of the toll-station, even though the toll is worth a quarter on the outer packet, because of its being joined as one with that [inner] packet, the inner packet—
He guards it. However, if he turns it over and places the inner part on the outside, it is a *pārājika* offense.

The same principle applies even when it is placed on a carrying-pole (*kāja*) after being tied together as one unit. But if he does not tie it and it is merely placed at the tip of the pole, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If he places it in a moving vehicle or on the back of a horse and so forth, thinking, "I will take it out," then even when it has been taken out, there is theft (*avahāra*).

There is no offense; there is not even the forfeiture of the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). Why? Because it was said, "Let them take the toll for one who has entered here," and this [item] stands outside the toll-station and was not taken away by him; therefore, there is neither forfeiture of goods nor a *pārājika* offense.
In the case of items placed on standing vehicles and the like, even if they depart without his exertion, there is no theft (*avahāra*) even if a thieving mind is present.
But if, having set aside vehicles and the like, he drives [the animal] and crosses the boundary;
or, because he is well-practiced in elephant-training sutras and such, he stands in front and calls out, "Come here, you!", then there is a *pārājika* offense upon crossing the boundary.

In the *Eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada*, at this point, if he causes another to carry it, there is no offense; here, however, there is a *pārājika*. In that case, regarding another person's vehicle or goods, for one who does not know [it belongs to another]...
"Having put [the goods] inside, if he carries them beyond three *yojanas*, they become subject to forfeiture; thus it is a *pācittiya*. Herein, there is no offense.
It is permissible to go after having paid the toll at the toll-house. One person goes with a specific intention, thinking:
"If they say, 'Pay the toll,' I will give it; if they do not say so, I will go. Seeing him, a certain toll-collector..."
If someone says, “That monk is going; seize him for the toll,” and another says, “How can there be a toll for one who has gone forth?
Let him go,” it is permissible to go. However, when it is said, “It is not permitted to go without paying the monks’ toll;
lay followers, seize [him],” then [if they say], “We will seize his bowl and robes while taking the monk’s toll...”
Even if it is said, "It will have to be taken; what does that matter? Let him go," it is still considered as if it has been obtained.
Even if the tax-collectors are sleeping, or playing at dice, or have gone somewhere else, and he calls out, "Where are the tax-collectors?

but does not see them, it is still considered as if it has been obtained. Even if, having reached the toll-station, he is distracted by something else... [he is still considered as if it has been obtained].
Whether he is reflecting, reciting, or applying his attention, if he is suddenly pursued by thieves, elephants, lions, tigers, or the like, or if,
seeing a great cloud risen, he wishes to enter a sala tree standing before him,
he passes that place having already attained the [appropriate] opportunity.
Regarding the phrase "one avoids customs duty," the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* states that even if one avoids it by entering the vicinity [of the toll station],

it is indeed theft (*avahāro*). However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, after merely demonstrating the disadvantage by saying, "The king’s men harass one who avoids [the duty]," it is stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who avoids it by entering the vicinity, but not for one who avoids it without entering [the vicinity].
"There is no offense," it is said. This accords with the Pāḷi. Here, the vicinity is to be delimited by two throws of a clod.
The Discussion on the Customs House is finished. Now follows the Discussion on Living Beings.
114. Beyond this, in order to show unilaterally a living being that constitutes theft, he says "a human being.
Even in the case of one who carries off a free person, there is no theft.

Even if a free person has been pledged by his mother or father, or if he himself has placed himself under [another] and accepted fifty or sixty [pieces of gold], there is still no theft for one who carries him away.
There is no [theft] in that case; however, wealth increases at the place where it has been taken.

But for one who carries away a slave—whether born in the house, purchased with wealth, or brought as a captive—the offense is indeed theft (avahāra). It is with reference to this very point that it was said:
"A 'living being' (pāṇa) is called a human being. And here, one born to a slave from the womb of a female slave of the household is "born in the house" (antojātaka); by means of wealth...
A "slave bought with wealth" is to be understood as one who, having been seized from a foreign land and brought back, has entered into servitude; he is known as one "brought by way of a debt.

If one touches such a living being with the intention, "I shall carry him away," it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If, taking him by the hand or the foot, one lifts him up and causes him to quiver, it is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
Having lifted him up, if one moves him even the width of a hair's breadth beyond his standing place while intending to flee with him, [it is a formal act of confession].
It is a *pārājika*. Having seized him by the hair or by the hands, he drags him; he must be made to proceed step by step.

If, intending "I will lead him on foot," he threatens or strikes him, saying "Go from here," then for one who goes toward the direction indicated by that [command], it is a *pārājika* with the second step. This applies to all those who are of one mind with him.

It is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*) in a single moment. If a monk, having seen a slave, asks about his well-being or does not ask, and says, "Go, live happily by fleeing," and if that slave flees, it is an offense entailing expulsion at the moment he takes the second step.
If another person tells him who has come near himself, "Flee," and if a hundred monks [are involved] in succession to himself...
If he speaks to one who has come near, it is a *pārājika* offense for all.
However, if he says, "Run away, before your owners catch you," to one who is fleeing in haste, there is no *pārājika* offense.
But if he speaks to one who is walking slowly, and that person speeds up because of his words, it is a *pārājika* offense. Or, having fled to another village...
If one sees [the victim] having gone to a country and causes him to flee even from there, it is likewise an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
The term "taking what is not given" (adinnādāna) is released by way of a figurative expression. For it refers to one who speaks thus:
"What are you doing here? Is it not fitting for you to flee? Or, is it not fitting for you to go somewhere and live in comfort?"

Or, if [someone] says, "The male and female slaves have fled and are living happily in such-and-such a place," and having heard those words, he flees, there is no offense of theft (*avahāra*). Furthermore, if someone says, "We are going to such-and-such a place;
once we have arrived there, we will live happily, and for those who go with us, there will be provisions for the journey (*pātheyya*) along the way..."
Having said, "There is no fatigue," she takes him who comes with her happily and goes along by way of traveling on the road, not with a mind of theft;
thus there is no taking away (*avahāra*). And when bandits arise on the way, even for one who says, "Hey! Bandits have arisen!
Flee quickly! Come, let us go!"—because this is spoken for the purpose of freeing [him] from the danger of the bandits, they do not say there is taking away.
The Discussion on Living Creatures is finished. The Discussion on Footless Beings:
