Regarding the footless creatures, "a snake" refers to a domesticated snake held by snake-charmers and others, which they cause to perform tricks.
They obtain half a *kahāpaṇa*, a quarter, or even a whole *kahāpaṇa*; and when releasing [the prisoner], they release him only after taking silver or gold.

They may go to the place where a certain bhikkhu is sitting, set down a basket containing snakes, and then either fall asleep or go elsewhere. If that bhikkhu, with a mind of theft, touches that basket—
It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If he makes it quiver, it is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*). If he moves it from its place, it is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
However, if he opens the basket and seizes the snake by the neck, it is an offense of wrong-doing. If he lifts it up, it is a serious offense.
For one who lifts it up straight, when even a hair’s breadth of the snake’s tail has emerged from the bottom of the basket, it is an offense entailing defeat. Having rubbed [it],...
If, while pulling [the snake] by its tail, semen is emitted from the opening of the mouth, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one slightly opens the mouth of a basket, strikes it, calls out by name saying, "Come here, you! and causes it to emerge, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Likewise, having opened it, if one makes the sound of a frog, the sound of a mouse, or scatters parched grain, and then calls out by name, snapping the fingers...
Or if he strikes [the snake], even when it has thus emerged, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Even if the mouth is not opened, if this is done, the hungry snake strikes the lid of the basket with its head, makes space, and escapes; it is still a *pārājika* offense.
But if, once the mouth is opened, the snake escapes by itself after coming out, it is a case of "goods to be paid" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). Furthermore, whether the mouth was opened or not opened—

Or, if he merely makes the sound of a frog or a mouse and scatters fried grain, but does not call out by name nor clap his hands, and the snake, being hungry, goes out with the thought "I will eat the frogs and so forth" and then flees, it is simply a matter of compensation (bhaṇḍadeyya).
The fish is included here by the mention of "footless creatures. As for what follows here:
That which ought to be said has already been stated regarding that which stands in water.
The discussion on footless beings is finished.
The discussion on two-footed beings.
115. Regarding bipeds—showing those that are capable of being stolen, he said, "humans who have grown wings.
However, deities cannot be stolen. Those for whom wings have grown are "wing-grown" (*pakkhajātā*).

They are of three kinds: feather-winged, skin-winged, and bone-winged. Among these, peacocks, chickens, and so forth are feather-winged; bats and so forth are skin-winged; [and others are bone-winged].
Bees and the like should be understood as having bone-wings. All of them—both humans and those born with wings—are included here solely by the mention of "two-footed" beings.
Whatever else needs to be said regarding this follows the same method as that explained for sky-dwelling creatures.
The discussion on two-footed beings is concluded.
Catuppadakathā 116.
Regarding the four-footed animals—apart from those already mentioned in the Canon, all remaining species of four-footed creatures should be understood as included here.
Elephants and so forth are well known. In this regard, for one who touches an elephant with a thieving mind, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for one who makes it quiver...

A *thullaccaya* offense. However, if one who possesses great strength, out of pride in his power, seizes a young elephant calf by the head at its navel while lifting it up, and yet does not release even a hair’s breadth of its four feet or its trunk from the ground, it is a *pārājika* offense.
As for elephants, some are kept tied up in an elephant stable, while others remain untied. Some...
Regarding "standing within the enclosure": someone may stand in the royal courtyard;
in that case, for one who has been tied by the neck and placed in the elephant stable, there are five locations: the neck-tie and the four feet.
For one bound by an iron chain at the neck and on one foot, there are six locations. For one bound at the neck and on two feet, there are seven.
The locations. By means of these, the instances of causing agitation and displacement should be understood. For one who is unbound, the entire elephant stable is the location;
if he goes beyond that, it is a *pārājika* offense. For one standing within the enclosure, the entire enclosure is the location;
if he goes beyond the door of the enclosure, it is a *pārājika* offense. For one standing in the royal courtyard, the entire city is the location.
Upon his crossing the city gate, there is a *pārājika* offense. For one standing outside the city, the "place" is simply the spot where he stands.
When carrying him away, it must be calculated step by step. For one who is lying down, there is only a single place.
For one who raises him with a thieving mind, there is a *pārājika* offense as soon as he has been raised up. This same analysis applies to a horse as well. However, if it is bound by its four legs...
There are eight points to be understood. This same method applies to the lips as well.
As for the ox: some are kept tied up in the house; some remain untied; some are kept tied up in the pen;
and some remain untied. Among these, regarding the one kept tied up in the house:
There are five locations: the four feet and the tethering post. For one not tied up, the entire cow-pen is his.
Even for one tied up within the pen, there are five locations. For one not tied up, the entire pen is his. If he passes beyond that gate of the pen, it is a *pārājika*.
If, having broken through the pen, he carries it out and passes beyond the broken gate, it is a *pārājika*. Or, having opened the gate or [broken] the pen...
Having broken through [the enclosure] and standing outside, he calls her by name and makes her come out; it is a *pārājika*.
The same rule applies even if he calls her after showing her a branch-bend (*sākhābhaṅga*).

If, without opening the door and without breaking the fence, he calls her by moving a branch-bend, and the cow, due to hunger, leaps over the fence and comes out, it is still a *pārājika*. But if at the door...
If the gate is opened or the enclosure broken and [the ox] goes out by itself, it is *bhaṇḍadeyya*.

Whether the gate is opened or not, and whether the enclosure is broken or not, if he merely shakes the branches but does not call out, and the ox—out of hunger—goes out on foot or by leaping over, it is indeed *bhaṇḍadeyya*. One [ox] is in the middle of the village...
One is bound and standing, one is lying down. For a cow that is standing, there are five positions; for one that is lying down, there are two.
According to these, the instances of trembling and the shifting from those positions are to be understood.
However, if one kills it right where it is, without making the one lying down stand up, it is a case of "value of the goods" (bhaṇḍadeyya). But if it has been well examined...
In a village with gates, the entire village is the "place" for a cow standing there.
For one standing or grazing in an unenclosed area, the place is only the area actually trodden by its feet. This same determination applies to donkeys, goats, sheep, and so forth.
The Discussion on Four-Footed Animals is finished.

**The Discourse on Many Words 117.** Regarding many locations—if the site is filled by a single centipede, for one who carries it away step by step, there are ninety-nine *thullaccaya* offenses and one *pārājika*. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The Discourse on Many Words is concluded.
Ocarakakathā 118.
"Ocaraka" means one who spies; it is said that he enters within here and there.
"Having spied" (*ocaritvā*) means having observed or having scrutinized. "He reports" refers to something improperly placed in other families or in monasteries and the like.
If one informs another who is capable of committing theft about property that has not been secured by protection, there is an offense of *pārājika* for both.
This means that when the property is inevitably to be taken, at the very moment the scout is commanded, the other person causes the property to be moved from its place;
thus, there is an offense of *pārājika* for both. However, if [one says], "There is no man in the house; the property is in such-and-such a place..."
If one gives an indirect explanation in such a manner as: "It was placed in a certain spot without protection, the door was not secured,
it could have been carried off by the mere act of walking past, and there is no one at all who lives by human effort who would go and take it," and another person,
having heard that, goes and takes it thinking, "I shall now carry it off," then [the offense occurs] upon its displacement from that place.
It is a *pārājika* offense for one [of them], but for the other there is no offense. For by means of this method, he is released from the taking of what is not given.
The Discussion on the Spy is finished. Now follows the Discussion on the Protector of the Well.
"One who guards what has been left behind" (oṇirakkho) is so called because he protects goods brought by another to his own dwelling place when told:
"Venerable sir, please look after this for a moment while I go and perform such-and-such a task.
This is the designation for such a person. For this very reason it is said: "One who guards goods brought [to him] is called an oṇirakkho."
In this context, regarding "protection against theft" (*oṇirakkha*): when one has mostly tied and hung up goods and, without having released them,
cuts the lower bag or pouch, takes even a small amount, and then restores the sewing and so forth to its original state—
such offenses corresponding to the acts of touching and so on performed with the thought, "I shall take [this]," are to be understood.
The Discussion on Protection by Others is finished.
The Discussion on Stealing by Agreement:
*saṃvidāvahāra* means stealing after having made an agreement; what is meant is stealing performed through mutual persuasion. *Saṃvidahitvā* means...
The meaning is: "having deliberated with a single desire and a single intention. Herein is the analysis:
A number of bhikkhus, having made an agreement, saying, "Let us go to such-and-such a house and, either breaking the roof-covering or breaking through a wall, steal the goods," they go there.
Among them, one steals the goods. In the taking away of those goods, [the offense belongs] to all.
It is a *pārājika*. This is also stated in the *Parivāra*:
"Four persons, having made an agreement, took away valuable property;
three were *pārājika*, one was not *pārājika*."
“This question was thought out by the wise.
This is its meaning: four people—a teacher and three students—became desirous of acquiring six *māsaka* coins’ worth of heavy goods.
Therein, the teacher said: “You take one *māsaka*, you take one, you take one, and I shall take three.”
He said: "Among the pupils, however, the first one said, 'Venerable sirs, you three take [three coins], you take one, and you take one;
I shall take one. The other two also spoke in exactly the same way.
In that case, for each of the pupils, one *māsaka* was directly handled by each individual; therefore, they incur offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); there are five instances of commanding."
For those [three], there is a *pārājika* offense for all three. However, for the teacher, there are three cases of acting by one's own hand;
for these, he incurs a *thullaccaya*. There are also three cases of commanding; for these as well, he incurs only a *thullaccaya*.

For in this training rule on taking what is not given, acting by one's own hand is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*) of commanding, nor is commanding a constituent factor of acting by one's own hand. Acting by one's own hand must be dealt with only by means of acting by one's own hand.
An instruction is [to be understood] by means of the instruction itself. Therefore it was said: “Four persons having made an agreement... this question was thought out by the wise.
Furthermore, for the sake of non-confusion regarding the acquisition of goods through an agreement, this tetrad should also be observed according to its meaning:
“one commodity in one place, one commodity in various places; various commodities in one place, various commodities in various places.”

In this context, "one article in one place" means that having seen five māsakas' worth of goods placed on a shop-counter belonging to a single family, several monks instruct one [of them], saying, "Go and bring this. Upon its recovery, there is a *pārājika* offense for all of them.
"One article in various places" means that five māsakas' worth of goods have been placed, one māsaka each, upon five shop-counters belonging to a single family.
Having seen [it], many direct one person, saying, "Go and bring these.
If there is an excess of five māsakas, it is a *pārājika* offense for all of them.

Regarding "various goods in one place": having seen various goods belonging to many people, worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas, placed together in one spot, many direct one person, saying, "Go and..."
If they say, "Bring [it]," then upon the removal of that [coin], there is a *pārājika* offense for all. Regarding "various goods in various places":

having seen one *māsaka* coin placed on each of five shop-slates belonging to five families, several people together command one person, saying, "Go, bring these," then upon the removal of the fifth *māsaka*, there is a *pārājika* offense for all.
The Discussion on the Conventional Usage of Consciousness is concluded. 119.
The Convention of Designation (*saṅketakamma*): This refers to the act of recognizing; the meaning is the making of a sign by way of delimiting time.
And here, when it is said, "Steal before the meal," whether he steals today before the meal, or tomorrow, or in a year’s time, there is no discrepancy;
for both, according to the method already stated for the scout, it is a *pārājika* offense.
However, if it is said, "Steal today before the meal," and he steals tomorrow before the meal, [the offense is incurred] because "today" was specifically determined.
Having passed that appointed time, it is considered stolen afterwards.

If, when told, "Take it tomorrow before the meal," one takes it today before the meal, then because it was taken before reaching the appointed time fixed as "tomorrow," there is a *pārājika* offense for the thief who took it, while there is no offense for the owner who remained at the spot. [Regarding the phrase] "tomorrow before the meal":

When this has been said, even if one brings it on that very day, or the next day after the meal, one should be understood as "bringing it at the appointed time" both before and after [the stated period].

This same method applies to the periods after the meal, during the night, and during the day. Furthermore, the distinction between the appointed time and the non-appointed time should be understood here by way of the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch; by way of darkness and light;
and by way of the month, the season, the year, and so forth. When it is said, "Bring it before the meal," [if one thinks], "I will bring it only before the meal"—
If it becomes afternoon while he is still striving, how is this to be understood? First, the Elder Mahāsumma said: "This is merely a preliminary effort for the morning meal;
therefore, the fundamental offense is not incurred. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "Because the time limit has been exceeded, there is a breach of the agreement;
therefore, the fundamental offense is incurred."
The Discussion on Conventional Acts is finished.
The Discussion on Symbolic Acts (120).
A symbolic act (*nimittakamma*) is the making of some sign for the purpose of producing recognition; that [is done] by means of the eye or...

It has been stated in three ways by way of such phrases as “I shall bury it,” and so forth. Furthermore, other various types of actions here should be included, such as leaping with the hands, striking with the palms, snapping the fingers, bending the neck, and clearing the throat.
The rest here follows the same method as that explained under the section on the ritual of signs (*saṅketakamma*).
The discussion on the ritual of signs is concluded.
121. Now, for the purpose of avoiding confusion regarding these very acts of signs and acts of marks, it is said: "A bhikkhu commands a bhikkhu," and so forth.
Therein, "he, thinking it to be that" refers to the thief; that which was spoken by the commander after making a sign-recognition (*nimittasaññā*).
Thinking "this is that," he steals that very thing; for both, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding the statement, "thinking 'that' [is] 'other,' he steals another," this means: thinking "this is that," he steals another item placed in that very same spot;
there is no offense for the one who was at the original location. Regarding "thinking 'other,' 'that'": this refers to the goods specified by the sender after making a sign.
Thinking, "This is of little value; this other thing placed near it is the valuable article," one steals that very [other thing] while imagining it to be something else;

for both, there is a *pārājika* offense. Thinking it to be one thing while imagining it to be another—in the same manner as before—one thinks, "This is another thing placed near it, the valuable article"; if it is indeed another thing, there is a *pārājika* offense for that very person.
In the passages beginning with "He tells so-and-so," one teacher and three pupils named Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, and Saṅgharakkhita are to be understood.
Therein, "a bhikkhu commands a bhikkhu" means that the teacher, having observed some goods somewhere, commands Buddharakkhita to take them away. "Tell so-and-so" means: "Go!"
“Buddharakkhita, you must inform Dhammarakkhita of this matter:
‘Let such-and-such a person inform such-and-such a person. Then Dhammarakkhita, being thus informed by you, must inform Saṅgharakkhita: “Let such-and-such a person steal such-and-such an article.
Thus, being commanded by Dhammarakkhita who was himself commanded by you, Saṅgharakkhita [informs such-and-such a person].
"Let him steal the goods; for he is of a heroic nature among us and capable in this task.
Regarding "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," first, there is a *dukkaṭa* for the teacher who gives such an order.

However, if that command proceeds according to its intended purpose, then at the moment of the command itself, there is precisely that which was later described as a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). Now, if that property is inevitably...

It is captivating that which is stated elsewhere: "For all [of them], the offense is a *pārājika*. Therefore, this logical principle—that for this person, it becomes a *pārājika* at that very moment—should be understood to apply everywhere.
He informs the other means that Buddharakkhita informs Dhammarakkhita, and Dhammarakkhita informs Saṅgharakkhita.
“If our teacher says, ‘Bring such-and-such an article;
you are indeed a hero among us,’ and he reports this, they too commit a *dukkaṭa* offense. ‘The thief accepts it’ means that Saṅgharakkhita agrees, thinking, ‘Very well, I shall take it.
For the one who was the original instigator, there is an offense of *thullaccaya* because of Saṅgharakkhita.”
At the very moment it is accepted, the teacher incurs a *thullaccaya* offense, for by that act he has incited the multitude toward evil.
If that person quarrels with him and Saṅgharakkhita then steals that property, there is a *pārājika* offense for all four people.
And this applies not only to these four; by this same method, even one who commands through a succession of others without breaking the chain of command incurs the same.
Whether there be a hundred ascetics or a thousand ascetics, for all of them it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the second instance: "He commands another" means that Buddharakkhita, having been commanded by his teacher, either not seeing Dhammarakkhita or being unwilling to speak [to him], approached Saṅgharakkhita and said, "Our teacher spoke thus..."
—“It seems you must steal such-and-such an item,” he commands. “There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)” means that for the command itself, there is an offense of wrong-doing for Buddharakkhita.

“If he accepts it, there is an offense of wrong-doing” means that when Saṅgharakkhita has accepted it, an offense of wrong-doing is to be understood as belonging to the one who originated the act (the instigator).
But if he actually steals that item, [there is an offense] for the one who gave the command.
For both Buddhārakkhita and Saṅghārakkhita the thief, there was a *pārājika* offense.
However, because the teacher Mūlaṭṭha had made no prior agreement, he was not guilty of a *pārājika*. For Dhammarakkhita, there was no offense at all because of his lack of knowledge.
But Buddhārakkhita, having ensured the safety of the two others, lost himself.
Regarding these four subsequent instances of command, first:
"Having gone, he returns again" means that after going to the place where the goods are kept, seeing the guards both inside and outside, and being unable to steal them, he comes back.
"When you are able, then..."—does this mean it must be stolen this very day? "Go; when you are able, then steal it. There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Likewise, even by such an instruction alone, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* offense. However, if that property is necessarily liable to be carried off, there is what is called "volition accomplishing the purpose," which is similar to the fruit immediately following the path;
therefore, this person becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense at the very moment of giving the instruction.
Even if the thief carries off that property only after sixty years have passed, and the instigator [gives the order] in the meantime—
Either he dies, or he returns to a lower state; having ceased to be a recluse, he will either die or return to a lower state.
However, for the thief, the offense of defeat (pārājika) occurs at the very moment of the theft.
Regarding the second instance: because he was speaking slowly, or because of that person’s deafness, [the thought] "Do not steal" [did not reach him].

He did not announce this statement; therefore, he who was at the root was not released. On the third occasion, however, because it was announced, he was released. On the fourth occasion, because it was announced by him and the other accepted it with "Very well" and desisted, both were released.
The Discussion on Commanding is finished. [Now follows] the Classification of Offenses.

122. Now, demonstrating the factors and the classification of offenses for the taking of what is not given—which was previously described in terms of being displaced from various locations—the author says, "by five modes," and so forth. Therein, "by five modes" means by five causes;
it is said, "by five factors. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: for one who takes what is not given...
“By the five modes stated in the manner beginning with ‘and it belongs to another,’ there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika), but not by fewer than these.

In this regard, these are the five modes: that it belongs to another, the perception that it belongs to another, the heavy nature of the requisite, the intent to steal, and the removal from its place.
However, in the two subsequent sections, regarding light requisites...
By way of the classification of the object, a grave offense (thullaccaya) and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) are shown.
Regarding the three sections stated by the method beginning with "In six ways," there are these six:
the perception that it is one's own, taking it on trust, taking it for a limited time, the preciousness of the requisite, the intention to steal, and moving it from its place. Thus, six.
The modes (ākāra) are to be understood. Furthermore, here too, according to the distinction of the object (vatthu), in the first section it is a *pārājika*;

in the second and third sections, a *thullaccaya* and a *dukkaṭa* respectively are stated. However, in the three subsequent sections, although there is a distinction of the object, because the object is not possessed by others, only a *dukkaṭa* is stated.
In that context, what is called "not possessed by another" refers to that which is unoccupied (*anajjhāvutthaka*).
Whether it be a discarded or root-cut plot of land belonging to no one, or property belonging to oneself— in both cases,
it is reckoned as "not taken possession of by another. However, because there is the perception that it is possessed by another in this instance,
and because it was taken with a thieving mind, it is not stated that there is no offense.
The classification of offenses is concluded. 131.
Having thus shown the classification of offenses by way of the subject matter and by way of the state of mind, the classification of non-offenses is now presented.
In explaining this, he said, "There is no offense in the case of one who has the perception [of ownership]," and so forth.

In that context, "one who has the perception" means one who possesses the perception, such as "this article belongs to me. For one who takes even another's property while having such a perception, there is no offense at the time of taking;
however, what was taken must be returned. If, when told by the owners, "Give it back," he does not give it, then upon their relinquishing responsibility for it, there is a *pārājika* offense.
"Taking on trust" means there is no offense even when taking on trust. However, the characteristics of taking on trust are to be understood from this Sutta:
"Monks, I allow you to take on trust from one who possesses five qualities:
