When [the object] has been taken, he is pleased; it is permissible for one who knows that such a person will be satisfied when his property is taken to take it.
These five factors are stated by way of taking everything without remainder. However, borrowing on trust succeeds through three factors:
being a friend, being alive, and being pleased when the item is taken; or being a close associate, being alive, and...
If he is glad when it is taken, and says, "He lives," then [the debt] is discharged.
However, if he does not live, and was not glad when it was taken, then even if his property was taken on the basis of trust, it must be given back again.
And when giving it back, as for the estate of the deceased, those who are the masters over that wealth—whether they be householders or...
Or it should be given to those who have gone forth. If one is displeased, the property belonging to him should be returned to him alone.

However, if someone has already expressed their approval—either by verbal expression or merely by a mental impulse—saying at the very outset, "You have done well in taking what belongs to me," then even if he later becomes angry for some reason, he is not permitted to demand its return. This applies even to one who is unwilling to give it back.
However, he accepts it mentally and says nothing; furthermore, that person is not permitted to demand its return.

But if someone says, "I have taken or used what belongs to you," and [the owner] replies, "Whether it was taken or used, I have set it aside for some purpose; it is proper to restore it to its original state."
He speaks. This person is permitted to have it returned.
Regarding "temporary use": there is no offense even for one who takes it temporarily with the thought, "I will give it back" or "I will make restitution.
However, if the owner of the goods—whether an individual or a group—grants permission, saying, "Let this remain yours," [then there is no offense].
This is wholesome. If he does not grant permission, it should be given when they bring it for him. However, as for what belongs to the Saṅgha, it is only proper to return it.

Regarding "the possession of the deceased" (*petapariggaha*): here, all those who have passed away—even those reborn in the realm of ghosts (*pettivisaya*), or those reborn in that very same existence, or even the gods of the Four Great Kings and so forth—have come to be reckoned simply as "deceased" (*petā*). In their possession...

There is no offense. For even if Sakka, the king of the gods, were sitting there having set out a shop, and a monk with divine vision, knowing this, were to take a cloth worth a hundred thousand for the sake of his own robe—even if the owner says, "Do not take it, do not take it"—it is permissible.
However, as for an offering made specifically for a deity...
There is no need to say anything regarding garments that have been hung on trees or similar objects by those who are making them.
Regarding "the property of animals": there is no offense even in the case of the property of animals.
For even if a dragon-king (*nāgarāja*) or a young garuḍa (*supaṇṇamāṇavaka*) were to set up a shop in human form, and some monk [were to take] what belongs to him from there...
If one takes it according to the previous method and goes along, it is permissible.

If a lion, a tiger, a deer, a wild buffalo, or other such animals, being oppressed by hunger, kill and eat [the prey], they should not be stopped from the very beginning; for they might even cause harm.

However, if one is able to stop them after they have eaten only a little, it is permissible to stop them and take [the meat]. This also applies when an army or similar group is departing after taking provisions.
It is permissible to take [the cloth] after having it dropped.
"With the perception that it is a refuse-rag" (paṃsukūlasaññissa): there is no offense in taking even that which is ownerless provided one has the perception, "This is a refuse-rag.
However, if it belongs to an owner, it must be given back when the owner asks for it. "Of one who is insane" (ummattakassa) refers to the type previously described.
There is no offense even for one who is insane. Regarding the phrase "for the first offender": here Dhaniya is the first offender; for him there is no offense.
However, for the rest—the thieves of the dyers' baskets and so forth, including the group of six—there is indeed an offense.
The classification of non-offenses is concluded.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis is finished.
Miscellaneous Discussion:
Origin, action, perception, and that which is accompanied by consciousness;
"Worldly offense, action, and wholesome [action] pertaining to feeling.
Now, regarding this miscellaneous section, this training rule has three origins: it originates from the body and the mind through personal action;
it originates from speech and the mind through command; and it originates from the body through both personal action and command.
It originates from speech and from mind. It is an origination by action, for one incurs this offense only while acting, not while not acting.
Because one is released through the absence of the perception, "I am taking what is not given," it is liberation-by-perception (*saññāvimokkha*).

It is accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), is a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*), and consists of bodily action, verbal action, and unwholesome consciousness; whether one is joyful, fearful, or neutral.
"He incurs that [offense] called 'the three feelings'"—all this is to be understood in the same manner as explained in the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
The miscellaneous discussion is concluded.
Commentary on the cases of legal procedure (*vinītavatthu-vaṇṇanā*).

132. Regarding the accounts of the cases concerning those who have been disciplined (*vinītavatthu*), the case of the group of six (*chabbaggiyavatthu*) has already been stated under the supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*). In the second case:
"Mind" (*citta*) means that for worldlings (*puthujjana*), by way of lust and other defilements, it abandons its natural state and runs, runs hither and thither, and rushes about.
If the Blessed One [were to declare] an offense even by a mere arising of thought (*cittuppāda*) without a breach of the doors of body or speech...
Who could possibly make himself free from offense? Therefore it was said: "There is no offense for a bhikkhu in the mere arising of a thought.
However, one must not be a slave to the mind; rather, by the power of reflection, the mind itself must be restrained. 133–4.

The cases concerning touching, shaking, and causing to move from its place have meanings that are self-evident. Those that follow, ending with "he took [it] from the ground with a thieving mind," constitute the conclusions of the cases.
135. In the section on the Path of Language (Niruttipathavatthu): "He took" (*ādiyī*) means he seized; he identified [the thief] by saying, "You are a robber.
But when the other asked, "By whom was it carried off?", he gave an admission in accordance with the nature of the question, saying, "It was carried off by me.
For had the other said, "By whom was it taken? By whom was it removed? By whom was it placed? then...
This person might also say, "I took it," "I removed it," or "I set it down. The mouth is indeed used for the purpose of eating and for the purpose of speaking;
however, there is no taking away (avahāra) without a thieving mind. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"There is no offense, monk, in the realm of conventional expression" (*niruttipathe*). The meaning is that there is no offense in mere conventional speech. Beyond that—
The entire section on the wrapping cloth, including the conclusion, is of plain meaning.
137. In the account of the undivided body, "inhabiting" means being reborn in that very body through craving for clothing.
"Not heeding" means not accepting his words, or not showing respect toward them. "That body having stood up..."
The peta, by his own supernatural power, raised that body up. Thus it is said: “That body having risen up.
He bolted the door: since the bhikkhu’s dwelling was right near the charnel ground, the bhikkhu, being of a timid nature, quickly entered there and bolted the door.
There he fell down: once the door was bolted, the peta fell right there.
Having become homeless in that very garment and having abandoned that body, he departed according to his karma; therefore, that body fell right there—it is said that it "fell.
Regarding the phrase "while the body was unbroken," one must not take a rag-robe while the body is still fresh and moist; for one who takes it while it is in such a state, [such consequences follow].
There are dangers, and one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, it is permissible to take [the fruit] once it has been broken.
To what extent is it considered "broken"? Even by the mere fact of being slightly split by the beak or the fang of crows, hawks, dogs, jackals, and so forth.
But when, through the impact of falling, only the outer skin is cut while the hide remains uncut, this is still not "broken."
Furthermore, when the skin has been cut, it is "burst. Also, if a boil, leprosy, carbuncle, or ulcer has burst while the body was still alive, this too is "burst.
From the third day onward, even that which has reached the state of a corpse through the stages of bloating and so forth is likewise "burst.
However, even if it is not burst in every respect, by the cemetery guards or others—
It is permissible to have it taken by people. If no one else is available, one may make an incision with a knife or some other instrument and take it oneself.
However, in the case of a body of the opposite sex, one must maintain mindfulness and arouse the perception of a recluse;
having done so, it is permissible to make an incision on the head or on the back of the hands or feet and take it.
138. The Discourse on the Matter of Shifting the Kusa Grass:
In the immediately following matter, it is said that he took the robe after shifting the kusa grass.

This refers to the explanation of the meaning of the phrase "he should take" (*ādiyeyya*) presented previously by way of mere names among the five types of taking: taking by theft, taking by force, taking by contrivance, taking by concealment, and taking by means of kusa grass.
The meaning is that one steals by means of a deceptive method.
Furthermore, the diversity among these types of stealing should be understood as follows:

when anyone, whether by night or by day, having broken into a wall or performed other such acts, steals property belonging to an owner while remaining invisible; or [when one uses] false measures, counterfeit coins, and so forth.
Or if one takes it after deceiving [the owner], for one who takes in such a manner, the taking away is to be understood as "taking by theft. However,
when one takes what belongs to others by overpowering them with force, or by intimidating them and showing them fear—
such as robbers and bandits who carry out highway robberies, village raids, and so forth, acting out of anger— [this is taking by violence].
It is like kings, royal ministers, and others who plunder the houses of others and seize by force more than their own share.
The theft committed by one who seizes in this manner is to be understood as "theft by force" (*pasayhāvahāra*).
However, the theft of one who seizes after having made a plan is called "theft by planning" (*parikappāvahāra*); this occurs by way of planning regarding the goods or planning regarding the location.
It is twofold. Herein, this is the "speculation regarding goods":
suppose someone here, needing a cloth, enters an inner room and, having speculated, "If it is a cloth, I will take it; if it is thread, I will not take it," takes a bag in the darkness.
If a cloth is there, he incurs a *pārājika* offense at the very moment of lifting it. If it is thread, [he does not].
He guards it. Having taken it outside and released it, and knowing it is "stolen," he brings it back again and places it in its original position;
he indeed guards it. Even if he knows it is "stolen," if he goes thinking, "Whatever has been found, that must be taken," he is to be dealt with according to the number of steps [taken].
If he takes it after placing it on the ground, there is a *pārājika* offense upon its removal. [If he is pursued] by owners crying out, "Thief! Thief!"...
If one who has been seized abandons it and flees, [the owner] guards it. When the owners see it and take it back, that is well.
If someone else takes it, there is an obligation to pay for the goods. Then, when the owners have turned back, if he himself sees it and takes it, thinking, "I already took this out;
it is mine now," he guards it; however, there is still an obligation to pay for the goods. "If..."

The same principle applies to one who takes [an item] after imagining it in such a manner as: "If it is thread, I will take it; if it is cloth, I will not take it"; or "If it is ghee, I will take it; if it is oil, I will not take it.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, it is stated: "Even one who needs cloth, having gone out having taken up only a bundle of cloth..."
It is stated: "Having stood there and released it, and seeing that 'this is a garment,' as he walks away, he should be made to pay by the mere lifting of his foot.
In this case, however, because of the thought, "If it is a garment, I shall take it," a hypothetical assumption (*parikappa*) is seen;

yet, because it was taken after he had already seen it, the application of the hypothetical assumption (*parikappāvahāra*) is not seen. But in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, that which was hypothetically assumed...
Theft is said to occur for one who takes away that which is unseen while it remains in a state of being merely imagined;
therefore, in that case, theft by way of imagination (*parikappa-avahāra*) is observed. This also accords with the canonical text: “Thinking it was that, he took it away.
In this context, the imagination that proceeds in such a manner as, “If it should be a cloth, I will take it,” and so forth—this is [the imagination referred to].
“Conjecturing about goods” is the name [of this offense].
However, the conjecture regarding place should be understood as follows:

here, a certain greedy bhikkhu, having entered another’s dwelling-pavilion, a family home, or a work-hall in the forest, sits there engaged in conversation and, seeing something that might provoke greed—

He looks at the requisites. Having looked and seen them, he delimits the area by way of the gateway, the front of the house, the lower terrace, the monastery courtyard, the gatehouse, the foot of a tree, and so forth, and reflects:
"If they see me within this range, I will give them [the requisites] as if I were taking them away out of a desire to see them; if they do not see me, I will carry them off. Taking them with him...
As soon as one has crossed the boundary that has been mentally defined, it is a *pārājika* offense.

If one defines a "vicinity boundary" (*upacārasīma*), and while walking toward it—whether attending to meditation subjects and the like or distracted by something else—one crosses the vicinity boundary through lack of mindfulness, it is an offense requiring restitution (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
Furthermore, even if he has reached that place, if a thief, an elephant, a wild beast, or a great storm [encounters him]...
Or he emerges [from the water], and if he passes that place in haste because of a desire to be freed from that calamity, it is merely *bhaṇḍadeyya*.
However, some here say: "Because it was taken at the very root with a thieving mind, therefore it does not protect [the owner];
it is indeed theft (*avahāra*). This, first of all, is the method of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. But in the *Mahāpaccarī*, however: "Even if..."

Thus, it is said: "If one mounts an elephant or a horse within the boundary and neither drives it nor causes it to be driven, there is no offense of defeat (pārājika) even when the boundary has been crossed;
there is only the obligation to pay the value of the goods. In this context, regarding the thought that arises:
"If they see me within this interval, I will give [the goods] to them as if I were taking them along out of a desire to show them."
This is called “conceited presumption” (*okāsa-parikappa*).
Thus, for one who takes after having presumed by means of these two kinds of presumption, it should be understood as “theft by presumption” (*parikappa-avahāra*).
However, theft committed by concealing [the act] is “concealed theft” (*paṭicchanna-avahāra*). It should be understood in this way: when a monk [takes from] people...

If, having seen an ornament or article of decoration that has been set down after being removed by those playing in or entering gardens and such places, he covers it with dust or leaves—thinking, "If I pick it up by bending down, they might recognize me and think, 'What is this ascetic doing? He is taking it!
and thus harass me"—and intends, "I will take it later," then for him there is no theft at that point.
It is not yet a theft. But when those people, wishing to enter the village, search for that property and do not see it, and having left with a lingering attachment, thinking, "It is dark now;
we shall find out tomorrow," then for one who takes it up, there is a *pārājika* offense regarding the removal.
Or, if they have gone [thinking], "Even while it was concealed, it was my own property," through the perception that it belongs to oneself...
Now, if one takes it with the perception that "this is discarded goods" (paṃsukūla), thinking "these are for you," it is an object to be given back (bhaṇḍadeyya).
Even if those [owners] come on the second day, search for it, do not see it, and depart having abandoned their responsibility, what was taken remains an object to be given back.
Why? Because they did not see it due to his effort; however, as for one who [sees it] in such a manner...

If, seeing a commodity left exactly where it was without being covered, one with a thieving mind steps on it with the foot and causes it to enter mud or sand, at the very moment it has entered, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
Furthermore, the removal by shifting a blade of grass is called "grass-removal" (kusāvahāra); that too should be understood in this way: whoever...
When a monk has cast down a blade of *kusa* grass while the robes are being distributed,
and— desiring to take another’s portion, whether it be of lesser value, greater value, or equal value in price, which stands near his own portion—

he lifts up the blade of *kusa* grass that had fallen in his own portion with the intent to cast it into the other’s portion, he is still protected [from an offense] as long as [the act is not completed]. Of the other...

If he causes it to fall into his own portion, he is protected. However, when that [portion] has fallen, if he extracts the toothpick from another person’s portion, at the mere moment of extraction, he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.

If he first extracts the toothpick from another person’s portion with the intention of causing it to fall into his own portion, he is protected during the extraction, but not protected during the falling. [In the case of] his own...
Furthermore, regarding the division [of the grain]: he extracts his own stalk of rice from it; as long as it remains extracted, he guards it.
Once he has extracted it, for one who causes it to fall into another's portion, there is a *pārājika* offense at the mere moment it leaves his hand.
However, if he causes the stalk that has fallen into both portions to disappear from sight, then, among the remaining monks...
When the other has gone through the gates, saying, "Venerable sir, my portion is not seen," and [the first] says, "Nor is mine seen, friend," [the other asks], "But what, venerable sir, is my share?
[The first] shows him his own share, saying, "This is your share.
Whether they have quarreled over it or not, once he has taken that share and departed, the other sets aside his own share.
In the case of the removal [of the goods], it is a *pārājika* offense. Even if he says, "I will not give my share to you;

you, however, take your own share after identifying it," and even though [the other] knows, "This is not mine," he nevertheless takes that person's share, it is a *pārājika* offense in the case of the removal. But if the other says, "This is your share, this is my share—what is the use of this dispute?"...
Having reflected, he says, “Whether the bowl be mine or yours, you take whichever is the superior portion”;

this is called “what has been given,” and there is no theft here. Even if that monk, fearing a dispute, is told, “Take whatever pleases you,” and having set aside his own bowl as the superior portion, takes only an inferior one—
Having taken [it], he departs; therefore, there is no theft even for the other who takes what remains after searching.
Furthermore, it is stated in the commentaries: "In this place, only the distribution of robes has been introduced by way of the example of the straw-mat;
however, having brought forth the arising and the distribution of all four requisites, they should be demonstrated."

Having spoken thus, [the Buddha] delivered the discourse on robes that arose beginning with the story of Jīvaka, starting from the words in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*: “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept from me this pair of Sīveyyaka cloths, and may he authorize householders’ robes for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
And in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*, it says: “Now at that time, Rājagaha was suffering from a famine; people could not find food...”

"May they be able to provide meals for the Saṅgha; may they wish to provide designated meals, invitations, tickets for meals, fortnightly meals, Uposatha-day meals, and meals on the first day of the lunar half-month"—starting from this sutta, there is the discourse on almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*). And in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* itself:
"Now at that time, the group of seventeen monks [stayed] at a certain remote great monastery..."

“They were repairing [the dwelling], thinking: ‘We shall spend the rains retreat here. The group-of-six bhikkhus saw the group-of-seventeen bhikkhus repairing the dwelling. Starting from this account of the group-of-six, the discourse on lodgings has been presented;
and at its conclusion, the discourse on medicinal requisites such as ghee and so forth is explained in detail.
We, however, shall explain all of that at the very point where it occurs in the text; the reason for explaining it in this manner has already been stated previously.
The account concerning the matter of the straw-matting is concluded. 139.
From here on, the account concerning the sauna (jantāghara) is of plain meaning.
140. Regarding the five bases for leftovers, those bhikkhus had what was allowable prepared by one who was not ordained and then consumed it.
However, when taking leftovers, one should take what has been discarded as the remains of what was eaten. If one is able to have it discarded while others are eating, this is also permissible.
Nevertheless, it should not be taken for the sake of protecting oneself or out of compassion for others.

141. Regarding boiled rice, hard foods, cakes, cucumbers, and things to be eaten with the hand, he said to another person who was not present, "Give a portion to such-and-such a person. "He took it without basis" means that while the owners were in the act of giving, he took it in this manner.

"There is no offense for the monk regarding a *pārājika*" means that because he took what was given by the owners, no *pārājika* offense is stated for him. There is an offense, however, for intentional lying.
"Regarding the *pācittiya*": he states that there is a *pācittiya* offense for the intentional lying spoken by him;
this is as in the subsequent case concerning the gruel with three spices (*tekaṭulayāgu*). However, regarding the taking [of the food], this is the analysis:

when something belonging to the Saṅgha is being given by those authorized or commanded by them, such as monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and so forth, or when something belonging to householders is being given by the owner or one commanded by him.
When something is being given and one takes it after saying, "Give another person's share," it is *bhaṇḍadeyya* (the value of the goods).
One who takes what is being given by another must be made to pay the value of the goods.

When something is being given by one who is neither authorized nor instructed, if one takes it after saying, "Give another share as well," or by counting false years [of age], it is like the case of the four bowls; it is only the removal of that [excess].
He must be made to pay the value of the goods. For one who takes what is being given by others in this manner, it is a "payment for the goods" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).

However, if the owner has caused it to be given, saying, "Give this to him," or if he gives it himself, it is considered "well-given. This is the essence here according to the decision of all the commentaries.
142–3. Regarding the matters of the kitchen and so forth: a "kitchen" (*odaniyaghara*) is a house for cooking food intended for sale. A "slaughterhouse" (*sūnaghara*)...
A "meat-house" (*maṃsaghara*) is a house for cooking meat for sale. A "cake-house" (*pūvaghara*) is a house for cooking cakes and snacks for sale.
The rest here, as well as in the section on requisites (*parikkhāra-vatthu*), is self-evident. 144.
Regarding the section on the bench (*pīṭha-vatthu*): that monk, having made a plan, thinking, "I will take it when it has reached this spot,"...
He shifts it. In that shifting, there is no theft. However, having shifted it, if he takes it from the designated place, a *pārājika* offense is stated.
And while carrying it thus, if there is no intent to steal regarding the bench, he is to be dealt with according to the value of the bag;
but if there is also [intent to steal] regarding the bench, he is to be dealt with according to the value of both. The three items beginning with the mattress (*bhisi*) are well known.
146. Regarding the three matters beginning with receiving on trust (*vissāsaggāha*), there is no offense in the act of taking;

however, those who cause it to be brought back must pay the value of the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). For one who has entered for alms, it is permissible to take a portion even while standing within the boundary of the monastery precincts (*upacārasīmā*).
But if the donors say, "Venerable sir, please take a portion even from outside the precincts; they will come and eat it," [then it is permissible].
In this way, it is also permissible to take [fruit] from within a village. The rest here is of plain meaning. 148–9. Regarding the seven cases beginning with the mango-thieves:
there is no offense if one takes [the fruit] with the perception that it is refuse-rag (paṃsukūla); if they cause it to be brought [to him], there is the obligation to pay for the goods;
if he uses it with the intention of theft, it is a Pārājika offense. Herein, this is the analysis: even if the owners still have a sense of attachment [to the fruit].
Even when the owners have attachment, if one eats [the food] with the perception that it is refuse-rags (*paṃsukūla*), there is the offense of *bhaṇḍadeyya* (value of the goods).
For one who takes it with a thieving mind, it is indeed theft (*avahāra*); having had the value of the goods appraised, he is to be dealt with accordingly.

The same principle applies whether the owners have attachment and the thieves are without attachment, or the owners are without attachment and the thieves have attachment. [In the latter case], thinking, "We shall take it again," they throw it into some place of concealment.

The same principle applies when [the fruit] has been taken away. Both [cases] are without a fixed abode; there is no offense for one who eats it with the perception that it is discarded rags (*paṃsukūla*), but there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) if done with a thieving mind.

However, regarding mangoes and other fruits belonging to the Saṅgha—whether grown in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha or brought and given there—if one steals them while they are worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas, it is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*). This also applies in border regions during times of harassment by bandits.
When villages are being vacated, monks also leave their monasteries and depart with determination, thinking, "We shall return when people settle there again.
When monks reach such a monastery, they may consume mangoes and other fruits with the perception that they are "discarded" (paṃsukūla);
there is no offense. However, for one who consumes them with a mind of theft, it constitutes an act of taking what is not given.
Having had the value of the goods assessed, he should be made to pay restitution.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated without distinction:
"If one uses fruits and other produce in an abandoned monastery with a thieving mind, it is a *pārājika*. Why? Because [the property] belongs to those who have come and those yet to come."
Regarding property belonging to the Saṅgha as well as that belonging to an individual, the measure [of the offense] is merely the act of making an offer.

However, if one gives mangoes or other fruits from those [resources] for the purpose of maintaining a family, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for corrupting a family. If one gives them with a thieving mind, one is to be dealt with according to the value [of the items].

This same principle applies to property belonging to the Saṅgha as well. If one gives what has been designated for the purpose of lodgings for the purpose of maintaining a family, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one acts out of a sense of ownership, it is a *thullaccaya*; if with the intent to steal, it is a *pārājika*. If the object is not available [to be taken], one must pay its value.
For one who sits outside the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīmā*) and consumes [the food] out of a sense of ownership, there is liability for compensation (*gīvā*).
If one strikes the bell, proclaims the time, and eats [thinking], "It falls to me," it is considered well-eaten. [But] if one does not strike the bell, even if the time has been proclaimed...

Having made a proclamation, or having struck the bell itself without proclaiming the time, or even without striking the bell or proclaiming the time, if one knows that there are no others present and thinks, "It falls to me," then eating it is indeed eating with ease.
The two cases concerning the flower garden are well known. Regarding the three cases concerning the speaker of what was said:
when one has been told by you, "I shall avoid this," one says, "I speak according to your word."
The meaning is: there is no offense for a monk regarding a *pārājika* because it was given by the owners.
Furthermore, monks, one should not say, "I speak because I have been told [to do so]";
the meaning is that one monk must not tell another monk, "I am speaking according to your word, having been instructed by you. However, having made a formal agreement, [one may say], "So-and-so..."
It is permissible to say, "I shall take it on your word. "Having been told, speak" means:
having been told by me, speak on my behalf. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
And in these two cases as well, it is permissible to speak after making a formal demarcation. For to this extent, one is freed from censure.
151–2. Regarding the middle case of the three cases on the jeweled cloth: “I am not unwell” means “I am not ill. The rest is self-evident. 153.

Regarding the two cases on the pig: although there is no offense for the first monk because he was released out of compassion upon seeing that the animal’s stomach was empty, nevertheless, since the owners did not consent, it is a debt to be paid for the goods (bhaṇḍadeyya), or [the value] must be as great as [the loss].
A dead pig should be brought and given, or goods of equivalent value.

If he does not see the owner of the snare anywhere, he should place an item of equivalent value—such as a cloth, a saffron robe, or a bowl—in a place near the snare where those who have come will see it, and only then may he depart. However, for one who releases it with a mind of theft, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.

And here, some boar, having dragged the snare with its foot, remains in its place once the snare is cut, though subject to being moved from that spot, like a ship moored in a violent current. Some remain by their own nature;
some lie down; and some are bound by a spring-snare (*kūṭapāsa*). A "spring-snare" is one at the end of which there is either a bow or a hook.
Or it may be some other stake that has been fixed, which, by being caught against trees or other objects here and there, prevents the pig from moving.
In that case, for one who stands having pulled the snare, there is only a single point of binding by the snare;
for he escapes as soon as the snare is released or as soon as it is cut. But for one who stands by his own nature [without pulling], there is binding.
There are five situations involving the four feet: two situations for one who is lying down, namely, being bound and being on a bed;
and for one bound by a snare, wherever he goes, that very place [is the situation].
Therefore, even ten, twenty, or a hundred monks who release him from here and there incur a *pārājika* offense. This applies to each respective case where it occurs.
It is as if one were driving away a single dog upon seeing it.
However, in the case of the first three, the shaking and the displacement from their place should be understood according to the method explained in the discourse on the four-footed animals.
Even for one releasing a pig bitten by a dog, there is the forfeiture of the goods if done with a compassionate intention; [but] if with a thieving mind...
It is a *pārājika* offense. However, if one goes toward the place where the dog is stationed or near the dog and makes it flee first, there is no theft.
Even if someone gives fodder and water to a tethered pig, makes it strong, and shouts, "It will flee in terror," if it then flees, it is a *pārājika* offense.
The same rule applies to one who, having weakened the snare, causes [the animal] to flee with shouts of exultation.
However, if one goes after giving fodder and water, thinking, "Having gained strength, he will escape," and if he then escapes, it is an offense requiring restitution (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
The same rule applies to one who goes after weakening the snare. [If] a weapon is near the snare...
Or he sets fire [to the trap], thinking, "When it is cut or burnt, the pig will escape. If the pig shakes the snare and escapes when it is cut or burnt, it is liable for the price of the goods.
If he knocks down the snare along with the pole, and afterwards the pig goes along trampling it, it is liable for the price of the goods.
If the pig is caught between the millstones, and [the owner] wishes to drive it away...
If one lifts up a plow out of compassion, it is an offense of forfeiture (*bhaṇḍadeyya*); if one does so with a thieving mind, it is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*).
If, immediately after lifting it, one does not go [with it] but goes later, it is only an offense of forfeiture.

If one causes a plow that was lifted and set aside to fall, and subsequently a pig goes along trampling it, it is an offense of forfeiture. Even if one rescues a pig that has fallen into a pit out of compassion...

It is an object to be restored; if he destroys it with the intent to steal, it is a *pārājika* offense. If he fills a pit and destroys [the animal], and afterwards a pig goes along trampling it, it is an object to be restored.
If he pulls out one pierced by a stake out of compassion, it is an object to be restored; if he does so with the intent to steal, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Having pulled out the stake, if he discards it, it is an object to be restored.
In the monastery grounds, however, those setting snares or traps should be stopped with the words: "This is a place of refuge for deer;
do not act thus here. If they say, "Venerable sir, please have them removed," it is permissible to have them removed.
If they remove them themselves, that is excellent. If they neither remove them nor allow them to be removed, one should request protection and [then proceed].
It is permissible to have them removed. During the time of guarding the crops, people set snares, stone-tethers, and so forth in the fields, thinking, "By eating meat, we shall protect the crops.
When the crop season has passed and those who had no attachment [to the field] have departed, it is permissible to release whatever was tied or fallen there.
The legal determination regarding the two cases concerning deer is exactly the same as that stated for the cases concerning pigs.
The same principle applies to the two cases concerning fish. However, this is the distinction:
if one causes fish to flee from a net by opening the mouth of the net, or by releasing the rear-end of the net, or by making a hole in the side, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Even for one who causes [the fish] to escape by showing cooked rice in this manner, it is a *pārājika*. Even for one who pulls [the net] up together with the fish-trap, it is a *pārājika*.

If he merely opens the mouth of the trap, releases the rear netting, or makes a hole, but the fish escape according to their own nature, it is an offense requiring restitution (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). Having acted in this way, [he shows] the cooked rice...
He shows [the fish], but the fish, having emerged to seek their food, flee away; it is merely a gift of goods.
Without opening his mouth, without releasing the back-pouch, and without making a hole on the side, he shows only the grains of rice;
however, the fish, being hungry, strike with their heads, make way, and flee away to seek their food.
It is merely a loss of goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). Whether he opens the mouth of an empty fish-trap, releases the rear-end of the net, or makes a hole in it;
when the fish that have come one after another reach the opening, they escape through the holes in the net—it is merely a loss of goods.
Or, having taken up an empty fish-trap, he throws it into the thickets—it is merely a loss of goods. In a vehicle, goods are like those in a bag on a seat.
In the case of the story of the piece of meat: if one takes it in the air, the very place where it is grasped constitutes the "place.

One should understand the displacement from that place by delimiting it in six ways. The rest here should be determined according to the method explained in the stories of the wood-gatherer, the washerman, the cloth, and the mango-thief, and so forth.

155. In the case of the Kumbha-vatthu: if one takes ghee, oil, and so forth, worth less than a pāda, and having established a restraint, thinking, "I will not do this again," yet on the second day and subsequent days, when the thought arises again, one likewise abandons the burden and consumes them—consuming all of that, there is no pārājika offense. There is either a dukkaṭa or a thullaccaya.
Or he incurs [the offense], yet it is a case of "value to be paid" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). This monk acted in exactly this way. Therefore it was said:

"There is no offense of *pārājika* for the monk. However, if he does not relinquish his intention but consumes it little by little, thinking, "I will enjoy it day after day," then on the day the value reaches one *pāda*, there is a *pārājika*.
The grounds for bringing about a formal agreement (saṃvidāvahāra) should be understood according to the method of decision stated regarding the grounds for bringing about a formal agreement;

the grounds for confusion (muṭṭhi) regarding the grounds for the house of gruel and so forth; the two grounds for dissension (vighāsa) regarding the grounds for mango-thieves and so forth. The two grounds concerning grass are of obvious meaning. 156.
Regarding the grounds for causing the distribution of mangoes and so forth: those monks went to a village residence that had a limited number of resident monks.
In that place, even while the monks were consuming various fruits, when those [visitors] arrived, they did not say to the attendant (*kappiyakāraka*), "Give fruits to the elders.

Then those monks, thinking, "Why should what belongs to the Saṅgha not reach us?", struck the gong, had it distributed, gave a share to them according to their seniority (*vassaga*), and consumed it themselves as well. Because of that—
Regarding them, the Blessed One said: "There is no offense, monks, for the purpose of consumption.

Therefore, even now, in a case where residents do not give to newcomers, and when the fruit season has arrived, they eat it themselves by stealth because they see others are present—it is permissible for the newcomers there to strike the bell, divide it, and consume it.

Furthermore, where the resident monks, having protected the trees, divide and eat the fruit when the harvest season arrives, and properly provide for the four requisites, there the incoming monks have no authority.
Even regarding those trees that were assigned for the sake of robes, the incoming monks have no authority;
the same principle applies to those assigned for the sake of the other requisites as well.
But as for those who, having been thus unassigned, take charge of and guard the resident monks' [share] and then consume it by theft—no agreement should be made with them regarding the residents.

However, as for those given for the purpose of consuming fruit, which the residents themselves guard and preserve and then properly present [to others], with them alone should an agreement be made on their behalf. (From the *Mahāpaccarī*)
However, it has been stated: "One who, with a thieving mind, consumes what has been assigned specifically for four types of requisites must be dealt with after having the value of the goods assessed.
For one who consumes it by dividing it up according to its use, there is an obligation to pay the value of the goods.
But as for that which was assigned here for the purpose of lodgings, for one who consumes it by dividing it up according to its use..."
“There is a grave offense (thullaccaya) and the value of the goods must be paid.
What is given specifically for the purpose of robe-cloth must be applied toward robe-cloth itself.

If there is a famine and the monks are distressed by lack of almsfood, but robe-cloth is easily obtained, one may perform an act of formal authorization (apalokanakamma) for the welfare of the Saṅgha.

It is also permissible to present [the gift] for almsfood. If they are distressed by lack of lodging or medicinal requisites, it is permissible to present them even for that purpose after performing an act of authorization (*apalokanakamma*) for the welfare of the Saṅgha.

The same principle applies even when [the gift] has been specifically given for the sake of almsfood or medicinal requisites. However, what is specifically given for the sake of lodging is considered "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*); having protected that, [one may use it].
Having protected it, one should bring it back for that very purpose.

However, if there is a famine and the monks cannot subsist on almsfood—where monasteries fall into ruin as people flee elsewhere due to fear of kings, disease, or thieves, and palm trees, coconut trees, and so forth are destroyed—it is possible to subsist by relying on the requisites of lodgings. In such circumstances...
The Blessed One has permitted the use of lodgings even after they have been relinquished at the proper time for the purpose of maintaining them.
Therefore, it is permissible to set aside one or two excellent lodgings and relinquish the others—even those of the lowest quality—for the sake of alms-food.
However, one must not relinquish them by cutting off the very root of their ownership.
However, in the case of a monastery that has been designated and given for the purpose of the four requisites, no formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*) need be performed regarding it.
It is permissible to bring in [resources] for the sake of whatever requisite is lacking. The monastery must be maintained;
it is even permissible to have it maintained by paying wages. As for those who, having received wages, live in the monastery itself after building houses there and guard it—
If they give coconuts or palm fruits to those monks who have arrived, they may receive only that which has been authorized by the Saṅgha—
namely, "Eat this much every day"— but it is not permissible for them to accept more than that, even if others offer it.
However, one who takes a monastery by purchase and gives it as allowable goods (kappiyabhaṇḍa) for the sake of the four requisites of the Saṅgha may give even a large amount.
A monastery given for the purpose of lighting lamps at a cetiya, or for the purpose of repairing what is broken or dilapidated, must also be maintained;
it may be made over to someone to maintain it by paying them wages. And here, the wages are...
It is permissible to give even what belongs to a cetiya or what belongs to the Saṅgha. This gift of the fruit arising from that [land]—
for those who dwell and guard this very monastery for wages, and for those who take it by lease and provide allowable goods—
should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
Regarding the cases of Ambapālī and others: “Monks, there is no offense for one who gives [food] to a cowherd.
Now, among these, which kind of gift to a cowherd is permissible, and which is not? First, the Elder Mahāsumma said:
“Only that which has been specifically allotted to the cowherd—such as when it is given with the instruction, ‘Take this much every day’—is permissible; anything beyond that is not permissible.”
But the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "Is there anything given after having made a written contract with the cowherds or having established a sign?
These people are the masters of what has been left in their hands; therefore, even if they give much, it is permissible.
However, in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "Of the groves belonging to people, or other fruits and crops..."
"If children are guarding [the property], what they give is permissible; however, one must not take it after having had it brought back.
But in the case of what belongs to the Saṅgha or what is dedicated to a cetiya, it is permissible for one who guards it after having purchased it by means of hire.
For one who guards it for wages, his own share is permissible. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it says: "Regarding those garden-guards of householders [who guard] for monks..."
Regarding teeth, this is permissible. As for gardeners belonging to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, what they give after having taken it from their own wages is permissible.
Even for one who guards half a monastery or some trees after receiving wages, it is permissible to give only from the tree that belongs to him personally.
However, for one who guards [the property] after taking it by means of a fee (keṇiyā)...
"Everything is also permissible," it is said. However, all of this is a difference in phrasing (*byañjana*), while in meaning (*attha*) it is one and the same;
therefore, it should be understood by knowing the underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
In the story of the wooden plank (*dāruvatthu*): "I am temporary, O Blessed One"—this was spoken by one who wished to say, "My mind is temporary, O Blessed One."
It is said: "with the thought ‘for the time being’" means it is stated that he had the thought, "I will bring it back and give it [again].
The Blessed One said, "There is no offense regarding what is for the time being.
Herein, this is the decision not found in the canonical text: if the Saṅgha has a communal work performed, such as a Uposatha hall...
Or from the dining hall; having asked permission from there, it may be taken for temporary use.
However, whatever building materials belonging to the Sangha are unprotected and become damp when it rains, or dry out in the sun—all that may be brought back and used for one's own residence.
When the Sangha is having these materials brought back, they should be persuaded [to consent] by means of other building materials or their value.
If it is not possible to convince him, one should say: "Venerable sir, this was made with the property of the Saṅgha;
you may use it as the property of the Saṅgha. However, this very bhikkhu is the master over the lodging.
Even if a stone pillar, a wooden pillar, a door, or a window is insufficient, he may bring back temporary items belonging to the Saṅgha and restore it to its original state.
It is permissible. This same principle applies to other material requisites as well.

Regarding the matter of water: when water is scarce and it must be brought from a distance of a league (*yojana*) or even half a league, there is the offense of theft (*avahāra*) regarding such enclosed water, whether it is being brought from that place or is situated in a pond (*pokkharaṇī*) and so forth.
They prepare only rice gruel and consume water, but not other great luxuries;
yet for one who takes even that with a thieving mind, it constitutes theft (*avahāra*).
However, from the point where it is permitted to take one or two jars to wash a seat, to sprinkle water as an offering at the Bodhi tree, or to cook dye—therein...

One should proceed solely according to the Sangha’s established agreement (*katikā*). One who takes more than the allotted amount, or one who puts in clay or other materials with a thieving intent, should be dealt with after having the value of the goods assessed.
If the resident monks maintain their agreement strictly, [they may not allow] the belongings of others to be washed or dyed.
They do not give [anything], but instead, seeing that others have nothing, they take everything for themselves;
one should not abide by an agreement with them. One should wash only as much as they wash.
If the Saṅgha has two or three lotus ponds or water cisterns, and an agreement has been made: "One should bathe here; drinking water [is to be taken] from there..."
"It should be accepted; here, full use [of it] may be made. Everything should be done according to the agreement (*katikavatta*).
Where there is no agreement, there full use is permitted.
Regarding the case of clay: where clay is scarce, or various kinds of colored clay have been brought in...
It was set aside; even a small portion of it there is worth five māsakas, therefore it is a *pārājika* offense.
However, when work for the Saṅgha or work for a shrine (*cetiyakamma*) has been completed, it is permissible to take [the materials] after having asked the Saṅgha, or to take them on loan.
This same principle applies to lime, as well as to colors for painting.
Regarding grass plots: if the grass has been burnt, since there is no removal from its place, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), but it must be made good.

If the Saṅgha has tended a grass plot and used it to thatch a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, and later is unable to tend it again, and another single monk tends it under the pretext of a duty, this belongs to the Saṅgha alone. If he does not tend it, [the Saṅgha] should appoint one...
The monk should be told, "Look after it and give [the produce] back. If he desires a share, even if he gives a share, he must still be made to look after it.

If he increases the amount, it must certainly be given. If he continues to increase it, he should be told, "Go, look after it, take everything, and roof over your own lodging. Why? Because there is no concern regarding what is lost. By those who give...
However, it should not be given with its foundation (the ground), for that constitutes a heavy object; rather, only the grass should be given.
If, after he has tended it, he covers his own lodging while the Saṅgha is still capable of tending it, he should be told:
"Do not tend it; the Saṅgha will tend it."

The seven items beginning with the bed are well known. However, even though not mentioned in the Pāḷi, for one who steals a stone pillar, a wooden pillar, or anything else worth a *pāda* [in value], it is likewise a *pārājika*.

The same principle applies to one who, having broken down a wall or a fence of the surrounding cloister (*pariveṇa*) or similar structures abandoned or fallen in the meditation hall (*padhānaghara*) and elsewhere, takes away bricks and so forth.
Why? Because that which belongs to the Saṅgha is sometimes inhabited and sometimes not inhabited.
This same principle applies even to one who takes away any requisite from abandoned monasteries and such places when the countryside has been evacuated due to fear of bandits on the frontier.
However, those who take things from there temporarily, and for whom monks have them brought back once the monasteries are re-inhabited, [are not at fault].
It must be given back. Even if a dwelling has been constructed using materials brought from there, that very material or something of equal value must be returned.
When people have departed after vacating their attachment with the thought, "We shall return to dwell here again," and the property—whether belonging to a community or to an individual—is taken;
if they subsequently give their consent, there is no need for restorative action. However, in the case of heavy goods belonging to the Sangha...
Therefore, a remedy must certainly be made.
157. The matter concerning the use of a dwelling is of plain meaning.
Regarding the phrase, "I allow you, monks, to take [a bed] for a limited time": here, it refers to whichever monk takes a bed belonging to the Saṅgha...
If one takes away a seat belonging to you for a limited time and uses it at one's own convenient place for even one or two months as the property of the Saṅgha,
giving it to those who arrive and are senior, and does not withhold it, there is no liability for him if it is lost,
worn out, or carried off by thieves. However, when departing after having stayed, it must be placed back in its original location.
However, if one uses [the robe] for private enjoyment and does not give it to those who arrive and are senior, he is liable for its value if it is lost.
But if, having taken it to another residence and using it there, a senior person arrives and asks for it back, he should say:
"I brought this from such-and-such a residence; I am going now, so let me restore it to its original state."
It should be stated: if that bhikkhu says, "I will restore it to its original state," it is permissible to go after entrusting the responsibility to him;
this is what is stated in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the case at Campā—*tekaṭulayāgu* means gruel made with sesame, rice, and green gram (*mugga*), or sesame, rice, and black gram (*māsa*), or sesame, rice, and horse-gram (*kulattha*).
Or, having added any other single side-dish together with sesame and rice, it is made of these three.
It is said that they prepare this by mixing milk—which has been blended with water in a fourfold proportion—with ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth. Regarding the case of Rājagaha:

"Honey-ball" (*madhugoḷaka*) refers to an extremely sweet cake; some also call it "honey-head" (*madhusīsaka*). The rest here, in both cases, is to be understood according to the method already explained in the section on the "sharing of alms-food" (*odanabhājanīya*).
158. Regarding the case of Ajjuka: “He said this” means he spoke while being ill. The Venerable Upāli was “on the side” of the Venerable Ajjuka;

this does not mean he was on his side by way of following an evil course. Rather, it should be understood that the Elder was on his side because of his perception that there was no offense, out of compassion for the modest, and out of support for the Vinaya. The rest here is self-evident.
159. Regarding the account of Bārāṇasī: "Plundered by thieves" means it was robbed by thieves. "Having brought it by supernormal power (*iddhi*) and placed it in the palace":

it is said that the Elder, seeing that family tormented by the dart of sorrow and wallowing in distress, out of compassion for that family and for the sake of preserving their faith, through the support of the Dhamma and by his own supernormal power, [brought back] those very...
He resolved: "Let the palace be near the children. The children, perceiving it as "our palace," climbed up.
Then the Elder withdrew his supernormal power (*iddhi*), and the palace remained in its own place.

However, it is said by way of conventional usage that "he brought those children by means of supernormal power and placed them in the palace. Regarding the phrase "within the scope of supernormal power": this refers to such supernormal power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*).
There is no offense. However, the supernormal power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*) is not permitted.
At the end, the two matters are self-evident. Thus ends [the section] from the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The commentary on the second *pārājika* is finished.
Herein is the instruction:
This second [offense], which was proclaimed by the Conqueror as being without a second, [is now explained].
Because it has overcome the defilements, this is the "Pārājika" here.
There is no other training rule equal to it;
it is interspersed with many methods and provides a profound analysis of its meaning.
Therefore, when a case has arisen, a monk who knows the Vinaya,
making his decision here with assistance from the Vinaya,
[should rely] entirely upon the Canon and the Commentary together with their underlying intent.
Having entered [the Order], one who is diligent should carry out the formal investigation.
One should never harbor the ambition of "I shall see the offense";
rather, one should form the thought: "I shall see the non-offense."
Even after having committed an offense, one should not speak of it again and again;
rather, having investigated it and consulted with the wise, one should declare it.
And even regarding a permissible matter, for one whose mind is fickle, [one should act with care].
By means of these qualities of a recluse, ordinary people pass away from this world.
Therefore, perceiving the requisites of others as one would a venomous snake or a blazing fire, the wise person should not honor them.
The first part of the Commentary on the Chapter on Defeat is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Section on Defeats in the Vinaya Piṭaka (Second Part) 3.
The Third Defeat (Pārājika)
The third [chapter], which was elucidated by the Buddha through three pure [methods],
is now reached in its sequence of commentary regarding the *pārājika* offense.
Therefore, that which was previously explained shall be easily understood.
Excluding that [case], this is the commendation regarding horses as well.
162. Commentary on the Origin of the First Proclamation:
"At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall. Regarding this:
"Vesālī" refers to the city known by that name, a designation applied according to its feminine gender.
For that city is called "Vesālī" because it became vast (*visālībhūta*) through three successive enlargements of its surrounding walls.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this city reached its full extent only when the Perfectly Enlightened One had attained omniscience. Having thus shown the village of his alms-round:
He stated his dwelling place as: "In the Great Forest, in the Gabled Hall.
Therein, what is called the "Great Forest" (Mahāvana) is a large forest that is self-grown, uncultivated, well-defined, and extensive.
However, the Great Forest in the vicinity of Kapilavatthu is connected as one with the Himalayas, being undefined and extending right up to the great ocean. This [forest] is not of such a kind.
They call it "Great Forest" because it is large and possesses boundaries. However,

the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) of the Blessed Buddha— constructed within a monastery built adjacent to the Great Forest, with its gabled hall forming the interior and its roof fashioned in the "swan-turning" style—
is to be understood as being endowed with every excellence.

“He speaks a discourse on foulness in many ways” means that he speaks a discourse intended to turn the mind away from the body, which proceeds by demonstrating the various aspects of foulness through numerous reasons.
Namely: “In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs...
[etc] ... urine. What is meant? Monks, in this fathom-long carcass, in every respect... [etc] ...
Searching through it, no one sees even the slightest bit of purity—neither a pearl, nor a beryl, nor aloeswood, nor sandalwood, nor saffron, nor camphor, nor perfumed powders and the like;

rather, one sees only various kinds of impurities, such as head hair and body hair, which are extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and unsightly to behold. Therefore, there is nothing here [to be found].
One should cultivate either dispassion or passion. For even those things called hairs that grow on the head, the highest limb, are indeed foul, impure, and repulsive.

And this quality of their being foul, impure, and repulsive is to be understood through five reasons: by way of color, shape, odor, habitat, and location. The same applies to the body hairs and so forth. This is the point here.
This is the summary; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus, the Blessed One teaches the discourse on foulness (*asubha*) through many methods, with fivefold divisions for each individual section.

He "speaks in praise of foulness" by first setting forth the matrix of foulness (*asubhamātikā*)—beginning with the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*) and so forth—and then [explaining it] through the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*).
Analyzing, praising, and extolling that [state], he speaks in praise of foulness (*asubha*). "He speaks in praise of the development of foulness" means:

regarding this development, increase, and mastery of the mind—which has taken up the aspect of foulness with respect to internal and external objects such as the head-hairs and so forth, or the bloated corpse and so forth—he speaks of the benefit (*ānisamsa*) of that development of foulness.
He speaks in praise and extols its virtues as follows:

"Monks, a monk devoted to the meditation on the foul, whether with respect to the parts of the body beginning with hair or to the [meditative objects] beginning with the bloated, attains the first jhāna—abandoned of five factors, possessed of five factors, good in three ways, and endowed with ten characteristics. He [attains] that which is reckoned as the first jhāna..."
“By relying on the casket of the mind, one increases insight and attains the supreme goal, which is Arahantship.
In this regard, these are the ten characteristics of the first jhāna:
purification of mind from obstacles, the practice of the sign of intermediate concentration, the plunging of the mind into that [sign], and the looking on with equanimity at the purified mind.
Equanimity toward one who has entered upon serenity; equanimity toward the establishment of unity; encouragement by way of non-transgression of the states arisen therein;
and encouragement by way of the single flavor of the faculties, by way of the driving of the energy directed toward them, and by way of cultivation.
In this regard, the text is as follows: “What is the beginning of the first jhāna? What is its middle? What is its end?
The purification of the way is the beginning of the first jhāna; the intensification of equanimity is the middle; the encouragement is the end.
The purification of the way is the beginning of the first jhāna; how many characteristics does the beginning have? The beginning has three characteristics.”
— His mind is purified from whatever constitutes an obstacle to it; because of that purification, the mind enters upon the middle sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*);

and because it has entered upon it, the mind leaps forward into it. Now, that which is the purification of the mind from obstacles, that which is the mind’s entering upon the middle sign of serenity through that purification, and that which is [the result] of its having entered upon it—
Therein, the mind leaps forward. The purification of the method for the first jhāna is its beginning;
these three characteristics belong to the beginning. Therefore it is said: "The first jhāna is beautiful in the beginning and endowed with the three characteristics.
"The intensification of equanimity for the first jhāna is its middle; how many characteristics does the middle have? The middle—
There are three characteristics: he looks on with equanimity at the purified mind; he looks on with equanimity at the mind engaged in serenity;

he looks on with equanimity at the establishment of unity. That which is looking on with equanimity at the purified mind, that which is looking on with equanimity at the mind engaged in serenity, and that which is looking on with equanimity at the establishment of unity—this is the intensification of equanimity regarding the first jhāna.
In the middle, these are the three characteristics of the middle. Therefore it is said: "The first jhāna is both beautiful in the middle and endowed with the three characteristics.
The conclusion of the first jhāna is its gratification; how many characteristics does the conclusion have? Of the conclusion—
There are four characteristics: encouragement by way of the non-transgression of phenomena arisen therein;
encouragement by way of the single flavor of the faculties; encouragement by way of the exertion of the appropriate energy;
and encouragement by way of repeated practice. Encouragement is the conclusion of the first jhāna; these four are the characteristics of that conclusion.
These are the characteristics. Therefore it is said: "The first jhāna is beautiful in its conclusion and endowed with four characteristics.

Thus the mind, having reached a threefold state, being beautiful in a threefold way and endowed with ten characteristics, is endowed with applied thought, endowed with sustained thought, endowed with rapture, endowed with pleasure, and endowed with the mind’s resolution."
"One endowed with faith, endowed with energy, endowed with mindfulness, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom.
"He speaks in praise of the attainment of the foul by pointing it out repeatedly" means that he speaks in praise of the attainment of the foul,
explains its benefits, and extols its virtues, pointing it out again and again by making a systematic determination [of its characteristics] in this way and that way.
For example: "Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells frequently with a mind cultivated by the perception of foulness, his mind recoils, shrinks away, and turns back from engaging in sexual intercourse;
it does not extend toward it, and either equanimity or revulsion becomes established. Just as, bhikkhus, a cock’s feather or a strip of sinew..."
Or just as a ball of cotton-wool thrown into a fire shrinks back, recoils, and rolls away, not spreading out; even so, monks,
when a monk dwells often with a mind cultivated by the perception of foulness,
his mind shrinks back, recoils, and rolls away from engaging in sexual intercourse, and does not spread toward it.
“Bhikkhus, I wish to retreat for half a month”—the meaning is: “Bhikkhus, I wish to retreat, to seclude myself, and to dwell alone.

“I am not to be approached by anyone except a single alms-food carrier”—this means that one who, without having spoken words on their own initiative, [brings food] for my sake from among those of faith...
"Having brought forth almsfood prepared for me from various families, he presents it to me;
except for that one monk who brings the almsfood, I am not to be approached by any other monk or householder.
But why did he speak thus? It is said that in the past, five hundred deer-hunters were in the forest with large nets and snares.
Having surrounded [the area], they were joyful and elated; by making their living solely through the act of killing deer and birds for as long as they lived, they were reborn in hell.

Having been cooked there, due to some previous wholesome karma and by virtue of a favorable supporting condition (*kalyāṇūpanissaya*), they were all reborn among humans and received both the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of the Blessed One.

They obtained [that state]. From that root unwholesome kamma of theirs, other volitions whose results had not yet matured created an opportunity for the severance of life—both through their own efforts and through the efforts of others—within that half-month; the Blessed One saw this.
Indeed, the ripening of kamma cannot be warded off by anyone. And among those monks, there were also worldlings (*puthujjana*).
There are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and those whose taints are destroyed. Among them, those whose taints are destroyed are free from rebirth;
the other noble disciples have a fixed destiny and are destined for a happy destination; but the destiny of worldlings is uncertain. Then the Blessed One thought:
"These beings, terrified by the fear of death due to desire and lust for their own personal existence, will not be able to purify their destiny."
"Come now, I shall speak on the foul (asubha) for the sake of abandoning their desire and lust.

Having heard this, they will purify their destiny by becoming free from desire and lust for their own bodies, and thus they will take rebirth in heaven. In this way, their going forth in my presence will become fruitful."
Then, for their benefit, he spoke on the subject of foulness (*asubha*) under the heading of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), not with the intention of praising death.
Having spoken thus, it occurred to him: "If the monks see me during this half-month, they will come again and again and report:
'Today one monk has died; today two... [and so on] ...today ten. And this is the ripening of karma."
“It cannot be warded off by me or by anyone else. Even having heard that, what shall I do?
What use to me is this useless hearing that leads to ruin and disaster? Come now, I shall go out of sight of the bhikkhus. Therefore he spoke thus:
“Bhikkhus, I wish to retire into seclusion for half a month; I am not to be approached by anyone.”
"Except for one person who brings almsfood.
Others, however, say: "Having spoken thus for the purpose of avoiding the censure of others, he entered into seclusion. For it is said that others might have censured the Blessed One, saying:
"This man, while professing 'I am omniscient' and 'I am the supreme wheel-turner of the true Dhamma,' [even] of himself..."
He was unable to prevent his disciples from killing one another. What else could he have done? Regarding this, the wise will say:
“The Blessed One was devoted to seclusion and did not know of this occurrence;
there was no one to inform him, and had he known, he certainly would have prevented it. But this is merely a wishful thought; for, right from the beginning, [the Buddha was already aware].
The reason [is as follows]. Regarding the phrase *nāssudhā*: here, *assudhā* is a particle used merely for the completion of the metrical line or for emphasis;
the meaning is that "no one at all approached the Blessed One.

That which has a separation (*vokāra*) by way of many causes such as color, shape, and so forth, is called "possessing manifold modes" (*anekākāravokāra*); it is "interspersed with manifold modes" (*anekākāravokiṇṇo*).
What is meant by "mixed with many causes"? It is the practice of the meditation on foulness (*asubha-bhāvanā*).
They dwell devotedly engaged in that practice of the meditation on foulness, which has many aspects and modes; thus they dwell "joined and intent.
"They are distressed" means they are troubled and pained by their own bodies. "They are ashamed" means they feel shame. "They are disgusted" means they have conceived a sense of loathing.

*Daharo* means young. *Yuvā* means endowed with youth. *Maṇḍanakajātiko* means one whose nature is to adorn himself. *Sīsaṃnhāto* means one who has bathed his head. Here, by the word "young" (*dahara*), he indicates the state of early youth;
for it is at the onset of early youth that beings especially become inclined toward adorning themselves. By the phrase "having bathed his head," [he shows... (Note:

It was the time for the pursuit of adornment. For even a young man, having performed some labor and having a body defiled by it, does not engage in adornment;
but once he has bathed his head, he devotes himself solely to adornment. He does not even wish to look upon things such as the carcasses of snakes.
At that moment, with the carcass of a snake, or the carcass of a dog, or the carcass of a human being fastened around his neck—

Just as one would be terrified, ashamed, and disgusted by an enemy who had brought a corpse and tied it around one's neck so that it hung down in front; even so, those bhikkhus, being themselves terrified, ashamed,
and disgusted by their own bodies, like that man, became desirous of abandoning their own bodies through the fading away of desire and lust for them.
Taking up a weapon, they deprive even themselves of life. Saying, "You deprive me of life;
I [will deprive] you," they thus deprive one another of life.
Regarding Migalaṇḍika: "Migalaṇḍika" is his name; "samaṇakuttaka" means one who wears the guise of an ascetic.

It is said that, having shaved his head leaving only a tuft, and having put on a single saffron robe draped over one shoulder, he lives right near the monastery by subsisting on the leavings of others.
People would approach that Migalaṇḍika, a mere sham ascetic, and speak thus. *Sādhu* is a particle used in the sense of a request. *No* is the plural accusative form.
"It is well, friend; take our lives," was what was said. And herein, the Noble Ones neither committed the destruction of life, nor incited others to do so, nor approved of it.
But the worldlings did all of these things. "Blood-stained" means smeared with blood.
"By which [flows] the Vaggumudā River"—the Vaggumudā is the river esteemed by the world as meritorious. It is said that even he [the Buddha] thought, "That evil deed occurred there..."
Thinking, "I shall wash it away," he went; yet by the power of the river, not even the slightest evil was actually abandoned.
163. "He indeed felt remorse": it is said that among those monks, no one made any movement of body or speech;
all lay down on their right sides, mindful and clearly comprehending. As he recalled that—
“Remorse arose” means that remorse indeed occurred. “There was regret” is said for the purpose of defining the specific nature of that very remorse;

it was the remorse of regret (*vippaṭisāra-kukkucca*), not the remorse regarding the Vinaya (*vinaya-kukkucca*). “Alābhā vata me” and so forth is said to show the manner in which the remorse manifested.
In that context, “Alābhā vata me” means: “Alas, I have lost my gain of welfare and happiness in the future.”
He laments, saying, "There is no gain. Furthermore, with the words "Alas, no gain for me," he makes that very point firm.
This is the intended meaning here: even if someone were to say, "It is a gain for you," that would be false; alas, there is no gain for me.
"Ill-gotten indeed is this"—even though this human state was obtained through the power of wholesome deeds, alas, it is ill-gotten for me.
“Alas, it has not been well-gained by me!”—this phrase, however, strengthens that very point. This is the intended meaning here:
even if someone were to say, “It has been well-gained by you,” that would be false; for alas, it has not been well-gained by me.
“Meritless has been produced” means meritless has been accumulated or generated. Why? Because I, a monk... [and so on]... have deprived [beings] of life.
The meaning of this is as follows: "I shall deprive of life those virtuous monks who possess wholesome qualities, supreme qualities, and excellent qualities, precisely because of that very virtue.
"A certain deity of Māra’s host" refers to a terrestrial deity belonging to Māra’s faction who holds wrong views and whose name is not well known.
Thinking, "In this way he will not transcend Māra’s domain, Māra’s sphere," those who follow Māra—
having adorned themselves with all their ornaments and displaying their own power, coming as if walking upon the surface of the earth even over water that cannot be crossed—
approached Migalaṇḍika, that sham ascetic, and said this. "Sādhu, sādhu" is an exclamation used for the purpose of encouragement.

Therefore, the dual number was used. "He delivered those who had not crossed" means that by this act of depriving them of life, he delivered—that is, liberated—those who had not yet crossed over from *saṃsāra*.
It is said that this foolish and dull-witted deity held the following view: "Those who have not died are not liberated from *saṃsāra*;
those who have died are liberated. Therefore, like a *milakkha* (outcaste) who liberates others from *saṃsāra*, she held such a view.
Having offered the sacrifice, she directed him toward that [result] and spoke thus.
Then Migalaṇḍika, the fake ascetic—though he was filled with intense remorse—saw the power of that deity and reached the conclusion: "This deity says so;
surely it must be exactly as she says regarding this matter. Thus, praising himself, saying, "It is indeed a gain for me," and so forth.
“Having approached one dwelling from another dwelling, and one courtyard from another courtyard, he speaks thus”:
having approached this or that dwelling and courtyard, opened the door, entered within, he says to the bhikkhus, “Who has not crossed over?
Whom shall I ferry across?”
“There is fear” means there is mental terror on account of death. “There is trepidation” means that, beginning with the flesh of the heart, there is a trembling of the body;
some say it is because the body becomes rigid due to extreme fear, for rigidity (thambhitatta) is called trepidation (chambhitatta).
“Horripilation” means the state of having hair standing erect; however, those whose taints are destroyed [do not experience this] because of the emptiness of beings.
Because they did not see even the dying being itself due to their clear vision, it should be understood that none of this occurred for them.

When it is said, "He deprived one bhikkhu of life, two... [and so on] ...up to sixty bhikkhus of life in a single day," it means that he deprived all those five hundred bhikkhus of life by way of counting.
164. “Having emerged from seclusion” means that, having learned of the passing away of those five hundred bhikkhus, he emerged from his solitary state;
and although he already knew, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda as if not knowing, for the purpose of initiating a conversation:
“Ānanda, why is it that the Saṅgha of bhikkhus seems so diminished? Previously, Ānanda...
"Many bhikkhus used to come together for attendance;
they would receive the recitation and the questioning, and they would practice their studies until the monastery appeared like a single lamp.
