But now, with the passing of only half a month, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has become as if thinned out—sparse, weak, small, and scattered. What indeed is the cause? What is it?"
"Have the bhikkhus departed in all directions?

Then the Venerable Ānanda, not perceiving through the ripening of kamma that they had met their end, but perceiving it rather through the condition of his application to the meditation subject of the foul (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna), said, "For thus indeed, Bhante, the Blessed One... and so forth, regarding the attainment of Arahantship by the bhikkhus.
Requesting another meditation subject, he said, "It would be well, Bhante, Blessed One," and so forth. The meaning of this is:
"It would be well, Bhante, Blessed One, if you would explain another method by which the community of monks might be established in Arahantship;

for there are indeed other categories—such as the ten recollections, the ten kasinas, the analysis of the four elements, the divine abidings, and mindfulness of breathing—which are like landing-stairs for descending into the great ocean."

There are many meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for ascending to Nibbāna. Among them, the intention was that the Blessed One, having comforted the bhikkhus, should explain one particular meditation subject.
Then, desiring to act accordingly, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Then, Ānanda," while dispatching the Elder. In that context, Vesālī—
"Dependent upon Vesālī" means: "Assemble all those bhikkhus who dwell within a league or even half a league around Vesālī.

Having assembled them all in the assembly hall, he himself went to the place where it was appropriate for him to go, and having sent junior bhikkhus elsewhere, in just a moment [he gathered] them all without exception.
The monks, having gathered in a great assembly in the assembly hall, said: "Venerable Sir, it is now time for the Blessed One to do as he deems fit.
Herein, the intended meaning is this: "The Blessed One, the Saṅgha of monks, has assembled;
this is the time for the monks to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma and to give instruction. Now, whatever you deem to be the appropriate time, that should be done."
The Discourse on the Concentration of Mindfulness of Breathing (Ānāpānassatisamādhikathā) 165. Then the Blessed One... [as before] ...addressed the bhikkhus:

"Bhikkhus, this too," having thus addressed them, he spoke another method for the attainment of arahantship by the bhikkhus, distinct from the previously taught meditation subject of foulness (asubha).
Explaining it, he said, "the concentration of mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*).

Now, since this passage was spoken by the Blessed One for the purpose of showing the monks a peaceful and sublime subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*), I shall provide a commentary here following the sequence of the construction of its meaning without omission. In that regard: "This too..."
Regarding this phrase, "O bhikkhus," the construction is as follows: "O bhikkhus, it is not only the development of foulness that leads to the abandoning of the defilements;
rather, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing also... [etc. ...leads to their subsiding. Herein, this is the commentary on the meaning:
"Mindfulness of breathing" (ānāpānassati) is the mindfulness that grasps the inhalation and exhalation. For this has been said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:

“In-breathing is inhalation, not exhalation. Out-breathing is exhalation, not inhalation. Mindfulness established by way of inhalation is mindfulness; mindfulness established by way of exhalation is mindfulness. It is established for one who inhales, and it is established for one who exhales.
“Concentration” (*samādhi*) refers to the one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*) that arises together with that mindfulness which grasps the breath.

This teaching is given under the heading of concentration, not under the heading of mindfulness. Therefore, concentration that is associated with mindfulness of breathing is “concentration through mindfulness of breathing” (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*).
Or, concentration in mindfulness of breathing is "mindfulness-of-breathing concentration"; this is how the meaning should be understood here. "Developed" means both arisen and increased.
"Cultivated" means done repeatedly. "Both peaceful and sublime": it is both peaceful and indeed sublime;
in both cases, the word "indeed" (eva) should be understood as a restriction. What is meant? This [concentration]— (End of fragment)
Just as the meditation subject of foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) is both peaceful and sublime solely by way of penetration,
yet is neither peaceful nor sublime by way of its object because its object is gross and repulsive,
so too it is not in any way unpeaceful or unsublime; rather, it is peaceful, stilled, and extinguished even by virtue of the peace of its object.
It is sublime because of the continuity of the factors known as penetration, because of the excellence of the object, and because of the excellence of the factors themselves;
thus it brings no satiety. Therefore it is said: "peaceful and sublime.
Regarding the phrase "an unadulterated and blissful abiding": here, "unadulterated" (asecanaka) means that there is no admixture (secanam) to it—it is unmixed and uninterrupted.

It is distinct and unique; here there is no continuity through either preliminary work (*parikamma*) or access concentration (*upacāra*), but from the very moment of initial attention (*ādi-manasikāra*), it is peaceful and sublime by its own intrinsic nature—this is the meaning.
Some, however, say that "unpourable" (*asecanaka*) means not being poured over, but being naturally rich in essence and sweet by its own nature.
Thus, this [jhāna] is unpourable, and at every moment of absorption, it leads to the attainment of bodily and mental happiness.
It should be understood that it is a pleasant abiding because it leads to such a state.
"As each one arises" means as each one has not yet been suppressed. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" means states produced by lack of skill.
"He makes them disappear on the spot" means he makes them disappear and suppresses them in an instant. "He pacifies them" means...
It thoroughly pacifies; or, because it partakes of penetration (*nibbedha*), it gradually eradicates and allays [the defilements] upon reaching the culmination of the Noble Path—this is the meaning.
"Just as if" (*seyyathāpi*) is an expression used to indicate a simile. "In the last month of summer" means in the month of Āsāḷha. "Dust and dirt have been swept away" (*ūhataṃ rajojallaṃ*).

The dust and fine particles that were raised and scattered into the air by the earth—which had been dried by wind and sun for half a month and broken up by the trampling of the hooves of cattle, buffalo, and other animals;

and the great unseasonable cloud, which arose covering the entire sky and rained for the whole half-month of the bright fortnight of Āsāḷha. For that [cloud] arose even before the rainy season had arrived.

"An unseasonal cloud" is intended here because it has arisen. "It makes [it] vanish and subside on the spot" means it leads it to invisibility in an instant and causes it to settle upon the earth. "In the same way" is the application of the simile.
What follows is exactly according to the method already stated.

Now, regarding the question, "And how, monks, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed?"—here, "how" is a question intended to explain in detail the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing by way of its various modes.
"And how, monks, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed" indicates the subject matter that was asked about for the sake of such a detailed exposition.
This same method applies to the second phrase as well.
This, however, is the summary of the meaning here: "In what manner, by what aspect, by what method, monks, is the concentration of mindfulness of breathing developed;
in what manner is it cultivated so that it is peaceful... [and so on] ...and completely tranquil?
Now, expanding upon that meaning, he said: "Here, monks... and so forth. In that context, "here, monks, a monk" means:

“Monks, a bhikkhu in this teaching. Here, the word *idha* (here/in this) indicates the teaching that serves as the support for the person who has produced the concentration of mindfulness of breathing in all its modes, and it precludes the existence of such a state in any other teaching.
For it has been said: “Right here, monks, is the ascetic... [and so on] ...empty are the doctrines of others of ascetics other than these.”
Therefore it was said: "In this teaching, monks.

"Having gone to the forest... or having gone to an empty hut"—this is an illustration of his selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati-samādhi*).
For this monk’s mind, which for a long time has been diffused among objects such as visible forms, [is now directed] toward the object of concentration through mindfulness of breathing.
He does not wish to mount; like a chariot yoked to a sham-bull, he runs only along the wrong path.

Therefore, just as a cowherd, wishing to tame a sham-calf that has grown fat by drinking all the milk from a sham-cow, would remove it from the cow, drive it to a secluded spot, drive a large stake into the ground, and bind it there with a rope—then for him...
Just as that calf, after struggling here and there, being unable to escape, would sit down or lie down right next to that very post;

even so, this bhikkhu—desiring to tame his corrupted mind which has long been nourished by drinking the flavors of sense objects such as forms—having withdrawn it from those objects like forms, [should go] to the forest... or to an empty hut.
Having established [the mind] there, it should be bound with the rope of mindfulness to the pillar of in-breathing and out-breathing.

Thus, although that mind may still quiver here and there, being unable to find its former habitual object and unable to escape by severing the rope of mindfulness, it sits down and lies down right upon that very object through access concentration (upacāra) and absorption (appanā). Regarding this, the ancients said:
"Just as a man here would tie up a young ox to be tamed by binding it to a post, so too should he bind his own mind firmly to the object of mindfulness.

In this way, that lodging becomes suitable for his development [of meditation]. Therefore it was said: "This is the explanation of his acquisition of a lodging suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing."
Alternatively, because this mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) meditation subject—

the pinnacle among the various meditation subjects, the proximate cause for the special attainments and the pleasant dwellings in this very life of the omniscient Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—
is not easy to accomplish without abandoning a village settlement crowded with the sounds of men, women, elephants, horses, and so forth, since sound is a thorn to jhāna; however, in a forest...
In the forest, it is easy for a practitioner of yoga to grasp this meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), to produce the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*),
and— taking that very state as a basis— to contemplate conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and thereby attain the supreme fruit,
which is Arahantship. Therefore, showing him a suitable dwelling place, the Blessed One said, "Having gone to the forest," and so forth.
For the Blessed One is like a master of site-selection (*vatthuvijjācariya*).

Just as a master of site-selection, having surveyed a piece of land for a city and examined it thoroughly, points out, "Build the city here," and when the city has been completed in safety, receives great honor from the royal court;
even so, [the Blessed One] examines a suitable dwelling for a practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*).
Herein, he indicates that the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be practiced.
Then, when a yogi devoted to that meditation subject attains Arahatship in due course, he receives great honor, thinking, "Truly, that Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One.
This bhikkhu, however, is called "one who resembles a leopard. For just as a great king of leopards [enters] a thicket of grass in the forest...
Just as a hunter, having hidden himself by relying on a forest thicket, a jungle, or a mountain cleft, captures wild animals such as deer, buffalo, oxen, and boars;

even so, it should be understood that this bhikkhu, while devoted to his meditation subject in the forest and other such places, captures the paths of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship, as well as the noble fruits, in their proper sequence. Thus said the ancients:
“Just as a leopard, having hidden itself, seizes a deer,
so too this son of the Buddha, devoted to practice and possessing insight,
having entered the forest, seizes the supreme fruit.”
Showing him a forest dwelling as a suitable ground for the speed of exertion, the Blessed One said, "Or having gone to the forest," and so forth.

Therein, "having gone to the forest" (*araññagato vā*) refers to the characteristics thus stated: "Having gone out beyond the threshold post, all this is the forest" (*arañña*), and "A forest dwelling (*āraññakaṃ senāsanaṃ*) is one that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant."
Having gone to the forest, he experiences whatever secluded bliss is appropriate for the forests. "Or having gone to the foot of a tree" means having gone near a tree.
"Or having gone to an empty place" means having gone to a secluded spot.

And here, apart from the forest and the foot of a tree, it is also permissible to say that one who has gone to any of the remaining seven kinds of lodgings has "gone to an empty place. Thus, in accordance with the three seasons...
Having pointed out a lodging suitable for his temperament and conducive to the development of mindfulness of breathing,

he said, "he sits," while indicating a peaceful posture that avoids both dullness and agitation. Then, showing the firmness of his sitting, the ease with which the inhalations and exhalations proceed,
and the method for grasping the object, he said, "having folded his legs crosswise," and so forth.
Therein, "pallaṅka" means a cross-legged posture with the thighs bound all around. "Having folded" means having bound [the legs].
"Having set the body erect" means having placed the upper part of the body straight, having aligned the tip of one vertebra against the tip of the next among the eighteen spinal vertebrae.
For when one is seated in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Then, for him, that which arises due to their bending—
Feelings might arise moment by moment, but they do not arise [in this case]. When they do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed;
the meditation subject does not fall away, and it attains growth and expansion.
"Having established mindfulness facing the front" means having placed mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject. Alternatively, "pari" means...
“Pariggaha” means the sense of embracing; “mukha” means the sense of outlet; “sati” means the sense of establishing. Therefore it is said:
“having established mindfulness facing the opening. The meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*.
This is the summary: “having made mindfulness the outlet that has been embraced. “Mindful he breathes in”: that bhikkhu, in this way...
Having sat down and established mindfulness in this way, not abandoning that mindfulness, he breathes in mindful, breathes out mindful;
it is said that he acts with mindfulness.

Now, in order to show the modes by which one acts with mindfulness, he says: "Breathing in long," and so forth. For this has been stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the very passage: "He breathes in mindful, he breathes out mindful."
“One practices with mindfulness by way of thirty-two aspects. For one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction through long inhalation, mindfulness is established.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one practices with mindfulness. [The same applies] through long exhalation... pe...
through inhalation while contemplating relinquishment, and through exhalation while contemplating relinquishment, for one who understands the unification of mind...”
"For one who understands non-distraction, mindfulness is established. By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, he acts with mindfulness.

Herein, "breathing in long" means while causing a long inhalation to proceed. "Inhalation" (*assāsa*) is the wind going out; "exhalation" (*passāsa*) is the wind coming in. However, in the commentaries on the Suttas, this is given in reverse order.
Therein, for all those dwelling in the womb, at the time of emerging from the mother's womb, first the internal wind...
It goes out externally. Afterwards, the external air, having taken up subtle dust, enters within and, striking the palate, is extinguished.
In this way, first of all, the in-breaths and out-breaths are to be understood. As for their length or shortness, that is to be understood by way of distance (*addhāna*).
For just as water or sand, having filled and occupied a space, remains there—
Or it is said: "Long water has long sand; short water has short sand.
In the same way, even though the inhalations and exhalations are broken into minute particles, in the bodies of elephants and snakes they slowly fill their long physical extent and slowly emerge;
therefore, they are called "long. [In the case] of dogs, hares, and so forth...
Having quickly filled a short duration of time known as a single lifetime, they emerge again very swiftly; therefore, they are called "short.
Among humans, however, some—like elephants, snakes, and so forth—inhalate and exhale for a long duration of time, while others—like dogs, hares, and so forth—do so for a short duration.
Therefore, in their case, it is by way of time that the duration is long.
Those [breaths] which go out and come in for a long duration are "long. Those which go out and come in for a short duration should be understood as "short.
In this regard, when a bhikkhu breathes in and breathes out long in nine ways, he understands:
"I breathe in and breathe out long. For one who understands in this way, there is the development of the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body in one aspect.
It should be understood that [this] is accomplished. As it is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
“How is it that, while breathing in long, one understands: ‘I am breathing in long’; and while breathing out long, one understands:
‘I am breathing out long’? One breathes in a long inhalation reckoned as a duration; one breathes out a long exhalation reckoned as a duration.”
He breathes out; he both breathes in and breathes out long inhalations and exhalations reckoned as a duration.

As he breathes in and breathes out long inhalations and exhalations reckoned as a duration, zeal arises. By way of that zeal, he breathes in a longer inhalation, more subtle than before, reckoned as a duration; by way of that zeal, he breathes out a longer exhalation, more subtle than before.

He breathes in and breathes out what is reckoned as a long duration by way of zeal. While breathing in and breathing out what is reckoned as a long duration by way of zeal, even more subtle than before, joy arises.
By way of that joy, [he breathes in and breathes out] what is even more subtle than before... a long [duration].
He breathes in a long inhalation reckoned as a course through the joy; he breathes out a long exhalation even more subtle than that through the joy...
[and so on] ...he both breathes in and breathes out a long inhalation and exhalation reckoned as a course through the joy.
While breathing in and breathing out a long inhalation and exhalation even more subtle than that through the joy, reckoned as a course, it is long.
With the in-breaths and out-breaths, the mind turns away [from the breaths] and equanimity becomes established. In these nine aspects: long in-breaths and out-breaths are the body;
the establishment is mindfulness; the contemplation is knowledge. The body is the establishment, but it is not the mindfulness; mindfulness is both the establishment and the mindfulness.

By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, one contemplates that body. Therefore, it is said: "The development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body as a body."
The same method applies to the short breath as well. However, this is the distinction:
whereas here it was stated, "He breathes in a long in-breath reckoned as a long duration," so here it comes down to, "He breathes in a short in-breath reckoned as a short duration.

Therefore, following that [method], the connection should be made up until the words, "Thus, it is called the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body in the body. Thus, this...

It should be understood that one who understands in-breaths and out-breaths through these modes—by way of duration and by way of brevity—knows, while breathing in long, "I am breathing in long," and so on, up to: while breathing out short, "I am breathing out short.
And for one who understands in this way:
“Long and short is the inhalation;
the exhalation is likewise.
Four colors proceed;”
"Right at the tip of the nose for the bhikkhu.

Regarding the training: "I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body... I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body," he trains himself while making known and making clear the beginning, middle, and end of the entire body of the in-breath. Of the entire...
Making known and making clear the beginning, middle, and end of the body of out-breathing, he trains himself, thinking, "I shall breathe out.
Making them known and making them clear in this way, he both breathes in and breathes out with a mind associated with knowledge;
therefore, it is said that he trains himself, thinking, "I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out. For a certain monk...
When the body of inhalation or the body of exhalation is scattered and shattered like fine powder, the beginning becomes manifest, but not the middle or the end.
Such a person is able to discern only the beginning, while they become exhausted by the middle and the end. For another, the middle becomes manifest, but not the beginning or the end.
Such a person is able to discern only the middle, while they become exhausted by the beginning and the end.

For one person, the end is clear, but not the beginning or the middle; he is able to comprehend only the end, while he falters regarding the beginning and the middle. For another, everything is clear;
he is able to comprehend everything and does not falter anywhere. Showing that one ought to become like the latter, he said: "Experiencing the whole body..."
“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in... ... ‘I shall breathe out.
In this context, “he trains” means he exerts himself or strives in this way. Alternatively, the restraint of one who has become such is here the training in the higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
The concentration of one who has become such is the training in the higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*). The wisdom of one who has become such is the training in the higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*).
These three trainings are practiced, cultivated, developed, and frequently repeated with that object, by means of that mindfulness, and through that attention;

this is how the meaning should be understood here. In that regard, because in the previous method there was only breathing in and breathing out to be done, and nothing else to be performed, but from this point on, there is the arising of knowledge and so forth.
Yoga must be practiced. Therefore, having stated the text for that [practice] according to the present tense as "he understands: 'I am breathing in';

he understands: 'I am breathing out'," it should be understood that from this point onward, the text is set forth in the form of the future tense—beginning with "I shall breathe in while experiencing the whole body"—for the purpose of showing the manner of generating knowledge and so forth that is to be performed.
"He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation... [and so on] ...I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
This means he trains with the thought, "I shall breathe in and breathe out tranquilizing, calming, stopping, and pacifying the gross bodily formation.
In this regard, both the grossness and subtlety, as well as the tranquility, should be understood as follows. For previously, when this bhikkhu had not yet comprehended [the body],...
The body and the mind become well-restrained. When the grossness of the body and mind has not subsided, the inhalations and exhalations are also gross;
they proceed with greater force until the nose is no longer sufficient, and one remains breathing in and out through the mouth.
But when both the body and the mind have been mastered, then they become calm.
They become stilled. When they have been stilled, the in-breaths and out-breaths proceed in a subtle manner, reaching a state where one must investigate whether they exist or not.
It is just as when a man has run, or descended from a mountain, or lowered a heavy burden from his head and stands still; his in-breaths and out-breaths are gross, and [his] nostrils...
He is not able [to stop them]; even while breathing out and breathing in through the mouth, he remains standing.

But when he has dispelled that fatigue, bathed, drunk, and lain down in the cool shade with a wet cloth over his heart, then those inhalations and exhalations of his become subtle, reaching a state where one must discern whether they exist or not.
In the same way, when this bhikkhu was previously uninvestigated, his body and so forth... reached a state where they were to be scrutinized.
Why is that? Because previously, when he was uninvestigated, there was no application of attention, mental engagement, or review with the thought, "I am tranquilizing gross bodily formations";
but when he has investigated them, such exists. Therefore, for him—
From the time when [the body] was unappropriated until the time it is appropriated, the bodily formation becomes subtle. Regarding this, the ancients said:
"When both body and mind are agitated, [the formation] proceeds excessively;
when the body is no longer agitated, it proceeds subtly."
It is gross in the case of possession, subtle in the access to the first jhāna; therein too it is gross in the access and subtle in the first jhāna.
It is gross in both the first jhāna and the access to the second jhāna, and subtle in the second jhāna.
It is gross in both the second jhāna and the access to the third jhāna, and subtle in the third jhāna. [It is gross] in both the third jhāna and the access to the fourth jhāna...
In the fourth jhāna, it becomes extremely subtle and reaches a state of non-occurrence. This, first of all, is the opinion of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas and Saṃyutta-bhāṇakas.

The Majjhima-bhāṇakas, however, maintain that "it is gross in the first jhāna and subtle in the access to the second jhāna," thus asserting that it becomes increasingly subtler in each successive access concentration (upacāra) compared to the jhānas immediately below them.
According to the view of all of them, however, during the time when it is not yet fully mastered—
The active bodily formation subsides at the time of comprehension; the active bodily formation at the time of comprehension [subsides] in the access to the first jhāna...
pe ...in the access to the fourth jhāna; the active bodily formation in the access to the fourth jhāna subsides in the fourth jhāna.
This, firstly, is the method regarding serenity (samatha).

In insight meditation (vipassanā), however, the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) occurring during the non-apprehension [of objects] is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of the primary elements (mahābhūta).
That too is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of derived matter (upādārūpa). That too is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of all material form.
That too is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of the immaterial (arūpa). That too is gross; it is subtle during the apprehension of both the material and the immaterial. That too...
It is gross in relation to the grasping of conditions, but subtle in relation to the grasping of conditioned name-and-form.

That too is gross in relation to the grasping of conditioned name-and-form, but subtle in relation to insight that takes the characteristics as its object. That too is gross in relation to weak insight, but subtle in relation to powerful insight.
In this context, according to the method already explained, each preceding stage is [surpassed] by each succeeding one.
Tranquility is to be understood by way of the latter [term]. Thus, both grossness-and-subtlety and tranquility are to be understood here.
In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, however, this meaning is stated together with the "exhortation" and "clarification":
"How does he train thus: 'I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation... I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation'? What are the bodily formations? Long..."
These in-breaths are bodily; these phenomena are bound up with the body, they are bodily formations.
He trains in calming, stopping, and pacifying those bodily formations. Long out-breaths are bodily; these phenomena...
[as before] ...short in-breaths... short out-breaths... in-breaths experiencing the whole body... out-breaths experiencing the whole body are bodily.
These phenomena are bodily, bound up with the body, and are bodily formations; he trains in calming, ceasing, and stilling those bodily formations.
By means of whatever bodily formations there are, there is the bending, the inclining, the leaning, the bowing, and the moving of the body.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in tranquillizing the bodily formation"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily formation.
By means of such bodily formations as do not cause the body to bend forward, to lean back, to incline to one side, or to incline to another side—
It is unshakable, unwavering, immovable, and unfluctuating. One trains thus: "I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation";
one trains thus: "I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation.
Indeed, it is in this way that one trains: "I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation," [and] "I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation."

"He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out. If this were the case, there would be no development of the perception of air, nor the development of inhalation and exhalation, nor the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), nor the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing;
and wise men would neither enter nor emerge from that attainment.
Thus, indeed, he trains himself: "Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe in... [and so on] ...I shall breathe out.

When this is the case, there is the development of the perception of air, there is the development of the in-breaths and out-breaths, there is the development of mindfulness of breathing, and there is the development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing; and he attains that meditative attainment.
The wise both enter and emerge from it.
How so? Just as when a bronze gong is struck, first coarse sounds arise;
because the sign of those coarse sounds has been well grasped, well attended to, and well retained, even when the coarse sounds have ceased—
Just as, after coarse sounds have ceased, subtle sounds subsequently arise, and because the sign of those subtle sounds has been well-grasped,
well-attended to, and well-retained, the mind continues to proceed even after the subtle sounds have ceased by taking the sign of the subtle sounds as its object;
in the same way, first the coarse inhalations and exhalations proceed, and [of] those coarse inhalations and exhalations...
Because the sign has been well grasped, well attended to, and well sustained, even when the gross in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased,
subsequently subtle in-breaths and out-breaths continue to occur; and because the sign of those subtle in-breaths and out-breaths has been well grasped,
well attended to, and well sustained, even when the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased, then—
Afterwards, the mind does not go to distraction even when taking the sign of the subtle in-breath and out-breath as its object.

This being so, there is the development of the perception of wind, the development of the in-breaths and out-breaths, the development of mindfulness of breathing, and the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing; and one attains that meditative attainment.
The wise both enter and emerge from it. "Tranquilizing the bodily formations":
here, the body refers to the inhalation and exhalation; the foundation is mindfulness; the contemplation is knowledge.
The body is the foundation but not the mindfulness; mindfulness is both the foundation and the mindfulness itself. By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, that...
He contemplates the body. Therefore it is said: "The development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body.
This, then, is the word-by-word commentary on the first tetrad stated here by way of contemplation of the body.
Since this very tetrad is taught here as the meditation subject for a beginner, whereas the others...
Three tetrads are taught here by way of the contemplations of feelings, mind, and mental objects for one who has attained jhāna.
Therefore, everything that must be done by a son of the Buddha— who, having developed this meditation subject,
desires to reach Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) through insight based on the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing— is contained right here.
This should be understood from the very beginning according to the case of a clansman who is a beginner.

First, the fourfold virtue must be purified. In this regard, there are three ways of purifying it: not transgressing, emerging from what has been transgressed, and not being oppressed by the defilements.
For one whose virtue is thus purified, the development of meditation succeeds. As for this duty regarding the shrine precinct (*cetiyāṅgaṇavatta*):

The morality of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*) is said to consist of these: the duties toward the Bodhi tree, the duties toward one’s preceptor (*upajjhāya*), the duties toward one’s teacher (*ācariya*), the duties regarding the sauna (*jantāghara*), the duties regarding the Uposatha hall, and the eighty-two rules of the Khandhakas, along with the fourteen kinds of major rules (*mahāvatta*).
This too must be fulfilled thoroughly. For one who thinks, "I am guarding my virtue; what is the use of the higher conduct?"...
If one were to say, "He will fulfill his virtue," this is impossible.
However, when the conduct of higher practice (*ābhisamācārika-vatta*) is fulfilled, virtue is fulfilled; when virtue is fulfilled, concentration takes conception.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Indeed, monks, that bhikkhu who, without fulfilling the Dhamma of higher practice, [claims] 'Virtues..."
‘...will fulfill it’—this possibility does not exist. This should be expanded in detail.

Therefore, he must also thoroughly fulfill that which is called the morality of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*), such as the duties regarding the shrine courtyard (*cetiyāṅgaṇa-vatta*) and so forth.
Then: “Residence, family, gain, the group, and action as the fifth;”
“Travel, relatives, illness, books, and psychic powers—these are the ten impediments.
When these ten impediments have been stated, whichever impediment exists must be severed.
Once the impediments have been severed in this way, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be learned. That too is twofold: the universal meditation subject and...

And the meditation subject for traveling. Therein, the "all-pervading meditation subject" (sabbatthaka-kammaṭṭhāna) is said by some to be loving-kindness (mettā), mindfulness of death (maraṇassati), and the perception of foulness (asubhasaññā) directed toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and so forth.

For a bhikkhu who practices meditation, he should first delimit a boundary and then develop loving-kindness toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus within that boundary; after that, toward the deities dwelling within that boundary; and after that, toward those in his alms-resort village.

[He should extend it] to the ruling class, and from there to all people therein, including all beings. For by means of loving-kindness toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he generates a gentle state of mind in those with whom he dwells, and thus he becomes easy to live with.

By means of loving-kindness toward the deities residing within the boundary, his protection is well-arranged through the righteous protection of those deities whose minds have been made gentle. In the village where he goes for alms...
Through loving-kindness toward the ruling class, he becomes one whose requisites are well-guarded by those rulers who, having softened their hearts with loving-kindness, provide righteous protection.
Therein, through loving-kindness toward human beings, he wanders about unscathed by them because they have become clear-minded through that loving-kindness.
Through loving-kindness toward all beings, his movement is unobstructed everywhere.
But by mindfulness of death, one who contemplates that "one must inevitably die" abandons wrong search and becomes one whose sense of urgency increases ever further and who lives without attachment.
By the perception of foulness, craving does not arise even for divine objects.
Therefore, because this triad is so very helpful, it is intended [here] as something that "should be cultivated and desired in all circumstances."
And because it is the foundation for the practice of yoga and its application, it is called the "universal meditation subject" (*sabbatthaka-kammaṭṭhāna*).
Furthermore, among the thirty-eight objects of meditation, whatever is suitable to one's own temperament should be constantly maintained;

thus, according to the method already stated, it is also called the "meditation subject to be maintained" (*pārihāriya-kammaṭṭhāna*). In this context, however, it is specifically this very meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).

This is called "the meditation subject for carrying about. This is the summary here; however, one who desires the detailed explanation of the purification of virtue and the cutting off of impediments should take it from the *Visuddhimagga*.
Now, by one whose virtue is thus purified and whose impediments are cut off, this meditation subject is to be learned as follows:
This should be learned in the presence of a son of the Buddha who, having produced the fourth jhāna by means of this very meditation subject, has increased his insight and attained Arahantship.
If such a person is not available, it should be learned from one who is an Anāgāmi; if he is not available, from one who is a Sakadāgāmi;
if he is not available, from a Sotāpanna; and if even he is not available, from one who has attained the fourth jhāna through mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna).
If one does not obtain even that, it should be learned in the presence of a teacher of the Vinaya who is undeluded regarding both the Pāḷi and the Commentary.
For while the Arahants and others teach only the path they themselves have realized, this teacher— like one leading a great elephant out onto a broad path—
is undeluded in all respects and speaks after having discerned what is suitable and what is unsuitable.
In this regard, here is the step-by-step instruction: That bhikkhu, living lightly and endowed with conduct in accordance with the Vinaya, should approach a teacher of the kind described above.
Having pleased the teacher’s mind by performing his duties, he should learn the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) consisting of five stages in that teacher’s presence.
These five stages are: learning (uggaha), questioning (paripucchā), establishing (upaṭṭhāna), absorption (appanā), and the characteristic (lakkhaṇa).
In this context, "acquisition" (uggaha) means the learning of the meditation subject; "inquiry" (paripucchā) means questioning regarding the meditation subject;
"establishment" (upaṭṭhāna) means the appearance of the meditation subject; "absorption" (appanā) means absorption in the meditation subject;

and "characteristic" (lakkhaṇa) means the characteristic of the meditation subject. What is meant is the grasping of the intrinsic nature of the meditation subject, thinking: "This meditation subject has such a characteristic."
One who learns the meditation subject with these five links does not weary himself, nor does he trouble his teacher.
Therefore, having had it recited in brief and having rehearsed it for a long time, one should learn the meditation subject with these five links.
If it is suitable there, one should dwell right there. If it is not suitable there, [one should approach] the teacher...
Having taken leave, if one is of dull wit, one should go no further than a league; if one is of keen wit, one may go even further.

Having approached a lodging that is free from the eighteen faults of a lodging and endowed with the five factors of a lodging, and dwelling there, having severed minor impediments and finished the meal, one should dispel the drowsiness following eating.

Having gladdened the mind by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem, one should attend to this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing without forgetting even a single word of what has been mastered from the teacher.
This is the summary here; however, one who desires a detailed exposition should take it from the *Visuddhimagga* along this path of discourse.
As for what was said, "This meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) should be brought to mind," the method for bringing it to mind is as follows:
"Counting, following, touching, fixing,
observing, Turning away, purification, and reviewing these."
“Counting” (*gaṇanā*) is simply counting. “Following” (*anubandhanā*) is continuous tracking. “Touching” (*phusanā*) is the point of contact. “Fixing” (*ṭhapanā*) is absorption (*appanā*).
“Observing” (*sallakkhaṇā*) is insight (*vipassanā*). “Turning away” (*vivaṭṭanā*) is the path (*magga*). “Complete purification” (*pārisuddhi*) is the fruit (*phala*).
“And the reviewing of these” (*tesañca paṭipassanā*) is reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*). In this regard, by means of counting first, that son of good family who is a beginner—
This meditation subject should be brought to mind. And when counting, one should not place the count below five, nor lead it above ten, nor show a gap in between.
For if one places it below five, the arising of consciousness flutters about in a cramped space, like a herd of cattle confined in a narrow pen. If [one goes] above ten...
For one who leads [the count] upward, the arising of consciousness is dependent solely on the counting.
For one who shows a break in between, the mind wavers, thinking, "Has my meditation subject reached its peak, or has it not? Therefore, avoiding these faults, one should count.
And when counting, one should first count by slow counting, like the counting of a grain-measurer. A grain-measurer...
Indeed, having filled the tube and said "one," he pours it out. While filling it again, seeing some refuse, he discards it saying "one, one.

This same method applies to "two, two," and so forth. In exactly the same way, by means of this [practice] as well, one takes whatever appears among the inhalations and exhalations, begins with "one, one," and continues until it proceeds to "ten, ten."
It should be counted only after observing it as it occurs. As he counts in this way, the incoming and outgoing breaths become manifest.
Then, abandoning that slow counting—like the counting of a grain-measurer—he should proceed with quick counting, like the counting of a cowherd.
It should be counted. For a clever cowherd, having taken pebbles in his lap and holding a rope and a staff in his hands, goes to the cattle-pen early in the morning;

striking the cows on their backs and sitting atop a crossbar, he counts each cow as it arrives at the gate by throwing a pebble, saying, "One, two. Throughout the three watches of the night, even in the crowded pen...
When a herd of cattle that has been standing in a cramped space goes out, they emerge in dense clusters, jostling one another with great speed.
As they rush out with such speed, they themselves count them, saying, "Three, four, five, ten.
In the same way, for this practitioner as well, as he counts according to the previous method, the inhalations and exhalations become manifest, and very quickly, again and again—
They move about. Then, knowing that they were moving about again and again, he did not catch them inside or outside, but catching them only as they reached the door, he quickly, quickly [counted]:
"One, two, three, four, five; one, two, three, four, five, six;
one, two, three, four, five, six, seven... eight... nine... ten."

It must indeed be counted. For when the meditation subject is connected with counting, the mind becomes one-pointed through the power of counting alone, like the steadying of a boat in a violent current by means of a prop.
As he counts thus very rapidly, the meditation subject appears as if it were occurring in an unbroken succession.
Then, knowing that it "proceeds without interruption," one should count with increasing speed in the same manner as before, without grasping at the wind either inside or outside.
For when one causes the mind to enter together with the inward-moving breath, the interior seems as if struck by the wind and filled with fat;
and when one leads the mind out together with the outward-moving breath, [the exterior seems likewise affected].
The mind is distracted by external, diverse objects. However, for one who establishes mindfulness at the point of contact [with the breath] and develops the practice, the meditation succeeds.
Therefore it was said: "Without grasping at the breath either internally or externally, it should be counted with increasing speed according to the previous method."
How long, then, should this counting be performed? It should be continued as long as mindfulness remains established upon the object of the inhalation and exhalation without the aid of counting.
For counting is solely for the purpose of establishing mindfulness on the object of the inhalation and exhalation by cutting off discursive thoughts that have strayed outward.
Having attended to it thus by means of counting, one should attend to it by means of following. "Following" means [continuing] the counting...
Having withdrawn [the mind], it is the continuous following of the inhalations and exhalations by means of mindfulness; however, this is not by way of following their beginning, middle, and end.
For the navel is the beginning of the air exiting outward, the heart is the middle, and the tip of the nose is the end.
The tip of the nose is the beginning of the air entering inward, the heart is the middle, and the navel is the end. As he follows that [air], it becomes distracted.
The mind becomes both agitated and restless. As it is said:

"For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath, because the mind has become distracted internally, both the body and the mind become agitated, restless, and trembling. [This applies likewise] to the out-breath, its beginning, middle, and end, through mindfulness..."
“For one who pursues [the breath] with a mind distracted outwardly, both body and mind become agitated, perturbed, and trembling.
Therefore, when attending to it for the purpose of following, one should not attend to it by way of its beginning, middle, and end;
rather, it should be attended to by way of touching and by way of fixing. By way of counting and following—
For there is no separate attention by way of touching and placing;
rather, while counting at each point touched, one attends both by means of counting and by means of touching.
Then, withdrawing the counting right there and following those [objects] with mindfulness, while placing the mind in absorption, one attends "by means of following and by means of touching."

"And he attends to it for the purpose of establishing [the mind]. This meaning is to be understood through the similes of the lame gatekeeper spoken of in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, and through the simile of the saw spoken of in the *Paṭisambhidā*.
Herein, this is the simile of the lame man: "Just as a lame man, having pushed the swing of his mother and son who are playing on a swing..."
Seated right there at the base of the swing’s pillar, he sees both ends and the middle of the swing’s plank as it comes and goes;
yet he does not exert himself for the purpose of seeing those two ends and the middle.
In the same way, this bhikkhu, standing at the base of the pillar of anchoring through mindfulness, [observes] the swing of inhalation and exhalation.
Having cast [the mind] right there upon the sign, he sits with mindfulness;

as the breaths enter and exit touch the place where they arrive and depart, he follows their beginning, middle, and end with mindfulness, fixing the mind there and seeing them, yet he is not occupied with the purpose of seeing them. This is the simile of the cripple.
Now, this is the simile of the gatekeeper: “Just as a gatekeeper does not examine the men inside or outside the city, asking, ‘Who are you?
Where have you come from? Where are you going? What is in your hand?
for such things are not his burden; he examines only those who have actually reached the gate—even so it is with this bhikkhu.”
The winds that have entered within and those that have gone outside are not a burden; only those that have reached the door are truly a burden.
This is the simile of the gatekeeper.
As for the simile of the saw, it should be understood from the very beginning as follows. For this has been said:
“The sign, the inhalation and exhalation, and the single-pointedness of mind without an object—
for one who does not know these three things, development is not found. The sign,
the inhalation and exhalation, and the single-pointedness of mind without an object...”
“And for one who knows these three things, development is found.
How is it that these three things do not become objects of a single consciousness, yet these three things are not unknown,
the mind does not fall into distraction, exertion is manifested, and the application is accomplished?
How does one attain distinction? Suppose, for example, a tree were placed on a level stretch of ground, and a man were to cut it with a saw.
By way of the teeth of the saw contacting the tree, the man’s mindfulness becomes established;
he does not attend to the teeth of the saw as they come or go, nor does he attend to the teeth of the saw that have come or gone.
They are not known [by others], yet striving is evident and the application is accomplished.
Just as a tree placed on level ground, so is the sign for anchoring.
Just as the teeth of a saw, so are the in-breaths and out-breaths. Just as a person’s mindfulness is established by means of the teeth of a saw that have struck the tree.
Just as a person with saw-teethed teeth does not attend to them when they come together or go apart, nor are those teeth unknown to him when they come or go,
yet his effort is evident and he accomplishes his task— just so, a bhikkhu sits having established mindfulness at the tip of the nose or on the feature of the mouth,
without attending to the incoming or outgoing breaths.
He attends to it; the inhalations and exhalations are not unknown whether they have come or gone, exertion is manifest, he accomplishes the application, and he attains distinction.
What is this "exertion"? For one who has aroused energy, both body and mind become wieldy—this is [exertion].
Exertion. What is the application? The defilements of one who has aroused energy are abandoned, and discursive thoughts are stilled—this is the application.
What is the distinction? The fetters of one who has aroused energy are abandoned, and the underlying tendencies are brought to an end—this is the distinction.
Thus, these three states do not become objects for a single moment of consciousness, nor do they...
When three things are fully understood, the mind does not become distracted, exertion is manifested,
application is accomplished, and one attains distinction.
“For one whose mindfulness of breathing is complete and well-developed...”
“Gradually accumulated, just as taught by the Buddha, it illuminates this world like the moon released from clouds. This is the Simile of the Saw.
Here, however, it should be understood that the sole purpose [of this simile] is non-attention (*amanasikāra*) according to its application.
For someone who attends to this meditation subject, the sign arises without long delay, and the "fixing" known as absorption—
adorned with the remaining jhāna factors— is accomplished. However, for another person, from the very moment they begin attending by means of counting,
as the gross in-and-out breaths are stilled through that process, both body and mind become tranquil.
The body becomes light; it is as if the body has attained a state of buoyancy in the air.

Just as when one with a rigid body sits on a bed or a chair, the bed or chair sinks down, creaks, and the coverlet gathers into folds, but when one with a non-rigid body sits, neither the bed nor the chair sinks, nor does it creak, nor does the coverlet gather into folds.
He takes up the posture, and his bed and chair become like they are filled with cotton wool. Why? Because when the body is not agitated, it becomes light.

In the same way, from the time of attention by means of counting onwards, as the bodily agitation is stilled through the gradual cessation of coarse inhalation and exhalation, both the body and the mind become light;
the body becomes as if it has attained the state of leaping in the air.
When his gross inhalation and exhalation have ceased, the mind proceeds with the sign of the subtle inhalation and exhalation as its object;
when that too has ceased, it continues to proceed with successively more and more subtle signs as its objects.
How so? Just as if a man were to strike a gong with a large iron bar, there would be a great sound at the first blow.
If it should arise, his mind would proceed with gross sounds as its object; when the gross sounds have ceased, then afterwards [the mind] proceeds with subtle sound-signs as its object;
when those too have ceased, the mind continues to proceed one after another with even more subtle and most subtle sound-signs as its object—it should be understood in this way.
And this has been said in detail: "Just as when a bronze gong is struck," and so forth.
For unlike other meditation subjects which become clearer and clearer as one develops them, this one does not do so.
On the contrary, as one develops it again and again, it becomes increasingly subtle and does not even come into focus.
When it does not appear in this way, that bhikkhu should not rise from his seat, shake out his leather mat, and [depart].
One must go. What should be done? One should not rise with the thought, "I will ask the teacher," or "Now my meditation subject is lost.
For if one goes by altering one's posture, the meditation subject becomes ever more fresh.
Therefore, while remaining exactly as one is sitting, one should bring it to mind from the place where it was left.
In this regard, this is the method for bringing it back. When that bhikkhu realizes that the meditation subject does not remain present, he should reflect thus:
"Where do these so-called in-breaths and out-breaths exist? Where do they not exist? In whom do they exist? In whom do they not exist?
Then, as he reflects in this way, [he understands]: "These do not exist within the mother's womb..."

Having understood that for those submerged in water, likewise for those who have become unconscious, for the dead, for those attained to the fourth jhāna, for those possessing existence in the fine-material or immaterial realms,
and for those attained to the cessation of perception and feeling, [craving] does not exist, one should thus reproach oneself by means of oneself: "O wise one,
is it not true that you do not possess craving while in the mother’s womb, nor when submerged in water, nor when unconscious, nor..."
“[He] is dead; he has not attained the fourth jhāna, nor does he possess existence in the fine-material or immaterial realms, nor has he attained cessation.
Those in-breaths and out-breaths are indeed still present, but because of his dull wisdom, you are unable to discern them.
Then, by means of the very area [of the body] normally touched [by the breath], one should establish the mind and apply attention. For these [breaths] belong to one with a long nose...
They proceed by striking against the nostril aperture, or, in the case of one with a short nose, against the upper lip.
Therefore, he should establish the sign by thinking, "It strikes this particular spot. It is precisely for this reason that the Blessed One said:
"Monks, I do not say that the development of mindfulness of breathing belongs to one who is muddled in mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension..."

"I say. For although any meditation subject whatsoever succeeds only for one who is mindful and clearly comprehending, this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) becomes manifest even to one who is attending to something else;
yet this is a weighty meditation subject, a weighty development, which constitutes the sphere of attention for great beings alone—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the sons of the Buddhas.
It is neither limited nor cultivated by limited beings. In whatever way it is brought to mind, in that very way it becomes both peaceful and subtle.
Therefore, in this matter, powerful mindfulness and wisdom are required.
For just as when sewing a fine cloth, a fine needle is required, so too is a fine needle-case.

Then it becomes even more subtle. In the same way, at the time of developing this meditation subject which resembles a smooth cloth, the wisdom associated with mindfulness must also be strong—possessing the appearance of a needle and the appearance of the needle's point.
And by a bhikkhu endowed with that mindfulness and wisdom, those in-breaths and out-breaths should not be sought outside the area normally touched by them.
Suppose, however, that a farmer, having plowed his field and released his oxen, were to let them go toward their pasture and rest in the shade;

then those oxen might quickly enter the forest. A skilled farmer who wishes to recapture and yoke them again does not wander through the forest following after their tracks. Rather, [he waits]—and then...
Taking both the reins and the goad, he goes straight to their watering-place and sits or lies down there.
Then, seeing those oxen after they have wandered for part of the day, descended to the watering-place, bathed, drunk, and come back up and stood still,
he ties them with the reins, prods them with the goad, leads them back, yokes them, and [drives them] again.
Just as one performs work, so too that bhikkhu should not seek those in-breaths and out-breaths anywhere other than the place normally touched by them.
Rather, taking hold of the goad of wisdom with the reins of mindfulness, he should fix his mind on the place normally touched and carry out his attention there.
For when he attends in this way, before long those breaths appear to him at the point of entry.

It is like oxen. Then, having bound them with a rope of mindfulness and yoked them to that very spot, he should again apply himself to the meditation subject while pricking them with the goad of wisdom. As he applies himself in this way, the sign will appear before long.
However, this does not arise in exactly the same way for everyone; rather, for some it is pleasant to the touch.
Some say that when it arises, it appears like a tuft of cotton, like a tuft of kapok, or like a stream of air.
However, this is the determination according to the commentaries: for some it is like the form of a star, like a round gem, or like a round pearl;
for others it has a rough tactile sensation, like a cotton seed or a needle made of hard wood.
To some it appears like a long silk cord, a garland of flowers, or a column of smoke;
to others it appears like a wide-spreading spider’s web, a mass of clouds, a lotus flower, a chariot wheel, or the disks of the moon and the sun. And furthermore, this [sign], when there are many...
While the bhikkhus were sitting after having recited the Sutta, one bhikkhu asked, "In what manner does this Sutta appear to you?
One replied, "To me it appears like a great mountain river.
Another said, "To me like a row of forest trees. Yet another said, "To me like a tree with cool shade, full of branches, and heavy with fruit."
"Because of diversity in perception. For to them, that single sutta appears as diverse due to the diversity in their perceptions.

In this way, even a single meditation subject appears as diverse due to the diversity in perception. Since this [subject] is born of perception, has perception as its source, and has perception as its origin, it should be understood that it appears as diverse due to the diversity in perception.
And here, the mind having the in-breath as its object is one thing, that having the out-breath as its object is another, and that having the sign as its object is yet another.
For one who lacks these three factors, the meditation subject reaches neither absorption (appanā) nor access (upacāra).
But for one who possesses these three factors, the meditation subject reaches both absorption and access. For this has been said:
“The sign, the inhalation and exhalation, and the single-pointedness of mind without an object—
for one who does not know these three things, development is not attained. The sign,
the inhalation and exhalation, and the single-pointedness of mind without an object.”
"And for one who knows three things, development is found.
When the sign has thus appeared, that bhikkhu should go to the presence of his teacher and announce:
"Venerable sir, such a sign appears to me. Then the teacher should determine whether it is "the sign" or "not the sign."
Or rather, it should not be said [either way]. After saying, "It is so, friend," one should say, "Continue to attend to it again and again.
For if one were told "the sign," he might fall into complacency; if told "not the sign," he might despair and become discouraged.
Therefore, without saying either of those two, he should be directed toward the act of attention itself. Thus, at least, say the Dīgha reciters. As for the Majjhima reciters:
They say: "Friend, this is the sign; you should repeat the meditation subject again and again, saying 'a true person'.
Then he should fix his mind on the sign itself. Thus, from this point onward, his development proceeds by way of fixing.
For this was said by the ancients:
“Fixing the mind on the sign, discerning its various aspects,
the wise man binds his own mind to the in-breaths and out-breaths.
From the moment the sign thus becomes established for him, the hindrances are indeed suppressed and the defilements are stilled.
When mindfulness is established, the mind is indeed concentrated. For the mind is said to be concentrated in two ways:
either by the abandoning of the hindrances on the level of access (upacāra-bhūmi), or by the manifestation of the factors on the level of attainment (paṭilābha-bhūmi).
In this context, "level of access" refers to access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), and "level of attainment" refers to absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). What of these two?
What is the distinction? Access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), having impelled through the wholesome cognitive process, descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

Absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), however, for one who has entered absorption during the daytime and remains seated, impels through the wholesome cognitive process for the duration of that day as well, and does not descend into the life-continuum.
Between these two types of concentration, it is by means of access concentration—through the manifestation of the sign—that the mind is concentrated.
Then he should not attend to that sign by way of its color, nor should he examine it by way of its characteristics.
Rather, it should be guarded with diligence— just as the womb of a Wheel-turning Monarch is guarded by the chief queen of a Khattiya,
or as the womb of rice and barley is guarded by a farmer— for when thus guarded, it yields fruit.
“For one who guards the sign, no decline is found;
when there is no guarding, whatever is gained is lost. In this regard, this is the method of guarding:
that bhikkhu [should consider] the dwelling, the alms-round, speech, the person, and food.
Having avoided these seven unsuitable factors— namely, the seasons and the postures—
one should repeatedly bring that sign to mind by cultivating those same seven suitable factors.
Having thus made the sign firm through the cultivation of what is suitable, and having brought it to growth and increase, one performs the purification of the basis.
The balancing of the faculties, skillfulness regarding signs, uplifting the mind at the time when the mind should be uplifted,
restraining the mind at the time when the mind should be restrained,
and gladdening the mind at the time when the mind should be gladdened.
Delighting the mind; at whatever time the mind should be looked on with equanimity, then looking on at the mind with equanimity; avoiding persons who are unconcentrated;
associating with persons who are concentrated; and being intent upon that—without abandoning these ten skills regarding absorption, one should practice yoga.

As he dwells thus devoted to this practice, thinking, "Now absorption will arise," the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is interrupted and mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana) arises with the sign as its object. When that has ceased, taking that same object, four or five impulsion moments (javana) arise;
of these, the first is the preliminary (parikamma), the second is access (upacāra), and the third is conformity (anuloma).
The fourth is the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhu*), and the fifth is the absorption consciousness (*appanā-citta*).

Alternatively, it is said that the first [moment] is both the preliminary (*parikamma*) and the access (*upacāra*), the second is conformity (*anuloma*), the third is change-of-lineage, and the fourth is the absorption consciousness.
Indeed, it enters absorption at either the fourth or the fifth moment, but not at the sixth or seventh, because of the imminent falling back into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
But the Elder Ābhidhammika Godatta said: "Wholesome states become powerful through the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya);
therefore, one enters the sixth or seventh [jhāna]. This is rejected in the Commentaries (aṭṭhakathā).

In this context, the preliminary consciousnesses (pubbabhāga-citta) belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), whereas the absorption consciousness (appanā-citta) belongs to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). Thus, by this means, one abandons the five factors.
He attains the first jhāna, which is endowed with five factors, possesses ten characteristics, and is good in three ways.
Then, having stilled applied thought and the other [mental factors] upon that very same object, he reaches the second, third, and fourth jhānas.
At this point, he has reached the culmination of development by way of fixing [the mind]. This is the brief explanation here.
The detailed exposition, however, should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga* by one who desires it. Thus, a bhikkhu here,
having reached the fourth jhāna and having expanded the meditation subject by means of observation and turning away,
desiring to attain complete purification, [should practice] that same jhāna through the five modes consisting of adverting, entering, resolving, emerging, and reviewing.

Having mastered and made familiar [the meditation] in five ways, he grasps form and formless phenomena—either form preceded by the formless, or the formless preceded by form—and establishes insight. How so?
For, having emerged from jhāna and grasped the jhāna factors, he grasps their support, the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), as well as the primary elements that support it, and their...
He sees the entire physical body as a support. Then he defines form and non-form, thinking: "The jhāna factors are non-form; the base and so forth are form.
Alternatively, having emerged from attainment, he [views] the parts such as the head-hairs and so forth by way of the earth element and the other elements.

Having discerned the primary elements and the forms dependent upon them, he sees consciousness together with its associated mental states, taking as his object either the form-objects as they were discerned or the doors of the bases of form as they were discerned.
Thereafter, he defines them thus: "The primary elements and so forth are form; consciousness together with its associated mental states is non-form (arūpa)."
Alternatively, having emerged from meditative attainment, he sees that the origin of the in-breaths and out-breaths is both the body born of karma and the mind.

For just as wind moves in dependence upon the bellows being blown by a smith, the bag, and the appropriate effort of the man, even so the in-breaths and out-breaths exist in dependence upon the body and the mind. Then, regarding the in-breaths and out-breaths...
He defines the body and form as "form," and the mind and its associated mental states as "the formless.
Having thus defined name-and-form, he searches for its condition;
and searching, having seen it, he dispels doubt concerning the occurrence of name-and-form throughout the three periods of time. With his doubts dispelled, by means of the comprehension of groups...
Having applied the three characteristics and abandoned the ten imperfections of insight— such as illumination— which arise during the preliminary stage of the contemplation of rise and fall,
he defines the knowledge of the way, freed from imperfections, as the "path. Then, having abandoned arising and reached the contemplation of dissolution,
he becomes disenchanted with all conditioned formations that appear as fearful through the uninterrupted contemplation of dissolution.
Becoming dispassionate and being liberated, he reaches the four noble paths in due order;

having established himself in the fruit of arahantship, he attains the culmination of the nineteenfold reviewing knowledge and becomes the most worthy recipient of offerings in the world with its devas.
At this point, the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing—beginning with counting and ending with insight—is completed.
This concludes the commentary on the first tetrad in all its aspects.

As for the other three tetrads, since there is no separate method for the development of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā-naya) in them, their meaning should be understood solely by way of a word-by-word commentary.
"Experiencing rapture" (pītippaṭisaṃvedī) means having rapture experienced.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out making [the breath] manifest. In this regard, rapture is experienced in two ways:
by way of the object and by way of non-delusion. How is rapture experienced by way of the object?

He enters the two jhānas accompanied by rapture; at the moment of attainment, through the acquisition of the jhāna, rapture is experienced by way of the object because the object has been experienced.

How is it through non-delusion? Having entered and emerged from two jhānas accompanied by rapture (*pīti*), one contemplates the rapture associated with those jhānas as subject to destruction and vanishing.
At the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), rapture is clearly understood through the penetration of its characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*) because of non-delusion.
For this has been said in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
“Mindfulness is established in one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction through long inhalation.
By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is experienced.
[The same applies to] long exhalation… short inhalation… short exhalation… inhalation while experiencing the whole body… exhalation while experiencing the whole body.”
Through out-breathing... through calming the bodily formation while breathing in...
through calming the bodily formation while breathing out, for one who understands the unification of mind and non-distraction, mindfulness is established;
by means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is experienced. As he adverts to it, that rapture is experienced; as he knows it...
...for one who sees... for one who reviews... for one who resolves the mind... for one who is intent upon faith... for one who exerts energy...
for one who establishes mindfulness... for one who concentrates the mind... for one who understands with wisdom... for one who directly knows what is to be directly known...

for one who fully understands what is to be fully understood... for one who abandons what is to be abandoned... for one who develops what is to be developed... for one who realizes what is to be realized...
"As he realizes it, that rapture is experienced. In this way, that rapture is experienced.
By this same method, the remaining terms should also be understood according to their meaning. However, this is the specific distinction here:
the experience of pleasure should be understood by way of the first three jhānas, and the experience of mental formations by way of all four.
“Mental formation” (*cittasaṅkhāra*) refers to the two aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*).
Regarding the phrase “experiencing pleasure,” the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* states that this is for the purpose of showing the plane of insight: “Pleasure is twofold—bodily pleasure and mental pleasure.
“Calming the mental formation” means calming and ceasing each gross mental formation as it arises.
Thus, this should be understood in detail according to the method already stated for the bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*).
Furthermore, here in the section on rapture (*pīti*), feeling (*vedanā*) is mentioned under the heading of rapture; in the section on pleasure (*sukha*), feeling is mentioned in its own right.

In the two sections on mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*), because of the statement, "Perception and feeling—these mental states are bound to the mind and are mental formations," they are associated with perception (*saññā*).
"Feeling. Thus it should be understood that this tetrad was spoken by way of the method of contemplation of feeling (*vedanānupassanā*).
In the third tetrad as well, the "experiencing of the mind" (*cittapaṭisaṃveditā*) should be understood by way of the four jhānas.
"Gladdening the mind": he trains himself, "I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out gladdening the mind, making it joyful, making it glad, causing it to laugh, and causing it to smile."
In this regard, there is gladdening in two ways: by way of concentration and by way of insight. How by way of concentration?

He attains the two jhānas accompanied by rapture; at the moment of attainment, he gladdens and rejoices his mind with the rapture associated [with those states]. How by way of insight? Having attained the two jhānas accompanied by rapture...
Having emerged from [jhāna], one comprehends the rapture associated with that jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing.

Thus, at the moment of insight, by taking the rapture associated with jhāna as the object, one gladdens and rejoices the mind. One who practices in this way is said to "train thus: 'I shall breathe in and breathe out gladdening the mind.'"

"Concentrating the mind": while placing the mind evenly upon the object by means of the first jhāna and so forth, or while entering and emerging from those jhānas and contemplating the consciousness associated with them as subject to destruction and vanishing—at the moment of insight through the penetration of characteristics—momentary one-pointedness of mind arises. Thus...
By means of the momentary one-pointedness of mind that has arisen, he who places the mind evenly upon the object and establishes it evenly is said to train thus:
“I shall breathe in and breathe out while concentrating the mind.
“Liberating the mind” means liberating and releasing the mind from the hindrances by means of the first jhāna, and by the second...
He liberates and releases the mind from applied and sustained thought by means of the second [jhāna], from rapture by means of the third, and from pleasure and pain by means of the fourth.
Or else, having entered and emerged from those jhānas, he contemplates the consciousness associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing.
At the moment of insight, by means of the contemplation of impermanence, he liberates and releases the mind from the perception of permanence.

While liberating and releasing the mind from the perception of pleasure by means of the contemplation of suffering, from the perception of self by means of the contemplation of not-self, from delight by means of the contemplation of disenchantment, from lust by means of the contemplation of dispassion, from arising by means of the contemplation of cessation, and from grasping by means of the contemplation of relinquishment, he breathes in and breathes out. Therefore it was said: "Liberating..."

“He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in mindful of the mind; I shall breathe out mindful of the mind. It should be understood that this tetrad was spoken by way of contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*).

As for the fourth tetrad, regarding the phrase “contemplating impermanence” (*aniccānupassī*): first, impermanence (*anicca*) must be understood, and the state of impermanence (*aniccatā*) must be understood.

The contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is to be understood, and the one who contemplates impermanence (aniccānupassī) is to be understood. In this context, "impermanent" refers to the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā).

Why? Because they possess the nature of arising, passing away, and change. "Impermanence" (aniccatā) means the non-existence of those very same aggregates after their arising, passing away, and change;
or, it means the breaking up through momentary destruction, as opposed to remaining in the same state once produced. "Contemplation of impermanence" (aniccānupassanā) means...
By way of its impermanence, there is the contemplation of "impermanence" regarding form and the other aggregates. One who is "contemplating impermanence" is one endowed with that contemplation.
