Therefore, it should be understood that one who is breathing in and breathing out while being thus established trains himself in this way: "I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence; I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence."
Regarding the phrase "contemplating fading away" (*virāgānupassī*): here there are two kinds of fading away—fading away as destruction (*khayavirāga*) and absolute fading away (*accantavirāga*).
In this context, "fading away as destruction" is the momentary dissolution of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*); "absolute fading away" is Nibbāna;

and "contemplation of fading away" is both insight (*vipassanā*) and the Path (*magga*), which proceed by way of seeing both of these. Breathing in while being endowed with both of these types of contemplation...
And while breathing out, it should be understood that he trains thus: "I shall breathe in and breathe out contemplating fading away.
The same method applies to the phrase "contemplating cessation.
Regarding "contemplating relinquishment," there too there are two kinds of relinquishment: relinquishment as giving up and relinquishment as leaping forward.
Relinquishment itself as contemplation is "contemplation of relinquishment"; this is a designation for insight and the path.
For insight, by way of its specific factor (tadaṅga), abandons defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates;

and by seeing the fault in the conditioned, it leaps forward into Nibbāna, which is its opposite, through being inclined toward it. Thus, there is both the relinquishment of abandoning and the relinquishment of leaping forward.

It is called "renunciation. The path abandons the defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates by way of their total eradication, and it leaps forward into Nibbāna by making it its object; thus, it is called both "renunciation as relinquishing" and "renunciation as leaping forward.
Furthermore, both of these are called "contemplation" because they are seen successively following one after another by means of preceding and preceding knowledges.

It should be understood that, being endowed with these two kinds of contemplation of relinquishment, while breathing in and breathing out, one trains oneself thus: "I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment; I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
"Developed in this way" means developed in these sixteen aspects. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The discourse on the concentration of mindfulness of breathing is finished. 167.
Now, as for the passage beginning with "Then the Blessed One," this is the summary of the meaning:

having thus comforted the bhikkhus with the discourse on the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, the Blessed One [then spoke] that which was both the origin and the formal setting for the proclamation of the third *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the occurrence of monks taking one another’s lives:

having convened the Saṅgha of monks on this account and on this occasion, and having questioned and rebuked them, [the Blessed One] excluded that case because, in that instance, the taking of one's own life by oneself or the inciting of Migalaṇḍika to take his own life does not constitute a *pārājika* offense. Therefore, he set that aside.
Taking only the mutual taking of life—which constitutes the actual basis for a *pārājika* offense—the Buddha, in prescribing the *pārājika*, said:

"Whosoever, however, a bhikkhu, intentionally [deprives a human being of life]," and so forth. Because this case involves a mixture with noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), the term "fools" (*moghapurisa*) was not used here;
instead, it says "those bhikkhus."

Thus, having made it firm by way of cutting off the root when the third *pārājika* was laid down, another case arose for the purpose of a supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) concerning the praising of death;
to illustrate its origin, the words beginning with "In this way indeed by the Blessed One" were spoken. 168.
Therein, "with minds bound" means with minds bound by desire and lust; "infatuated and full of longing."
The meaning is as follows: “I shall praise the beauty of death” means that, having shown the disadvantage of life, I shall praise the excellence of death;

that is, I shall show its benefit. Regarding the phrases beginning with “one who has done what is beautiful,” this is the word-meaning: “Beautiful” (*kalyāṇa*) refers to pure action; since you have performed such [action], you are indeed “one who has done what is beautiful.
Likewise, “wholesome” (*kusala*) refers to blameless action; since you have performed such [action], you are “one who has done what is wholesome.”

When the time of death has arrived, there arises in beings a state of fear known as dread; because you have performed for them the act of protection (*tāyaṇa*)—that is, guarding (*rakkhaṇakamma*) from that [fear]—you are one who has provided a refuge from dread (*katabhīruttāṇo*).

Because you have not committed base actions, you are one who has not committed evil (*akatapāpo*). Because you have not committed cruel, harsh, or immoral deeds, you are one who has not committed cruelty (*akataluddo*).
*Kibbisa* refers to reckless acts characterized by an abundance of defilements such as greed.
"By you nothing was done" means "you have committed no evil. Why is this said? Because every kind of merit has been performed by you, and no evil has been done by you;
therefore we say to you: "What use is this wretched, evil, and miserable life to you, which is so full of suffering due to being overcome by disease?
"Death is better for you than life" means that death is preferable for you to living.
Life is more beautiful than that. Why? Because from here, having passed away—having reached the end of time, having completed one's lifespan, having died—is the meaning.

"With the breakup of the body... you will be reborn. And having been thus reborn there, you will be endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, the objects of desire consisting of pleasing forms and so forth, which arise in the divine world of the gods.
"Being fully endowed," means that having become associated and united, you will move here and there;
the sense is that you will roam about and take delight. 169.
"Unsuitable things" means those which are harmful, which do not bring about growth, and which lead very quickly to the destruction of life.
Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis (Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 172.
*Sañcicca* (intentionally): this is the extraction of the word *sañcicca* as it occurs in the matrix (*mātikā*) phrase, "intentionally [killing] a human being.
In that context, *sam* is a prefix; together with it, *sañcicca* is a term expressing exertion (*ussukka*). Of that...

"Having intended, having well-intended"—this is the meaning. However, since one who deprives [a being] of life intentionally is one who knows and perceives, and that act of depriving is a transgression committed after having willed and resolved upon it, therefore, without regard for the literal phrasing, in order to show the actual meaning, it is stated of him thus:
"knowing, perceiving, having willed, and having resolved, there is a transgression."
The word-commentary has been stated. Therein, "knowing" means knowing [the victim] as a "living being. "Perceiving" means perceiving [the intention], "I shall deprive him of life";
thus the meaning is: knowing together with that very mode of knowing the living being. "Having intended" means having intended and planned by way of the volition of killing.
"Having resolved" means having exerted effort and dispatched a mind free from apprehension.
"Transgression" means that the transgression occurring in such a manner is the ultimate sense of the word "intentionally"—this is what is meant.
Now, in order to show from the beginning the human state mentioned in the phrase "one should deprive a human being of life," he says:
"A human being, so-called," and so forth. Therein, it is for the purpose of showing the most subtle state of existence by way of those in the womb.
It is said: “That which [arises] in the mother’s womb. “The first consciousness” refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*). “Arisen” means born.

“The first consciousness has appeared”—this is a synonym for that very same thing. By the expression “the first consciousness in the mother’s womb,” the entire rebirth-linking process of the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokāra*) is indicated here. Therefore, that first...
That consciousness, the three formless aggregates associated with it, and the kalala-materiality produced together with them—this is the very first human composition.
Therein, "kalala-materiality" consists of thirty material phenomena by way of the body-base decad and sex-decad for females and males;
for those who are neuter, it consists of twenty by way of the body-base decad alone. Therein, for females and males...
The form of the *kalala* is, at birth, like a drop of oil drawn up by a single fiber of wool—clear and serene.
And this has been said in the Commentary:
"Just as a drop of sesame oil, or the purest cream of ghee, is unclouded..."
“Thus, what has the appearance of such color is called *kalala*.

Thus, beginning with this minute basis, the personal existence (*attabhāva*) that gradually reaches growth until the time of death for a being whose natural lifespan is one hundred years—this is what is called the human form.
“One should deprive him of life”: even at the stage of the *kalala*, [one might do so] by means of heating or crushing, or by the administration of medicine, or from that [state].
The meaning is: "one might deprive [the victim] of life even by means of an effort corresponding to that [intention].

However, since the taking of life in its actual sense is nothing other than the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), it is therefore stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for this [offense]:
"one cuts off the life-faculty, obstructs it, and disrupts the continuity (*santati*). In that context, the connection of the succession of the life-faculty...
When one cuts off and obstructs, it is said that "one cuts off and obstructs the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
This meaning is shown by the phrase "it disrupts the continuity" (*santatiṃ vikopeti*). "Disrupts" means to separate.

In this context, the life-faculty is twofold: the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) and the immaterial life-faculty (*arūpa-jīvitindriya*). Among these, regarding the immaterial life-faculty...
There is no means by which that [immaterial life-faculty] can be cut off; it is impossible to deprive one of it.

However, there is a means to deprive one of the material life-faculty, and in depriving one of that, one also deprives one of the immaterial life-faculty. For it ceases together with that very [material life-faculty], since its existence is dependent upon it.
But when one deprives one of it, does one deprive one of the past, the future, or the present?
Neither the past nor the future [is subject to killing], for among them one has ceased and the other has not yet arisen;

thus both are non-existent. Because they are non-existent, there is no effort [to kill them]; and because there is no such effort, it is impossible to deprive even one of life. And this has been said:

“In the past moment of consciousness, he lived, he does not live, and he will not live. In the future moment of consciousness, he will live, he did not live, and he does not live. In the present moment of consciousness, he lives, he did not live, and he will not live.”
Therefore, since an effort is appropriate where there is life, one deprives [the being] of its present existence.
And this "present" is threefold: the momentary present (*khaṇapaccuppanna*), the serial present (*santatipaccuppanna*), and the temporal present (*addhāpaccuppanna*).
Among these, the "momentary present" is that which possesses arising, decay, and dissolution; it is that which one deprives of [life].

It is not possible. Why? Because it ceases of its own accord. What is called "present continuity" (santatipaccuppanna) is that which ceases after proceeding for the duration of seven or eight impulsion-moments by way of a homogeneous continuity;

or, for one who has come from heat and entered a room and sat down, until darkness arises, or for one who has come from cold and sat down in a room, until there is the manifestation of a dissimilar temperature.
The preceding temperature does not subside; that interval is called "present by continuity" (*santatipaccuppanna*).
From rebirth-linking until death, however, this is called "present by duration" (*addhāpaccuppanna*). Both of these can be destroyed.
How so? For when that effort is made, the life-nonad (*jīvitanavaka*), having received that effort, ceases while being weak and its momentum exhausted.

It becomes a condition for the continuity. Then, whether it is the present continuity or the present duration, it ceases prematurely before reaching the time as delimited. Thus, both of these can be deprived;
therefore, it should be understood that this statement, "he disrupts the continuity," was said with reference to that very thing.
To clarify this matter, one must understand: the living being, the taking of life, the taker of life, and the application of the taking of life.
In this context, "the living being" refers to a sentient creature in conventional usage, but in the ultimate sense, it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
For it is said that one who destroys the life-faculty "takes the life of a living being," and that [life-faculty] is of the very nature just described.

“Taking life”: that volition by which one instigates an action that severs the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is called the murderous volition, “taking life. “One who takes life” should be understood as the person possessing the aforementioned volition.

“The means for taking life”: there are six means for taking life—namely, by one’s own hand, by command, by relinquishment, by persistence, by means of spells (*vijjāmaya*), and by means of supernormal power (*iddhimaya*).
In this context: "By one's own hand" (*sāhatthiko*) means striking with the body or with something connected to the body while killing oneself.
"By command" (*āṇattiko*) means commanding another, saying, "Kill by piercing or striking in such a manner.

"By relinquishing" (*nissaggiyo*) refers to the case of one wishing to kill someone standing at a distance, using the body or something connected to the body to discharge a spear, arrow, machine, stone, or the like.

The renunciation [of the object]. "By means of a stationary thing" (*thāvara*) refers to the digging of a pit, the provision of a precipice, the placing of a trap, or the preparation of medicine by one desiring to kill with a non-mobile instrument.
These four will also be explained in detail later in the commentary on the text itself.

However, those consisting of science (*vijjāmaya*) and those consisting of psychic power (*iddhimaya*) are not mentioned in the text; they should be understood as follows. Briefly stated, for the purpose of killing...
The employment consisting of science (*vijjāmaya*) is the recitation of spells (*vijjāparijappana*). However, in the Commentaries it is asked: "What is the employment consisting of science?
It is when practitioners of *āthabbaṇa* employ *āthabbaṇa*; when a city is besieged or a battle is imminent, they cause calamity to arise against the opposing army, the enemies, and the adversaries;
they cause misfortune to arise, they cause disease to arise, they cause fever to arise."
“They produce colic, they produce dysentery, they produce convulsions. Thus do the practitioners of *āthabbana* employ *āthabbana*.
Having recited their spells, the holders of *vijjā* [perform magic] when a city is besieged... [and so on] ...they produce convulsions.
Having thus shown the employment consisting of *vijjā*, there are many [instances] of those killed by both the *āthabbana*-practitioners and the holders of *vijjā*.
The bases have been stated; what is the use of them? Herein, the recitation of a spell for the purpose of killing is a practice consisting of science (*vijjāmaya*).

The application of a practice resulting from the ripening of kamma is a practice consisting of psychic power (*iddhimaya*). And this so-called "psychic power born of the ripening of kamma" includes the psychic power of nāgas, the psychic power of supaṇṇas, the psychic power of yakkhas, the psychic power of devas, and the [psychic power] of kings.

"Royal power" (*rājiddhi*) is of many kinds. Therein, when nāgas who have seen, bitten, or touched poison cause harm to others after having been seen, bitten, or touched, it should be understood as "nāga-power" (*nāgiddhi*).
When supaṇṇas extract nāgas from the great ocean measuring two or three hundred fathoms, it should be understood as "supaṇṇa-power" (*supaṇṇiddhi*).
As for the yakkhas, they are seen neither coming nor striking; by them—
But those beings struck down in that very place die; in their case, it should be understood as "the psychic power of a *yakkha*.

Regarding the death of *kumbhaṇḍas* looked upon by Vessavaṇa with his weapon before he attained stream-entry, and regarding the respective psychic powers of other deities, these should be understood as "the psychic power of a god.
As for the King of the Wheel-turning Monarch traveling through the air together with his retinue, and so forth—

The exercise of authority over a league (yojana) both below and above the Aśoka tree, and the death of the merchant Cūḷasumana due to the crushing of his teeth by his father, the King of Siṃhala, should be understood as "royal supernormal power" (*rājiddhi*).
However, some [commentators] say: "Furthermore, monks, a recluse or a brahmin who possesses supernormal power and has attained mastery over the mind..."
Having shown such suttas as, “She regards with an evil mind the embryo in another’s womb, thinking:

‘Oh, may this embryo in her womb not emerge safely’—in this way too, monks, there is destruction of a family,” they say that even by means of supernormal power consisting of mental development (bhāvanāmaya-iddhi), there is the act of harming others; together with the performance of such harm to others...
And they maintain that there is a destruction of psychic power (iddhi) like the breaking of a water-pot placed within a burning house; however, that is merely their wish.
Why? Because it does not accord with the triads of wholesome feeling, thought, and the limited. How so?
For this so-called "psychic power consisting of development" is both wholesome and indeterminate according to the triad of the wholesome, whereas the taking of life is unwholesome.
In the triad of feeling (*vedanāttika*), killing living beings associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure is associated with pain.

In the triad of applied thought (*vitakkattika*), [the mind] without applied or sustained thought; killing living beings is with applied and sustained thought. In the triad of limited (*parittattika*), [the mind] sublime; killing living beings is limited.
Regarding the phrase "he might seek out one who carries the knife": here, "carrier" (*hāraka*) means that which carries. What does it carry? Life. Now...

"Or it may be taken away" means "that which carries it away"; the meaning is "it should be deposited. "The weapon and that which carries it" is "weapon-and-carrying. "Of him" refers to the person in human form.
"Should seek" means he should act in such a way as to obtain it; the meaning is "he should deposit it.
By this, he shows the application involving a stationary object. For otherwise, one would become subject to a *pārājika* offense merely by the act of seeking.
And this is not logical. However, in the Pāḷi, without taking into account every single word, the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) states, "a sword...
or a rope," in order to show specifically that weapon which is included within the application of a stationary object (*thāvarappayoga*).
Therein, whatever remains after what has been mentioned as "weapon" should be understood as being face-to-face (*samukha*). And regarding the clubs, stones, and loose ropes—
The inclusion of the "knife" (sattha) should be understood as being due to the state of destroying life. Regarding the phrase "or the praise of death":
here, even when one points out the danger in living by such means as, "What is the use of this wretched, miserable life for you, since you do not get to eat choice foods?
and so forth, [one might say], "You, lay follower, have performed what is wholesome... [but] you have not done... [the rest].
Even when speaking in praise of death by such means as, "Evil is life; death is better for you;
having passed away from here, you will attend upon [the gods] and dwell having attained happiness in the Nandana Grove, surrounded by celestial nymphs," he is indeed praising death.
Therefore, the word-commentary (padabhājana) is stated by dividing it into two parts: "he shows the danger in living and speaks in praise of death."
"Or he might incite him to death" means he would cause him to adopt a means for the sake of dying.

Regarding the phrases "or take up a weapon," and so forth, even that which was not explicitly stated—such as "fall into a pit, a chasm, or a precipice"—should be understood as already expressed by way of meaning, because it follows the method explained later. For it is not possible to state everything in its literal form.

“Thus-minded and thus-intentioned” means one whose mind is such and whose intention is such. In the phrase “death is better than life,” the meaning is one whose mind is set on death and whose intention is for death.

However, since the word “intention” (mano) is used here to clarify the meaning of the word “mind” (citta), and these two are in fact identical in meaning, he says “whatever is mind, that is intention” in order to show their non-difference in meaning.
It is said: "That which is mind (mano), that is consciousness (citta). However, even though the word *iti* has been extracted [from the compound], its meaning has not yet been stated.
In this phrase, "consciousness-intention" (*cittasaṅkappo*), the word *iti* must be brought in by virtue of the context.

For it should be understood that although this is not explicitly stated as "thus consciousness-intention" (*iti-cittasaṅkappo*), it is indeed stated by implication through the context. Thus, showing that very same meaning:
He said, “one who perceives death,” and so forth. Furthermore, in this context, “intention” (*saṅkappa*) is not a name for applied thought (*vitakka*);
rather, it is a designation for mere mental preparation. And that mental preparation, in this sense, is included within perception (*saññā*), volition (*cetanā*), and purpose (*adhippāya*).
Therefore, the meaning is: one whose intention is manifold—that is, one who has various kinds of intentions—is “one of manifold intention” (*citrasaṅkappa*). Thus is the meaning.
It should be understood thus; for its word-commentary (*padabhājana*) is also stated by way of perception, volition, and intention (*adhippāya*).
And here, "intention" should be understood as applied thought (*vitakka*).
"By means of high and low modes" means by means of great and small methods. In that regard, first, concerning the praise of the beauty of death:
The low manner [of speech] should be understood as seeing the danger in life; the high manner [of speech] should be understood as praising death.
Furthermore, in the case of inciting [others], the high manner should be understood as inciting death by means of such acts as striking with fists or kicking with knees;
the low manner should be understood as inciting death and so forth by putting poison into the nails of one who is eating together with him.
Regarding the phrase "in a pit, in a ravine, or on a precipice": here, a "pit" (*sobbha*) is a deep hollow with its sides cut away on all sides.
A "ravine" (*naraka*) is a great natural cave formed spontaneously in ground that breaks apart here and there, where even elephants fall and thieves remain hidden.
A "precipice" (*papāta*) is a place where the slope is cut off on one side, whether between mountains or across a plain.

...there is. "With reference to the former" means with reference to persons who, having engaged in sexual intercourse and having taken what was not given, have fallen into an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
The remainder is clear, as it follows the method already explained previously and its meaning is self-evident. 174.
Having thus analyzed the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) according to the sequence of its words, now, since in the previous word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*)—
The *pārājika* offense involving a human being has been shown only in brief; the formal rule (*tanti*) was not established by setting forth the offense in full detail.

Furthermore, when a matter is shown in brief, monks are not able to grasp the underlying method in all its aspects, and there would also be an opportunity for wicked persons in the future [to misinterpret it]. Therefore, for the sake of monks grasping the method in all its aspects—

And for the purpose of warding off future opportunities for evil persons, [the Buddha] again established the matrix (mātikā) by way of the method beginning with "having resolved for oneself" (*sāmaṃ adhiṭṭhāya*), and showing the full detail of the *pārājika* offense regarding human beings, he said: "‘For oneself’ (*sāman*) means one kills by oneself," and so forth.
Herein, this is the exposition of the legal decision (*vinicchaya-kathā*) together with a commentary on the words not [yet] explained: "By body" (*kāyena*) means by hand or by foot.
"Either with the hand, or with the fist, or with the knee, or with any limb whatsoever. "Connected with the body" means by a weapon such as a sword that has not been detached from the body.
"Detached" means by a weapon such as a spear or an arrow that has been detached both from the body and from what is connected to the body.
By this much, two modes of action are stated: the one performed by oneself (*sāhatthika*) and the one involving something detached (*nissaggiya*).
In that regard, each one is twofold, distinguished by being specified (*uddissa*) or unspecified (*anuddissa*).

Among these, in the case of the specified, one is bound by the karma through the death of that very person for whose sake one strikes. In the case of the unspecified—where one thinks, "Let whoever dies"—one is bound by the karma through the death of anyone at all due to the cause of the blow.
And in both cases, whether [the victim] dies immediately upon being struck or later...
Or, one is bound by that very same karma at the mere moment of striking with that disease.
Furthermore, having struck with the intention to kill, if the victim later dies from a second blow given with a different state of mind, one is still bound by the karma of the first blow alone.
However, if the victim dies from the second blow, there is no offense of taking life.
Even when both strike, one is bound by the karma of the first blow alone. When neither strikes, there is no act of taking life at all.
This same principle applies when many people strike a single person; for even in that case, one is bound by the karma of whichever blow causes death.
In this context, the "sheep-tetrad" should also be understood for the purpose of clarifying the nature of the offense of intentional action (*kammāpatti*).
Suppose a man hides a sheep lying in one place with the thought, "I will come at night and kill it.
Yet, in the place where the sheep is lying, its mother or father—or even an Arahant—is lying down covered by a yellowish-white garment. At the time of night, [he arrives].
Having arrived, thinking "I will kill a sheep," one kills one's mother, one's father, or an Arhat.
Because the volition exists with the thought "I will kill this being," one becomes a murderer, incurs an immediate offense (ānantariya-kamma), and falls into a defeat (pārājika).
If another person who has arrived happens to be lying there, and one kills them thinking "I will kill a sheep," one is a murderer.
If one lies down and commits an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*), yet does not incur an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*):

if a *yakkha* or a *peta* is lying there and one kills them thinking, "I am killing a sheep," one is indeed a murderer, yet one does not incur an immediate retribution nor commit an offense entailing defeat;
rather, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). However, if no one else is lying there and it is actually a sheep that one kills...
If he kills someone, he commits an offense entailing confession (*pācittiya*).

If, thinking, "I will kill one of these—my mother, my father, or an arahant," he kills one of those very persons, he is both the killer and incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*), and he commits an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
If, thinking, "I will kill one of them," he kills another who has arrived, or kills a *yakkha* or a *peta*, [he commits an offense entailing confession].
Or if one kills a sheep; this should be understood according to the method previously explained. However, in this case, the volition (*cetanā*) is particularly cruel.

Other objects here should also be understood, such as a heap of straw and so forth. For instance, one who, thinking "I will ask for a red sword or spear," thrusts it into a heap of straw, thereby killing his mother, father, or an *arhat* lying therein—
If one kills a visitor, a human being, a *yakkha*, a *peta*, or an animal, one is called a "murderer" by way of common usage;
however, because of the absence of the intention to kill (*vadhaka-cetanā*), one neither incurs the kammic result nor falls into an offense.
But as for one who, entering in this manner, perceives physical contact and thinks, "I believe a living being has gone inside..."

If one causes someone to enter [a place] with the thought, "Let him die," and then kills them, one should understand that there is both a karmic bond and an offense corresponding to those specific bases (*vatthu*).
This same principle applies to one who causes someone to enter for the purpose of burying them there, or to one who throws them into forests, thickets, and the like.
Furthermore, if one kills one's own father—who is traveling in the guise of a thief—with the intent, "I am killing a thief," one incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) as well.

He is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. Furthermore, if someone, seeing another warrior and his own father performing their duties in the enemy army, hurls an arrow at the warrior with the thought, "By piercing him, he will pierce my father," he becomes a patricide when the intended object is reached.
If he hurls it with the thought, "When the warrior is pierced, my father will flee," and the arrow reaches an unintended object—[he is not a patricide].
Having gone and killed his father, one is called a "patricide" by way of conventional usage, yet there is no immediate retribution (*ānantariya*).
"Having resolved" means having stood nearby. "Commands" means he commands either specifically or generally.
In that regard, when an enemy army has drawn up its ranks, he commands without specifying [the individual]: "Pierce thus! Strike thus! Kill thus!"
As many as are commanded, and as many as the one commanded causes to be killed, for all of them there is the offense of taking life (*pāṇātipāta*).

If the parents of the one who gave the command are present there, he incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) as well. If the parents belong only to the one who was commanded, he alone incurs the immediate retribution.
If [the victim] is an *arahant*, both incur the immediate retribution. Having specified this, [the text continues]: "This is long..."

When it is commanded: “Kill and strike down that short man wearing a red tunic or a blue tunic, who is seated on the neck of the elephant or seated in the middle,” if he kills that very person, there is the offense of taking life for both [the commander and the executor];

and in the case of an object of an immediate (ānantariya) deed, it is an immediate offense. If he kills someone else, there is no offense of taking life for the commander. By this, the instigatory application (*āṇattika-payoga*) is explained.
Thus it is said. In this regard:
"Having weighed these five factors—the object, the time, the place, the weapon, and the posture—a wise person should carry [the sword] for the sake of his purpose."
Another method:
The object, the time, the place, the weapon, the posture,
and the specific action— these six are the determinants of an instruction.
In this context: "The basis" (*vatthu*) refers to the sentient being to be killed. "The time" (*kāla*) refers to times such as morning or evening, and times such as youth or old age.
"The place" (*okāsa*) refers to such locations as a village, a forest, the door of a house, the middle of a house, a street, or a crossroads.
"The weapon" (*āvudha*) refers to such instruments as a sword, an arrow, or a spear. "The posture" (*iriyāpatha*) refers to [the posture] of the one to be killed...
“Going or sitting,” and so forth. “A specific action” means piercing, cutting, splitting, or shaving the head with a conch-shell razor, and so forth.
For if, having deceived the object and being commanded, “Kill this one,” he kills someone other than that person, [it is as if] having struck in front...
Or, being commanded with the words “Kill him,” he kills by striking from behind, from the front, or in another location.

In this case, there is no karmic bond for the commander; the karmic bond belongs only to the one who gave the command. However, if he kills without deceiving the victim and acts exactly according to the command, then there is a karmic bond for both:
for the commander at the moment of commanding, and for the one commanded at the moment of killing.

Furthermore, in this case, there is a distinction of action and a distinction of offense based on the specific object. Thus, first of all, the conventional and non-conventional nature regarding the object should be understood.
As for the time, however, one who is commanded—without specifying "today" or "tomorrow"—saying, "Kill him in the morning," [commits an offense] whenever it happens to be the morning.

If he kills [the victim] at the very time specified, there is no discrepancy in the appointment. However, if one who has been told, "Kill him this morning," instead kills him at midday, in the evening, or on the following day's morning, there is a discrepancy in the appointment;
the giver of the command incurs no karmic bond. The same principle applies even if the intended time for killing is the morning, yet it occurs at midday.
By this method, the nature of the agreement and the discrepancy regarding all divisions of time should be understood.
Even in the case of a location, if one is commanded without specifying, "Kill him when he is in this village," and kills him wherever he may be, there is no discrepancy in the command.
However, if one who was commanded with the specification, "Only in the village," kills him in the forest; or likewise, if one commanded "in the forest" kills him in the village;
or if one commanded "at the door of the house" kills him in the middle of the house—this constitutes a discrepancy (*visaṅketa*). By this [it is understood...]
By this method, the state of being conventionally designated or non-designated should be understood in all cases involving distinctions of location.

Even regarding weapons, if one is commanded, "Kill with a weapon," without specifying whether it is "with a sword or with an arrow," and he kills with whichever weapon [is used], there is no breach of the convention (*visaṅketa*).
However, if he is told "with a sword" but uses an arrow, or if he is told "with this sword" [but uses another]...

He is told by another, "Kill with this sword. Or, being told of that very sword, "Kill with this edge," he kills with the other edge, or with the flat of the blade, or with the point, or with the hilt;
this is a breach of convention (*visaṅketa*). By this method, the nature of convention and breach of convention should be understood regarding all varieties of weapons.

Regarding the modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*), however, if one says, "Kill him as he is walking," and the person so commanded kills him while he is walking, there is no discrepancy in the instruction.
But if one is told, "Kill him only while he is walking," yet kills him while he is sitting;

or if one is told, "Kill him only while he is sitting," yet kills him while he is walking—there is a discrepancy. By this same method, [the principle applies] to all divisions of the modes of conduct.
The state of being in accordance with or contrary to the convention should be understood.
Even regarding a specific action, if one who is told, "Pierce and kill," kills by piercing, there is no contrariety to the convention.
But if one who is told, "Pierce and kill," kills by cutting, there is contrariety to the convention. By this method, [the same applies] to all distinctions among specific actions.
The state of agreement and disagreement regarding the convention should be understood as follows:

If, however, one gives an order without specifying by means of gender—saying, "Kill the tall one," "the short one," "the dark one," "the fair one," "the thin one," or "the fat one"—and the person ordered kills anyone of that description, there is no disagreement; both incur a *pārājika* offense.

But if he commands with reference to himself, and the one commanded, thinking "this very person is such [as described]," kills the commander himself, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the commander and a defeat (*pārājika*) for the killer. If the commander commands with reference to himself, but the other kills someone else who is similar, the commander is released;
the defeat belongs to the killer alone. Why? Because the specific object was not defined.
But if, even when commanding with reference to himself, he specifies the occasion, saying,
"Kill such-and-such a person while they are sitting in such-and-such a night-station, or a day-station, or on a senior’s seat, or a junior’s seat,
or a middle seat," and another person happens to be sitting there, if the one commanded kills that other person, the killer is not released from the offense.
He is not an instigator. Why? Because the scope [of the command] has been restricted. However, if he causes death outside of the restricted scope, the instigator is released;
this principle is stated very firmly in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Therefore, one should not show disregard in this matter.
"Having resolved": the discussion on the application of an instruction according to the summary (mātikā) is concluded.
Now, for the purpose of showing the exposition of this summary-point "by means of a messenger," four sections beginning with "A bhikkhu instructs a bhikkhu" have been stated.
Among those, "he, thinking it was he": "he" refers to the one who was instructed by the instructor [with the words] "such-and-such a person."
Thinking it was that [person], he deprives that very person of life; for both, there is a *pārājika* offense. Thinking it was that [person], but [it was] another:
thinking "the one you told me to deprive of life" was someone else, he deprives another such person of life;
for the one who was the original instigator (*mūlaṭṭha*), there is no offense. Thinking it was another, but [it was] that [person]: the strong companion of the one mentioned by the commander.
Seeing someone standing nearby, [one thinks]: “It is by his power that this [other person] roars; I shall first deprive him of life.
While striking, however, the other person turns around and stands in that very spot; thinking, “This is my companion,” one deprives him of life. For both, there is a *pārājika* offense.
Thinking it is one person while it is another, as in the previous method: “I shall first [deprive] this companion of his...”
If one says, “I shall deprive him of life,” and then deprives that very companion of life, there is a *pārājika* offense for that person alone.

In the section explaining the phrase regarding the succession of messengers, such as “inform so-and-so,” one teacher and three disciples named Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, and Saṅgharakkhita are to be understood.
In that context, “a monk commands a monk” means that a teacher, desiring to have a certain person killed, [gives the order].
Having explained that matter, he instructs Buddharakkhita: "Go, Buddharakkhita, and inform Dhammarakkhita of this matter, saying, 'Let so-and-so inform so-and-so.
Let Dhammarakkhita also inform Saṅgharakkhita, saying, 'Let so-and-so deprive so-and-so of life.'"
"Thus, having been commanded by her, Dhammarakkhita commanded Saṅgharakkhita: 'Kill the person named so-and-so;
for he is energetic among us and capable of this task. 'There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)':
first, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the teacher who thus commands. He informs the other: [Buddharakkhita informs] Dhammarakkhita."
Dhammarakkhita informs Saṅgharakkhita: “Our teacher says this: ‘Kill such-and-such a person.
You, it seems, are a hero among us. Thus, they too commit a dukkaṭa offense.
“The killer accepts” means that Saṅgharakkhita agrees, thinking, “Very well, I shall kill him. For the one who is the root [of the instigation]...
"An offense of thullaccaya": as soon as Saṅgharakkhita has accepted [the gift], the teacher incurs a thullaccaya.

For he has incited the great multitude to evil. "He" (so): if that Saṅgharakkhita deprives that person of life, there is a pārājika for all four people. And not only for the four; by this same method...
Whether it be a hundred or a thousand ascetics, if they transmit [the instruction] through tradition without making a formal convention (*visaṅketa*), all of them incur a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the explanation of the phrase "the messenger who has been authorized": "He instructs another" means that Buddharakkhita, having been instructed by his teacher, either not seeing Dhammarakkhita or being unwilling to speak to him, approached Saṅgharakkhita and said, "Our teacher spoke thus..."
—“He gives the order while creating a misunderstanding, thinking, ‘I shall have such-and-such a person deprived of life.

Indeed, it is because of this creation of a misunderstanding that he is called a ‘misleading messenger. “There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)”: first, there is an offense of wrong-doing for Buddharakkhita due to the mere giving of the order.
“He accepts, there is an offense of wrong-doing”: when Saṅgharakkhita has accepted [the message], there is an offense of wrong-doing for the one who originated it (mūlaṭṭha).

It should be understood as an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). This being the case, while there would be no offense in the mere act of receiving [the message], there is an offense even in the receiving of a matchmaker’s mission or in rejoicing at death;
so how could there not be one in the receiving of [an intent for] death? Therefore, this *dukkaṭa* applies only to the one who receives it.

For that very reason, the phrase "of the one who is the root" (*mūlaṭṭhassa*) is not stated here. Furthermore, in the previous method as well, this should be understood as applying only to the one who receives it.

However, it was not stated because there was no opportunity [for it to occur]. Therefore, our view on this matter is that for whomever accepts [the gift], there is indeed an offense for each of them due to that condition.
And as it is here, so it is also in the case of taking what is not given.
But if he deprives him of life, then for both the instigator, Buddharakkhita, and the murderer—
For Saṅgharakkhita, it is a *pārājika* offense for both. However, because the teacher who was at the root [of the matter] had no prior agreement, there is no offense regarding the *pārājika*.
For Dhammarakkhita, because of his lack of knowledge, there is no offense whatsoever.
But Buddharakkhita, having ensured the safety of the two others, was lost himself.

In the explanation of the messenger who goes and returns: "He goes and returns again" means that having gone into the presence of the one whose life is to be taken, he returns because he is unable to deprive him of life due to the well-guarded protection [provided for the victim].
"When you are able" means: does he have to be killed this very day? Go; when you are able, then deprive him of life.
"Kill him" means: "There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Thus, even by a subsequent command, there is only an offense of wrong-doing.
However, if he must necessarily be deprived of life, the volition aimed at accomplishing that purpose is like the fruit immediately following the path;
therefore, one becomes defeated (*pārājika*) at the very moment of the command. Even if the executioner kills him only after sixty years have passed, [the offense remains].
If the one who gave the command dies in the interim, or returns to a lower state, or dies while no longer being a recluse,
or returns to a lower state; or if, having given such a command regarding his mother, father, or an Arhat during his time as a householder, he goes forth into homelessness,
and after he has gone forth, the one commanded kills him— then the one who gave the command [is guilty] even while still a householder.
He is a matricide, a patricide, or a murderer of an arahant; therefore, neither his going-forth nor his full ordination is valid.

Even if the person to be killed was an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) at the moment of the command, but becomes an arahant when he is commanded to kill him—or if, having received a blow from the commander, he relies on faith rooted in suffering and practices insight (*vipassanā*)—[the offense remains].
If, having attained Arahatship, he dies from that very affliction, the instigator becomes a murderer of an Arahant at the very moment of the command.
However, the executioner incurs a *pārājika* offense everywhere at the very moment he performs the lethal act.
Now, regarding all these points stated by way of the messenger in the summary headings (*mātikā*), [the following is] for the purpose of showing the conventional and non-conventional:
Three rounds have been stated. Regarding the first round: because he spoke slowly, or because of the other’s deafness, he did not make himself heard say the words “Do not kill”;
therefore, the one who was at the root [of the act] was not released from the offense. In the second round: he was released because he had made himself heard.
In the third round, however, both were released—the one who spoke because he had made himself heard, and the other because, having accepted with “Very well,” he desisted.
The Discussion on the Messenger is finished. 175.

Regarding the explanations of "one worthy" (*arahā*) and "one who perceives as secret" (*rahasaññī*), etc.: "Worthy" (*arahā*) refers to being face-to-face. "Secret" (*raha*) refers to being out of sight.
In that context, when at the time of attendance, even while sitting right in front of a hostile monk who has arrived together with other monks, [if one acts] due to the fault of darkness...
Not knowing that he has arrived, one who exclaims such words as, "Oh, may so-and-so be killed! May even thieves not kill him!
May a snake not bite him! May neither weapon nor poison reach him!
while thus rejoicing in his death—this is what is meant by "speaking in private when one perceives it as private," even in the very presence of that person.

The meaning is "perceiving [the person] as being out of sight. However, if one sees that person sitting in front of oneself, and after they have departed while the monks remain behind, one nevertheless speaks according to the previous method while perceiving, "He is still sitting right here," this is called speaking while perceiving one who is not alone as being alone.
By this same method, one who is alone but perceives himself as being alone, and one who is alone...

And it should be understood that one must perceive [the victim] as being in private. Furthermore, for each of these four cases, a *dukkaṭa* offense should be understood to occur for every single utterance.

Now, regarding the five explanations of the matrix (mātikā) beginning with "praising death by means of the body" which were stated for the purpose of showing the distinctions in the praise of the beauty of death—[in the first case:
"he makes a bodily gesture" means that he acts so that the person understands: "Bring a weapon, or consume poison..."
"By means of a rope, or by hanging oneself, or by falling into ravines and the like—whosoever dies thus, it is said, gains wealth, or gains fame, or goes to heaven";
this is the meaning expressed by this [statement], and he likewise indicates it by means of hand gestures and so forth.
"He speaks with speech" means he speaks that very same meaning by breaking it down into distinct sentences. The third section is by way of both.
[The offense is] declared. In every instance of the application of the commentary, there is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).

When that [person] experiences suffering, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for the commentator. If the person for whose sake the commentary was made has died, at the very moment of the commentary, there is a *pārājika* (defeat) for the commentator.
He does not know this; another, having learned it, thinks, "I have indeed found a means for my own happiness," and by means of that commentary...
If [the person] dies, there is no offense. If a description is made specifically for two people and one of them dies upon learning of it, it is a *pārājika*.
If both die, it is both a *pārājika* and a mass of unwholesome karma (*akusalarāsi*). This same principle applies to many people.
When one wanders about praising death without specifying anyone in particular, whoever learns of that praise and dies—all of them are considered killed by him.

Regarding the praise by messenger: as soon as the message is announced in the instruction, saying, "Go to such-and-such a house or village and praise death in this way for such-and-such a person," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When the one for whose sake he was sent experiences suffering, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya) for the instigator;
with his death, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika). The messenger [thinks], "Now this path to heaven is well known."

If, without informing him, he informs his own kinsman or blood relative, then when that person dies, there is a breach of the agreement (*visaṅketa*), and the original instigator (*mūlaṭṭha*) is released from the offense.
If the messenger, having thought the same way, dies after performing what was stated in the praise (*saṃvaṇṇanā*), there is likewise a breach of the agreement.
However, if it is announced in the teaching (*sāsana*) without specifying a particular person, then as many as die because of the messenger’s praise, [so many are affected].
These are the various forms of taking life. If one’s mother or father dies [as a result], it constitutes an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense.
176. Regarding the commentary on writing: "One cuts writing" means one writes letters upon a leaf or in a book, such as:
"Whoever, having taken up a weapon, or having fallen from a precipice, or by other means such as entering fire or entering water..."

Or [if one says], "He dies by these means and obtains this and that," or "This is his Dhamma"—here too, the offenses of *dukkaṭa* and *thullaccaya* are to be understood according to the method already stated.
However, in the case of what is written specifically for someone, it is a *pārājika* offense upon the death of the very person for whom it was written.
When many are written for, there are as many acts of taking life as there are who die.
There is an immediate offense (ānantariya) through the death of one's mother or father. The same principle applies even when [the book] was written not specifically for them.
If remorse arises upon thinking, "Many have died," one is freed from the offense by burning that manuscript or by making it so that the letters are no longer recognizable.
If that manuscript belongs to another, whether it was written specifically for him or not, [the same applies].

Or, having placed it in the location where it was seized, it is released. If it was purchased for a price, the manuscript is released by paying the price to the owners of the manuscript—that is, to those from whose hands the price was received.

If several people, with a single common intention, thinking, "We shall write a description of death," one person climbs a palmyra tree and cuts a leaf while another brings it down, [the offense is incurred].
One person prepares the manuscript, another writes it;

if there is a scratch, another applies ink, and having applied the ink and prepared that manuscript, they all place it in an assembly hall, a marketplace, or wherever many people gather out of curiosity to see the writing.
Having read it, even if only one person dies, there is a *pārājika* offense for all of them.

If many die, the principle is exactly as stated before. However, if remorse arises and they hide that book in a chest, and another person sees it, takes it out, and shows it to many again, they are not released from their guilt.
Let alone a chest; even if they throw that book into a river or the ocean, or wash it away, they are still not released.

Or they cut it into pieces, or they burn it in fire; as long as even when the bowl has been scrubbed or washed, or when it has been poorly burned, the letters are still discernible, for so long they are not released.
But when it is done in such a way that the letters are no longer discernible, then they are released.
Now, for the purpose of showing the classification of the permanent method (*thāvarapayoga*), regarding the explanations of the matrix-terms (*mātikā*) such as "pit" (*opāta*) that have been stated:

"he digs a pit aiming at a person" means that having designated a certain person, thinking "so-and-so will fall and die," he digs a hole in a place where that person wanders about alone; while he is digging, even if it is with soil already formed...
He digs; because it is an application of the taking of life, for each application there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
For the one on whose account he digs, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) upon the arising of suffering, and a defeat (*pārājika*) by death. If another falls and dies, there is no offense.
If he digs without a specific person in mind, thinking "whoever shall die," then for as many as fall and die, [there is an offense].

Regarding the taking of life: among the bases for an offense entailing immediate retribution (*ānantariya*), there is the immediate retribution; among the bases for a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) or an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), there are the grave offenses and offenses of expiation.
There are many volitions (*cetanā*) therein; by which one does the *pārājika* offense come to be? Regarding this, it is first stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"Having dug a pit according to its depth, length, and width, having fixed its dimensions, having trimmed [the wood], having wiped it clean, and having prepared a basket of earth..."
The volition that brings about certainty and accomplishes the purpose for one who is pulling [the victim] out is similar to the fruit immediately following the path.
Even if the victim inevitably dies after falling into the pit a hundred years later, it is still a *pārājika* offense solely on account of the volition that brought about the certainty.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "Even if [one thinks], 'He will fall into this pit and die'... [and so forth].
It is said: "If, when a blow from a spade has been struck, someone stumbles there, falls, and dies, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
However, the Suttantika Theras take [the offense] based on the volition of instigation (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*).
One person commands another: "Having dug a pit, bring such-and-such a person, drop him here, and kill him. He...
If, having caused him to fall, one kills him, there is a *pārājika* offense for both.

If one causes another to fall and kills him, or if one falls oneself and dies, or if another falls and dies of his own accord, in all such cases there is a lack of correspondence [between the intended victim and the actual victim], and the one who initiated the act is released from the offense.

The same principle applies even when one has been summoned with the thought, "So-and-so will bring so-and-so here and kill him. This is also the case when those desiring to die think, "We shall die here."
He digs; if one person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense. If many die, it is a mass of unwholesome karma (*akusalarāsi*). If mother or father die, it is an immediate transgression (*ānantariya*).
In cases involving a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) or an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), there are grave offenses and offenses of expiation respectively.
If he digs thinking, "Whoever wishes to kill [them], they shall drop them here and kill them," and they drop them there and kill them—

According to one opinion, there is a *pārājika* offense in a single instance, while in many instances there is a heap of unwholesome karma; regarding bases such as the *ānantariya* (immediate) offenses, they are classified as *ānantariya* and so forth.

In this very system, even those who have become *arahants* are included [in the category of those who fall]. However, in the former method, because "there is no falling due to a desire to die" on their part, they are not included.
In both methods, however, there is no disagreement regarding those who die after having fallen by their own nature.
Thinking, “Whoever might throw their enemies here and kill them,” one digs [a pit]. And there, enemies throw their enemies into it and kill them.
When one is killed, it is a *pārājika* offense; when many are killed, it is a mass of unwholesome karma (*akusalarāsi*).

If one’s mother, father, or an *arahant* is brought there by enemies and killed, it is an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense. There is no transgression regarding those who die after having fallen down of their own accord.
But he who digs without specifying at all— thinking, "Whether they wish to die or do not wish to die, whether they wish to be killed or do not wish to be killed,
whoever falls here or is caused to fall here shall die"—
incurs both the corresponding kamma and the offense for the death of whichever individual dies. If a pregnant woman falls...
If she dies while pregnant, there are two acts of taking life. If only the fetus perishes, there is one.
If the fetus does not perish but the mother dies, there is only one. If one who is pursued by thieves falls and dies, it is a *pārājika* offense for the ditch-digger alone.
If the thieves cause him to fall there and kill him, it is likewise a *pārājika*. If they carry him out after he has fallen there and kill him, [it is likewise a *pārājika*].

It is indeed a *pārājika*. Why? Because it was taken by means of causing [the victim] to fall into a pit. If, after emerging from the pit, he dies from that very same affliction, it is indeed a *pārājika*.
If, after many years have passed, he dies again from that same affliction which had flared up, it is indeed a *pārājika*.
If another disease arises in one who is already ill due to a disease produced by the cause of falling into the pit...

If the disease of the pit is more powerful, then even when the person has died, the one who dug the pit is not released from the offense. If the disease that arose later is more powerful, then he is released upon the death [of the victim].
If both are equally powerful, he is not released upon death. If a person born spontaneously (*opapātika*) in the pit dies because they are unable to climb out, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
If, having been intended for a human, [the victim] falls among *yakkhas* or other beings after being thrown into the pit...

There is no offense for those who die among humans and so forth when [the pit] was dug specifically for yakkhas and the like. This same principle applies even when humans and others die after a pit has been dug for the sake of yakkhas and the like.
However, for one who digs for the sake of yakkhas and the like, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense both at the moment of digging and when they experience pain.

Upon their death, depending on the specific circumstances, there is either a *thullaccaya* or a *pācittiya* offense. In the case of a pit dug without such intent, if a yakkha-form or a peta-form appears in that pit...
The Elder Upatissa says: "It falls; it dies in the form of an animal; the form of falling is the measure [of the offense]; therefore, it is a *thullaccaya*.
The Elder Phussadeva says: "Death is the measure; therefore, it is a *pācittiya*.
This same principle applies even if, after falling in the form of an animal, one dies in the form of a *yakkha* or a *peta*.
If one who has dug a pit sells that pit to another or gives it away for free, then whoever falls into it and dies, the offense and the karmic bond belong to that person alone on account of it;

the one by whom it was obtained is blameless. However, if he too thinks, "Those who fall in this way will be unable to get out and will perish, or they will not be easy to rescue," and makes that pit deeper...
Or if he makes it more level, or longer, or shorter, or wider, or narrower, for both there is an offense and a karmic bond.

Thinking, "Many will die," if, after remorse has arisen, he fills the pit with earth, and if anyone falls into the earth and dies, even though he has filled it, the one who was at the root [of the act] is not released. While the rain is falling...
If there is mud there, one is not released from the offense even if someone dies after clinging to it.

Or, when a tree falls, or the wind, or rainwater carries away the earth, or people digging for roots and tubers make a pit there—if anyone dies by clinging to or falling into it, one who was at the root does not escape. However, if there is a large pond in that place...
Or having had a lotus pond constructed, or having established a shrine (*cetiya*), or having planted a Bodhi tree, or having constructed a dwelling or a cart-road, one is released.
Even when a pit has been filled firmly and the roots of trees and so forth have become interwoven with its base, and the soil has grown over it, even then one is released.
Even if a river comes and washes away the pit, even in that case—
"He is released. This, first of all, is the discourse on the pit.
Furthermore, regarding the palaces and other structures that follow the pattern of the pit:

if one sets a snare with the thought, "Beings will die here after being caught," then by virtue of the beings who are inevitably caught, at the mere moment of release from the hand, there are offenses of *pārājika*, *ānantariya*, *thullaccaya*, and *pācittiya*.
These things should be understood. Regarding what was prepared specifically for someone: there is no offense in binding others who were not intended for that specific purpose.
Even if a snare is given for its price or for free, the karmic consequence belongs only to the one who provided the price.
If the person by whom it was obtained repairs a broken snare, or sees someone passing by the side and, having set up a fence, leads them into the front, or makes it tighter—
Or he sets up a snare-pole, or ties a stronger snare-rope, or drives in a firmer stake; neither of them escapes.
If, when remorse arises, he causes the snare to be removed and departs, others see him and set it up again;
they die one after another as they are bound, and the original perpetrator is not released.
If, however, the snare-stake was not made by him himself, he is released after setting it aside at the place where it was taken;
he is released after cutting down a stake grown there naturally. But even if he merely guards a stake made by himself, he is not released.
For if another person takes that stake and sets up the snare, then for those who die because of it, the original owner (mūlaṭṭha) is not released. If he burns it...
If one makes a firebrand and throws it away, even if one dies after being struck by that firebrand, one is not released from the offense.
However, one is released only after having completely burnt it or destroyed it; or even in the case of a rope, if it was spun by others and placed where it was taken, one is released.
Having obtained the yarn, if one spins it oneself and then unwinds it, or if it was spun with wool...
Having made it into a diamond [or a hard stone], one is released. But even if one brings the flax from the forest oneself, twists it, and guards it, one is not released.
One is released only by completely burning it or destroying it.
When setting up the mortar, one places the mortar-stand on its four legs and sets the stones upon it; with each application of effort...

It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Once it has been made ready in every respect and is released from the hand, the offenses—such as those involving defeat (*pārājika*) and others—must be understood according to whether the beings to be covered are specifically designated or not, and in accordance with the gravity of the act.
Even if a price is paid at a non-auction (*adūhala*), whether for a sum or for free, the legal liability for the deed attaches only to the one who holds the price.
If the person by whom it was obtained picks up what has fallen, [the responsibility remains with him].
Or, having placed other stones [on top], he makes it even heavier; or, seeing them moving toward the slope, he builds a wall and directs them into the threshing floor;

in both cases, they are not released from the offense. Even if, after remorse has arisen, he removes the stones from the threshing floor and goes away, and another person sees this and restores them, the one who was at the root of the act is not released. As for the place where the stones were taken—
Except for the base of a mortar, or having placed it on a bedpost in the manner already described, one is released [from the offense] by either taking hold of it or burning it.

Even in the case of one who impales [a victim] on a stake, once everything is prepared and the stake has merely been released from the hand, the offenses—Pārājika and so forth—should be understood according to whether the victim was designated or not, based on the fact that they are beings destined to die once they have fallen upon the point of the stake. [The text continues: "On the stake, by the base..."
Whether it is given intentionally or unintentionally, the karmic bond belongs only to the one who originally planted it.
If the person by whom it was received thinks, "They will die all at once," and makes the stake sharper; or thinks, "They will die in pain," and makes it duller;
or, perceiving it as "high," plants it lower, or perceiving it as "low," plants it higher—[the original planter remains bound].
Whether it is bent, straight, too straight, or slightly leaning, neither [of these] are exempt.

However, if one places it in another location, thinking, "It was placed in the wrong spot," and if that [plant] was sought from the very beginning for the purpose of killing, the person who planted it (the *mūlaṭṭha*) is not exempt.
But if it was planted after being obtained without having been sought for that purpose, the person who planted it (*mūlaṭṭha*) is exempt.
He is released. When remorse has arisen, he is released by either placing [the knife] in the spot where it was grasped according to the method described for the "bedpost" or by burning it.

177. Regarding the phrase "or a weapon on a support": here, "support" (apassena) means a bed, a chair, a leaning board used for daily enjoyment, or a supporting pillar for one sitting in a daytime resting place, or a tree growing there.
Furthermore, for one standing leaning against a walking path, a support tree, or a support board—
all these are called "reliance" (*apassena*) in the sense of being something to lean upon.
Having acted in such a way that one leaning on that reliance might be pierced or cut, he places a weapon such as an axe, a hatchet, a spear, an arrow, or a thorn.

It is a *dukkaṭa*. For one who sits or lies down in a place where [the seat] is always used, being free from apprehension, but not seeing [the danger], there is a *thullaccaya* due to the arising of suffering caused by contact with the blade; if death occurs, it is a *pārājika*.
If another monk, an enemy of his, sees him while wandering through the monastery and thinks, "This [action] is surely for the sake of his death..."
If he goes along rejoicing, thinking, "It has been placed [there]; let it die well and properly," it is a *dukkaṭa*.
But if he also performs some action there—such as making it sharper—in the thought, "When this is done, it will be well-made," for him too it is a *pārājika*.
However, if he removes it, thinking, "It is in the wrong place," and places it in another location, [there is no offense].
If it is placed there for that very purpose, the one who planted the root does not escape [liability]. If it is placed after obtaining something natural, he escapes.
If, having removed that, he plants another sharper one, the one who planted the root still escapes.

This same principle applies even regarding the smearing with poison, up to the point where there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for delighting in death. However, if he [the one who planted the root] is also... [small/insignificant]...
Having observed that it is unevenly circular, she makes it larger, or she makes what was large smaller, thinking "it is excessive";
or she makes what was thin thick, or makes what was thick thin;

or, having heated it with fire, she moves it from below to above or from above to below—there is a *pārājika* offense for her as well. Thinking, "This is situated in the wrong place," she cuts it all away.

Having wiped it, he places it in another location; if he himself has prepared the medicines, the status of being the root-cause (mūlaṭṭha) is not relinquished, but if he has not prepared them himself, it is relinquished.

However, if he thinks, "This poison is too little," and brings in more and adds it, then for whichever person dies from the poison, there is a *pārājika* offense for him. If [the victim] dies from the property belonging to both, then for both.
It is a *pārājika* offense. If, thinking "this is poison, this is non-poison," one removes that [poison] and leaves only one's own [non-poisonous] poison, there is a *pārājika* for him;
the original offender is released from the root.
Or, "he makes it weak" means: having cut the lower part of a bed or chair with a saw, or with splinters or ropes...
Or, having cut those parts by which it is traversed, or having left only a small remainder, he places a weapon below [the path], thinking, "He will fall here and die.

He also cuts the far side of the handrails, etc., at the end of the walking path, the support trees, and the railings, and places a weapon below; or, in the case of ravines and such, he cuts a bed, a chair, or a handrail.
Or, having brought [someone] there, he places them so that they fall as soon as they sit down or merely look around;
or, it is a bridge for walking across a ravine and the like, and he makes it weak. For one who acts in this way, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of doing so.

For the other [person], if suffering arises, there is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*); if death occurs, there is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*). If he brings a bhikkhu and places him on the edge of a ravine or similar place...
“Having seen [him], trembling with fear, he will fall and die”—this is a *dukkaṭa* offense. If he falls right there, it is a *thullaccaya* due to the arising of suffering;

if he dies, it is a *pārājika*. Whether one causes him to fall oneself, or causes another to cause him to fall, or another causes him to fall unbidden of his own accord, or a non-human being causes him to fall, or he falls by the force of the wind, or by his own nature...
If [the victim] dies, there is a *pārājika* offense in every case of death. Why? Because by his action, [the perpetrator] stands on the edge of a precipice or similar place.

"Placing near" (*upanikkhipana*) means placing in the vicinity. In that regard, having praised the beauty of death by such means as, "Whoever dies by this sword shall obtain wealth," and so forth, one says, "Let those who desire death die; let those who do not desire death..."
If, having said, "Kill him," one places a sword down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for that placing.

Whether one who desires to die strikes himself with it, or one who desires to kill strikes another, in both cases there is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*) for the placer of the weapon due to the arising of suffering in another;
if death occurs, it is an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*). If it was placed without specifying a particular person, and many die, [the same applies].
A mass of unwholesome states. Regarding the grounds for offenses such as *pārājika*, there are the *pārājika* offenses and so forth.
When remorse has arisen, one is released by setting aside the sword at the place where it was seized. If it was taken after having been purchased, it is the sword of those who do not own it;
one is released by paying the price to those from whose hands the price was originally received. If, having taken a lump of iron, a plowshare, or a hoe, a sword was subsequently fashioned [from it].
He is released by doing exactly what he was made to do with the goods he took.
If he takes a hoe and, having destroyed it, makes a plough, even if living beings die from being struck by that plough, he is not released from the offense of taking life.
However, if he had the iron produced solely for the purpose of depositing it [as collateral], and another person strikes it...

When it has been reduced to powder and scattered about, one is released. Even if [the offense] was committed by many people with a single intention, like a commentary manuscript, the determination of the bond of kamma should be understood according to the method stated for manuscripts. This same principle applies to spears and clubs.
For a mallet, the determination is similar to that for a noose or a staff. Likewise for stones. For a sword, it is exactly like a blade. Or [it may be] poison.

Regarding one who places poison [as a gift], the offenses—such as *pārājika*—should be understood according to the specific objects (*vatthu*) involved, whether they are designated or not, and in accordance with the relevant rules such as *pārājika*.
If the poison was purchased and set aside, one is released from the offense by restoring it to its original state according to the aforementioned method.

If one has personally prepared it with medicinal ingredients, one is released from the offense by making it non-poisonous. The legal determination for a rope is exactly the same as that for a noose-rope.

Regarding medicine: if a monk, when a hostile monk has contracted a wasting disease or a disease of a dissimilar nature, intends his death and gives him unsuitable ghee and so forth while claiming they are suitable, or gives him some other root, bulb, or fruit for that purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of giving such medicine.
If the other person experiences pain or dies, there are offenses of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*) and defeat (*pārājika*), respectively.
In the case of an immediate offense (*ānantariya-vatthu*), it should be understood as an immediate offense. 178.

Regarding the infliction of a disagreeable form: "inflicts" means either that one places a disagreeable form near another person, or that one stands there having assumed the guise of a *yakkha*, a *peta*, or the like.
By the mere act of inflicting it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For the other person, that...
Upon seeing a form, if fear arises, there is a thullaccaya offense; if death occurs, it is a pārājika offense.
However, if that very same form is pleasing to someone else, yet he dies from dehydration due to not obtaining it, there is no transgression (visaṅketa).
This same principle applies even in the case of what is pleasing. In that regard, specifically, the male form is pleasing to women, and the female form is pleasing to men. That [is the distinction].
Having adorned [the animal], he brings it near; he merely shows it [to the victim] and does not allow it to be seen for too long.
The other [victim] withers from lack of food and dies: this is a *pārājika* offense. If it dies out of fear, there is no transgression (*visaṅketa*).
However, if one brings it near without considering whether it will die from fear or from lack of food, thinking only, "It will die from seeing [me]," [then it is a *pārājika*].

If [the victim] has become terrified or has withered away, or is dead, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense. By this same method, cases involving the offering of sounds and so forth should also be understood.

However, in this context, the sounds of non-humans and the like, which cause terror, are "unpleasant sounds"; whereas for men, the sounds of women, sweet music, and the like, which bring delight to the mind, are "pleasant sounds.
Furthermore, the scents of the roots and so forth of *visarukkha* trees in the Himalayas, as well as the scent of corpses, [are also included].
Unpleasant odors are those such as the smell of black aloe-wood root; pleasant odors are [the opposite]. Unpleasant tastes are those such as the taste of bitter roots;
pleasant tastes are those such as the taste of non-bitter roots. Unpleasant tangibles are to be understood as those such as the touch of poison or the touch of severe itch;
pleasant tangibles are those such as the touch of fine Chinese silk, lotus fibers, or cotton mattresses.

Regarding "the presentation of the Dhamma" (*dhammūpahāra*): "Dhamma" should be understood here as the Dhamma of the teaching. Or, by way of the teaching, it refers to the objects of the Dhamma consisting of the distinctions between misfortune and success in both hell and heaven.

"To one destined for hell" means: he tells the story of hell—such as the fivefold binding and the performance of labor—to a being who has broken his vows, committed evil, and is fit to be reborn in hell.

If, having heard that [account], he dies out of fear, there is a *pārājika* offense for the speaker. But if he dies by his own nature even after hearing it, there is no offense. If one speaks a discourse on hell with the thought, "Having heard this, he will not commit such evil;
he will restrain himself, he will desist," and the other, having heard it, dies out of fear, there is no offense. A "discourse on heaven" refers to [accounts of] celestial musicians and so forth.
And [he speaks] the account of the splendors of the Nandana Grove and other such realms.
