Having heard this, the other person—intent on heaven and desiring to quickly attain that splendor—inflicts suffering by means of carrying heavy loads, eating poisonous food, cutting off food intake, suppressing inhalation and exhalation, and so forth.
For the one who tells the story, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; if the listener dies, there is a *pārājika* offense. But if, even after hearing it...
If one dies according to one’s own natural law after remaining for the full extent of one’s lifespan, there is no offense.

If one speaks with the thought, “Having heard this, he will perform meritorious deeds,” and the other person, having heard it, passes away while being intent upon that [merit], there is no offense. 179.
Regarding “speaking when asked”: “He speaks when asked” means that when asked, “Venerable sir, how does one who has died obtain wealth or be reborn in heaven? he speaks thus.
Regarding the instruction: "Unasked" means that he speaks on his own initiative without being asked.
The acts of signs and acts of conventions are to be understood in the same manner as explained in the discourse on taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
Having thus shown the classification of offenses in various ways, now, in order to show the classification of non-offenses, [he says]: "There is no offense..."
He said, “Unintentionally,” and so forth. Therein, “unintentionally” means not having thought, “By this means I shall kill this person.
For indeed, there is no offense even if another dies by a means employed without such an intention; and he will say, “There is no offense, monk, if unintentional.
“Of one who does not know” means [employing] a means while not knowing, “By this, this person will die,” regarding another.
There is no offense even when [the person] dies; and in the case of the story regarding the alms-food containing poison, it will be said: "There is no offense, monk, for one who did not know.
"One who does not intend death" means one who does not desire death.
For by whatever means another dies, even if that person is killed by that very means, there is no offense for one who does not intend death. And it will be said: "There is no offense, monk..."

“...with the intention of death. Those such as the insane and so forth are exactly as described by the method previously stated. However, in this case, there is no offense for those monks who were the first offenders (*ādikammika*) and who killed one another;
for them there is no transgression. For all others, however, there is indeed an offense for such acts as praising the virtues of death and so forth.
The commentary on the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*) is concluded.
Regarding the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors: this training rule has three origins; it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.

It is an action (*kiriya*), liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), and painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
For even if one has ascended to a royal bed and is experiencing the bliss of the success of sovereignty...
When it is said, “Your Majesty, the thief has been brought,” the king says, “Go, kill him,” as if laughing;
yet it should be understood that he speaks with a mind of dejection. Because it is interspersed with happiness and lacks continuity, this is difficult for ordinary people to discern.
—Commentary on the Basis of Discipline (Vinītavatthu-vaṇṇanā)
180. In the accounts of the cases concerning those who have trained, regarding the first case:

"Out of compassion" means that those bhikkhus, seeing his great suffering from illness, gave rise to compassion and said, "You are virtuous and skilled in what ought to be done; why are you afraid while dying?
Is it not the case that for one who is virtuous, heaven is dependent upon nothing more than death? Thus, they were themselves desirous of death and manifested their state of being desirous of death.
Being ignorant, they praised the beauty of death. That monk, too, having cut off his food supply due to their praise, passed away in the interim;
therefore, they incurred an offense. However, it was said "they praised the beauty of death out of compassion" by way of common parlance.
Therefore, even now, a wise monk [should act] toward a sick monk...

In this way, one should not praise death. For if, having heard such praise, someone takes their own life through an act such as cutting off food, and dies prematurely even while there is still the remainder of a single conscious moment (*javana*) of life, they have been killed by that very person.
However, instruction should be given according to this method: "It is no wonder that the arising of the paths and fruits occurs for one who possesses virtue."
"Therefore, without forming an attachment to dwellings and the like, one should establish mindfulness directed toward the Buddha,
the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the body, and apply diligence to mental attention. And even when the description of death has been delivered,
he who makes no effort whatsoever on account of that description, but [remains] according to his own nature, according to his lifespan, and according to the natural sequence of events—
"He dies; because of that, the one who praised him should not be made to undergo an offense.
Regarding the second case—"And you, monks, should not [sit] without having examined"—here, what kind of seat should be examined and what kind should not be examined?
That which is a plain seat, without any covering, and...
When it is spread out while people have arrived and are watching, that should not be reviewed; it is permissible to sit there.
Even when people, having stepped on it with their own hands, offer it saying, "Venerable sir, please sit here," it is also permissible.
Even if those who first arrived and sat down later move upward or downward, there is no need for review.
There is no need [for formal reflection]. Even when it is covered by a thin cloth such that the palm is visible through it, there is likewise no duty of reflection.

However, that which is already spread out beforehand with a cloak (*pāvāra*), a *kojava*, or similar items, should be sat upon after touching and inspecting it with the hand. In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however, it says: "Even with a thick outer robe..."
It is said that whatever is laid out such that no creases are visible need not be inspected. Regarding the case of the pestle:

"unintentionally" means that there was no murderous intent (*avadhaka-cetana*) and the application of effort was mistaken. Therefore he said, "I did it unintentionally. The case of the mortar is self-evident.
Regarding the cases of those who went forth when old, in the first case: "for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus..."

"Do not create an obstacle," he said, and dismissed him. In the second case—being addressed in the midst of the Saṅgha and in the midst of a group as "the son of an elder elder," and being distressed by those words—he said, "Let this man die," and dismissed him.
In the third case—by causing him suffering, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
181. The three subsequent cases have their meanings self-evident. Regarding the case of the alms-food containing poison:

that bhikkhu, being one who fulfills the qualities conducive to cordiality (*sārāṇīya-dhamma*), eats only after having given the first portion of the alms to his fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*). Therefore it is said: "She gave him the first portion.
"The first portion" (*aggakārika*) means the act of giving the first portion; or, the very best of the alms-food obtained first, or the most excellent of the excellent.
The meaning is "alms-food. As for that foremost act of giving, which consists of his gift, it was not possible to give [it away];
for he gave the alms-food starting from the seat of the elders. "Those monks" refers to the monks who had consumed the alms-food starting from the seat of the elders;
it is said that they all passed away. The rest here is self-evident. However, regarding those who are faithless and hold wrong views...
Having received fine food with due respect from families, one should neither consume it oneself nor give it to others without first examining it.
Even if one receives from there food that has been kept overnight, or edible snacks, that too should not be consumed.
For anything that has been slept upon by snakes, scorpions, and the like—even if its covering has not been removed—is of a nature to be discarded.
Those families give [the food]. Even if the alms-food is smeared with perfumes, turmeric, and so forth, it must not be accepted from them;
for they think that even food set aside after wiping away spots of disease from the body should be given.
Regarding the matter of testing: one who tests tests in two ways—“Is he able to kill this person or not?”
Or one examines the poison, thinking, "Will this person die after eating this poison, or not? Or one examines the person.
In either case, if it is given with the intention of testing, whether the person dies or not, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).
However, if it is given with the thought, "May this poison kill him," or "After eating this poison, may this person die," and the person consequently dies, there is a *pārājika* (defeat).
If not, it is a thullaccaya offense.
182–3. The three subsequent rules concerning stones and the three rules concerning bricks, rafters, and roof-tiles are self-evident.
Furthermore, this distinction between offenses and non-offenses does not apply solely to stones and the like; it also applies to sticks, clubs, wedges, awls, and so forth.
It is indeed by way of this [principle] that it occurs; therefore, even though it is not explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi, it should be understood according to the method already established.
Regarding the cases concerning "aṭṭaka": *aṭṭaka* refers to a bedstead suspended from the air, which people construct for the purpose of white-washing, garland-making, creeper-work, and so forth.
In that context, the phrase "Friend, bind it where you are standing" is spoken with the intention of death toward the place where one is standing.
Having fallen, one might break against a stump, or die in a swamp, a precipice, or similar places; it is with reference to such a place that this was said.
And in this regard, someone determines the upper location, thinking, "Having fallen from here, he will die"; someone determines the lower location, thinking, "Having fallen here, he will die";
and someone determines both, thinking, "Having fallen from here and here, he will die. Among these:
If one falls elsewhere instead of falling at the designated upper spot, or falls elsewhere instead of falling at the designated lower spot,
or falls having failed to observe either one of the two designations, there is no offense because the agreement has been broken when that person dies.
This same principle applies to the case of roofing a monastery as well.

Regarding the story of the monk who found no delight: it is said that this monk, seeing the arising of sensual thoughts and the like, and being unable to restrain them, became dissatisfied with the Teaching and turned his face toward the life of a householder.
Then he thought, "Before I fall into a breach of morality, I shall die. Thereupon, having climbed that mountain, while falling down a precipice, [he encountered] another...
Having spread out a bamboo-weaver’s mat, he killed him. "Bamboo-weaver" means a worker in bamboo. "And you must not cause yourself to fall," means that one must not cause oneself to fall.
This is stated, however, by way of a change in grammatical case. And here, it is not only that one must not cause oneself to fall;
one must not be killed by any means whatsoever, even by the withholding of food. For whoever...
If a sick person, while medicine and attendants are available, cuts off food because he desires to die, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* offense.

However, in the case of one who has a severe illness that has persisted for a long time, and where the monks, though attending to him, become exhausted and disgusted, thinking, "When indeed shall we be freed from this sickness?
and feel distressed; if that person [thinks], "Even if this physical existence were to be tended to..."
If he says, "The illness does not subside, and the monks are becoming exhausted," it is permissible for him to cut off food and not use medicine.

Furthermore, if he thinks, "This illness is severe, the life-formations do not persist, and this attainment of distinction appears as if already within my grasp," it is likewise permissible for him to cut them off.
Even for one who is not ill, if a sense of spiritual urgency has arisen, [the thought] "the search for food..."
"It is mere conceptual proliferation; I shall devote myself to the meditation subject alone"—it is permissible for one who cuts off [food] under the pretext of the meditation subject.
However, if he cuts off food after announcing his attainment of a specific distinction, it is not permissible.
For it is permissible to speak thus to fellow bhikkhus who possess a sense of shame.
Regarding "at Silāvatthu": *davena* means by way of sport; the meaning is "for amusement. *Silā* means a stone;
and it is not only a stone, but any other fragment of wood or brick that may be thrown with the hand or by means of a machine is likewise forbidden.
Stones and such things may indeed be rolled along while laughing and joking for the sake of shrines and the like.
It is permissible to throw [things] or to toss them up during the time for work.
Likewise, it is permissible when performing similar new construction work, or when washing utensils, or when tossing up and striking a tree or a washing-stick.
It is also permissible to drive away crows, jackals, or other animals by throwing a piece of wood or a stone during meal times and the like.
184. All the bases for weariness and so forth have already been explained. Furthermore, in this context, thinking "I am timid" is not a reason to fail to attend to the sick;
rather, out of a desire for their welfare, one should attend to them after carefully observing the patient's strength and weakness, their preferences, and what is beneficial or harmful for them.
185. In the case of the adulteress pregnant by another: "whose husband has gone abroad" means one whose husband has departed on a journey.
"Causing an abortion" means a medicinal substance by which, when consumed, the fetus is expelled. The two cases concerning co-wives have their meanings already explained.
In the case of destroying the fetus: when told, "Having crushed it, cause it to fall," if she causes it to fall by having someone else crush it, there is no breach of the agreement (*visaṅketa*).

Even when it is said, “Having had it crushed, cause it to fall,” if she crushes it herself and causes it to fall, there is still a breach of the agreement (*visaṅketa*). Regarding a human being, there is no such thing as a formal pretext (*pariyāya*).
Therefore, when it is said, “The fetus falls once it has been crushed,” whether she crushes it herself or causes another to crush it before causing it to fall, there is no breach of the agreement;
it is indeed a *pārājika*. This same principle applies even in the case of the matter of burning (*tāpanavatthu*).
In the story of Vañjhitthī—*vañjhitthī* means one who does not conceive. There is no woman who simply does not conceive at all;
rather, this term is said with reference specifically to her whose conceived embryo does not remain stable.
It is said that during the fertile period (*utusamaya*), all women conceive. As for this woman who is called "barren" (*vañjhā*), her...
The unwholesome result (akusalavipāka) reaches those beings reborn in the womb.

Having taken rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) by means of a limited wholesome result, they perish when overcome by the unwholesome result. Indeed, at the very moment of a new rebirth-linking, through the power of karma, the embryo does not become established in two ways:
either by wind or by microorganisms (pāṇaka). The wind dries it up and causes it to disappear.
The fetus was devoured by worms. However, if medicine had been administered to ward off that wind or those worms, the fetus might have been stabilized;
yet that monk did not do so, but instead gave another harsh medicine. Because of that, she died.
The Blessed One, because the medicine had been administered, prescribed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The same principle applies to the second case as well. Therefore, one should not provide medicine to outsiders who come to one;
if one does so, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, one may provide it to the five who share the same Dhamma:
a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a female trainee (*sikkhamānā*), a male novice (*sāmaṇera*), and a female novice (*sāmaṇerī*). For these possess equal virtue, faith, and wisdom regarding the three trainings.
It is not permissible for one who is capable to fail to provide medicine;
and when providing it, if they have it, one should take what belongs to them, compound it, and give it. If they do not have it, one should use what belongs to oneself.

If one does not have it either, one should seek it through the practice of alms-round or from a place where one has been invited by relatives. If nothing can be obtained, [one must act] for the sake of the sick person.
It may be made even by requesting what has not yet been prepared for one's own benefit;
it is also permissible to make [robes] for five others: for one's mother, for one's father, for those who attend upon them, for one's own attendant, and for a *paṇḍupalāsa*.
A *paṇḍupalāsa* is one who is seeking the going-forth and is preparing his bowl and robes.
He dwells in the monastery. Among them, if his parents are wealthy and do not expect anything in return, it is permissible for him not to provide for them.
However, if they are even established in royalty and do expect something, it is not permissible for him not to provide for them.

To those who expect medicine, medicine must be given; to those who do not know how to compound it, it must be compounded and given. For the sake of all, [he should act] toward his fellow practitioners...

It should be sought in the same manner as previously described. However, if he brings his mother to the monastery and looks after her, he must perform all the attendant services without touching them.
He should give her hard food and soft food with his own hands.
As for his father, however, he should attend to him just as he would a novice, performing services such as bathing and massaging with his own hands. And those parents whom one attends to...

They look after [the sick]; for them also, it should be done in exactly the same way. One called a "servant" (*veyyāvaccakara*) is one who, having received wages, cuts wood in the forest or performs some other work;
when illness arises in such a person, medicine must be administered until his relatives see him. However, as for one who remains entirely dependent on the bhikkhus and performs all tasks...
If he does so, medicine must certainly be given to him. One should behave toward even a mere withered leaf as one would toward a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*).
It is also permissible to do so for ten others:
an elder brother, a younger brother, an elder sister, a younger sister, a junior mother, a senior mother, a junior father, a senior father, a paternal aunt, and a maternal uncle.
When preparing for all of them, however, one should take medicine belonging to those very individuals, compound it, and give it to them.
But if they are insufficient and they request, saying, "Venerable sir, please give us;
we will repay you," it should be given on a temporary basis. Even if they do not request it, one may say, "We have medicine; take it on a temporary basis."
Having said this, or having made the intention, "When it comes to them, they will give," one may give.
If they return it, it should be accepted; if they do not give, they should not be pressured. Apart from these ten types of relatives, this should not be done for others.

However, regarding the lineage of their children, as long as it is within the seventh generation of the family circle, for one who causes the four requisites to be brought [for him], [there is no offense].
For one who prepares medicine without a formal request, there is no offense of medical practice (*vejjakamma*) or of corrupting a family (*kuladūsaka*).
If the brother’s wife or the sister’s husband are ill, it is permissible even if they are relatives.
If they are not relatives, [the medicine] should be prepared by the brother and sister and given with the instruction: “Give this where you are looking after them. Then...
Or, having prepared it for those sons, it should be given [to them] with the words, “Give this to your mother and father.

By this method, the decision should be understood for all cases as well. And when novices are being made to bring medicine from the forest for their sake, it should be brought by novices who are relatives.
Or, having had it brought for his own sake, he should give it. They too, under the pretext of their duties, should bring it, saying, "We are bringing it for the preceptor.

If the preceptor’s parents, being ill, come to the monastery while the preceptor has gone abroad, the student (saddhivihārika) should give the medicine belonging to the preceptor. If there is none, [he should give] his own.

Having relinquished it, medicine should be given to the preceptor. Even if one does not have any oneself, one should seek it in the manner described, make it the property of the preceptor, and give it.
The preceptor should also act in exactly the same way toward the mother and father of the student living with him.
This same method applies to the teacher and the resident pupil as well. As for any other person, whether a visitor or a thief...
Or if a lord defeated in battle, or one abandoned by his kinsmen, or a pauper, or a traveler,
or one who is ill enters a monastery, medicine should be prepared for all of them without expecting anything in return.
There may be a faithful family that serves the Saṅgha of monks with the four requisites, acting as parents to them.
If there is anyone who is ill there, and they say out of trust for his sake, "Venerable sir, please prepare medicine and give it," one must neither give it nor prepare it.

However, if they ask after knowing what is allowable (kappiya), saying, "Venerable sir, what medicine do you prepare for such-and-such a disease? one may say, "Having taken this and that, we prepare it."
It is permissible. However, when asked, "Venerable sir, my mother is ill;
please tell me what medicine she should take," one must not give a direct instruction. Rather, they should converse with one another:

"Friend, what medicine did they prescribe for such-and-such a monk suffering from this same ailment? [The other replies: "This and that, venerable sir. Having heard that, the other [should say] regarding his mother...
If one prepares medicine, it is indeed permissible.
It is said that when Queen Vasabha’s illness arose, the Elder Mahāpaduma was approached by a certain woman who asked him about it;
instead of saying, "I do not know," he conversed with the monks in exactly this manner. Upon hearing that, they prepared medicine for her.

When the illness had subsided, they filled a medicine basket with his three robes and three hundred kahāpaṇa coins, brought it back, and placing it at the feet of the Elder, said, "Venerable sir, please perform an offering of flowers.
The Elder, having had them accept it as a permissible gift under the category of "the teacher’s portion," performed the flower offering. This, then, is how one should deal with medicine.
Regarding the *paritta*, however, when it is said, “Venerable sirs, perform a *paritta* for the sick person,” one should not do so;
but when it is said, “Recite it,” then one may do so. Even if he thinks, “People are ignorant; if this is not done, they will feel regret,” one may still do it.
But when told, “Give him water consecrated by the *paritta* and thread consecrated by the *paritta*,” [one should do so].
One should stir the water with one's hand, wipe the thread, and give it to them.

If the monastery gives water that belongs to oneself, or if one gives one's own thread, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If people take the water and the thread, sit down, and say, "Recite the protective charms (*paritta*)," it should be done.
If they do not know [how to do so], it should be explained to the monks.
Having poured water on the feet of those sitting [in the assembly] and having placed the thread, they depart, saying, "Perform the protection;
recite the protective chant. The feet must not be removed [from the water]. For people become remorseful.
If they send for a monastery within the village for the sake of one who is ill, one should say, "Recite the protective chant. Within the village, in places such as the royal palace...
When a disease or a calamity has arisen, they should summon [the monks] and have them recite; the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta and others should be recited.

Even if they are sent with the message, "Come and give the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) to the sick person, preach the Dhamma," or "Come to the royal palace or the minister’s house and give the training rules, preach the Dhamma," they must go and give the training rules.
The Dhamma should be taught. If they summon one, saying, "Come for the sake of attending to the dead," one must not go.
However, it is permissible to go under the pretext of a meditation subject, thinking, "I shall obtain mindfulness of death by visiting a charnel ground and observing the foulness.
This is how one should proceed in such minor matters.
Regarding almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*), however: to whom should unselected almsfood be given, and to whom should it not be given? First, it should be given to one’s mother and father;

even if it is worth a *kahāpaṇa*, there is no transgression in giving what has been offered out of faith. It should also be given to those who attend upon one’s mother and father, to one’s servant, and to a *paṇḍupalāsa* (one whose leaves have turned pale). In that regard, for the *paṇḍupalāsa*, [it should be placed] in a bowl...
It is permissible to give it even after having mixed it [with other food]. Apart from that, it is not permissible for others who are householders, nor even for one's own parents.
For the use of requisites belonging to those gone forth is equivalent to a shrine (cetiyatthāniya) for householders.
Furthermore, this unclaimed alms-food should be given even to a bandit-thief or a lord who has arrived. Why? Because if it were not given to them, they would say, "They are not giving."
Even when food is being given after they have touched it, they become angry, thinking, "She is giving me what is left over.
Being angry, they even deprive others of life and create obstacles for the Teaching. In this regard, the story of the thief-nāga who wandered about longing for sovereignty should be told.
This is how one should conduct oneself regarding almsfood.

Now, to whom should hospitality be extended, and to whom should it not? Hospitality—meaning toward any newcomer who has arrived at the monastery, whether they be poor or a thief, whether they be a pauper or a lord—must certainly be extended. How so?
First, seeing a newcomer who has arrived at the monastery with his provisions exhausted, one should give him drinking water and oil for rubbing the feet.
It should be given. To one who arrives at the proper time, rice-gruel and food should be given; to one who arrives at the improper time, if there is rice, the rice should be given.
One who has arrived at an untimely hour must not be told, "Go away. A place for sleeping should be provided.
All this should be done without expecting anything in return. "People, indeed, are givers of the four requisites when such hospitality is rendered."
One should not give rise to the thought, "Having gained confidence again and again, they will do me a favor. However, even property belonging to the Saṅgha may be given to thieves.
And for the purpose of illustrating the benefits of hospitality, there is the story of the thief Nāga and [the account] of one who went to Jambudīpa with his brother.

The story of the Great King of the City, the story of the four ministers during the reign of King Pitu, the story of the robber Abhaya, and many other such stories are recounted in detail in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Herein is the illustration of one such story: it is said that in the island of Sri Lanka, a robber named Abhaya, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, [lived] in a certain...
Having established his camp at that place, he dwelt there after causing a three-league radius around him to be cleared.
The inhabitants of Anurādhapura did not cross the Kadamba River, and the movement of people along the path to Cetiya Mountain was cut off.
Then one day, a bandit went there thinking, "I shall plunder Cetiya Mountain. When the monastery attendants saw him, they [informed] the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya.
They reported this. The Elder asked, "Is there ghee, molasses, and so forth? "There is, venerable sir," they replied. "Give these to the bandits;
is there rice? "There is, venerable sir; there is rice brought for the sake of the Saṅgha, as well as leaf-vegetables and milk-rice.
"Prepare a meal and give it to the bandits. The monastery attendants did accordingly. The bandits [received] the meal...
Having eaten, they asked, "By whom was this hospitality provided? "By our noble Elder Abhaya," they replied.
The bandits went to the Elder, paid homage, and said: "We came intending to seize whatever belongs to the Saṅgha and the Cetiya by force;
however, we have become inspired with faith by this hospitality of yours."
“From this day forward, let the righteous protection of the monastery be under our control; let the citizens come and give alms, and let them pay homage to the cetiya.
From that time on, when the citizens came to give alms, they would go out to meet them right at the riverbank and escort them to the monastery while guarding them;
even inside the monastery, they remained there providing protection for those giving alms.
The monks gave the leftovers from their meal to the robbers. Even when it was time for them to depart, those robbers would bring them to the riverbank and then turn back.
Then one day, a disparaging talk arose among the community of monks: "The Elder, out of a sense of lordship, gave what belonged to the Saṅgha to the robbers.
The Elder had an assembly convened and said: "The robbers [are providing] the Saṅgha’s natural requisites..."
They came thinking, “We shall seize and take what belongs to the cetiya.
Then I offered them such hospitality as this, thinking, “In this way they will not carry it off”; now, having gathered all of that together, have it appraised.
For that reason, have all the goods that were not stolen gathered together and appraised. Thereupon, everything given by the Elder—
In the shrine hall, even a single fine cloth-painted carpet was not worth as much as that. Then they said:
"The welcome extended by the Elder was so well-performed that it cannot be challenged or recalled; there is neither debt nor forfeiture.
Thus, having recognized that a welcome has such great benefit, it should be offered by a wise bhikkhu.

187. In the case concerning the poking with the finger: *uttanta* means being exhausted. *Anassāsaka* means breathless. However, as for the offense that would have occurred in this case, it has been pointed out in the *Khuddaka* (Minor Rules) and therefore is not mentioned here.
In the case immediately following: *ottharitvā* means having stepped upon. It is said that he fell while being pulled by them. One man climbed onto his belly and sat there;
the remaining fifteen people also covered him over with their bodies on the ground.
They killed the deer like hunters using stones. However, because they intended [the act] as a ritual for the spirits (*kamma*) and not with the intent to kill, a *pārājika* offense was not mentioned.
In the case of the "Exorcist" (*bhūtavejjaka*) story—where it says "he killed a *yakkha*"—it refers to those who recite the *bhūtavejjā* texts and desire to release one seized by a *yakkha*.
They say, "Summon the yakkha and release him. If he does not release him, they fashion an image out of dough or clay and cut off its hands, feet, and so forth;
whatever part of it is cut off, that very part of the yakkha is as if cut off.
When the head is cut off, the yakkha also dies. Thus, he too is killed by this means; therefore, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is stated. And not only this...
It is indeed a *yakkha*; for even one who would kill Sakka, the king of the gods, incurs only a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
Regarding the case of the fierce *yakkha*: "A dwelling of a fierce *yakkha" refers to that monastery in which a fierce, violent *yakkha* resides.
For if one sends someone to such a monastery without knowing its nature, merely for the purpose of staying there, there is no offense.
If one who intends death sends [someone] away, he incurs a *pārājika* offense upon that person’s death, and a *thullaccaya* offense if they do not die.

And just as in the case of sending someone to the Vāḷayakkha monastery, so too should the distinction between offenses and non-offenses be understood for one who sends someone to a "wilderness" (*vāḷavihāra*) where predatory animals such as lions,
tigers, and other beasts, or long-bodied creatures such as pythons and black snakes dwell.

This is the method [of analysis] independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimuttakanaya*). And just as it is for one who sends a monk to a dwelling place of predatory spirits (*vāḷayakkha*), so too should the distinction between what constitutes an offense and what does not be understood for one who sends a predatory spirit to the presence of a monk.

This same method applies to cases such as a wilderness inhabited by predators (*vāḷakantāra*) and so forth. The only difference here is that a wilderness in which there are predatory beasts or long-tailed serpents is called a "wilderness inhabited by predators. In which...
"There are thieves; that is a thicket of thieves"—thus, there is only a difference in the literal meaning of the words. Furthermore, this offense of defeat regarding the human form is subtle;
one is not released by figurative speech. Therefore, if someone were to say, "In such-and-such a place a thief is sitting;
whoever brings back his head after cutting it off shall receive special honor from the king," [he would still be guilty].
If, having heard these words of his, someone goes and kills him, this [monk] becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the phrase "thinking it was he," and so forth: it is said that the monk, desiring to kill a monk who was his enemy, thought, "It would not be easy for me to go safely if I were to kill him during the day; I shall kill him at night."
Having observed him and arrived at night, thinking he was that person in a place where many were lying down, he deprived that very person of life.
Another, thinking it was that person, [deprived] another; another, thinking it was his companion, [deprived] him;
and another, thinking it was his companion, [deprived] yet another companion of his life. For all of them, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the first of the cases concerning those possessed by non-human spirits (*amanussa*): [the monk] struck him with the intention, "I will drive away the *yakkha*," while the other thought, "This one is no longer capable of escaping; I will kill him.
And here, it is stated that there is no offense for one who intends death. However, a blow should not be given to one possessed by a non-human spirit merely on this account; rather, a palm leaf—
A protective discourse (*parittasutta*) should be tied to the hand or the foot; protective discourses such as the *Ratana-sutta* should be recited;
and a Dhamma talk should be given, saying, "Do not harass a virtuous bhikkhu. The discourses on heaven and so forth are of plain meaning.
Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated.
189. The story of the tree-felling is similar to the story of the eightfold bondage. However, this is the distinction:

even if one is crushed by a tree and does not die, and it is possible to escape by cutting the tree from one side or digging into the earth, and if one has an axe or a hatchet in hand, one should still sacrifice one's life.

Nor should a tree be cut down, nor should the earth be dug up. Why? Because by doing so, one incurs an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), violates the Buddha’s command, and fails to maintain virtue for the duration of one's life.
Therefore, even if one must sacrifice one's life, one should not act in this way while clinging to one's virtue. However, [this does not apply] to another monk...
It is permissible to cut down a tree or dig up the earth to remove it.
If the mortar must be removed by rolling a tree against it, the Elder Mahāsumma said that one should cut down that very same tree and take the mortar.
The Elder Mahāpaduma said that it is also permissible to cut down another tree and take it. Regarding pits and the like:
The same principle applies to rescuing someone who has fallen by constructing a ladder for them. One should not construct a ladder oneself by cutting down a living grove (*bhūtagāma*);
however, it is permissible to rescue others using one that has been made by another.

190. Regarding the matters concerning the burning of a forest (*dāya*): "They set fire to the forest" means they set a fire in the woods. Here, however, [the distinction] is made according to whether it is dedicated (*uddissa*) or not dedicated (*anuddissa*).

The nature of the offenses—Pārājika, Ānantariya, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, and so forth—as well as their status as a mass of unwholesome states (akusalarāsi), should be understood according to the method already explained above, in accordance with the specific basis for each offense.
For one who sets fire [to a forest] with the thought, "May all the grass, trees, and thickets burn," there is a Pācittiya offense.
For one who sets it on fire with the thought, "May the wooden implements be destroyed," there is a Dukkaṭa offense. This applies even when done with the intention of mere play.

“An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” so it is stated in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*. For one who sets fire [to anything] with the thought, “Let whatever is wet or dry, whether possessing sense-faculties or lacking them, burn,” the offenses of defeat (pārājika), grave offense (thullaccaya), expiation (pācittiya), and wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) are to be understood according to the specific object.
However, the giving of fire and the performance of protective charms were permitted by the Blessed One; therefore, in the forest, [one may act] by means of forest-workers...
Or, seeing a fire approaching—whether given by another or arisen spontaneously—it is permissible to provide a counter-fire so that "the grass huts may not be destroyed.
The fire coming with it shall merge with this one and be extinguished for lack of fuel.
It is also permissible to perform protective measures (paritta) such as clearing the ground around the grass huts or digging a trench.
Or, just as a fire that has been kindled goes out when it finds no fuel, so too must this be done. All of this may be performed only while the fire is still burning.
If it has not yet been kindled, it must be caused to be done by those who are not fully ordained (anupasampanna) using appropriate terminology.
Furthermore, those extinguishing it with water must pour only water that contains no living organisms.

191. Regarding the case of a lethal blow (*āghāta*): just as it is in the statement "with a single blow," so too in statements such as "with two blows" and so forth, a *pārājika* offense is to be understood.
When "two" is stated, even if the person is killed by only one blow, it is still a *pārājika* because the limit has been reached;
however, if they are killed by three, there is no transgression. Thus, whether within the specified limit or inside that limit.
Or, if there was no agreement [on the number], then upon exceeding the limit, there is disagreement in all cases;
the commander is released, and the fault lies with the executioner alone. And just as it is with the blows, so it is with the men:
when it is said, "Let one kill," if he is killed by one, there is a *pārājika* offense; if he is killed by two, there is disagreement. When it is said, "Let two kill," whether by one or by two...
It should be understood that if one kills by means of three [steps], it is a *pārājika* offense due to the lack of a prior agreement (*visaṅketa*).

When one person in battle cuts off the head of a man running with speed using a sword, and the headless trunk continues to run until another strikes it down, if it is asked, "Whose [act constitutes] a *pārājika*?
half of the elders said, "Of the one who interrupted the movement. This was the view of the Elder Ābhidhammika Godatta.
“Of one who cuts off the head. Such instances as these should also be cited to illustrate the meaning of this case. 192.
In the case concerning buttermilk—when it is said without specification, “Give him buttermilk,” and he is killed after being given any kind of buttermilk whatsoever, there is a *pārājika* offense.
However, if it is specified—such as “cow’s buttermilk,” “buffalo’s buttermilk,” or “goat’s buttermilk”—or [if it is specified as] “cold...
When it is asked, "Is it hot? Is it smoked? Or is it unsmoked?", if one gives him something other than what was stated and he dies, there is a discrepancy (*visaṅketa*).
Regarding the case of the fermented salted sour gruel (*loṇasovīraka*): "salted sour gruel" is a single medicinal preparation compounded from all flavors.
It is said that those preparing it [use] the decoctions of *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, and *vibhītaka*, as well as all grains and all vegetables—even those of the seven [types].
Having added rice from grains, plantains and all other fruits, the shoots of vetta, ketaka, dates, and so forth— all such shoots— as well as pieces of fish and meat,
and various medicinal ingredients such as honey, molasses, rock salt, sea salt, and bitter substances,
they smear the mouth of the jar and set it aside for one, two, or three years; once that has fully matured...

It has the color of rose-apple juice. For those who have eaten unctuous food due to wind-diseases, coughs, skin diseases, jaundice, fistula-in-ano, and so forth, there is no other post-meal drink that is as effective for digesting the meal as a medicine as this. Furthermore, it is permitted for monks even after the midday meal;
for the sick, it is used exactly as prescribed, while for those not ill, it is to be consumed by mixing it with water.
The explanation of the third *pārājika* in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, is completed. 4.
The fourth *pārājika*.
The Teacher, the Knower of the Four Truths, has now proclaimed the fourth [Truth].
It is now the turn for the commentary on the *Pārājika* rules.
Therefore, that which was explained previously is easy to understand.
Excluding that [case], this is the praise for horses as well.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Bhikkhus of the Vaggumudā River 193:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī... [as before] ... "Let us undertake the work of the householders."
It is said: "We determine the duties to be performed by householders in their fields, monasteries, and so forth;
we both explain and instruct them, saying, 'It should be done thus,' and 'It should not be done thus. *Dūteyya* means the work of a messenger.
*Uttarimanussadhammassa* means of that state which transcends human beings; having surpassed ordinary humans, it refers to the state of a Brahmā.
The meaning is: "of a state that leads to Nibbāna" or "of the Dhamma of those superior to humans, of the best of persons, and of the noble ones who meditate.
In such cases as "this monk named so-and-so," having first deliberated among themselves, they later speak to householders, saying:
"The monk named Buddharakkhita is an attainer of the first jhāna; Dhammarakkhita is [an attainer] of the second."

It should be understood that they spoke of the excellence [of the life] by way of its name alone. In this context, "This indeed, friends, is better" refers to the undertaking of manual labor and the carrying of messages—tasks which involve many enemies, great exertion, and are not befitting of a recluse.
Therefore, it is better, more praiseworthy, and more excellent than both of those, namely, when we householders [discuss] one another's superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*).

The praise was spoken. What is meant? When householders—whether they have asked or not—approach one who is sitting having composed his posture or walking, and say, "This monk named so-and-so is an attainer of the first *jhāna*," and so forth;
such is the praise by us of another regarding a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*).

"will have been spoken"—this alone is better. However, since it is not logical that he [the Buddha] spoke those very words at that moment if there were no connection to the future, one must understand the meaning here by establishing a connection to the future:
"That which will thus have been spoken—that alone is better. As for the grammatical characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), it should be sought from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
194. "They were beautiful" means that a fresh, unprecedented bodily complexion arose for them; by virtue of that complexion, they became beautiful (*vaṇṇavanta*).

"With full faculties" means that because the space occupied by the five sensitive organs was complete, their faculties—including the mind as the sixth—were not withered, and thus they were "full-facultied.
"With serene facial complexion" means that although they were beautiful without distinction [in general], [they were specifically so].

Furthermore, as for their bodily color, the color of their faces is more exceptionally clear; the meaning is that it is limpid, unclouded, and perfectly pure. Regarding the phrase "with a very clear complexion":

while other humans may possess a complexion similar to theirs—such as the color resembling a great *kaṇikāra* flower and the like—their skin color is not [clear] in the same way as that of these [beings].
It was serene. Therefore it was said: “with serene skin and complexion.

Thus those bhikkhus, neither applying themselves to the recitation, nor to questioning, nor to the meditation subject, but instead consuming the choice foods obtained through their display of fraudulent, untruthful qualities, devoted themselves as they pleased to the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of socializing.
They have attained this beauty of the body, like foolish deer that have strayed from their herd.
"Those of Vaggumudā" means those who dwell on the banks of the Vaggumudā River. "I hope, monks, it is endurable" means:
I hope, monks, that for you this body-machine—with its four wheels and nine gates—is endurable, capable of being endured, and tolerable.
"It does not produce any suffering that cannot be avoided. "Is it sufficient for maintenance? means:
is it possible to carry on and proceed with all necessary duties, or does it show any obstacle? "The belly is cut" means: it would be better if the belly were cut open;
the reading "parikatta" is also appropriate. Thus, in many ways, [the Buddha spoke] to those from the banks of the Vaggumudā River.

Having rebuked them, and because the deed they had committed was a criminal act, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus in order that others in the future might not commit such an act. Having addressed them, he said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these five great thieves," and so forth. In this context, "existing" means being found present.
"It exists and is found"—this is what is meant. "Here" means in this world of sentient beings. "It occurs thus" means that in this way, a desire arises in the prior stage.
Regarding the phrase "When indeed shall I...", *su* is a particle; the meaning is "when indeed.
"At a later time" means that having thought thus in the prior stage, he gradually increased his retinue and performed the work of clearing the roads.

"Plundering border villages," and so forth; having thus become a band of people who have reached great proliferation, they act—whether in villages or non-villages, in districts or non-districts—killing, causing to kill, slaying, cutting, causing to cut, cooking, and causing to cook.
Having thus shown the great external robber, [the Buddha] says "In the same way" in order to show the five great robbers within the Dispensation that are similar to him.

He said, beginning with "He," and so forth. In that context, a "bad bhikkhu" (pāpabhikkhu) is called such in other places when he has been cut off at the root by having committed a *pārājika* offense.

However, here the term "bad bhikkhu" is intended for one who, though not having committed a *pārājika*, remains established in misconduct (*icchācāra*), wandering about while trampling upon the minor and lesser training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
For him, too, as in the case of an external thief, [the result arises] in the prior stage...
Thus it occurs to him: "When indeed shall I... [and so on] ...of requisites? In this context, "honored" means having attained honor.
"Venerated" means having attained veneration. "Revered" means cherished in the mind. "Worshiped" means worshiped by the offering of the four requisites.
"Honored" means having attained the state of being honored. In this regard, for one who has honored the four requisites and prepared them well—
When they give after making [the gift] most excellent among the excellent, he is honored (*sakkata*). When they give while manifesting a sense of respect toward him, he is revered (*garukata*).
One whom they love even with the mind is esteemed (*mānita*). One toward whom they perform all these things is worshiped (*pūjita*).

One toward whom they perform the highest act of homage by way of prostrating, rising from their seat, joining the palms, and so forth, is venerated (*apacita*). And for one who desires all this worldly bait, it happens in this manner.

"Then at a later time" means: having first thought thus, he gradually gathered around himself wicked bhikkhus who were excessively conceited regarding the training, arrogant, haughty, fickle, talkative, loose of speech, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, with unrestrained faculties, abandoned by their teachers and preceptors, and devoted to gain;
[he gathered them] through hypocritical practices such as the maintenance of deportment.

Having trained them, [he entrusted them] to those bhikkhus who were endowed with eloquence, well-versed in the Jātaka and other texts, capable of ripening the world through skillful means such as praising the dwellings esteemed by the world, saying:

"This elder, having entered the rains retreat at such-and-such a monastery, completed his duties and observances, and has now emerged after spending the rains. Thus, their virtues were being extolled by those bhikkhus.
“Having sacrificed [his wealth], surrounded by a hundred or a thousand [followers]... [and so on]... [providing] medicinal requisites. This, monks, is the first great thief.
This should be understood as the “first great thief” because, unlike a thief who breaks into houses and so forth, he does not deceive just one family or two;
rather, having deceived the masses, he takes the four requisites. As for those who are experts in the Suttas...
Whether they be Abhidhamma specialists or Vinaya experts, those bhikkhus who, while not being fully proficient in the practice of alms-gathering,

travel on tour through the countryside— teaching the Pāḷi, expounding the commentaries, gladdening the world with their expressions of thanks, their Dhamma discourses, and their perfection of deportment,
and being honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected— they should be understood as "those who maintain the continuity of the lineage and illuminate the Dispensation."
“Proclaimed by the Tathāgata” means that which has been penetrated, realized through direct experience, or made known by the Tathāgata.

“He displays it for himself” means that, having reconciled the Pāḷi and the Commentary in the midst of the assembly and having delivered a pleasing Sutta with a sweet voice, the wise people—struck with wonder and amazement by way of the Dhamma talk—exclaim: “O Venerable Sir!...”
When asked, "The Pāli and the commentary are perfectly pure; from whom did you learn them? he replied, "Who is capable of teaching someone like me?
Without naming a teacher, he proclaimed the Dhamma and Vinaya realized by his own self-dependent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*).
This [Dhamma] was attained by the Tathāgata after four incalculable eons (*asaṅkheyya*) and one hundred thousand aeons.
The second great thief is one who, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), has with difficulty and toil penetrated the meaning of the Dhamma.
"Pure celibacy" refers to a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted. "Practicing the utterly pure holy life" refers to one practicing the supreme conduct free from defilements;
or alternatively, it includes anyone from a non-returner (anāgāmī) down to a virtuous worldling (puthujjana).

While he is living a pure holy life (brahmacariya) based on such grounds as freedom from remorse, someone slanders him with a groundless charge of unchastity—that is, they reproach and accuse that person with a final ground (antimavatthu) that does not exist in him.
This is the third great thief: one who conceals existing virtues and feigns noble qualities.

"Valuable goods" (*garubhaṇḍāni*) and "valuable requisites" (*garuparikkhārāni*): as in the case of the offense of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), where it is said, "Four men having made an agreement took away valuable goods," and here "valuable goods" refers to something worth five *māsaka*s; however, it is not so here.
Rather, [it refers to] these five things, O monks, which are not to be relinquished and must not be distributed by the Saṅgha or a group (*gaṇa*).
or by an individual. Even those things that have been distributed become undistributed [if they are heavy goods]. Whoever should distribute them commits a *thullaccaya* offense.

What are the five? Because of the statement: "A monastery, the site of a monastery... [and so on] ...wooden articles, earthenware articles," these are heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*) because they must not be distributed.
"Monks, there are these five things which are indivisible and must not be divided, whether by the Saṅgha or..."
Whether by a group or by an individual, even those things that have been distributed become undistributed. Whoever should redistribute them incurs a *thullaccaya* offense.
What are the five? Because of the statement, “A monastery (*ārāma*), the site of a monastery (*ārāmavatthu*)...

[and so on] ...wooden articles, earthenware articles,” they are heavy requisites due to their status as common property, since they are not subject to redistribution (*avebhaṅgiya*). Regarding what is to be said concerning the monastery, the site of a monastery, and so forth:
I shall explain all of that in the commentary on the sutta found in the Khandhaka, which states: "Bhikkhus, these five things are not to be given away.
He "wins over householders" means that by giving those things again and again, he wins them over and assists them.
He "flatters" means that he makes them affectionate, following after them with such talk as, "Oh, what a noble master we have! This...
The fourth great thief is one who, having stolen heavy requisites—which are not to be given away nor to be shared—on account of their high value, seeks to win over householders.

Furthermore, by disposing of these valuable goods for the sake of winning over families, he incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* for corrupting families and becomes subject to the formal act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*). Having thus overcome the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...
If he disposes of it out of a sense of lordship, he commits a thullaccaya offense. If he disposes of it with the intent to steal, he must be dealt with according to the value of the goods.
This is the foremost great thief; this is the chief thief among these thieves; there is no thief equal to him.
He who deceives others regarding the supramundane state (lokuttara-dhamma), which is exceedingly subtle and delicate and beyond the grasp of the five sense-faculties.
But is it possible to deceive and steal the supramundane state like gold, silver, and so forth? It is not possible; for this very reason it is said:
"He who proclaims a non-existent, unreal superhuman state (uttarimanussa-dhamma). For he [proclaims] that [state] which does not exist within himself.
He merely utters the Dhamma, saying, "This is mine," yet he is unable to move from his position or to make it manifest within himself.
Why, then, is he called a thief? Because, having uttered that [Dhamma], he takes the requisites arising from the false reputation he has gained.
For by taking them in this way, he deceives and steals those requisites through subtle means.
They have been taken. For this very reason he said: "For what reason? Because, monks, you have eaten the alms of the kingdom by theft.

This is the meaning here: as for what we said—"This is the foremost great thief, who proclaims a non-existent, unreal superhuman state"—for what reason did we say this? "Because, monks, [you have eaten] by theft."
“Monks, the alms of the country have been eaten,” [it is said] because he has eaten that alms of the country by means of theft, with a thieving mind.
For here the particle *hi* is a mere expletive used for the purpose of filling out the meter, as in such passages as “Those noble ones who [dwell] in forest thickets and woodlands.
Therefore, its meaning should not be understood as “it was eaten by you.”
Now, making that very same meaning clearer by means of verses, he said: "Being otherwise... and so forth.
Therein, "being otherwise" (*aññathā santaṃ*) means being in another manner, such as through impure bodily conduct and the like.

"Whoever should proclaim otherwise" (*aññathā yo pavedaye*) means whoever should proclaim [himself] in another manner, such as through pure bodily conduct and the like. "I am supremely pure... [and so on].
He should make it known thus: “There is the supramundane Dhamma within me. Having made it known, he then eats the food obtained through that announcement as if he were an Arahant.
"Nikacca" means having cheated, like a gambler; it refers to eating what was obtained by theft.
"Tanti" means having deceived, showing one thing to be otherwise than how it actually is. It is merely a thicket and a bush.
Having shown himself as a thicket or a grove by covering himself with branches, leaves, shoots, and so forth— just like a cheat,
a deceiver, a hunter who makes his living by capturing whatever birds come to the forest under the pretext of a thicket or a grove—
the phrase "his food was obtained by theft" refers to the state of being an arahant in one who is not actually an arahant.

Regarding one who eats food obtained by showing [something]: that which has been eaten is called "eaten by theft" because it was obtained by deceiving people—just as a fowler catches birds by deceitfully tricking them.
Those who eat in this way without understanding this underlying meaning, though they wear the saffron robe around their necks... [they] are reborn in hell.
“With yellow robes around their necks” means having their necks wrapped with yellow robes.
This implies that they possess nothing more than the mere bearing of the noble one’s banner; all else of the ascetic life is absent.

This is a designation for those of immoral conduct who were spoken of thus: “But there will be, Ānanda, in the future time, those of the lineage (gotrabhuno) with yellow robes around their necks. “Of evil nature” means of base character.
"Unrestrained" means unrestrained in body and so forth. "Evil ones" refers to base persons.

"By evil deeds" means by evil deeds such as deceiving others, which were committed without seeing the danger at the time of doing them. "They are reborn in hell" means they are reborn in a miserable destination devoid of satisfaction;
therefore, [the verse says] "an iron ball is better. Its meaning is: if this immoral person...
A person who is unrestrained, established in a course of desire, and a deceiver of the world through hypocrisy,
might eat and swallow a red-hot iron ball, glowing like a crest of flame; compared to that and the alms-food of the country which he eats,
between these two, the eating of the iron ball alone would be better, more excellent, and more refined, for there is nothing [unwholesome] in the iron ball.
Because he has consumed it, he experiences suffering in the future that is difficult even for one possessing omniscient knowledge to fully comprehend.
Thus, because he has consumed that alms-food obtained from the kingdom, he undergoes the aforementioned kind of suffering in the future;
for this is the most extreme form of wrong livelihood.

Having thus shown the danger to those who do not see the peril in evil deeds, and having rebuked the monks from Vaggumudā in many ways for their difficulty in being supported and difficulty in being nourished...
[as above] ...and having said, "You should recite this training rule," he spoke the words beginning with "Whatever monk, not knowing... while enacting the fourth *pārājika*.

Thus, having made it firm by way of cutting off the root when the fourth *pārājika* was laid down, another occasion for overweening pride (*adhimāna*) arose so that no further rule might be prescribed.
To illustrate its origin, this was said: "In this manner, this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks."
Commentary on the Basis for Overestimation (Adhimānavatthu-vaṇṇanā) 196.

Therein, "perceiving what has not been seen as seen" means that regarding Arahatship, which has indeed not been seen by the eye of knowledge, they perceive it as seen, thinking, "Arahatship has been seen by us.
The same method applies to "not attained," and so forth. However, this is the distinction: regarding "not attained"—
"Without having reached" means by way of its arising within one's own continuum. "Not attained" means not attained through the cultivation of the path;
the meaning is also "not acquired. "Not realized" means not penetrated, or not made manifest through reflective contemplation.
"By overweening conceit" means by the conceit of attainment; the meaning is by the conceit arisen thus, "We have attained," or by excessive conceit, that is, stiffened conceit.
The meaning is as follows: "They declared another" means they declared their attainment of *arahantship*; they announced to the monks, "Friends, we have attained *arahantship*;

what was to be done has been done. Because their defilements were not yet abandoned by the [supramundane] path, although their defilements were suppressed for a time by the power of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), on a later occasion, when encountering suitable conditions, their minds incline toward passion.
The meaning is that he inclines toward passion. This same method applies to the others as well.

"And yet this is not subject to formal designation" means that this explanation given by them is not subject to formal designation; it does not enter into the conventional usage for establishing an offense; the meaning is that it is not a factor for an offense.
Now, in whom does this overestimation arise, and in whom does it not arise? First of all, it does not arise in a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka).
For he has become joyful through the reviewing of the path, the fruit, Nibbāna, the defilements abandoned, and the remaining defilements;

thus, he is free from doubt regarding the penetration of noble qualities. Therefore, in those such as stream-enterers, overestimation (*adhimāna*) in the form of "I am a once-returner," and so forth, does not arise.

It does not arise in one who is immoral, for he has no hope at all for the attainment of noble qualities. Nor does it arise in one who possesses virtue but has abandoned his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
It does not arise for one who is devoted to such things as delighting in sleep. However, it arises for one who possesses perfectly pure virtue,
who is diligent in his meditation subject, who has defined name-and-form, who has crossed over doubt by discerning conditions,
who has applied the three characteristics and is comprehending formations— such a person being one who has begun insight— and for one who has already attained pure serenity.

Or he places the one who has attained pure insight (suddhavipassanālābhi) in between; for such a person, having seen no manifestation of defilements even for ten, twenty, or thirty years, conceives the notion:
"I am a stream-enterer," or "a once-returner," or "a non-returner. However, he places the one who has attained serenity and insight (samathavipassanālābhi) only at the stage of Arahantship.
This is because, through the power of his concentration, [he does not perceive any defilements].
The defilements have been suppressed; by the power of insight, conditioned phenomena have been thoroughly mastered.
Therefore, for sixty years, eighty years, or even a hundred years, the defilements do not manifest, and his mental activity is that of one whose taints are exhausted.
Not seeing the manifestation of defilements for such a long time, he does not stop midway but conceives the thought, "I am an arahant."
Commentary on the Training Rule with its Analysis (Savibhaṅgasikkhāpada) 197:
*Anabhijānaṃ* means "not knowing. Because one practices this non-knowing, it is "unreal" (*abhūta*) since it has not arisen in one's own continuum and has not been realized through knowledge.
Therefore, in the word-commentary, it is said: "that which is non-existent, unreal..."
Having said, "not being found," it is stated, "not knowing, not seeing.
*Uttarimanussadhammaṃ* means the state (*dhamma*) of those superior to humans, namely both the meditators and the noble ones (*ariya*).
*Attupanāyikaṃ* means that which leads [the claim] toward oneself, or that which leads oneself toward that [state]; thus it is *attupanāyika*, and that is what is meant by *taṃ attupanāyikaṃ*.

The connection is: "Having done so, one should behave [in this way]. However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), because various states such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth are stated—namely, "the so-called 'superhuman state' (*uttarimanussadhamma*) consists of jhāna, liberation (*vimokkha*), concentration (*samādhi*), attainment (*samāpatti*), knowledge-and-vision (*ñāṇadassana*), ...
pe ... delighting in empty dwellings"—therefore, he shows the quality of referring back to oneself (*attupanāyika-bhāva*) by means of all of those.
"He brings those wholesome states into himself"—thus he made this expression in the plural.

In that context, it should be understood that when one behaves toward oneself thinking, "These qualities are seen in me," one brings them into oneself; and when one behaves toward them thinking, "I am seen in these," one brings oneself into them.
"Knowledge and vision of the noble ones" (*ariya-ñāṇadassana*): herein, mundane and supramundane wisdom is "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of knowing;
it is "vision" (*dassana*) in the sense of seeing, because it makes the Dhamma directly manifest as if seen with the eye. Thus, it is "knowledge and vision.

It is the "noble knowledge and vision" (*ariya-ñāṇadassana*) because it is noble, purified, and supreme. It is "adequate" (*alaṃ*), "sufficient" (*pariyattaṃ*), and capable of destroying the defilements.
"Superior human state" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) refers here to the various distinctions such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).

"Possessing sufficient noble knowledge and vision" (*alamariyañāṇadassano*) means that his noble knowledge and vision is sufficient; thus, "that superior human state is one possessing sufficient noble knowledge and vision"—in this way the connection between the words is to be understood.
In this context, it is by means of that specific knowledge and vision that he is called "one possessing sufficient noble knowledge and vision. To demonstrate that very point:

“Knowledge” (*ñāṇa*) refers to the three types of clear knowledge (*tisso vijjā*); “vision” (*dassana*) means that which is knowledge is vision, and that which is vision is knowledge—thus the word-commentary is stated by way of the heading of clear knowledge.
Furthermore, all wisdom (*paññā*) here, whether sublime (*mahaggata*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*), should be understood as “knowledge.
“One would display” means that one would report this aforementioned superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) by making it refer to oneself.
The phrase "or by a woman," and so forth, is an indication of the persons to whom one must report. For when reporting is made to these [persons], it is considered reported;
it is not reported to devas, māras, or brahmās, nor to petas, yakkhas, or animals. "Thus I know, thus I see" is an indication of the manner of practice.
In its word-by-word commentary, however, it says: "I know these states; I see them..."
"‘These states’" is an indication of the occurrence of knowing and seeing regarding those states such as the jhānas; "‘And these states exist in me,’ etc.
is an indication of the state of referring [the realization] back to oneself. 198.
"Then at a later time" is a demonstration of the time of confessing the offense. However, this [confession occurs] at the very moment it is announced.
One commits a *pārājika* offense. However, because one who has committed an offense acknowledges it—whether exhorted by another or not exhorted—it is therefore said:

"Whether being examined or not being examined. In that regard, first, when being examined: "What have you attained? is a question regarding attainment; [it refers] to the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), liberations (*vimokkha*), and so forth.
Or [the question] regarding the path of stream-entry and so forth: "What have you attained? This is a question concerning the means by which one has attained, asking:

"In what manner have you attained it? For this is the intended meaning here: "Did you attain it by making the characteristic of impermanence primary, or one of the other two characteristics—suffering or non-self?
Or did you attain it by way of concentration through directed attention (*abhinivesa*), or rather by way of insight (*vipassanā*)? Likewise, what..."
"Did you become attached to form, or rather to the formless? Or did you become attached internally, or rather externally?
This is a question concerning time: "When was it attained by you? It means: "At which time—forenoon, midday, or the like?
"Where was it attained by you? This is a question concerning place: "In which location—in a place for standing at night, or a place for standing during the day?"
"At the foot of a tree, in a pavilion, or in which monastery?"—this is what is meant. "Which defilements have you abandoned?"—this is a question regarding abandoned defilements.
"Which defilements were to be destroyed by which path have been abandoned by you?"—this is what is meant.
"Of which states are you a possessor?"—this is a question regarding attained states. "Of which states among the first path and so forth..."
It is implied that you are an attainer.
Therefore, even if some bhikkhu were now to declare the attainment of a superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*), he should not be honored on that account alone.
However, for the sake of purification regarding these six points, he should be asked: "What have you attained? What..."
“Is it jhāna, or is it one of the liberations (vimokkha) and so forth? For whatever Dhamma has been realized by someone, that is clear to him.
If he says, “This is what I have realized,” then he should be asked, “How was it realized by you? [He should be asked:

“Among the characteristics such as impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), etc., or among the thirty-eight objects of meditation (ārammaṇa) classified as material, immaterial, internal, external, and so on—which did you take as the primary focus?”
"Or by what means among phenomena does one become intent? For whatever one's intent is, that is evident to oneself.
If he says, "This is my intent; it was attained by me in this way," then he should be asked, "When was it attained?
Was it in the morning, or at some other time such as midday? For all [who have attained]...
The time at which one has attained [realization] becomes clear. If he says, "I attained it at such-and-such a time," then he should be asked, "Where did you attain it?
Was it in a daytime resting place, or in one of the other locations such as a night resting place?
For the place where one has attained by oneself becomes clear to everyone. If he says, "In such-and-such a location for me..."

If he says, "I have attained it," he should then be asked, "Which defilements have been abandoned by you?"—specifically, "Are they those to be abandoned by the first path, or rather those to be abandoned by the second and subsequent paths?
For the defilements abandoned by whichever path one has personally attained become manifest to oneself.
If he says, "These specific defilements have been abandoned by me," then [he should be asked], "Of which phenomena..."
He should be asked, "Of what are you an attainer?"—"Is it of the stream-entry path, or of one of the others, such as the once-returning path?
For all the qualities attained by oneself are evident to oneself.
If he says, "I am an attainer of these specific qualities," even then his word is not to be trusted; for those who are learned are skilled in their mastery and inquiry.
Bhikkhus are able to purify these six points.
However, the path by which this bhikkhu has come must be purified. If the path by which he has come is not pure, he should be sent away with the thought:
"By means of such a path, the supramundane Dhamma cannot be attained. But if his path by which he has come...

He is purified; it is known that "for a long time he has been diligent in the three trainings, devoted to wakefulness, unattached to the four requisites, and dwells with a mind like the open sky. Thus, the declaration of that bhikkhu accords with his practice.
It is just as the water of the Ganges accords with the water of the Yamunā.
It meets [with it]; even so, the path leading to Nibbāna well-laid out by the Blessed One for his disciples converges with Nibbāna and the path. This is similar to what was said.
Furthermore, however, one should not offer honor on that account alone. Why? Because even some worldlings (puthujjana) possess it.
The practice is similar to that of one whose taints are destroyed; therefore, that bhikkhu must be made to feel alarmed by various means.
For one whose taints are indeed destroyed, there is no fear, trepidation, or horripilation even when a thunderbolt falls upon his head.
If fear, trepidation, or horripilation should arise in him, [one should say]: "You are not an Arahant."

It should be removed. However, if one sits like a lion—courageous, undaunted, and fearless—this bhikkhu is possessed of excellent exposition and is worthy of the honor sent from all sides by kings, royal ministers, and others.
As for "one of evil desires," it refers to that which was stated: "In this case, someone who is actually immoral desires: 'May people know me as virtuous,'" and so forth.

"By way of method" means he is one who possesses those evil desires as they have been described. "Overpowered by desire" means being overcome and defeated by that evil desire, having become one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
"Seeking purity" means looking toward, desiring, and longing for one's own purification. For this [person], because...
One who has committed a *pārājika* offense, remaining in the state of a monk, is incapable of attaining the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth;
for his status as a monk becomes both an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the Path. Indeed, it has been said: "The ascetic life, when wrongly grasped, drags one down to hell.
And it has also been said: "For a lax wandering life scatters even more dust [of defilement]."

Thus, for him, there is no such thing as purity in the state of being a bhikkhu. However, because one who is a householder, a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*), or a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*) is capable of attaining the path to heaven through giving, taking refuge, and the restraint of virtue, or the path to liberation through the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and liberations (*vimokkha*), therefore his status as a householder and so forth is called "purity. Therefore, that purity—
Because he looks toward purification, he is called “one who looks toward purity. For this very reason, it is said in the word-commentary (padabhājana):
“He may wish to be a householder,” and so forth. “He might speak thus” means he would say this. How? “Friend, though not knowing, I said ‘I know’; though not seeing, I said ‘I see.
However, in the word-commentary, without even citing the phrase “he might speak thus,” it is explained how one who speaks thus—“though not knowing... [and so on].
When one says, "Friend, though I did not know, I say 'I know'; though I did not see, I say 'I see,'" that is what is meant by [the phrase] "he speaks.

To show this manner of speaking, it was said: "I do not know these things," and so forth. "I prattled empty falsehoods" means: because it lacked the actual meaning of the words, I prattled what was empty;
because of the intention to deceive, it was false; that is to say, I spoke what was untrue. However, in the word-commentary (padabhājana) for this...
In order to show the mere meaning by means of other words and phrases, it was said: "I have spoken falsely," and so forth.

"With reference to the preceding" means with reference to persons who have committed the three preceding *pārājika* offenses. The remainder is clear because it follows the method already explained and its meaning is evident.
This concludes the commentary on the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*).

199. Having thus analyzed the training rule (sikkhāpada) according to the sequence of its words, now, since in the previous word-analysis (padabhājaniya) the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) was shown only in brief—as "jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision...
[and] delighting in empty dwellings"—and the textual tradition (tanti) was not established by setting forth the offense in detail, [the following is said] regarding what was shown in brief:
Furthermore, not everyone is able to grasp the method (naya) in its entirety and in all its aspects;
