therefore, in order to facilitate the grasping of the method in all its aspects, he again places that same word-commentary (padabhājana) in the position of a matrix (mātikā), and having shown the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) in detail, wishing to show the classification of offenses (āpattibheda), he says:
"Jhāna means the first jhāna, the second jhāna," and so forth. Therein:

The first jhāna and so forth include the jhānas of loving-kindness (mettā), the jhānas of the foul (asubha), the jhānas of concentration on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), mundane jhānas, and supramundane jhānas. Therefore: "They attain the first jhāna...
[and so on] ...the fourth jhāna, the jhāna of loving-kindness, the jhāna of equanimity (upekkhā), the jhāna of the foul, and the jhāna of concentration on mindfulness of breathing."
It should be understood that one who says, "I have entered upon a worldly jhāna" or "I have entered upon a supramundane jhāna," is indeed guilty of a pārājika offense.

Liberation (vimokkha) is so called because it is well-liberated, or liberated from various defilements. Furthermore, this liberation is "empty" (suññato) because of its emptiness of lust, hatred, and delusion;
it is "signless" (animitto) because of its signlessness through the signs of lust, hatred, and delusion; and it is [wishless] because of the absence of longing for lust, hatred, and delusion.
It is called "the wishless. It is *samādhi* because it places the mind evenly and establishes it upon the object. It is *samāpatti* because it is to be attained by the Noble Ones.
The rest here is exactly as previously explained. And herein, by the triad of liberations and the triad of concentrations, the Noble Path itself is described;
but by the triad of attainments, the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is meant. Among these, even a single word [of each]—
Having taken [the name], one becomes guilty of a *pārājika* offense simply by saying, "I am a possessor of this.
"The three knowledges" (*tisso vijjā*) refer to the recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavā*).
In that regard, even by taking the name of only one of them and saying, "I am a possessor of this knowledge," one becomes guilty of a *pārājika*. This is stated in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*.

However, it is stated: "Even one who says, 'I am a possessor of clear knowledge (vijjā),' or even one who says, 'I am a possessor of the three clear knowledges,' is defeated (pārājika). In this context, the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) mentioned in the word-commentary on the development of the path (maggabhāvanā)—being associated with the path and supramundane (lokuttara)—are what is intended.
Therefore, [it refers to] the supramundane foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and right efforts (sammappadhāna).

In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that for one who says, "I am an attainer of the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda), the faculties (indriya), the powers (bala), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga),

and the Noble Eightfold Path," it is a *pārājika* offense. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries, it is said that even according to each individual category— such as by saying, "I am an attainer of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)," or "I am an attainer of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body" (*kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*)— [the same offense applies].
Thus, it is stated that even for one who speaks there by way of each individual factor, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense; this too is consistent. Why?

Because it was stated with reference specifically to those factors arising at the moment of the Path (*magga*). It should be understood that regarding the realization of the fruits (*phala-sacchikiriyā*) as well, it is a *pārājika* offense by way of each individual fruit.

In the tetrad beginning with "the abandoning of lust" (*rāgassa pahāna*), only the abandoning of the defilements (*kilesappahāna*) is mentioned. However, since that [abandoning] does not exist without the Path, [it is implied].

For by the third path there is the abandoning of lust and hatred, and by the fourth, delusion; therefore, even for one who says, "Lust has been abandoned by me," and so forth, a *pārājika* offense is stated.

In the triad beginning with "the mind is unobstructed from lust," only supramundane consciousness is intended. Therefore, even for one who says, "My mind is unobstructed from lust," and so forth, it is indeed a *pārājika*.

However, in the word-commentary on the "empty hut," since a mere statement such as "I delight in the empty hut" without connecting it to jhāna is not intended to constitute a *pārājika* offense, it is therefore stated:
"One delights in the empty hut with the first jhāna," and so forth.
Consequently, it is only one who connects it with jhāna and says, "I delight in the empty hut with this specific jhāna," [who is subject to the offense].
"He becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense" is how it should be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the five types of higher knowledge (*vijjā*)—namely, insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), mind-made psychic power (*manomaya-iddhi*), the various forms of supernormal power (*iddhividha*), the divine ear (*dibbasota*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*)—which are mentioned among the eight knowledges (*aṭṭha vijjā*) in the word-commentary on this term "knowledge" in such discourses as the Ambaṭṭha Sutta:
it should be understood that among those, only one, namely insight, is not a ground for a *pārājika* offense, while the remaining ones are.
Therefore, for one who says, "I am an attainer of insight" (*vipassanā*) or "I am an attainer of the knowledge of insight" (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), there is no offense involving defeat (*pārājika*).
However, the Elder Phussadeva says: "The other four types of clear-knowledge (*vijjā*) also do not constitute grounds for defeat when they are not conjoined with [supramundane] knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

Therefore, [there is no offense] for one who says: 'I am an attainer of the mind-made body, of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*), of the divine ear-element (*dibbā-sotadhātu*), or of the penetration of others' minds (*cetopariya*')."
"Even for one who says, 'I am an attainer,' there is no *pārājika* offense. This was refuted by his own students: "The teacher is not an expert in the Abhidhamma;
he does not understand the distinction between planes of existence. What is called 'direct knowledge' (*abhiññā*) is merely a sublime state (*mahaggata-dhamma*) based on the fourth *jhāna*;
it is accomplished by means of *jhāna* alone. Therefore, [the claim] that 'I am an attainer of the mind-made body' or 'of the knowledge of the mind-made body'..."
Whether he says, "I have attained it," or says it in any other way, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
And here, although *nibbāna* is not explicitly mentioned in the Canon, nevertheless, for one who says, "I have attained *nibbāna*" or "I have realized it," it is indeed a *pārājika* offense. Why?
Because *nibbāna* is a supramundane state that has been produced. Likewise, [it is a *pārājika* offense] for one who says, "I have penetrated the Four Truths; they have been penetrated."
Even for one who says, "By me," it is indeed a *pārājika*. Why? For "penetration of truth" (*saccappaṭivedha*) is a synonym for the Path.

However, because the three analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) arise from the wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) in the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge, and they arise from the functional states (*kriya*) in the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge, while the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)...
"It arises in these very [states], and it arises in the four paths and the four fruits"—thus it is stated in the Vibhaṅga.
Therefore, even if one says, "I am an attainer of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā)," or "I am an attainer of the analytical knowledge of language...

[or] of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā)," or "I am an attainer of the mundane analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā)," there is no offense of defeat (pārājika).
When one says, "I am an attainer of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)," it does not yet strike upon the head [of the offense].
However, when one says, "I am an attainer of the supramundane analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)," it constitutes a pārājika offense.

In the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated that even for one who says without qualification, "I have attained the analytical knowledge of meaning," it is a pārājika offense. In the *Kurundi* as well, it is stated that "one is not released. In the *Mahāaṭṭhakathā*...
However, because it has been deliberated that "up to this point there is no *pārājika*, up to this point it does not descend upon the head,
up to this point it is not a *pārājika*," it is not possible to establish another measure.
Even for one who says, "I am entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)" or "I am an attainer of it," there is a *pārājika*.
There is none. Why? Because the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is neither mundane nor supramundane.
However, if he thinks, "Only a non-returner or one whose taints are destroyed enters cessation;

they will know me as one of them," and he answers accordingly, and they indeed know him as such, it is a *pārājika* offense according to the *Mahāpaccarī*, the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*, and other commentaries.
This has been stated. That should be accepted after investigation.
Even for one who says, "In a past existence, during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, I was a stream-enterer," there is no *pārājika* offense.
For because it refers to past aggregates (*khandhas*), it does not "descend" upon the head [as a formal offense]. However, in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "In the past..."
For one who says, "I am an attainer of the eight meditative attainments," there is no offense of defeat (pārājika);

however, it is stated here that because [the attainment] is subject to fluctuation (kuppadhamma), some say that it is not subject to fluctuation. That too has been rejected right there [in the Vinaya], stating:
"For one speaking with reference to a past existence, there is no offense of defeat; it is only for one speaking with reference to the present existence that there is an offense."
Commentary on the Chapter on the Pure (Suddhika-vāra): 200.
Having thus expanded upon the ten matrix-headings beginning with jhāna, [the author] now speaks of the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).
Demonstrating the factors for the deliberate falsehood one utters therein, he presents a wheel-rotation (cakkapeyyāla) according to that very expansion.
In order to show the manner of binding and the classification of offenses, he said, "in three ways," and so forth.
Therein, there are three great sections: the section on the pure [formulation], the section on those desiring to speak, and the section connected with the conditions.

Among these, in the section on the pure formulation, beginning from the first jhāna up to the phrase "the mind is free from the hindrance of delusion," for each individual phrase, one has entered, enters, [and will enter] into attainment.
Having attained [the first jhāna], "I am a gainer," "I am a master," "it has been realized by me"—
having thus applied each one of these six terms in three ways, four ways, five ways, six ways, and seven ways,
it is called the "pure method" (*suddhikanaya*). Then, [applying them] with the first jhāna, such as "the first jhāna" and "the second jhāna," and so forth...
By joining each individual term and thereby joining all the terms, it is described by that very same detailed method as the "Broken Wheel" (*khaṇḍacakkam*).
For that [previous wheel] was not again brought back and joined with the first jhāna and so forth; therefore, it is called the "Broken Wheel.
Then, [joining] the second jhāna and the third jhāna—in this way, each individual term together with the second jhāna...
Having joined them again and brought them back, connecting them with the first jhāna, it is called the "bound wheel" (*baddhacakkam*) by that same detailed method.
Then, just as with the second jhāna, so too with the third jhāna and the others,
having joined each single phrase again and brought them back, connecting them with the second jhāna and the rest by that same [method]...
Having explained in detail the other twenty-nine bound wheels (*baddhacakkāni*), the method based on a single root (*ekamūlaka-naya*) is concluded.
The text, however, has been shown in brief; it should be understood in detail by one who does not become confused.
And just as with the single-rooted method, so too for those starting from the two-rooted (*dumūlaka*) up to the end of the all-rooted (*sabbamūlaka*), there are more than four hundred [methods].
Thirty-five methods have been stated. Namely: twenty-nine based on two roots, twenty-eight based on three roots, twenty-seven based on four roots;
in this way, from those based on five roots onwards, each successive number being reduced by one, they should be understood up to those based on thirty roots.
In the text, however, having abbreviated even their names, only one method—the thirty-rooted method—is shown under the heading "This is the All-Rooted."
And because the state of an empty dwelling does not enter the head unless it is joined with jhāna, one should understand that without touching upon that [state],
the application is shown everywhere as ending with the "unobstructed state" due to delusion.
Thus, the first jhāna and so forth— whether in direct order or reverse order, and whether joined or unjoined with the second jhāna and so forth— [should be understood].
For one who speaks in such a manner as "I shall enter [the attainment]," etc., there is no liberation; he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
This is the brief commentary on the meaning of this "Pure Great Chapter" (*suddhikamahāvāra*), stated by way of demonstrating this point:
"By three ways" means by the three causes that constitute the factors of a conscious lie (*sampajaññamusāvāda*). Prior to this...
"It occurs" means that even in the preliminary stage, this person thinks: "I shall speak falsely. "It occurs while speaking" means it occurs for one who is in the act of speaking.
"It occurs when spoken" means it occurs for him once the speech is finished; the meaning is that it occurs when what was to be said has been uttered.
Alternatively, "bhaṇitassa" means it occurs for the speaker once the speech is completed. Thus, [this applies] even in the preliminary stage.
He knows; even while speaking he knows; and afterwards he also knows, "I have spoken falsely.
Thus, it is shown here that one who says, "I attained the first jhāna," incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Although this has been shown, there is nevertheless this distinction here: first, there is the preliminary stage [of the thought], "I shall speak falsely."
"Is there no 'after-stage' in the thought, 'I have spoken falsely,' such that someone might forget it as soon as it was uttered;
does he thereby incur a *pārājika* offense, or not? This was answered thus in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*):
In the prior stage, for one who thinks "I will speak falsely" and knows "I am speaking falsely," and in the subsequent stage, [the thought] "I have spoken falsely."
It is not possible for it not to be [an offense]. Even if it does not exist, it is indeed a *pārājika*. For the first two factors alone are the measure.

Even for one who has no prior intention (*ābhoga*) in the preliminary stage, thinking "I will speak falsely," but while speaking knows "I am speaking falsely," and after speaking knows "I have spoken falsely"—he is not to be dealt with according to the offense. This refers to the preliminary stage.
For it is more authoritative. In its absence, there is either what is called "speaking falsely" or "uttering a lie.
And here, both the state of knowing that [specific intention] and the convergence of knowledges must be relinquished. Regarding the phrase "the state of knowing that must be relinquished":
by whichever consciousness one knows, "I will speak falsely," by that very same [consciousness] one knows, "I am speaking falsely," and "A falsehood has been spoken by me."
And because it is said that "one knows," one might think that thus, by means of a single consciousness alone, one knows across the three moments;

this notion of knowing that [consciousness] must be abandoned. For it is not possible for that very same consciousness to know itself, just as it is not possible for a sword to cut that very same sword with which it cuts.
Rather, each preceding consciousness serves as the cause for the arising of each succeeding consciousness in such a manner.
Having served as a condition, it ceases. Therefore, this is said:
“The measure is only the preliminary stage; when that exists, the [other] two will not be.
Since the remainder does not exist, the word ‘measure’ (miti) consists of three factors.”

One should not take it to mean that these three types of consciousness arise simultaneously in a single moment with the thought, “The convergence of knowledges must be relinquished. For this is what consciousness is:
While the first has not yet ceased, the subsequent does not arise;
Because they arise without interval, they appear as if they were one.
But hereafter, regarding this person who speaks a conscious lie, saying, "I attained the first jhāna," since he holds the view, "I have no first jhāna"—for he indeed possesses this conviction;
likewise, it is both acceptable and pleasing to him that "I have no first jhāna. And such is his very nature.

The mind thinks, "I do not possess the first jhāna. However, when one wishes to speak falsely, then—having set aside, deposited, concealed, and rendered unreal that view, or the approval associated with that view, or the liking associated with both view and approval, or the disposition associated with view, approval, and liking—one speaks; therefore, for those [factors] as well...
In order to show the classification of the factors (*aṅga*) by way of their basis, the passage beginning with “in four ways” was stated.

Furthermore, because it is said in the *Parivāra* that “there is lying consisting of eight factors,” another method should be applied here—namely, that there are “eight ways”—together with the specific perception intended therein.
And in this context, the phrase “setting aside one’s view” is stated by way of setting aside a strong factor; [the same applies to] “setting aside one’s preference” and so forth.
Then, by way of misrepresenting what is very weak. Here, "misrepresenting the perception" refers to the misrepresentation of every very weak factor.
It is impossible that one would speak a conscious lie without even misrepresenting a mere perception.
However, since there is no offense of defeat (pārājika) through future tense expressions such as "I shall enter [meditation]," therefore [the text uses] "entered," and so forth.
It should be understood that only the past and present bases are stated in the text. 207.
From here onwards, everything in this "Pure Great Chapter" (Suddhika-mahāvāra) is of plain meaning.
For there is nothing herein that cannot be understood by means of this exposition, with the exception of the term for the abandoning of the defilements (kilesappahāna).
In the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*), the meaning of the phrases beginning with “lust has been abandoned by me, cast out by me” is as follows:
here, “abandoned” (*catta*) is said in the sense of relinquishing its own being; “cast out” (*vanta*) is said in the sense of showing that it will not be taken up again;

“freed” (*mutta*) is said in the sense of liberation from the continuity [of existence]; and “given up” (*pahīna*) is said in the sense of showing that even what has been freed does not remain anywhere.
"Relinquished" (*paṭinissaṭṭha*) is said by way of showing the relinquishing of that which was previously taken up.

"Shaken off" (*ukkeṭita*) is said by way of showing the state of not clinging again, because of having been terrified by the Noble Path. This meaning should be sought from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
"Completely shaken off" (*samukkeṭita*) is stated by way of showing the state of not clinging again even to what is associated with subtle [defilements], after having thoroughly terrified [the mind].
The Discourse on the Chapter on the Pure Ones is finished.

Regarding the Discourse on the Chapter on Those Desirous of Speaking (Vattukāmavāra): here, the meaning of the phrases beginning with “in three ways,” as well as the entire classification of the chapter’s repetitive formulae (vārapeyyāla), are [to be understood].

It should be understood in the same manner already stated. For this [statement] was spoken solely for the purpose of closing the door to those wicked persons who seek an opportunity, thinking, "Since I intended to say one thing but, having slipped up, said another, there is no offense for me.
Indeed, just as one intending to say, "I renounce the Buddha," might instead say, "I renounce the Dhamma," and so forth...

In the cases of renouncing the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*), even if one says this or that, because one has entered the field [of the offense], one becomes one who has indeed renounced the training.

Likewise, regarding the cases of superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) such as the first jhāna and so forth, even if one wishes to say one thing but says something else entirely, because one has entered the field, one is indeed guilty of a defeat (*pārājika*). If [one speaks] to someone...
He knows that matter at that very moment. Herein, the characteristic of knowing should be understood in the same manner as stated regarding the renunciation of the training.
However, this is the distinction: the renunciation of the training does not apply even by means of a hand gesture;

whereas this false report does apply even by means of a hand gesture. For whoever, by means of gestures of the hands or by movements of the limbs and members, [claims] a non-existent superhuman state—
If one informs a person standing within range of hearing, and that person understands the matter, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
However, if the one to whom it is informed does not understand, thinking, "What is this person saying?"; or if they fall into doubt;
or if, after investigating for a long time, they later come to know; then the informant is reckoned as one who has not made themselves understood. Thus...
If one speaks to someone who does not understand, a *thullaccaya* offense occurs. However,
if someone does not know the jhānas and so forth through their own attainment, nor by way of study or inquiry, but has merely heard the mere words "jhāna" or "liberation," and even he,
upon being told that, thinks, "He says, 'I have entered jhāna,'" if [he understands] even this much—
He knows; he indeed comes to be reckoned as one who knows. When this has been said by him, it is indeed a *pārājika*.

The rest—the distinction regarding whether [the offense applies] to one, two, or many, and whether [the person] is specified or unspecified—all should be understood according to the method already stated in the discussion on the renunciation of the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*).
The section on those desiring to speak is concluded.
220. Discussion on the Section Connected with Conditions (Paccayapaṭisaṃyuttavārakathā).

In the section connected with conditions as well—having understood the entire classification of the sections and the meaning of the words already introduced according to the method previously stated—the sequence of the text (*pāḷikkama*) should first be known in this way. For here, "he who dwelt in your monastery... [and so forth].
“He who used your robe, he who used your almsfood, he who used your lodging, he who used your medicinal requisites for the sick”—these are five sets of expressions in the nominative case;
“he by whom your dwelling was used,” and so forth, are five sets of expressions in the instrumental case;
“having come to whom you gave the dwelling,” and so forth... [are five sets of expressions in the ablative case].

Five modes of application for the word have been stated; by means of these, one should understand the classification of the modes of application for all the terms previously mentioned—beginning with the first jhāna—in conjunction with the term "empty hut" used here.
However, because it has been stated in various ways as "the dwelling which is yours," "that by which you dwell," and "that resorting to which you dwell," [it is not simply] "I."

Furthermore, for one who understands [the meaning] even when it has not been stated, there is a *thullaccaya* offense here; for one who does not understand, even when it has been stated, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense—this is the analysis (*vinicchaya*) in this matter.
Discussion on the Classification of Non-offenses (*anāpatti*).
Having thus shown the classification of offenses in detail, he now says, "There is no offense when [it is done] out of overweening pride," and so forth, in order to show the non-offenses.
In this context, "out of overweening pride" means there is no offense for one who acts while possessed of the conceit of having attained what has not been attained.

"One whose intention is not to misrepresent" means that, without remaining in hypocrisy or a life of sensual indulgence, one who intends not to misrepresent explains something else in the presence of fellow celibates.

There is no offense. Those such as the insane and so forth are exactly as described in the previous method. However, in this case, there are the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā who were beginners;
for them, there is no offense.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis is finished.
Regarding the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors: this training rule has three origins. For one who makes it known by means of hand gestures, it originates from body and mind;
for one who makes it known through verbal expression, it originates from speech and mind; for one who performs both, it originates from body, speech, and mind.

It is an action (*kiriya*), liberated from perception (*saññāvimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), vocal action (*vacīkamma*), and an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*).
For even when laughing, one experiences three kinds of feeling; likewise, whether speaking with joy, or with fear, or with equanimity. 223.
Commentary on the Cases of Discipline (*Vinītavatthu*):
Regarding the case concerning overweening pride (*adhimāna*), the method is exactly as stated in the subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*).
In the second case—*paṇidhāya* means having made an aspiration. Thinking, "Thus people will esteem me," he thinks:
"While I am dwelling thus in the forest, people will esteem me as one who has attained either Arahantship or the stage of a trainee (*sekkha*);
consequently, I shall be honored, revered, respected, and worshipped by the world. There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for making such an aspiration while [dwelling] in the forest.

For one who goes [to the forest] thinking, "I will live there," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) at every step along the way. Likewise, for all activities in the forest—such as building a hut, walking meditation, sitting, or putting on robes and outer garments—there is an offense of wrong-doing for every instance of such action.
Therefore, one should not live in the forest in this manner;
for by living thus, whether or not one gains respect, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing. However, for one who has undertaken the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) [thinking], "The ascetic practice..."
Or thinking, “I shall protect [my mind]”; or thinking, “While living near a village my mind is distracted; the forest is suitable for me”;
or thinking, “Surely in the forest I will attain one of the three kinds of seclusion”;
or thinking, “Having entered the forest, I will not come out until I have attained Arahantship”; or thinking, “Forest-dwelling is praised by the Blessed One.”

Or, thinking, "While I am living in the forest, many of my fellow celibates will leave the vicinity of villages and become forest-dwellers as well," he desires to live in such a blameless dwelling; by that [desire], he should dwell there.

In the third case as well—thinking, "Having composed myself with regard to the 'excellent' and so forth, I shall go for alms"—[this refers to] the duty of wearing the lower garment and the upper robe.
From the beginning until the conclusion of the meal, for every single action, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Whether or not one gains esteem, it is simply *dukkaṭa*. However, when entering for alms with graceful movements such as approaching and departing, either for the sake of fulfilling the duties of the Khandhaka and the training rules (*sekhiya-vatta*) or for the sake of following the example of one's fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*), [there is no offense].
"It is blameless in the eyes of the wise.

Regarding the fourth and fifth bases: in the case of "he who dwells in your monastery," because the word "I" is not mentioned there, as explained by the method already stated, there is no *pārājika* offense. For a *pārājika* is said to apply only to one who behaves in a way that refers back to oneself.
As for "he walks with longing," and so forth, these follow the same method explained below.

Regarding the basis of fetters (*saṃyojanavatthu*): whether one says, "the fetters have been abandoned," or "ten fetters have been abandoned," or "one fetter has been abandoned," it is the very abandoning of the defilements that is being announced; therefore, it is a *pārājika*. 224. Regarding the bases of secrecy (*raho-vatthu*):
"speaking in secret" means saying, "Having gone into seclusion, I am an Arahant," rather than merely acting upon what was thought in the mind. Therefore, a *dukkaṭa* offense is stated here.
The bases of the monastery (*vihāra-vatthu*) and the bases of attendance (*upaṭṭhāna-vatthu*) are exactly as previously described.
225. Regarding the point that it is not difficult: this is the conviction of that bhikkhu—“Only noble persons are disciples of the Blessed One.
Therefore he said, “Those who are disciples of the Blessed One would speak thus. And because his intention is this:
“For one who is virtuous and has initiated insight, it is not difficult to declare final knowledge; he is capable [of doing so].”
"...so that he might attain arahantship. Therefore, he said, "I am one whose intention is not to boast.
Regarding the basis of energy, "one who is to be propitiated" means one who can be propitiated, accomplished, or brought about. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Regarding the basis of death, that bhikkhu thought: "He for whom remorse arises would be afraid; but as for me..."
"Since my precepts are pure and constitute a basis for freedom from remorse, why should I fear death?
It was with reference to this meaning that he said, "Friends, I do not fear death. Therefore, there is no offense for him.
The same principle applies even in the case of a basis for remorse. The three subsequent bases are identical to the basis for energy.

Regarding the first basis for feeling (*vedanāvatthu*), that bhikkhu, by the power of reflection, stood firm in patient endurance and said, "Friends, it is not possible to endure [the insult] in this way or that. Therefore, there is no offense for him.

In the second case, however, because he did not apply it to himself but spoke by way of a general statement, saying, "Friends, it is not possible for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*)," there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
Regarding the third basis for feeling, it is said that the brahmin did not merely say, "Come, sirs, you who are arahants."
Whatever words issued from his mouth, they were all connected with talk concerning the Arahants, such as: "Prepare seats for the Arahants;
give them water for their feet; let the Arahants wash their feet.
This was his inspired discourse, spoken because he was of a faithful temperament and was emboldened by the power of his own faith. Therefore, the Blessed One—
“There is no offense, monks, in the case of a declaration of confidence,” he said. However, when this is being said, the monk should not enjoy the requisites merely out of joy and satisfaction;
rather, he should apply himself with the thought: “I shall fulfill the practice that leads to the attainment of Arahatship.
These cases are similar to those in the *Aññabyākaraṇa-vatthu* and the *Nisaṃyojana-vatthu*. In the *Agārava-vatthu*, that monk [was in] the state of a householder...

Because he was without need and without regard [for sensual pleasures], he said, "Indeed, friend, one such as I am is incapable," not with the intention of boasting. Therefore, there is no offense for him. 227.

Regarding the case of the monk who said his desires were closed off: that monk was without regard for both objective sensual desires (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-based sensual desires (*kilesakāma*) due to a purely mundane vision of their danger.
Therefore, he said, "Friend, my desires are closed off. Consequently, there is no offense for him. And here, "closed off" means...
“Restrained” means prevented or prohibited; it means refused.

Regarding the matter of his delight, that bhikkhu said, “I am delighted, friends, with the highest delight,” because of his lack of weariness toward the Teaching and his delight in recitation, interrogation, and so forth—not with the intention of boasting. Therefore, there is no offense for him.

Regarding the case of departing: if, having made an agreement by delimiting a certain place—whether it be a residence (*āvāsa*), a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), a boundary (*sīmā*), or any other location—with the thought, "Whoever departs first from this residence," [and] if one departs first from that place with the intention, "Let them know me as an *arahant*," he becomes one who has committed a defeat (*pārājika*).
However, if it is due to a duty toward one's teacher (*ācariya*) or preceptor (*upajjhāya*)...

If he passes beyond that place for some business of his parents, or for the purpose of going on almsround, or for the sake of recitation or questioning, or for some other similar business, there is no offense.
Even if, after having gone there, a desire arises in him later, thinking, "I will not go there now; it does not suit me."
If they think, “They will honor us,” there is likewise no offense.
Furthermore, if one has arrived at that place for some business and is distracted by recitation, mental attention, and so forth;
or if one is pursued by thieves and the like; or if, seeing a cloud rising, one wishes to enter a shelter from the rain—there is no offense.
If he passes beyond that point, there is no offense. Even one traveling by vehicle or by psychic power (iddhi) does not incur a defeat (pārājika);
it is incurred only by traveling on foot. Furthermore, if he travels neither before nor after those with whom he has made an agreement, he does not incur the offense;
for all who travel in this manner protect one another. Even if [they meet] in a pavilion, at the foot of a tree, or elsewhere...
If, having demarcated a certain area, they make an agreement in such a manner as, "Whoever sits or walks here,
we shall know him to be an Arahant," or by placing flowers, "Whoever takes these and performs an offering,
we shall know him to be an Arahant," then for one who acts accordingly through the influence of desire, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense— even if...

If a lay follower has built a monastery along the way, or has placed robes and other requisites there, thinking, "May those who are Arahants dwell in this monastery and take these robes and so forth," even in that case, for one who dwells there or takes the robes and so forth out of a desire for personal gain, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
This, however, is an unrighteous practice established by private agreement; therefore—

One should not do so, nor anything else of this kind, such as: "Within these three months, let everyone become forest-dwellers, or let them all observe the remaining ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas) such as the alms-food-eater's practice, or else let everyone become those whose taints are destroyed. For monks from various regions assemble there;
among them, some are weak and lacking in strength, and are unable to maintain such a regimen. Therefore, even this kind [of resolution]...

No formal duties (vatta) should be performed. However, one must certainly not carry out such things as: "During these three months, no one at all shall give exhortation, no one shall ask questions, no one shall grant the going-forth;
the vow of silence must be observed, and the Saṅgha’s alms-food must be given even to one standing outside the boundary. And so forth.
228. Regarding the Venerable Lakkhaṇa mentioned in the *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta*, he is the Elder Lakkhaṇa;

he should be understood as one of the great disciples who was ordained by the "Come, monk" (*ehi-bhikkhu*) formula in the midst of a thousand matted-hair ascetics, and who attained Arahantship at the conclusion of the discourse on the Burning (*Āditta-pariyāya*).
For he was endowed with the marks of perfection, complete in every aspect, and equal to a Brahmā.
Because he was endowed with such a personal form, he came to be designated as a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*).
As for the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, he attained *arahantship* on the seventh day after his day of going forth; he was the second chief disciple.
"He manifested a smile" means he displayed a gentle smile; it is said that he made it manifest and showed it. But why?

Having seen [this], why did the Elder manifest a smile? It was because he saw, with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*)—and not with the physical eye (*pasāda-cakkhu*)—a certain being born in the world of hungry ghosts (*petaloka*) as a skeleton.
For such bodily forms do not come within the range of the physical eye. Having seen such a state of existence, compassion should be exercised.
"Why did he break into a smile? [The answer is: Because he recollected his own attainment and the attainment of the Buddha's knowledge.
Upon seeing him, the Elder recollected his own attainment, thinking: "I have been liberated from such states of existence as must be experienced by a person who has not yet seen the Truths;
what a gain for me! What a great blessing for me! And then, [recollecting] the Buddha's [attainment]: "Oh, the Buddha..."
Recalling the perfection of the Buddha’s knowledge—wherein he taught, “Bhikkhus, the ripening of kamma is inconceivable;

it is not to be pondered”—and considering that Buddhas teach having made [the truth] manifest before their very eyes, for the Dhamma-element of the Buddhas is well-penetrated, he displayed a smile. For those whose taints are destroyed do not act without cause.
They broke into a smile; therefore, the Elder Lakkhaṇa asked: "Friend Moggallāna, what is the cause, what is the reason for this breaking into a smile?
However, since those who have not personally witnessed such a rebirth find it difficult to believe, the elder, wishing to provide an explanation with the Blessed One as his witness, said:
“Friend, it is not the right time,” he said, and so forth. Then, questioned in the presence of the Blessed One, he answered in the manner beginning with, “In this case, friend.
In that context, “a skeleton” refers to a collection of bones, white, devoid of flesh and blood.
As for “vultures, crows, and hawks,” these should be understood as *yakkha*-vultures, *yakkha*-crows, and *yakkha*-hawks, rather than ordinary ones.
However, this form does not even come within the range of sight of vultures and other such creatures. "Anupatitvā anupatitvā" means having pursued it again and again.
"Vituḍentī" means they go piercing through it; or the reading is "vitudentī," which means they pierce it with iron beaks that are sharp like the edge of a sword.
"Sā sudaṃ aṭṭassaraṃ karoti" (she indeed makes a cry of distress)—here, "sudaṃ" is used as an emphatic particle.
"nipāto" means that this skeleton-frame utters a cry of pain, a cry of distress.

It is said that for the sake of experiencing the result of unwholesome kamma (*akusala-vipāka*), such personal bodies (*attabhāva*) as large as a league (*yojana*) are produced, and they are so sensitive that they resemble ripe boils;
therefore, that skeleton-frame, afflicted by powerful sensations, made such a sound. Having spoken thus:

Again, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, out of compassion for beings—thinking, "Beings subject to the cycle of existence do not escape such forms of individuality"—and wishing to demonstrate the spiritual urgency that had arisen in him, said, "Then, friend, this occurred to me:
'How wonderful indeed! and so forth.

"The monks were indignant" means that those who had not personally witnessed that rebirth in the peta realm were indignant. However, the Blessed One, in order to manifest the power of the elder, said:
"Monks, indeed disciples dwell as if they have become vision," and so forth.

In this context, "those for whom vision has become [their own], has arisen, has appeared" means they are "vision-become"; they are those who have become possessed of vision, those who have attained vision.
The meaning is: "having produced the eye, they abide. The same method applies to the second phrase as well.
Regarding the expression *yatra hi nāma*: here, *yatra* is a word signifying a cause. The construction of the meaning there is as follows:
since even a disciple might know such a thing, or see it, or bear witness to it, therefore we said: "O monks, truly they have become the eye!"
“Monks, the disciples dwell as those who have become knowledge; indeed, monks, the disciples dwell as those who have become knowledge.

Monks, that being was seen by me even before this, when at the seat of enlightenment, through the penetration of the knowledge of omniscience, I directly perceived the immeasurable world-systems and the immeasurable classes of beings within their various states of existence, destinies, wombs, stations, and abodes.
"I saw that being even before," he says.
"A cow-slayer" is a being who makes his living by repeatedly slaughtering cows, cutting off their flesh, and selling it.
"By the remainder of the ripening of that very karma" refers to the karma of successive rebirths (*aparāpariya-kamma*) accumulated through various volitions (*cetana*).
For in that case, when the ripening (*vipāka*) of that volition (*cetanā*) by which rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in hell was produced has been exhausted,
rebirth-linking arises again among the hungry ghosts (*peta*) and so forth, taking either remaining karma or the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*) as its object;
therefore, that rebirth-linking— whether by way of similarity of karma or similarity of object— is called "the remainder of the ripening of that very same karma."
It is said: "And this being was reborn in such a way. Therefore he said, "By the remaining result of that very same kamma.
It is said that at the time of his death from hell, a heap of bones of fleshless oxen became the sign for him.
Making even that concealed kamma as manifest as if it were evident to the wise, he was born as a skeleton-ghost (*aṭṭhisaṅkhalika-peta*).
229. In the story of the Meat-Cake: A cow-slaughterer made meat-cakes from beef, dried them, and sustained his livelihood for many years by selling dried beef.
Consequently, at the time of his death and falling from hell, a meat-cake alone appeared as his sign.
He was reborn as a meat-cake *peta*.
In the story of the lump of flesh, that fowler made his living by catching birds and selling them at the time of sale,
having stripped them of their wings and skin until they were mere lumps of flesh. Consequently, at the time of his death and descent into hell, a lump of flesh became his sign,
and he was reborn as a *piśāca* (flesh-lump spirit).

In the case of the "Skinless" (Nicchavi) hell, that sheep-slaughterer—who made his living by constantly slaughtering sheep and flaying them—had, according to the same method as before, a flayed sheep carcass as his objective sign (*nimitta*). He was thus reborn as a skinless peta.
In the case of the "Hairy-Blade" (Asiloma) hell, that pork-butcher made his living for a long time by repeatedly slaughtering with a sword pigs that had been fattened on fodder.
Therefore, his very state of having a raised sword became his objective sign; consequently, he was reborn as a hairy-blade peta.

In the story of the dart-hair ghost, that hunter took a deer and a dart, went into the forest, and whenever a deer approached the one he was after, he pierced and killed it with the dart; the very act of piercing with the dart became his defining characteristic.
Therefore, he was reborn as a dart-hair ghost (*sattilomapeta*).

In the case of the *Usuloma-vatthu*, the "executioner" (*kāraṇika*) refers to the man who, after having tormented a criminal against the king with many tortures, finally kills him by piercing him with an arrow.
It is said that he pierces him only after knowing, "He will die when pierced in such-and-such a place.
Having thus made his living, when that person is reborn in hell and subsequently escapes from there, he is reborn here [in this world] with the remainder [of his karma], and [is struck] by an arrow.
The very act of piercing was the cause for his becoming a *nimitta*. Therefore, he was reborn as a needle-haired ghost (*sūciloma-peta*).

In the *Sūciloma-vatthu*, the term "charioteer" refers to a trainer of horses; it is also stated in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* that he was called Godamaka. For him, the very act of piercing with the needle-pointed goad was the cause. Therefore, he was reborn as a needle-haired ghost.
In the second *Sūciloma-vatthu*, the term "slanderer" refers to one who practices backbiting; it is said that he indeed caused dissension among people.
In the royal court, he repeatedly incited discord by whispering, "He has this [fault], and he did this [deed," thereby bringing about ruin and calamity for them.
Therefore, having made his own past karma the cause, he was born as a Needle-Hair Ghost (sūciloma-peta) in order to experience the suffering of being torn apart by needles,
just as he had caused men to be divided by his whispering.
In the account of the one who carried eggs, the term "village headman" (*gāmakūṭa*) refers to a judicial official.
Because of his similarity in action to that [animal], his eggs were the size of jars, the measure of large water-pots.

For, since he would take bribes in secret, hidden places, and by means of fraudulent judgments cause manifest harm—rendering owners ownerless—therefore his secret organ was produced as something manifest.
Because, when he laid down the rod of punishment, he imposed an unbearable burden upon others, therefore his private parts became an unbearable burden and were thus produced.
Because, standing in a place where one ought to be impartial, he stood there and became partial,
therefore his private parts had an uneven sitting posture.
In the case of the adulterer, that being— having touched the protected, guarded, and owned body of another,

and having delighted his mind with the filth of pleasure and sensual pleasure— was reborn there to experience suffering by touching the touch of excrement due to the similarity of his karma. The story of the wicked brahmin is well known.
230. Because a woman is not her own mistress regarding her own touch—
having stolen that touch belonging to her husband and thereby produced delight in others—
she has been reborn as a skinless woman, having exhausted pleasant contact through the similarity of her karma and now experiencing painful contact.
In the story of the woman Maṅguli, "ugly" (*maṅguli*) means deformed, unsightly, and loathsome. It is said that she,
while performing the work of a fortune-teller and the service of a servant to the *yakkhas*,

would deceive the great multitude by taking their perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, saying, "If this and that sacrificial offering (*balikamma*) is made, such and such prosperity will come to you," thereby leading the people into wrong views.

She caused her to adopt wrong view; therefore, due to that similarity of kamma—because she had stolen perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and because she had adopted foul odors and ugliness—she was reborn as one who is ill-smelling, unsightly, hideous, deformed, and loathsome.
In the story of Okilinī, she is called "Okilinī" (the one smeared) or "Okirinī" (the one scattered) because she was lying on a bed of burning coals, writhing in agony.
As it turns over, it is cooked; therefore, its body is both scorched and roasted by a fierce fire.
It is drenched, its body soaked, and drops of liquid stream down from its body.
It is strewn about, surrounded on all sides by embers—for beneath it there are embers the color of *kiṃsuka* flowers, as are those on both its sides, and even from above it in the air.
Embers fell; therefore it is said: "boiling, bespattering, and sprinkling. Out of jealousy, she bespattered her co-wife with a basin of embers.

It is said that a certain dancer of King Kaliṅga, having placed a basin of embers nearby, would wipe the moisture from her limbs and rub away the sweat with her hand. The king, too, would converse with her...

She did so and displayed an air of great satisfaction. The chief queen, unable to endure this and overcome by jealousy, took that brazier of embers while the king had not long departed and scattered the embers over her.
Having performed that deed, she was reborn in the world of hungry ghosts (*petaloka*) to experience a corresponding result.

In the case of the thief Coraghātaka, by the king’s command he had the heads of thieves cut off for a long time; consequently, when being reborn in the world of ghosts (petaloka), he was reborn as a headless trunk (kabandha).

In the case of the monk, "evil monk" means a base monk. It is said that after consuming the four requisites given to the world out of faith, he wandered about unrestrained in the doors of body and speech, with a broken livelihood, playing with his own mind.

Then, after being boiled in hell for one interval between Buddhas (*buddhantara*), as he was being reborn in the world of hungry ghosts (*petaloka*), he was reborn with a physical form exactly like that of a monk.
This same analysis applies to the cases of the nun, the female trainee (*sikkhamānā*), the novice monk (*sāmaṇera*), and the novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*).
231. In the case of the Tapodā (Hot Springs) story: *acchodaka* means clear water; *sītodaka* means cool water; *sātodaka* means... [tasteful water].
It has sweet water; it is pure at its extremities, free from moss, aquatic plants, and mud.
It is well-situated, being endowed with beautiful landing places. It is delightful, meaning it generates joy. "The size of a wheel" means the measure of a chariot wheel.
"Boils and flows" means that having become heated there, it flows. "From where this, monks" means *yato ayaṃ bhikkhave*.
Therefore, it is called "Soṇa" (the Hot Water). From where, then, does this stream flow?

It is said that beneath Mount Vebhāra there is a nāga abode belonging to the Bhummaṭṭhaka nāgas, five hundred yojanas in extent, resembling the world of the gods, with a floor made of jewels and provided with parks and gardens.
There, in a place for the nāgas' recreation, is that pool of water; from there this Tapodā flows forth.
"It comes from between two great hells" means that, it is said, the world of the great *peta*s is drawn toward the city of Rājagaha;
there, this Tapodā flows between two great hells of molten iron, and for that reason it flows boiling hot.
"In the matter of battle, Nandī goes about" means he parades with the victory drum. "The King, friends, [was defeated] by the Licchavis," [said] the Elder.
It is said that while sitting in his own daytime and nighttime resting places, reflecting with his divine eye, "The Licchavis have gained the upper hand and established their position;
the king is engaging in combat with them," he saw the king defeated and fleeing.
Then, addressing the bhikkhus, he said, "Friends, the king is your supporter, yet by the Licchavis—"
He said, “It is broken. “Moggallāna spoke the truth, monks,” [the Buddha said], for having reflected at the time of his defeat, he spoke what he had seen;
thus he spoke the truth. 232.
In the account of the elephant’s plunge, “Sappinikā” refers to one who has that name. “The imperturbable concentration” means the unmoving, unshakable concentration.
The fourth jhāna concentration, which is devoid of the agitation of body and speech. "Of the nāgas" means of elephants.
"Plunging in and coming out again" means having plunged in—that is, having entered—and then coming out again.
It is said that they descend into deep water, bathe there, drink, take up water with their trunks, and come out while splashing one another; of those who thus plunge in...
"Those who were crossing over" is what is meant. "Crying out like cranes" means standing on the riverbank, putting their trunks into their mouths, and making the cry of cranes.
"I heard the sound" means I heard that sound of the crane-cry.
"There is this concentration, bhikkhus, but it is not purified" means that Moggallāna possesses this concentration, and yet it is not completely purified.
It was not so. It is said that on the seventh day after his going forth, the Elder attained Arahantship on that very day;

yet, having not yet fully mastered the eight attainments in five ways, and without having thoroughly purified the states that obstruct concentration, he performed merely the mere act of perception regarding the advertence, entering, resolving, emerging, and reviewing of the fourth jhāna.
Having entered [the attainment] and sat down, he emerged from the factors of jhāna and, hearing the sound of the elephants, perceived that he had heard it while within the meditative absorption.
Therefore it was said: "There is this concentration, monks, but it is not completely purified.
In the story of Sobhita, when he said, "Friends, I recollect five hundred aeons," he meant that he recollected them with a single act of adverting the mind (*ekāvajjana*).

He said: "Otherwise, it would not have been surprising for noble disciples to recollect their various past dwellings in succession by means of different acts of attention (*āvajjana*), and thus the monks would not have complained.
But because he said, 'I recollect by a single act of attention,' the monks complained. This [power], monks, belongs to Sobhita, and it is..."
"Only one birth"—this refers to what Sobhita said when he declared, "I recollect my birth.
There was indeed this birth for Sobhita, and it was recollected as being only one immediately preceding [the present], not out of sequence; such is the intended meaning.
But how did he recollect this? It is said that he [was born] in a heretical sect more than five hundred aeons ago.
Having gone forth and attained the attainment of non-perception (*asaññasamāpatti*), he passed away without falling away from that jhāna and was reborn in the realm of non-perception (*asaññabhava*).

Having remained there for the full span of his lifespan, he was eventually reborn in the human world. There, having gone forth in the Dispensation, he realized the threefold knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*).
Recalling his former births, he perceived his rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in this present existence, and from there...
However, he saw only his own death in the third existence.
Then, unable to recollect the mindless existence between those two, he discerned it through inference: "Surely I was reborn in the non-percipient realm.
By making such an observation, he performed a difficult feat; he pierced the tip of one hair, split a hundredfold, with the tip of another.
A footprint was shown in the sky. Therefore, regarding this very matter, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position:
"Bhikkhus, among my disciples, monks who recollect their past lives, the foremost is Sobhita.
The commentary on the account of his training is finished.
Commentary on the Conclusion (Nigamanavaṇṇanā) 233.
“Venerable friends, the four rules involving defeat have been recited”—this merely indicates the rules of defeat that have been recited here.
However, when taken together, all twenty-four rules of defeat are to be understood. Which are the twenty-four?
First, there are eight [types of persons] mentioned in the Pāḷi: four for bhikkhus and four non-common [obstacles] for bhikkhunīs.
There are eleven types of persons incapable [of attaining the path]; among them, the paṇḍaka, the animal, and the hermaphrodite—these three are "defective in basis" (vatthuvipanna).
Those with rootless rebirth-linking (ahetuka-paṭisandhika) have heaven barred to them, but the path is not barred; for they are incapable of attaining the path.
"Because they have failed in the basis. Even their going forth has been rejected; therefore, they too are defeated (pārājika).

These eight—the one who lives in communion through theft, the one who has gone over to another sect, the matricide, the patricide, the murderer of an arahant, the defiler of a bhikkhunī, the shedder of blood [of a Buddha], and the schismatic—are defeated precisely because they have reached a state of incapacity due to the failure of their own actions.

Among them, for these three—the one who lives in communion through theft, the one who has gone over to another sect, and the defiler of bhikkhunīs—heaven is not barred, but the path [to hell] is indeed barred.
For the other five, both are barred; for they are beings destined to be reborn in hell in their very next existence.
Thus, these eleven and the previous eight make nineteen. These [nineteen] are in the guise of householders.
Having aroused desire, there are twenty cases involving a nun who, though dressed in lay clothing, has not committed an act of transgression beyond the bounds of conduct;
yet for this much alone she is no longer a *samaṇī*. These, then, are the twenty *pārājika* offenses.

There are also others: one who is "hanging" (*lambī*), one who is "flat-backed" (*mudupiṭṭhikā*), one who takes another's sexual organ into her mouth, and one who [takes it] into another's sexual organ...
Regarding the phrase "he sits down," they say that there are four *anuloma-pārājikas* (reverse pārājikas) by way of these four [cases].
For since the act (*dhamma*) of two who have attained a state of similarity through passion is called "the act of sexual intercourse" (*methunadhamma*),
therefore, by this method, even without actually engaging in sexual intercourse, it occurs merely by way of the entrance of one organ into another.
They are called "conformable offenses entailing defeat" (*anuloma-pārājika*) because they lead to the commission of the offense of sexual intercourse, which is itself an offense entailing defeat.
Thus, by combining these four with the previous twenty, all twenty-four offenses entailing defeat (*pārājika*) should be understood.
One does not obtain communion with the monks—namely, the various formal acts of the Saṅgha such as the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the recitation of the Pātimokkha, and other sangha-procedures.

He does not obtain communal living with the bhikkhus. "As before, so after" means that just as previously—during his time as a householder and during his time prior to full ordination—so too, even after having committed a *pārājika* offense, there is likewise no communal living;

for him, there is no communal living with the bhikkhus consisting of the various *saṅghakamma*s such as the *uposatha*, the *pavāraṇā*, the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*, and other formal acts of the Saṅgha.
One does not obtain co-residence with them. Regarding this, I ask the Venerable Ones: "I ask the Venerable Ones, 'Are you pure in this regard?

"Kaccittha" means "Is it so in this?"—the meaning is: "In these four *pārājika* offenses, are you pure? Alternatively, "Kaccittha parisuddhā" means "Are you pure in this? (i.e., *kacci parisuddhā attha*).
The meaning is "be [thus]. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the fourth *pārājika* in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the exposition of the Vinaya, is finished.
2. The Section on Saṅghādisesa Offenses 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule on the Emission of Semen:
That which was recited immediately after the Section on Pārājika offenses;
This is the commentary on the first phrase of the Thirteen-Sectioned [Sutta].
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Seyyasaka was living the holy life without enthusiasm.
Here, “Venerable” (*āyasmā*) is a term of affection. “Seyyasaka” is the name of that bhikkhu.
“Dissatisfied” (*anabhirato*) means having a distracted mind, burning with the fever of sensual lust; it does not mean wishing for the state of a householder.
“He became emaciated because of that” means that Seyyasaka became emaciated because of that state of dissatisfaction.
"Āyasmā Udāyī saw"—here, "Udāyī" is the name of that elder.
For he was the preceptor of Seyyasaka, named Lāḷudāyī, resembling a restless deer, one of those greedy monks devoted to the pleasure of sleep and so forth.
"Kacci no tvam" means "I hope that you. In expressions such as "yāvadatthaṃ bhuñja," *yāvadattha* means "as much as is needed."
"As much as needed. This is what is meant: eat as much food as you require, whatever amount you desire;
sleep for as long as you wish, whether by night or by day;
bathe as much as you like, having rubbed your body with clay and so forth and scrubbed it with powder and such; [and study] by means of recitation.
"Whether by questioning, or by the performance of duties, or by the meditation subject, there is no purpose [in these].
When dissatisfaction arises in you means: at whatever time a state of longing or distraction of mind arises in you due to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
"Lust ruins the mind" means: sensual lust ruins, destroys, distracts, and withers the mind.
"And then, having exerted yourself with your hand, discharge the impurity. At that time, "exerting yourself with your hand, perform the discharge of the impurity;
for in this way you will achieve one-pointedness of mind. Thus the preceptor instructed him, as a fool instructs a fool, as a deluded person instructs a deluded person.
(235) "Of those who fall asleep with mindfulness lost and lacking clear comprehension" means: having abandoned mindfulness and clear comprehension.

For those falling asleep: although for those who have fallen asleep the indeterminate life-continuum (bhavaṅga) process occurs and the process of mindfulness and clear comprehension lapses, nevertheless, at the time of lying down, one should apply attention. One who sleeps during the day should do so with resolve, thinking:
"I will wake up after sleeping as long as it takes for the hair of a washed bhikkhu to dry."

One should sleep with mindfulness. When sleeping at night, one should sleep with determination, thinking: "Having slept for this much portion of the night, I shall wake up when the moon or a star has reached such-and-such a position.

Regarding the phrase "except in a dream": here, a dream itself is "supinanta"; the meaning is that it is stated [the offense occurs] excluding or setting aside that [dream].

Or, whether out of a desire for welfare or a desire for harm, they present various kinds of objects;

[This is] like [the dream of] the acquisition of a son, like the five great dreams of the Bodhisatta, or like the sixteen dreams of the King of Kosala.
In this regard, a dream that one sees due to a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*) or from what has been previously experienced does not come true.

Those desiring to destroy [the truth] present even what is perverted as such. However, that which one sees from a portentous sign (*pubbanimitta*) is exclusively true.
Furthermore, a distinction in dreams also arises from the combination or separation of these four root causes.
And it is only those still in training (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*), because their distortions (*vipallāsa*) have not been abandoned, who see these four kinds of dreams.

Or it does not exist; and such thoughts arise in one seeing a dream. Then, if one sees [something] after waking, a violation of the Vinaya occurs;

Even when there is a transgression, it is entirely without offense. Now, if he neither sleeps nor wakes and does not see anything—who indeed would see?
And if this were so, it would follow that dreams do not exist at all. But they are not non-existent. Why?
Because one who is overcome by "monkey-drowsiness" sees them. For this has been said: "Great King, one who is overcome by monkey-drowsiness sees a dream."
“He sees,” it is said. “Overcome by monkey-sleep” means possessed by the sleep of a monkey.

It is both unwholesome and indeterminate. In this context, it should be understood that for one performing such acts as worshipping a cetiya, listening to the Dhamma, or teaching the Dhamma in a dream, it is wholesome;

Even though it yields a result, nevertheless, because it arises in a sphere that is not its proper domain, dream-intention is indeed not reckoned as such. Therefore he said:
"excepting dream-time. *Saṅghādisesa* is the name of this class of offenses. Therefore, that which is intentional, excluding dream-time—

Since not even a single formal act (*kamma*) can be performed here without the Saṅgha, it is called a *saṅghādisesa* because the Saṅgha must be sought at the beginning and in the remainder.
However, in order to show the meaning without regard for the phrasing, the word-commentary on this is as follows:

"The Saṅgha alone grants probation for that offense, sends back to the beginning, grants the trial period (mānatta), and rehabilitates; neither a group nor a single individual does so; therefore it is called a *saṅghādisesa*."
“Listen to the truth regarding what is called ‘an offense entailing suspension’ (saṅghādisesa):

The reason for the statement is given in the *Parivāra*. Therein, the granting of the *parivāsa* probation and so forth are set forth in detail in the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*;

Although this is indeed a single offense, it is called a "class" (*nikāya*) by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhisadda*), either by applying the term for the whole to a part or by treating the collection as a single unit—just as one speaks of "a single aggregate of feeling" (*vedanākkhandha*).
As in such passages as, “There is one aggregate of consciousness,” and so forth.
Having thus analyzed the training rule (sikkhāpada) that was recited according to the sequence of its words, he now says, “He emits within his own body,” and so forth,

238. Hereafter, however, for the purpose of explaining these very terms, "internal form" and so on, it is said:

however, one incurs the *saṅghādisesa* offense of indecent speech. If one is lustful through relishing speech...
If, having relished it again, he makes an effort toward the sign for the purpose of emission and emits, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.

If, out of worldly affection, he repeatedly touches and embraces his mother with the affection one has for a mother, or his sister with the affection one has for a sister, and semen is emitted, there is no offense.
However, if it is due to contact based on worldly affection, it is an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If, being impassioned by domestic affection, he relishes it again and makes an effort toward the signs for the sake of emission and emits, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.

When men and women in a forest retreat send some kind of gift—such as betel, perfumes, flowers, or incense—to one another for the sake of strengthening their state of friendship, this is called "forest-gathering" (*vanabhaṅga*). If a woman...
If he sends it to a certain bhikkhu with whom he is intimate and who visits his family, and while that bhikkhu— being lustfully attached to it and thinking,
"This was sent for me"— repeatedly plays with that flower-cluster with his hands, and semen is emitted, there is no offense. However, if he,
being lustfully attached to the flower-cluster, again relishes it and makes an effort toward the sign for the purpose of emission...
If it is emitted, it is a *saṅghādisesa*. If it is not emitted even though one makes the effort, it is a *thullaccaya*.
Thus, having examined these eleven applications by way of these eleven [types of] lust, one should discern whether there is an offense or no offense.
Having discerned it, if it is grave, it should be declared as "grave."
If it is light, it should be declared as "light. And a disciplinary act (vinayakamma) appropriate to that should be performed.
For when it is done in this way, it is well-done—just like medicine administered by a physician after diagnosing the cause of a disease—and it leads to the well-being of that person.

262. Regarding the phrases "he intends but does not make an effort," and so forth: if he intends with the intention of relishing the pleasure of emission but does not make an effort, and emission occurs, there is no offense.
If, oppressed by the desire for the pleasure of emission, he intends, "O, may I be released," but does not make an effort and emission does not occur, there is no offense.
If he does not intend through the desire for the pleasure of emission, but makes an effort through the desire for contact or the desire for scratching, [there is no offense].
He is released; there is no offense. Likewise, he does not intend it, he makes an effort, but he is not released; there is no offense.
While thinking sensual thoughts, he does not intend for the sake of emission, nor does he make an effort, yet he is released; there is no offense.

Furthermore, if he is not released even while thinking such thoughts, this is already implied by the statement: "If he does not intend it, does not make an effort, and is not released, there is no offense."

There is no offense on account of a dream means: for one who emits semen due to the very cause of a dream—just as if one were engaging in sexual intercourse or committing bodily contact and so forth while dreaming—there is no offense.
However, if the object of a dream becomes real through the volition of enjoyment that has arisen within the dream, one must remain motionless; one must not [use] the hand.

The sign may be played with; however, it is permissible to take it in the hollow of one’s hands and go to a water source for the purpose of cleaning it, provided it is for the sake of protecting the saffron-colored rug.
"With the intention of releasing" refers to one who, while applying the sign with medicine or while voiding excrement and so forth, intends to release it.
If one releases with the intention of rescuing [the animal], there is no offense for that person as well. For one who is insane, there is no offense in either of the two cases.
Here, Seyyasaka was a first-offender; for a first-offender, there is no offense.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis is finished.
Regarding its origin and other characteristics: this training rule originates from the first *pārājika*; it arises from body and mind.

It is an action (*kiriyā*), with perception as its liberation (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*), associated with two feelings (*dvivedana*), namely pleasure and equanimity (*sukhamajjhattadvaya*).
263. Regarding the *Vinītavatthu*, the account of the dream follows the same method as that stated in the *Anupaññatti*. The accounts concerning excrement and urine are of plain meaning.
In the account concerning thoughts (*vitakkavatthu*), "thoughts of sensual desire" (*kāmavitakka*) refers to sensual thoughts based on the household life.

Although it is stated therein that there is no offense, nevertheless, one must not fall under the sway of such thoughts. Regarding the accounts of hot water, the first is of plain meaning. In the second—
That bhikkhu, desiring to discharge [semen], bathed by repeatedly striking the sign with warm water;

for that reason, an offense is stated for him. In the third case, because there was an intentional effort (*upakkama*), it is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*). The cases concerning medicinal ointments and scratching are of obvious meaning.
264. Regarding the cases concerning walking on a path: for the first, in the case of one with thick thighs walking on a path, it refers to the friction against the narrow parts of the body.

The first [monk] discharged the impurity; because his intention was merely to release it, there is no offense. For the second, it likewise discharged, but because he had the intention to discharge it, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
For the third, it did not discharge; however, because of the presence of the effort, there is a *thullaccaya* offense.

Therefore, when feverish passion arises while traveling on a road, one must not continue; rather, having halted the journey, one should attend to the mind with the contemplation of the foul (*asubha*) and so forth.
Having calmed the mind, one should proceed with a pure mind, taking up the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
If, while standing, one is unable to dispel [the defilements], one should step off the path, sit down, dispel them, and then proceed with a pure mind, taking up the meditation subject.
Regarding the "cloth and bladder" [simile]: those monks were like village boys who, having firmly grasped a bladder, filled it again and again, and then released its contents.

They passed urine as if it were excrement. In the case of the sauna (jantāghara) incident, for one who is warming his belly, there is no offense whatsoever regarding the emission of semen, whether he intended to emit it or did not intend to emit it.
However, when impurity was emitted by one performing preparatory work through the movement of the organ, an offense is stated because it occurred at a point where an offense would otherwise arise.

265. Regarding the cases of *ūrughaṭṭāpana* (rubbing the thighs), it should be understood that those for whom an offense has been stated are also included when causing the sexual organ to be touched; thus it is said in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*.

The cases concerning novices (*sāmaṇera*) and others are self-evident. 266. In the case of "stiffening the body" (*kāyatthambhana*), "stiffening the body" means stretching oneself after sitting or lying down for a long time, or after performing manual labor, in order to dispel lethargy.
In the case of "intense gazing" (*upanijjhāyana*), even if she is clothed in a hundred layers of cloth, [the offense occurs] by standing either in front of her or behind her.
For one who gazes intently at a sign thinking, "The sign is in this place," there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
What more need be said for one who gazes intently at the signs of village girls who are not clothed? The same principle applies to the signs of animals as well.
However, for one who gazes intently with a single continuous effort even for a whole day, looking here and there, there is only one [offense].
It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For one who looks here and there and gazes repeatedly, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each such act.
However, this does not apply to the mere opening and closing of the eyes.

There is no offense for one who, having gazed impulsively, subsequently reflects and stands firm in restraint; but for one who abandons that restraint and gazes again, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing.
267. The locations such as the gaps between the rafters and so forth have meanings that are self-evident.
Regarding the bathing locations, the offense for those who struck the current of water with a sign has been stated. The same principle applies to the cases of the "water-offering" (*udañjali*).
And here, "water-offering" refers to a puddle of water. By this very method, all subsequent cases involving splashing water and so forth in the water [are to be understood].

These points are to be understood. However, this is the distinction: in the cases concerning flower-garlands and so forth, even if there is no offense for one whose intention is merely to honor [the Buddha], there is nevertheless an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) if it is for the purpose of play.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the emission of semen is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Physical Contact (Kāyasaṃsagga-sikkhāpada) 269.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One—this refers to the training rule concerning physical contact. Herein is the commentary on the words not [previously] explained:
“He dwells in the forest” means not in a secluded forest, but on a single side at the edge of the Jetavana monastery itself. In the middle...
"A cell" means there was a cell in the middle of that monastery. "Surrounded on all sides by a circular gallery" means it had a circular pavilion enclosure all around it.

It is said that having constructed a square cell in the center, it was built with an external circular pavilion enclosure so that one could walk about while remaining entirely within [the cell] by pulling oneself along.
"Well laid out" (*supaññatta*) means well-arranged; it has been placed in such a way and in such locations that it is pleasing and delightful to the world.
It has been arranged in each respective place so that, by way of its proper conduct (*vatta*), it does not even perform a single function [of obstruction].
"Opening some of the windows" refers to opening those through which darkness would otherwise prevail when they are closed.
"Closing those [doors] through which light was shining when they were open.
When this had been said, that brahmin woman spoke thus to the brahmin:
having been praised in this way by that brahmin, she observed, "This brahmin is inspired with faith; I think he wishes to go forth," and even though it was something to be concealed...
Manifesting her own failure and being solely intent on destroying his faith, she spoke these words beginning with, "Whence can he have such nobility?
In this context, one who has a noble self (*attā*) is "noble-souled" (*uḷārattā*); the state of having a noble self is "nobility of soul" (*uḷārattatā*).
Regarding the terms "women of good family" (*kulitthīhi*) and so forth: "women of good family" refers to mistresses of the household; "daughters of good family" (*kuladhītaro*)...
"Women who have gone into another's house" refers to daughters of good family (*kuladhītara*). "Maidens of good family" (*kulakumāriyo*) refers to those who have not yet been betrothed.
"Daughters-in-law of good family" (*kulasuṇhā*) refers to the wives of sons of good family brought from another family. 270.
"Immersed" (*otiṇṇa*) means that beings are immersed by passion arising within them, just as [beings are possessed] by *yakkhas* and so forth; it is like [falling into] wells and the like.
