Not considering existence, one who becomes attached to an object of attachment either by himself descending into lust, or because this term is a designation for anyone possessing lust in either way;
therefore, its word-commentary is stated thus: "One who has descended is called 'one who is lustful,' 'one who has regard,' and 'one whose mind is bound'."
In this context, "infatuated" (*sāratto*) means thoroughly impassioned by the lust for physical contact.

"Longing" (*apekkhavā*) means longing through the longing for physical contact. "With mind bound" (*paṭibaddhacitto*) means having a mind bound to that object precisely by the lust for physical contact.
"By what has changed" (*vipariṇatena*) means by that which has occurred otherwise, having abandoned its natural state consisting of the continuum of the pure life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
"Or ugly through transformation" means ugly through change; the intention is that it remains ugly just as it was while changing, even after it has changed and come to rest. 271.
But because this does not transcend association with lust and the other [defilements], therefore it is said: "It is transformed, being lustful... and so forth.

Having stated the word-commentary for this [term] by way of "citta" and so forth, he finally says, "Furthermore, in this context, 'mind' (citta) is intended in the sense of being 'stained' (ratta) and 'transformed' (vipariṇata)," while showing the meaning intended here.
"Born on that very day" means born on that same day, just born, having the color of a piece of raw meat; for even with such [a mind]...

In the case of physical contact, there is a *saṅghādisesa*; in the case of transgression involving sexual intercourse, there is a *pārājika*; and in the case of consenting to sitting in private, there is a *pācittiya*.
"Even before" means first of all.
"Should engage in physical contact" means one should engage in bodily union, such as grasping the hand, or bodily mingling.
However, because for one who enters this attainment, that which is called "bodily contact" is in fact transgression (*ajjhācāra*)—
an action that overcomes the boundary of restraint through the power of lust— it is therefore said, in order to show its concise meaning,
that the word-commentary states: "It is called transgression."

The detailed exposition of its meaning begins with the classification starting from "taking by the hand" (*hatthaggāha*) and so forth. Therein, for the purpose of showing the distinctions of the hand and other parts, he said:
"The 'hand' (*hattha*) is that which begins from the elbow (*kappara*)," and so on. Regarding this, "beginning from the elbow" means beginning from the second joint (*mahāsandhi*).
In other contexts, however, the hand extends from the wrist (*maṇibandha*) up to the fingertips; here, it includes the upper arm as well.
This refers to what is intended from the time of the *kappa-ratta* (the period of the world's duration).

"Pure hair" (*suddhakesā*) means hair that is pure, unmixed with thread or other materials. "Braid" (*veṇī*) is the name for a mass of hair fashioned by binding it together with three strands of hair.
"Mixed with thread" (*suttamissā*) means made by mixing the hair with thread of five colors.
“Mixed with garlands” (*mālāmissā*) means made by binding together three braids of hair after mixing them with *vassika* flowers and the like;
or alternatively, even a single braid of hair mixed solely with flowers should here be understood as a “tress” (*veṇī*).

“Mixed with gold” (*hiraññamissā*) means made by mixing it with a string of coins (*kahāpaṇa*). “Mixed with gold” (*suvaṇṇamissā*) means made by mixing it with golden *cīraka* ornaments or with *pāmaṅga* necklaces and so forth. “Mixed with pearls” (*muttāmissā*)...
"Made by mixing with strings of pearls" means made by mixing with gems strung on threads.
For regarding these, whoever takes even a single braid incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense. There is no escape for one who says, "I took a mixed braid.
And here, by the taking of the braid, the hair itself is also taken; therefore, whoever [takes] even a single hair...
If she takes hold of it, there is likewise an offense for her.

"Excluding the hand and the braid": here, with the exception of the hand as defined in this context and every kind of braid, the remainder of the body should be understood as the "limb" (aṅga). Thus, among the hand and so forth as thus delimited, regarding the hand—
"Seizing" means taking by the hand; "seizing by the braid" means grasping the hair-braid;
"touching" means touching the remainder of the body or touching one or another limb.
Whoever should engage in that seizing by the hand, or seizing by the braid, or touching one or another limb, for him there is an offense-class called *saṅghādisesa*.
"Occurs"— this is the meaning of the training rule (sikkhāpada).
Furthermore, since both the grasping of the hand, the grasping of the hair, and the touching of any remaining limb—
all of which constitute twelve types according to their classification— therefore, in order to demonstrate that classification, [the text] says "touching, stroking," and so forth.

The word-commentary for this has been stated according to the method. In that regard, there is this distinction between what was said—“touching (*āmasanā*) means merely being touched”—and what was said—“contact (*chupana*) means merely being contacted”: “Touching” (*āmasanā*) means rubbing;
it is the friction right there without crossing over the area already contacted. This is what is called “merely being touched. “Contact” (*chupana*), however, [is contact that does cross over].
It is merely touched without being rubbed together.
Furthermore, in the description of both "pushing upward" (*ummāsana*) and "leaping up" (*ullaṅghana*), only the single phrase "sending upwards" (*uddhaṃ uccāraṇā*) is stated.
Even there, this is the distinction: the first is stated by way of sending one's own body upward into the body of a woman.
The second [offense] is by way of lifting up a woman’s body; the rest is self-evident.

Now, regarding one who has descended [into passion] and, with a perverted mind, engages in physical contact, the Teacher shows the detailed classification of the offenses according to these terms: "It is a woman, and he perceives her as a woman, and he is lustful..."
And he said: “A bhikkhu [touches] her with body against body,” and so forth. In that context, “a bhikkhu [touches] her with body against body” means:
that bhikkhu, being lustful and perceiving her as a woman, [touches] her with his own body. *Naṃ* is merely a particle.
Alternatively, *taṃ* refers to her body, consisting of the hand and other parts. “He touches, he touches closely”—if by even one of these...

If one commits an offense by means of a bodily gesture, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa). In that regard, if one touches [the body] once, there is a single offense; if one touches it repeatedly, there is an offense entailing suspension for each individual act.
Even if one is fondling [the body], if one does not let go of the body but moves one’s own hand or body here and there, [there is an offense].

If one touches [a woman] while carrying her or sending her along, there is a single offense even for the duration of the day. If one touches her after repeatedly releasing her from the body, there is an offense for each individual act of contact.
Even if one is insulting her, if one does not release her from the body but instead insults her starting from the top of her head down to the back of her feet, [there is an offense].
There is one offense. However, if, having reached various places such as the belly and so forth, he strokes her again and again, there is an offense for each individual act.
The same principle applies to tickling: for one who tickles from the feet up to the head, it is exactly the same.
Regarding pulling down, if he seizes a woman by the hair and pulls her down to perform acts such as kissing, whatever transgression he intends to commit—
If one releases [the monk] after having lifted him up, it is a single offense. If one repeatedly bends [him] back once he has risen, there is an offense for every individual effort (*payoga*).
The same principle applies to lifting him up by seizing him by the hair or by the hands.
Regarding dragging: while dragging him toward oneself, as long as one does not let go, it is a single offense. Having let go...
For one who lets go and then pulls [the other] back, there is an offense for every instance of the act. The same principle applies to pulling back as well;
if one takes hold of the other's back while they are facing away and turns them around, it is likewise.
For restraining, if one takes hold firmly by the hand or the arm and drags them even a league’s distance, it is a single offense.
The Elder Mahāsumma said: "For one who releases and then takes hold again and again, there is an offense for every single act;
likewise, for one who touches and embraces again and again without releasing, there is an offense for every single act. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said:
"Only the initial grasping is the measure; therefore, as long as one does not release, it is only a single offense."

When one presses [the body] together with a garment or an ornament for the purpose of squeezing, if it does not touch the limb, there is a *thullaccaya*; if it touches it, there is a *saṅghādisesa*. With a single act of application (*ekapayoga*), there is a single offense; with various acts of application (*nānāpayoga*), there are various offenses.
Even if one does not produce any other alteration during seizing or touching, one incurs an offense by the mere fact of seizing or the mere fact of touching.
Thus, among these acts such as touching and so forth, through any one mode, if there is transgression against a woman while perceiving her as a woman, there is a *saṅghādisesa*.
For one who is doubtful, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; likewise, for one who perceives him as a paṇḍaka, a male, or an animal, there is also a *thullaccaya*.
For one who perceives a paṇḍaka as a paṇḍaka, there is a *thullaccaya*; for one who is doubtful, there is a *dukkaṭa*.

For one who perceives him as a male, an animal, or a female, there is also a *dukkaṭa*. This applies even for one who perceives a male as a male, or who is doubtful, or who perceives him as a female, a paṇḍaka, or an animal.
It is indeed a *dukkaṭa*. Even in the case of an animal, in every respect it is indeed a *dukkaṭa*.

Having observed these offenses stated according to the method of the single root (*ekamūlaka-naya*), by this same means, one should understand that in the method of the double root (*dumūlaka-naya*)—stated as "two women [committing] against two women," and so forth—the offenses are doubled. And just as there are two *saṅghādisesa* offenses for two women;
In this way, the cases involving many [women] should be understood as numerous.
For if one encircles and seizes many women standing together by their arms,
he incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense according to the number of women touched, and a *thullaccaya* according to the number of those standing in the middle.
For those [parts] are indeed touched by that which is connected to the body.

However, he who takes hold of several fingers or hairs together, having not counted the fingers and the hairs but having counted them as women, is to be dealt with according to the *saṅghādisesa* rules.
And in the case of those women whose fingers or hairs are situated in the middle, the count is according to those [women].

One incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. For when those [women] have been touched by that which is connected to the body, one who seizes several women after surrounding them with ropes, garments, or other items connected to the body incurs a *thullaccaya* for each of them according to the count of those who have entered within the enclosure.
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for those not touched. In that regard:
Since there is no such thing as touching by means of what is connected to what is connected to the body (*kāyappaṭibaddhappaṭibaddha*) mentioned in the Canon, therefore,

including all that is connected to what is connected to the body within "what is connected to the body" itself, the method stated previously— in both the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Kuruṇḍī*— is seen to be more appropriate here.
For when one has taken hold of the hand with a hand among women standing in a row and possesses equal lust for them, [if he touches] one hand...

He takes [her]; by virtue of having taken that woman, he incurs one *saṅghādisesa* offense, while for the others, according to their number, there are *thullaccaya* offenses in the same manner as previously stated.
If he takes it from a garment or a flower attached to her body, he incurs *thullaccaya* offenses according to the number of all [women involved].
For just as when one encircles [them] with a rope, cloth, or the like, all [of them] are [encircled] by what is attached to the body.
They are "touched" (āmaṭṭha); likewise here too, all [women] are touched by means of what is connected to the body.

However, if those women are standing while holding onto each other by the corner of their garment, and if he first takes hold of one woman by the hand in the manner previously described, he incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense on account of her who was taken; for the others, there are *dukkaṭa* offenses according to their number.
For in all those cases, by that same previous method, the body-bound [object] is touched by means of what is body-bound.
However, if he too takes hold of that very thing which is body-bound, he incurs a *thullaccaya* offense by virtue of that;
for the others, there are *dukkaṭa* offenses according to the immediately preceding method of counting.
If, however, out of lust for bodily contact, one touches the garment of a woman dressed in thick clothing, there is a *thullaccaya* offense. If one touches her when she is dressed in thin clothing,
and if the hairs emerging from the woman’s body through the gaps in the cloth touch the monk,
or the hairs on the monk’s body touch the woman, or if their hairs merely touch each other— [there is a *thullaccaya*].

If one touches [it], it is a *saṅghādisesa*. For even by means of derived matter born of karma (*kammajarūpa*), whether one touches something derived or non-derived, or even if one touches something derived or non-derived by means of some non-derived [matter] such as hair and so forth, one incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Kurundi*: "Having counted the body hairs, it is a *saṅghādisesa*. However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*...
It has been said: "Having counted the body hairs, one should not be made to undergo the penalty for the offense; he incurs only a single *saṅghādisesa*.
However, if he lies down on a monastic bed without having spread a coverlet, he should be made to undergo the penalty by counting the body hairs. That alone is correct.
For this offense is according to the female sex, not according to the number of parts [of the body].
Here it is asked: "But if one who thinks, 'I will take what is connected to the body,' takes the body;

or if one who thinks, 'I will take the body,' takes what is connected to the body—what offense does he incur? Regarding this, the Elder Mahāsumma says, "It is exactly according to the basis [of the object].
This, it is said, is his position:
“The object, perception, and lust, the discerning of contact;
as they are pointed out in the exposition, one should apply weight accordingly.
Here, “object” (*vatthu*) means a woman. “Perception” (*saññā*) means the perception of a woman. “Lust” (*rāga*) means lust for bodily contact. “Discerning of contact” (*phassappaṭivijānanā*)...

[This refers to] the knowing of contact born from bodily contact. Therefore, even one who, perceiving a woman as a woman, acts with lustful intent toward bodily contact, thinking, "I shall take hold of what is connected to her body," and touches her body, incurs a heavy offense of *saṅghādisesa* alone.
Another, however, incurs a *thullaccaya*—so said the Elder Mahāpaduma.
“When passion for perception has faded away, and passion for grasping has faded away;
in the explanation as it was pointed out, no weightiness is seen therein.
For it is stated that there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for one who perceives a woman as a woman when approaching her. And by this, the perception of a woman [is addressed].
Dispassion (*virāgitā*) has been produced regarding what is connected to the body (*kāyappaṭibaddha*), and the perception of what is connected to the body has arisen;
however, for one who takes that [object], a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) is stated. By this, even the taking was dispassionate; having not taken that, a woman was taken.
Therefore, because the perception of a woman is absent here, a *saṅghādisesa* is not seen, and because what is connected to the body was not taken, a grave offense is not [incurred].
It is seen [as no offense], but because of being touched by lust for bodily contact, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For there is no case where one who touches such an object with lust for bodily contact incurs no offense; therefore, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa*.
Having said this, he stated this tetrad: "If, being lustful, thinking ‘I will take [her] while she is lustful,’ he takes her while she is lustful, it is a *saṅghādisesa*."
“If one takes [a woman] who is dispassionate, thinking, ‘I will take one who is dispassionate,’ it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If one takes one who is dispassionate, thinking, ‘I will take one who is impassioned,’ it is an offense of wrong-doing. If one takes one who is impassioned, thinking, ‘I will take one who is dispassionate,’ it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.

Even though he says this, nevertheless, in this matter, the doctrine of the Elder Mahāsumana alone is correct: “When there is a woman, and one perceives her as a woman, and the monk is impassioned...”
And if he touches with his own body, or something connected to his body, a woman’s body...

[as before] ...takes hold of her, or makes contact with her, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*—according to this canonical passage, "if one takes hold of many women standing together by encircling them with one's arms, one incurs an offense of *saṅghādisesa* according to the number of women touched; for those who are in the midst..."
This is consistent with the commentarial expositions beginning with “by counting [the offense] as a thullaccaya.

For if it were indeed called "dispassioned" by virtue of being dispassionate toward perception and so forth, the Pāli would have stated a specific distinction in the same manner as in passages such as “he is a paṇḍaka and perceives himself as a woman,” by saying instead, “he is bound to the body and perceives himself as the body,” and so on. Since, however, that was not said, [it is not so].
Therefore, when there is the perception of a woman as a woman, for one who touches that woman, it is a *saṅghādisesa*;
for one who touches something attached to the body, it is a *thullaccaya*. This is consistent with the nature of the offense (*yathāvatthuka*).
This is also stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "Thinking, ‘I shall touch the body of a dark-skinned woman who is lying down having put on a blue garment...’"
"If he touches the body, it is a *saṅghādisesa*; if he touches the blue [object] thinking, 'I will touch the body,' it is a *thullaccaya*;
if he touches the body thinking, 'I will touch the blue [object],' it is a *saṅghādisesa*; if he touches the blue [object] thinking, 'I will touch the blue [object],' it is a *thullaccaya*.
This is the method of mixed bases that was stated in the manner beginning with "a woman and a *paṇḍaka*," and so forth.
In that case as well, the offenses stated according to perception and doubt regarding the object should be understood by one who is not confused about the Canon (Pāḷi).
In the section on "body-to-body-connected," for one who takes a body-connected object from a woman while perceiving her as a woman, there is a Thullaccaya;
in all other cases, there is a Dukkaṭa. The same method applies to the section on "body-connected-to-body. In the section on "body-connected-to-not-body-connected," [the same applies].
And in all cases involving the section on bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) and so forth under the *nissaggiya* [pācittiya] rules, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

However, the section beginning with “If she is a woman, he perceives her as a woman, he is lustful, and the woman [touches] him with her body” is stated with reference to a monk’s lust toward a woman. In that context, “the woman [touches] him with her body... [and so on].
A woman, being passionately attached to a bhikkhu, goes to the place where he is sitting or lying down and, with her own body, touches or...

[as before] ...contacts the body of that bhikkhu. If, with the intention of seeking sexual union, she makes an effort with her body and perceives the contact—thus, if he is touched or contacted by her while having the intention of seeking sexual union...
If one moves or shakes the body even slightly for the purpose of discerning contact, one incurs a *saṅghādisesa*.
Regarding "two women": here one incurs two *saṅghādisesas*; with respect to a woman and a *paṇḍaka*, there is a *dukkaṭa* along with the *saṅghādisesa*.
By this method, [the offenses continue] up to: "if one touches what is to be relinquished with what is to be relinquished, with the intention of indulgence..."
“If one makes an effort with the body but does not perceive contact, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Thus, the classification of offenses should be understood according to the previous method.
And herein, “one makes an effort with the body but does not perceive contact” refers to a flower that has been relinquished by oneself, or...
Or, having seen a woman striking him with her own flower or fruit that she has relinquished,
he makes a bodily gesture, wiggles a finger, raises an eyebrow, rolls his eyes,
or makes some other such gesture; this is called "exerting himself with the body but not experiencing contact."

This too constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because of the exertion of the body; in the case of two women, there are two [offenses], and in the case of a woman and a paṇḍaka, one likewise incurs two offenses of wrong-doing. 279.
Having thus shown the classification of offenses in detail according to the basis (*vatthu*), now, by way of characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), in brief:
Demonstrating both the classification of offenses and the classification of non-offenses, he says: "One whose intention is to engage," and so forth.

In that regard, according to the first method, when one who has been touched by a woman exerts himself with the body with the intention to engage and perceives the contact, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense due to the fulfillment of three factors.

According to the second method, as in the case of [the rule on] exchanging what is to be relinquished for what is to be relinquished, having exerted oneself and not touching—just as in the case of not touching—[there is a different result].

And because of not discerning the contact, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to the failure to fulfill two factors. In the third case, there is no offense for one who does not exert himself with the body.

For if one, though having the intention to engage in sexual intercourse, merely discerns the contact, consents to it, and experiences it with a motionless body, there is no offense because there is an absence of an offense even in the mere arising of the thought. But in the fourth case, by means of emission...
As in the case of the *nissaggiya* offense regarding a seat, there is no discernment of contact; it is merely the arising of a thought.
Therefore, there is no offense. For one whose intention is liberation, there is indeed no offense in any circumstances.
However, in this case, if one who has been seized by a woman moves away or strikes her with the desire to release himself from her body, [there is an offense].

Or, one makes an effort with the body and experiences contact. One who, seeing a [snake] approaching, desires to release it from there and frightens it away so that it flees, makes an effort with the body but does not experience contact.

One who, seeing such a long-bodied creature mounted upon his body, does not strike it—thinking, "Let it go slowly; being struck, it might lead to harm"—[does not make an effort with the body and does not experience contact].
Or, having perceived that a limb is being touched in this very way, he remains motionless as if unaware, thinking, "She will depart of her own accord, realizing she has no interest in me.
Or, when a young bhikkhu is firmly embraced by a strong woman, even though he wishes to flee, he becomes motionless because he is held so tightly;
thus he does not exert himself with the body, nor does he [respond to] the contact.
He perceives the contact. However, one who, seeing someone approaching, thinks, "Let him come for now;

after I have struck him or driven him away, I will depart," remains motionless—this person should be understood as one whose intention is liberation, who does not exert himself with the body, and who does not perceive the contact.

280. "Unintentionally" (*asañcicca*) means: not having thought, "By this means I shall touch her. For indeed, if one has not so intended, there is no offense even when touching a limb of a woman while receiving a bowl or performing similar acts.

"Without mindfulness" (*asatiyā*) means: he is distracted; there is no mindfulness [thinking] "I am touching a woman. Thus, for one who touches while extending a hand or foot and so forth at such a time without mindfulness, there is no offense.

"Not knowing" (*ajānantassa*) means: not knowing that a girl standing in the guise of a boy is a "woman," he touches her for some purpose. Thus, for one who touches without knowing she is a "woman," there is no offense.
"Of one who does not consent" means of one who does not consent to physical contact;

there is no offense for him, just as in the case of the monk who was led away by a succession of arms. Those such as the insane and so forth are to be understood in the manner already stated. However, in this instance, the Elder Udāyī is a beginner;
for a beginner, there is no offense.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis (*padabhājanīya*) is finished.
Regarding the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors: this training rule has its origin in the first *pārājika*; it originates from body and mind; it is an action (*kiriya*);

it is liberated by perception (*saññāvimokkha*); it is accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*); it is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*); it is bodily action (*kāyakamma*); it is unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*); and it possesses two feelings (*dvivedana*).
"By means of the two [feelings], pleasure and equanimity.
(281) Regarding the cases for disciplinary rules (*vinītavatthu*): "With motherly love for his mother" means he touched the body of his mother with motherly love.
This same method applies to the cases concerning daughters and sisters. In that regard, whether she be a mother or a daughter, every woman indeed [is an obstacle] to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).

They are like highway robbers. Therefore, it is stated that even for one who touches [a woman] out of domestic affection, thinking, "This is my mother," "This is my daughter," or "This is my sister," there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, if one, recollecting this command of the Blessed One, should see one's own mother being carried away by the current of a river, [one may touch her].
One must not touch it with the hand. However, a wise bhikkhu should bring along a boat, a plank, a plantain trunk, or a log of wood.
If these are unavailable, even a yellow robe may be brought and placed in front [of the person], but one must not say, "Take it here.
Once it has been taken, one may walk while pulling the requisites, thinking, "I am pulling the equipment."
If she is afraid, one should go ahead of her and comfort her, saying, "Do not be afraid.
If, while afraid, she suddenly climbs onto her son's shoulder or takes hold of his hand, he should not shake her off, saying, "Get away, old woman!
Rather, he should bring her to dry ground. The same rule applies even if she becomes stuck in mud or falls into a well.
For even there, having placed either a cord or a cloth [over it] and knowing that it has been grasped by the hand, it may be lifted out, but it must never be touched.
Not only is the body of a woman untouchable, but her lower garment, upper robe, ornaments, or articles—even down to a grass mat or a palm-leaf ring—are likewise untouchable; and that—
However, the lower robe (*nivāsana*) and the upper robe (*pārupana*) must be set aside specifically for the purpose of wearing them.
But if one exchanges the lower or upper robe and places it at the monk's feet for the purpose of [making] a robe (*cīvara*), it is permissible.

Regarding ornaments and articles, however, if an allowable article such as a *sīsapa*-flower ornament, a needle, or a toothpick is being offered with the words, "Venerable sir, please take this," it may be accepted for the purpose of [obtaining] a case, a needle, or other such requisites.
However, that which is made of gold, silver, pearls, and so forth, is "untouchable" (anāmāsa) even when being given; it must not be accepted.

Not only are their physical bodies untouchable, but even wooden figures, ivory figures, iron figures, copper figures, tin figures, paper figures, figures made of all kinds of gems, and even figures made of clay, if they are fashioned in the form of a woman, are untouchable.

It is indeed untouchable (*anāmāsa*). However, having received [an object] for the purpose of use with the thought, "Let this be yours," one may set it aside, break the remainder made of all kinds of gems, and bring what is suitable as an accessory to the accessories, and what is suitable for use to the use.
And just as a female figure is untouchable, so too the sevenfold grain is untouchable. Therefore, by [passing] through the middle of the field...
While walking, one must not tread upon grain or fruit grown there.
If grain is spread out at a house door or along the path, and there is a side-path available, one must walk without treading on it.
If no such path exists, one should resolve upon a path and proceed. Within a house, one should not sit upon grain.
Having prepared [a seat], it is permissible to sit down. Some people scatter grain in the assembly hall;
if it is possible to have it removed, it should be removed. If not, one should prepare a stool and sit down without trampling the grain.
If there is no space, people may prepare a seat right in the midst of the grain and give it to one.
One should sit down. One must not touch with a playful mind any vegetables grown there, such as mung beans or peas, nor fruits such as palm or jackfruit.

The same rule applies even when these have been heaped up by people. However, it is permissible to pick up fruits that have fallen from a tree in the forest with the intention, "I will give these to those who are not fully ordained."

Regarding these ten gems—pearl, mani-jewel, beryl, conch-shell, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and masāragalla—some say that among them, the pearl, even if unwashed and unpierced, may be touched as it is when first produced;
the others, however, are not to be touched. But in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "The pearl, whether washed or unwashed, is not to be touched, except for the purpose of its value as merchandise."
"It is not permissible to accept [it], but it is permissible for the purpose of medicine for leprosy," so it was said.
Even including the *jātiphalika* (cinnamon-fruit) stone, every variety of gemstone—whether blue, yellow, or otherwise—is *anāmāsa* (unblemished) when washed, pierced, and polished;
however, it is stated that a gemstone in its natural state, as it comes from the mine, is permissible to accept for the purpose of providing materials such as bowls and other utensils.
That too is rejected in the *Mahāpaccarī*; it is stated that only one made by boiling [the material] and resembling a glass gem (*kācamaṇi*) is permissible.
The determination regarding beryl (*veḷuriya*) is the same as for gems.
A conch shell, a *dhamana* conch, a polished and perforated one, and one mixed with precious substances are not counterfeit. Even a drinking-conch, if polished...
Even though it has not been washed, it is like raw clay; it is permissible to accept it for the purpose of medicinal ointments and the like, or as raw material for goods.

Stones that have been washed, polished, and set with gems, being the color of mung beans, are indeed unapproachable (untouchable). Other stones may be taken for the purpose of sharpening knives and so forth.
And here, "set with gems" means those made by joining them with gold and then smelting them together.
They say: coral that has been washed and pierced is *anāmāsa* (untouchable); the rest is *āmāsa* (touchable).

It is permissible to accept it for the purpose of the value of the goods. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "Whether washed or unwashed, all [coral] is *anāmāsa*, and it is not permissible to accept it.
Silver and gold, whether fashioned into articles or unfashioned, are entirely *anāmāsa* from the seed onwards.
And regarding what is not accepted: it is said that Prince Uttara, having had a golden cetiya made, sent it to the Elder Mahāpaduma.
The Elder rejected it, saying, "It is not allowable. There are golden lotuses, golden bubbles, and so forth in cetiya houses; these too are untouchable.
However, the guardians of the cetiya house stand in the place of those who discard silver; therefore—
It is stated that it is permissible for them to play with these [objects]. However, in the *Kurundi*, this is prohibited.

It is permitted only to remove refuse from a golden cetiya; this much alone is authorized. Furthermore, it is stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that even brass is of the same category as gold and is untouchable.
As for the use of lodgings, however, it is allowable in every respect; therefore, [the use of] things made of gold and silver...

All the requisites for the lodgings were new. At the site where the monks were expounding the Dhamma and Vinaya, they constructed a jeweled pavilion adorned with pillars of crystal and festooned with jeweled garlands; there, it was fitting that all the necessary articles be maintained for the monks.
Red and emerald gems that have been washed and pierced are "untouchable" (anāmāsa); others are "touchable" (āmāsa) and are said to be permissible for the purpose of providing the cost of the goods.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "Whether washed or unwashed, they are entirely untouchable and are not permitted to be accepted.
All weaponry and implements are untouchable; even when being given for the purpose of providing the cost of the goods, they must not be accepted.
Trade in weapons is not permitted. Even a simple wooden staff, a bow, a slingshot, a goad, or a hook—even down to tools such as axes and hatchets—when categorized as weapons, are untouchable.
If a spear or a javelin has been placed in a monastery by someone, the one looking after the monastery should send word to the owners, saying, "Please take this away. If...
They do not take them away; therefore, one must maintain that dwelling by remaining unshakable.
Upon seeing a sword, spear, or javelin fallen on a battlefield, it is permissible to break the blade with a stone or some other object and take it for the purpose of making knives.
It is also permissible to separate the other parts and take some for the purpose of making knives, and some for the purpose of making walking sticks and so forth.
However, when something is being given with the words, “Take this,” it is permissible to accept even the whole lot if one intends,
“I will destroy it and turn it into allowable goods.
Fish-nets, bird-nets, and so forth, as well as shields, screens, and protective amulets against arrows— all these are not to be touched (anāmāsa).
However, when items are obtained for the purpose of personal use, it is permissible to take a net with the thought, "I will tie it over a seat or a cetiya," or "I will wrap it around a parasol.
All items intended for protection against arrows may be accepted as merchandise for resale.
For this serves to ward off the obstruction caused by others and does not itself cause obstruction; thus, it is permissible to accept a wooden board or a tooth-stick container.
It is permissible to take [an instrument] with the intention, "I shall play.
Lutes, drums, and the like that are covered with leather are not to be touched. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated:
"Even the frame of a drum, the frame of a lute, an empty sound-box, the leather fastened to the rim, and even the neck of a lute—all of these are not to be touched."
It has been stated: it is not permitted at all to cover it up, to have it covered up, to play [an instrument] upon it, or to have it played upon.
Even if one sees that what was discarded by people after making an offering on the cetiya-precinct has been left there, one should sweep it up from time to time without moving it.
However, when the time comes to discard rubbish, it is permissible to carry it away according to the usual practice for rubbish and deposit it to one side; thus it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī.
It is permissible even to accept [skins] for the purpose of making musical instruments. However, when they are being offered for the purpose of personal use,

it is permissible to take them for the sake of various requisites and accessories— such as thinking, "We shall make a lute case, a drumhead, a tooth-stick box, or a leather sheath for a knife"— and then to fashion them accordingly.

The story of the former wife is self-evident. In the story of the yakkhinī, even if one enters into physical contact with a goddess of the Paranimmitavasavatti realm, it is only a thullaccaya offense.
The stories of the paṇḍaka and the woman who has recently given birth are likewise clear.
In the story of the dead woman, there is a thullaccaya at the time when it would constitute a pārājika offense, and after that point, it is a dukkaṭa. In the story of the animal...
For a female *nāga* maiden, a female *supaṇṇa* maiden, a *kinnarī*, or a cow, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
In the case of the wooden image (*dārudhītalikā*), it is an offense of wrong-doing not only for a wooden one, but even for a female form depicted in painting.
282. The case of the pressure (*sampīḷana*) is of plain meaning. In the case of the bridge (*saṅkama*), whether it be a footpath or a cart-track, [it is an offense].
Or, having merely made an effort with the thought, "I will move it," whether it moves or not, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The case of the path is self-evident.
Regarding the case of the tree: whether the tree is large, the size of a great rose-apple tree, or small, whether one is able to move it or not, by the mere effort there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The same principle applies to the case of the boat. Regarding the case of the kingdom:
If one is able to move a rope from its place by pulling it, there is a *thullaccaya* offense. If it is a heavy rope that does not move even slightly from its place, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The same principle applies to a staff (*daṇḍa*). For even a large tree fallen on the ground is included here simply by the mention of a "staff.
The case concerning the leaf (*patta*) is self-evident. In the case concerning the salutation (*vandana*), [it refers to] a woman.
If she massages his foot with the intention of worshipping him, he should prevent her, or he should cover his foot, or he should remain motionless.
For there is no offense even if one consents with a motionless mind. At the end, the object of contact is indeed manifest.
The commentary on the training rule concerning bodily contact is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Lewd Speech (Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpada) 283.
"At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... refers to the training rule regarding lewd speech. In this context, "pointing out" means by way of reference.
"He speaks even in praise," and so forth, will be explained further below. "Chinnikā" means one whose sense of shame has been cut away. "Dhuttikā" means...
"Deceitful" means they are shameless. "Laughing" means they smile with a gentle, smiling look.
"Chattering" means they speak various kinds of seductive talk in a high-pitched voice, saying things such as, "Oh, noble sir! and so forth. "Guffawing" means they laugh with loud laughter.
"Mocking" means they make jokes by saying things such as, "This man is a eunuch; he is no man at all," and so forth.
285. "Passionate" (*sāratta*) means one who is impassioned by the lust for lewd speech. "Having regard, with a mind bound" is exactly as explained in the previous method;

the only difference here is that the lust for lewd speech (*vācassāda-rāga*) should be applied. To show what is intended here by "a woman" (*mātugāma*) in the phrase "with lewd words toward a woman," he says "a woman" and so forth.
In that context, a "wise person" (*viññū*) is one capable of discerning well-spoken and ill-spoken speech.
"To know what is grave and what is not grave" means that she who is wise and capable of discerning speech that is meaningful and meaningless,
as well as speech associated with what is not the True Dhamma and what is the True Dhamma, is intended here. However, it is shown that one who is elderly but foolish and mute is not intended here.
“Should illuminate” means he should shine forth; he should speak words of various kinds that are not the true Dhamma.

However, for one who illuminates in this way, that which is called “illumination” is, in its actual meaning, transgression (*ajjhācāra*); it is conduct that, having been overcome by lust, exceeds the bounds of restraint.
Therefore, showing this meaning, he said: “‘Should illuminate’ is what is called ‘transgression. As the text says:
In this context, *tanti* is merely a particle; the meaning is "the young man, the young woman," for example.
"Having pointed out two ways," and so forth, is stated to show the manner in which it becomes a *saṅghādisesa* offense due to its appearance.
Therein, "two ways" refers to the anus and the urinary tract. The rest is already clear from the summary (*uddesa*). In the detailed exposition (*niddesa*):
"But he praises" means: if he says, "You were endowed with female characteristics and auspicious characteristics," it does not yet amount to a formal charge.

If he says, "Your anus and urinary tract are such that you were indeed endowed with such female characteristics and auspicious characteristics," it amounts to a formal charge; it is a *saṅghādisesa*. "He extols" means he praises.
These, however, are synonyms for the words of praise themselves.
"He reviles" means he strikes with the goad of speech. "He despises" means he disparages. "He censures" means he attributes fault.

As for the eleven phrases beginning with "you are signless" that appear later in the text, if they are not combined [with the preceding], it does not constitute the head [of the section]; yet even when they are combined, [it remains so].
Among those, it is only when combined with these three—“you are a *sikharaṇī*,” “you are a *sambhinnā*,” or “you are a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanā*)”—that there is a *saṅghādisesa*.

Even with a request such as “give me that,” the offense does not reach its full extent by that alone; it is only when combined with sexual intercourse, as in “give me the act of sexual intercourse,” that there is a *saṅghādisesa*.
Even in words of entreaty such as “When will your mother be pleased? and so forth, the offense does not reach its full extent by that alone; [when one asks] “When...? [the offense is complete].
If one is engaged in sexual intercourse by means of such phrases as “Your mother will be pleased;

when shall we have sexual intercourse? or “When your mother has been won over, we shall have sexual intercourse,” it is an *saṅghādisesa* offense. Even in the case of interrogative statements such as “How do you instruct your husband?

it is an *saṅghādisesa* offense only when the word “sexual intercourse” (*methunadhamma*) is mentioned, and not otherwise. This same principle applies to responsive statements such as “I instruct my husband in this way.”
“Being asked for an explanation, he speaks”: being asked, “How is it that by giving she becomes dear to her husband?
he explains. And in this context, even if it were said, “Give in such a way; by giving in such a way,” it would not be the main point.

Rather, it is [the explanation] beginning with, “By giving sexual intercourse in such a way, by approaching in such a way, by giving and approaching in sexual intercourse in such a way, she becomes dear. And so forth.
However, according to this method, it is only when one has engaged in sexual intercourse that there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
This same principle applies to the words of instruction as well. In the description of abuse: "You are signless" means you are devoid of the [sexual] signs;

what is meant is that your vaginal canal is merely the size of a keyhole. "You are a mere sign" means your female characteristics are incomplete and are merely a matter of perception. "You are bloodless"...

“Dry-streamed” means having a dry vaginal canal. “Constantly bleeding” means having a perpetually bloody, moist vaginal canal. “Constantly wearing a cloth” means she always wears a cloth inserted [into the vagina];
what is meant is that she constantly uses an artificial penis (*āṇicōlaka*). “Dripping” means flowing; what is meant is that urine flows from her constantly.
“Sikharaṇī” means one whose artificial flesh has protruded outside. “Female eunuch” (*itthipaṇḍaka*) is said to be one who lacks sexual organs.
*Vepurisikā*: a woman who has the appearance of a man, with a full beard and mustache. *Sambhinnā*: one whose anus and urinary tract have become confluent.
*Ubhatobyañjanā*: one endowed with both sexual characteristics, namely, the female characteristic and the male characteristic.
And among these eleven categories, only those who are *sikharaṇī*, *sambhinnā*, or *ubhatobyañjanā* [are included].
Three pure words enter the head. Thus, these three and the preceding three—the words regarding the anus, the urinary tract, and sexual intercourse—make six pure words that constitute offenses.

The remaining ones, such as "animitta" (signless) and so forth, [apply] by way of sexual intercourse, such as saying, "Give me sexual intercourse with one who is signless," or "You are signless, give me sexual intercourse," and so on.
It should be understood that these very things constitute offenses. 286.

Now, regarding one who has fallen [into misconduct] and makes a proposal with a perverted mind, showing the detailed classification of offenses by way of praising the anus and the urinary tract and so forth, it says: "And a woman..."
He said, “...perceiving her as a woman,” and so forth. The meaning of these terms should be understood in the same manner as explained regarding bodily contact.
However, this is the distinction: *adhakkhaka* means below the collarbone;
*ubbhajāṇumaṇḍala* means above the kneecaps; *ubbhakkhaka* means above the collarbone; and *adho jāṇumaṇḍala* means below the kneecaps.
Starting from below [the collarbone], the collarbone and the kneecaps are included within this field of *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing), just as in the case of physical contact with a bhikkhunī.
For the Buddhas do not prescribe a grave offense that leaves a remainder.
"Connected to the body" refers to clothing, flowers, or ornaments.
287. “One who has the meaning as the priority” means one who is explaining the meaning of such words as “signless,” etc., or one who is reciting the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

“One who has the Dhamma as the priority” means one who is teaching the Pāḷi or reciting it. Thus, for one who speaks while prioritizing both the meaning and the Dhamma—for one who has the meaning as the priority and for one who has the Dhamma as the priority—there is no offense. “One who has instruction as the priority” means:
“Even now you are signless and possessed of both characteristics; you should now practice heedfulness.”
There is no offense for one who speaks with the intention of instruction, placing such guidance foremost as: "In the future, may you not become like this.

However, for one who, while teaching the Pāḷi to the bhikkhunīs, abandons the normal method of recitation and repeatedly says, laughing and laughing, "You are a *sikharaṇī*, you are a *sambhinnā*, you are a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanā*)," there is indeed an offense.
There is no offense for one who is insane. Here, the Elder Udāyī was a beginner; for him there is no offense as he was a beginner.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis is finished.
Regarding the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and other factors, this training rule has three origins: from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
And it arises as: an action, liberation through perception, accompanied by consciousness, a worldly offense, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and associated with two feelings.
288. Regarding the cases for disciplinary rules (*vinītavatthu*), in the case concerning blood:
that monk spoke with reference to the female organ’s appearance resembling blood; the other did not understand, therefore it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

"Coarse-haired" means having much hair with short hairs. "Thickly-haired" means having matted hair. "Harsh-haired" means having stiff hair. "Long-haired" means having long hairs. All this is said with reference specifically to the female characteristics.
289. "You have sown," he said with reference to unrighteousness (*asaddhamma*); she, not having noticed it, said, "But it has not been harvested.
"Harvested" means [in the case of] a water-sowing, where the seed has not taken root in the place, or where the seed has been destroyed by insects.
Having replanted the seed in a suitable place and sprinkled it with water;
or, for the purpose of leveling seeds that have fallen unevenly on dry land, having smoothed them out again with a tooth-stick—referring to one of these cases, she said this.
Regarding the phrase "the path sinks" in the section on the path, she said it referring to the path of the genitals (*aṅgajāta*). The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the training rule regarding indecent speech is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Service for One’s Own Pleasure (Attakāmapāricariyā-sikkhāpada) 290.

At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... [this refers to] the training rule regarding one's own pleasure (*attakāma*). In this context, "one who frequents families" (*kulūpaka*) means one who visits families for the sake of the four requisites, being constantly engaged in approaching such families.
"Requisites consisting of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick" means: robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick.
Herein, "requisite" (*paccaya*) is used in the sense of a support; it is a designation for whatever is suitable [for the sick]. For a physician...
It is medicine because it is authorized by that [kamma]. "Medicine as a requisite for the sick" (*gilānapaccaya-bhesajja*) means medicine that is a requisite for the sick;
what is meant is whatever is suitable for the sick, such as the physician’s treatment, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth.
As for "requisite" (*parikkhāra*), in such passages as "well-furnished with the seven requisites of a city," it refers to an accessory or equipment. "A chariot..."

In such passages as “the sīsa-parikkhāra (head-ornament), the jhāna-eye, the wheel-valiant,” it means an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). In such passages as “these requisites for life that must be procured by one who has gone forth,” it means a provision (*sambhāra*).
But here, both “provision” (*sambhāra*) and “retinue” (*parivāra*) are appropriate.
For that medicinal requisite for the sick is a retinue for life, since it protects it by not allowing an interval for the arising of diseases that destroy life.
The equipment (sambhāra) is also called "requisite" (parikkhāra) because it serves as its cause so that [the practice] may proceed for a long time;
thus, medicine as a requisite for the treatment of the sick is "medicine-requisite-for-the-treatment-of-the-sick" (gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāra),
and this is how the meaning should be understood.
*Vasala* means low and vile. Alternatively, *vasala* is so called because he "flows" (*vassati*); the meaning is that he "oozes. Thus, it is said that a *vasala* is one who oozes impurity.
*Niṭṭhuhitvā* means having spat out saliva. *Kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmi* means: "In comparison with which other woman do I fall short by what wealth, ornament, or beauty?
Who indeed is superior to me? This is what she indicates. 291. *Santike* means standing in the vicinity, nearby; this same meaning is also indicated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).

"Attending to one's own desires" (*attakāmapāricariyā*): "Desire-attendance" (*kāmapāricariyā*) is attendance for the sake of desire, which is designated as the act of sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*).
"Attendance to one's own desires" (*attakāmapāricariyā*) is attendance for the sake of desire for oneself;

or, it is "desired by oneself" (*attakāmā*), meaning it is wished for or longed for by oneself through the lust of sexual intercourse. It is "desire-attendance to one's own desires" (*attakāmapāricariyā*) because it is both a desire for oneself and an act of attendance.
Regarding the phrase "one should speak in praise of that service for one’s own sensual pleasure": one should proclaim its quality (*guṇa*) and its benefit (*ānisansa*).

In this regard, according to the interpretation of the meaning as "service for one’s own sake through sensual pleasure," both the sensual pleasure (*kāma*), the cause (*hetu*), and the service (*pāricariyā*) constitute the meaning (*attha*), while the rest is the phrasing (*byañjana*).

Alternatively, it may be understood as "that which is both a desire for oneself and a service" (*attakāmā ca sā pāricariyā ca*); thus, it is "service for one’s own sensual pleasure" (*attakāmapāricariyā*).
In this interpretation of the meaning, *adhippāya* (intention) and *pāricariyā* (service) constitute the sense (*attha*), while the remainder is the phrasing (*byañjana*).
Therefore, without placing emphasis on the phrasing, in order to show merely the sense, the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) states:
"one's own desire, one's own cause, one's own intention, one's own service. "One's own desire, one's own cause... [and so forth].
For when it is said, "one's own service" (*attano pāricariyā*), the wise will understand: "To this extent, the service of one's own sensual desires has been described.

And even when it is said, "one's own intention is one's own service," they will understand: "To this extent, the service of one's own desires has been described in the sense of what is wished for and craved by oneself."
Now, in order to show the manner of praising that service for one’s own pleasure, he said, “This is the foremost,” and so forth.
Its meaning is clear both from the summary and the detailed exposition. Here, however, is the connection of the words and the determination of the offense:
“This is the foremost... [omitted] ...one should serve”—that is, one who serves someone like me, who is virtuous, of good character, and a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī).
One should serve her with this Dhamma; for one who serves me in such a way, this service—which is called "service"—is the foremost of all services.

Regarding the offense of *saṅghādisesa* connected with sexual intercourse: if anyone should speak in praise of serving according to one's own desire by means of speech connected with sexual intercourse—that is, speech associated precisely with the act of sexual intercourse—for him there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.

Now, since a *saṅghādisesa* offense was stated only for one who speaks in connection with sexual intercourse, therefore there is no *saṅghādisesa* even for one who praises service by means of such statements as, "I too am a khattiya, you too are a khattiya;
it is fitting for a khattiya to give to a khattiya because of our common birth. Regarding the phrase "I too am a khattiya," and so forth:

However, even after speaking by way of many methods, if one speaks with reference specifically to sexual intercourse, saying, "You ought to give me the act of sexual intercourse," it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
The phrase "and she is a woman," etc., follows the same method as previously stated. In this case, the Elder Udāyin was a first-offender; for a first-offender, there is no offense.
The origin and all other details are the same as for the offense of indecent speech. The grounds for the offense are self-evident.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the pursuit of one's own pleasure is concluded.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning matchmaking.
296. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, [was staying] regarding the matter of matchmaking (*sañcaritta*).

In this context, "wise" (*paṇḍita*) means endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*), possessed of insight (*gatimant*). "Clever" (*byatta*) means endowed with proficiency (*veyyattiya*), endowed with skillful means (*upāya*), knowing the means, and confident. "Intelligent" (*medhāvinī*) means endowed with intelligence (*medhā*);
she makes what has been seen [clearly] manifest. "Dexterous" (*dakkhā*) means skillful. "Unwearying" (*analasā*)...
Endowed with initiative and energy. "Suitable" (channā) means appropriate. "In what way?"—the intention is:

"It is like a hardship, like a defilement, yet it is like a sense of shame for us. "To speak on behalf of the maiden" means to speak for the sake of the maiden, saying, "You must take her. Regarding "marriage and so forth":
marriage (*āvāha*) is the bringing of a girl from another family for the sake of a boy; wedding (*vivāha*) is [the taking] of one's own daughter...
"Sending to another family" means requesting, "Give us a girl for our boy," or determining the day, the lunar mansion, and the auspicious moment.

297. "The former courtesan": she was the wife of a certain accountant; while he was alive, she was known as a "courtesan" (*gaṇikā*), but when he died, she came to be designated as a "former courtesan" (*purāṇagaṇikā*).
"To another village" means outside the village; the intention is that it is a different village.
"Men" refers to those people who knew that Udāyī was engaged in and occupied with the act of matchmaking.

"By means of the enjoyment due to a daughter-in-law" means they enjoyed her by means of whatever resources a daughter-in-law is to be provided with, such as having food prepared, cooked, and brought in;
thereafter, "by means of the enjoyment due to a slave-girl" refers to what is to be provided after a month has passed, by which means a slave-girl is to be provided.
There is [work] such as clearing away the refuse from the fields, performing agricultural labor, fetching water, and so forth; they ate by means of that.
"Duggatā" means poor, or having gone to a family where one becomes poor—that is, having gone to such a family.
"Māyyo imaṃ kumārikaṃ" means "O Noble Ones, do not [take] this girl. "Āhārūpahāro" means both food and an offering, both taking and giving; nothing was brought by us.
They indicate: "We have no trade or business dealings with her regarding what has been brought here. [One should think: "A recluse must be uninvolved;

he should be a true recluse. Thus, a recluse indeed must be uninvolved and free from concern in such matters, thinking, "In this way, the venerable one will be a recluse, a true recluse. Having thus discouraged him, [he says: "Go!"
“We do not know him,” they said. 298.
“Equipped” means provided with all requisites, or adorned and decorated. 300. “Scoundrels” means women-scoundrels.
“Amusing themselves” means [indulging] here and there, on all sides, in pleasing forms and so forth.
"Moving the dice" means playing, sporting, and taking delight; this is what is meant. "They made a wager" means they set a stake, saying, "If you win, you shall give this much;
if you do not win, I shall give this much. However, it is not permitted for monks to make a wager.
It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that whoever makes such a wager must pay the forfeit to the one who loses.
"How indeed could the venerable Udāyī [act]?"—here, "that moment" (*taṅkhaṇo*) refers to a short time. "Momentary" (*taṅkhaṇikaṃ*) means pertaining to that short time.
"He should engage in matchmaking" (*sañcarittaṃ samāpajjeyyā*): he should enter into the state of acting as a go-between.
For, by one who enters into that, it is necessary to go somewhere when sent by someone; and because of the subsequent statement, "the mind of a woman toward a man," and so forth.
Here, women and men are intended; therefore, to show that meaning, its word-commentary is stated as:
"Either sent by a woman, he goes to the presence of a man, or sent by a man, he goes to the presence of a woman.
Regarding the phrase "or [he] should inform a woman of a man's intention, or a man of a woman's intention," the words "should inform" (*āroceyya*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the text.
It must be seen; for that very reason, its word-by-word commentary states: "He reports a man's thought to a woman; he reports a woman's thought to a man.
Now, as for the purpose for which he reports their thought, intention, disposition, desire, and preference—this...

He spoke the passage beginning with “In the state of a husband (*jāyattana*) or in the state of a lover (*jārattana*)” in order to show this. Therein, “in the state of a husband” means in the capacity of a husband; “in the state of a lover” means in the capacity of a lover.
For one who conveys a man’s intention to a woman conveys it in the state of a husband, while one who conveys a woman’s intention to a man conveys it in the state of a lover;
furthermore, even when conveying a man’s intention to a woman, it is [conveyed] in the state of a husband.
One makes known [the intention] regarding the state of being a bound wife, or regarding the state of misconduct in the form of being a paramour.
Since, however, one who makes this known must say such things as, "Will you indeed become his wife," etc., therefore, in order to show that mode of speech, its word-commentary is:
"In the state of being a wife means 'you will be a wife'; in the state of being a paramour means 'you will be a paramour.'"
Thus it was said. By this same method, when a woman’s intention is communicated to a man, the manner of what should be said is to be understood as:
"You will become a husband," "you will become a master," or "you will become a lover.
"At least for that moment" means, at the very minimum limit, that which lasts for just a brief instant.
It is called "momentary" because it must be shared for only that moment; the meaning is "lasting for a short while.
If one conveys this intention to a man by saying, "You shall be her momentary [lover]," there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.

By this same method, it should be understood that if one conveys this intention to a woman on behalf of a man by saying, "You shall be his momentary [lover]," one likewise incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense.

303. Now, having shown the various types of women intended by the phrase "a woman with a man's mind," the text says "ten kinds of women" and so forth, in order to show the classification of offenses based on acting as a go-between among them.

In that context, "protected by her mother" means protected by her mother; she is protected by her mother in such a way that she does not permit cohabitation with a man. Therefore, for him [who acts as a go-between],...
It is also stated in the *Padabhājana*: “The mother protects, guards, exercises authority, and wields power.
Therein, “protects” means she does not allow [the child] to go anywhere. “Guards” means she places him in a protected place so that others do not see him.
“Exercises authority” means she acts by overcoming him, preventing him from living according to his own will. “Wields power”...
"She controls" means she exercises control over her by saying, "Do this; do not do that.
By this same method, those protected by their father and so forth should also be understood. Neither lineage nor the Dhamma protects her;

rather, she is "protected by lineage" when she is protected by kinsmen, or by fellow practitioners of the Dhamma who have gone forth under the same Teacher, or by those included in the same monastic group.
She is called "protected by the Dhamma. Therefore, the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for those terms is stated in the manner beginning with "those of the same clan protect her" and so forth.

"With protection" means *sārakkhā*. "With punishment" means *saparidaṇḍā*. Their detailed explanations are indeed well-known. Among these ten, sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*) occurs only for the last two who go to another man, and not for the others.

Those purchased for wealth, whether little or much, are "purchased with wealth" (*dhanakkītā*). However, because she is not merely purchased but becomes a wife through being purchased for the purpose of cohabitation, it is said in its definition:

"having purchased her with wealth, one causes her to dwell. One who dwells according to her own desire or preference is "one who dwells by choice" (*chandavāsinī*). However, because she does not become a wife by her own choice alone but through being accepted by the man, it is said in its definition: "the beloved causes the beloved to dwell."

“Bhogavāsinī” means she who dwells with enjoyment; this is a designation for a woman from the countryside who, having obtained household utensils such as a mortar and pestle, enters into the state of being a wife.
“Paṭavāsinī” means she who dwells with a cloth; this is a designation for a poor woman who, having obtained even a mere lower garment or a mere cloak, enters into the state of being a wife.
“Odapattakinī” refers to those two [types of women] who, having been made to place their hands into a single water-bowl, are joined together like that water.
Having said, "Be inseparable," this is merely a conventional name for one who has been formally accepted as a wife;
its meaning should be understood in the commentary as: "having touched the water-vessel with her, he causes her to dwell there.

*Obhaṭacumbaṭā* means one whose head-cloth (*cumbaṭa*) has been removed (*obhaṭa*, i.e., *oropita*); she is a certain woman such as a wood-gatherer, and this is a designation for her whose head-cloth has been taken off from her head and she is made to dwell in the house.
A *dāsī* is both a slave-girl and a wife of one’s own.
A *kammakārī* is one who performs work in the house for wages; someone, being without need for his own wife, establishes a household with her. This is called “a female laborer and a wife.
One brought by a banner (*dhajāhaṭā*) is one brought after having gone to another territory with an army that has raised its banners, plundered it, and returned.
It is said that someone takes her as a wife; this is called "one carried off by the flag" (*dhajāhaṭā*). A "momentary woman" (*muhuttikā*) is in the same manner as described.

For these ten types of women, sexual misconduct occurs when one approaches another man's wife. However, for twenty types of men, sexual misconduct occurs when they approach these [ten] women, and for a monk, it constitutes the offense of acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*).
305. Now, regarding the phrases "a man sends a monk" and so forth:
"accepts" means that the monk, having been told by that man, "Go, venerable sir, say this to the woman protected by her mother:
'May you become the wife of such-and-such a person, purchased for a price,'" replies, "Very well, lay follower," or "So be it," or "I shall inform her."
In whatever manner—either by making a verbal communication or by means of a nod of the head and so forth—one accepts [the message].
"Investigates" means that, having thus accepted it, one goes to that woman and communicates the message.
"Returns [the answer]" means that when he has communicated it, that woman either accepts it, saying "Very well," or rejects it, or remains silent out of modesty.
"Let it be," she says; then, having returned, she reports that matter to the man.
At this point, through the fulfillment of these three factors—consisting of the acceptance, the reporting, and the bringing back—it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
Whether she is his wife or not is irrelevant; this is no cause for concern. However, if she is one protected by her mother...
If one sent to the presence [of a person] does not see that person and reports the message to their mother instead, it is called "communicated outside" (*bahiddhā vimaṭṭha*);

therefore, the Elder Mahāpaduma said it is "a breach of the convention" (*visaṅketa*). However, the Elder Mahāsuma stated that whether it be the mother, the father, or even a domestic slave, or whoever else might carry out that action—it is [still a breach] even if it is reported to them.
It is not called "rubbed" (vimaṭṭha); rather, when the three factors are fulfilled, it is indeed an offense.
Is it not just as if one who wishes to say, "I renounce the Buddha," should by mistake say, "I renounce the Dhamma"—the training has nonetheless been renounced?
Or as if one who wishes to say, "I attain the first jhāna," [should instead say something else]...
Having become dispassionate, if he were to say, "I am entering the second jhāna," he would incur a *pārājika* offense.

He said, "It is just like this. However, this is consistent with the rule: "If he accepts [the gift], having had his pupil test it and then returning it himself, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*"; therefore, it is well said.
And just as there is no discrepancy when one who has been told, "Speak of her who is protected by her mother," goes and speaks even to the mother and others capable of informing her,

so too, when it should have been said, "Be the wife of such-and-such a man, purchased for a price," the same applies to the terms such as *chandavāsinī* (one who lives by consent) and so forth mentioned in the Canon.
Whether by way of one or another among such statements—even if not explicitly stated—such as those indicating cohabitation:
"Be the wife, the spouse, the mistress, the mother of children, the housewife, the mistress of the home, the cook, the obedient servant, or the attendant of so-and-so," there is no lack of consensus;
rather, due to the fulfillment of the three factors, there is indeed an offense.

However, for one who has been sent with the instruction, “Speak to a woman protected by her mother,” and having gone there, speaks instead to someone else—such as one protected by her father or others—that constitutes a breach of the agreement (*visaṅketa*).
This same principle applies to instructions such as, “Speak to a woman protected by her father,” and so forth.
Herein, however, according to the classification of single-rooted, double-rooted, and so on, it may be that a man’s mother sends a bhikkhu to a woman protected by her mother.
The distinction lies solely in the various permutations of the formula (*peyyālabheda*), based on the root cases such as "a mother sends a bhikkhu," and so forth.
Since that too can be understood by following the textual sequence according to the method previously explained, we have not taken the trouble to show its detailed analysis.
However, regarding the two sets of four terms beginning with "accepts" (*paṭiggaṇhāti*), in the first set, by the initial term, there is the perfection of the three factors (*tivaṅgasampatti*).
There is a *saṅghādisesa* offense when two factors are fulfilled in the middle; a *thullaccaya* when one factor is fulfilled at the end; and a *dukkaṭa* when one factor is fulfilled at the beginning.
In the second tetrad, there is a *thullaccaya* due to the fulfillment of two factors by the first term; a *dukkaṭa* due to the fulfillment of one factor by the two middle terms;
and no offense (*anāpatti*) at the end because of the absence of any factor. In this context, "accepts" means the instruction of the sender.

He accepts. "He investigates" means that having gone to the place where he was sent, he reports it. "He brings back a report" means that having returned, he reports it to the one who was at the source.
"He does not bring back a report" means that after reporting it, he departs from there. "He accepts but does not investigate" means by a man...

When one is told, "Go to such-and-such a person and speak," and having accepted that message with the words "Very well," one then—whether having forgotten it or not—goes into her presence for some other business and sits down while saying something else entirely;
to this extent, it is said that "one accepts [the message] but does not investigate. Then, regarding her...
That woman says of her own accord, "It seems your attendant wishes to take me into his household.
Having said this, she speaks thus: "I shall become his wife," or "I shall not become his wife.
Without rejoicing in her words and without rejecting them, he simply rises from his seat in silence and goes into the presence of that man.
He reports that news; up to this point, it is said: "He does not investigate, but he returns [the message].
"He does not investigate and does not return" means that at the time of reporting the teaching, he merely receives it, but does not perform the other two actions.
"He does not receive it, but investigates and returns" refers to a certain person who, while a bhikkhu is standing or sitting...
Or, when someone speaks in such a manner, even though not sent by him, the bhikkhu goes to the woman as if he were sent;
having tested her by saying, "It is said you should become the wife of so-and-so," and so forth, he returns and reports her acceptance or rejection to this man.
Having tested her in that same manner, if he does not report back... [he commits an offense].

"He accepts, examines, and does not report back" is what is said. By that same method, one who has gone [to the teacher] and, without examining, hears the discussion raised by him, returns according to the method stated in the third phrase of the first tetrad and reports it to this person;
he is said to "not accept, not examine, and report back. The fourth phrase is self-evident.
The methods beginning with "he instructs many bhikkhus" are already evident.
Just as many [bhikkhus] may incur [an offense] regarding a single object, so too should it be understood that a single [bhikkhu] may incur many offenses regarding many objects.
How so? A man instructs a bhikkhu: "Go, venerable sir, to such-and-such a palace where there are about sixty or seventy..."
"Tell those women standing there: 'May you indeed become the wives of such-and-such a man.
Having accepted this, he goes there, delivers the message, and returns that report. For as many women as there are, so many offenses does he incur.
For this has been stated in the Parivāra as well:
“By merely stepping on [the shadow of] one’s footprint, and by what is spoken with the voice;
all these grave offenses, which require expiation—
sixty-four such offenses— one might incur them all at once.”
“This question was conceived by the wise.
It is said that this question was stated for this very purpose. Furthermore, it is expressed as “sixty-four offenses” here for the sake of the elegance of speech;
however, by acting in such a way, one may incur even a hundred or a thousand offenses. And just as by one person...
When one man who has been sent [as a messenger] approaches many women, there are many offenses;
likewise, when one man sends many monks to the presence of one woman, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for all of them.
When one man sends many monks to the presence of many women, there are *saṅghādisesa* offenses according to the number of women. When many men [send one monk...]
If they send one man to the presence of one woman, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for each man counted.
If many men send one man to the presence of many women, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for each basis counted.
If many men send many men to the presence of one woman, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for each basis counted. Many men [send many men] to many monks...
If they send [a messenger] to many women, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for each instance according to the number of cases.
This same principle applies to such cases as "one woman to one monk," and so forth. Furthermore, in this context, whether the parties are similar or dissimilar is irrelevant;
even if one acts as a go-between for one's own mother or father, or for five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, there is indeed an offense.
"A man instructs a bhikkhu, saying, 'Go, venerable sir,'"—this is stated for the purpose of showing the classification of offenses according to the four factors.
Regarding the final phrase, "the pupil, having investigated, reports it back externally":
this means that after returning, he does not inform his teacher, but instead goes directly from there and informs the man himself. For both of them, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
Because it was accepted by the teacher and because it was tested, there is a *thullaccaya* offense due to two factors;
because it was tested by the pupil and because it was brought back, there is a *thullaccaya* offense due to two factors. The rest is self-evident. 339.
"While going, he accomplishes [the act]" means that he both accepts and tests [the food]. "While coming, he deceives" means...

"He does not bring back [the robe]" means that because he goes away, he deceives [the donor], and thus he does not accept it. "He brings it back upon returning" means that he both investigates and brings it back.
Thus, in both cases, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for two factors. In the third phrase, there is an offense; in the fourth, there is no offense. 340.
There is no offense if one goes on account of the Saṅgha, or the shrine, or being ill, or on some business, or if one is insane.
Regarding the phrase "for the first offender": here, the Uposatha hall of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha or something else has been left unfinished.

In that case, if a lay follower (upāsaka) should send a bhikkhu to a laywoman (upāsikā), or a laywoman should send a bhikkhu to a lay follower, for the purpose of providing food and wages to the craftsmen—there is no offense for one who goes on such business for the sake of the Saṅgha. [This applies] regarding work at a cetiya.

The same principle applies even when [the offense] is being committed.
