There is no offense for one who goes to the presence of a layman (*upāsaka*) or a laywoman (*upāsikā*)—or for a laywoman going to the presence of a layman—if sent by a layman or a laywoman for the sake of medicine for the sick. Those such as the insane and first-time offenders are to be understood according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis (*padabhājanīya*) is finished.
Regarding the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors: this training rule has six origins.

It originates from the body in the case of one who, having received a message through a bodily gesture such as nodding the head, goes, tests it by means of a hand-sign, and then returns and reports it back by means of a hand-sign.
It also originates from the body in the case of one sitting in the assembly hall who says, "So-and-so will come; you should know her mind."
Having accepted with "Very well" when someone has spoken, and having told her that he had arrived, when she has departed and that man returns again,
it arises from the speech of one who reports [the matter] to him.
Having received the message with "Very well," and having gone to her house for some other business or while going elsewhere, upon seeing her, one examines her by means of verbal expression and then—
If, having departed from that place for some other business, one sees that person at some later time and informs them, it arises from speech alone.
However, for one who does not know the formal rule—even an arahant—it arises from both body and speech. How so?
For instance, if his parents, being angry, have become "unfit to be spoken to," and a monk enters their house...
The father says, "My dear son, your mother has abandoned me, an old man, and gone to her own family home;
go, send her back to attend upon me. If he goes, speaks to her, and then reports back to his father whether she has returned or not, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
These three cases originate from lack of intention (*acittaka*).

However, having understood the designation (*paṇṇatti*), for one who enters into sexual intercourse by means of these same three modes (*naya*), it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
These three originate with consciousness (*sacittaka-samudhāna*) through the consciousness that knows the designation.

They are functional (*kiriya*), not-liberated-from-perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), blameworthy by designation (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), bodily action (*kāya-kamma*), and verbal action (*vacī-kamma*); [they are further classified] according to the wholesome and so forth.
And herein, there are three types of consciousness; and by way of pleasure and so forth, there are three feelings.
341. Regarding the *Vinītavatthu* (cases of discipline), in the first five cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because [the food] was merely accepted.
In the case of the quarrel, regarding the phrase "he made a friendly greeting," having informed him of that, [he should go] again to the house.
"Did she? "She is not one to be spoken to with 'enough' (nālaṃvacanīyā)," which means she has not been relinquished.
For a woman who, however much she may be relinquished in various regions, still remains relinquished and does not transcend the status of a wife, is called "one to be spoken to with 'enough'.
But this woman was not one to be spoken to with 'enough'; she departed after having quarreled for some reason. It is for this very reason that the Blessed One [said this].

He said, “There is no offense. However, since a grave offense (thullaccaya) was stated for a female yakkha in the case of physical contact, it should be understood that in the cases of indecent conduct and so forth, female yakkhas and petīs likewise constitute grounds for a grave offense.
This, however, has not been discussed in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā).
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the training rule concerning matchmaking is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning the building of a hut (Kuṭikārasikkhāpada). 342.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning the building of a hut. In this context, "the people of Āḷavī" refers to children born in the province of Āḷavi.
They were known as the Āḷavakas; even at the time of their going forth, they were designated simply as “the Āḷavakas. It is with reference to them that it is said, “the Āḷavaka bhikkhus.
“By means of requisites obtained by begging” means those things taken after having been requested by themselves. “They have them built” means they both build themselves and have others build;
for it is said that they had abandoned both the duty of insight (vipassanā-dhura) and the duty of study (gantha-dhura) within the Teaching, and were occupied solely with building work.
Making it their primary task, they took it up. "Ownerless" means having no master; the meaning is that they were devoid of one who would cause them to be given away.
"Dedicated to oneself" means undertaken for the sake of oneself, directed toward oneself.
"Immeasurable" means those whose measure is not limited in this way, thinking "they will reach completion with just this much," or rather, those whose measure is increasing.
The meaning is "of great magnitude.
They are "abundant in begging" because begging itself is their primary activity and other work is dull for them; thus they should be understood as being abundant in requests (*viññatti*).
In terms of actual meaning, however, there is no difference here [between *yācanā* and *viññatti*], as it is said many times: "Give a man, give a man-doer."
"Give [us] a man! is a designation for those who beg. In this regard, it is not permissible to beg for a man for the purpose of cutting down a tree;
however, it is permissible to beg for a man "to give us a man" for the sake of companionship or for the sake of performing labor.
"Man-work" (*purisatthakara*) refers to manual labor to be performed by a man; it is permissible to beg for that. As for "manual labor," it is something... [some specific task].
The object itself is not [inappropriate]; therefore, with the exception of the personal work of deer-hunters, fishermen, and the like, everything else is allowable.
Whether asked, "Venerable sir, why have you come? or not asked, it is permissible to request [the goods];
there is no fault arising from the condition of a formal request (*viññatti*). Therefore, deer-hunters and the like [may provide] their own work...
They should be requested [for manual labor], but they should not be requested without specifying, saying, "Give us manual labor.
For if requested in that way, they might dismiss the monks with "Very well, Venerable Sir," and then go out and kill even a deer to bring it back. However, one should request by specifying:
"There is something to be done in the monastery; please provide manual labor for that. Tools such as plows, hoes, and so forth [should be provided].
It is indeed appropriate to ask for manual labor from a farmer or anyone else who is engaged in their own duties while going about to plow, sow, or reap.
However, if someone is a glutton or otherwise idle, dwelling in sleep or engaging in useless talk, one may approach such a person even without asking: "Come..."
"Or do this, or do that"—it is permissible to have whatever one desires done.
However, they explain this method for the purpose of illustrating that manual labor (*hatthakamma*) is entirely allowable.
For if a monk wishes to have a palace built, he may go to the house of stone-cutters to obtain pillars and say: "Manual labor..."
“It is permissible for you to receive them, lay followers. “What should be done, venerable sir? “The stone pillars should be removed and given [to us].
“If they give them after having removed them, or if they give their own pillars that have been set aside after being removed, it is permissible.
Or if they say: ‘Venerable sir, we have no time to do manual labor; please have someone else remove them,’ [then it is also permissible].”
Thinking, “We shall give him the price for it,” one may have it removed and say,
“Give the price for those people who have removed the stone pillars. By this same method, [one may ask] carpenters for the sake of palace timber,
bricklayers for the sake of bricks, roofers for the sake of roofing, and painters for the sake of painting.
Whatever purpose one may have, it is permissible to go to those various craftsmen and ask for their manual labor for that specific purpose.
And by way of requesting such labor, it is permissible to accept everything obtained, whether through cutting down trees or through the provision of food and wages.
Furthermore, by one who has things brought from the forest, everything that has not been previously inhabited must be brought.
Not only by one desiring to have a palace built, but also by one desiring to have beds,

stools, bowls, water-strainers, water-pots, robes, and so forth made, having obtained wood, metal, thread, and the like, one should approach the respective craftsmen and request manual labor in the manner already described.
And by means of requesting manual labor, either through the cutting down of the price (mūlacchejjā) or by the provision of food and wages—

Or, even if it has been obtained, all of it may be accepted. However, if they do not wish to do the work themselves and expect payment for their food, one must not give them unallowable coins and the like.
It is permissible to seek out rice and other provisions according to the practice of alms-gathering and give them.
Having had a bowl made by manual labor and having cooked [the rice] in that same manner, [one may use it] for the purpose of wiping a newly baked bowl with oil.
Having entered the village and perceived that [the donor] has come for alms, when rice gruel or a meal is brought, the bowl should be covered with the hand.
If a female lay devotee asks, "What is it, venerable sir?", one should say, "The bowl is newly washed;
there is need of oil for wiping. If she says, "Give it, venerable sir," and takes the bowl, one should wipe it with oil and [pour] the rice gruel...
If one gives after having filled [the bowl] with food, it is not called a formal request (*viññatti*); it is permissible to accept.
The monks, having already wandered for alms early in the morning, went to the assembly hall and stood there not seeing any seats.
If lay followers, seeing the monks standing there, themselves have seats brought and, after [the monks] have sat down, depart—

One must depart after having taken leave. For those who have departed without taking leave, although there is no liability for what is lost, departing only after taking leave is the proper duty (*vatta*).
If seats have been brought by monks who were told, "Bring the seats," one must still depart only after taking leave.
For those who depart without taking leave, there is both a breach of duty and liability for what is lost. The same principle applies to rugs, blankets, and so forth.
If there are many flies, one should say, "Bring a fly-whisk.
If they bring branches of the *pucimanda* tree or similar items, these should be accepted after having them made allowable (*kappiya*).
If the water vessel in the dining hall is empty, one should not say, "Take the water-pot (*dhamakaraṇa*)," for by placing the water-pot into an empty vessel, one might break it.
It is permissible to say, "Go to the river or the pond and bring water.
However, it is neither permissible to say, "Bring it from the house," nor should one consume what has been brought in that manner.

When those performing their meal duties in a dining hall or in the forest take any leaf or fruit suitable for a secondary course (*uttaribhaṅga*) that grows there and has not been inhabited by others, [it is permissible].
Alternatively, if he causes someone to bring something while performing some work, it is permissible to use it after having it brought by means of manual labor (*hatthakamma*).
However, one must not have manual labor performed by shameless monks or novices.
This, first of all, is the procedure regarding those who perform services for men.
However, it is not permitted to have an ox brought from a place where one is neither known nor invited; for one who has it brought there, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Even from a place where one is invited by kinsmen, it is not permitted to ask for it with the intent of cutting off its roots [of ownership];
in all other cases, it is permitted on the basis of temporary use. Having thus had the ox brought, one should protect and tend it, and then return it to the owner. If, however, it...
If a leg or a horn is broken or lost, it is well if the owners accept [the responsibility]; if they do not accept it, there is a fine.
If they say, "We shall give it back to you yourselves," one should not accept this.
But when they say, "We shall give it to the monastery," one should say, "Inform the monastery attendants so that they may look after it."
It is not permitted to say, “Give us a cart,” even to one who is unrelated and has not invited [one to accept]; it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) as soon as the request is made.
However, it is permitted in the case of a relative who has invited [one], and it is permitted for temporary use, provided that after the work is done, it must be returned.
If the rims or other parts are broken, they must be repaired before being returned. If it is lost, there is liability for its value.
When it is said, “We give it to you,” it is permissible to accept what is called a wooden vessel.

This same principle applies to axes, adzes, hatchets, hammers, and pickaxes, as well as to creepers and the like that belong to others. A formal request (*viññatti*) is permitted only for creepers and such items that are worth a heavy article;
it is not allowed for those of lesser value. However, anything that is unoccupied may be had brought to one. For a formal request is only valid in the case of places that are guarded and protected.
This is what is called [soliciting]. That is not permissible in any way whatsoever with respect to two requisites;
however, regarding the lodging-requisite, merely making a request such as "bring it" or "give it" is not permissible, whereas indirect talk, hinting, and giving signs are permissible.
In that regard, for one who desires a Uposatha hall, a dining hall, or any other kind of lodging, [the thought] "in this..."
To speak in such a manner as “It is proper to build such a dwelling in this place,” or “It is suitable,” or “It is appropriate,” and so forth, is called *parikathā* (indirect talk).

To ask, “Lay followers, where do you live? and when they reply, “In a mansion, Venerable Sir,” to then say, “But lay followers, is a mansion not proper for monks?”—speech such as this is called *obhāsa* (hinting). [Regarding] people...
Having seen [the site], he stretches out a rope and has stakes driven in. When asked, "What is this, venerable sir? he replies, "We shall build a dwelling here.
Such acts as these are called "preliminary work" (*nimittakamma*). However, even requesting requisites for the sick is permissible, let alone indirect speech and so forth.
For people are harassed by begging; they are harassed by requests. Therefore, because of those monks' begging...
And they are oppressed by the [threat of] command. They become terrified (*ubbijjanti*): they experience agitation, trembling, and shaking, thinking, "What will they have us bring?
They are frightened (*uttasanti*): like seeing a snake, they suddenly startle and flee.
They run away (*palāyanti*): from afar, they flee in this or that direction. They go by another way: that path which they had set out upon—
They turn back after leaving, or they go taking either the left or the right [path],
and they even bolt the doors. "In the past, monks," said the Blessed One, having thus rebuked those monks and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma appropriate to that,
he again made the fault of requesting [for requisites] manifest by means of this passage beginning with, "In the past, monks."

By this method, he showed three instances. Therein, "Maṇikaṇṭha" is said to have been that Nāga king who used to wander about with a precious, wish-fulfilling gem fastened around his neck; therefore, he was known as "Maṇikaṇṭha.
He stood having formed a great hood over his head; it is said that he was the youngest of those two seers.
The seer was dwelling in loving-kindness; therefore, the Naga king, having emerged from the river, assumed the form of a deity and sat near him.
After exchanging greetings, he abandoned that divine form and resumed his own natural appearance.
Then, surrounding the seer and manifesting an attitude of faith, he raised a great hood over the seer’s head.
Standing for a moment as if holding up a parasol, he departed; therefore it is said: "He stood having formed a great hood over his head.
"A jewel was fastened upon his neck" means a jewel was bound upon his neck; the sense is that it was worn.
"He stood to one side" means that, having arrived in the form of a deity, he stood exchanging greetings with the ascetic.
He stood in one place.
"My food and drink" means my food and my drink. "Abundant" means plentiful. "Exalted" means refined.
"You are a constant beggar" means you are an excessive beggar; it is said that you beg again and again. "Susū" means young, endowed with strength.
"A man who has reached the prime of youth. A "pebble" (*sakkharā*) is called a black stone; a sword polished on such a stone is called "pebble-polished" (*sakkharadhota*).
One who has such a pebble-polished sword in his hand is "one with a pebble-polished hand" (*sakkharadhotapāṇi*); the meaning is that he holds a sword sharpened and polished on a rock.
Just as that man with the sword in his hand would strike out in terror, so did he terrify me while begging for the rock—meaning, while begging for the jewel.
One does not beg that from which one should not beg. Which [is that]? That which one desires to win over as dear to a being; one should know what is dear to that being.
How much more so, then, regarding those who have become human—what need is there to say that what is unpleasant to them [should not be done]?
345. "Harassed by the cry of a flock of birds": it is said that this flock of birds [was present] during both the first watch and the last watch.
He made a continuous sound; that bhikkhu, being oppressed by that sound, went into the presence of the Blessed One.
Therefore he said: "I approached him.
Regarding the question, "From where have you come, bhikkhu?", that bhikkhu was sitting there and had not actually come from anywhere in the immediate vicinity.
But it is permissible to speak thus. Therefore he said: “From where, monk, do you come? The meaning is: “Whence have you come?
The same principle applies here as well in the phrase, “From there, Blessed One, I am coming. “Ubbāḷho” means oppressed; the meaning is, having become distressed.

Regarding the statement, “That flock of birds [thought], ‘The monk asks for a bowl’”—those birds did not understand the words of the monk, but the Blessed One, by his own power, acted in such a way that they came to know them.
346. "I do not know you"—even among people, I do not know who these are or to whom they belong.
"Begging together" means having gathered together, they beg in groups. "The beggar is unpleasant" means that whoever begs becomes unpleasant.
"One who does not give what is begged for is unpleasant": "begged for" refers to what is requested; even one who does not grant the thing requested [is unpleasant].
He becomes unloved. Or else, when people beg, he who does not give to the one begging becomes unloved; thus, by not giving, he becomes unloved. "May there be no estrangement for me" means:
may there be no state of being unloved for me; that is, "may I not be a stranger or unloved to you, nor may you be a stranger or unloved to me.
(347) "Difficult to acquire" means: things that are to be acquired with difficulty through means such as plowing, cattle-herding, and so forth.
348–9. Regarding the phrase "a nun by means of a *saññācikā*": here, *saññācikā* refers to a request made by oneself;
therefore, "by means of a *saññācikā*" means "by means of one's own request. The sense is: "by means of requisites requested by oneself.
Since that [robe] is being made from things requested by oneself, it is "being made after having requested them oneself"; therefore—
In order to demonstrate this method of exposition (*atthapariyāya*), the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for this [verse] was stated as: “Having requested it himself, even from a man.
*Ullitta* means smeared on the inside. *Avalitta* means smeared on the outside. *Ullittāvalitta* means smeared both inside and outside; this is what is meant.
Regarding the phrase “by one having it made,” in the word-commentary for this, only “by one having it caused to be made” (*kārāpentena*) should have been said; for in this way—

The phrasing is consistent. However, since one who builds a hut by means of a formal request must also proceed according to the method stated here, whether he is building it himself or having it built, both are included by the very term "by one who is having it made.
To show this meaning, it is said: "whether building or having it built. But if [the offense applies] to one who is either building or having it built...
If one were to speak thus, the phrasing would be inverted; for one who causes another to do [an action] is not called the "doer" himself.
Therefore, it should be understood that only the meaning is shown here. Regarding *attuddesa*:
it is called *attuddesa* because the self (*atta*) is the designation (*uddesa*)—"this belongs to me"—thus it is *attuddesa*; that which is such is *taṃ attuddesaṃ*. Since...
However, for one who designates it for oneself, it is for one's own benefit; therefore, showing the method of the meaning, he said: "Designated for oneself means for one's own benefit.
"It should be caused to be built according to measure" means it should be caused to be built with appropriate proportions.
"In this regard, this is the measure": this is the measure for that hut. "By the Sugata-span": now, a Sugata-span is [defined as] that of a person of medium height.
Three spans of a man measured by the carpenter’s cubit is one and a half cubits.
"By the external measurement" means by the measurement outside the wall of the hut; however, when measuring, the first layer of large plaster applied [to the wall] must not be included.
It should be measured up to the limit of the straw-bundle. Any white plaster work above the straw-bundle is not counted.
If he does not require even that much clay, but finishes it with just large lumps of clay, then the large lumps of clay themselves constitute the limit.
"Horizontally" means in width. "Seven" means seven *sugata-vidatthis*. "Internally" is this explanation for that term:
"by the internal measurement"; that is, when measuring by the inner edge, without taking the outer edge of the wall.
It is said that the measurement is seven Sugata-spans across.
However, if one who makes a false claim intends to make it exactly the stated measurement,
yet makes it eleven spans long and eight spans across, or thirteen spans long and six spans across;
It is not allowable. For even if it exceeds the measure by only one side, it is indeed considered to have exceeded the measure. Let alone a span;

it is not allowable to shorten it by even as much as a hair’s breadth either in length or in width and then increase the length again—how much less so when increasing both dimensions? For this has been said: “Even if [it exceeds] in length or in width, at the very least...”
"If one makes it or causes it to be made exceeding even the measure of a hair's breadth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the preliminary effort," and so forth.

Only that which is of the aforementioned dimensions is permissible. However, that which is sixty cubits in length but only three cubits or less than four cubits in width—where a bed of standard size cannot turn from side to side—is not reckoned as a "hut" (kuṭī).
Therefore, this too is permissible. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that at the maximum limit, it may be four cubits in width;

anything smaller than that is a hut (*akuṭi*). Furthermore, even if it is within the prescribed measure, it is not permissible if the site has not been formally assigned, if there is construction work underway, or if there is no space for circumambulation.

Only that which is within the prescribed measure, where the site has been formally assigned, where there is no construction work, and where there is space for circumambulation, is permissible—even if it is slightly less than the full measure.
When constructing [a dwelling] four or even five cubits in size, it must be built on a site already authorized by the Teacher.
Furthermore, one who constructs it exceeding the prescribed measurement incurs a grave offense at the completion of the plastering.
In this context, "plastered," "unplastered," "place for plastering," and "place not for plastering" should be understood. To explain: "plastered" means...

There are two kinds of plastering: clay plaster and lime plaster. However, setting aside these two types of plaster, all other varieties such as ash, cow dung, and so forth, are non-plastering (alepa).
Even if it is a thick paste-like plaster, it is still considered non-plastering. "The place for plastering" refers to walls and ceilings;
however, setting aside walls and ceilings, everything else—such as pillars, beams, floor-joists, door-frames, windows, smoke-vents, and so on—is not included.
Every place that is unfit for plastering should be understood as "a place unfit for plastering.
"Bhikkhus should be brought for the selection of the site" means that bhikkhus should be led to the place where one intends to have the hut built, for the purpose of selecting the site.
The phrase beginning with "by that builder of the hut," however, refers to the procedure by which those bhikkhus should be brought.
This was said for the purpose of showing that. In this context, "having cleared the site for the hut" means that one should not go taking monks into a rugged forest;

rather, it shows that first the site for the hut must be cleared, made level like the circle of a boundary (sīmamaṇḍala), and only afterwards should one approach the Saṅgha, make the request, and lead them there. "In this way he should speak" [is the instruction].
The Saṅgha should be addressed in this way. However, the plural form in the subsequent phrase, “it should be requested a second time,” is used with reference to the monks.
“If the entire Saṅgha is not able” means if the entire Saṅgha does not consent, because those various monks are occupied with recitation, mental attention, and so forth.
“With construction” means with a calamity; “without construction” means without a calamity. “With space for circumambulation.”
"Unenclosed" means with or without a precinct (*upacāra*).
"The time has arrived" (*pattakalla*) means that the time for this looking has arrived; thus it is *pattakāla*, and *pattakāla* itself is *pattakalla*.

Furthermore, this formal act of authorization (*sammuti-kamma*) for the purpose of inspecting the site may be performed even after having inspected it by way of a formal proclamation (*anusāvana-naya*).
Furthermore, the act of designating the site must be performed by means of the motion (*ñatti*) and the proclamation (*anusāvana*) exactly as previously described;
it is not permitted to do so merely by looking [at the site].
353. *Kipillikānaṃ* refers to any kind of ants whatsoever, such as the red, black, brown, and other varieties. It is also written as *kipīllakānaṃ*.

The reading is as follows. "Abode" (*āsaya*) means a place where one dwells permanently; and just as it is for ants, so too for termites and the like, their abode should be understood as a place where they dwell permanently.
However, as for the places where they come and go for the sake of foraging, such areas of movement are unrestricted for all of them;
therefore, it is permissible to remove them from there, clear the area, and build [the hut]. These, first of all, are...
Six places are prohibited out of compassion for living beings.
"Of elephants" means that it is not permitted [to stay] even at a place where elephants reside permanently or a place where they regularly graze;
nor is it permitted at the lair of lions and other such animals, or on the regular path taken by them when setting out to forage.
The range of their activity has not been included. "Of any whatsoever" refers to other predatory animals as well, such as those belonging to the animal realm (*tiracchānagata*).
These seven places, being full of danger, are prohibited for the sake of the monks' health.
The remaining ones are fraught with various calamities. Therein, "dependent on standing crops" means dependent on the seven types of standing crops.
It stands adjacent to a field where grain grows. This same method applies to those dependent on other crops and so forth.
Here, however, *abbhāghāta* refers to a slaughterhouse, a house of enmity, or one built for the purpose of killing thieves, according to the *Kurundi-ṭīkā* and other sources.

*Āghātana* is called a place of execution. *Susāna* refers to a great cemetery. *Saṃsaraṇa* refers to a path that must be traversed back and forth without being able to turn away. The rest is self-evident.

"It is not possible with a cart yoked as usual" means that it is not possible to maneuver a cart yoked with two oxen by turning one wheel in a place where water falls and keeping the other outside. However, in the *Kurundi* it is stated: "with four [oxen] yoked.
"To go all around along the ladder" means by those covering the house while standing on the ladder.

It is not possible to climb all around it by means of a ladder. Thus, in such a place that involves harm to living beings (*sārambha*) and lacks a path for circumambulation (*aparikkamana*), a hut must not be built.

However, it may be built in a place where there is no harm to living beings and where there is a path for circumambulation; this is already included in the text according to the method opposite to what was previously stated.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Now, as for 'by means of a request' (*saññācikā*)," etc., is stated for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of "by means of a request" and so forth, as spoken in the rule: "If a monk, by means of a request, should have a hut built on ground involving harm to living beings and lacking a path for circumambulation."

"An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding the use": thus, if one intends, "I shall have a hut built whose site has not been formally designated or which exceeds the prescribed dimensions," and lays down an axe or a hatchet for the purpose of felling trees from the forest, there is an offense of wrong-doing; if he enters the forest, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
if he cuts green grass there, there is a formal offense of expiation (pācittiya) together with an offense of wrong-doing; if he cuts dry [grass], there is an offense of wrong-doing.

The same method applies to trees as well. When one clears the ground, digs, removes soil, and piles it up—in this way, everything up until the binding of the embankment is called "preliminary effort" (*pubbapayoga*).

Regarding that preliminary effort, in all cases where there would otherwise be a *pācittiya* offense, there is a *pācittiya* together with a *dukkaṭa*; in cases where there would otherwise be a *dukkaṭa*, there is a *dukkaṭa*. From that point onward, it is called "concurrent effort" (*sahapayoga*).

In that regard, for one who erects a pillar when a pillar is to be made, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For one who piles bricks when bricks are to be built, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
Thus, for every application of whatever accessory material is being prepared, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each such application.
For one who fashions it with a knife, there is an offense of wrong-doing for every stroke of the hand; for one who goes for that purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing at every step. Thus...
Furthermore, regarding a wooden wall, a brick wall, or a stone wall—
even down to a leaf-hut provided with walls and a roof— if one intends, "I shall plaster this," and applies either lime or clay,
for every application until the *thullaccaya* (grave offense) occurs, there is *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). However, this *dukkaṭa* applies only when the plastering is extensive.
There is no offense in making a red color or in painting.
"When one lump has not yet arrived" means when that single final lump of plaster has not yet reached the construction of the hut.
This is what is meant: when it is known, "Now it will reach completion with two lumps," there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) at the giving of the first of those lumps.

"Regarding 'when that last lump has been brought': when that one final lump which, if not yet brought, would constitute a *thullaccaya* offense for the construction of a hut—once that final lump has been brought, given, and set aside, because the plastering has been joined together, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
Thus, for one who is plastering, whether it be internal plaster, or having made the wall and the roof a single unit together with the internal plaster..."
If it is joined with an external plaster, or if an external plaster is joined [with the wall], it is a *saṅghādisesa*.

However, if one applies clay without leaving a gap for a door-panel or a window, and that plaster does not join with the existing surface—whether the space for it is subsequently increased or not—it remains protected for the time being; but when one applies more clay again, as soon as it has joined, [the offense occurs].
It is a *saṅghādisesa*. If, while being plastered, it stands in immediate contact with the first layer of plaster already applied, it is a *saṅghādisesa* from that very first moment.
There is no offense if one plasters the wall after leaving a space of eight finger-breadths uncovered for the purpose of preventing termites.
Likewise, there is no offense if one constructs a stone floor below for the very same purpose of preventing termites.
If one applies plaster over [a surface] without first plastering it, it is called "the plaster does not adhere," and there is no offense at all.
If one makes windows and smoke-vents in a brick-walled house using bricks themselves, there is an offense only when the plaster adheres.
If one plasters a leaf-hut, there is an offense only when the plaster adheres. In that case, for the sake of light, [one may leave] a space measuring eight finger-breadths...
If one applies plaster while leaving a portion aside, such that the plaster does not join together, there is no offense at all.
If one builds with the thought, "I will place it here once I have obtained a window," there is an offense when the plaster joins together once it has been placed at the window.
If one builds a wall with clay, there is an offense when it joins together with the plaster for the roof. If one person sets aside a remainder of a single lump, [there is no offense].
If another person, seeing that [work], says "this is a *dukkaṭa* offense" by way of formal procedure, there is no offense for either of them. 354.
The thirty-six tetrads beginning with "a bhikkhu builds a hut" are stated for the purpose of showing the classification of offenses;

therein, for building on a site where there is danger, there is a *dukkaṭa*; for building where there is no space for circumambulation, there is a *dukkaṭa*; for exceeding the prescribed measurement, there is a *saṅghādisesa*.
There is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for one who has not confessed the basis [of the offense]; by means of these, mixed offenses (*vomissakāpatti*) are to be understood. 355.

Regarding such cases as "an offense of two *saṅghādisesas* and two *dukkaṭas*," the meaning should be understood according to the method beginning with "two *dukkaṭas* together with two *saṅghādisesas*.
361. However, regarding such passages as "If he returns when it is unfinished," this is the analysis of the meaning: "He" refers to the one who gave the command.

"A monk who has departed. "Incomplete" means while the construction of the hut is not yet finished. "Or it should be given to another" means it should be relinquished and given to another person or to the Saṅgha.
"Or having demolished it, it should be built again": by how much is it considered demolished?
If the pillars were driven into the ground, they must be pulled out; if they were placed on top of stones, they must be removed.
In the case of a brick-built [stupa], the walls must be dismantled down to the auspicious bricks. Briefly stated, it is considered destroyed when reduced to level with the ground;
even if it remains standing four finger-breadths above the ground, it is not yet destroyed. The rest is clear in all the fourfold sets.
There is nothing else here that would be difficult to understand, as it follows the sequence of the canonical text itself.
363. Regarding the phrases beginning with "one's own unfinished" (*attanā vippakataṃ*), "one's own" refers to a hut commenced by oneself.
"One completes it oneself" means that when one desires to bring it to completion using either great clay or husk-clay—whichever was used—one completes it by applying the final layer of plaster.
"One has it completed by others" means one has it completed by others for one's own sake; for [the hut] may indeed have been left unfinished by oneself.
Whether it be by others or by both, if one brings it to completion for one's own benefit— either completing it oneself, having it completed by others,
or completing it through a combination of oneself and others— it is indeed a *saṅghādisesa*;
this is the legal determination in this matter.
In the *Kurundi* it is also said: “If two or three bhikkhus make an arrangement, thinking, ‘We shall dwell together,’ it is still protected;
because there has been no formal division, there is no offense. If they make an arrangement after dividing it, saying, ‘This place is yours, this is mine,’ there is an offense.
When a novice and a bhikkhu make an arrangement together, it is protected as long as there has been no division. According to the previous method...”
"If they build by dividing [the work], there is an offense for the monk.
(364) Regarding "there is no offense in the case of a shelter" and so forth: there is no offense for one building even a large shelter, for here plastering is not involved.
There is also no offense for one building even a large cave—whether it be a brick cave, a stone cave, a wooden cave, or an earthen cave.
"Of a grass hut": even a seven-storied palace with a roof of grass and leaves is called a "grass hut.

However, in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is specifically stated that a "hen-pecked house" refers only to a small hut covered with grass or leaves after the roof has been constructed as a lattice-work of sticks;
in such a case, there is no offense. It is permissible to build even a large house with a grass roof.
For the very state of being plastered over and so forth is the characteristic of a hut (*kuṭī*), and it should be understood that this was stated with reference specifically to the roofing.

Statements such as, "Monks, I allow you to make [the floor] plastered over and whitewashed after having smeared it with mud," in the context of the walking-hall (*caṅkama-sālā*) where grass and dust fall, serve as proof for this.
Therefore, whether it be double-sided, gabled, or circular, it is permissible.
Or, regarding that which is square and is designated as the "roof" of this house by way of being a roof-covering:
when the plaster has been joined with the plaster of the walls, there is an offense.

However, if they cover it above with grass for the purpose of protecting the plaster of a house that has already been plastered inside and out, it does not, at this point, constitute what is called a "grass hut."

But here, is there an offense-free state (anāpatti) only due to the conditions of the site not being specified, the construction not exceeding the proper measure, and the materials being provided? Or is there also an offense-free state due to the conditions of there being no new construction and sufficient space around it?
[The answer is: There is an offense-free state in all these cases. For, with reference to such a hut, it is stated in the Parivāra:
"A bhikkhu builds a hut by means of a formal request..."
“There is no offense for that which has not been designated as a site, which exceeds the proper measure, where there is harm to living beings, or where there is no space on all sides.
This question was conceived by those who are skilled.”

"For the sake of another" means that there is no offense for one who builds a hut— even if it possesses the characteristics of a "crooked" (excessive) hut— for the sake of another, such as another preceptor,
a teacher, or the Saṅgha. As for what is stated in the Pāḷi, "there is an offense of three *dukkaṭas* for the craftsmen," etc.,
that was stated on account of their failure to act according to the instructions given.

"Except for his own dwelling place, in all other cases": having set aside the house he uses for his own residence, if he has another building made—whether it be an Uposatha hall, a bathhouse, a dining hall, or a fire-hall—there is no offense in all such instances.
Even if he thinks, "There will be an Uposatha hall, and I shall reside there, as well as a bathhouse and a dining hall..."
Even if one has it built with the thought, "There shall be both a fire-hall and a place for me to dwell," there is no offense.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, after stating "there is no offense," it is further said: "But for one who builds it specifically for the purpose of his own dwelling-house, there is an offense.
There is no offense for one who is insane or for the *ādikammikas* (first offenders), such as the monks of Āḷavī.
Regarding the origins and so forth, it has six origins: both action (*kiriya*) and non-action (*akiriya*).

For this [offense] arises from action when one makes the object exceed its measure after having had it pointed out; it arises from non-action when one does so without having had the object pointed out.

It is not liberated by perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*), is without consciousness (*acittaka*), is an offense by rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), is bodily action (*kāya-kamma*) and verbal action (*vacī-kamma*), consists of three types of consciousness (*ticitta*), and consists of three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the building of a hut is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning the building of a monastery (vihārakāra). 365.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning the building of a monastery. In this context, "at Kosambī" means in the city of that name.
"At Ghositārāma" means in the monastery of Ghosita. It was reportedly built by a merchant named Ghosita; therefore, it is called "Ghositārāma.
"Of Channa" refers to Channa, who was his attendant during the time of the Bodhisatta. "Vihāravatthuṃ, bhante, jānāhi" means:
"Venerable sir, know the site for the monastery"—that is, know the place where the monastery is to be established. And here, "vihāra" does not refer to the entire monastery, but to a single...
It is a dwelling; for this very reason it was said: “I shall have a monastery built for the noble one. Regarding the term *cetiyarukkha*:
here, in the sense of being honored (*cittīkata*), it is a *cetiya*; this is a designation for shrines worthy of worship (*pūjārahāni devaṭṭhānāni*).
A tree that is recognized as a *cetiya* is a *cetiyarukkha*. That which is honored by a village, or that which belongs to a village’s honor, is a *gāmapūjita*.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Furthermore, in this context, "province" (*janapada*) refers to each individual district within the kingdom of a single king.
"Kingdom" (*raṭṭha*) should be understood as the entire kingdom; for even the whole kingdom sometimes performs worship to that tree, which is why it is called "honored by the kingdom.
"Single-facultied" (*ekindriya*) is said with reference to the body-faculty (*kāyindriya*).
"Perceiving it as a living being" means perceiving it as a sentient being.
"Large" (*mahallaka*): it is called "large" because it possesses a state of greatness compared to a hut built by begging with a designated owner;
or alternatively, because it is permissible to build it even beyond the prescribed measurements after having had the site assigned, it is large by virtue of its great dimensions.

"Large" means that which is large in size. Since such magnitude is obtained only because it has an owner, the word-commentary "A 'large' dwelling is said to be one with an owner" was stated in order to show that meaning.
The rest of it—all of it—should be understood according to the method already explained in the training rule on building a hut, together with its origin and other details.
For here, the distinction consists merely in the fact that there is no arising from an action and no restriction regarding the measurement;
and because of this lack of restriction on the measurement, there is the forfeiture of the fourfold [set].
The commentary on the training rule concerning the building of a monastery is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Malice (Paṭhamaduṭṭhadosasikkhāpada) 380.
"At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... refers to the training rule concerning malice (*duṭṭhadosasikkhāpada*).
In this context, "in Veḷuvana, at Kalandakanivāpa": *Veḷuvana* is the name of that park; it is said to have been surrounded by bamboos (*veḷu*) eighteen cubits (*hattha*) high.
And because it was surrounded by a wall provided with gate-towers and watchtowers, blue in luster, and delightful, it was called "Veḷuvana" (the Bamboo Grove).
Furthermore, because they gave fodder for the squirrels there, it was called "Kalandakanivāpa" (the Squirrels' Feeding Place).
It is said that formerly a certain king came there for the purpose of a pleasure excursion in the park; intoxicated by wine, he fell asleep during the day.
While he was sleeping, his attendants also fell asleep; thinking, "The king is a man," and being tempted by flowers, fruits, and other such things, he wandered here and there.
Then, drawn by the scent of the liquor, a black snake emerged from a hollow tree and came toward the king.
Seeing this, a tree deity, thinking, "I shall give life to the king," approached him in the guise of a crow.
He made a sound at the root of the king’s ear; the king woke up, and the black snake retreated.
Seeing this, the king thought, "My life has been saved by this black one," and he established a supply of fodder there for the black ones and had a proclamation of safety made.
Therefore, from that time on, it became known as Kalandakanivāpa. For "Kalandaka" is indeed a name for black ones.
Dabba was the name of that elder. "Son of the Malla" means the son of the Malla king. Regarding the statement that he realized arahantship at seven years of age:

it should be understood that the elder, having attained a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) while still only seven years old, went forth into homelessness and reached arahantship on the very day his hair was cut.
Whatever can be attained by a disciple, all that was attained by him.

That which is to be attained by a disciple consists of this collection of qualities: the three types of higher knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*), the four analytical insights (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidāḥ*), the six direct knowledges (*ṣaḍ abhijñāḥ*), and the nine supramundane states (*nava lokottara-dharmāḥ*). All of that has been reached by him. There is nothing further to be done for him;
because he has performed the sixteenfold function through the four paths regarding the four truths, there is now nothing further for him to do.
"There is nothing further to be done" means that there is no further increase of what has already been accomplished;
it is like washing a garment that has already been washed, grinding a scent that has already been ground, or picking a flower that has already blossomed.
"Of one who has gone into seclusion" means of one who has gone to a private place. "Of one who is withdrawn in meditation" (paṭisallīnassa) means...
“Having withdrawn from here and there, having become secluded,” this is what is meant;
that is, having attained solitude. Then it occurred to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
“What if I were to assign lodgings for the Saṅgha and designate the meals? It is said that the Elder, seeing that his own task was accomplished, thought: “I—”
"I bear this final body, yet it stands at the mouth of impermanence like a lamp placed at the mouth of the wind;
it is subject to extinction before long. While it has not yet gone out, what service might I perform for the Saṅgha?
Thinking thus, he reflected: "In foreign lands there are many sons of noble family who [serve] the Blessed One..."
Having seen [the Blessed One], they go forth; thinking, "We shall see him and pay homage to him," they come from afar.
There, those for whom there is no lodging prepare their beds even on stone slabs.
Indeed, by my own power, I am able to provide for those sons of good family, according to their wishes, palaces, monasteries, half-stories, couches, seats, and coverlets.
and having conjured up an army and its commander, he could provide for them. Furthermore, on the following day, some of them would become exceedingly exhausted;
out of deference, they would stand before the bhikkhus and not even request meals to be assigned.
"But I am indeed capable of assigning meals for them"—as the Venerable Dabba was thus reflecting, [the thought occurred to him: "Then, indeed, the Venerable Dabba..."
It occurred to Mallaputta: "What if I were to assign lodgings for the Saṅgha and designate meals?

Now, are not these two matters appropriate for one devoted to delighting in talk and such activities? And yet, this [monk] is one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) and delights in the non-proliferated (nippapañca);
why did these thoughts occur to him? Because he was impelled by a former aspiration. It is said that for all Buddhas, this...

Disciples indeed attain such a station. And this man, having been reborn in a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, saw the power of that bhikkhu who had attained this station;
he then invited the Blessed One together with six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus for seven days, and having given a great almsgiving, [he made a vow].

Prostrating at the Blessed One’s feet, he made this aspiration: “In the future, when a Buddha such as you appears, may I also, by the name of so-and-so, be like your disciple, serving as both your assigner of lodgings and your distributor of meals.
The Blessed One, having dispatched his knowledge of the future, saw this; and having seen it, [he declared that] after the passing of one hundred thousand eons from now...

“A Buddha named Gotama will arise; at that time, you, having become a Malla youth named Dabba and having gone forth into homelessness at the age of seven, will realize Arhatship and obtain this very position,” he prophesied.
From then on, fulfilling the perfections of generosity, virtue, and so forth, and having experienced the prosperity of gods and humans, [he was born] under our Blessed One.
In due course, he realized Arahantship exactly as had been prophesied by the Blessed One. Then, while he was alone in seclusion, thinking,
"What service might I perform for the Saṅgha?", these two matters occurred to him, prompted by his former aspiration.
Then it occurred to him: "I am indeed not independent regarding myself; I live in the same place as the Teacher.
If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I shall undertake these two practices. He went into the presence of the Blessed One.
Thus it is said: "Then the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta... [and so on] ...to assign the meals."
Then the Blessed One, having encouraged him with the words, “Excellent, excellent, Dabba,” said:

“Since a bhikkhu such as you—one who is excluded from going on wrong paths—is worthy to deliberate upon these two matters, therefore, Dabba, you shall assign lodgings for the Saṅgha and designate the meals.
He replied to the Blessed One, meaning he listened to the word of the Blessed One.
"Face-to-face" means he heard it; "accepted" is what is meant.
Why did the Blessed One cause Dabba to be requested [to perform the task]? For the sake of releasing him from blame.
For the Blessed One foresaw: "In the future, there will be a great calamity for Dabba on account of this matter, arising through the Mettiya-Bhummajaka monks."
“...it will arise, and therein some will criticize him, saying: ‘Why does this man, remaining silent and not performing his own work, concern himself with such a matter?
Then others will say: ‘What fault is there in him? He was appointed by these very people after being requested. In this way, he will be freed from criticism.
Having thus had him request [permission] for the sake of being freed from criticism, [the Buddha said: “Furthermore, since [one who is] unappointed...”
When a bhikkhu says something in the midst of the Saṅgha, the tendency to criticize arises:
"Why does he make such a loud noise in the midst of the Saṅgha? He is showing off his authority! But when one who has been formally appointed speaks, people say:
"Venerable sirs, do not say anything; this one has been appointed, let him speak as he pleases. And when one who is unappointed speaks falsely...

For one who falsely accuses [an unappointed monk], there is a light offense, merely a *dukkaṭa*. However, for one who falsely accuses a monk who has been appointed, there is a more serious offense, a *pācittiya*.
Furthermore, because of the gravity of the offense, the appointed monk is even harder for his adversaries to overcome;
therefore, in order to have such a venerable one appointed, the text says, "by a competent monk," and so forth. But what [is meant by "competent"]?
Is it permissible to give two formal agreements (*sammuti*) to one person? Not only two; if he is capable, even thirteen may be given.
However, for those who are insufficient [to receive all], it is permissible to give even one to two or three.
382. "Of those who are similar" means similar in virtue (*guṇa*), not similar in terms of friendship or intimacy. For this very reason, he said: "Those monks..."

"Those who are experts in the Suttas [should be assigned] together," and so forth. For as many as there are experts in the Suttas, having selected them, he assigns suitable lodgings for them all together;
and likewise for the others. "Devoted to bodily fortitude" means those who are frequently engaged in strengthening the body;

the meaning is that they are frequently engaged in nourishing the body. "And these venerable ones find delight in this"—in this [state], which is like a state of being an animal on the path to heaven.
"Delighting in frivolous talk. "They will dwell" means they will live.

"Having entered the fire-element attainment and by that very light" means: having entered the fourth jhāna of the fire-kasina, and having emerged, one resolves upon the blazing of the fingers through the knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññā-ñāṇa); it is by that very light from the blazing of the fingers produced by the attainment of the fire-element.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, this power of the Elder soon became well known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa;
having heard of it, even monks desiring to see his miracle of psychic power would intentionally arrive late.

Knowing that they were intentionally making excuses for being far away, they would indeed make excuses for being far away. How so? By way of saying, "Friend Dabba, we are at Vulture Peak," and so forth.

"Going ahead and ahead with his finger burning": if there is only one bhikkhu, he goes by himself. If there are many, he emanates many bodies. All of them, being identical to himself, prepare the lodgings.

However, when the Elders say "this is a couch" and so forth, even the emanated forms say "this is a couch" in each respective place they have gone to; this applies to all such instances. For this is the nature of emanations:
"When one speaks, all the emanated ones speak."
“When one sits in silence, they all become silent.

Furthermore, in whatever monastery couches, chairs, and so forth were lacking, he would fill them there by his own power; thus, for those things created by him, there was no statement lacking a physical basis.
Having prepared lodgings, he returned again to Veḷuvana; this means that he did not sit down with them to engage in talk about the countryside, but returned instead to his own dwelling place.
383. *Mettiya-bhūmajaka*: Mettiya and Bhūmajaka; these were the foremost among the group of six.
Regarding "inferior meals": it is not surprising that inferior lodgings first fall to the newcomers.
As for the meals, however, they would place the voting sticks (*salākā*) either in a basket or within the folds of their robes, mix them together, and [distribute] one by one...
Having set it aside, they designate [other food], yet due to their own meager merit, even those [designated portions] turn out to be poor quality and reach them as the very last of all.
Furthermore, when there is a meal for a single wanderer, on the day these [monks] receive their alms, that meal is either of poor quality, or else, upon seeing them,
people do not give fine food but give only what is poor.

"Prepared" (*abhisaṅkhārika*) means made by preparing it with various ingredients; the meaning is that it is well-arranged and well-prepared. "Barley-gruel" (*kaṇājaka*) means rice mixed with broken grains. "With sour gruel as the second" (*bilaṅgadutiya*) means having sour gruel as the companion [food].
"One who eats fine food" (*kalyāṇabhattika*) means one for whom the food (*bhatta*) is fine, beautiful, and exceedingly refined;
he is known by his food because he gives such refined [food]. "He gives four meals" (*catukkabhattaṃ deti*) means he gives four [meals].
However, it is expressed by way of derivative terminology (*taddhita*) as “the four-meal meal.
“He serves after standing near” means that having set aside all his own duties and performed great honor and respect, he stands nearby and serves.
“Inquiring about the rice” means that approaching with rice in their hands, they inquire, saying, “Venerable sir, what rice shall we give?”; thus, it is used precisely in the sense of the instrument.
The word "karaṇa" (instrumental) is used here. This same method applies to the case of the soup and so forth.

"For the sake of tomorrow" (*svātanāya*) means: that which exists for tomorrow is "tomorrow's meal" (*svātana*); for its sake, that is, for the sake of the consumption of the meal to be prepared for tomorrow—this is what is meant.
"It has been assigned" (*uddiṭṭhaṃ*) means it has been brought and given. [This refers to] the case of Mettiya and Bhūmajaka.
“Householder,” [the Elder] said this without having reflected. For so powerful is their lack of merit that even those who have attained fullness of mindfulness fail to reflect.
In the phrase “Ye jeti,” *jeti* is used as a vocative addressing the slave-girl.
In the phrase “rātriṃ sammantayamānā atītaṃ divasabhāgaṃ sandhāya ‘hiyyo’ ti,” [the word] “hiyyo” (yesterday) refers to the past portion of the day while they were reflecting on the night.

They say: "Not according to mind" means not in accordance with their minds; whereas previously they would sleep for as long as they wished, they did not sleep in that way then—it is said that they slept only a very little.

"Outside the monastery gatehouse" means outside the gatehouse of the Veḷuvana Monastery. "With drooping shoulders" means with shoulders slumped, sitting with the backbone bent. "Fainting away" means emitting smoke (of distress).

"Where there was no wind, there is now wind" means that where there was no wind at all, a great wind has arisen; this is the intended meaning. "As if the water were burning" means it is as if the water itself were on fire.
384. "Do you remember, Dabba, doing such a thing? means: "Dabba, do you remember being the one who did such a thing? Or alternatively:
"Dabba, do you remember doing such a thing, as this bhikkhunī says? Do you recall being the one who did such a thing, as this [bhikkhunī] says?"
The meaning here should be understood by connecting it thus: "The bhikkhunī said. As for those who read "having done," for them [the meaning] is straightforward.
When the Elder says, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One know me as I am," what does he show? He shows: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is omniscient, and I am one whose taints are destroyed;
there is no further indulgence in objects for me. The Blessed One knows me as such; what then shall I say in that regard?"
"As the Blessed One knows me, so am I to be seen.
Regarding the statement, "Dabba, the wise do not resolve matters in this way," the meaning is: "Dabba, the wise do not resolve matters by relying on the testimony of others as you have done;
rather, they resolve them by that which has been known by themselves."
It must be seen. By the phrase "If it was done by you, it was done," what does he show?
For it is not possible, either through the power of an assembly or through the support of a faction, to make a non-doer into a doer, or to make a doer into a non-doer;
therefore, he shows that only that which was actually done or not done by oneself should be spoken of. But why did the Blessed One, though knowing [the answer], say "I..."?
“Did he not say, ‘I know you, you are one whose taints are destroyed; there is no fault in you, this bhikkhunī is a liar’?

It was out of compassion for others. For if the Blessed One were to say whatever he knew, then when another who had committed a *pārājika* offense was questioned, he would have to say, “I know you, you are a *pārājika*”; consequently, that person...
“Previously he made Dabba Mallaputta pure, but now he makes me impure;
whom shall I speak to now, since even the Teacher falls under the influence of favoritism toward his disciples? Where is his omniscience?
Having harbored such resentment, one might fall into the states of misery; therefore, out of compassion for others, the Blessed One did not say anything, even though he knew [the truth].
Furthermore, he did not say this even to avoid censure. For if the Blessed One had spoken thus, there would have been this censure:
"The renunciation of Dabba Mallaputta was indeed difficult, yet he renounced having obtained the Perfectly Enlightened One as his witness.
And those who considered this to be the characteristic of renunciation [would have thought]: "Even in the time of a Buddha, purity comes through a witness..."
"Whether it be impurity or not, we know; this person is impure"—in this way, evil monks might destroy even those who possess a sense of shame.

Furthermore, in the future, when monks are involved in a matter, they will, after having accused and reminded them, take a confession from those possessing shame by saying, "If you did it, say 'I did it,'" and then carry out the formal act (*kamma*); such is the characteristic of the Vinaya.
When establishing the tradition, he did not say, "I know," but rather said, "If it was done by you, say 'it was done.
"I do not recall having engaged in sexual intercourse even in a dream" means that he does not recall engaging in sexual intercourse even in a dream;
the sense is that he has never been one who engaged in it. Or alternatively, even if he had been one who engaged in it, [he does not recall it] even in a dream.
It means: "I do not know the act of sexual intercourse. For those, however, who read the text as "having practiced it," the meaning is straightforward.
"Even before waking" means that while still awake, she first said, "I do not know [it].
Therefore, "Monks, expel the nun Mettiyā"—this was said because the statements of Dabba and of this nun did not coincide; thus, it is meant: "Expel the nun Mettiyā."

In this context, there are three types of expulsion (*nāsanā*): expulsion by means of the [monastic] marks (*liṅganāsanā*), expulsion by means of communal living (*saṃvāsanāsanā*), and expulsion by means of disciplinary action (*daṇḍakammanāsanā*). Among these, the statement "the violator is to be expelled" refers to "expulsion by means of the marks.

When they carry out an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) for failure to acknowledge an offense, for failure to make amends for an offense, or for failure to relinquish an evil view, this is "expulsion by means of communal living. [The phrase] "Go away! Perish! Be lost!"...

They perform the act of punishment; this is "expulsion by means of punishment" (*daṇḍakammanāsanā*). However, here he speaks with reference to expulsion by means of the [monastic] emblem (*liṅganāsana*), saying:
"Expel the nun Mettiyā.

By the words "and you, monks, investigate these [others]," he illustrates this: "This nun is not acting of her own accord; she has surely been incited by others. Therefore, investigate, search for, and find out those by whom she was incited—these monks."
But was the nun Mettiyā expelled by the Blessed One with her admission (*paṭiññā*) or without her admission (*appaṭiññā*)? What is the point here?

If she was expelled with her admission, then the Elder is the perpetrator and is at fault (*sadosa*). If she was expelled without her admission, then the Elder is not the perpetrator and is without fault (*niddosa*).
Even during the time of King Bhātiya, regarding this very point, there was a dispute between the Elders dwelling at the Mahāvihāra and those dwelling at the Abhayagiri.
A dispute arose. The residents of the Abhayagiri monastery also stated their own sūtra and said, "In your doctrine, the Elder is the one who acts [as the author].
The residents of the Mahāvihāra monastery also stated their own sūtra and said, "In your doctrine, the Elder is the one who acts.
The question was not resolved. Having heard this, the King convened the Elders and [summoned] Dīghakārāyaṇa.
He commanded a minister of the Brahmin caste, saying, "Listen to the words of the elders.
The minister was reportedly wise and skilled in various languages; he said, "Let the elders recite the *sutta* first.
Thereupon, the elders of Abhayagiri recited their own *sutta*: "In that case, monks, expel the nun Mettiyā on her own confession."
The minister said, "Venerable sir, according to your doctrine, the Elder is the perpetrator and is guilty.
The Mahāvihāravāsins also recited their own Sutta: "In that case, monks, expel the nun Mettiyā.
The minister said, "Venerable sir, according to your doctrine, the Elder is not the perpetrator and is innocent. Which of these, then, is correct? That which—

This was later discussed by the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā: "If a monk falsely accuses another monk of an unfounded offense involving an antima-vatthu (an offense entailing expulsion), it is a *saṅghādisesa*;
if he falsely accuses a nun, it is a *dukkaṭa*. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "In the case of lying, it is a *pācittiya*."

In this regard, the following is the investigation: first, according to the previous system, because the intention was not to cause a formal accusation (*anuddhaṃsana*), only a *dukkaṭa* offense is appropriate.
Just as, even though there is lying, for a monk [to lie] to another monk [regarding a grave offense] results in a *saṅghādisesa*;

and just as, even though there is lying, for one who perceives purity in what is impure and speaks with the intention of reviling, there is a *pācittiya* only for abusive speech (*omasavāda*) and not for intentional lying (*sampajānamusāvāda*); so too [in this case].
Here too, because the intention is not to cause a scandal, an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for intentional lying is not applicable;
rather, a simple offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) alone is appropriate. In the latter case as well, since it is indeed a lie, an offense of expiation alone is appropriate.

For, according to the authority of the wording, if a monk, with the intention of causing a scandal, [accuses] one monk of a formal meeting offense (*saṅghādisesa*), it is an offense of defamation (*omasavāda*); and if he intends to abuse, it is an offense of verbal abuse (*akkosa*). But for a monk...
There is no statement that it is a *dukkaṭa* for a bhikkhunī; rather, there is the statement that it is a *pācittiya* for intentional lying.
Therefore, *pācittiya* alone is appropriate.
In this regard, however, the following must be examined: "When there is no intention to defame, it is a *pācittiya*; in that case..."

"In what case would there be an offense? In this regard, since a separate *pācittiya* is stated for falsely accusing someone of a *saṅghādisesa* offense with groundless charges—even though the *pācittiya* for speaking falsehood is already established—therefore, when the intention is to accuse, no room is seen for a *pācittiya* in the case of a conscious lie;
nor is it possible for there to be non-offense for one who is accusing.

It appears that "it shall be" is even more clearly purified according to the previous method. Likewise, if a nun falsely accuses another nun of an unfounded offense involving the ultimate ground (antimavatthu), it is a *saṅghādisesa*;
if she falsely accuses a monk, it is a *dukkaṭa*. In that case, the *saṅghādisesa* leads to rehabilitation (*vuṭṭhānagāmī*), while the *dukkaṭa* leads to confession (*desanāgāmī*);
by these [offenses], there is no expulsion (*nāsanā*). However, because she is inherently immoral (*dussīlā*) by nature...
"The evil bhikkhunī now says of herself, 'I am immoral'; therefore, because she is indeed impure, the Blessed One has expelled her.

Then, after the Blessed One had said, "Expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā and investigate these bhikkhus," and had risen from his seat and entered his dwelling, those bhikkhus said, "Now give her the white robes!"
Seeing that bhikkhunī being dragged away, those bhikkhus, desiring to release her, confessed their own transgression;
to show this matter, it is said: "Then the Mettiya-Bhūmajakas," and so forth.
(385–6) *Duṭṭho doso* means both corrupted and corrupting. For when hatred has arisen, a person is corrupted by that very hatred.
It has abandoned its natural state; therefore, it is called "corrupt" (*duṭṭha*). It corrupts and destroys another; therefore, it is called "hatred" (*dosa*).
Thus, the expression "corrupt hatred" (*duṭṭho doso*) is a designation for a single individual according to his different modes of manifestation.
Therefore it was said: "Corrupt hatred means that which is both corrupted and a corrupter. In this regard, the characteristic of the word (*saddalakkhaṇa*) should be investigated.

However, because that which has attained the designation "hate as a defilement" exists in a person possessing aversion precisely in a state of being angry and so forth, it is therefore said in the word-commentary:
"angry," and so on. Therein, "angry" means having reached a state of agitation, a state of falling away from one's natural composure.
"Displeased" means not having a mind of one's own, with the mind not remaining under its own control; furthermore, [devoid] of joy and happiness...
"Not pleased" (*anattamano*) means not having a pleased mind. "Discontented" (*anabhiraddho*) means not happy or not serene.

"With a struck mind" (*āhatacitto*) means one whose mind has been struck by resentment. "One in whom a thorn has arisen" (*khilajāto*) means one in whom a thorn of resentment—consisting of mental rigidity and the dross of the mind—has arisen.
"Unconvinced" (*appatīto*) means not convinced, being devoid of joy, happiness, and so forth.

The meaning is "he has not been assailed. In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, the phrase beginning with "by that anger" is stated in order to show those states by means of which one becomes displeased.
Therein, "by that anger" refers to that by which one is called both "corrupt" and "provoked"; for both of these [terms] refer to the state of being natural (or inherent).
"From which [state] it becomes of a single form": by that "fault" (dosa), which is what is called "fault"; by these two, he shows only the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).

"By that dissatisfaction" (anattamanatā), which is what is called "displeased" (anattamano); and "by that lack of delight" (anabhiraddhi), which is what is called "unhappy" (anabhiraddho); by these two, he shows the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). Regarding the phrase "by a groundless offense involving defeat" (amūlakena pārājikena):
here, "groundless" (amūlaka) means there is no root (mūla) for it; and its state of being groundless is because—
It is intended by way of the accuser (*codaka*), not by way of the accused (*cuditaka*). Therefore, to show that meaning, it is said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*):
"What is called 'groundless' (*amūlaka*) is what has not been seen, not heard, and not suspected. By this, he illustrates the following:

"That which is a *pārājika* offense which has neither been seen, nor heard, nor suspected by the accuser with respect to the person being accused—this [is groundless] among these things known as seeing, hearing, and suspecting..."
Because it lacks a basis, it is called "baseless" (*amūlaka*); however, whether he has actually committed that offense or not, this [term] here is of no account.

In this context, "not seen" (*adiṭṭha*) means not seen by one’s own physical eye or by the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). "Not heard" (*asuta*) likewise means not heard when being spoken of by someone. "Not suspected" (*aparisaṅkita*) means not suspected by the mind.
"Seen" (*diṭṭha*) means seen by oneself or by another, either with the physical eye or the divine eye. "Heard" (*suta*)...
The name is likewise heard. "Suspected" means suspected either by oneself or by others.
In this regard, what was seen by oneself remains simply as "seen"; what was seen by others is "heard" by oneself;
and what was heard by others or suspected by others—all of this, moreover, stands in the very place of what was heard by oneself.
Suspicion, however, is threefold: suspicion based on what has been seen, suspicion based on what has been heard, and suspicion based on what has been sensed.
Therein, "suspicion based on what has been seen" means: a certain bhikkhu entered a thicket near a village to attend to the business of defecation or urination;
a certain woman also entered that same thicket for some business and then turned back, yet neither...
A monk saw a woman, and the woman did not see the monk; without seeing one another, both departed as they pleased.
Then, another monk, observing their departure from that place, suspects: "Surely something has been done by these two, or they will do so.
This is what is called "suspicion based on having seen."
What is called "suspicion based on what has been heard" is as follows: here, someone hears a certain kind of friendly conversation between a bhikkhu and a woman in the dark or in a concealed place;

although another person is nearby, he does not know whether they exist or not, and he suspects, "Surely these people have done it, or will do it. This is what is called suspicion based on what has been heard.
"Mutaparisaṅkitaṃ" means that several rogues, having taken flowers, perfumes, meat, liquor, and so forth during the night, went with women to a certain frontier monastery;
having played as they pleased in a pavilion or in the dining hall and other such places, they scattered the flowers and other items and departed.
On the following day, when the monks saw that disorder, [they wondered], "Whose is this?"...

They investigate, "What is the kamma? In that regard, if a certain bhikkhu has risen early and, in the course of his duties, has been tending to the pavilion or the dining hall, he may have touched flowers and such;
or if another has performed an offering with flowers and such brought from a family of supporters; or if another has drunk *ariṭṭha* for the sake of medicine—then...
Investigating, "Whose work is this?", the monks smell the odor of their hands and the odor of their mouths and become suspicious of those monks;
this is called suspicion based on what has been released (muta-parisaṅkita).
In that regard, there is what is seen with a basis (samūlaka), and there is what is seen without a basis (amūlaka); likewise, there is what is seen with a basis of perception (saññā-samūlaka).

There is that which is based on perception (*saññāmūlaka*). This same method applies to what is heard (*suta*) as well. Regarding what is suspected (*parisaṅkita*), there is that which is suspected on account of what was seen (*diṭṭhaparisaṅkita*) that is with a basis (*samūlaka*), and there is that which is without a basis (*amūlaka*);
likewise, that very same suspected-on-account-of-what-was-seen is based on perception (*saññāmūlaka*), and there is that which is without perception (*saññāamūlaka*).

This same method applies to what is suspected on account of what was heard or what was suspected. In this context, "with a basis" regarding what was seen refers to one who has committed an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*).

Having seen [the offense], one says, "I have seen it. What is called "groundless" (amūlaka) means that having seen someone emerging from a concealed place, one says, "I have seen it," even though one has not seen the transgression.
What is called "based on perception of what was seen" (diṭṭhasaññāsamūlaka) means that having actually seen it, one accuses while being conscious of having seen it.
What is called "not based on perception" (saññāamūlaka) means that although one previously saw a transgression involving a defeat (pārājika), afterwards...
One who perceives that he has not seen, having made his perception baseless, accuses another, saying, "I have seen him.
By this same method, the cases of what is heard, suspected, or expected should also be understood in detail.

And herein, there is no offense for one who accuses in any manner whatsoever—whether with a basis or with a perception based on a basis; however, there is an offense only for one who accuses without a basis or without a perception based on a basis.
"Anuddhaṃseyya" means he would destroy, utterly destroy, overcome, or overwhelm.
Since that act of overcoming is performed both by one who reproaches himself and by one who causes another to reproach him,
it is therefore stated in the word-commentary as "he reproaches or causes to be reproached."

In this context, "he accuses" means he himself accuses him by means of such statements as, "You have committed an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika)," and for every word of his speech, there is an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa). "He causes another to accuse" means that, standing near him, he commands another bhikkhu;
when that other bhikkhu accuses him according to his instruction, for every word of the accuser's speech, there is an offense of formal meeting for the one who caused the accusation. Now, if he...
