If one accuses another, saying, "I have seen it, I have heard it," there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for each word spoken by both persons.
For the sake of skill in distinguishing the various types of accusation, one should first understand the fourfold scheme here, beginning with a single subject and a single accuser.
In that regard, if one monk accuses another monk on account of a single matter, this constitutes one subject for this accusation.
There is one accuser. Many monks accuse one monk on a single ground, as in the case of the five hundred Chabbaggiya monks led by Mettiya and Bhūmajaka accusing the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta;
in this accusation, there is one ground and multiple accusers. A single monk accuses another monk on many grounds; in this accusation...
There is one accuser regarding various matters; there are many accusing many with many matters.
In this case of accusation, there are various matters and various accusers.
But who is permitted to accuse, and who is not? First, taking the words of a weak accuser as the standard, someone...
He does not obtain [the offense]. One who accuses weakly (*dubbalacodaka*) is as follows:

while many are sitting together in conversation, one person, making it general and not naming anyone specifically, speaks regarding another on a matter involving a *pārājika* offense. Another hears this and goes to tell the other person.
That person approaches him and says, "I believe you said such and such to me. He replies, "I did not say anything of that sort."
"I know; however, I spoke that matter in general conversation without specifying [the person].
Had I known of this arising of suffering for you, I would not have said even so much. This is the "weak accuser.
No one is permitted to accuse that bhikkhu by taking up such conversational exchange. But setting this aside, a bhikkhu endowed with virtue...
The Elder Mahāpaduma said that only a bhikkhunī who is endowed with virtue may reprove a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī.
However, the Elder Mahāsiva said that all five [classes of practitioners] who are in accordance with the Dhamma may do so.
The Elder Godatta, on the other hand, stated that "no one is excluded," and added: "Having heard it from a bhikkhu, one reproves; having heard it from a bhikkhunī..."
Having heard it, he reproves him... [and so on] ...he reproves him after having heard it from the disciples of other sects. He cited this Sutta.
According to the doctrine of all three elders, the matter must be dealt with based solely on the admission of the one who has been reproved.
However, this so-called “reproving” does not apply to one who reproves by sending a messenger, a letter, or a message.
However, for one who stands right next to the person and reproaches them either by means of a hand gesture or by verbal expression, the offense reaches its culmination (sīsaṃ eti).
Indeed, it is only the formal renunciation of the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*) that does not reach its culmination through a hand gesture;

but this act of reviling (*anuddhaṃsana*) and the reporting of what is untrue (*abhūtārocana*) do indeed reach their culmination. Furthermore, if one standing in the presence of two people designates one of them and reproaches him... [if he]... then... [the offense reaches its culmination].
If one person knows, the matter goes to the head [of the offense]. If the other knows, it does not go to the head.

Even if he accuses after having restricted both parties—whether one or two know—it still goes to the head. This same method applies when there are many. Furthermore, knowing at that very moment is difficult;

however, once it is known by reflecting upon it at a later time, it is indeed considered "known. If he knows it afterwards, it does not go to the head. [This concludes] the section on the renunciation of the training.

The training rules concerning the reporting of what is untrue, offensive speech, acting for one's own benefit, and the reporting of what is truly a fault—all of these indeed share the same definition.
Thus, this censure is twofold according to body and speech. Furthermore, there is censure based on what has been seen, censure based on what has been heard, and censure based on suspicion.

It is threefold. There is also another fourfold classification: censure for failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), censure for failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*), censure for failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*), and censure for failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*).
In this context, censure for failure in virtue should be understood by way of the two heavy classes of offenses;
censure for failure in conduct by way of the remaining [classes]; and [censure for failure in view] by way of wrong view and extremist views.

The censure for failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*) and the censure for failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*)—the latter being understood by way of the six training rules (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed on account of livelihood—should be known.

There is also another fourfold [censure]: the pointing out of the basis (*vatthusandassanā*), the pointing out of the offense (*āpattisandassanā*), the prohibition of communal living (*saṃvāsapaṭikkhepa*), and the prohibition of respectful treatment (*sāmīcipaṭikkhepa*).
Among these, "pointing out the basis" means: "You have committed sexual intercourse."

The "exposing of an offense" (*āpattisandassanā*) is that which proceeds in such a manner as: "You have taken what was not given," "You have caused a human being to be killed," or "You have spoken what is untrue.
The "refusal of communal living" (*saṃvāsapaṭikkhepa*) is that which proceeds in such a manner as:
"There is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha with you."
However, at this point it does not reach the head; it reaches the head only when combined with such statements as, "You are no longer a samaṇa, you are no longer a son of the Sakyan.
What is called a "proper rejection" (sāmīcipaṭikkhepa) is the non-performance of acts such as bowing, rising to greet, joining the palms in salutation, and fanning.
This should be understood as occurring at the time when one performs the remaining acts—such as the successive acts of veneration and so forth—after having omitted one of them.
Up to this point, it is merely called "reproach" (*codanā*), but the offense does not reach its head.

However, when one is asked, "Why do you not perform prostrations and so forth for me? and this is joined with statements such as, "You are no longer a *samaṇa*, you are no longer a son of the Sakyan," only then does it reach its head.
But when one asks for whatever one desires, such as rice gruel or food, by that much alone it is not "reproach."

In the *Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhaka*, another hundred and ten charges are stated, beginning with: "Monks, there is one illegitimate suspension of the Pātimokkha and one legitimate suspension," and so on, up to: "There are ten illegitimate suspensions of the Pātimokkha and ten legitimate suspensions.
Thus, fifty-five are illegitimate and fifty-five are legitimate, totaling one hundred and ten.
There are one hundred and ten for one who accuses by what is seen, one hundred and ten for one who accuses by what is heard, and one hundred and ten for one who accuses by what is suspected;

thus, there are three hundred and thirty. These, when multiplied by three—namely, for one who accuses by body, for one who accuses by speech, and for one who accuses by both body and speech—become nine hundred and ninety. These...
Whether accusing oneself or causing another to accuse, there are exactly two thousand minus twenty;

furthermore, it should be understood that when classified according to the divisions of what was seen and so forth, as well as by way of being with or without root, there are many thousands of accusations.
However, standing at this point, the Commentary states: "By a monk named Upāli who wishes to take formal admission (*attādāna*), [he must] possess five factors..."

Having cited many discourses such as those in the *Upālipañcaka* and elsewhere— such as "the formal charge (*attādāna*) should be taken up," and "O Upāli, a monk who wishes to accuse another should first examine five qualities within himself before accusing the other"—
[one should explain] the characteristics of the formal charge, the duty of the accuser, the duty of the accused, and the tasks to be performed by the Saṅgha.
The entire duty of the investigator has been explained in detail; we shall describe it in its proper place as it occurs in the text.

Regarding these various types of accusations already mentioned, whenever a matter comes before the Saṅgha by means of any such accusation, the accused and the accuser should be told: "You will be satisfied with our judgment."
If they say, "We shall take it," the Saṅgha should accept that legal case.

But if they say, "Venerable sirs, first settle it; if it is acceptable to us, we will take it," one should dismiss them by making a long detour, saying things such as, "First pay homage to the Cetiya. If they become exhausted after a long time...
When the assembly has departed and their faction has been severed, they request [a decision] again;
after refusing them up to three times, when they have become free from pride, then their legal case should be adjudicated.
And while adjudicating it, if the assembly is full of the shameless, that legal case should be adjudicated by a committee (*ubbāhikā*). If the assembly is full of fools...
“Seek out a fellow-bearer of the Vinaya who is like-minded with you.

Having had such a bearer of the Vinaya sought out, that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) must be settled in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction by which that legal issue is pacified.
In this context, “Dhamma” refers to the factual basis; “Vinaya” refers to the formal charge and the reminder; and “Teacher’s instruction” refers to—
There is the perfection of the motion and the perfection of the proclamation. Therefore, when the accuser has announced the matter, the accused should be asked:

"Is this true, or not? Having thus examined the matter, and having accused and reminded him based on the actual facts, that legal issue should be settled through the perfection of the motion and the perfection of the proclamation. In that case...
If one who is shameless accuses someone who is conscientious, and that shameless person is foolish and incompetent such that no guidance should be given to him, he should instead be addressed thus:
"On account of what do you accuse him? He will certainly say, "What is this, venerable sir? On account of what indeed?
You do not even know on account of what he is accused; it is not proper for a foolish person like you to accuse another.

He should be sent away and not subjected to questioning. However, if he is shameless yet wise and competent, and is able to overcome and refute [the charge] by means of what has been seen or heard, then after subjecting him to questioning, the formal act should be carried out on the basis of the confession of one who possesses shame.
If one who possesses shame accuses one who is shameless, and that shameless person is foolish and incompetent, he is unable to provide a defense through questioning.
The procedure for him should be given thus: "In respect of what do you charge him—with failure in virtue, or with one of the others such as failure in conduct?
Why, then, should this procedure be given only to this person and not to the other? Is it not improper for those who uphold the Vinaya to follow a wrong course?
It is indeed not improper; however, this is not a wrong course, but rather what is called "supporting the Dhamma."
This training rule was indeed laid down for the purpose of restraining the shameless and supporting the conscientious.
In this regard, the shameless person, having found an opportunity, will come forward with overbearing conduct;

but the conscientious person, having found an opportunity, will speak by establishing himself on what is seen according to the continuity of what is seen, and on what is heard according to the continuity of what is heard. Therefore, it is appropriate to provide him with spiritual support (dhammānuggaha). If...
However, that person is modest, wise, and competent; he speaks with firm standing. But the shameless one does not give his consent, saying, "This is not so, that is not so.
In such a case, it must be done according to the consent of the shameless one.
To illustrate this point, this story should be understood: it is said that the Elder Cūḷābhaya, who was well-versed in the Tipiṭaka, [was at] the Lohapāsāda...
Having taught the Vinaya to the monks below, he emerged at the time of evening. At the moment of his emergence, two adversaries of his self engaged in conversation.
One did not grant an admission, saying, "This too does not exist; that too does not exist.
Then, when only a small portion of the first watch of the night remained, regarding that person, the Elder thought: "This one speaks by relying [on a basis]."
But he did not give his consent, thinking, "Many grounds have been brought forward; surely this must have been done.
Thus, a conviction of impurity arose [in him]. Then, signaling with the handle of a fan upon the footstool, he said, "Friend, I am not fit to decide this case;
let it be decided by another. "Why so, venerable sir? [asked the other]. The Elder [explained] that matter...
He reported this, and a burning fever arose in the body of the person who had reproached him. Thereupon, having paid homage to the Elder, he said:
"Venerable sir, it is fitting for one who is capable of judging to be like you, a master of the Vinaya; and it is likewise fitting for the accuser to be like this.
Having spoken thus, he put on white robes, apologized, saying, "I have caused you much distress," and departed.

Thus, when one who is conscientious accuses one who is unconscientious, the latter does not give a confession even when many grounds for accusation have arisen; he should be described neither as "pure" nor as "impure. He is called a "living corpse" or a "raw corpse.
However, if another similar ground for accusation arises against him, it need not be adjudicated; he will simply be discarded in that manner.
But if an unconscientious person accuses another unconscientious person, he should be told: "Friend, by your word this [accused]..."
Having said to the other person as well, "What can be done?", both should be dismissed after saying, "Live together, sharing the same enjoyment and use.

No formal adjudication should be made for the sake of their moral discipline (*sīla*); however, for the sake of their alms-bowl, robes, dwelling cell, and so forth, it may be done if a suitable witness is obtained.

Now, if one who is modest reproves another who is modest, and they have a dispute over some very minor matter, they should be persuaded, made to confess their transgression with the words "Do not do this," and then dismissed.

However, if in this case the one being reproved has acted impulsively, there is no such thing as a person who is inherently shameless from the very beginning. And he [the accuser] should give his formal consent for the sake of protecting his own faction.
If he does not grant it, many people will arise, saying, "We have faith, we have faith.
On their word, let him be pure once or twice; but from the time he has failed, he must not remain in his position, and no legal decision should be granted to him.

Thus, when a matter has been brought into the midst of the Saṅgha by means of any kind of accusation, having understood the conduct of both the accused and the accuser, the legal determination (vinicchaya) regarding that very accusation must be known by way of its beginning, middle, and end, for the purpose of discerning its success or failure.
For example: what is the beginning of an accusation, what is its middle, and what is its end? Regarding the accusation:
“I wish to speak to him; let the Venerable One give me the opportunity”—thus the formal act of requesting permission (*okāsakamma*) is the beginning.

Having accused and reminded [the person] by means of the matter under dispute, the legal decision (*vinicchaya*) is the middle. The settlement (*samatha*) is the conclusion, by way of establishing [the case] as either an offense or a non-offense.
How many roots, how many matters, and how many grounds are there for an accusation? There are two roots for an accusation: that which has a root (*samūlikā*).

Or it may be groundless. There are three grounds: what has been seen, what has been heard, and what has been suspected. There are five bases: "I will speak at the proper time, not at an improper time;
I will speak what is true, not what is untrue; I will speak gently, not harshly;
I will speak in a way that is beneficial, not in a way that is unbeneficial; I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of ill-will."

Furthermore, by means of this accusation, the person who accuses must establish himself in the fifteen qualities described in the *Upālipañcaka* by way of the method beginning with, "Am I indeed pure in bodily conduct? and so forth;
the person being accused must establish himself in two qualities: truthfulness and imperturbability.
"Perhaps they might cause him to fall away from this holy life"—that is, "perhaps I might cause this person to fall away from this supreme conduct";
it is said that one would revile [him] with the intention: "It would be well indeed if I could cause this person to fall away from this holy life.
However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it says "might cause him to fall away from the holy life."
To demonstrate the meaning of this very method, it was said: "he would cause him to fall from the state of a bhikkhu," and so forth.

*Khaṇa*, *laya*, and *muhutta* are synonyms for time (*samaya*). "He passes that moment, that instant, that brief duration" means when that moment, that instant, and that brief duration have passed. This accusative case ending is used here because it expresses the locus of the action.
In the description of "being pressed with an accusation," "by whatever matter he has been censured" refers to among the four matters constituting a *pārājika* offense.
By which matter the one who is reproached is overwhelmed, overpowered, surpassed, and eclipsed. "Being interrogated regarding that matter" means:
while that accuser is being investigated, examined, and scrutinized by the investigator according to the method beginning with, "What have you seen?
How was it seen by you? concerning the very matter stated by that accuser.
In the exposition of "not being pursued" (*asamanuggāhiyamāna*), "not being spoken to by anyone" means not being addressed by either the investigator (*anuvijjaka*) or anyone else;
or alternatively, it means not being accused regarding any of the bases such as what was seen (*diṭṭha*) and so forth.

Furthermore, the connection for these two matrix-terms (*mātikāpada*) is to be understood with the subsequent phrase: "and the bhikkhu maintains his innocence. For this is what is meant: "In this way..."
"Whether being interrogated or not being interrogated, if a bhikkhu maintains, persists in, and admits to hatred, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
This was stated merely to show the time when the groundlessness of the matter becomes manifest;
however, he incurs the offense at the very moment he brings the charge forward.
Now, regarding the phrase “that legal issue is indeed baseless,” since the characteristics of what is baseless have already been stated previously, he says “A legal issue (adhikaraṇa) is...

and so forth, without repeating that, in order to show what has not been mentioned before. In this context, because a legal issue—though one in its nature as a legal issue—is differentiated according to its subject matter (vatthu), he states its various types in order to demonstrate that diversity: “There are four... and so forth.
He says, "The legal issues (adhikaraṇāni) are the legal issue of disputes," and so forth. But what is the meaning of "legal issue" (adhikaraṇa), by virtue of which this [category] is one?

It is the state of being subject to settlement by means of the methods of settling (samatha). Therefore, that with reference to which, on account of which, depending upon which, and concerning which the methods of settling proceed—that should be understood as "the legal issue."

In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is said: "Regarding 'legal issue' (*adhikaraṇa*), some say it is grasping (*gāha*), some say volition (*cetanā*), some say intolerance (*akkhanti*), some say legal procedure (*vohāra*), and some say designation (*paṇṇatti*). Furthermore, it was investigated as follows:

"If grasping is what is called a legal issue, then when one person, having taken up a formal charge (*attādāna*), is deliberating with a fellow monk who shares the same view, [he perceives] the danger therein..."
Having seen [the fault], he relinquishes it again; thus that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) of his will have reached settlement.
If volition (cetanā) is the legal issue, then the volition that arose with the thought, "I take this upon myself," ceases.

If intolerance (akkhanti) is the legal issue, then even after having taken the matter upon himself out of intolerance, either because he later fails to obtain a formal decision or because he has asked for forgiveness—
He abandons it. If the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is discourse, then by wandering about while speaking and later becoming silent and voiceless, that legal issue of his will have reached settlement;
therefore, the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*) is the legal issue. Furthermore, this [is illustrated by]:
"An offense of defeat for sexual misconduct is a factor pertaining to an offense of defeat for sexual misconduct... and so forth.

This contradicts such statements as: "In this way, an offense-dispute (āpattādhikaraṇa) is a part of an offense-dispute," and "A dispute over litigation (vivādādhikaraṇa) may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
For they do not maintain that the designation (paṇṇatti) possesses the quality of being wholesome and so forth;
nor is the offense against the Pārājika rules mentioned in the phrase "by means of a groundless charge of an offense involving defeat" itself the designation.
It is so named because it is absolutely unwholesome (*akusala*). For it has been said: "An issue arising from an offense may be unwholesome or it may be indeterminate (*abyākata*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by means of a groundless *pārājika*," that which was indicated there as a "groundless *pārājika*" is precisely what is being restated here by the words "and that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is indeed groundless.
This does not refer to the formal designation (*paṇṇatti*), for one does not indicate one thing and then [refer to] another.

It points to another [factor]. However, because that designation by which, and that expression by which, the accuser designates the person as having committed an offense of defeat (*pārājika-dhamma*), that designation is itself rootless (*amūlika*) due to the lack of a basis for the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) termed "defeat";
and because it occurs within a legal issue, it is also a legal issue. Therefore, by this method:
It would be appropriate to say that "designation" (*paṇṇatti*) is "legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*), because that legal issue which is called "rootless" does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature;
it exists merely as a designation. For this reason also, it would be appropriate to say that designation is the legal issue.
However, this applies only here and not everywhere; for the designation of disputes (*vivāda*) and so forth is not itself the legal issue. Rather, the meaning of "legal issue" is...

Their state of being subject to legal settlement (*adhikaraṇīyatā*) is by means of the methods of pacification (*samatha*) previously mentioned. Thus, in this sense of being a legal matter (*adhikaraṇa*), a certain dispute (*vivāda*) here is both a dispute and a legal matter;
therefore, it is called a "legal matter of dispute" (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). This same method applies to the remaining [three] as well.
In that regard, "here monks dispute whether it is Dhamma or non-Dhamma"—thus are the eighteen bases for schism.

A dispute arising on account of [something] is a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). “In this case, monks reprove a monk for failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) or [for failure in conduct, view, or livelihood]”—thus, a reproach arising on account of the four failures is a legal issue arising from reproach (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*).
“The five classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) are a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*); the seven classes of offenses are also a legal issue arising from an offense”—thus...
An offense itself is a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). As for the fourfold business of the Saṅgha—namely, "whatever is the duty or obligation of the Saṅgha:

a formal act by consultation (*apalokanakamma*), a formal act by a motion (*ñattikamma*), a formal act by a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*), and a formal act by a motion and a fourth resolution (*ñatticatutthakamma*)"—this should be understood as a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
However, in this context, only the legal issue arising from an offense consisting of a *pārājika* offense is intended. The others are mentioned merely by way of enumeration.
These have been stated, for such are the meanings of the term *adhikaraṇa*. Among them, it is specifically the *pārājika* that is intended here.
That becomes a groundless legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) through roots such as what was seen and so forth. And this monk establishes a fault;
he relies upon it and admits it, saying things such as, "I spoke falsely," and so on. Of that monk...
"At the very moment it is not denied, it is a *saṅghādisesa*": this, first of all, is the meaning of this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) which provides a sequential exposition.
387. Now, demonstrating the imposition of an offense in detail by way of those grounds for accusation—beginning with "seen" and so forth—which were stated in brief, he says:
"It occurs for one who has not seen," and so on. In that context, "it occurs for one who has not seen" means: for one who has not seen.
He has it. By this "accuser," he is not seen; the meaning is that this person has committed an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*).
This same method applies to the phrases "he has heard it" and so forth.
"I have seen you" means "you have been seen by me. This same method applies to "I have heard you" and so forth. The rest is based on what was not seen.

The meaning is exactly as it appears on the surface. However, regarding the section based on what was seen, if one accuses [the monk] by saying, "I have heard it," the lack of foundation (*amūlaka*) should be understood through the absence of those discourses and so forth mentioned in that way.
And in this entire section concerning the accuser, just as here it is said of those who have come before: "You have committed an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika-dhamma*),"...
In each of these statements—“You are not an ascetic; you are not a son of the Sakyan”—there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for every single utterance.

Likewise, when other [terms] are used, such as: “You are immoral, of evil nature, impure, of suspicious conduct, one whose actions are concealed, not an ascetic though claiming to be an ascetic, not a practitioner of the holy life though claiming to be a practitioner of the holy life, internally rotten, leaking, and putrid.”
In these statements as well, according to each individual word, it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa* offense for every single utterance.
However, the pure phrases, "There is no Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremony with you, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha," do not constitute the opening charge;
rather, it is when one uses terms such as "you are immoral" in the manner of "You are immoral, there is no Uposatha with you," that they do so.

However, in such phrases as "you have committed an offense entailing expulsion" (*pārājikaṃ dhammaṃ ajjhāpannosi*), when these words are joined with anything whatsoever, they take the initial [case endings] and become offenses entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*). But the Elder Mahāpaduma said:
"It is not only the phrases 'one who is immoral' (*dussīlo*) and 'one of evil nature' (*pāpadhammo*) that are not included here in the Canon..."
They come with their heads bowed, saying: "You are a eunuch; you are one living in communion by theft; you are one who has gone over to another sect; you are an animal; you are a matricide;
you are a patricide; you are a murderer of an arahant; you are a schismatic of the Saṅgha; you are a great novice; you are a great lay follower;
you are a senior probationer; you are a Nigaṇṭha; you are an Ājīvaka; you are an ascetic; you are a wanderer."
“You are one who causes blood to flow, you are a violator of a bhikkhunī, you are a hermaphrodite”—these [accusations] too cause the head to nod.
And the Elder Mahāpaduma himself says: “In cases such as ‘one who is doubtful regarding what has been seen,’ at the very moment he is doubtful, he does not consider it allowable;
at the moment he does not consider it allowable, he does not remember it; at the moment he does not remember it, he forgets it.”
The Elder Mahāsumma, however, divides each [of these] into two and demonstrates a separate method for all four.
How so? Regarding the phrase "one who is doubtful about what was seen" (*diṭṭhe vematikō*): this refers either to doubt regarding the seeing itself or to doubt regarding the person.

In that context, one is "doubtful about the seeing" when one wonders, "Was this seen by me, or was it not seen? Or one is "doubtful" when one wonders, "Was this person seen by me, or was it another? Thus...

He is doubtful about the person. Thus, he either does not resolve upon the seeing or the person, or he forgets the seeing or the person, or he has lost the memory of the seeing or the person. And herein, "doubtful" means one in whom doubt has arisen.
"Does not resolve" means he does not have faith. "Forgets" means that, while not being reminded, he forgets. But when [someone says], "In such-and-such a place..."

When they remind him, saying, "Venerable sir, at such-and-such a place, at such-and-such a time," he then remembers. "Forgotten" means that even when being reminded by those various means, he simply does not remember.
By this same method, the section concerning the accuser (*codāpaka*) is also to be understood;
for there, only the word "by me" is omitted, while the rest is exactly the same as in the section concerning the accuser (*codaka*).

389. Following that, in order to show the classification of offenses (*āpatti*) and the classification of non-offenses (*anāpatti*), the fourfold set beginning with "one who perceives purity in what is impure" is established.
Each individual term is explained by means of fourfold classifications; all of this can be understood according to the method of the Pāḷi itself.
Only the distinction of the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) here needs to be known. For this so-called "intention" is as follows: the intention to cause a fall (*cāvanādhippāya*),...

It is of many kinds: with the intent to abuse, with the intent to bring legal action, with the intent to cause [the monk] to leave, with the intent to suspend the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, with the intent to investigate, and with the intent to give a Dhamma talk.
Among these, for one who does not ask for permission regarding the first four intents, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Even if permission has been asked, if [one accuses him] in his presence with a groundless charge of a Pārājika offense...
If one accuses [another] of a *saṅghādisesa* offense, it is a *saṅghādisesa*. If one accuses [another] of a groundless *saṅghādisesa* offense, it is a *pācittiya*.
If one accuses [another] of a failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*), it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one speaks with the intention of reviling, it is a *pācittiya*.
However, if one speaks in the absence [of the accused], even regarding all seven classes of offenses, it is a *dukkaṭa*. Even in the absence [of the accused], there are seven kinds [of offenses].
For one who performs [this] action, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "If one says with the intention of restoring [the person]: 'You have fallen into such-and-such an offense;
you should make amends for it,' there is no requirement for [the recipient] to grant leave. In all cases, however, [it is an offense] for one who suspends the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā.

It is said, "there is no formal act of granting permission. However, the ground for setting aside [the Uposatha] must be known. For it is permissible to set it aside while the syllable *re* in the words, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs;
today is the fifteenth Uposatha; if it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha," has not yet been passed.
But after that, when the syllable *yya* has been reached...

It is not permitted. This same principle applies to the *pavāraṇā* ceremony. Furthermore, when a matter has come before an investigator, there is no formal opening of the case for one who speaks with the intent of investigating, saying, "This belongs to you.
Likewise, for a preacher of the Dhamma sitting upon the Dhamma-seat, there is no such opening when he says, "The monk who does this and that is not a true ascetic," and so forth.
For one who teaches the Dhamma indiscriminately according to the method [of general preaching], there is no need for obtaining formal permission (*okāsakamma*).

However, if one speaks by specifying and limiting the audience, saying, "So-and-so and so-and-so are not monastics and not disciples," one must descend from the Dharma-seat, confess the offense, and then depart.
As for what is stated here and there regarding "having obtained permission" (*anokāsaṃ kārāpetvā*), it means "without having obtained permission."
The meaning should be understood in this way: for there is no such thing as a "non-occasion" (anokāsa) by making which one incurs an offense;
rather, one incurs an offense by not making an occasion (okāsa). The rest is self-evident.
Regarding the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth, it has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
It is functional, liberation through perception, associated with consciousness, worldly-offense, bodily action, verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and painful feeling.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning corrupting faults is finished.
9. Commentary on the second training rule concerning corrupting faults.
391. At that time, "the Buddha, the Blessed One"—this refers to the second training rule concerning malice. Therein, [it says]: "Come, friends, let us make this goat Dabba Mallaputta.
It is said that because they were unable to fulfill their own desire in the first instance and had received a rebuke, having fallen into distress, they thought, "Now we shall see."
They wandered about searching for such a person. Then one day, having seen him and being delighted, they looked at one another and said:
"Come, friends, let us make this goat the name 'Dabba Mallaputta'";
that is to say, "Let us give him the name 'Dabba Mallaputta'. This same method applies to Mettiya.
Regarding the phrase "the nun named Mettiyā," here too [it is the same].
Those monks interrogated the monks of the Mettiyabhūmajaka group; they interrogated them thus:
"Friends, where was Dabba Mallaputta seen by you together with the nun Mettiyā? "At the foot of Mount Gijjhakūṭa."

“At what time? “At the time for going on alms-round. “Friend Dabba, they say this: ‘Where were you then? “I was assigning meals in Veḷuvana. “Who knew of your presence in Veḷuvana at that time? “The Saṅgha, Bhante. They questioned the Saṅgha: “Do you know...? At that time, the Blessed One was seated with a large assembly of monks. The venerable Dabba Mallaputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Bhante, at that time when the venerable Channa was being tormented by painful feelings, he said: ‘Friends, where was Dabba Mallaputta at that time? When asked, ‘At what time? he replied, ‘At the time for going on alms-round. When asked, ‘Friend Dabba, where were you then? he replied, ‘I was assigning meals in Veḷuvana. When asked, ‘Who knew of your presence in Veḷuvana at that time? he replied, ‘The Saṅgha, Bhante. Then they questioned the Saṅgha: ‘Do you know...? (The Blessed One said: “Dabba, it is good that you remember this matter. It is good that the Saṅgha remembers this matter. It is good that the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people, remembers this matter. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, I authorize you to appoint as an assigner of meals a monk who possesses five qualities: one who does not assign a meal to himself; one who does not assign a meal to his relatives; one who does not assign a meal to a regular visitor; one who does not assign a meal to one who has been staying there for a long time; and one who does not assign a meal to one who has arrived late. Monks, you should appoint as an assigner of meals a monk who possesses these five qualities in this way. A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: ‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint monk so-and-so as the assigner of meals. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. The Saṅgha appoints monk so-and-so as the assigner of meals. If it is pleasing to the venerable ones to appoint monk so-and-so as the assigner of meals, let them remain silent; if it is not pleasing, they should speak. Monk so-and-so is appointed by the Saṅgha as the assigner of meals. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I hold it. (The Blessed One said: “Monks, I authorize you to appoint as a distributor of meals a monk who possesses five qualities: one who does not distribute a meal to himself; one who does not distribute a meal to his relatives; one who does not distribute a meal to a regular visitor; one who does not distribute a meal to one who has been staying there for a long time; and one who does not distribute a meal to one who has arrived late. Monks, you should appoint as a distributor of meals a monk who possesses these five qualities in this way. A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: ‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of meals. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. The Saṅgha appoints monk so-and-so as the distributor of meals. If it is pleasing to the venerable ones to appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of meals, let them remain silent; if it is not pleasing, they should speak. Monk so-and-so is appointed by the Saṅgha as the distributor of meals. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I hold it. (The Blessed One said: “Monks, I authorize you to appoint as a distributor of lodgings a monk who possesses five qualities: one who does not distribute a lodging to himself; one who does not distribute a lodging to his relatives; one who does not distribute a lodging to a regular visitor; one who does not distribute a lodging to one who has been staying there for a long time; and one who does not distribute a lodging to one who has arrived late. Monks, you should appoint as a distributor of lodgings a monk who possesses these five qualities in this way. A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: ‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of lodgings. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. The Saṅgha appoints monk so-and-so as the distributor of lodgings. If it is pleasing to the venerable ones to appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of lodgings, let them remain silent; if it is not pleasing, they should speak. Monk so-and-so is appointed by the Saṅgha as the distributor of lodgings. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I hold it. (The Blessed One said: “Monks, I authorize you to appoint as a distributor of minor requisites a monk who possesses five qualities: one who does not distribute minor requisites to himself; one who does not distribute minor requisites to his relatives; one who does not distribute minor requisites to a regular visitor; one who does not distribute minor requisites to one who has been staying there for a long time; and one who does not distribute minor requisites to one who has arrived late. Monks, you should appoint as a distributor of minor requisites a monk who possesses these five qualities in this way. A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: ‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of minor requisites. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. The Saṅgha appoints monk so-and-so as the distributor of minor requisites. If it is pleasing to the venerable ones to appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of minor requisites, let them remain silent; if it is not pleasing, they should speak. Monk so-and-so is appointed by the Saṅgha as the distributor of minor requisites. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I hold it. (The Blessed One said: “Monks, I authorize you to appoint as a distributor of bathing robes a monk who possesses five qualities: one who does not distribute a bathing robe to himself; one who does not distribute a bathing robe to his relatives; one who does not distribute a bathing robe to a regular visitor; one who does not distribute a bathing robe to one who has been staying there for a long time; and one who does not distribute a bathing robe to one who has arrived late. Monks, you should appoint as a distributor of bathing robes a monk who possesses these five qualities in this way. A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: ‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of bathing robes. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. The Saṅgha appoints monk so-and-so as the distributor of bathing robes. If it is pleasing to the venerable ones to appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of bathing robes, let them remain silent; if it is not pleasing, they should speak. Monk so-and-so is appointed by the Saṅgha as the distributor of bathing robes. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I hold it. (The Blessed One said: “Monks, I authorize you to appoint as a distributor of fruit a monk who possesses five qualities: one who does not distribute fruit to himself; one who does not distribute fruit to his relatives; one who does not distribute fruit to a regular visitor; one who does not distribute fruit to one who has been staying there for a long time; and one who does not distribute fruit to one who has arrived late. Monks, you should appoint as a distributor of fruit a monk who possesses these five qualities in this way. A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha: ‘
“At that time, we knew of his presence in Veḷuvana. “Yes, friends, we know;
from the day the Elder attained supernormal powers, he has been in Veḷuvana itself. Then they said to the Mettiya-Bhūmajakas:
“Friends, your account does not agree; do you perhaps speak while casting a slur upon us? Thus were they questioned by those monks.
Having said, "It is so, friends," they reported this matter.

But as for the phrase, "Friends, why did you [approach] the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta regarding a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) belonging to another category?"—here, *aññabhāgiya* means "belonging to another part" (*aññabhāga*), or that which has another part; *adhikaraṇa* means a basis or foundation.
It is to be understood; what is meant is that the "basis" (vatthu) is the "adhiṭṭhāna.
For that goat which was called "Dabba Mallaputta" is distinct from the portion, part, or side consisting of the venerable Dabba Mallaputta’s human birth and his status as a monk;
it belongs to another portion, part, or side, namely the animal birth.
And because there exists either that very state of being a goat or another state [of being], it receives the designation "pertaining to another" (*aññabhāgiya*).
Furthermore, since for those saying, "We shall give this person the name Dabba Mallaputta," that naming-convention has its support,
its basis, and its foundation in him, it should therefore be understood as a "legal question" (*adhikaraṇa*).

For it was with reference to this that they said, "Those bhikkhus [are dealing] with a legal issue belonging to another category," and not with any one of the others, such as a dispute-legal-issue (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) and so forth. Why? Because it is impossible.

For they did not take up even a portion or a mere trace of any legal issue belonging to another category among the four types of legal issues. Nor is there a trace of the four types of legal issues [in them].
There is a name [for this]. For the "stains of birth" (*jātilesā*) and so forth are said to be stains pertaining only to persons, not to legal issues such as disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).

And this name "Dabba Mallaputta" was merely a pretext for someone to groundlessly charge the Elder with a *pārājika* offense, while that goat-skin was actually situated within a legal issue of a different category (*aññabhāgiyādhikaraṇa*).

And here, "place" (*desa*) is so called because it is seen, pointed out, and designated as that from which [something] comes; this is a designation for any one of the categories beginning with birth (*jāti*).
Furthermore, "trace" (*lesa*) is so called because it is licked, adhered to, or slightly clung to by mere conventional expression;
this is a designation for any one of the categories beginning with birth itself. Beyond that, the meaning is self-evident.
This same meaning applies to the laying down of the training rule (*sikkhāpada-panñatti*) as well. However,

regarding the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it should be understood that although one might accuse someone of an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika-dhamma*) by taking up some portion or mere semblance of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) belonging to another category,
this [case] has not been analyzed because it is already made manifest by way of the origin of the matter (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
393. Furthermore, regarding the four *adhikaraṇas* (legal issues) that occur by way of extracting the meaning from the commonality of the term "legal issue":

since their distinctness (*aññabhāgiyatā*) and their belonging to the same category (*tabbhāgiyatā*) are not evident and must be understood by those who uphold the Vinaya, [the author], relying on the term "legal issue" obtained through that commonality of expression, reveals it as follows: "Of a distinct legal issue..."
"An *adhikaraṇa* (legal case) may be either *āpattiaññabhāgiya* or *adhikaraṇaññabhāgiya*," he said.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this summary of the classification of all *adhikaraṇas* as being either *tabbhāgiya* (of the same category) or *aññabhāgiya* (of a different category) was stated in order to show that very same point which was mentioned at the conclusion regarding the *codanā* (accusation) concerning an *adhikaraṇa* that is *āpattiaññabhāgiya*.

And therein, because the category of "belonging to another case" (*aññabhāgiya*) regarding offenses was recited first, one might have expected the exposition to begin with: "In what way is an offense belonging to another case than an offense?

However, since this matter will be understood through the very investigation of "belonging to that same case" (*tabbhāgiya*) within the context of legal issues concerning offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), it was not begun in that manner; instead, it begins:
"In what way is a legal issue belonging to another case than a legal issue? (*kathañca adhikaraṇaṃ adhikaraṇassa aññabhāgiyan*?).
It should be understood that the exposition has begun by taking up only the final phrase.

In this regard, the section on "belonging to another" (*aññabhāgiya*) is of plain meaning. For each individual legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) belongs to another, belongs to another side, and belongs to another category in relation to the other three, because its subject matter (*vatthu*) is dissimilar; [this is explained] in the section on "belonging to that" (*tabbhāgiya*).

Furthermore, a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is related to, belongs to the faction of, and is of the same category as another legal issue arising from a dispute because their underlying subject matter (*vatthu*) is similar;
likewise for a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*). How so?
For the disputes that have arisen since the time of the Buddha based on the eighteen grounds for schism, and the disputes that are arising now, [are of the same nature].
And because of the similarity of the underlying matter (*vatthusabhāgatā*), there is only one legal question of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).

Likewise, from the time of the Buddha onwards, both an accusation that has arisen based on the four failures (*vipatti*) and an accusation that is about to arise now are considered one single legal question of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) due to the similarity of the underlying matter.
However, since a legal question of offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) [is distinguished] by the similar and dissimilar matters of offenses...
Because it is not invariably "of that same category" (*tabbhāgiya*) either by way of being similar in kind (*sabhāga*) or similar in appearance (*sarikkha*), it is therefore said:
"A legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) may, with respect to another legal issue arising from an offense, be either of the same category or of a different category.
In this context, since the "of a different category" was explained first starting from the beginning, here too the "of a different category" is explained first.

In this regard, its being "of another category" (*aññabhāgiyatā*) and its being "of that same category" (*tabbhāgiyatā*) should be understood according to the method already stated. Regarding the statement,

"A legal issue arising from formal acts (*kicca*) is of the same category as a legal issue arising from formal acts," here [it refers to] both the legal issues that have arisen based on the four sangha-formal acts since the time of the Buddha, and the four sangha-formal acts themselves at present.
A legal issue arising in dependence [on another] is, by virtue of its commonality and similarity, one and the same as a legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
Now, is a legal issue that has arisen in dependence on sangha-proceedings (*saṅghakamma*) a legal issue of business, or is this merely a designation for the sangha-proceedings themselves?
It is a designation for the sangha-proceedings themselves. Even so—
What is called a "sanghakamma" (an act of the Sangha) is that which arises depending on the characteristics of an act—
such as "this and that must be done in this way"— and because it arises depending on each preceding sanghakamma,
the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that has arisen based on such sanghakammas is called a "legal issue arising from business" (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

394. Regarding the phrase "taking some small portion (lesa) of a place (desa)": since "place" and "small portion" differ only in phrasing but are identical in meaning according to the method explained previously, he therefore said:
"A 'portion' (lesa) means ten portions: the portion of birth (jātileso), the portion of name (nāmaleso)," and so forth.
In this context, birth itself is the "portion of birth. The same principle applies to the remaining [portions].
395. Now, in order to show that very *lesa* (taint) in detail, and to demonstrate how, based upon it, there is an accusation (*anuddhaṃsanā*) by providing a concrete instance, he said:
“A *jātilesa* (taint of birth) occurs when a khattiya is seen,” and so forth.
In this context, “a khattiya is seen” means that some other person belonging to the khattiya caste has been seen by this accuser. [If] a *pārājika*...
"Practicing a forbidden act" means practicing any one of the forbidden acts, such as sexual intercourse and so forth.

"Having seen another khattiya, he accuses him" means that then, having seen another bhikkhu of the khattiya caste who is his own enemy, he seizes upon the mere appearance of being a khattiya and accuses him thus:
"A khattiya was seen by me practicing a forbidden act involving a pārājika offense; you, too, are a khattiya."
“You have committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika-dhamma),” or alternatively, “You are that very khattiya, not another; you have committed an offense entailing defeat;
you are no longer a samaṇa, you are no longer a follower of the Sakyan (asakyaputtiya); there is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) with you.
For every such statement, there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa. And here, regarding those khattiyas—

The state of being "belonging to another" (*aññabhāgiyatā*) should be understood by way of their mutual dissimilarity—such as being long or short, or seen or unseen—and the state of being the "locus" (*adhikaraṇatā*) should be understood as the basis for the designation of the *khattiya* caste. By this method, the application [of the analysis] should be understood for all terms. 400.

In the description of the bowl (*patta*), a "cloth-bowl" (*sāṭakapatta*) refers to a clay bowl that is well-shaped like a metal bowl, with a beautiful surface, glossy, and the color of a bee. A "Sumbhaka-bowl" (*sumbhakapatta*) refers to a bowl made of natural clay.

406. Since, however, the brief exposition of the class of offenses was stated by means of a single phrase, it was therefore said—"a bhikkhu is seen committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense," and so forth—in order to show that also from an extensive perspective.
But why was its exposition not given right there [in the previous section] and instead stated separately here? Because it is dissimilar to the remaining expositions. The remaining expositions...

For [the previous case] was stated by way of accusing one person after having seen another; this, however, is stated by way of accusing someone of one offense after having seen that very person committing another offense.
If this is so, how does it become a legal issue belonging to another category (*aññabhāgiya*)? It is by way of the offense.
Therefore it was said: "In this way, there is both a legal issue belonging to another category and a stain has been taken up."
For that which he has committed as a *saṅghādisesa* offense is a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) belonging to a different category than a *pārājika*.

Now, the "trace" (*leśa*) of that legal issue belonging to a different category is what is common to all offenses—the nature of being an offense—just as the status of being a kshatriya is common to all kshatriyas.
By this same method, the remaining systems based on the roots of offenses and the section concerning the accuser (*codāpaka*) are to be understood.
408. There is no offense for one who, perceiving it as such, accuses or causes another to accuse, thinking, "This person has indeed fallen into a pārājika offense.
For whoever, perceiving it as such, accuses or causes another to accuse, there is no offense. The rest is clear everywhere.
The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are also exactly like those of the first *duṭṭhadosa* rule.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning malice is finished.
10. Commentary on the first training rule concerning schism in the Saṅgha.
409. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... [this is] the training rule concerning schism in the Saṅgha. In this regard, concerning the passage beginning with "Then Devadatta," etc.:
Who Devadatta was, how he went forth, and for what reason Kokālika and the others approached him and said,
"Come, friends, let us cause a schism in the Saṅgha of the ascetic Gotama,
a breaking of the wheel"— all that has already been related in the Saṅghabhedakkhandhaka. As for the request for the five points, although it is indeed found in that very same [section],...
"He will come. But rather, having first said whatever needs to be said here regarding his arrival, we shall then depart.

"Excellent, venerable sir," is the request. "Let the bhikkhus be forest-dwellers for as long as they live" means that all the bhikkhus, having undertaken the forest-dwelling ascetic practice (*araññika-dhutaṅga*), should remain forest-dwellers for as long as they live, dwelling only in the forest. Whoever [dwells] near a village...

"May he fall into blame; may blame touch him"—this means that if even a single bhikkhu, having abandoned the forest, should descend to a village boundary for the sake of dwelling there, may blame touch that bhikkhu;
may fault touch him; may the Blessed One deal with him according to an offense.
This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

410. "I shall convince the people" means: "I shall make the people know our state of having few desires and so forth," or alternatively, it means "I shall satisfy them" or "I shall inspire confidence in them.
However, as soon as the Blessed One heard Devadatta’s words as he was requesting these five points, he knew:
"He requests these because he intends to cause a schism in the Saṅgha. For if those points had been permitted, they would have become an obstacle to the Path for many sons of noble family.

They lead [to such consequences]; therefore, the Blessed One, having rejected [Devadatta’s proposal] with the words, “Enough, Devadatta,” said, “Whoever wishes, let him be a forest-dweller,” and so forth.
Here, however, having understood the Blessed One’s intention, a son of good family should know what is appropriate for himself.
This, indeed, is the Blessed One’s intention here: “A single bhikkhu may have great aspiration and great energy; he is capable...”
Having rejected a lodging within a village, one dwells in the forest in order to bring an end to suffering.
One person is weak and lacks strength; he is unable to dwell in the forest, but is able to do so only within a village.

Another is very strong, with well-balanced elements, endowed with patience and endurance, and even-minded toward the pleasant and the unpleasant; he is indeed capable of dwelling both in the forest and within a village.
One person is able neither in the vicinity of a village nor in the forest; he is merely one who follows the footsteps [of others].

In this regard, as for the one who has great aspiration and great energy, who is able to bring an end to suffering by rejecting a lodging in the vicinity of a village and dwelling in the forest—it is fitting that he dwell in the forest alone. His students and others [should likewise do so].
Training in accordance with this, they will think that one must dwell only in the forest.
However, if there is one who is weak and lacking in strength, yet is able to reach the end of suffering even while living near a village, let him dwell right there in the vicinity of a village.
But as for one who is of great strength, whose elements are well-balanced, and who is endowed with patience and endurance—
One who is even-minded toward the pleasant and the unpleasant is capable both in the forest and in the vicinity of a village;

let this one also abandon lodgings in the vicinity of a village and dwell in the forest, for it is appropriate for him, and his co-residents, following his example, will think that they too should dwell in the forest.
But as for one who is capable neither in the vicinity of a village nor in the forest, being merely a follower of words—let him dwell in the forest alone.
For this practice of the ascetic virtues (dhutaṅga) and the cultivation of the meditation subject will serve as a decisive support for his future attainment of the paths and fruits.
Furthermore, his co-residents and others, emulating him, will think that they too ought to dwell in the forest.
Thus, even one who is weak and lacking in strength can bring an end to suffering while dwelling right within the village.
"Not in the forest"; it was with reference to this person that the Blessed One said, "Whoever wishes, let him dwell near a village.
And by this person, the way has been opened for others as well.
For if the Blessed One had accepted Devadatta's proposal, then for this person who is weak by nature—

There is one who lacks sufficient strength; even if he was able to endure living in the forest during his youth, he is unable to do so later in old age, or at a time when the humors are disturbed by wind, bile, and so forth.
Yet, while dwelling right within a village, he is able to bring an end to suffering.
For such individuals, there would be a severance of the Noble Path, and they would not attain the fruit of Arhatship.

If [the teaching] were contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, subversive, and not leading to liberation, and if the Teacher were not omniscient, he would be censurable for having abandoned his own doctrine and established himself in Devadatta’s doctrine.
Therefore, the Blessed One, while gathering such persons [to himself], rejected Devadatta’s doctrine. By this very means...

The detailed exposition should be understood regarding the practice of eating only almsfood (*piṇḍapātika*), the practice of wearing robes made from discarded rags (*paṃsukūlika*), and the practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree (*rukkhamūlika*) for eight months.
However, for four months, dwelling at the foot of a tree as one's lodging is strictly prohibited.

Regarding the practice concerning fish and meat, "pure in three respects" (*tikoṭiparisuddha*) means pure with respect to the three points, being free from the impurities of having seen [the animal being killed] and so forth.
The meaning is "devoid of. For this very reason it is said: "not seen, not heard, not suspected.
Therein, "not seen" means that which is taken after killing deer or fish for the sake of the bhikkhus, without having been seen [by them].
"Not heard" means that it has been heard that deer or fish were killed for the sake of the bhikkhus. "Not suspected," however, refers to what is suspected because it was seen [to be so].
Having understood that which is suspected of being heard and that which is suspected of being both [heard and seen], it should be known by way of their opposites.
How so? Here, monks see people with nets, snares, and other such implements leaving a village or wandering in the forest;
and on the following day, when those people have entered that village for alms, they see them receiving alms-food consisting of fish and meat.
They bring it forward. Seeing that [food], they suspect it, thinking, "Has this been prepared for the sake of the monks?
This is what is called "suspected upon seeing" (*diṭṭhaparisaṅkita*); it is not permitted to accept it. However, that which is not suspected in this way is permitted.
But if those people ask, "Venerable sir, why do you not take it? and having heard the reason, say, "This is not..."
If they say, "Venerable sir, this was made for the sake of the bhikkhus, or it was made by us for our own sake, or for the sake of royal officials and others," it is allowable.
It may be that the bhikkhus do not actually see it, but they hear it: "People, it seems, with nets, snares, and other such things in their hands, [are coming] from the village..."

“...or they go out, or they wander in the forest. On the second day, when they have entered that village for alms, thinking, “Was this made for the sake of the monks?”—this is called “suspicion based on what was heard.
It is not permissible to accept such [food]; however, that which is not suspected in this way is permissible. But if those people say, “Venerable sir, why...?”
Having asked, "Do you not take it? and having heard that matter, if they say, "Venerable sir, this was not made for the sake of the bhikkhus;
it was made by us for our own sake or for the sake of those connected to the king and so forth," it is allowable.
Furthermore, even if the bhikkhus neither see nor hear [of its making], but rather, when they have entered the village for alms...
Having taken a bowl and prepared almsfood consisting of equal portions of vegetable and meat, they offer it;
those people suspect, "Has this been prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus? This is called "suspected as being for both [the donor and the recipient].
It is not permissible to accept this. That which is not suspected in this way is permissible. But if those people say, "Why..."
Having asked, "Venerable sir, do you not accept it? and having heard that matter, they say, "Venerable sir, this was not done for the sake of the bhikkhus by us;
nor was it done for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and the like.

It was prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus after obtaining only what is allowable (kappiya) meat that was already available. This is permissible. [Also permissible is meat] intended for the funeral rites of the deceased.
The same principle applies even when [a gift] is made for the sake of auspiciousness and so forth.
Indeed, whatever has not been made specifically for the sake of monks, and regarding which one is free from doubt, all that is allowable.
However, if it has been made for the sake of monks in a particular monastery, and they themselves acknowledge that it was made for their own sake—
They do not know; others know. For those who know, it is not permitted; for others, it is permitted.
Others do not know; they themselves know; for them alone it is not permitted; for others, it is permitted.
They know, "This was done for our sake," and others also know, "This was done for their sake"; for all of them it is not permitted; for all...

They do not know; for it is permissible for all. Regarding the five types of fellow practitioners (sahadhammika), whatever is prepared specifically for the sake of one or another among them is not allowable for any of them.
However, if someone kills an animal specifically for one bhikkhu and gives it to him, filling his bowl, he—
If one takes food knowing full well that it was prepared for oneself, yet gives it to another bhikkhu who consumes it out of faith, whose offense is it?
There is no offense for either. For there is no offense for the one for whom it was intended because he did not eat it;
nor is there an offense for the other because he was unaware [of the origin]. Indeed, there is no offense in the acceptance of allowable meat (*kappiyamaṃsa*). Regarding that which was intended...
There is no requirement to confess an offense for one who has eaten meat without knowing it was "prepared on purpose" (uddissa kata), provided one only learns of it after having already consumed it;
however, even if one learns of it afterwards, an offense committed by eating unallowable meat (akappiya-maṃsa) must still be confessed.

For an offense occurs only when one eats while knowing it was prepared on purpose. Even for one who eats without knowing it is unallowable meat, there is indeed an offense. Therefore, one who fears transgression...
Even when observing the form, one must receive the meat only after asking.
At the time of consumption, one should either take it with the intention of "I will eat after asking," or consume it only after having asked. Why?
Because it is difficult to discern. For the flesh of a deer is similar to the flesh of a pig, and the flesh of a leopard and so forth is also similar to the flesh of a wild animal; therefore—
They say that after asking, one should indeed proceed with the taking [of the robe].

"Joyful and elated" means being both satisfied and having a body and mind uplifted. It is said that Kokālika perceived the Bhagavā’s gesture and thought, "The Blessed One does not permit these five points;
now I shall be able to cause a schism in the Saṅgha."
Having shown this, it is just as when a man desiring death— having either consumed poison, hanged himself with a rope, or taken up a weapon—

finds any one of those things such as poison and, not perceiving even the immediate suffering of death resulting from them, becomes joyful and elated; in the same way, [one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha], due to the cause of that schism,
does not perceive even the immediate [suffering] to be experienced after being reborn in Avīci.
Not understanding this suffering, [Devadatta] thought, "Now I have found the means for the schism of the Saṅgha. Elated and overjoyed, he rose from his seat together with his followers;
with that same state of elation, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Regarding the phrase, "We are living having undertaken these five points," the expression "these five points" refers to the following:

Although they should have said, "We shall convince the people by means of these five grounds," they failed to notice the grammatical shift resulting from their frequent reflections; instead, following the very pattern of those frequent reflections,
they said, "We [shall convince] them by means of these five grounds," just as one whose mind is distracted might speak.

“Dhutā sallekhavuttino”: one who possesses that practice which shakes off (*dhunāti*) defilements is called *dhuta*. And since their way of life (*vutti*) scrapes away (*sallikhati*) defilements, they are "those whose way of life is scraping away" (*sallekhavuttino*).
"Bāhuliko": "abundance" (*bāhulla*) is the state of having an abundance of requisites such as robes;

one who has this abundance, or who is devoted to or established in that abundance, is "one who is abundant" (*bāhuliko*). "He intends for abundance" means he intends for, or prepares for, the state of abundance.

He makes an effort. The intention is that he has exerted himself with the thought: "How indeed might there be an abundance of requisites such as robes for both me and my disciples? "For the breaking of the wheel" means for the breaking of the authority.
"Having given a discourse on the Dhamma" refers to the method stated in the Khandhaka: "Enough, Devadatta; let not the schism in the Saṅgha be pleasing to you."
“Devadatta, schism in the Saṅgha is indeed grave.
Devadatta, whoever divides a harmonious Saṅgha produces an evil that lasts for an eon; he will burn in hell for an eon.
But whoever, Devadatta, reunites a divided Saṅgha, produces sublime merit; he will rejoice in heaven for an eon. Such was his teaching.
Having given a Dhamma talk of many kinds to Devadatta and the bhikkhus—talk that was appropriate and suitable for them—he [spoke].
411. "Of one who is united" (samaggassa) means of one who is together, not separated in mind and body;
for this very meaning is shown in the word-analysis as well. Indeed, by saying "one who belongs to the same communion" (samānasaṃvāsako), the non-separation in mind is demonstrated.
By saying "standing within the same boundary," it is meant by way of the body. How so?

For one who shares the same communion (*samānasaṃvāsaka*) is not separated from one with whom he shares different views (*laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka*) or different formal acts (*kammanānāsaṃvāsaka*), being inseparable from him through a mind of equanimity.
Standing within the same boundary, he is inseparable from him by way of the body through the granting of communal unity (*kāyasāmaggidāna*).
"A legal issue conducive to schism" (*bhedanasaṃvattanikaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ*) means a cause conducive to, that is, leading toward, a schism in the Saṅgha.

In this context, "legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to mean "cause," as in such passages as "with sensual desire as the cause, with sensual desire as the source, with sensual desire as the legal issue. And since that [cause] is of eighteen kinds, therefore, in the word-commentary, it says: "eighteen..."

"...the grounds for schism," it is said. These, moreover, are recorded in the Khandhaka according to the method beginning with: "Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma," and so forth;
therefore, we shall explain their meaning right there.

And as for this [schism] which, based on these grounds, occurs through other means—namely, by formal act (kamma), recitation (uddesa), terminology (vohāra), proclamation (anusāvanā), and the drawing of lots (salākaggāha)—it is likewise explained there.
There are five causes for a schism in the Saṅgha; we shall explain those as well in their proper place.
In brief, however, regarding the phrase "having taken up a legal issue conducive to schism," the meaning should be understood as follows:
having grasped a cause that is conducive to a schism in the Saṅgha—that is, capable of producing a schism in the Saṅgha.
“Having taken up” means having grasped, lifted up, and made manifest. “Should stand” means he should remain exactly as he has undertaken and exactly as he has taken up [the precept].

However, because for one who thus takes up and stands [firmly], that [precept] becomes both illuminated and not relinquished, therefore it is said in the word-commentary: “he should illuminate” and “he should not relinquish.”
"He should be addressed thus by the bhikkhus" means he should be spoken to in this way by other bhikkhus who possess a sense of shame.
In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), "those who see" refers to those who see him standing having taken up [the dispute] in their presence.
"Those who hear" refers to those who also hear: "In such-and-such a monastery, bhikkhus are standing having taken up and maintained a legal issue conducive to schism."

"Let the venerable one be united with the Saṅgha" means that the venerable one should unite with, come together with, and become of one view with the Saṅgha. For what reason? Because a Saṅgha that is harmonious, living in concord, without dispute, and reciting the same code dwells in comfort.
In this context, "living in concord" means rejoicing well in each other’s success.

"Without dispute" means not disputing in such a manner as, "This is the Dhamma; this is not the Dhamma. "Having one recitation" (*ekuddeso*) means having a single recitation of the Pātimokkha occurring together.
"Does not yield" means he does not relinquish. "He dwells in comfort" means he dwells in happiness.
"This is wholesome" means that this relinquishing is wholesome, secure, and a state of safety for that bhikkhu.
"If he does not relinquish, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that for one who does not relinquish after it has been stated three times, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
"Having heard it, they do not speak: there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)"—this means that for those who, having heard it, do not speak, there is also a dukkaṭa.
To what distance does "having heard it" extend for those who do not speak so as to incur a dukkaṭa? First of all, in the case of a single dwelling (ekavihāra), there is no need to specify a distance.

However, it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā): "The responsibility lies with the monks within a radius of one and a half yojanas. Even if one speaks by sending a messenger or a letter, there is release from the offense."
There is none. Having gone there himself, he should be restrained, saying: “Friend, schism in the Saṅgha is a grave matter; do not strive for a schism in the Saṅgha.
However, one who is capable should go even a long distance, for even a long distance is merely a burden for those who are not ill.
Now, in order to show the mere meaning of the passage beginning with “And when that bhikkhu is being spoken to thus by the bhikkhus,” [it says] “he...”
"A bhikkhu should be dragged even into the midst of the Saṅgha and addressed," and so forth, he said. In that context, "dragged even into the midst of the Saṅgha" means:

if, when being spoken to according to the previous method, he does not relinquish [his position], then even by seizing him by the hands and feet, he should be dragged into the midst of the Saṅgha and addressed three times again according to the method beginning with, "Venerable sir, do not [do this]."
"Up to the third time he should be exhorted" means that he should be exhorted for as long as it takes until the third exhortation;
what is meant is that the formal act (kamma) should be performed with three formal proclamations of exhortation.
However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), taking only the meaning of this [phrase], in order to show the procedure for the exhortation, it says: "That bhikkhu is to be exhorted. And thus..."
"But, monks, he should be formally admonished," and so forth, was said. 414.
In that regard, the *dukkaṭa* [offense] incurred by means of the motion (*ñatti*) and the two formal proclamations (*kammavācā*) are extinguished;
thus, both the *dukkaṭa* offense committed at the conclusion of the motion and the two *thullaccaya* offenses incurred through the two formal proclamations—these three as well—[are extinguished].

The offenses are extinguished at the third *kammavācā*—the point reached by the syllable "yya" in the phrase, "He to whom it does not please, let him speak"—but the *saṅghādisesa* itself remains. Now, do the offenses committed become extinguished, or those not yet committed?
Regarding this, the Elder Mahāsiva says: "He who shall relinquish [the offense] at the end, for him those offenses..."
"It does not incur [an offense]; therefore, those who have not incurred [an offense] are pacified. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said:

"Just as with offenses that are not shared [by both genders], those who have incurred [an offense] are pacified through a change of gender; but for those who have not incurred [an offense], what is there to be pacified?
415. "One who perceives a legitimate legal act as a legitimate legal act": if that act of formal admonition is indeed a legitimate legal act, [then it is so].
"In that case, he perceives it as a legitimate legal act" is the meaning. This same principle applies everywhere. In this instance, perception does not protect [the monk];
because the act is indeed legitimate, he incurs the offense even while refusing to relinquish [his position].
416. "Without having been formally admonished": there is no offense by Saṅghādisesa for one who has not been formally admonished, even if he refuses to relinquish [his position].
"For one who relinquishes" means: for one who relinquishes prior to the motion, at the moment of the motion, at the conclusion of the motion,
or during the first, second, or third proclamation— so long as one does not reach the syllable *yya*—
there is no offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
"Of the first offender": here, however, because it is stated in the Parivāra, "Devadatta strove for the schism of the united Saṅgha;
