in that matter," Devadatta is the first offender. And that [status] applies only to his striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, not to his refusal to relinquish [the schismatic views].
For that formal act (kamma) was not performed against him. If one asks, "How is this to be known? [it is so known from the aforementioned source].

From the Sutta: For instance, because it is stated in the Parivāra—"The monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-keeper, did not desist from that matter even after being admonished up to three times"—it is understood that a formal act (kamma) was performed against Ariṭṭha;
however, such is not the case for Devadatta. Even if someone were to say, on the mere basis of their own preference, that one must have been performed against him as well, [it would be baseless].
Nevertheless, for one who does not relinquish [the offense], there is no such thing as being a "first-offender" (ādikammika) who incurs no offense.
For indeed, apart from cases where an action is specifically permitted, no exemption from offense is seen for one who transgresses a prescribed training rule (sikkhāpada).

As for the fact that the phrase "for a first-offender" is written in the manuscripts regarding the exemption from offense in the case of the Ariṭṭha-sikkhāpada, that is a scribal error. The nature of it being a scribal error...

This is to be understood from the statement regarding the imposition of an offense in the *Kammakkhandhaka*: "First, the monk Ariṭṭha should be charged; having been charged, he should be reminded; having been reminded, the offense should be imposed.
Thus, because that formal act was not performed against Devadatta—the original instigator who strove for schism—therefore, for him...
No offense was actually committed; however, because the training rule (sikkhāpada) was promulgated with reference to that case, he is called an "original offender" (ādikammika).
Thus, it is precisely due to the absence of an offense that his non-offense is stated.
Although this [non-offense] is already established by the phrase "even though he does not admonish," nevertheless, one who "does not admonish" refers to one whom others simply do not admonish at all.
Thus he is called "not a beginner. But this Devadatta was indeed a beginner; therefore it is said, "of a beginner.
By this method, the explanation for all formal admonitions should be understood, with the exception of the training rule concerning Ariṭṭha.
The rest is clear everywhere.

Regarding the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors: it consists of three factors, has a single origin, and its name is "originating from admonition" (*samanubhāsana-samuṭṭhāna*). It originates from body, speech, and mind.
Because one incurs the offense even without making a physical gesture or uttering a word when saying "I renounce," it is a non-action (*akiriya*);

it is resolved by perception (*saññā-vimokkha*), associated with consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), an unwholesome state of mind (*akusalacitta*), and a feeling of pain (*dukkhavedanā*).
The commentary on the first Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada is finished.
11. Commentary on the second Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada. 417–8.
"At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... refers to the second Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada. In this context, "those who follow" means...
Those who do not follow by adopting his views, inclinations, and preferences are the "factional speakers" (vagga-vādaka), because they speak words that belong to a faction and promote discord.
In the word-commentary (padabhājana), however, it is said: "They stand for his praise and for his side";
this means they stand for the sake of praising him when he is striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, and for the sake of increasing the strength of his faction.
The meaning is as follows: Those who speak in factions are invariably of such a nature; therefore, it was said thus.
However, since those beyond three do not deserve a formal act (*kamma*), and because the Saṅgha does not perform a formal act against itself, it was stated:
"one, two, or three."
"Knows" means he knows our inclinations and so forth. "Speaks" means he speaks with us, saying, "Let us do it thus. "This is agreeable to us" means that whatever he does is pleasing to us as well.
"Let the venerable ones' minds be in harmony with the Saṅgha" means let the minds of the venerable ones be in harmony and come together with the Saṅgha;
what is meant is that they should attain unity. The rest here is clear, as it follows the method explained in the first training rule and its meaning is self-evident.
The origins and other details are also exactly like those of the first training rule.
The commentary on the second Saṅghabheda (schism) training rule is finished.
12. Commentary on the Duvaca (difficult-to-speak-to) training rule.
424. At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, [laid down] the training rule concerning the one who is difficult to speak to.
Therein, "he practices improper conduct" means he commits various kinds of transgressions through the doors of body and speech.
"What on earth is this? is a word of contempt. "I am indeed such-and-such" is a boastful statement. "You might say" refers to saying, "Do this; do not do that."

He shows that he is worthy to speak to you. Why? Because he spoke with reference to such matters as: "Our Buddha, the Blessed One, having climbed upon Kaṇṭaka, went forth together with me and became a renunciant.
Having said, "Our Dhamma," he then demonstrates the justification for it being his own possession by saying, "The Dhamma was realized by our Noble Son."
He said: "Because the Noble Son has realized the Dhamma of the Four Truths, it follows that the Dhamma is ours as well.
However, thinking that the Saṅgha stands on the side of his enemies, he does not say, 'The Saṅgha is ours.
Having given a simile, wishing to disparage the Saṅgha, he said, 'Just as if,' and so forth. [The phrase] *tiṇakaṭṭhapaṇṇasaṭa*..."
"Grass, sticks, and leaves fallen here and there. Alternatively, "grass and sticks" refers to sapless, light wood.
"Decayed leaves" means old leaves. "Should clear away" means one should make a heap. "Mountain-born" means originating from a mountain;
for that [water] has a swift current, and therefore one takes that very [water]. "Shells, seaweed, and moss."
Here, *saṅkho* refers to a long-rooted leaf-moss (*paṇṇasevāla*). *Sevālo* refers to blue-green moss;
all the rest—such as water-crust (*udakapappaṭaka*), sesame seeds, and so forth—is reckoned as *paṇako*. "Heaped up together" means gathered in one place by someone and made into a pile. 425–6.
"Of a harsh-natured disposition" means having a character that is difficult to speak to; the meaning is that he is impossible to address. In the word-analysis (*padabhājana*) for this as well...
“Difficult to speak to” (*dubbaco*) means one who must be addressed with pain and difficulty; the sense is that he cannot be spoken to easily.

“By means of the qualities that make one difficult to speak to” (*dovacassakaraṇehi*) means by those things which produce the state of being difficult to speak to; the sense is that he is possessed of those [qualities] which make a person difficult to speak to.
These, moreover, are described as follows: “And what, friends, are the qualities that make one difficult to speak to? Here, friends, a bhikkhu has evil desires,” and so forth.
In due order according to the method [of the Suttas], as set forth in the *Anumāna-sutta*, these are: having evil desires,

praising oneself and disparaging others, being prone to anger, harboring resentment on account of anger, being obsessed by anger on account of anger, uttering speech bordering on anger on account of anger,
counter-attacking one who reproaches, rebuffing one who reproaches, throwing accusations back at the reproacher, and evading the issue by changing the subject.

Nineteen qualities are to be understood: lack of courtesy in conduct, being smeared with and defiled by [faults], envy and avarice, craftiness and deceitfulness, stubbornness and excessive pride, and adherence to one's own views while grasping them dogmatically and refusing to relinquish them.

One who does not tolerate or endure instruction is "intolerant" (*akkhamo*). Because he does not practice according to what has been taught, he does not accept instruction in a proper manner; thus he is "one who does not grasp instruction properly" (*appadakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaniṃ*).

“Included in the recitation” means included within the recitation, contained therein. The meaning is: while it is being recited within the Pātimokkha, because it is summarized by the words, “Whosoever has an offense, let him reveal it. “Being addressed by one who shares the Dhamma” means being addressed by one who shares the Dhamma;
this is the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental, because one must train together with the five [factors] who share the Dhamma.
The meaning is: "being addressed by a training rule (sikkhāpada) proclaimed by the Buddha and known by the name 'sahadhammika' because it belongs to them. "Viramathāyasmanto mama vacanāyā" means:
"Refrain, venerable sirs, from that speech with which you address me"; the sense is: "Do not speak such words to me. "Vadatu sahadhammenā" means:
[let him speak] by means of a training rule that is *sahadhammika*, or by another *sahadhamma* (in accordance with the Dhamma) that conduces to inspiring confidence (*pāsādikabhāva*).
"Let him speak with words. The phrase *yadidaṃ* is a particle used for the purpose of indicating a cause of growth.

By this, the cause of growth for the assembly is shown as follows: "The assembly has grown through these mutual words of benefit and through their mutual restoration from offenses. The rest is clear everywhere.
The origins and other details are exactly the same as in the first rule on schism in the Saṅgha.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those who are difficult to speak with is finished.
13. Commentary on the training rule concerning the defiler of families.
431. At that time, the Blessed Buddha [laid down] the training rule concerning those who corrupt families. In this context, "Assaji and Punabbasuka" refers to Assaji and Punabbasuka.
"In Kīṭāgiri" means in the district of that name. "Were residents" (*āvāsikā*):

they are called "residents" because a residence (*āvāsa*) belongs to them; "residence" here refers to a monastery (*vihāra*). It is that which is under their authority, as they bear the burden of overseeing new construction, maintaining what is old, and so forth.
Those are the *āvāsikas* (resident monks). However, those who merely dwell in the monastery are called *nevāsikas* (local residents).
These were the *āvāsikas*. "Shameless, wicked bhikkhus" means they were shameless and base bhikkhus; for they were the leaders among the group of six (*chabbaggiyas*).
It is said that in Sāvatthī there were six friends who thought, "Agricultural labor and such tasks are difficult; come now, let us go forth properly!"

Having deliberated, "It is fitting for those going forth to go forth when there is a duty that has arisen and a need to overcome it," they went forth in the presence of the two Chief Disciples. When they had been ordained for five years and had mastered the *mātikā*, they consulted together:
"The countryside is sometimes well-supplied with food and sometimes ill-supplied; let us not remain in one place."
“We have lived there; we lived in three places. Then Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka said:

“Friends, there is a place called Sāvatthī, inhabited by seven million five hundred thousand families, the gateway to the revenues of the two kingdoms of Kāsi and Kosala, which consist of eighty thousand villages and extend for three hundred leagues.
There, you should build your dwellings in the very heart of the city.”
“Having had mango, breadfruit, coconut, and other trees planted, and supporting families with flowers and fruits,
ordain the children of those families and thus increase the assembly.
The Mettiya-Bhūmajaka monks said, “Friends, Rājagaha is inhabited by eighteen koṭis of people.”
“It is the source of revenue for the two kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha, which are adorned with eighty thousand villages and extend three hundred yojanas;
there you should establish yourselves at the very center... [and] increase your following.
Assaji and Punabbasuka said, “Friend, Kīṭāgiri is favored by two clouds and yields three harvests a year...”
“They are giving birth; therefore, you should have monastic cells built right where your respective seats are...
[and so on]... and thus increase your following. They did accordingly. Each one of them had a retinue of five hundred monks, so that there were more than fifteen hundred monks in total.
Therein, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, along with their followers, were indeed virtuous.

They even traveled on tour through the countryside together with the Blessed One; they gave rise to what had not been established as a practice, yet they did not trample upon the training rules that had been laid down.
All the others, however, being shameless, both gave rise to what had not been established as a practice and trampled upon the training rules that had been laid down.
Therefore it was said: "shameless, evil monks."
"Of such a kind" means of such a nature. "Practicing improper conduct" means they practice what should not be practiced; they do what should not be done.
"A flowering shrub" refers to a young flowering tree; for even young flowering trees and flowering creepers are called "flowering shrubs.
They themselves plant various kinds of flowering shrubs and have others plant them as well.
Therefore it is said: "They plant flowering shrubs themselves, or they have them planted. "They sprinkle" means they sprinkle with water themselves.
"They have sprinkled" means they have someone else sprinkle it.
In this context, however, there are these five: unallowable expression, allowable expression, synonym, indication, and sign-making.
These things are to be understood. In this context, "improper speech" (*akappiyavohāra*) refers to: the pounding or causing to be pounded of fresh greens;
the digging or causing to be dug of a pit; the planting or causing to be planted of a sapling; the binding or causing to be bound of a fence; the sprinkling or causing to be sprinkled of water;
and the clearing out of a channel or the sprinkling of "proper water" (*kappiya-udaka*), such as water for washing the hands, face, or feet, or for bathing.

"Permissible speech" (*kappiyavohāra*) refers to such statements as "Know this tree," "Know this pit," "Know this flowering shrub," or "Know that there is water here," as well as the straightening of a dried-up irrigation channel.
"Indirect method" (*pariyāya*) refers to such statements as "A wise person indeed should have flowering shrubs and the like planted;
before long, they will lead to benefit. "Hinting" (*obhāsa*)...
"Taking up" means taking hold of such things as a hoe, a spade, and so forth, as well as a flower-garden hoe;

for when novices and others see him standing thus, they go and perform the work, thinking, "The Elder wishes to have it done. "Sign-making" (nimittakamma) means bringing a hoe, a spade, an axe, a hatchet, and a water vessel and placing them nearby.
These five [types of trees] are not permitted for planting for the purpose of supporting one's family;

however, regarding their use for fruit, only the two modes of expression—*kappiya-vohāra* (permissible terminology) and *akappiya-vohāra* (impermissible terminology)—are restricted, while the other three are permitted.

In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however, it is stated: "Even *kappiya-vohāra* is permitted. And that which is permitted for one's own consumption is also permitted for the sake of another person, the Saṅgha, or a *cetiya*."
However, for the sake of a pleasure grove, a forest, or shade, even the mere use of improper terminology is not permitted;

the rest is permitted. Furthermore, it is not only the rest that is permitted, but one may also straighten any part of the boundary markers, sprinkle water that has been made permissible (*kappiya-udaka*), build a bathing platform to bathe, and discard there the water used for washing hands, feet, and face.
It is permissible. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kuruṇḍī*, it is stated: "It is also permissible to plant [trees] oneself on land that is allowable (*kappiyabhūmi*).
Furthermore, it is permissible to consume the fruit of what has been planted or caused to be planted for the sake of a monastery or similar purpose.
Gathering or causing to gather [fruit] is a *pācittiya* offense by its very nature. But if it is done for the purpose of corrupting a family, it is both a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa* offense.

And in the case of constructing [buildings] such as granaries, up to those ending with roof-coverings, for one who builds them for the purpose of defiling a family or for some other purpose, there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense. Why?
Because it is improper conduct (*anācāra*), and because it constitutes "evil conduct" as stated in the passage, "one of evil conduct. If it is asked:

"Why is there no offense in this case, as there is none when planting trees for the sake of a monastery and so forth, since here too it is for the purpose of honoring the site?"—there is indeed no offense. Just as...

For in that case, there is no offense due to the use of allowable terminology (*kappiya-vohāra*) and various indirect methods; likewise, there is indeed no offense even for the purpose of honoring the site. But has it not been stated there:
"It is also permissible to plant [trees] oneself on allowable ground (*kappiya-pathavī*)"? It was so stated, but not in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Or perhaps you might think that what is stated in the other [commentaries] is also authoritative. Yet, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*...
The sprinkling of allowable water has been mentioned; how is that so? That too is not contradictory.

For there, where it could have been stated without qualification that "they plant trees themselves and have them planted, they sprinkle them themselves and have them sprinkled," by saying instead "flowering shrubs" (*mālāvaccha*), he makes it known:
"This was said with reference specifically to those that bear flowers and fruit for the purpose of supporting one's family; otherwise..."

"But there is a method [of explanation]. Therefore, having understood that there is a method in that case and the absence of a method here, what has been stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) is indeed well-stated. And this has been said:
"The Dhamma and the Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha;"
He who was likewise known by his sons as such— those [sons] who,
having abandoned their own opinions,
formerly composed commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) for them.
Therefore, having set aside whatever has been stated in the commentaries that contains careless errors, [one should follow] everything else for those who possess reverence for the trainings.
"Because this is the measure for the wise here.
All of this should be understood according to the method already stated. Herein, it might be asked:

"If there is an offense even for the purpose of worshipping the physical object [of the Buddha] in cases such as taking [the requisites], why is there no offense in cases of taking and so forth when it is for the sake of women and others? This is because they are taken for the sake of women and others; thus, under the heading of "taking," [there is no offense].
For it was stated, having made a distinction, "those [garlands] of women of good family," and so forth; therefore, there is no offense for one who takes them for the sake of the Buddha and others.
In that context, *ekatovaṇṭika* refers to a garland made by placing the stalks of the flowers on one side. *Ubhatovaṇṭika* refers to a garland made by placing the flower-stalks on both sides.
Regarding *mañjarika* and the others, however, they are flower-arrangements made in the shape of a cluster (*mañjarī*).
It is called *mañjarikā*. *Vidhūtikā* refers to [garlands] made by piercing flowers such as *sinduvāra* with a needle or a skewer.
*Vaṭaṃsaka* means an ear-ornament (*vataṃsaka*). *Āveḷā* means a crest-jewel (*kaṇṇikā*). *Uracchada* is a flower garland placed upon the chest, similar to a necklace (*hāra*).
This, then, is the word-by-word commentary on this passage.
This, however, is the detailed determination of offenses from the beginning.

For one who plants flowering shrubs on unsuitable ground for the purpose of disgracing a family, there is both a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa*; likewise for one who causes them to be planted by means of an improper transaction.
Even when planting or causing to be planted on suitable ground, there is only a *dukkaṭa*. In both cases, even if many are planted through a single command, [the offense remains the same].
In the case of planting, there is only one offense: either a *pācittiya* together with a *dukkaṭa*, or a simple *dukkaṭa*.

For there is no offense in having [a tree] planted in a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an area where it is permitted) or even in a non-permitted area (*akappiya-bhūmi*), provided it is for the purpose of consumption and done using a permissible formula (*kappiya-vohāra*).

However, for one who plants in a non-permitted plot of land—even for the sake of a monastery (*ārāma*) and so forth—or for one who has it planted by means of a non-permissible formula, there is a *pācittiya*. This...
However, this method is not clearly explained in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, but it is explained in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
Regarding sprinkling and causing another to sprinkle with unallowable water, there is a *pācittiya* offense in all cases;

there is also a *dukkaṭa* offense if it is for the purpose of corrupting families or for personal enjoyment. If [unallowable water] is used for those same two purposes with allowable terminology, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense. And here, regarding the purpose of personal enjoyment, even by means of allowable terminology—

There is no offense in causing [flowers] to be sprinkled. However, regarding the point of the offense, one should understand that due to the multiplicity of applications by way of cutting the stream [of water], there is a multiplicity of offenses.
When plucking flowers for the purpose of corrupting a family, there are *dukkaṭa* and *pācittiya* offenses according to the number of flowers; elsewhere, they are simply *pācittiya*.
But when one plucks many flowers with a single application, one is to be dealt with according to the application. Regarding causing others to pluck [flowers] for the purpose of corrupting a family...
If he is commanded once, even if he gathers a great quantity, there is only one offense of *pācittiya* and *dukkaṭa*; otherwise, it is simply *pācittiya*.

Regarding weaving and so forth, all six varieties of flower-work are to be understood: the knotted (*ganthima*), the sewn (*gopphima*), the pierced (*vedhima*), the wrapped (*veṭhima*), the stuffed (*pūrima*), and the woven (*vāyima*).
Among these, "knotted" refers to [flowers] such as blue lotuses or red lotuses together with their stalks.
Or it may be seen in other flowers with long stalks. Having tied stalk to stalk or stem to stem with a cord, that which is thus made is indeed a "knotted" (ganthima) flower.

It is not permitted for a monk or a nun to make such a thing themselves, nor to have it made by others, even with words that are technically improper, thinking, "If it is made in this way, it will look beautiful so that these flowers do not scatter."
However, it is permissible to have it made using allowable speech such as, "Please do so.
"Tying" (*gopphima*) means tying together jasmine flowers and the like by means of thread or materials such as bark-fiber, either as a single-stalked garland or a double-stalked garland;
or, having doubled a strip of bark-fiber or a cord, inserting stalkless flowers such as *nīpa* blossoms therein.
They bind them in sequence; this too is merely "gopphima" (anklet-style). All of it is not permissible in the same manner as previously described.

What is called "vedhima" (pierced) refers to flowers with stalks, such as *vassika* flowers, which are threaded through their stalks, or stalkless flowers, such as *vakula* flowers, which are pierced through the central cavity with needles, awls, and so forth, and then strung together;
this is called "vedhima," and that too is [not permissible] in the same manner as previously described.
It is not permissible. However, some insert thorns, palm-splinters, or similar objects into a plantain trunk and fix flowers there;
some [fix them] on thorny branches; some, for the purpose of making flower-umbrellas or flower-pavilions, insert them into thorns fixed within umbrellas or on walls;
and some [fix them] on thorns tied to the canopy of a Dhamma-seat.
Some pierce *kaṇikāra* flowers and the like with needles and arrange them like a parasol above a parasol; that is indeed too coarse.

However, for the purpose of piercing flowers, it is not permitted to tie even a thorn to the canopy of the Dhamma-seat, nor to pierce even a single flower with thorns and the like, nor to insert one flower into another. [This applies to] the lattice-canopy, the pedestal, and the *nāgadantaka* (peg).
However, there is no fault in inserting flowers into the holes of flower-receptacles, palm-leaf tubes, and the like, or into the gaps between *asoka* clusters;
this is not what is called "woven" (*vedhima*). The same principle applies to "dhamma-rope" (*dhammarajju*) as well.
"Woven" (*veṭhima*) should be understood as referring to flower garlands and flower bouquets. For some, when making a crest-garland (*matthakadāma*), [place the flowers]...
To show the shape of a small pot at the bottom, they wrap them with flowers;
some bind eight or ten blue lotuses (*utpala*) and so forth onto handles made of thread or bark-fiber, making them into "lotus-hand" or "lotus-bunch" offerings.
All of this is not permitted according to the previous method. As for the blue lotuses and other flowers that novices have plucked and placed on dry land:
It is not permitted to tie even a bundle together with saffron-colored cloth.
However, it is permitted to tie it with their own cotton thread or with a cord, or to make a shoulder-bundle (*aṃsabhaṇḍikā*).
What is called a "shoulder-bundle" is when one brings both ends of the saffron robe placed upon the shoulder, forms them into a bundle, and puts flowers into it as if into a bag; this is it.
This is called a shoulder-bag; it is permissible to make one. Having pierced a lotus leaf with sticks and wrapped the blue lotuses and other flowers with the leaf, they carry them away;
in that case as well, it is permissible to tie only a lotus leaf over the flowers.
However, it is not permissible to tie a stick underneath.
"Filled up" (*pūrima*) should be understood in the case of a flower garland and a flower cloth.

For if one who is encircling a shrine (*cetiya*), a Bodhi tree, or a railing with a flower garland brings it back and passes beyond its original starting point, even to that extent it is called "filled up.
How much more so for one who encircles it many times, or [uses] the gaps between the pegs?
Having inserted [the flowers] and carried them away, one makes them hang down and then encircles them again with a peg (*nāgadantaka*);
this too is called "filling" (*pūrima*). However, it is permissible to insert a circle of flowers onto the pegs. They make flower-canopies (*puṣpapaṭa*) with strings of garlands (*mālāguṇa*).
Even there, it is permissible to carry only a single string of garlands. For one who carries it back again, it is likewise "filling"; that—

Everything else is not permitted exactly as in the previous method. However, having received a flower garland made even from many strings of flowers, it is permissible to tie it to the top of a seat or similar places.

But if the string of flowers is too long, it is permissible to take it once, either by carrying it away or by encircling it, and give it to another bhikkhu. It is likewise permissible for that bhikkhu to do the same with it.
“Woven” (*vāyima*) should be understood as referring to flower-lattices, flower-cloths, and flower-figures.
For one making a flower-lattice on a cetiya, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for each individual opening of the lattice.

The same principle applies to walls, canopies, Bodhi-tree pillars, and so forth. Furthermore, it is not permitted to weave a flower-cloth even if it has already been filled by others. Elephant, horse, and other such figures may be made using only *gopphima* flowers.
They make them, and those too remain in the weaving place. In the same manner as before, everything is not permitted.
However, it is permitted for one placing flowers within a boundary made by others to even make figures of elephants, horses, and so forth.
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, eight varieties of flower arrangements are mentioned, including the *kalambaka* and the *addhacandaka*. Therein, the *kalambaka* is—
Between the half-moons, a hanging garland of small bells (*ghaṭikadāma*) is mentioned. A "half-moon" (*aḍḍhacandaka*) is a circular arrangement of flower strings in the shape of a half-moon;

both of these are included within the "filling" (*pūrima*). However, the *Kurundi* states: "Making flower garlands by joining two or three strings of flowers together is also considered 'woven' (*vāyima*). That too is included here within the category of "filling."
And it is not only flower-garlands and honeycomb-garlands that are mentioned in the *Kurundi*;

flour-garlands and ball-flower garlands are also mentioned there. Furthermore, because the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is common to both monks and nuns, even for monks, it is not permitted to make or have made harsh-leaf garlands.
However, for the purpose of worship, the term "allowable" (*kappiya*) may be used everywhere.
It is permissible. Discourses, illuminations, and symbolic acts are indeed permissible.
"They roll about" means they lie down. "They dance" means that, as if floating with rapture, they rise up and perform the dance of the *lāsiya* dancers;
they give vent to their breath. "They dance when she dances" means that when the dancing woman dances, they too [dance].
Those walking in front of her or behind her dance. Regarding "they sing as she dances": when she dances, they sing in accordance with the dance.
This same method applies everywhere. Regarding "playing at eight-squares":
they play dice on an eight-square board. Likewise, "at ten-squares" and "in the air": just as with the eight- and ten-square boards, they play right there in the air.
"On the path for avoidance" means that on the ground they have made a circular area with various paths; there, avoiding the path that must be avoided, they play.

"They also play at 'nearby'" means they play at the game of "nearby," where pieces of wood or pebbles placed together are moved neither too far nor too near by the fingernail alone, provided that none of them— [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated.*
If he moves [the piece], there is defeat. "At Khalikā" means they play with dice on a gaming board.
"With ghaṭikā" means a ghaṭikā is called a stick-game; they play with that. They move about striking a short stick with a long stick.
"With a hand of sticks" means having moistened a hand of sticks with lac, or with lac-resin, or with flour-water, [they ask]: "What?"
Saying, “Let it be so,” they strike the ground or a wall and play, displaying the forms of elephants, horses, and other creatures.
*Akkhena* means with dice. *Paṅgacīrena*: a *paṅgacīra* is called a leaf-pipe; blowing through that, they play. *Vaṅkakena*:
with a small plough, which is a toy for village children. *Mokkhacikāya*: a *mokkhacikā*...
It is called "the game of tumbling" (*samparivattakakīḷā*); the meaning is that they play by tumbling up and down, either holding a staff in the air or placing their heads on the ground.
"With a spinning-top" (*ciṅgulakena*): a spinning-top (*ciṅgulaka*) is said to be a wheel made of palm leaves or similar materials that revolves by the force of the wind;
they play with that. "With a cupped hand" (*pattāḷhakena*): a cupped hand (*pattāḷhaka*) is said to be...
A *paṇṇanāḷi* is a leaf-tube; they play by measuring sand and other substances with it. *Rathakena*: with a small chariot. *Dhanukena*: with a small bow. *Akkharikāya*:
"Akṣarikā" refers to a game for learning letters either in the air or on the back [of one's hand]; they play with that. *Manesikāya*:
"Manesikā" refers to a game for knowing what has been thought of by the mind; they play with that. *Yathāvajjena*: [as appropriate].
"According to their defects" means that they apply whichever defect they have—such as being one-eyed, having crooked limbs, or being lame—and play at showing it off, like the Velambhakas.
"They train in elephant-riding" means they train in whatever craft must be learned for the purpose of handling elephants.
The same method applies to horses and so forth. "They run away" means they go away from the presence [of their teacher].
They run about. "They run back as well" means that for however far they run away, they run back toward [the monks] for exactly that same distance.
"They wrestle" means they engage in a wrestling match. "They even give a 'forehead-scratch'" means that saying, "Excellent, sister!
Excellent!", they place their own finger on their own forehead and then place it on her forehead. They also commit various kinds of improper conduct.
"They practice" means they practice various forms of improper conduct (*anācāra*) not mentioned in the Canon, such as playing mouth-drums and so forth.
(432) "With inspiring" means with that which brings about confidence; "with becoming" means with that which is suitable for ascetics.
"In advancing" means in going forward. "In retreating" means in turning back. "In looking ahead" means in seeing before one. "In looking around" means [looking] hither and thither.
"By seeing. "By contracting" means by the contraction of the limbs. "By extending" means by the extension of those very same limbs.

In all instances, the instrumental case is used in the sense of expressing an accompaniment (*itthambhūtākhyāna*). What is meant is that, because they are thoroughly conditioned by mindfulness and clear comprehension, one becomes graceful in advancing, retreating, looking ahead, looking aside, contracting, and extending.
"With downcast eyes" means with eyes cast downwards. "Endowed with deportment" means by that...
He possesses perfected modes of deportment due to his being pleasing and graceful in his approach and so forth.
"Kvāyaṃ" means "Who is this? "Abalabalo viya": it is said that "abala" refers to a dog (*bonda*);
this repetition is used in the sense of excess, therefore it means "like an exceedingly weak dog. "Mandamanda" refers to the lack of agitation in his approach and other such behaviors.
"Too dull" and "too harsh"—in this way they perceive virtue as a fault. "As if one who is constantly frowning":
thinking that because of his downcast eyes he moves about with a contracted face as if angry, having made a frown, they say this. "Gentle" means subtle;
it refers to those who are skillful at leading laypeople to their appropriate place by saying things like "Mother, Father, Sister," unlike this person.
The intended meaning is that they are thus "weak and powerless. "Gentle" (sakhilā) means endowed with gentleness (sākhalyena).

"Easy to converse with" (sukhasambhāsā): this is a statement of the reason for the former [term]. For those whose conversation is pleasant, their friendly talk is blameless and pleasing to the ear, they are called "gentle.
Therefore they said: "Gentle, easy to converse with. This, however, is the intended meaning here:
“Our noble ladies, upon seeing lay followers, engage in sweet and friendly conversation;
therefore they are sociable and pleasant to talk with, unlike this woman, who seems so very dull.
“Preceded by a smile” means that a smile is the precursor to their speech; having first smiled, they speak afterwards.
The meaning is as follows. "Those who say 'Come, welcome'": seeing a lay follower, they speak thus, "Come, welcome to you," unlike this person;

having thus shown by way of meaning the state of being non-frowning (*abhākuṭika*)—as opposed to those who are frowning and constantly scowling due to their contracted faces—they spoke again, showing it by its actual form: "Non-frowning, with open faces."
"Those who speak first. Or rather, it should be understood that this is a demonstration of the absence of all three modes out of their proper sequence.
How so? For here, by the term "without frowning," the absence of the mode of being frowning or excessively frowning is shown.
By the term "with open faces," the absence of the mode of being dull or sluggish is shown; for those who have opened their eyes and look about with open faces are not [dull].
They were very slow. By the phrase "speaking first," the absence of a faltering manner is shown;
for those who, through skill in addressing others, speak first with words such as "Mother" or "Father," they are not faltering.
"Come, venerable sir, let us go home"—it is said that the lay devotee [said this] thinking, "Friend, no alms-food is to be obtained."

When he said this, [the man] replied, "This was done by your own monks; even if you wander through the entire village, you will find nothing," and then, wishing to give almsfood, he said, "Come, venerable sir, let us go home.

But is this considered a prearranged speech (*payuttavācā*)? It is not. This is what is called a "questioned question" (*pucchitapañha*), and it is permissible to speak in such a case. Therefore, even now—
If someone should ask a bhikkhu who has entered among the houses in the morning or in the evening, “Venerable sir, for what purpose are you wandering?

he should explain the purpose for which he is wandering. When asked whether he has received anything or not, if he has not received anything, he may say, “I have received nothing,” and it is permissible for him to accept whatever that person gives.
"Corrupt" means corrupt by way of the destruction of faith and so forth; it is corrupt by way of the person.
"Paths of giving" refers simply to acts of giving. Alternatively, "paths of giving" means those things connected with giving, namely the duties of giving.
"Severed" means they have been cut off by the donors; they do not give them now. "They fall away" means they become separate or distinct.
"He departs" is what is meant. "He should stand firm" means he should stand rightly; he should become a support for well-behaved bhikkhus.
"Very well, friend," that bhikkhu accepted the message of the faithful, confident lay follower.
Indeed, it is proper to carry such a message as this, which is allowable; therefore [the lay follower said], "In my name, pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One."
Or, when one receives such instructions as: “Worship the cetiya, the image, the Bodhi tree, or the senior monk of the Saṅgha”;
or “Offer perfumes at the cetiya; offer flowers”; or “Assemble the bhikkhus; we shall give alms and listen to the Dhamma”—one should not feel remorse regarding such instructions.
These are permissible instructions; they are not connected with the worldly affairs of householders.
When it is asked, "From where have you come, monk?", that monk does not actually come while he is sitting;
nevertheless, the present tense is used here because it refers to what has just occurred. Thus, there is no fault.
The same principle applies to the statement at the conclusion: "From there, Blessed One, I am coming."
433. First, the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka are to be charged thus:
"We wish to speak to you," having thus obtained their leave, they are to be charged with both the matter and the offense. Having charged them, whatever they do not remember is to be reminded of.
If they acknowledge both the matter and the offense, or if they acknowledge only the offense and not the matter, [then] the offense—

They should be charged with the offense. If they admit only to the basis (vatthu) but not to the offense, they must still be charged with the specific offense corresponding to that basis, saying, "In this basis, this is the offense. If they admit neither the basis nor the offense, the offense should not be charged.

This is the legal decision (*vinicchaya*) in this matter. Having charged them with the offense according to their admission, the act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*) should be carried out accordingly.
Showing that it must be performed, he said, "by an experienced bhikkhu," and so forth; the meaning of this is already clear.

Thus, a bhikkhu who has undergone the act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma) must not reside in the monastery where he lives, nor in the village where he committed the act of defiling families. While residing in that monastery...
One should not wander for alms even in a neighboring village. Even while residing in a neighboring monastery, one living there should not wander for alms in that village.
However, when the Elder Upatissa was told by his pupils, "Venerable sir, a city is large;
it may even extend for twelve yojanas," he replied, "It is forbidden only in that street where the act of corrupting families was committed."
He said: "Then, when it was stated, 'The street is also as large as a city,' he replied, 'Of which there is a succession of houses.
When it was stated, 'The succession of houses is also as large as a street,' he replied, 'Seven houses were excluded here and there.
But all of that was merely the Elder’s own fancy. Even if the monastery were three leagues in extent.
And even a city twelve *yojanas* at most—neither is it permitted to dwell in its monasteries, nor is it permitted to wander through its streets. 435.
They had a formal act of banishment (*pabbājanīya-kamma*) performed against them by the Saṅgha. How did the Saṅgha perform that act for them?
It was not done by going there and overwhelming them; rather, while meals for the Saṅgha were being prepared after they had been invited to various families, in that...
In that place, the elders, having explained the way of the ascetic life and having informed the people, saying, "This one is an ascetic;
this one is not an ascetic," established a boundary for one or two bhikkhus and, by this very means, performed the act of banishment against all of them.
And for one against whom the act of banishment has been performed, if he fulfills the eighteen duties and makes a request, the act [is to be revoked].
It must be pacified. Even by one who has had that legal act pacified, requisites should not be accepted from those families where he previously committed an act of defiling a family;
they should not be accepted even by one who has attained the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*), for they remain indeed improper.
If, when asked, "Why do you not accept them?", he says, "Because I previously did such a thing," and if they say:
“They should not be accepted [with the thought], ‘We do not give for that reason; we give now because of their virtuous conduct.

In such cases, a deed that defiles the family has been committed right at the place of giving by nature. Therefore, it is proper to accept only the natural gift; that which they give after having increased it is not proper.
‘They do not behave properly’ means that those Assaji and Punabbasuka monks do not behave properly in the eighteen matters of proper conduct.”
“They do not let their hair grow” means that because they do not practice the conformable way (*anulomapaṭipadā*), they do not have their hair down.
“They do not proceed toward deliverance” means that they do not enter upon the path of their own deliverance.
“They do not ask the monks for forgiveness” refers to asking forgiveness from the monks in this manner: “Venerable sirs, we have committed a wrong; we shall not do so again. Please forgive us.”
They do not act [in accordance with the Dhamma]. "They revile" means they revile the Saṅgha of those who perform [the formal acts] by means of the ten grounds for reviling.
"They abuse" means they show them fear. "They cause them to fall into favoritism... [etc]...

and into intimidation" means they cause them to fall into favoritism and... [etc]... into intimidation; the meaning is that they lead them into, or join them to, favoritism and... [etc]... intimidation.
“They depart” means that some among the five hundred ascetics who were their followers departed for various directions.

“They fall away” means that some become householders. In the phrase “how indeed could the monks Assaji and Punabbasu,” all of them are referred to as “Assaji and Punabbasu” by way of designating them after their two leaders.
436–7. Regarding the phrase "village" (*gāma*): here, even a city (*nagara*) is included by the mention of "village.

Therefore, it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "A village, a market town (*nigama*), and a city—all these are 'village' and 'market town'. In this context, a market town should be understood as a place surrounded by a wall and provided with shops.
He "corrupts families" (*kuladūsaka*); and in corrupting them, he does not corrupt them with filth, mud, and the like, but rather through his own...
Improper conduct destroys their confidence; for this very reason, it is said in the word-commentary (padabhājana) regarding this: "with a flower," and so forth.

In that context, if one—whether having carried [the flowers] oneself, or having had them carried, or having summoned [the recipient] oneself, or having had them summoned, or having approached them oneself—gives any flower belonging to oneself for the purpose of maintaining the family (kulasaṅgaha), it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If one gives what belongs to another...
It is indeed a *dukkaṭa*. If one gives with the intent to steal, one is to be dealt with according to the value of the goods.

This same principle applies to property belonging to the Saṅgha as well. However, this is the distinction: for one who gives away what has been designated for the purpose of lodgings out of a sense of ownership, there is a *thullaccaya*.
Regarding flowers: to whom is it permissible to give them, and to whom is it not permissible? First, even if one takes them from one’s mother or father...
It is permissible to give [the robes] after having them brought back, or after having summoned [the relatives], or after having caused them to be summoned;
however, in the case of other relatives, they must be summoned first. Furthermore, this is for the purpose of honoring the material [of the robe];

it is not permissible to give it to anyone else for the purpose of decoration or for the worship of Śiva-liṅgas and the like. And when having [the robes] brought back from one's parents, they should be brought back by the relatives who are novices (sāmaṇera). As for the others...

However, if they themselves so desire, it is permissible. When the officially appointed flower-distributor is distributing them, it is permissible to give half a portion to the novices who have arrived.
According to the *Kurundi*, half a portion is to be given to laypeople who have arrived.
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "It is permissible to give a small amount. One who is not officially appointed should distribute them after seeking permission.

When novices, out of respect for their teachers—the preceptors and instructors—bring many flowers and set them down in a heap, and the elders, having arrived at dawn, give them to their resident pupils or lay followers who have come, saying, "You take this;
you take that," it does not constitute an offering of flowers. This is also the case when they take them while going with the thought, "We shall worship the cetiya."
Even when performing worship, if they give [flowers] for the purpose of worshipping a cetiya encountered here and there, this too does not count as a gift of flowers (*pupphadāna*).
However, seeing lay followers (*upāsaka*) worshipping with *akkapuppha* and other such flowers, it is appropriate to say: "There are *kaṇikāra* flowers and so forth in the monastery;
lay followers, take them and perform worship. Having performed the flower-worship, the bhikkhus [should depart] early in the morning.
When they had entered the village, people asked, "Venerable sir, why have you come so late?

They replied, "We performed an offering with many flowers in the monastery. Hearing that there were indeed many flowers in the monastery, on the following day the people took abundant hard and soft food, went to the monastery, performed flower offerings, and gave alms.
It is permissible. People say, "Venerable sir, we shall make an offering on such-and-such a day," and having requested the turn for flowers, they come on the authorized day.
The novices have already gathered the flowers and set them aside earlier;
not seeing the flowers on the trees, they ask, "Venerable sir, where are the flowers? [The answer is: by the novices having gathered them...
"But you, having made offerings, may depart; the Saṅgha will make offerings on another day.

If they depart after making offerings and giving alms, it is permissible. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kuruṇḍī*, it is stated: "The elders are not permitted to have the novices give [the offerings].
If the elders themselves give those flowers to them, it is permissible. But by the elders..."
It is stated: "One should say only this much: 'They were gathered and set aside by the novices.

However, if they request a flower-offering and, having brought rice porridge, food, and so forth in place of flowers that have not been gathered, they tell the novices, "Gather [flowers] and give them," it is permissible to gather them and give them only to those novices who are relatives.
For those who are not relatives, one should lift them up onto a tree branch.
They place [the flowers] [there]; one must not descend and flee. It is permissible to pluck [them] and give them.

However, it is stated in both the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kuruṇḍī* that if a certain Dhamma-preacher says, "Lay followers, take many flowers, rice-milk, food, and so forth to the monastery and perform flower-worship," it is not allowable for him alone. This is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
However, it was stated without distinction that "this is not allowable and is not permitted.
Even fruit belonging to oneself may be given to one's mother and father, as well as to other relatives, in the manner already described.

Furthermore, for one giving for the sake of maintaining the family, [it is permissible] in the same manner already described regarding what belongs to oneself, what belongs to others, and what belongs to the Saṅgha.
When [lodgings] have been assigned for the purpose of housing, offenses such as *dukkaṭa* should be understood.

It is permissible to give what belongs to oneself to sick people, or to those who have arrived as masters of the situation, or to those whose travel funds are exhausted; however, it does not constitute a "gift of fruit" (*phaladāna*).
Even by one appointed as the distributor of fruits, it is permissible to give half a portion to people who have arrived at the time when the Saṅgha is distributing the fruits.
It should be given by one who has not been formally appointed after seeking permission.
Within the monastery grounds as well, a boundary should be established either by delimiting the fruit or by delimiting the trees.

Then, when sick people or others request fruit, four or five fruits should be given according to that established boundary. Alternatively, the trees should be pointed out, saying, "From here it is permitted to take [fruit]. "In this place..."
However, one should not say, "The fruits are beautiful; take them from here.
Regarding "with powder": if one gives one's own sirīsa-powder or any other astringent substance for the sake of winning over a family, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
The analysis regarding the property of others and so forth should be understood according to the method already stated. This, however, is the distinction:
— Here, even the bark of a tree that has been guarded and protected by the Saṅgha is indeed a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*).

Regarding clay, tooth-sticks, and bamboo as well, having recognized them as falling under the category of heavy articles, the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) should be understood in the same manner as that stated for powder.

However, the giving of leaves is not mentioned here; that too should be understood in the same manner as stated. Furthermore, we shall explain everything in detail in the subsequent section on the determination of heavy articles.
Regarding "by means of medical practice": here, the procedure for medical work is to be understood in the same manner as explained in the commentary on the third *pārājika*.
Regarding "by means of running errands on foot": here, "running errands on foot" refers to the work of carrying messages and errands for householders; that must not be done.
For one who goes taking a message from householders, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at every step. That work—
Even for one who eats food obtained by relying [on a message], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) with each mouthful swallowed.
Even for one who, without first receiving the message, later descends from the road thinking, "Now that village has been reached;

come, I shall announce the message," there is an offense of wrong-doing at every step. For one who eats food obtained after announcing the message, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the same manner as previously described.
However, for one who has come without having received a message, if they are asked, "Venerable sir, what is the news regarding such-and-such a person in that village?
it is permissible to speak; there is no fault in answering the question asked. But it is permissible to carry a message for five types of persons:
fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, parents, a *paṇḍupalāsa* (one whose leaves have withered), one’s own attendant, and laypeople, provided it was previously [authorized].
This is a permissible message of the kind already described; for this is not what is called "work on the legs" (*jaṅghapesaniyakamma*).
However, requisites obtained through these eight acts of corrupting families are not permissible for any of the five types of fellow practitioners (*sahadhammika*);
they are exactly like requisites obtained through false proclamation or trading in money.
"One of evil conduct" means one whose conduct is evil.
Since, however, the planting of flower trees and so forth are intended here, its word-commentary is stated in the manner beginning with "they plant flower trees. "Tirokkhā" means behind one's back.
Regarding the phrase "and families are corrupted by him," here "families" is merely a conventional designation; for in actual fact—
People become hostile toward him; therefore, in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*), it says, "having previously been faithful," and so forth.
"Those who follow through favoritism" (*chandagāmino*) means those who proceed by way of favoritism (*chanda*). This same method applies to the remaining terms.

"He should be formally admonished for the sake of relinquishing [that behavior]"—here, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the act of corrupting families. However, as for that which he said after having insulted the Saṅgha, namely, "those who follow through favoritism," and so forth...

The meaning should be understood as follows: "A formal act of admonition (samanubhāsanakamma) must be performed for the sake of his relinquishing [the offense]. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and other factors are also exactly the same as in the first case of schism in the Saṅgha.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the corrupter of families (kuladūsaka-sikkhāpada) is finished.
Commentary on the Conclusion (Nigamanavaṇṇanā) 442.
Regarding the passage, “What has been recited... thus do I remember it”: here, “those for which there is an offense first” are *paṭhamāpattika*;
the meaning is that they are to be incurred at the very moment of the first transgression. As for the others, however, as in the third and fourth [categories]...

And because it occurs on the day [of the offense], it is called "fever" (*jara*); thus, because they occur during the formal act of admonition up to the third time, they should be understood as "up-to-the-third" (*yāvatatiyaka*).
"As many days as he knowingly conceals": this refers to however many days he knowingly conceals, thinking, "I am such-and-such a person..."
“He has fallen into an offense,” [thinking this], he does not inform his fellow celibates. “For so many days” means for that many days.
“He must undergo the probation against his will” means not by choice, nor by his own power, but rather he must undertake and live out the probation against his will and without his own power.

“For more than six nights” means for more than six nights beyond the period of probation. “For the sake of the monks’ formal act of reconciliation” (bhikkhumānattāya) means for the purpose of the state of being honored by the monks.
"It is for the sake of restoration" is what is meant. "A group of twenty" means one who has a community (saṅgha) consisting of twenty members;
"therein" means wherever there is a community of monks consisting of at least twenty members.
"Is to be restored" means he is to be received, he is to be reinstated by means of the act of restoration (abbhāna-kamma); or the meaning is that he is to be summoned.
*Anabbhito*: not terrified; it means not accepted, not something that has been done out of obligation, or alternatively, the meaning is "not invited.
*Sāmīcī*: accordance with the Dhamma (*anudhammatā*), instruction and teaching following the supramundane Dhamma; it means "the state of proper conduct" (*sāmīci-dhammatā*).
The rest here is according to the method already explained.
The commentary on the Thirteenfold Section of the *Samantapāsādikā*, the exposition of the Vinaya, is completed. 3.
The Section on the Indeterminate Rules (*Aniyata-khaṇḍa*).
1. Commentary on the First Indeterminate Training Rule (Paṭhama-aniyata-sikkhāpada) 443.
“At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... refers to the first indeterminate training rule.
In this context, “speaking at the appropriate time” means having observed the proper time, when no one else is either going by or coming near.
Or, at that time, speaking in accordance with that situation, he would engage in worldly conversation such as, "Are you not weary? Are you not fatigued?
Are you not hungry? Speaking the Dhamma at the appropriate time means observing the proper occasion;
when someone else is passing by or approaching nearby, he speaks accordingly, saying, "You should observe the Uposatha; [you should give] *salākabhatta*..."
While he was delivering a discourse on the Dhamma beginning with the words, “Would you give...,” [he said]:
“One who has many daughters and sons is ‘one with many sons’ (bahuputtā). It is said that she had ten sons and ten daughters.
One who has many grandsons is ‘one with many grandsons’ (bahunattā). For just as she did, so too her sons and daughters each had twenty [children].”
...were boys; thus she had a retinue of four hundred and twenty sons and grandsons. "Considered most auspicious" means considered the highest of blessings.
"In sacrifices" means in the giving of gifts. "In festivals" means in domestic celebrations such as marriages and other auspicious occasions.
"In great festivals" means in major celebrations such as the Āsāḷhī festival, the Pavāraṇā ceremony, and auspicious constellations. "Feeding first" means [feeding] these boys as well.
"May they have an equal lifespan and be free from disease," thus praying, she fed him first;
and even those who were faithful and confident, having first fed the bhikkhus, would feed her immediately thereafter.
"He did not accept" means he did not take up her words, nor did he grasp them, nor did he show them respect.
444–5. *Alaṃkammaṇiyaṃ*: "Kammaṇiya" means that which is capable of action or fit for action. "Alaṃkammaṇiyaṃ" means that which is sufficient or adequate for the state of being fit for action;
the meaning is: in such a place that is *alaṃkammaṇiya*, where those who commit transgression are able to perform that act.
For this very reason, it is said in the word-commentary: "It is possible to engage in sexual intercourse..."
"To practice" means that it is possible to practice the act of sexual intercourse; this is what is intended.

"Should arrange a seat" means he should make a seat, i.e., he should sit down; this is the meaning. However, since one lies down only after having sat down, both [actions] are mentioned for him in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
In that context, "having approached and sat down" means having gone near and sat down. Thus...

It should also be understood that this applies when one has sat down nearby (*upanipanna*). "A monk is seated" means when a monk is seated. "Both are seated" means both are seated without one being earlier or later than the other.

And here, although the word "secrecy of the ear" (*sotassa raho*) appears in the text, the delimitation should be understood as the secrecy of the eye (*cakkhussa raho*). For even in the case of a room with its door closed...
If a wise person is sitting at the door, he does not commit an offense. However, if he is sitting at the door of one whose bolt is not closed, he commits an offense.
Not only at the door, but even if he is sitting within a space of twelve cubits inside, if he has eyes—even if he is distracted or asleep—he does not commit an offense.
Even if he is standing nearby, a blind person does not commit [an offense].
Even one who possesses vision does not commit [an offense] while lying down and sleeping; however, even with a hundred women, she certainly does not commit an offense.
"One whose word is to be trusted" means one whose speech is credible. Since she is indeed an Ariyan female disciple, it is therefore said in the word-commentary (padabhājana):

"one who has attained the fruit," and so forth. In that context, "one who has attained the fruit" means one for whom the fruit has arrived—that is, one who has obtained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti).

The meaning is as follows: "One who has fully realized" means one who has penetrated the Four Noble Truths. "One who has understood the teaching of the three trainings" means one by whom the teaching of the three trainings has been comprehended.

Regarding the phrase "a monk who claims to be sitting": even though she speaks thus upon seeing such a laywoman, nevertheless, a monk who claims to be sitting must be dealt with according to one of the three rules.
The meaning is "not by one who does not confess.
Or rather, that monk should be dealt with according to whatever reliable testimony that female lay follower (*upāsikā*) might speak;
that is to say, by whichever mode—such as sitting and so forth—together with which [mode] she would charge him with sexual intercourse or other such acts, provided he indeed confesses it.
That monk must be dealt with by him. The meaning is that he must not be dealt with merely on the word of such a female lay follower.
Why? Because what is called "seen" may be as it is, or it may be otherwise.
And to illustrate this point, they cite this story: it is said that in the Mallārāma Monastery, there was a certain elder who had destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsavatthero*).
One day, having gone to the family of his supporters, he sat down inside the house; the laywoman was also standing near her couch.
Then a certain alms-collector, standing at the door, saw them and, perceiving that "the Elder is sitting on the same seat with the laywoman," looked back again and again.
The Elder also [thought], "This man is one who gains his livelihood through impurity..."
Having observed that [the other] had been born [into the human state], and having finished his meal, he went to the monastery, entered his own dwelling place, and sat down inside.
That monk also, thinking, "I shall reprove the Elder," came and cleared his throat to open the door.
The Elder, knowing his intention, rose into the air and sat cross-legged leaning against the pinnacle of the gabled roof.
That monk also entered inside, looked at the couch and the space beneath it, and not seeing the Elder, looked upward.
Then, seeing the Elder seated in the air, he said, "Venerable sir, you who possess such great psychic power, how can you say that you were sitting on the same seat with a woman?
The Elder replied, "This, friend, is merely the interior of a house."
"I am guilty; however, being unable to convince you of that, I did this. Please protect me," he said, and then descended.
From here on, the passage beginning with "If she should speak thus" and so forth is stated for the purpose of showing the reasons and manner of the confession.
In that context, "practicing the sexual act with a woman" means practicing the sexual act with a woman on the road.
The meaning is "while engaging in [sexual intercourse]. "He is to be dealt with for sitting" means:

having admitted to the sitting, but not admitting to the engagement in sexual intercourse, he is not to be dealt with for the offense entailing defeat (pārājika) for sexual intercourse; rather, he is to be dealt with for whatever offense he incurs by the mere act of sitting—that is, he is to be dealt with for an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).
By this method, the legal analysis is to be understood for all fourfold sets.

451. At the conclusion of the training rules, for the purpose of showing the delimitation between what constitutes an offense and what does not, regarding the statements beginning with "he admits to going," etc.:
"He admits to going" means he admits to going thus, "I went for the sake of enjoying private sitting.
"He sits" means he admits to sitting solely out of a desire for sitting. "An offense" refers to any one of the three [offenses].

"An offense. "He is to be dealt with according to the offense" means that he is to be dealt with according to whichever of the three [offenses] he confesses. The rest here in this tetrad has its meaning already explained.
However, in the second tetrad, "he does not confess to going" means he does not confess it by way of delighting in sitting in private;
rather, he says, "I went on my own business for the sake of tickets for meals and so forth, but she was at the place where I sat."
"He has come," he says. The rest here also has its meaning plain.
This, however, is the analysis for all cases: "The relish of sitting in private" refers to the defilement associated with sexual intercourse.
If a bhikkhu, desiring to go into the presence of a woman due to that relish, applies collyrium to his eye, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
He puts on the lower garment, fastens the waistband, and puts on the upper robe;

for every such act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). As he walks, for every step, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Having gone and sat down, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing.
When a woman has come and merely sat down, there is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*). If that woman, due to some business, rises up again and again—

If she sits down, for each act of sitting there is a *pācittiya* offense. If the person with whom she went is not seen, and another woman comes and sits down, then when enjoyment arises, there is a *pācittiya*.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "From the moment of departure, because of the impurity of the mind, there is indeed an offense.
If several women come together, there are *pācittiya* offenses according to the number of women. If...
Rising again and again, they sit down repeatedly; for each act of sitting, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

Even for one who has gone with the intention, "I will engage in secret conversation with whomever I see," and sits down, the offenses should be understood according to the same method described above, based on the successive arrivals of people and the repeated acts of sitting. If, however, one goes and sits down with a pure mind...
There is no offense if the secret conversation arises for a woman who has come into one's presence and is seated there.
The origin and other factors are exactly the same as those for the first *pārājika*.
The commentary on the first *aniyata* training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Indeterminate Training Rule (Aniyata Sikkhāpada) 452.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... [this is] the second indeterminate training rule. Therein, regarding the passage beginning with "it was prohibited by the Blessed One," [it refers to]:
"If one should sit down alone with a woman in a secluded place, a concealed seat, sufficient for sexual intercourse—that sitting..."
The connection should be understood as: "it is forbidden to use [it]. Otherwise, one would have to say "of one [person] by one [person]," for what reason?
Because it is stated, "it is forbidden. Alternatively, this accusative case-ending should be understood in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*). 453.
Regarding the phrase "nor even that which is concealed," here, even that which is enclosed on the outside but open on the inside—
The courtyard of the cell and so forth—this too should be understood as being included within [the area].
For such a place is taken as being uncovered (*appaṭicchanna*), as stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. The remainder should be understood according to the method of the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
For here, whether it be a woman or a man, anyone who is conscious, not blind, and not deaf, standing within a space of twelve cubits (*dvādasahattha*) [is considered a witness].
Whether standing or sitting, even if distracted or sleeping, one incurs no offense. However, one who is deaf—even if sighted—or one who is blind—even if not deaf—does not incur it.
Having excluded the offense of a *pārājika*, the offense of indecent speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*) is stated;
this is the distinction. The rest is exactly as before. In both cases, there is no offense for those who are insane or for first-time offenders.
Regarding the origin and other characteristics: this training rule has three origins—it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.

It is an action (kiriya), liberated by perception (saññāvimokkha), associated with consciousness (sacittaka), a worldly offense (lokavajja), bodily action (kāyakamma), verbal action (vacīkamma), unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta), and possesses two feelings—pleasant and neutral. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the second *aniyata* training rule is finished.
The commentary on the *Aniyata* [chapter] in the *Samantapāsādikā*,
the commentary on the Vinaya, is finished.
4. The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa) 1. The Chapter on Robes (Cīvaravagga) 1.
Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning the Kathina (Paṭhamakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā)
The thirty *nissaggiya* rules, which were spoken by the One who has Stilled the Defilements—I shall now provide a word-by-word commentary on them. 459.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī at the Gotamaka Shrine. Now, at that time...

"At that time, the three robes were authorized for the bhikkhus by the Blessed One"—here, "the three robes" refers to the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*); this triad of robes was authorized for use.
As for where they were authorized, when they were authorized, and for what reason they were authorized—all of that is [explained] in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*.

This is already explained in the *Jīvakavatthu*. "Entering the village with another set of the three robes" means that they wear robes other than those by which they stay in the monastery or enter for bathing;
in this way, they wear nine sets of robes day after day.

460. "It arises" means it arises by way of acquisition (*paṭilābhavasena*) as an occasion for a supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) that provides an opening, not by way of its actual production (*nipphattivasena*).

"He wished to give it to the Venerable Sāriputta": it is said that the Venerable Ānanda, out of great esteem for his virtues, cherished the Venerable Sāriputta exceedingly, thinking that there was no other person so distinguished in virtue as the Blessed One himself.
Thus, whenever he obtained a pleasing robe, he would dye it, apply the *kappa-bindu* (the mark of validity), and give it to the Elder before the morning meal.
Even when he received excellent rice gruel, solid food, or alms-food, he gave it to the Elder; even after his meal, when he received honey, molasses, and so forth, he gave those to the Elder as well.

Having had children removed from their families of supporters, having had them ordained, and having had them take formal admission (upajjhāya) under the Elder, he himself performed the act of proclamation (anusāvanakamma). The Venerable Sāriputta [said]: "Father..."

"The duty that must be performed is the responsibility of the eldest son; Ānanda performs for me that duty which was to be performed by the Blessed One, and through Ānanda I am able to dwell free from anxiety. Thus he cherished the Venerable Ānanda exceedingly.
And when he obtained a pleasing robe, he gave it to the Elder Ānanda; all else remained exactly as before.
Thus, through his great esteem for such qualities, it should be understood that he then desired to give even that robe which had arisen to the Venerable Sāriputta.
Regarding the phrase "on the ninth or tenth day," if one were to ask, "How does the Elder know [this]?
he knows it by many reasons. It is said that when the Elder Sāriputta was setting out on a journey through the countryside, he [instructed] the Elder Ānanda...
Having taken leave, he departs, saying: "I shall return after such-and-such a time; in the meantime, do not neglect the Blessed One.
If he does not take leave in person, he sends monks to take leave before departing.
If he is spending the rains retreat elsewhere, he sends this message to those monks who arrive there first.
“By my word, pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One with your head, and after inquiring after Ānanda’s health, say to him:
‘On such-and-such a day, he will come. And indeed, he always arrives on the very day previously determined.
Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda knows by inference: “For so many days the Blessed One has endured and patiently borne separation from me.”
“Venerable Sāriputta has passed away; from this day forward, the day named so-and-so will not pass by—he will surely come.
For those whose wisdom is great, their love for and reverence toward the Blessed One are likewise great;
he knows this by this method as well. Thus he knows by many reasons. Therefore he said: “The ninth…”

“Or perhaps the Blessed One [taught it] for ten days. When this was said, since this training rule is a transgression by way of formal prescription (*paṇṇattivajja*) and not a transgression by way of worldly convention (*lokavajja*), the Blessed One—establishing a limit exactly as spoken by the Venerable Ānanda—said:
“Then the Blessed One… [as above] …let it be remembered. However, had the Elder taught it for half a month or for a month, [the limit would have been different].
That too would have been permitted by the Blessed One.
Regarding the phrase "when the robe is finished": it refers to when the robe is finished by whatever means of completion.
Since that robe is finished both by the act of making it and by its loss or other such causes, therefore, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), only the essential meaning is given.
To demonstrate this, it is said: "the robe of a bhikkhu has been made," and so forth. In that context, "made" means completed by the conclusion of the needlework;
"conclusion of the needlework" refers to the final insertion of the needle after having performed whatever must be done with the needle, ending with the border, the binding-strip, and the knot.
"Lost" means carried off by thieves and the like; for this too [falls under] the impediment of making.
Because it has been finished, it is said to be "finished. "Spoiled" means gnawed by termites and the like. "Burnt" means consumed by fire.

Or, "the expectation for a robe has been cut off": this refers to the expectation that had arisen, thinking, "I shall obtain a robe from such-and-such a family," and that expectation has been severed.
For in these cases as well, the state of being "finished" should be understood as the completion of the obstacle consisting in the act [of making the robe].
"Once the kaṭhina has been removed" means when the kaṭhina has been taken up. By this, he shows the absence of the second impediment.
Furthermore, since that kaṭhina is removed either by one of the eight headings (*mātikā*) or by an intermediate removal (*antarubbhāra*), it is therefore said in its definition:
"of the eight headings," and so forth. Therein: "Monks, there are these eight headings..."
Regarding the suspension of the *kathina*—the eight headings (*mātikā*) appearing in the *Kathinakkhandhaka* are as follows:

"suspension due to departure," "suspension due to completion," "suspension due to determination," "suspension due to loss," "suspension due to hearing," "suspension due to the cutting off of hope," "suspension due to crossing the boundary," and "simultaneous suspension. Furthermore, regarding intermediate suspension:
"Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me. If it is agreeable to the Sangha, the Sangha..."
"I propose this motion: Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The Saṅgha is now suspending the kaṭhina.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the suspension of the kaṭhina, let him remain silent; whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The kaṭhina has been suspended by the Saṅgha; it is approved by the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this."
Thus it is found in the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga. Whatever needs to be said regarding that matter, we shall explain it in its very place of occurrence.
However, if it were explained here, the Pāḷi would have to be cited and the meaning also stated; and even if stated, it would not be easily understood because it would be out of context.
*Dasāhaparamaṃ* means that ten days is the maximum limit; thus it is *dasāhaparama*. The meaning is that it should be kept for that period of time up to ten days.
However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it is stated as "it should be kept for a period not exceeding ten days" (*dasāhaparamatā dhāretabbaṃ*) merely to show the sense.
For this is what is meant: regarding the term *dasāhaparamaṃ*, there is the state of being limited by ten days (*dasāhaparamatā*).
"Having ten days as the maximum limit" means that it should be kept for as long as this period does not exceed.

It is called "extra robe-cloth" (*atirekacīvara*) because it is not included among those [robes] that have been either formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhita*) or assigned to another (*vikappita*). For this very reason, it is stated in its word-commentary:
"not resolved upon and not assigned. "One of the six kinds of robe-cloth" refers to linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, or jute.
