"Any one of these six kinds of robes. Having thus shown the type of robe by this [statement], he now says "the last one suitable for assignment" (*vikappanupaga*) in order to show its measurement.

Its measurement is two spans (*vidatthi*) in length and one span across. On this point, the canonical text (*pāḷi*) is as follows: "I allow you, monks, [a robe] eight finger-breadths in length according to the Sugata’s finger-breadth..."
"One may assign the lower robe (pacchima-cīvara) as being four fingerbreadths wide.

For one who exceeds that [limit], it is an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya-pācittiya). This means that for one who lets the robe—of the aforementioned type and measurement—exceed the ten-day limit, and who does not act in such a way that it does not become an "extra robe" (atireka-cīvara) during that interval, it is an offense entailing relinquishment.
The meaning is that it is a *pācittiya* offense, and that robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), and there is an offense of *pācittiya* for him.

Alternatively, *nissaggiya* means "that which involves forfeiture"; this is the name for the disciplinary procedure (*vinayakamma*) to be performed in its preliminary stage. It is called *nissaggiya* because it possesses forfeiture.
What is that? It is the *pācittiya*. For one who lets that [period] pass, there is the disciplinary procedure involving forfeiture.

"It is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya)"—this is the meaning here. In the word-by-word commentary (padabhājana), however, first establishing the matrix (mātikā) by saying, "For one who exceeds that [time limit], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya)," in order to show the alternative explanation of the meaning, it is stated:

"At the rising of the sun on the eleventh day, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment; it must be relinquished. Furthermore, as for whom it must be relinquished and how it must be relinquished:
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “or to the Saṅgha” was stated. Regarding the phrase “on the eleventh dawn after”:

the dawn of the day on which the robe was acquired is dependent upon that day of acquisition; therefore, it should be understood that it becomes an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) when the dawn breaks on the eleventh day from the day the robe was acquired. This remains true even if many [robes] were acquired together at once.
If they are placed there after being tied or wrapped, it is a single offense. If they are neither tied nor wrapped, the offenses are according to the number of items.
"Having relinquished them, the offense is to be confessed"—how is it to be confessed? As it is stated in the Khandhaka;
and how is it stated there? It is stated thus: "Monks, that monk, having approached the Saṅgha, with one shoulder bared..."

Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, having sat down on his heels and extended his hands in reverential salutation, he should speak to them thus:
"Venerable sirs, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense; I confess it.
But in this case, if there is only one robe, it should be said: "one *nissaggiya pācittiya*. If...
If there are two, it should be said, "Two. If there are many, it should be said, "Many. Regarding the relinquishment as well:
if there is one, it should be said exactly as in the text, "Venerable Sir, this robe of mine... If there are two or many, [it should be said]:
"Venerable Sir, these robes of mine have exceeded ten days and are to be relinquished; I relinquish them to the Saṅgha."
It should be stated. One who is unable to recite the Pāḷi may state it in another way.

An offense should be accepted by a learned and competent monk; it should be accepted precisely according to the method set forth in the Khandhaka. For it is said there: “The Saṅgha should be informed by a learned and competent monk:”

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this bhikkhu named so-and-so remembers an offense; he discloses it, reveals it, makes it clear, and confesses it. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, may I receive the confession of the offense of the bhikkhu named so-and-so.

He should then be asked: “Do you see [the offense]? “Yes, I see it. “You should exercise restraint in the future. However, in the case of two or many [offenses], the variation in wording should be understood according to the same method as before.

In the case of giving robes as well, the distinction in speech should be understood according to the object, such as: "The Saṅgha, this robe, these robes. The same method applies to the relinquishing [of property] to a group and to an individual.
However, regarding the confession and receiving of offenses here, the Pāḷi is as follows:
"Monks, that monk, having approached several monks, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and having bowed at the feet of the senior monks..."
Sitting in the squatting posture and raising his joined palms, he should speak thus:
"Venerable sirs, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense; I confess it. A competent and capable monk should inform those monks:

"Let the venerable ones listen to me. This monk, so-and-so, remembers an offense, discloses it, makes it plain, and confesses it. If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, I shall receive the confession of the offense of the monk so-and-so."
He should be asked, "Do you see it? "Yes, I see it. "You should exercise restraint in the future.

Then that bhikkhu, having approached another bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his heels, and having raised his joined palms in salutation, should speak to him thus: "Friend, I have committed such-and-such an offense..."
‘I have fallen into that; I confess it. He should be told: ‘Do you see it? ‘Yes, I see it; I shall exercise restraint in the future.
In this regard, the naming of the offense and the phrasing of the speech should be understood according to the same method as before.
And just as it is in the case of relinquishing to a group, so too should the text be understood for relinquishing to two individuals, provided there is a distinction.

It would be as follows: having stated, "I allow you, monks, to perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* for three [monks], and it should be performed in this way: 'A competent and capable monk should inform those monks,'" and so forth, he further said, "I allow you, monks..."
Regarding the performance of the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* for two [monks], it was stated by way of the method beginning with, "And thus, monks, it should be done:
the elder monk should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder," etc., that the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* for two is indeed performed separately.

If this were the case here as well, the text (*pāḷi*) would have stated it separately; however, since there is no such separate statement, it is not mentioned and has been passed over. Therefore, the very text prescribed for a group (*gaṇa*) is what constitutes the text here.
However, regarding the formal acceptance of an offense (*āpattipaṭiggahaṇa*), there is this distinction:

whereas when an offense is being confessed after having been relinquished to a group, the monk who accepts the offense establishes a motion (*ñatti*), so too, without establishing a motion, the offense should be accepted by one person from among the two, just as a single individual accepts it. For indeed, the establishment of a motion by two [monks] is not permitted.
It does not exist; for if it did, one would not speak of the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* separately for two people.

Also, regarding the giving away of a robe that has been relinquished, just as one person says, "I give this robe to the Venerable One," so too it is permissible to say, "We give this robe to the Venerable One.
For even formal acts (*kamma*) consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) are more serious than this.
There are certain acts stated to be "to be performed after having obtained permission"; this [case] is in accordance with those. However, a robe that has been relinquished must indeed be given back;
it is not permitted not to give it, for this is merely a formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma).
It does not mean that it has already been given to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual by that [person].

468. "When ten days have passed, one perceives that they have passed" means: when the robe has passed the ten-day limit, one perceives it thus, "This has passed," or when the ten days have passed, one perceives it thus, "The ten days have passed.

"An offense entailing relinquishment and confession" (nissaggiya-pācittiya) means that here perception does not protect one. Even for one who perceives it thus, that robe is subject to relinquishment, and there is an offense of confession.
And so, both alternatives—whether it is a formal act of forfeiture (*sanissaggiya-vinaya-kamma*) or an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)—are applicable.
This same method applies everywhere. "Perceiving as given what was not given" means: when something has not been handed over or relinquished by anyone, one perceives, "It has been relinquished by me.

"Perceiving as lost what was not lost" means: many robes belonging to others have been placed together with one's own robe, and thieves carry them off. In this case, although one's own robe has not been stolen, one perceives it as lost. This same method applies to "not destroyed" and so forth.
Regarding the term "plundered" (*avilutta*): here it should be understood as plundering by breaking open the womb and carrying it away by force.

"If one uses [the robe] without relinquishing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)" means that if one wears it once or puts it on once and does not remove it from the body even while wandering about for the whole day, it is a single offense.
If, however, one removes it again and again before putting it on or wearing it, [there is a separate offense for each act].
For every act of application, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). There is no offense for one who adjusts what is poorly dressed or poorly clad.
There is also no offense for another who uses it; the statement, "There is no offense for one who, having obtained what was made by another, uses it," and so forth, is the proof here.
Regarding the phrase "when not exceeded" (*anatikkante*), the offense of wrong-doing is stated with reference to the use [of the robe] by one who perceives it as exceeded or who is in doubt.

469. “There is no offense if one determines [the robe] within ten days or assigns it” — here, however, one should understand what pertains to determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and what pertains to assignment (*vikappana*).
In this regard, the following is the canonical text: Then it occurred to the monks:
“Those things which have been permitted by the Blessed One—namely, ‘the three robes,’ ‘the rainy-season robe,’ ‘the sitting mat,’ or ‘the spread’...”

“Or a ‘sweat-protector,’ or a face-cleaning cloth, or a requisite cloth—all these, should they be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) or should they be assigned to another (*vikappetabba*)? They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow you to determine the three robes, but not to assign them; the rain-cloak during the rainy season...”
One may resolve upon [a robe] for four months and thereafter designate it; one may resolve upon a sitting mat but not designate it;
one may resolve upon a sheet but not designate it; one may resolve upon a cloth for covering itchiness as long as the affliction lasts and thereafter designate it;
one may resolve upon a face-cloth but not designate it; [and likewise for] a requisite-cloth.
"One should resolve upon it, not alter it.
In this regard, one who resolves upon the triple robe (ticīvara) must first dye it, apply the "wholesome mark" (kappabindu), and then resolve upon it only when it is of the proper measure.
Regarding its measure: at the upper limit, it is permissible for it to be smaller than the robe of the Sugata; at the lower limit, [it must be sufficient].
The measurement for the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) is five fist-breadths in length and three fist-breadths across;

this is permissible. The inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) is five fist-breadths in length, and two cubits across is also permissible, for it is possible to cover the navel even with that much when wearing it as an outer covering.
However, anything exceeding the stated measurements or falling short of them should be determined as an accessory cloth (*parikkhāracola*).
In this regard, since it is said: "There are two ways of determining a robe:

one determines it by means of the body, or one determines it by means of speech," therefore, having relinquished the old outer robe (saṅghāṭī) with the words, "I relinquish this outer robe," and having taken the new outer robe in hand, one should make a mental application (ābhoga), thinking, "I determine this outer robe," and perform a bodily gesture.
It must be resolved by means of the body. This is resolution by the body; it is not permissible for one who does not touch [the robe] with any part of the body to do so.
However, in the case of resolution by speech, one must resolve it by speech after making a vocal utterance.
In that regard, there are two kinds of resolution: if [the robe] is within arm’s reach, one says by speech, "I resolve this outer robe."
It must be dismantled. Then, having observed a place where it is kept—whether in the inner chamber, on the upper terrace, or in a nearby monastery—one should dismantle it by means of speech, saying:
"I resolve upon this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*). This same method applies to the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*).
For the only difference is the name; therefore, [one should say] for all of them: "the outer robe," "the upper robe," and "the inner robe."

In this way, they must be determined by means of their own names. If, having determined them, one makes a *saṅghāṭī* or other robes from the fabrics thus set aside, then once the dyeing and the cutting are finished, one should relinquish them with the words, "I relinquish this," and determine them again.
However, when sewing on a second patch or a piece that is even larger than the determined robe, [one must do so] together with that which has already been determined.
It must indeed be determined again. There is no need for determination regarding what is equal or small.
But as for the three robes that are requisites—does it or does it not become allowable to determine them as such?
Regarding this, the Elder Mahāpaduma reportedly said: "The three robes must be determined as the three robes themselves. If one were to obtain the determination of them as requisites-cloths..."
"In that case, the exemption regarding the rule on stored goods (*udosita-sikkhāpada*) would be rendered meaningless. When this was said, it is reported that the remaining monks said:
"It has been stated by the Blessed One himself that even the requisites cloth (*parikkhāra-coḷa*) must be formally determined; therefore, it is permissible. It is also stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*:
"What is called 'requisites cloth' is a separate category of storage; [it refers to] the three robes (*ticīvara*)."
"It is permissible to use [a cloth] after having determined it as 'requisite-cloth' (*parikkhāra-coḷa*).
However, in the *Udosita-sikkhāpada*, an exemption is stated for one who carries about the three robes (*ticīvara*) after having determined them.
It is said that the Elder Mahātissa, resident of Puṇṇavālika and reciter of both the *Vibhaṅgas*, also said: "In the past, we heard from the great elders that monks dwelling in the forest..."
Having placed their robes in hollows of trees and similar locations, they go forth to exert themselves in meditation.
When they have gone to a neighboring monastery to hear the Dhamma, at sunrise, novices or junior bhikkhus take their bowls and robes and depart.
Therefore, for the sake of comfortable use, one may resolve that the three robes are "accessory cloth."

"It is permissible. It is also stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "In the past, forest-dwelling bhikkhus, finding it difficult to maintain [the robes] within an unbounded boundary (*abaddhasīmā*), used the three robes after resolving that they were merely requisites for clothing (*parikkhāracoḷa*).

Regarding the "rainy-season robe" (*vassikasāṭikā*): having taken its name as being of a size not exceeding the prescribed measure, one should use it according to the method already described during the four months of the rainy season.

It must be formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhātabba*), and thereafter, having relinquished it, it must be assigned (*vikappetabba*). This is permissible even if it is dyed only slightly different in color;
however, two [such items] are not permitted. A "sitting mat" (*nisīdana*) must indeed be resolved upon according to the stated method, and that too must be of the proper measure and only one;
two are not permitted. A "bedspread" (*paccattharaṇa*) must also be resolved upon. That...
However, it is permissible whether it is large, or even a single one, or many; it is permissible of every kind—whether blue, yellow, with figures, or with flower designs.
Once determined, it remains determined for good. A "sore-covering cloth" (kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi) should be determined as being of the proper size as long as the illness exists.
When the illness has subsided, it should be relinquished and then formally assigned to another.
Only one is permitted. A face-cloth must indeed be determined [as such], but as long as one is being washed, another may be desired for use; thus two are permitted.
However, other elders say, "This is merely a place of storage, so even many are permitted. Regarding requisites-cloths, there is no limit; as much as one desires, that much is allowed.

It must indeed be formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhātabba*). A bag for robes and a water-strainer, if they are of the size of the last [allowable] robe and fit for assignment, must also be formally resolved upon as "accessory cloth" (*parikkhāracoḷaka*).
It is likewise permissible to collect many such items together and resolve upon them, saying: "I resolve upon these robes as accessory cloths.
This applies even when preparing medicine or for the sake of one's mother, father, and so forth.
Even when setting it aside, one must indeed perform the formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated that there is no offense.

Furthermore, regarding a mattress for a bed, a mattress for a chair, a bolster, a woolen rug, and a goatskin rug—as well as spreadings given for the purpose of bedding requisites—there is no need for the formal act of determination at all.
But for one who uses a robe that has been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*), how is that determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) lost?

It is lost through these nine causes: by giving it to another, by taking it back after having given it away, by taking it on trust, by returning to the lower state, by renouncing the training, by death, by change of gender, by relinquishing it, and by its becoming torn.
In this regard, by means of the first eight [causes], all robes lose their determined status (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

However, in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated that for the three robes (*ticīvara*) alone, the loss of determined status occurs through the state of being torn; and that [tearing] must be a tear the size of a fingernail’s surface.
In this context, the measure of a fingernail’s surface should be understood by way of the fingernail of the little finger, and the tear must be one that has been completely pierced through.
For if even a single thread remains uncut within a hole, it protects [the robe].

In that regard, for the *saṅghāṭī* and the *uttarāsaṅga*, a hole situated beyond a distance of one span from the long edge and eight finger-breadths from the crosswise edge breaks the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*); beyond that, it does not break it. For the *antaravāsaka*...

However, from the long end, a hole measuring only one span (vidatthi) breaks the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna), while from the crosswise end, a hole measuring only four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) breaks it;
beyond that, it does not break it. Therefore, once a hole has arisen, that robe remains in the status of an extra robe (atirekacīvara);
after performing needlework [to mend it], it must be formally determined again. Thus says the Elder Mahāsumma.
But he said: "A hole anywhere in a robe of the correct measurement breaks the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*);
however, a hole outside the measurement of a large robe does not break the determination, though it does break the determination for one born inside [the robe].
The Elder Karavīkatissa said: "Smallness or largeness is not the measurement; rather, when one is wearing two robes, having folded them in the left hand..."
"In the place where it is fixed, the determination does not break the gap; it breaks on the side beyond that.
When making a waistband for the inner robe (antaravāsaka) as well, one does not break the gap at the place where it is folded together; one breaks it from there onwards.
However, in the *Andhaka-ṭīkā*, having taken the opinion of the Elder Mahāsumma regarding the three robes as authoritative, [it states] this also for the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
It is said: “One maintains the determination regarding the final measurement.
If there is a hole anywhere in the requisites cloth that is eight finger-breadths long by four finger-breadths wide according to the Sugata’s finger-breadth, the determination is lost.
In a large cloth, a hole larger than that does not cause the determination to be lost. This same principle applies to all robes that must be determined.
In this regard, since there is no other "minimum measure" for any robes that must be formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) apart from the minimum measure suitable for assignment (*vikappanupaga*),
that which is stated as the measure for the sitting mat (*nisīdana*), the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*),
and the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) is the maximum; for it is prohibited to exceed that, while it is not prohibited to go below it, and thus it is not the minimum.
For the three robes as well, being smaller than the measure of the Sugata’s robe constitutes the maximum limit.
However, there is no separate rule stated in the Suttas regarding the last [robe]. There is likewise no upper limit specified for face-towels, bedspreads, and accessory cloths.
But the lower limit is stated by means of the "suitable for dedication" (*vikappanupaga*) robe; therefore, as for that which—

In the *Andhakavattiya-kathā*, after stating, "One maintains the resolution regarding the minimum measurement," it demonstrates that for the requisite cloth alone, the minimum measurement is eight finger-breadths by four finger-breadths according to the Sugata’s finger-breadth;

then, referring to the minimum measurements of the other robes, such as the three robes (*ticīvara*), which consist of various divisions starting from five handfuls (*muṭṭhi*), it says: "This same method applies to all robes that must be resolved upon."
What has been stated does not agree with that.
Even in the doctrine of the Elder Karavīkatissa, a breach is shown only from the long side, but not from the horizontal side;
therefore, according to him, it remains undefined. In the doctrine of the Elder Mahāsumma, [it is said]: "Wherever there is a breach in a robe of standard measurement..."
It is said: "One breaks the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) [if the robe exceeds the size], but one does not break the determination if there is a hole outside the measurement of the large [robe].
However, this was not stated: "This is a robe of the prescribed measure; any robe larger than this is [excessive].
Furthermore, in this context, what is intended by the "lower limit" (*pacchima-ppamāṇa*) is the five-fist-measure and so forth for the three robes (*ticīvara*) and the rest. In that regard:

If a hole outside the final measurement would not break the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna), then even for a large bowl or a medium bowl, a hole outside the minimum measurement would not break the formal determination; yet it does break it.
Therefore, this position is also undecided.
However, this very first statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) is the authority here. Why?

Because it possesses a definite delimitation (*pariccheda*). For the final measurement of the three robes, the measurement of the hole, and the measurement of the location where the hole arises have all been defined and stated only in the *Aṭṭhakathās*;
therefore, that statement alone is the authority. Indeed, it certainly [conveys] the Blessed One’s intention.
It is stated [only] after having followed through [the entire robe]. However, in other cases, there is no demarcation, nor do the preceding and following parts coincide.
But if one first applies the bolt (aggaḷa) to a weak spot and later removes it by cutting that weak spot, the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is not broken.
This same principle applies even when turning a circular patch. Regarding one layer of a double-layered robe (dupaṭṭa):

If a hole has formed or a part has torn away, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is not broken. If one makes a small robe large, or makes a large robe small, the formal determination is not broken.

If one brings both ends together in the middle, if one cuts first and then joins them later, the formal determination is broken. But if one joins them first and then cuts, [the determination is not broken].
It does not break [the determination]; even for one who has it washed by dyers and has it made white, the determination remains a valid determination.
This, then, is the exposition regarding determination in the context of the rule: "Within ten days, he determines or designates. Regarding designation, however, there are two types of designation:
designation in the presence (*sammukhā-vikappanā*) and designation in the absence (*parammukhā-vikappanā*). How [is this so]?

What is meant by "assignment in the presence"? Having ascertained whether the robes are one or many, and whether they are present or absent, one should say: "I assign this robe," or "I assign these robes," or "I assign that robe," or "I assign those robes, to you.
This is one form of assignment in the presence. Up to this point, it is permissible to store [the robe].
However, it is not permitted to consume it, to give it away, or to resolve upon it as one's own.
But when it is said, "This is my property; use my property, give it away, or do with it as you see fit," then it is called a renunciation (*paccuddhāra*).
From that point onward, even the consumption and other uses of it are permitted.
There is another method: having likewise understood whether the robes are one or many,
and whether they are stored or not stored, one should speak in the presence of that same bhikkhu,
saying either "this robe" or "these robes," or "that robe" or "those robes," and then [offer them] to whichever among the five types of fellow practitioners one prefers.
Having taken the name of anyone whatsoever, one should say: "I dedicate it to the monk Tissa," or "I dedicate it to the nun Tissa, the trainee Tissa, the novice monk Tissa, or the novice nun Tissa.
This is another form of dedication in the presence of the recipient. Up to this point, it is permissible to set it aside; however, regarding its use and so forth, even a single [instance]—
It is not permissible. However, when that bhikkhu says, “Use the property belonging to the bhikkhu Tissa...
[or] the property belonging to the female novice Tissa, or dispose of it, or deal with it as you see fit,” this is called relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*).
From that point onward, even using it and so forth are permissible.

How is there an assignment in the absence of the person (*parammukhā-vikappanā*)? Having ascertained the singular or plural nature of the robes, as well as whether they are present or absent, one should say, "This robe" or "These robes," or "That robe" or "Those robes," and then say, "I give this for your assignment. He should then be asked: "Who is your friend?"
“Or has he been seen? Then the other must reply in the same manner as before: “Three bhikkhus... [or] ‘three novice nuns.
Again, that bhikkhu must say: “I give to the bhikkhu Tissa... [or] ‘I give to the novice nun Tissa’”;
this is an assignment made in the absence of the recipient. Up to this point, it is permissible to set aside [the robe].
However, among the uses such as consumption, not even one is permitted.
But when that bhikkhu has said, in accordance with the method explained for the second type of face-to-face assignment:

"Enjoy this belonging to so-and-so, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit," then it is called a relinquishment (paccuddhāra). From that point onward, even uses such as consumption are permitted.

What is the difference between the two types of assignment (*vikappanā*)? In the case of face-to-face assignment (*sammukhā-vikappanā*), one assigns it oneself and then has another person relinquish it. In the case of indirect assignment (*parammukhā-vikappanā*), one has another person assign it and then has that same person relinquish it;
this is the difference here. However, if the person to whom one assigns it is not skilled in the formal rules (*paññatti*) and does not understand them...
To relinquish it, one should take that robe, go to another competent person, and after making a formal assignment (vikappa) again, have it relinquished.
This is what is called "assignment-after-assignment" (*vikappita-vikappanā*), and it is permissible. This is the analysis of the term "assigns" (*vikappeti*) in this context.
Furthermore, from such statements as, "Monks, I allow you to determine (*adhiṭṭhātuṃ*) the triple-robe, but not to assign it," this [distinction] follows.
The statement "he designates" (*vikappeti*) appears as if it were contradictory when stated without qualification; yet the Tathāgatas do not speak what is contradictory.

Therefore, its meaning should be understood in this way: for one who maintains the three robes by means of the very summary of the three robes, I allow only the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), not the designation (*vikappa*).
However, for the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*), one must designate it after the four months have passed.

It cannot be formally determined [as one's own]. This being the case, for one who wishes to stay apart from one of his three robes, he is permitted to rescind the formal determination of the set of three robes and provide an opportunity for the assignment (*vikappanā*) for the sake of the ease of staying apart.
Furthermore, there is no offense if ten days have elapsed; by this method, it should be understood that in all such instances, the assignment is not prohibited.
"Vissajjeti" means he gives it to another. But how is it given? And how is it received?
If one says, "I give this to you," "I bestow it," "I grant it," "I offer it," "I relinquish it," "I renounce it," or "I hand it over"; or if one says, "I give it... [etc.
...I renounce it to such-and-such a person"—whether in the presence of the recipient or behind their back—it is indeed considered given. "To you..."
When it is said, “Take it,” and he says, “I am taking it for myself,” it is well given and well received.
When it is said, “Make it yours; let it be yours; you shall make it yours,” and he says, “I am making it mine;
let it be mine; I shall make it mine,” it is ill given and ill received. Neither...
The giver knows how to give, but the other does not know how to receive. However, if, when told, "Make this yours," he says, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I take it," then it is well-received.

But if the first person says, "Take it alone," and the other replies, "I will not take it," and the first person then says, "I have given this to you, take it," yet the other still says, "I will not..."
"I have need of this," he says. Then the first person lets ten days pass, thinking, "It was given by me," and the latter also lets them pass, thinking, "It was refused by me.
For whom is there an offense? For neither is there an offense. However, whichever one desires it, he should determine it as his own and then use it.
But what should one who is doubtful about the formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) do?
Having declared his state of doubt, he should say, "If it remains unresolved, then this shall be allowable for me," and then he should relinquish it according to the method already stated.
For there is no falsehood in performing a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) after having made such a declaration. Some, however, [say] that by means of a single monk... [trust...]
The claim that "it is permissible to take it back and give it again" is incorrect.
For this is not a formal disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) against him, nor does it become a different offense simply by that much.

The phrases "it is lost," and so forth, are self-evident. Regarding the statement, "if one does not give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," here [the meaning is]: "It was given to me..."

"By this" means that for one who does not give because of this perception, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, having recognized that it belongs to him, if one seizes it by means of a pretext, one should be dealt with according to the value of the goods after they have been appraised.
Regarding the origin and other factors, this training rule is known as originating from the *kathina*; it arises from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind.

It arises through both [intention and action]; because it is incurred through non-determination and non-intention, it is an act of non-doing (*akiriya*). One is not released even in the absence of perception;

since one incurs it even without knowing, it is "not released by perception" (*no-saññā-vimokkha*). It is without mental concomitants (*acittaka*), a fault of formal rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*), bodily action (*kāya-kamma*), and vocal action (*vacī-kamma*);
it consists of three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the first Kathina training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Udosita training rule: 471.
"At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One... refers to the Udosita training rule. Therein, "santaruttarena" means "with the inner and outer [robes]. Regarding "antara":
The *antaravāsaka* is called the inner robe; the *uttarāsaṅga* is the upper robe. Together with the *antara* (inner) and the *uttara* (upper) is the *santaruttara*;
by means of that *santaruttara*, the meaning is: together with the *antaravāsaka* and the *uttarāsaṅga*.
"Scabby" refers to blackish-grey circular patches that have appeared in places touched by sweat. The Venerable Ānanda saw [this] while walking on tour of the lodgings.
Regarding the phrase "wandering about": it is said that when the Blessed One had entered the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭī*) for his midday seclusion,
the Elder, having found that opportunity, was putting away wooden and earthenware vessels that had been poorly set out,
sweeping the unswept places, and exchanging greetings with the sick monks at their lodgings.
Having arrived, he saw it. Therefore it is said: "The Venerable Ānanda, while wandering on a tour of the lodgings, saw it.
(473) "To grant permission for non-separation" (*avippavāsa-sammuti*): *avippavāsa-sammuti* is the permission regarding non-separation;
or, *avippavāsa-sammuti* is the permission for the sake of non-separation. What, then, is the benefit here? [It is that] one may dwell apart from whatever robe one possesses.
There is no forfeiture, nor does one incur an offense. For how long a time? To this, the Elder Mahāsumma said:
"As long as the illness has not subsided; but once the illness has subsided, one must return quickly to the place where the robe was kept.
The Elder Mahāpaduma said: "If one returns too quickly, the illness might recur; therefore, one should return slowly."
"From the moment one either searches for a teacher or makes the mental application (ābhoga), thinking, 'I am going,' from that point on it is permissible.
However, by one who lays down the burden, thinking, 'I shall not go now,' it must be relinquished [with the thought], 'It shall remain in the status of an extra robe (atirekacīvara).
"But if a disease flares up for him, what should be done? asked Phussadeva Thera.
He said: “If that very same disease recurs, it is the same convention; there is no need to perform the act of granting the convention again.
But if another [disease] recurs, the convention must be granted again. The Elder Upatissa said:
“Whether it be that same disease or another, there is no need to perform the act of granting the convention again.”

475–6. Regarding the phrase "a bhikkhunī whose robe is finished" (*niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunī*): here, one should understand the meaning of the instrumental case not by taking the sense as in the preceding rule, but rather as "when the robe is finished for a bhikkhunī.
For there is no such thing as "this must be done by a bhikkhunī" in the sense of an agentive instrument; rather, it is in the sense of a possessor—that is, "for a bhikkhunī."

"When the robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, for one whose impediments have thus been severed, it is appropriate to say: 'If a bhikkhu should be separated from his three robes even for a single night.
In this context, "with the three robes" means with any one of the three robes that have been determined [as such].
For even if one is separated from only one, one is considered separated from the three robes, provided it is one included among those [robes] that are permitted.

Because of being separated. For that very reason, it is said in the word-commentary (padabhājana) for him: “by the outer robe,” and so forth. “Should live separated” means he should live dissociated [from his robes]. 477–8.
The passage beginning with “A village with a single precinct” is stated for the purpose of defining the characteristic of non-separation (*avippavāsa*).
Thereafter, expanding upon those same fifteen matrix-heads (*mātikāpada*) in their respective order, he says: “A village with a single precinct is called... and so forth.
In this context, "a village of a single family" means a village belonging to a single king or a single lord.
"Enclosed" means surrounded by any kind of wall, fence, or enclosure. By this much, the fact that a village of a single family has a single access point is shown.
"One must dwell within the village" means that having deposited one's robe in such a village, one may stay anywhere within the village according to one’s preference.
It is appropriate to cause the dawn to rise while staying in that place. By the word "unenclosed" (*aparikkhita*), it is shown that there is no distinct precinct (*upacāra*) for that very village.
In such a village, one must reside in whichever house the robe has been deposited;
or else, one must not depart from hand’s-reach (*hatthapāsa*) of that house—that is, one must not leave a space measuring two and a half *ratana*s on all sides.
It is said that one must not abandon [the robe] above [the ground]. However, it is permissible to store it within a distance of two and a half ratanas.
If one exceeds that measure, even if a monk possessing psychic power causes the dawn to rise while in the air, it is indeed an offense of expiation (nissaggiya).
And here, regarding "in whatever house," the definition of a house is as stated in such passages as, "it is the dwelling of a single family."
It is to be understood by its characteristic.
479. "A village of various clans" means a village belonging to various rulers or chieftains, such as Vesālī, Kusinārā, and so forth.
By the word "enclosed," the fact that such a village of various clans constitutes a single precinct (ekūpacāra) is shown. "In the assembly hall or at the gate" [is the location].
Here, by the change of gender (*liṅgavyattayena*), "sabhāyaṃ" refers to the assembly hall (*sabhā*). "At the gate" (*dvāramūle*) means in the vicinity of the city gate.
This is what is meant: in such a village, one should reside in whatever house the robe has been deposited;
or, for one who is unable to live there due to the noise of voices or the crowding of people, one may reside in the assembly hall.

Or at the foot of the city gate. If he is unable to dwell even there, he may stay in any comfortable place and, having returned before dawn, must not go beyond the reach of hand from those very same assembly halls or the foot of the gates.
However, there is no need to mention staying within the reach of hand of a house or a robe.
"Having placed the robe within arm's reach while going to the assembly hall": if one goes to the assembly hall thinking, "I will not leave it at home,
but will place it in the hall," then by that person going to the assembly hall "within arm's reach"—

meaning when the robe is within reach of the hand so that it is easy to deposit it by stretching out the hand and thinking, "Now I shall place this robe"— the robe [is deposited] in some shop within arm's reach.
Having deposited it, one should stay in the assembly hall or at the door in the same manner as before; nor should one go beyond the reach of one's hand.
Herein is the analysis: First, the Elder Phussadeva said, "One need not stay within the reach of one's hand of the robe;
it is permissible to stay anywhere within the reach of one's hand, whether that be on the street, in the assembly hall, or at the door."
But the Elder Upatissa said: "A city has many gates and many assembly halls; therefore, it is not permissible in every place.

However, one must not leave the reach of one's hand from the spot where the robe was placed in that street, nor from the assembly hall and gate facing it, nor from the gate of that assembly hall. For in this way..."

"It is possible to know the whereabouts of the robe-cloth. However, when going to the assembly hall, if it is placed in the hand of a shopkeeper and he carries it home and puts it away in his house, the "hand-span of the street" does not provide protection;
one must remain within the hand-span of the house. If the house is large, [one must remain within] two streets.
Having encompassed it, the dawn must be made to rise while [the object] is still in front or behind him,

within the reach of his hand. But having deposited it in the assembly hall, the dawn must be made to rise either in the assembly hall, or in the presence of that person, or at the foot of the city gate, within the reach of their very hands.
By the phrase "unenclosed" (*aparikkhitto*), the fact that there is no distinct precinct (*nānūpacāratā*) for that very village is shown.
By this same method, in all instances, both the state of having a single precinct (*ekūpacāratā*) and the state of having multiple precincts (*nānūpacāratā*) should be understood.

However, in the Canon (*pāḷi*), after citing the single summary heading (*mātikāpada*) at the beginning as "a village is called 'having a single precinct'" and at the end as "an open space is called 'having a single precinct'," the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)...

This has been explained in detail. Therefore, following that very passage, one should understand the state of being a single sphere of activity (*ekūpacāratā*) and the state of being multiple spheres of activity (*nānūpacāratā*) everywhere by way of the enclosure and so forth.

480–1. Regarding "dwelling places" (*nivesana*) and so on, "chambers" (*ovarakā*) is a synonym specifically for inner rooms (*gabbha*). "Within arm's reach" (*hatthapāsā va*) refers to the inner room.
"Within arm's reach": at the base of the door common to all; "or within arm's reach" means within the reach of the hand of either the inner chamber or the base of the house door. 482–7. *Udosita*:
a hall for goods such as vehicles and so forth. From this point onward, it is according to the method already stated regarding the dwelling (*nivesana*).
The detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*) should be understood as follows:

*Aṭṭa* is a specific type of dwelling constructed with bricks, having thick walls and four or five stories, for the purpose of warding off rival kings and the like. *Māḷa* is a square palace comprised of a single roof-peak.
*Pāsāda* is a long palace. *Hammia* is a palace with a flat roof.
489. Regarding "seven *abbhantara*s": here, one *abbhantara* is twenty-eight cubits (*hattha*).

If a caravan, while traveling, stops having encircled a village or a river, and stands connected with those who have entered inside, covering both this side and the far side, it receives the same exemption as the caravan itself. Or, if [it stops] at a village...
Or if he has entered and is included within a river, both the exemption from the village and the exemption from the river apply.
If he stands having crossed the monastery boundary, but his robe is within the boundary, he must go to the monastery and stay there.
If his robe is outside the boundary, he must stay right near the caravan. If, while going...
If a cart breaks down or an ox is lost, and one is separated from the group, one must stay where the robe is located.

490. Regarding the "hand’s reach" (*hatthapāsa*) on the field of a single family: it is the hand’s reach of the robe itself. Regarding the "hand’s reach" on the field of various families: it is the hand’s reach of the field’s entrance. On an unenclosed area, it is the hand’s reach of the robe itself. 491–4.
"Grain-processing place" (*dhaññakaraṇa*) refers to a threshing floor. "Garden" (*ārāma*) means either a flower garden or a fruit garden. In both cases...
The determination is similar to that stated regarding a field. A monastery (*vihāra*) is like a dwelling (*nivesana*).

"Within the shadow at the foot of a tree" means precisely within the area touched by the shadow; however, for a tree with sparse branches, what is placed in an area touched by the sun is indeed subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
Therefore, [it is permissible] under the shadow of such branches or the shadow of the trunk.
It should be placed [on a branch]. If one places it on a branch or a bough, it must be placed only in a spot touched by the shadow of another branch above.
Even if the shadow of a crooked tree extends far, it is indeed permissible to place it in the place where the shadow has reached.
Here too, "the reach of the hand" refers specifically to the reach of the hand holding the robe.

"In a forest devoid of villages" (*agāmake araññe*): a "forest devoid of villages" is found in places such as the Vindhya wilderness or in islands in the middle of the ocean that are not accessible to fishermen.
"Seven *abbhantara*s on all sides": from the center, in every direction, there are seven *abbhantara*s;
thus, including the diameter, they total fourteen. Sitting in the center, [facing] the east...
Or he protects the robe-cloth placed at the boundary in the western direction.
However, if at the time of sunrise it moves even a hair’s breadth toward the eastern direction, the robe-cloth in the western direction becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
This same principle applies to the other directions as well. But at the time of the *uposatha*, starting from the monk seated at the edge of the assembly...
The seven-intermediate-space boundary must be cleared. To whatever extent the Saṅgha of bhikkhus increases, the boundary also increases to that same extent.
Regarding the rule, "If one uses [the robes] without relinquishing them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)":
here, if a bhikkhu engaged in meditation, having devoted himself to meditation throughout the entire night, intends to bathe at dawn and places his three robes on the bank before entering the river—
He enters the water, and while he is still bathing, dawn breaks. What should be done?

For if he, having stepped out of the water, puts on his robe, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for using a robe that has not been relinquished after it was subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
But if he goes naked, does he likewise incur an offense of wrong-doing? He does not incur one. For as long as he [remains there] until another monk...
If one sees [the robes] but does not perform the formal act of the Vinaya, then, because those robes are unfit for use, one stands in the position of one whose robes have been lost.
For one whose robes are lost, there is nothing that is technically "unallowable" (akappiya).
Therefore, having put on one robe and holding two others in the hands, one should go to the monastery and perform the formal act of the Vinaya. If the monastery is far away, then along the way—
People are walking about. One should go having put on one [robe], covered with another, and placed one over the shoulder.

If he does not see like-minded monks in the monastery—because they have gone out for alms—he should place his outer robe outside the village, go to the assembly hall wearing only the inner robe and the sarong, and perform the disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*). If there is danger from thieves outside the village...

[The robes] must be worn while traveling. If the assembly hall is crowded and congested with people such that it is impossible to perform the legal act of the Vinaya after removing the robes to one side, one should take a monk and go outside the village;
having performed the legal act of the Vinaya there, the robes may then be used.
If monks, having placed their bowls and robes in the hands of junior monks while traveling on the road, wish to sleep during the last watch of the night,
they should sleep keeping their own robes within reach of their hands. If dawn breaks while they are still traveling and before the juniors have arrived,
the robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), but the formal support (*nissaya*) is not [lost].
It subsides. The same applies even when young monks are walking ahead and the elders have not yet caught up.
The same applies even if they lose their way in the forest and cannot see one another.
However, if the young monks say, "Venerable sirs, we shall sleep for a moment and then reach you at such-and-such a place," [and remain there] until—
If they sleep after sunrise, the robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is suspended.
The same rule applies even if, after sending away the junior monks, the elders sleep [there]. Having seen a forked path, the elders say, "This is the way," and the juniors say, "This is the way";
if they go without heeding one another's words, at the rising of the sun, the robes [become forfeited].
The robes become subject to forfeiture and the formal support (nissaya) is suspended. However, if the novices leave the road and, thinking,
"We shall return before dawn," enter a village for the sake of medicine and return,
and the dawn rises while they have not yet arrived, the robes become subject to forfeiture, but the formal support is not suspended.
If, however, out of fear of cows or fear of dogs, they stop or sit down while thinking, "We will go after staying for a moment," then when dawn has risen in the meantime,
the robes become subject to forfeiture and the formal support (nissaya) is suspended.
If, thinking, "We will return before dawn," they have entered a village within the boundary—
If dawn breaks while they are still within [the monastery], the robes do not become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), nor does the formal dependence (*nissaya*) cease.
However, if they remain sitting with the thought, "Let it first grow light," then even when dawn has broken, the robes do not become subject to forfeiture, yet the formal dependence does cease.
This also applies to those who, thinking, "We will return before dawn," go to a neighboring monastery for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
They set out with enthusiasm, but the dawn breaks upon them while they are still on the way;
their robes become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), yet the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is not dissolved.

If, out of respect for the Dhamma, they sit down thinking, "We will go only after we have heard the conclusion," then at the moment the dawn breaks, both the robes become subject to forfeiture and the formal dependence is also dissolved.

It subsides. When an elder sends a junior monk to a village for the purpose of washing robes, he should give [the robe] after first relinquishing his own robe. The junior monk’s robe should also be relinquished and set aside.
If he goes away through forgetfulness, he should relinquish his own robe and take the junior monk’s robe on trust.

It should be set aside. If the elder does not remember, but the junior monk remembers, the junior monk should relinquish his own robe, take the elder’s robe on trust, go [to him], and say: "Venerable sir, having determined your robe, please use it.
He should also determine his own robe. In this way, even through the mindfulness of one person, there is release from the offense.
"...it happens. The remainder has its meaning already explained.

Regarding the origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth: in the first Kathina training rule (*sikkhāpada*), non-determination (*anadhiṭṭhāna*) and non-assignment (*avikappana*) constitute non-action (*akiriya*); here, however, the non-removal (*apaccuddharaṇa*) is the specific distinction. The rest is entirely according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the Udosita training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Third Kathina Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 497.
"At that time" refers to the third Kathina training rule.

In this context, "having spread it out, he repeatedly smooths it" means that, thinking "when the wrinkles have disappeared, this will become large," he sprinkles it with water and tramples it with his feet.
Having lifted it up with his hands and tossed it, he rubbed it on his back; while still wet, it dried in the sun as soon as it was applied.
He did this again and again; thus it is said: “Having tossed it up, he rubs it repeatedly.
Seeing him thus exerting himself, the Blessed One, while seated in the Fragrant Chamber, went out and began his inspection of the lodgings.
He went there as if wandering about. Therefore it was said: “The Blessed One saw,” and so forth. 499–500.
“In the eleven months” means in the remaining eleven months, excluding the single month of the later *kattika*.
“In the seven months” means in the remaining seven months, excluding the month of *kattika* and the four winter months, thus making five months. [This applies] specifically to the time as well.
"Given" means either given to the Saṅgha with the designation, "This is an out-of-season robe-cloth," or given to a single individual with the words, "I give this to you.
"From the Saṅgha" means it may arise from the Saṅgha by way of one's own allotted share. "From a group" means [it arises] from a group of those who specialize in the Suttas.
"‘This is for the Abhidhamma group’—in this way they give it to the group. Then, according to the portion each has received, it may arise from the group.

‘And there is no completion’ means: if there were no completion; that is to say, if the robe required to suffice for the *adhiṭṭhānacīvara* being prepared should not be so much, but rather less—that is the meaning."
Regarding the phrases "there is expectation from the Saṅgha," and so forth: "On such-and-such a day, the Saṅgha will receive robes; the group will receive them;
from that, a robe will accrue to me"—thus there is expectation from the Saṅgha or from the group.
"It has been sent by my relatives for the sake of a robe; it has been sent by my friends; they have arrived and will give me a robe"—thus [there is expectation].
There is an expectation from relatives or from friends. Regarding the phrase "or a rag-robe," it should be construed here as: "there is an expectation in the form of 'I shall obtain a rag-robe.
Regarding "or with one's own wealth," the meaning is: "there is an expectation in the form of 'I shall obtain [it] on such-and-such a day,' using one's own wealth such as cotton thread and so forth."

"If one should set it aside beyond that, even with the expectation [of more], it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). This is the meaning: "If one should set it aside for more than a month.

However, this not being stated, because when an expected robe arises in the interim, from the day the original robe arose until the twentieth day, the expected robe that has arisen [during that time] is considered part of the original robe.
One makes it one's own property; thereafter, one makes the basic robe (*mūlacīvara*) and the expected robe (*paccāsācīvara*) one's own property.

Therefore, in order to show that distinction, the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) is stated in the manner beginning with "when the basic robe has arisen on that very day," and its meaning is self-evident.
Regarding "when the basic robe has arisen from an unrelated source": if the basic robe is fine and the expected robe is coarse, [it is not so].
It is possible to apply [the rule]. There are still nights remaining; the month has not yet been completed, and one must not have the robe made under compulsion against one's will.
Only after obtaining another expected robe (*paccāsā-cīvara*) within the time limit may it be made. Furthermore, that expected robe should be determined as a requisite cloth (*parikkhāra-coḷa*).
Now, if the original robe (*mūla-cīvara*) is coarse and the expected robe is fine, [one may proceed accordingly].
Having determined the basic robe as a requisite cloth, one should set aside the expected robe itself as the basic robe.
That [expected robe] again receives the one-month grace period; by this method, it is permissible to set aside successive robes as basic robes for as long as one wishes. The rest is self-evident.
The origins and other details are exactly the same as those for the first *kathina* rule.
The commentary on the third *kathina* training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Old Robes (*purāṇacīvara*).
503–5. “At that time” refers to the training rule concerning old robes (*purāṇacīvara-sikkhāpada*). In this context, “as far as the seventh generation of ancestors” means:

the father’s father is the grandfather; the generation of the grandfather is the “grandfather-generation. “Generation” (*yuga*) is a term for the measure of a lifespan. This is merely a matter of verbal expression;
however, in terms of actual meaning, the grandfather himself is the “grandfather-generation. Beyond that, all [subsequent generations] are included.

The ancestors are included by the mention of the grandfather alone. Thus, up to the seventh person, that which is unconnected is called "unconnected for up to seven generations of grandfathers. This is merely a way of presenting the teaching;

however, because of the statement, "whether from the mother's side or the father's side," this includes the paternal grandfather’s generation, the paternal grandmother’s generation, the maternal grandfather’s generation, and the maternal grandmother’s generation.
It should be understood that their brothers, sisters, nephews, sons, grandsons, and so forth, are all included here.
In this regard, the detailed method is as follows: father, paternal grandfather, his father, and his father as well—thus up to the seventh generation;
and father, paternal grandmother, her father and mother, brother, sister, sons, and daughters.

In this way, both upwards and downwards as far as the seventh generation—father, paternal uncle, paternal aunt, paternal sons, and paternal daughters, along with their successive sons and daughters—in this way as far as the seventh generation;
mother, maternal grandmother, her mother, and her mother also—in this way as far as the seventh generation; mother, maternal grandfather, his mother and father, and [his] brother.
And [her] sister, sons, and daughters— likewise, upwards and downwards as far as the seventh generation: mother, mother’s brother, mother’s sister, mother’s sons, and mother’s daughters,

and even the succession of their sons and daughters— as far as the seventh generation— if one is not related by either maternal or paternal connection, she is called "one who is not a kinswoman" (aññātikā).

"From both Saṅghas" means she is fully ordained by a formal legal act (*vinayakamma*) consisting of eight proclamations—namely, by a motion followed by the fourth proclamation in the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha and by a motion followed by the fourth proclamation in the Bhikkhu-saṅgha.
"Even though once wrapped and once covered" means that after dyeing it and making it permissible, she has worn it or covered herself with it even once.
At the very least, she has traveled along a road having placed it on her shoulder or on her head as a mere token of its use.
Or if one lies down having made it a pillow, this too is merely an old robe.

However, if one lies down having placed it beneath a bedspread, or if one lifts it with the hands and carries it through the air like a canopy without touching it with the head, this is not called "use" (paribhoga); so it is stated in the *Kurundi*.
"Regarding 'washed and forfeitable' (*dhotaṃ nissaggiyaṃ*): here, when thus commanded, the nun prepares the hearth for the purpose of washing, gathers wood, makes a fire, and brings water;

as long as she has not yet washed it and set it aside, for every single act of effort on her part, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the monk. At the very moment she has washed it and set it aside, it is forfeitable."

It occurs thus. If, thinking it is not well-washed, she sprinkles or washes it again, then for every such act until the process reaches its conclusion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This same principle applies to dyeing and beating [the cloth].
For after having poured dye into a dye-vat, whatever one does for the purpose of dyeing prior to the first time the robe is dyed, or if one subsequently re-dyes it, [there is an offense].
In every instance of such action, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the monk. The same application of the rule should be understood regarding the act of beating [the robe].

506. If a monk causes an unrelated woman—who he perceives as unrelated—to wash an old robe, even if he does not say, "Wash this," but rather makes a physical gesture for the purpose of washing, or gives it from hand to hand, or places it at her feet;

If she throws it upward, or sends it into the hands of a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*), a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*), a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*), a lay follower (*upāsaka*), or a member of another sect (*titthiya*), or if she throws it into the vicinity of one who is washing at a river crossing—provided she stands within a space of twelve cubits—it is considered as having been washed by her.
However, if she places it outside the vicinity and she brings it back after having washed it herself, there is no offense. [The same applies for] a trainee nun.

If she gives it into the hand of a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*), a female lay follower (*upāsikā*), or anyone else for the purpose of washing, and she washes it after having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), there is indeed an offense.

If she gives it into the hand of a male lay follower (*upāsaka*), and he, having changed his gender, goes forth among the nuns and receives full ordination and then washes it, there is indeed an offense.
The same principle applies even when it has been given into the hand of a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*) or a fully ordained monk (*bhikkhu*), provided there is a change of gender.
In such cases as "has it washed" or "has it dyed," there is a *nissaggiya* offense for the first item and a *dukkaṭa* offense for the second.
For one who has three items made, there is a *nissaggiya* offense for the first and two *dukkaṭas* for the remaining ones.
Since there is no exemption for one who has these acts of washing and so forth performed either in sequence or out of sequence, three sets of four are stated here. Even if...

For if it is said, "Having dyed this robe-cloth and washed it, bring it," and that bhikkhunī first washes it and afterwards dyes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the offense of relinquishment (nissaggiya).
This same principle should be applied to all instances of inverted instructions.
However, if she is told, "Having washed it, bring it," and she both washes and dyes it, there is an offense only on account of having it washed.

There is no offense in dyeing. In all such cases, when performing more than what was prescribed, it should be understood that there is no offense by the criterion of "she washes what was not told [to do].
However, one who says, "Whatever must be done with this robe-cloth, all of that is your responsibility," incurs several offenses with a single utterance.
"Being uncertain whether she is unrelated, yet perceiving her as related to one who is unrelated"—these phrases should also be understood in detail by way of the three tetrads already mentioned.

Regarding "one who has received full ordination from one side": for one who causes [a robe] to be washed by a woman who has received full ordination in the presence of the nuns, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

However, for one who has received full ordination in the presence of the monks, it is according to the specific basis [of the offense]; that is, for one who has received full ordination in the presence of the monks...
There were five hundred Sākiyan women by name.

507. "Washes without being told" means that when she sees a soiled robe—whether they have come for instruction or for exhortation—she takes it from where it was placed, or causes it to be brought back, saying, "Give it here, Noble Lady, I will wash it," and then she both washes, dyes, and beats it.

And this is what is called "washing without being told": when a monk, having heard a junior monk or a novice being commanded, "Wash this robe," says, "Bring it, venerable sir, I will wash it," and then washes it;
or when he takes it on loan, washes it, dyes it, and returns it—this too is called "washing without being told."

"Another requisite" refers to sandals, bags for robes, bags for bowls, shoulder-straps, waist-bands, beds, stools, needle-cases, and so forth; if one has any such thing washed, there is no offense. The rest here is of obvious meaning.

Regarding the origin and other factors: this training rule has six origins, is an action, is not liberated by perception, is without [evil] intention, is an offense of formal prescription, is bodily action and verbal action, consists of three types of consciousness, and consists of three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning old robes is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Acceptance of Robes (Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpada) 508. "At that time" refers to the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes.

In this context, "having returned from almsround" means having come back from the almsround. "She approached the Blind Men’s Grove" means that, while the training rule had not yet been laid down, she went toward the Blind Men’s Grove.
He approached her. "One who has committed a deed" means one who has performed acts of theft; it is said that he had carried away the property of others by means of breaking into walls and so forth.
"The village headman of the thieves" refers to the chief of the bandits. It is said that he had known the Elder Nun previously;
therefore, seeing her as he was walking in front of the thieves, he said, "Do not go this way! All of you come this way! and having seized them, [he led them] by another path.
...he arrived. "Having emerged from concentration" means that the elder nun, it is said, emerged from concentration at the very time she had predetermined.
He too spoke thus at that very moment; therefore she heard him.
Having heard it, she thought, "Now there is no other ascetic or brahmin here besides myself," and she took that meat. Hence it was said: "Then..."
“The nun Uppalavaṇṇā,” and so forth.
*Ohiyyako* means one who is left behind or remaining; the meaning is that having reached the turn for the monastery, he was the only one remaining in the dwelling.
Why did he say, “If you would give me your inner robe (*antaravāsaka*)”? It was because he saw that the inner robe was soft, thick, and smooth.

Out of greed; moreover, her greed for that inner garment was slight, but the Elder Nun, having developed improper greed with the thought, "I shall see the perfection of her body, for she has reached the pinnacle of excellence in her physical proportions," spoke thus.
"The last" (*antima*) means it is the final limit among the five types of robes; it is the last, meaning the final one. Having made another [robe] even by way of a mere pretext...

Or, having set it aside, there is no robe remaining; thus he spoke by way of wearing the five types of robes as they have been permitted, not out of greed—for there is no greed in those whose taints are destroyed.
"Being pressed" means pressing firmly, showing this by means of a simile.
"Having given him an inner robe, she went to her dwelling" means that, having put on her bodice, she went away showing only the palm of her hand so that his desire was not fulfilled.

Why did they complain to her when she would not accept the robe in exchange? Because they were distressed by their state of destitution, thinking, "If even this much trust from the noble ladies is not placed in us, how shall we survive?"
"I allow you, monks, for these five" means: "I allow you to take [robes] by exchange with these five who share the same Dhamma, who have equal faith, equal virtue, and equal view.

512. "In the attempt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means: an offense of wrong-doing occurs in acts such as stretching out the hand for the purpose of taking [the robe]. "By acquisition" means: by way of receiving it.
And in that case, whether he gives it hand-to-hand, or places it at the base of one's feet, or hurls it overhead—if one consents to it...

It is indeed considered accepted. However, if one accepts [robes] that have been sent into the hands of a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), a novice monk (sāmaṇera), a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), a male lay follower (upāsaka), a female lay follower (upāsikā), or others, there is no offense.

When one is preaching the Dhamma, the fourfold assembly may bring robes and garments of various colors and place them at the feet [of the preacher], or stand within reach and throw them [there], or release them from within reach—whatever [is thus offered].
In that case, if one takes what belongs to the nuns except by way of exchange, there is indeed an offense for the one taking it.
However, if they have been discarded during the night and it is impossible to know, "This belongs to a nun; this belongs to others," there is no need for an exchange;
thus it is stated in the Mahāpaccarī and the Kurundi. This is because [the act] is devoid of intentional thought (*acittaka*).
It does not agree. If a bhikkhunī gives a *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe), it must be exchanged.
However, if she places it on a rubbish heap or similar location, thinking, "They will take it as rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*)," it is permissible to take it after resolving it as a rag-robe.

513. Regarding "one who is unrelated and perceives her as unrelated": this constitutes a *pācittiya* offense for each of the three permutations. "From one fully ordained together with oneself" refers to bhikkhunīs.
For one who receives [an item] from the hand of a person ordained in the presence [of the Saṅgha], it is a dukkaṭa; however, for one ordained in the presence of monks, it is indeed a pācittiya.

514. Regarding "the small for the large": if, having caused a costly robe to be bartered for a cheap robe—whether by means of a robe of little value, or by means of sandals, a needle-case, a bowl-bag, a shoulder-strap, a waist-band, and so forth—even if he accepts the robe, there is no offense. However, in the Mahāpaccarī...
“It is said: ‘even with a single piece of *harītakī*. Or, “the small by means of the abundant”—this should be understood as a reversal of what was previously stated.

Regarding “any other requisite”: this refers to items such as a bowl-bag and so forth; however, anything that falls short of the minimum size for a robe permitted for distribution—even a cloth or a water-strainer—is not allowed.
That which is neither fit for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) nor fit for distribution is...

Everything is permissible. Even if the lotus skin is the size of a bed, it is still permissible; what need then to mention cases such as bags for alms bowls? The rest is self-evident. Regarding the origin and other factors:

this offense has six origins; it is both an act and a non-act; it is not released by mere recognition; it is without mental consciousness; it is an offense of formal rule (paṇṇatti-vajja); it consists of bodily and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning requesting from one who is not related. 515.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning requesting from one who is not related. In this context, "Upananda the son of the Sakyans" [was among] approximately eighty thousand [monks].
Among the monks who have gone forth from the Sakyan clan, he is of a base character and fickle.
"A speaker" means one who is clever, capable, competent, endowed with a fine voice, and possessed of sweetness of throat. "Like what? means like what? Like defilement;
the meaning is that it is like trembling and shaking by way of moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*).
“On a long journey” means a long road reckoned as a journey, not a city street; this is the meaning. “They cut them off” means they plundered them;
the meaning is that they took away their bowls and robes. “Inquire” means ask for the purpose of knowing whether they are monks.
“Being questioned” means being asked about their going forth, full ordination, the formal determination of their bowl and robes, and so forth.
“They reported this matter” means: having made themselves known as monks, they reported this matter in the manner stated beginning with, “We are traveling on the highway from Sāketa to Sāvatthī.
517. Regarding the phrases “an unrelated householder,” etc., that which follows—“having covered it with grass or leaves”—[is what is meant].
This has been stated; beginning from that point, the gradual discourse should be understood as follows.

If, upon seeing the thieves, the young monks flee after seizing their bowls and robes, and the thieves depart taking only the undergarments and upper robes of the elders, then the elders must not yet request robes, nor should they break off branches and foliage. But when the young monks [have returned] with everything...
Having abandoned their belongings, they fled; the thieves took the robes and the belongings of the elders and departed.
The young monks, having returned, must not yet give their own robes and undergarments to the elders.
For those whose robes have not been stolen are not permitted to break off branches and foliage for their own use. [This applies] to those whose robes have been stolen.
However, they may obtain [robes] for the sake of others; even when their own robes have been stolen, they may obtain them for the sake of themselves or others.

Therefore, the elders should either break off branches and foliage and tie them together with grass and such to give to the juniors, or the juniors should break off and tie together [branches] for the sake of the elders—either by placing them in their hands or without placing them there—and then wear them themselves.
One's own lower and upper robes should be given to the elders; in that case, there is no offense of expiation for destroying living plants, nor is there an offense of wrong-doing for their wearing.
If, however, on the way there is a dyer’s cloth or one sees other such people, [one should leave] the robe...
It should be requested. And as for those robes which they, or the people who have been requested by them, or others, having seen monks dwelling among the branches and foliage,
give out of their own initiative— whether they have fringes or are fringless, whether they are various colors such as blue and so forth, and whether they are allowable or unallowable— all of these,
because they stand in the place of a robe that has not been cut [from a loom], may be worn by them as undergarments.
And it is permissible to wear them. This too has been said in the Parivāra:
“Even that which is not made allowable, nor dyed with a dye, one who is clothed in such may go wherever he wishes.”
There is no offense for him;
that Dhamma was taught by the Sugata.
This question has been pondered by those skilled in wholesome qualities.
For this question was stated with reference to a monk whose robe had been stolen.

However, if they go together with members of other sects (titthiya), and they give them robes made of kusa grass, bark, or wood-shavings, it is permissible to wear them even without adopting their tenets;
yet, once worn, one must not adopt those tenets.
Now, regarding the phrase "whatever dwelling he first enters, if there is there a *vihāracīvara* belonging to the Saṅgha," and so forth:

a *vihāracīvara* is a set of three robes that people, having built a dwelling, prepare and place within the dwelling they themselves have constructed, thinking, "May all four requisites remain as our own property for our use."
This is what is called "monastery robe" (*vihāracīvara*). "Upper covering" (*uttarattharaṇa*) refers to that which is spread over a bedstead.
"Ground-covering" (*bhūmattharaṇa*) is a mat made of felt-wool (*cimilika*) used for the protection of the prepared ground;
having spread a wooden plank upon it, one walks back and forth. "Cushion-skin" (*bhisicchavi*) refers to either a cushion for a bedstead or a cushion for a chair.
Or the skin; if it is full, it is permissible to take it even after shaking it out.

Thus, among these items such as monastery-robes and so forth, whatever is there in the dwelling, it should be understood that monks whose robes have been lost are permitted to take it and wear it as an inner robe or an upper robe, even without asking permission.
However, having obtained it, they must think: "I will put it away and return it again."

This is done with the underlying intention [of preservation], not for the sake of cutting off the root. Once it has been obtained, however, one must restore it to its original state from relatives, attendants, or anyone else from whom it was received.
If one has gone abroad, it should be deposited in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha for the purpose of being used as property belonging to the Saṅgha.
If, through that very use, it becomes worn out or lost, there is liability for compensation.
