It does not exist. However, if nothing is obtained from these aforementioned items for householders, such as robes and so forth, ending with a skin of a water-snake, one may come after covering oneself with grass or leaves.
519. Regarding the phrase "or by anyone who has not cut [the robe]," here, even if the preceptor and teacher have their robes cut, others [should say], "Bring them."
It is appropriate to say that even when one takes a robe after having requested it, saying “Friend, this robe [is for you],” or by way of trust, it is included in the category of *saṅgaha*.

Regarding the phrase “or worn out through use,” it is also appropriate to say here that even a robe given by oneself—having covered it with grass and leaves—to teachers, preceptors, and others who have lost their robes, is included in the category of *saṅgaha*. For in this way, they [the recipients] stand in the place of those whose robes were stolen.
And they will be standing in the place where robes were lost; therefore, there will be no offense for them in making a request or in using an unallowable robe, as it will be appropriate. 521.
Regarding the phrase "those invited by relatives": here, it refers to one who requests or asks, saying, "Give what belongs to these [relatives]."
"Non-offense" (anāpatti) should be understood in this sense. For there is neither offense nor non-offense for those who have been invited by their relatives.

Regarding the phrase "with one's own wealth," here too the meaning should be understood as follows: there is no offense for one who requests, causes to be purchased, or exchanges a robe using one's own allowable goods and in accordance with allowable terminology. Regarding the term "those who have been invited" (pavāritānaṃ): [here...]
When invitations are made by way of the Saṅgha, it is permissible [to request] only the standard measure.
In an invitation made by an individual, one may ask for whatever that person invites.

For one who, having invited according to the four requisites, observes for himself and gives from time to time—whether robes, or daily portions of gruel and food—whatever is needed, there is no further need for him to make a formal request.
There is no offense. However, if one who has invited [others] does not give because of foolishness or through loss of mindfulness, he should be made to understand.
If someone says, "I invite you to my house," one should go to his house and sit or lie down as one pleases, but nothing should be taken.
But if someone says, "Whatever is in my house, that I invite you to," [one may take it].
He speaks. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Kurundi* that one may request whatever is allowable there, but it is not permitted to sit or lie down in a house.
As for the phrase "for the sake of another," here it means that when invited by one's own relatives, it is not only for one's own sake, but indeed for the sake of another.
“There is no offense for one who makes a request on behalf of another”: this is one meaning. This, however, is the second:

“on behalf of another” means that there is no offense for one who makes a request on behalf of someone else—such as one known by the designation “another,” like Buddharakkhita or Dhammarakkhita—who has been invited by his own relatives. The rest is self-evident.

Regarding its origin and other characteristics: this too has six origins; it is an action; it is not a liberation through perception; it is mindless; it is an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*); it consists of bodily and vocal action; it involves three types of consciousness; and it involves three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning requesting from one who is unrelated is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Excess.
522–4. *Tena samayena* means: this is the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) that follows. Therein, *abhihaṭṭhuṃ*: *abhi-* is a prefix;
*harituṃ* is the meaning, which is to say, "to take. *Pavāreyya*: one should cause [the other] to desire; one should arouse a wish or a preference;
the meaning is "one should speak" or "one should invite. Now, as for the manner in which one who invites by bringing [food] should speak, that form [is as follows]:
To demonstrate this, the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) was stated for him as: "Take as much as you wish.

Alternatively, just as in the phrase "having seen renunciation as safety" (*nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato*), the meaning is "having seen" (*disvā*), so too here, "he should invite after having brought forth" (*abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyā*) means "he should invite after having brought forward" (*abhiharitvā*).
In that regard, there are two kinds: bringing by body (*kāyābhihāra*) and bringing by speech (*vācābhihāra*).
"Bringing forth" (*abhihāra*) means: either by physically bringing robes and placing them at the feet [of the recipient] while saying, "Take as much as you wish," one invites [the other];
or by speaking with words, saying, "Our storehouse of cloth is full;
take as much as you wish," one invites. Combining both of these together is called "bringing forth."
"one should invite [the donor to choose]," it is said.
"With the inner and outer robes as the maximum" (*santaruttaraparamaṃ*) means that for this robe, the inner and outer robes are the limit;
what is meant is that the upper robe together with the lower robe constitutes the highest permissible extent. Beyond that, the robe—
“Sāditabbaṃ” means that from the robe brought from there, only this much robe should be accepted, and not more than this; such is the meaning.

However, since a monk who possesses a complete set of robes and is already wearing the three robes must practice in this way, whereas another may do so differently, the following is stated in order to show that distinction: “If three [robes] have been lost,” and so forth.
The explanation of the terms has been stated.
Herein is the analysis: he whose three [robes] are lost must accept two;
having dressed in one and wrapped himself in another, he will seek a replacement from a suitable place. He whose two are lost must accept one.
If she goes about in her ordinary attire consisting of an inner and outer robe, two [robes] may be accepted. In this way, by accepting one [robe], she will become equal [to those who have three].
For one who has lost one of the three, none should be accepted. But for one who has lost one of the two, one may be accepted.
For one who possesses only one and that too is lost, two may be accepted. [This applies to] a bhikkhunī.
However, even when all five are lost, two may be accepted. When four are lost, one may be accepted;
when three are lost, nothing at all may be accepted—let alone when two or one are lost. For one must remain with at most an inner and outer garment;
beyond that, nothing more is permitted. This is the defining characteristic here.

526. “I will bring the remainder” means: having made two robes, [he thinks] “I will bring the remainder again. “Not because of being cut off” means they give out of virtue such as great learning (*bāhusacca*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrases beginning with “from relatives,” the meaning is that there is no offense for one who consents when relatives are giving, for one who consents when those who have been invited (*pavārita*) are giving, or for one who consents by means of his own wealth. In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*),...
However, it has been stated that "in a place where one has been invited by relatives, even a large amount is permissible;

only a measured amount is permissible when there is no reason for cutting down. This does not accord with the Pāḷi. Since this training rule was laid down specifically regarding the case of requesting for the sake of another, therefore the phrase "for the sake of another" is not mentioned here. The rest is self-evident.

Regarding the origins and other characteristics: this [offense] also has six origins; it is an action (*kiriya*); it is not a liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*); it is without thought (*acittaka*); it is an offense by rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*); it consists of bodily and verbal action (*kāya-kamma* and *vacī-kamma*); it involves three types of consciousness (*ti-citta*); and it involves three types of feeling (*ti-vedana*).
The commentary on the subsequent training rules is finished. 8.
Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Set Aside (*Paṭhama-upakkhaṭa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā*).
527. "At that time" refers to the training rule concerning what has been prepared (*upakkhaṭasikkhāpada*). Regarding this, "Is there, friend, such a supporter for me as you say?
means, "Friend, is there such a person who is my supporter?"—this is the meaning here.
"It occurs to me too, noble lady, that it is so" means, "It occurs to me too, noble lady, that it is so"; *api mayyā evam* is also a reading.
528–9. Regarding the phrase "having designated a bhikkhu" (*bhikkhuṃ paneva uddissa*): here, "designated" (*uddissa*) means having pointed out or having taken as a basis.

Furthermore, since that which is prepared for the sake of someone is said to be "prepared for his benefit," it is therefore stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "for the sake of a bhikkhu."
“Making a bhikkhu the object” means making a bhikkhu the condition (*paccaya*).
For whatever is prepared specifically for a bhikkhu is necessarily prepared by making that bhikkhu the condition; therefore it is said, “making a bhikkhu the object.
Indeed, even a condition is referred to as an “object” in such passages as, “Māra obtains an object,” and so forth. Now...
Regarding the word “uddissa”: in this context, it is stated “desirous of clothing a bhikkhu” in order to show the manner of the agent.
For that [agent] has prepared it specifically for that bhikkhu, and not for any other reason; thus he is one who desires to clothe him.
Therefore it is said: “desirous of clothing a bhikkhu.”
"Of an unrelated householder" means "by an unrelated householder"; for this is a genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental.
However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), in order to show merely the meaning without analyzing the phrasing, it is said:
"An unrelated person is called... a householder is called... and so forth.
"Cīvaracetāpanna" means the price for a robe; since that consists of one or another of the items such as gold and so forth, it is therefore stated in the word-commentary (padabhājana) as "gold or...
and so on. "Upakkhaṭaṃ hoti" means it is prepared, set aside, or kept in reserve;
however, its state of being prepared is demonstrated by the expression beginning with "gold or... and so forth.
Therefore, having extracted the word "prepared" (*upakkhaṭaṃ*), no separate word-commentary was given for it.
By the phrase "by this," he refers to what is prepared; for that very reason, it is stated in its word-commentary as "presented" (*paccupaṭṭhitena*).
For that which has been gathered and set aside is what is "presented. "I shall cover" is a conventional expression.
“‘I will give it to the bhikkhu named so-and-so’—this is the meaning here. For that very reason, ‘I will give’ is stated even in its word-analysis (*padabhājana*).

In that regard, ‘if that bhikkhu,’ meaning if that bhikkhu, having approached where that householder or housewife is, without being previously invited, should engage in specifying the kind of robe-cloth—this is the connection of the words here. In that context, ‘having approached’ means...”
Regarding the phrase *imassa gantvā* (“having gone to him”): although the meaning is already established by this alone, it is stated as “to his house” (*gharaṃ*) by way of common usage.
However, the actual meaning here is “having gone to where that donor is”; therefore, it is further stated, “having approached anyone whatsoever.
*Vikappaṃ āpajjeyyā* means he would enter upon a special mode, an additional specification; [this is explained] in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
However, in order to show precisely the manner in which [the mind] has undergone conceptualization (*vikappa*), the words "long" (*āyataṃ*) and so forth were spoken.
*Sādhu* is a particle used for making a request. *Vata* is used in the sense of reflection (*parivitakka*). *Maṃ* refers to oneself. *Āyasmā* is used to address or call out to another.
Since all of this is merely a matter of phrasing and its meaning is already evident, therefore, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) of this...
The meaning has not been stated. "Having taken up the desire for what is beautiful" means having grasped with the mind the desire for what is lovely, the desire for what is distinguished;

this is connected with the phrase "if he should incur [an offense]. However, because one who incurs [an offense] out of a desire for what is beautiful is one who seeks a good purpose and a great value, therefore, in the word-commentary (padabhājana), setting aside the literal phrasing—

That very statement was spoken in order to demonstrate the intended meaning. However, since the offense does not reach its head merely by one’s own undertaking of it, the words "by his word," and so forth, were spoken. 531.
Regarding the phrase "there is no offense for [those who act] for kinsmen" and so on: there is no offense for one who effects the distribution of a robe for kinsmen.

The meaning should be understood in this way: "If one who wishes to have something of great value purchased obtains something of little value," means that if a householder wishes to have a robe worth twenty [units] purchased, and [the agent] says, "That is enough for me;
give me one worth ten or eight instead," there is no offense.
Furthermore, the phrase "something of little value" is stated solely for the purpose of prohibiting an excess; however, it applies even in the case of an equivalent [value].
There is no offense, but that is only by way of value, not by way of measurement; for this training rule concerns an increase in value.
Therefore, one who wishes to have an inner robe worth twenty [units] made may also say, "Give me a robe worth exactly that much. The rest is self-evident.
The origins and other details are also exactly like those of the preceding training rule.
The commentary on the first *upakkhaṭa* training rule is finished.
9. Commentary on the second *upakkhaṭa* training rule.
532. In the second case involving what has been brought, the meaning should be understood by this same method. For that is similar to a subsequent rule (anupaññatti).
The only difference here is that in the first training rule, harm was done to one person, whereas in the second, it was done to two;
everything else is exactly like the first. And just as with two people, so too should the offense be understood for one who takes [the goods] after having harmed many.
The commentary on the second *Upakkhaṭa* training rule is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Rāja* training rule: 537.
"At that time" refers to the *Rāja* training rule. Therein, "having informed the lay follower" means having made him know; "by this... [text continues].
The intention [of the phrase] "having bought a robe with the root-coin (mūla), give it to the elder" is as follows.
"A fine of fifty" means a penalty of fifty kahāpaṇas; this is what is stated. There is also a reading, "bound by fifty," which means that having been defeated by fifty, he must be made to pay fifty.
"Venerable sir, wait until tomorrow" means: Venerable sir, stay for one day today; please accept our hospitality.
"Parāmasī" means you have seized. "Jīnosī" means you have been conquered. 538–9. "Rājabhoggo":
one who desires to enjoy what is to be enjoyed from the king is a *rājabhoggo*; "rājabhogo" is also a reading, meaning "one who has enjoyment (*bhoga*) from the king. "Pahiṇeyya" means he would send;
however, because its meaning is obvious, no word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*) was given for it. And as with this, [so it is with the following].

In this way, it should be understood that the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*) for phrases such as "the robe [for] the monk named so-and-so" was not stated precisely because their meaning is already obvious.
"Brought" (*ābhataṃ*) means carried there. "At the proper time, what is allowable" (*kālena kappiyaṃ*) means at the appropriate and suitable time;
the sense is: "when we have need of it, then we shall take the allowable robe."
*Veyyāvaccakara* means one who performs services; the meaning is "one who does what is allowable" (*kappiyakāraka*). *Saññatto so mayam* means he has been instructed by me;
the meaning is that he has been told, "In such a way that, when you have need of a robe, he will give you a robe.
"I have need of a robe, friend" is an indication of the characteristic of the formal request (*codanālakkhaṇa*); for these words must be spoken, or else...

The meaning may be expressed in any language whatsoever; this is the characteristic of a formal charge (*codanālakkhaṇa*). However, such expressions as "Give me a robe" and so forth are stated for the purpose of showing forms that are not to be used;
for these words, or their meaning, are not to be expressed in any language whatsoever.
As for the second and third times, one should say: "Friend, I have need of a robe"—this alone is to be said up to the third time.

"It should be said. Having thus shown the limit of the urging prescribed in the passage, "He should be urged and reminded two or three times," [the author] now shows, in brief, the meaning of these words: "If, while urging and reminding two or three times, he should cause that robe to be produced, this is good," by saying: "If he produces it..."

"It is well," he said. Thus, if while being urged up to three times he brings that robe-cloth to completion—meaning he is able to bring it to completion for his own acquisition—"it is well" means it is good, excellent, and beautiful.
"He should stand silently, designated [for him], at most four, five, or six times" is the indication of the characteristic of standing.
“*Chakkhattuparaman* (at most six times) is a neuter noun in the locative case;
for by this [rule], one must stand silently with the robe in mind for at most six times, and nothing else should be done—this is the characteristic of standing.
Therein, first, in order to show the silence which is common to all instances of standing, the word-commentary says: ‘Having gone there...’”
"By remaining silent," and so forth, was said. In that context: "One should not sit on a seat" means that one should not sit even when addressed with the words, "Venerable sir, please sit here.

"One should not accept material gifts" means that one should not accept any kind of material gift—such as varieties of rice gruel or solid food—even when requested with the words, "Venerable sir, please take this. "One should not speak the Dhamma" means...
Even when requested, "Please speak words of auspiciousness or approval," one should not say anything at all;
however, when asked, "For what reason have you come? one should simply say, "You know, friend. Regarding the term "pucchiyamāno" (being asked):
this is a nominative singular form used in the sense of the instrumental case. Alternatively, it can be understood here as "one who is making a question is being asked."

The meaning should be understood as follows: for whoever asks a question, he breaks the ground—that is, he destroys the reason for the matter being brought forward by saying, "Only this much should be said.
Now, regarding the three censures and the six grounds that have been mentioned, the text says, "Having censured four times," and so forth, in order to show the increase and decrease therein.
And because, in this context, with the increase of one censure, there is an increase of two grounds...
The loss has been stated; therefore, the characteristic is shown by the rule: “One admonition is two-fold standing.
Thus, by this characteristic, having admonished three times, one must stand six times; having admonished twice, one must stand eight times;
and having admonished once, one must stand ten times. And just as “having admonished six times... [the rest follows].
It has been stated, "one should not stand [in silence]"; likewise, it follows that it has also been stated, "having stood twelve times, one should not accuse.
Therefore, if one only accuses and does not stand, six accusations are obtained.
If one only stands and does not accuse, twelve instances of standing are obtained. If one both accuses and stands, then for each accusation there are two...
There are points that must be forfeited. In this regard, one who goes back again and again on a single day and urges [the donor] six times;
or one who goes only once and says, "I have need of a robe, friend," six times.
Likewise, one who goes back again and again on a single day and stands twelve times; or one who goes only once and stands in various places there.
Even he who remains [in the Saṅgha] destroys all accusations and all grounds [for them]. What need is there to mention one who acts thus over many days?
In this matter, such is the legal decision (*vinicchaya*) to be understood.
Regarding the phrase "from whom the robe-fund has been brought for him": from whichever king or royal official it was brought for that bhikkhu...
“The robe-fund has been brought. *Yatvassā* is also a reading; it has this same meaning.
They also read *yatthassā*, explaining the sense as: “in whatever place that robe-fund was sent”; however, the phrasing does not agree [with the grammar].
*Tattha* means “in the presence of that king or royal official”; for this locative expression is used in the sense of proximity.
"It brings no benefit whatsoever to that bhikkhu" means that those robe-funds do not accomplish even the slightest purpose for that bhikkhu.
"Venerable sirs, apply yourselves to what is your own" means: may the venerable ones obtain their own property;
"let not what is yours go to waste" means: let not your own property be lost.
But he who neither goes himself nor sends a messenger incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for a breach of the rule.
However, should one proceed in this same manner toward all those who provide what is allowable (*kappiyakāraka*)? One should not so proceed.
For this person known as a "provider of what is allowable" is briefly explained to be of two kinds: the designated (*niddiṭṭha*) and the non-designated (*aniddiṭṭha*). Among these, the designated...
It is twofold: designated by a bhikkhu and designated by a messenger. That which is not designated is also twofold:

one who makes it allowable in the presence [of the owner] and one who makes it allowable in the absence [of the owner]. Among these, that which is designated by a bhikkhu is fourfold, according to whether it is done in the presence or in the absence [of the owner].
Likewise, that which is designated by a messenger is also fourfold.
How so? Here, someone sends an improper article to a monk for the sake of robe-cloth by means of a messenger.
The messenger approaches that monk and says, "Venerable sir, this was sent for you for the sake of robe-cloth by such-and-such a person;
please accept it. The monk refuses, saying, "This is not allowable. The messenger says, "But is there..."
“Venerable sir, those are the service-providers,” he asks; or they have been instructed by lay followers seeking merit to “perform services for the monks”;
or there are certain service-providers who are friends or associates of the monks;
one of them is sitting near the monk at that moment, and the monk points him out.
“This man is the attendant for the monks. Having placed an unallowable object in his hand, the messenger departs with the instruction, “Buy a robe for the Elder and give it to him”;
this is one designated by the monk in his presence. If he is not sitting near the monk, yet the monk designates him—“In such-and-such a place...”

“Such-and-such a person in the village is the attendant for the monks. Having gone there, he gives an improper article into that person's hand and says, “Please buy a robe for the Elder and give it to him,” and having returned, he informs the monk and departs;
this is one case where the person has not been designated in the presence of the monk.
Not only does that messenger, having come himself, announce it; rather, he sends another, saying:
"Venerable sir, I have given the robe-fund into his hand; you should accept the robe. This is the second case of one not designated in the absence [of the recipient] by a monk.
Not only does he send another, but while going himself, he says to the monk: "I [have given it] into his hand..."
“I will give you the price for robes; you may take the robe”—this is the third case of one who has been designated by a monk without being present.
Thus, there are four types of persons designated as service-providers by a monk: one designated in their presence and three designated in their absence.
Regarding these, one should proceed according to the method stated in this training rule concerning kings.

Another monk, having been questioned by a messenger in the same manner as before, either because there was no one present or because he did not wish to investigate, says, "We have no one to act as a kappiyakāraka. At that moment, a certain person arrives;
the messenger gives the unallowable article into that person's hand and says, "You may take the robe from this man's hand."
He goes; this is one who is designated in person by means of a messenger.

Another messenger, having entered the village, gives an improper object into the hand of someone he chooses and returns in the same manner as before to report it, or he sends another, saying: "I [have given] the price for a robe into the hand of such-and-such a person."
If he says, "I will give it; you may take the robe," and then departs, this is the third case of one designated by messenger who is not designated in person.
Thus, there is one designated in person and three designated not in person; these four are called "messengers-designated attendants.
Regarding them, one should proceed according to the method stated in the Meṇḍaka-sikkhāpada. For this has been said: "There are..."
“Monks, there are people who have faith and confidence; they place gold in the hands of those who prepare what is allowable, saying:
‘With this, give whatever is allowable to the noble one.
Monks, I allow you to accept from that whatever is allowable, but by no means, monks, should gold or silver be accepted in any way whatsoever.”
"I say it must be sought out. In this matter, there is no limit to the number of times one may be urged;

even if the owner does not give it up, it is permissible for one who has not accepted the purchase price to accept a suitable article (kappiyabhaṇḍa) through being urged or by means of a formal standing.
If he still does not give it, it should be brought back even by appointing another steward (kappiyakāraka). If he so desires, it should also be told to the original owners.
If he does not wish to speak, he should not speak.
Suppose another monk, questioned by a messenger in the same manner as before, says, "We have no attendant to prepare what is allowable.
Then another person standing nearby, having heard this, says, "Bring it, sir; I will purchase a robe for the venerable one and give it to him."
If a messenger, having placed [the item] in the hand of another with the words, “Come now, sir, you should give this,” departs without informing the bhikkhu,
he is a *mukhavevaṭika-kappiyakāraka* (one who makes it permissible by mouth). Another, having placed an impermissible object in the hand of a bhikkhu’s attendant or someone else,
and departing with only the words, “You should give this robe to the Elder,” is a *parammukha-kappiyakāraka* (one who makes it permissible out of sight).
These two are called "unspecified makers of what is allowable. Regarding them, one should proceed as if they were unrelated persons who have not been invited.
If they themselves bring a robe and give it, it may be accepted. If they do not, nothing should be said to them.

This [instruction], "he should send a messenger with the means for purchasing a robe," is merely for the purpose of teaching; even if one brings it oneself, it applies to alms-food and so forth as well.
The same principle applies even when others are giving. It is not permissible to accept it only for one’s own benefit;
nor is it permissible to accept it even if someone brings gold and silver and says, "I give this to the Saṅgha;
you may use it to build a monastery, a shrine, or any of the other requisites such as a dining hall. This too is not permissible to accept. For whom...
For it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that for one who accepts [an offering] for the sake of another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
However, if, after it has been refused on the grounds that "this is not permissible for monks to accept," one says, "It will be in the hands of carpenters or laborers;
you need only know whether it is well-made or poorly made," [then there is no offense].
If he hands them over into their hands and departs, it is permissible.

Furthermore, if he says, "They shall come into the hands of my people, or they shall remain in my own hands; you need only send them as required for whomever they are to be given," even in this case it is permissible.
However, if they do not specify the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, but say, "We give this gold and silver to the cetiya;
we give it to the monastery; we give it for new construction," it is not permissible to refuse it.
One should inform the kappiyakārakas (those who handle allowable goods), saying, "These people are saying this. [One may then say: "For the sake of the cetiya and so forth, you should accept it..."
When told, "Set it aside," however, one must refuse, saying, "It is not permissible for us to accept it.
But if someone brings much gold and silver and says, "I give this to the Saṅgha;
please use it for the four requisites," and if the Saṅgha accepts it, there is an offense both in the acceptance and in the use.

In that case, if one bhikkhu rejects it, saying, "This is not allowable," and the lay follower goes away thinking, "If it is not allowable, it shall be mine alone," that bhikkhu must not be spoken to by anyone at all, saying, "You have created an obstacle to the Saṅgha’s gain.
For whoever reproves him becomes guilty of an offense; however, by that one [who refuses], [the offense is incurred].

Many instances have been rendered non-offenses. However, if monks reject it saying, "It is not permissible," and [the donor] says, "It will be in the hands of the kappiyakārakas, or in the hands of my men, or in my own hands;
you simply use these requisites," then it is permissible.
And what has been given for the purpose of the four requisites should be applied to whichever requisite is needed;

what has been given for the purpose of robes should be applied to robes themselves. If there is no such need for robes, and the Saṅgha is distressed by a lack of alms-food and so forth, it may be applied even for that purpose after obtaining the consent of the Saṅgha for the sake of its well-being. This same method applies to what is given for the purpose of alms-food and medicinal requisites.
Even when it has been given, that which was given for the purpose of lodgings must be kept at the lodging itself because it is a heavy article (garubhaṇḍa).
However, if the lodging is destroyed after the monks have abandoned it and departed, it is permitted for monks to use the lodging even after it has been relinquished at such a time;
therefore, for the sake of maintaining the lodging, [the property] may be cut off at the root.
One should consume only what is sufficient for maintenance.
Not only gold and silver, but other unallowable things such as fields and land must also not be accepted.
For if someone were to say, "I have a large tank that produces three harvests a year; I give it to the Saṅgha," [one must not accept it].
If he speaks [of it] and the Saṅgha accepts it, there is an offense both in the acceptance and in the consumption.
However, as for one who rejects it, he is not to be addressed by anyone in any way according to the previous method. For whoever accuses him becomes the one with the offense;
yet by that single person, many have been rendered free from offense.

But if one who has said, "I shall give such a pond," is refused by the monks saying, "That is not permissible," and he replies, "The Saṅgha already possesses such-and-such and such-and-such ponds; how can that be permissible? he should be told:
"It will become permissible once it has been made allowable. How does it become allowable when given? [By being designated as] the four requisites.
Having said, "Enjoy it," it is considered given. If he gives it while saying, "Excellent, Bhante; let the Saṅgha enjoy the four requisites," it is allowable.
Furthermore, if after saying, "Take the pond," he is refused with "It is not allowable," and one asks, "Is there a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable)?
and upon being told "There is none," [he says], "So-and-so by name will manage this, or it is in the hand of so-and-so..."
If he says, "It shall be in my hand; let the Saṅgha enjoy the allowable goods," it is permissible.

Even if he has been refused on the grounds that "it is not permissible," if he says, "They will drink the water, they will wash the goods, or wild animals and birds will drink [from it]," even then it is permissible.
Furthermore, even if he has been refused on the grounds that "it is not permissible"…

He says, "Take it under the pretext that it is allowable. Having said, "Very well, lay follower, the Saṅgha will drink the water, the Saṅgha will wash its requisites, and the wild animals and birds will drink," it is permissible to use it.
Furthermore, if he says, "I give my pond or lotus-pool to the Saṅgha," [and the other replies], "Very well, lay follower..."
It is indeed permissible to use [water] after saying, "The Saṅgha will drink this water," and so forth. However, if a pond has been constructed by monks for the purpose of using water—
either by requesting manual labor from others or by digging the earth themselves with their own hands—
and people, having produced a crop by depending on that [pond], provide articles for the monastery's use...

[If] they give [the produce], it is permissible. Furthermore, if people themselves, for the sake of assisting the Saṅgha, dig up land belonging to the Saṅgha and give allowable goods from the crops produced in dependence upon that [land], it is likewise permissible.
And if they say, "Appoint one of us as a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable)," it is also permitted to appoint one. However, if those people [are forced] by royal tax...

If they depart because they are harassed, or if others take over [the land], and they give nothing to the monks, it is permitted to block them from water—but only during the time for plowing, not during the time for harvesting.
If they say, "Venerable sir, have not people in the past also cultivated crops depending on this [water]? then they should be told: "They [did so] for the sake of the Saṅgha."
“They have rendered this service and given these various allowable goods. If they say, “We too shall give,” this is also permissible.
However, if anyone who is incompetent accepts a pond or has one constructed using unallowable terminology, the monks [should address him].
It must not be used; even a permissible article obtained by depending upon it is indeed impermissible.

However, if the owner, or his sons or daughters, or someone else born into the lineage, having learned that it has been relinquished by the monks, gives it again using permissible terminology, it is allowable. If the family lineage has been extinguished, whoever is the owner of that district [may take it].
If one takes it back after having seized it and gives it again— just as the chief queen of King Aḷanāga gave back the water-carrier that had been carried away by a monk on Cittalapabbata—
it is likewise permissible.

Even in the case of allowable transactions (*kappiya-vohāra*), for those with pure minds, activities such as digging up clay or binding embankments are permitted in a pond that has been accepted for the sake of water.
And it is permissible to do so. However, seeing those who cultivate crops depending on that [water], it is not permissible to appoint a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable).
If they themselves give allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*), they may be accepted. If they do not give them, one must neither urge nor remind them.
It is permissible to appoint a *kappiyakāraka* for a tank that has been accepted as a requisite. [This applies to] the digging out of clay, the binding of embankments, and so forth.
However, it is not permissible to do so [oneself]. If the kappiyakārakas (those who prepare what is allowable) do it themselves, it is permissible.

But when things are caused to be made by an unskilled yet conscientious bhikkhu, although they are allowable at the time of acceptance, because they are mixed with what arose through the bhikkhu’s own initiative, they are like food mixed with poisonous meat-soup, or like alms-food mixed with unallowable meat-soup.
And it becomes difficult to remove; thus, it is indeed unallowable for everyone.
However, if one directs the water itself, saying, "There is space for the water; the embankment of the pond is firm;
act in such a way that it takes in much water; place the water near the bank," this is permissible. [Regarding] the hearth:
They do not set fire [to the fields], and it is permissible to say, "Let the lay followers receive water for irrigation.
However, it is not permissible to say, "Go and bring back grain after you have harvested it.
But if, seeing too much water in the reservoir, he has a channel dug either in front of or behind the observer, or has a forest cleared and fields created in the old fields—

Or, if one does not take the customary share but takes an excess; or, regarding a new crop or a non-seasonal crop where the shares have not been demarcated, one demands coins by saying, "Give so many *kahāpaṇas*"; all such acts are improper.
However, he who, without saying "Plough and sow," says, "In this much land, such-and-such a share [is yours]," [is not at fault].

Or he establishes a boundary on the ground; when the cultivators say, "We have cultivated the crop on this much area of land, so take this much portion," he measures it with a rope or a staff for the purpose of determining the extent of the land;
or he stands in the threshing floor and guards it, or has it removed from the threshing floor, or stores it in the granary—this is not allowable for him alone.
If farmers bring coins and say, “These have been brought for the Saṅgha,” and a certain monk, with the perception that “the Saṅgha does not consume coins,” says, “Bring robes with this many coins;
prepare rice gruel and other foods with this many,” whatever they bring is unallowable for everyone. Why? Because the coins have been handled.

If, after grain has been brought, they say, "This has been brought for the Saṅgha," and a certain bhikkhu says, in the same manner as before, "Bring this and that with so many measures of rice," then whatever they bring is indeed unallowable. Why?
Because the grain has already been processed [into a specific purpose].

If they bring rice or other food and say, "This has been brought for the Saṅgha," and a certain bhikkhu says, in the same manner as before, "Bring this and that with so much rice," then whatever they bring is allowable for all. Why?
Because the rice and other such items are allowable things that have already been processed. This also applies to buying and selling.
There is no offense, because it was explained to the attendant (kappiyakāraka).

Previously, however, at Cittalapabbata, a certain bhikkhu drew a circle on the ground at the door of the four-hall building for the purpose of making the monastery attendants aware, thinking: "Oh, may they bake this much quantity of cakes for the Saṅgha tomorrow! Seeing that, a clever [person]...
The monastery attendant did exactly as instructed; on the following day, when the drum was beaten and the Saṅgha had assembled, he took some cakes and said to the senior monk of the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sir, neither by our fathers nor by our grandfathers has such a thing ever been heard before.
A certain noble one has given a signal at the door of the four-hall building for the sake of the cakes. From this day forward, let the noble ones [partake]."
"Let each speak according to his own inclination; there will be a comfortable dwelling for us as well.
The Great Elder turned back from that very spot, and not even a single monk took any of the cakes. Thus, in the past, they did not consume even what was produced on the spot. Therefore:
By a bhikkhu who is diligent, Transcending the practice of effacement...
"Even in the case of allowable things (kappiya), one should not act out of greed for the sake of material gain.
This same principle applies to ponds, lotus pools, water channels, and irrigation ditches that were mentioned regarding tanks.
Any field or plot of land where early grains, late grains, sugarcane, fruits, or other such produce grow is also included.

Even when someone says, "I give [this]," if one refuses it, saying, "It is not allowable," and only later speaks using an appropriate expression (kappiya-vohāra), saying, "I give this for the purpose of using it as the four requisites," then it may be accepted.
However, if they say, "I give a grove" or "I give a forest," it is allowable. If people, even without being instructed by the bhikkhus, [plant] trees there...
If, having cleared away the wild vegetables and so forth, they prepare [food] and give a portion to the bhikkhus, it is permissible; those who do not give should not be reproached.
If, due to some obstacle, they have departed and others take over the work but do not give anything to the bhikkhus, they should be stopped.
If they say, "Venerable sir, did people not cultivate crops here in the past as well?"
Then they should be told: “They gave such and such allowable goods to the Saṅgha.
If they say, “We too shall give,” it is permissible.
If, referring to some area of land suitable for crops, they say, “We give the boundary,” it is permissible. This is *sīmā*.
However, for the purpose of demarcation, one must not personally set up pillars or stones. Why?

Because "land" is of incalculable value, and even for a small amount, one might incur a *pārājika* offense. But one may say to the monastery attendants (*ārāmikas*), "The boundary extends to this place.
Even if they take more than that, there is no offense because it was spoken by way of a circuitous method.
However, if kings, royal ministers, and others themselves cause pillars to be erected and give [the land], saying, "Enjoy the four requisites," it is indeed permissible.

If someone digs a pond within the boundary (sīmā), or leads a watercourse through the middle of the monastery, thereby defiling the courtyard of the shrine (cetiyāṅgaṇa), the courtyard of the Bodhi tree, and so forth, he must be stopped.
If the Saṅgha, having received something, does not stop him out of a preoccupation with material gain, then a single bhikkhu...
If one bhikkhu prevents [the act], that bhikkhu alone is the master. If no single bhikkhu prevents it, saying, "You may go," then they themselves are on the side [of the majority];
if the Saṅgha prevents it, the Saṅgha alone is the master. For in matters belonging to the Saṅgha, whoever performs a legal action (*dhammakamma*) is the master.
Even if he performs it despite being prevented, having thrown back the dust already taken up below, [it is still considered valid].
Having thrown the soil taken from above back on top,
it should be filled. If someone wishing to give sugarcane, other crops, or things such as gourds, pumpkins, and the like— whether they be vines or fruits— as they were originally grown, says,
"I give all this sugarcane field, the plot of other crops, and the enclosure for vines and fruits," [one may accept it].
Because it is taken together with the object itself, the Elder Mahāsumma said, "It is not allowable. The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, said, "This is a mere matter of expression;
for that plot of land belongs to the owners themselves, therefore it is allowable. If one says, "I give a slave," it is not allowable.
If one says, "I give a monastery attendant (ārāmika), I give a service-provider (veyyāvaccakara), I give a preparer of what is permissible (kappiyakāraka)..."

If he says, "I give [it]," it is permissible. If that monastery attendant performs work for the Saṅgha both before and after the meal, then all duties regarding the care of medicines must be performed for him just as they are for a novice (sāmaṇera).
If he performs work for the Saṅgha only before the meal, and performs his own work after the meal, then in the evening...

No food or fodder should be given [to them]. Even those who perform work for the Saṅgha on a five-day rotation or a fortnightly rotation, but perform their own work at other times—for them also, food and fodder should be given only at the time they are performing that work.
If there is no work for the Saṅgha and they live by performing only their own work, then [they must provide] the wages for manual labor.
If they bring [the goods] and give them, they should be accepted. If they do not give them, nothing should be said.
It is permissible to accept anything—even a gift from a dyer or a weaver—under the name of an *ārāmika* (monastery attendant).
If they say, "We shall give cows," they should be refused with the words, "It is not permissible. For the wise, [one should ask]: "Where did these cows come from?"

If it is said, "These five products of the cow have been given for the purpose of consumption," and one says, "We too shall give them for the purpose of consuming the five products of the cow," it is permissible.
The same principle applies to goats and so forth. If they say, "We give an elephant;
we give a horse, a buffalo, a chicken, or a pig," it is not permissible to accept them. If some people say, "Venerable sir, be free from anxiety..."
If they say, "You were there; we will take these and give them to you as allowable goods (kappiya-bhaṇḍa)," it is permissible to accept them.
It is permissible to release chickens and pigs into the forest with the thought, "May they live happily.
When it is said, "We give this pond, this field, or this site to the monastery," one is not permitted to refuse. The rest here is of plain meaning.

Regarding its origin and other characteristics: this too has six origins; it is an action; it is not accompanied by liberation through perception; it is mindless; it is an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*); it consists of bodily and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness; and it involves three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning kings is finished.
The first chapter, the Chapter on Robes (*cīvaravagga*), is completed.
2. The Chapter on Silk (Kosiyavagga) 1.
Explanation of the Training Rule on Silk (Kosiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) 542.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning silk. Therein, "it was made by spreading [the material] out" means on a level patch of ground.
It is made by layering silk threads one upon another and sprinkling them with sour gruel and so forth.
"Even by mixing with a single silk thread" means: let alone what is mixed according to one's own preference;
even if the wind brings and drops a single silk thread into the place where it is being made, it is still considered to have been made by mixing. The rest is of plain meaning.
It originates from chance, is functional, is not a liberation through perception, is without consciousness, is an offense by formal rule, consists of bodily and verbal action,
involves three types of consciousness, and involves three types of feeling.
The commentary on the Kosiya training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Pure Black [Wool] (Suddhakāḷaka-sikkhāpada) 547.
"At that time" refers to the training rule on pure black [wool]. Therein, "pure black" means purely black;
the meaning is "black unmixed with others. The rest is of obvious meaning. The origin and so forth [of this rule] are also [to be understood in the same way].
"These are indeed similar to the Kosiya training rule.
The commentary on the Suddhakāḷaka training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Dvebhāga training rule.

552. "At that time" refers to the training rule concerning two parts (*dvebhāga*). Therein, "having taken at the edge" means having shown the edge of the rug as if it were a trailing wind, and having caused the white [wool] to adhere to it.
"Two parts" means two portions. "To be taken" means to be grasped. "Of the *gocariya* wool" means of the Kapila-colored wool.
"Two *tulā*s to be taken" is said with reference to one who wishes to have it made from four *tulā*s. In terms of meaning, however, by how many...

If one wishes to make [a rug] from sheep’s wool, it should be understood that this very point is demonstrated: two portions of those [wools] must be black, one white, and one tawny. The rest is of plain meaning.

The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and other factors are also the same as for the rule on silk (kosiya-sikkhāpada). It should be understood as being both an action and a non-action, depending on whether one makes it by taking [the materials] or not taking them.
The commentary on the training rule concerning two parts is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Six Years (Chabbassa-sikkhāpada) 557.
“At that time” refers to the training rule concerning six years. In this context, “they urinate and they defecate” means that they discharge feces and urine upon the spread-out [rugs].
"By the Saṅgha, the authorization for a rug has been granted to the monk named so-and-so.
Having thus obtained the authorization, as long as his illness has not subsided, that monk is permitted to spread a rug wherever he goes.
If, having recovered, he becomes ill again with the same original disease, he receives that very same privilege; there is no other.
Thera Phussadeva said it is "the duty of formal authorization" (*sammutikicca*). Thera Upatissa, however, said:
"Whether that same illness recurs or another arises, once the name 'one who is ill' has been obtained, it is indeed obtained; there is no further need for the duty of formal authorization.

Regarding the phrase "within six years," the meaning is "on this side of six years," that is, within [them]. In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, it is stated as "less than six years" for the purpose of showing the mere number.
“There is no offense if one makes it within six years”: this means that when the six years are completed, he then makes the blanket.
In the second phrase as well, the meaning should be understood thus: “when more than six years have passed, then he makes it.
For it is not the case that he makes it for exactly six years. The rest is of plain meaning.
The origins and other details are exactly like those of the Kosiya training rule.
The commentary on the six-year training rule is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning sitting mats.
565. *Tena samayena* refers to the training rule concerning sitting mats (*nisīdana-santhata-sikkhāpada*).
Regarding this, the Blessed One said, "I wish, monks," because it is said that during those three months he did not see any being capable of being awakened; therefore, he spoke thus.

Even so, the teaching of the Dhamma ought to be performed according to the sequence of the discourse. However, it occurred to him: "While I am remaining in seclusion after having granted [the people] an opportunity..."
“The monks will establish an unrighteous formal agreement (*katikavatta*), and Upasena will break it.
Having gained confidence in him, I will grant the monks permission to see him; consequently, many monks desiring to see me will undertake the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
And because of their use of discarded bedding, I shall lay down a training rule (*sikkhāpada*); for this reason he spoke thus. Thus...
"For there are indeed many benefits herein.

[The Elder] approached the Blessed One together with his retinue; it is said that regarding this training rule in the Khandhaka which states, "Bhikkhus, one who has fewer than ten years [of seniority] must not grant full ordination;
whoever should so ordain commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," [the Elder thought], "How indeed..."
"O foolish man, having yourself been exhorted and instructed by others, do you think you can exhort and instruct others?"—having received such censure in this manner, [he thought]:
"The Teacher has censured me on account of my assembly;
now, therefore, I shall [proclaim] the Brahma-voice with that face of the Blessed One, which possesses the splendor of the full moon and is perfect in every aspect."

Thinking, "Having dismissed the assembly, I shall have them give their applause once they are dependent upon me alone," the well-disposed noble son retreated more than a hundred yojanas, gathered an assembly, and surrounded by about five hundred bhikkhus, he approached the Blessed One again.
Therefore it is said: "Together with his retinue, he approached the Blessed One. For it was not possible [otherwise].
There is no other way to please the Buddhas than through the perfection of one’s conduct (*vattasampatti*).

"Seated not far from the Blessed One" means that, being fearless due to the purity of his conduct, he sat near the Blessed One like a lion on a mountain of gold. "He said this" is for the purpose of initiating the discourse.
He said: "Bhikkhu, these rag-robes are pleasing to you. This means: "Bhikkhu, these rag-robes of yours are pleasing;
they were taken by your own preference and consent. "No, venerable sir, they are not pleasing to me. This shows: "Venerable sir, they were not taken by my own preference;
I was seized against my will, as if by the throat or as if by a blow to the head."
"Paññāyissati" means "it will be known" or "it will be recognized"; what is meant is that it will be manifest therein.
"We shall not lay down what has not been laid down" means that we, who are called disciples, shall not lay down what has not been laid down;

for this—namely, the laying down of training rules not previously laid down in the manner of "an offense of expiation" (pācittiya) or "an offense of wrong-doing" (dukkaṭa)—is the domain of the Buddha.
Or, it is the cutting off of what has been prescribed. "Having undertaken" means having undertaken each respective training rule;
it shows that one will train in all the training rules as they have been prescribed, having accepted them with the words, "Excellent!
Well done! With a mind thus aroused, he again gave his approval, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!"
"566. 'Anujñātāvuso' means 'It is permitted, friend. 'Pihentā' means 'desiring.
'Ujjhitvā santhatāni' means having discarded all the rugs, which are designated as the fourth requisite. Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
the Blessed One, seeing the rugs strewn about, [thought], 'There is no reason for the misappropriation of what has been given in faith.'"
"Thinking, 'I shall show them the means for their enjoyment,' he gave a discourse on the Dhamma and addressed the bhikkhus:
'Once wrapped and once covered' means both when one has sat down and when one has lain down.
'Around' means having cut a circle or a square from one side, the area taken is such that it measures a span (vidatthi)."

It should be understood in this way. However, when spreading it, one should either spread it in one place according to the method stated in the Pāḷi, or spread it by interweaving or mixing [the materials];
in this way, it becomes more durable. The rest is of plain meaning.
Regarding the origin (samuṭṭhāna) and other factors, because this training rule is both an action and a non-action, they are similar to those of the Two-Part Training Rule.

Regarding these five kinds of rugs (*santhata*), it should be understood that the first three are not permitted to be used after having been obtained by performing a formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*); however, the latter two are permitted.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the sitting rug (*nisīdana-santhata*) is concluded.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning sheep’s wool (*eḷakaloma*).
571. "At that time" refers to the training rule concerning wool (eḷakaloma). Therein, "they mocked" means they laughed at him by saying things such as, "Venerable sir, for how much were these bought?

"He threw them down while standing" means that just as people, having brought a large load of timber from the forest and being exhausted, throw it down while still standing, so too did he throw them down; this is the meaning.
572. "With one's own hand" means by one's own hand; it is said that they are to be carried away by oneself.

"Throws beyond three yojanas" means he throws it outside of three yojanas. Even if there is no obstacle, as soon as it is released from the hand and falls, there are offenses of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) according to the count of hairs [on the object].
If, having struck against a tree or a pillar beyond the three yojanas, it falls back inside, there is no offense.
If a bundle of wool falls to the ground and, rolling over and over again, enters back inside [the robe], it is indeed an offense.
If, having remained inside, one rolls it with the hand, the foot, or a stick—whether remaining still or not—the bundle moves along;
it is indeed an offense. If one sets it down thinking, "Another will carry it," even if it is carried by that person, it is indeed an offense.

If something placed with a pure mind is blown away by the wind or by some other natural force outside [the boundary], it is indeed an offense, because this training rule involves both intention and the presence of a conscious state.
However, in the *Kurundi* and other commentaries, it is stated that "there is no offense here";
yet that non-offense does not accord with the Canon (*pāḷi*). If two bundles are tied together as one and one bundle is [placed] within the boundary...
If one places a single [article] outside the boundary, it remains protected for that time. The same principle applies even when it is placed on a cart that is still hitched together.

However, if it has not been tied down and is merely placed at the edge of the cart, it is no longer protected. Even if it is on a cart that is still hitched together, if it is placed after being turned around, there is indeed an offense.
Regarding the phrase "in another's vehicle," this refers to a vehicle that is moving or to the backs of elephants and so forth, while the owner is unaware.
He places it [the bowl] with the thought, "It will be carried," and when it has passed three *yojanas*, there is an offense. The same principle applies even while it is being brought back.
However, if, after placing it on a vehicle that is returning or on the back of an elephant and so forth, he mounts it and causes it to be conveyed;
or if, while walking below, he urges it on; or if, calling out, he causes someone to follow it—there is no offense, because of the statement, "he causes another to carry it."
In the *Kurundi* and other commentaries, however, it is stated that this constitutes an "offense" (*āpatti*); yet that does not accord with the phrase "having caused another to carry it.

Regarding the taking of what is not given, there is an offense in the case of evading customs duties. For whatever constitutes an offense in that context is here a non-offense (*anāpatti*), and whatever constitutes an offense here is there a non-offense.
If, having reached that place, one goes while distracted by other matters or harassed by thieves and the like, [there is no offense].
It is indeed an offense. In all cases, the determination of the offense should be understood by counting the hairs [of the body]. 575.
Regarding "having gone with the intention of staying for three *yojanas*, he carries it beyond that":

this means that having gone to a certain place, because of not obtaining instruction, questioning, or the like, or because of not obtaining requisites and so forth, he goes from there to another place, and from that place to yet another—thus it is.
There is no offense for one who carries it even a hundred yojanas. "Having recovered what was stolen" means that after thieves have stolen it, they return it upon realizing it is useless;

there is no offense for one who carries it [in such a case]. "Having recovered what was relinquished" means having recovered what has been formally forfeited through a legal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma).
"Kata-bhaṇḍa" means a prepared bundle; it refers to anything whatsoever, such as blankets, *kojava* rugs, or mats, even if they are merely tied together with a string.

Furthermore, it includes a small leaf-wallet, or a case for the *āyoga*, shoulder-straps, waist-bands, and so forth, or a small box used for protecting against the filth of fleas and the like, or even for one afflicted by wind-disorders (*vātābādhika*).
If one goes about after inserting even hair into the ear canal, it is indeed an offense.

However, if it is inserted after being tied with a thread and remains in its place as a finished article, or if it is carried after being fashioned into a braid—this is called a "repository-opening," and it is indeed an offense.
The rest is self-evident.

Regarding the origins and other characteristics: this is known as the origin by means of sheep’s wool (*eḷakaloma-samuṭṭhāna*). It originates from both body and from body-and-mind; it is an action (*kiriya*); it is not liberated through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*); it is without thought (*acittaka*); it is an offense by rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*); it is bodily action (*kāya-kamma*); it involves three types of consciousness (*ticitta*) and three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning sheep’s wool is concluded. 7.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Washing Sheep’s Wool (*eḷakaloma-dhovāpana-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā*)
576. "At that time" refers to the training rule concerning the washing of wool. Therein, "neglecting" means they abandon it, they discard it;

what is meant is that they are unable to apply themselves to it. The rest here is to be understood according to the method already stated for the training rule on old robes, including its origin and other characteristics.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the washing of sheep’s wool is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Money (Rūpiya-sikkhāpada).
582. “At that time”: this refers to the training rule concerning money. In this context, “a counter-part” (paṭivisa) means a portion.
583–4. Regarding the phrase "gold and silver" (*jātarūparajata*): here, *jātarūpa* is a name for gold.
Because that [gold] resembles the color of the Tathāgata, it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) that "it is called the Teacher’s color. Its meaning is:
"That particular kind of metal which has the Teacher’s color is what is called *jātarūpa*. As for silver, however, [the commentary lists]: "conch, stone, coral..."
In such passages as "silver" and "gold," *rūpiya* (precious metal) is mentioned. However, here whatever is fit for commercial transaction, such as the *kahāpaṇa* and so forth, is intended.
For this very reason, its word-commentary (*padabhājana*) states: "The *kahāpaṇa*, the copper *māsaka*, etc.
In that context, a *kahāpaṇa* may be made of gold, or made of precious metal, or it may be the ordinary [coin]. A copper *māsaka* is a coin made from copper, bronze, and so forth.
A wooden māsaka is a coin made by cutting a shape from heartwood or from a bamboo splinter, or even from a palm leaf.
A resinous māsaka is a coin made by forming a shape out of lac or sap.
By the phrase "those which enter into commerce," however, it is meant that whichever [coins] are used in whichever region, whenever they are used...
It comes under common usage; even that which consists of bone, leather, or seeds of trees, whether it is produced by artificial means or not produced by artificial means—all of it is included.
Thus, all this is "gold" (jātarūpa), "gold coin" (jātarūpamāsaka), and likewise all the aforementioned varieties of "silver coin" (rajatamāsaka).

There are four kinds of objects involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, stones, coral, rubies, emeralds, the seven grains, female and male slaves, fields, lands, flower gardens, fruit orchards, and so forth—these are objects of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).
Thread, ploughshares, cloth, cotton, various kinds of non-food, and medicinal requisites such as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, and so on.
This is an allowable object. Regarding that, it is not permitted to accept an object involving forfeiture for one’s own sake, or for the sake of the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or a shrine.
For one who accepts it for one’s own sake, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture;
for the sake of the others, it is an offense of wrong-doing. Regarding an object involving wrong-doing, for one who accepts it for the sake of any [of these], it is simply an offense of wrong-doing.

There is no offense regarding an allowable object (*kappiyavatthu*). Even when one accepts [an item] for the purpose of storing it under the pretext of being a storekeeper, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to what is set forth in the subsequent Jewel Precept (*ratana-sikkhāpada*).

"Should take" means he should take. Since one incurs an offense by taking, therefore it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*): "If he takes it himself, it is an offense of expiation involving relinquishment (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well.
In that regard, for one who takes or causes another to take gold, silver, or articles such as *kahāpaṇa* coins and *māsaka* coins, there is one offense.
Even if one takes or causes another to take a thousand [coins] all at once, there are offenses according to the number of items.

However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kuruṇḍī*, it is stated that in the case of a bag with loose fastenings or a vessel filled loosely, the offense is calculated by the number of [individual pieces of] metal.
It is an offense. However, it is stated that when [the items] are packed together or filled together, there is only a single offense.

But regarding the acceptance of what has been set aside, if one says, "Let this be for the venerable one," even if one consents in the mind and desires to take it, yet rejects it with body or speech, saying, "This is not allowable," there is no offense. [This applies] when [acting] with body or speech.
Or even if one has not formally declined [the gift], if one remains pure in mind and does not consent, thinking, "This is not allowable for us," there is indeed no offense.
For among the three doors, what is declined by any one of them is indeed considered declined.
However, if one does not decline through body or speech but consents mentally, this is because one fails to perform the refusal that ought to be performed through body and speech.
An offense arising from non-action (akiriyasamuṭṭhāna) is incurred at both the door of the body and the door of speech; however, there is no such thing as an "offense" at the door of the mind.
Suppose someone places a hundred or a thousand [pieces of money] at the feet [of a monk], saying, "Let this be yours";
the monk refuses it, saying, "This is not allowable," and the lay follower departs with the thought, "It has been relinquished by me to you. Then another person comes there and asks:
—“What is this, venerable sir? He should explain whatever he himself has said. If he says, “I will keep it, venerable sir;
show me a secure place,” then even if it is a seven-storied palace, having ascended it, he should point out, “This is a secure place”;
he must not say, “Place it here. Up to this point, it is allowable (*kappiya*).
And it stands supported by what is not allowable (*akappiya*). One who guards it must live having closed the door.
If some merchandise for sale, such as a bowl or a robe, comes there, and someone says, "Venerable sir, please take this," he should say:
"Lay follower, we have need of this, and such a site exists for us; however, there is no one to prepare what is allowable (*kappiyakāraka*)."
"It does not exist," he should say. If he says, "I shall act as the steward;
open the door and give [the goods] to me," then having opened the door, he should say, "It has been placed in this spot," but he must not say, "Take this.
Even in this way, it remains dependent upon both what is allowable and what is unallowable. If he, taking that [item],...
If he gives him an allowable article, it is permissible. If he takes more than that, he should be told, "We do not take your goods; go away.
Regarding the instruction "it must be relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha," since what is called "money" (rūpiya) is indeed unallowable, therefore it must be relinquished.

It was not said, "To the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual. However, because that [gift] has merely been accepted and nothing suitable for use has yet been purchased with it, it is therefore stated, "It should be relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha," in order to show the means by which it may be used.
Regarding the instruction, "The allowable [substance] should be pointed out—ghee, for example": "For those who have gone forth, ghee..."
"Or oil is permitted, lay followers"—thus it should be explained.
"It is to be used by all except the receiver of money" means that it should be divided and used by everyone;
the receiver of money must not take a share. Even the portion allotted to other monks or to the monastery attendants [must not be taken].
It is not permitted to consume [these things] after having obtained them;

even if they have been carried away from monkeys or other animals and placed in the forest, or if they have fallen from their hands—even if they are the property of animals—it is still not permitted, even if they are discarded rags (*pāṃsukūla*).
Furthermore, it is not permitted to fumigate lodgings with molasses brought from there. Nor is it permitted to use ghee or oil for a lamp [from such sources].
It is not permitted to lie down using the light of a lamp, nor to perform the preliminary work for a *kasiṇa* meditation, nor to read a book.
Furthermore, it is certainly not permitted to smear an ulcer on the body with oil, honey, or molasses.
If, by means of that material, one takes beds, chairs, and so forth, or constructs an *uposatha* hall or a dining hall, it is not permitted to use them.
Even a shadow that remains within the boundaries of the dwelling is not permitted;

however, one that extends beyond those boundaries is permitted because it is considered "incoming. It is not permitted to go by way of a path, a bridge, a boat, or a raft constructed after relinquishing that site.
One may neither drink from nor make use of the water emerging from a lotus pond excavated at that site.
It is permissible. However, if there is no water inside [the vessel], it is permissible for other incoming water or rainwater to have entered.
In the case of insects, even that incoming water with which the insects are present is not permissible;
if the Saṅgha uses requisites after setting aside that object as a deposit, those requisites are not permissible for him either.
The grove has been acquired; it is not permissible to enjoy even that. If both the soil and the seed are unallowable (*akappiya*), it is not permissible to enjoy either the soil or the fruit.
If, having purchased only the soil, other seeds are planted, the fruit is permissible; however, if seeds are purchased and planted in allowable soil (*kappiyabhūmi*), the fruit is not [permissible].
It is permissible; it is permissible to sit or lie down on the ground.
"If he discards it" means if he throws it anywhere; even if he does not discard it, but takes it himself and goes away, he should not be stopped.
"If he does not discard it" means if he neither takes it and goes away nor discards it—what is that to me?
"By this procedure": one who departs at will [from the community] must appoint a "discarder of silver" (*rūpiya-chaḍḍaka*) possessing the characteristics already described.
One who, out of greed (*lobha*), acts for his own sake regarding that object or exalts himself, goes toward what is called "bias through desire" (*chandāgati*).
Out of hatred (*dosa*), thinking, "This man knows neither the *mātikā* nor the Vinaya," he [denigrates] another...
By disparaging [the donor], one goes to the "wrong course" of hatred (*dosāgati*). By falling into a state of forgetfulness due to delusion, one goes to the "wrong course" of delusion (*mohāgati*).
Being unable to discard [the object] out of fear of the recipient of the silver, one goes to the "wrong course" of fear (*bhayāgati*).
By not acting in this way, one does not go to the wrong course of desire, nor to the wrong course of hatred, nor to the wrong course of delusion.
It should be understood that he goes, but does not go by way of fear.

"Having made it signless" means having made no sign; having closed one's eyes, one should throw oneself like excrement—without regard for a river, a precipice, or a dense forest—and without attending to the place where one falls. Thus...
Although money is something to be loathed, the Blessed One explained by way of a particular method that it may be used by monks.
However, for one who has accepted money, the use of requisites arising from it is not permitted by any method whatsoever.
Just as this is not permitted for him, so too [the use of requisites] obtained through false reputation, through corrupting families, or through hypocrisy and the like, is likewise forbidden.
It is not permissible for him, nor for anyone else; even if obtained righteously and justly, it is not permissible to consume it without having reflected upon it.
For there are four ways of consuming: consumption as theft, consumption as debt, consumption as inheritance, and consumption as ownership.
Among these, the consumption by one who is immoral, even while sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, is "consumption as theft."

...so it is called. For one who possesses virtue, using things without reflection is called "using on credit. Therefore, one should reflect each time one uses a robe, and with every morsel of almsfood.
If one is unable to do so, one should reflect before the meal, after the meal, during the first watch of the night, and during the last watch.
If dawn should rise while one is still not reflecting, one stands in the position of using on credit. This applies to the lodging as well.
One must reflect upon each act of consumption. Regarding medicinal requisites, mindfulness is required both at the time of receiving and at the time of consuming;

nevertheless, while this is so, there is an offense for one who exercises mindfulness when receiving but fails to do so when consuming, whereas there is no offense for one who fails to exercise mindfulness when receiving but does so when consuming.

Purification is indeed fourfold: purification by confession (*desanāsuddhi*), purification by restraint (*saṃvarasuddhi*), purification by search (*pariyeṭṭhisuddhi*), and purification by reflection (*paccavekkhaṇasuddhi*).
In this context, "purification by confession" refers to the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha; for since it is purified through confession, it is called "purification by confession.
"Purification by restraint" refers to the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties; for that is purified solely by the restraint consisting in the mental resolve: "I shall not do so again."
Because it is purified, it is called "purity of restraint. "Purity of search" refers to the virtue of livelihood-purification;
for that is called "purity of search" because the search is pure when one abandons wrong means of livelihood and procures requisites in accordance with the Dhamma and justice.
"Purity of reflection" refers to the virtue dependent on the use of requisites.
For it is called "purity through reflection" because it is purified by the kind of reflection described in such passages as, "He uses the robe with wise reflection.
Therefore it was said: "But there is no offense for one who applies mindfulness at the time of use, even if they were not mindful at the time of receiving it."
The enjoyment of requisites by the seven types of trainees (sekkha) is called "enjoyment as an inheritance," for they are indeed the sons of the Blessed One;
therefore, being heirs to the requisites belonging to their father, they enjoy those requisites.
But do they enjoy the requisites of the Blessed One, or do they enjoy the requisites of householders? Even when given by householders—
Because they have been authorized by the Blessed One, they belong to the Blessed One; therefore, it should be understood that they enjoy the requisites of the Blessed One.
In this regard, the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* is the supporting proof.
The enjoyment of those whose taints are destroyed is called "enjoyment as owners," for they are owners because they have transcended the servitude of craving.
"Having offered, they consume. Among these modes of consumption, both the master’s consumption (*sāmiparibhoga*) and the inheritance’s consumption (*dāyajjaparibhoga*) are permissible for everyone.
Debt-consumption (*iṇaparibhoga*) is not permissible, and as for theft-consumption (*theyyaparibhoga*), there is no discussion even of it.

There are yet four other modes of consumption: the consumption of the conscientious (*lajjiparibhoga*), the consumption of the unconscientious (*alajjiparibhoga*), the righteous consumption (*dhammiyaparibhoga*), and the unrighteous consumption (*adhammiyaparibhoga*).
In this regard, it is permissible for one who is conscientious to share communal use with one who is unconscientious, and he should not be made to incur an offense.

It is permissible for one who is conscientious to share communal use with one who is unconscientious as long as he does not know [of that person’s state]. For from the very beginning, there is no such thing as an "unconscientious one";
therefore, when he knows of that person’s unconscientiousness, he should be told: "In both the bodily door and the verbal door..."

“Do not commit a transgression; that is improper, do not act in this way. If, disregarding this, he nevertheless commits it, and if one shares in the enjoyment [of requisites] with him, that person too becomes shameless.
Even one who shares in the enjoyment [of requisites] with a shameless person who has become a burden to oneself should be restrained. If he does not desist, he too is indeed shameless.

Thus, one who is shameless even makes another shameless. However, for one who is shameless, there is no such thing as an offense regarding the use [of requisites] together with another who is shameless.
The use of requisites by one who is conscientious together with one who is conscientious is like two princes eating from a single golden bowl.
