The use of requisites—whether in accordance with the Dhamma or contrary to the Dhamma—is to be understood according to the conditions [of the individuals involved]. In that regard, if the person is shameless and the alms-food is also...
Both are unrighteous and loathsome. Almsfood is righteous for a person who is shameless; however, having felt disgust for that person, the almsfood should not be accepted.

In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however, it is stated: "If one who is immoral, having received meals for recitation (*uddesabhatta*) and so forth from the Saṅgha, gives them back to the Saṅgha itself, these are permissible because they have returned to their original state of being given. Almsfood [is likewise] for a person who is conscientious...
If the person is unrighteous, the alms-food is loathsome and should not be accepted. If the person is conscientious, the alms-food is righteous and is permissible.

There are two further types of support and two types of enjoyment: the support of the conscientious and the support of the unconscientious; the enjoyment of the Dhamma and the enjoyment of material things.
In this regard, it is permissible for the unconscientious to support the conscientious, and he should not be made to undergo punishment for an offense. However, if the conscientious...
He accepts the shameless man; he requests him to offer thanks; he requests him to give a Dhamma talk; and he provides support for him among families.
The other, too, speaks in praise of him in his assembly, saying, "Our teacher is such and such.
This should be understood as causing the Dispensation to decline and disappear.
Regarding the enjoyment of the Dhamma and the enjoyment of material goods, wherever the enjoyment of material goods is permitted, there the enjoyment of the Dhamma is also permitted.

However, it is said that it is permissible to learn through support for the Dhamma a text that stands at the very limit [of preservation] and would perish after the passing away of that particular person.
Here is the story: It is said that during a time of great peril, the *Mahāniddesa* alone was well-mastered by a single bhikkhu.
Then, the Elder Mahātipiṭaka, who was the preceptor of the Elder Catunikāyika Tissa, said to the Elder Mahārakkhita:
"Friend Mahārakkhita, learn the *Mahāniddesa* from him. [Mahārakkhita replied: "This man is indeed wicked..."
“Venerable sir, I will not take it up. “Take it up, friend; I shall sit near you,” [the Venerable Ānanda said]. “Very well, venerable sir;
I will take it up when you are seated,” [the other replied]. Having thus established himself, he mastered the text continuously day and night.
On the final day, seeing a woman beneath his bed, he thought: “Venerable sir, I have heard this before; had I known it was so...”
"One should not learn the Dhamma in the presence of such a person," he said. Yet, many great elders, having learned it in his presence, established the *Mahāniddesa*.
586. Regarding the phrase "perceiving gold as gold":
here, it should be understood that all gold and silver are included within the category of "money" (*rūpiya*).
“Having doubt about money” means having arisen into a state of uncertainty by way of such methods as, “Is this gold, or is it coarse cloth?

“Perceiving what is not money as money” means perceiving coarse cloth and so forth in gold and so forth. Furthermore, queens, court ladies, and others who desire merit place gold and bullion among their food, snacks, perfumes, and alms-morsels, and give them to those wandering for rag-robes.

When they give cloths together with kārṣāpaṇa coins and so forth to those standing there, and the monks accept them either perceiving them as food or perceiving them as cloths—in this case too, it should be understood that "one takes money while perceiving it as not money.
Furthermore, by the one who accepts it, it should be noted: "This was obtained in this house. For if, through lack of mindfulness...
It has been given; having regained mindfulness, he returns again, and then he should be told: "Look for your rag-robe.
The rest here is of plain meaning. Regarding the origins and so forth: it has six origins;
it may be an act (*kiriya*) because one incurs the offense through the act of taking, or it may be a non-act (*akiriya*) because of the prohibition.
By way of non-transgression, the three training rules concerning money, speaking otherwise, and eavesdropping have a single delimitation;

they are not to be released through recognition, are without mental concomitants, are offenses by formal precept, consist of bodily and verbal action, involve three types of consciousness, and involve three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning money is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Trade in Coin (Rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpada) 587.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning trade in coin. In this context, "of various kinds" means manifold, by way of what has been done and what has not been done, and so forth.
"Trade in coin" means the exchange of gold and silver. "Engaging in" refers specifically to the act of accepting [the coin].
Because it has been refused, they act without seeing any fault in exchanging what has already been accepted.
589. Regarding "head-reaching" (*sīsūpaga*) and so forth: it is called "head-reaching" because it reaches the head;
however, in manuscripts it is written as "head-attached" (*sīsūpaka*), which is a designation for any kind of head ornament. This same method applies everywhere. By what has been made...
Regarding the terms "what" and so forth, it is simply pure trading in money.

In the section beginning with "perceiving money as money," when one exchanges an article subject to forfeiture for another article subject to forfeiture among the objects mentioned in the preceding training rule, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) at the time of taking the original price; furthermore, for each successive exchange, [there is an offense].

By this, it is indeed an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). The same principle applies even when one exchanges an article subject to forfeiture for an article that is merely an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) or an allowable article (*kappiya-vatthu*).
For this second triad mentioned—namely, "one who perceives money as money in what is not money and exchanges money," and so forth—is a corollary;
therefore, although not explicitly stated, this other case is also included: one who perceives money as money in what is not money [and exchanges it].
The triad beginning with "causes to be exchanged" (cetāpeti) should be understood as follows:

for whether one causes another’s non-monetary object to be exchanged for one’s own monetary object, or causes one’s own monetary object to be exchanged for another’s non-monetary object—in both cases, a transaction involving money has indeed been performed.
Therefore, in the Pāḷi, only a single triad is stated exclusively on the side of monetary objects.

However, for one who exchanges an article involving an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for an article involving an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*), there is an offense of wrong-doing under the previous rule at the time of taking the original price; subsequently, upon the exchange, there is an offense of expiation entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) under this present rule, because of having exchanged something grave.

For one who exchanges an article involving an offense of wrong-doing for another article involving an offense of wrong-doing, or for a permissible article (*kappiya-vatthu*), there is an offense of wrong-doing under the previous rule at the time of taking the original price.
It is a *dukkaṭa*; even if the exchange occurs later, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa* for this reason. Why? Because it was purchased with an improper object (*akappiyavatthu*).
However, in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "If one should engage in buying and selling, it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
That is poorly stated. Why? For there is no such thing as "buying and selling" other than the act of giving and taking.

And the training rule concerning buying and selling was spoken with reference specifically to the exchange of allowable goods for allowable goods, and that only when other than among fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.
This training rule concerns the exchange of money for money or non-money, and the exchange of non-money for money.
However, the exchange of an article involving an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for an article involving an offense of wrong-doing is not [included].
This is not stated in the text there, yet it cannot be that there is no offense here. Therefore,

those who know the Blessed One’s intention have stated that just as there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the acceptance of an object of wrong-doing, so too is an offense of wrong-doing appropriate in its exchange by him or for him.

However, for one who exchanges an allowable article (*kappiyavatthu*) for an article that entails relinquishment (*nissaggiyavatthu*), there is no offense at the time of taking the original price according to the preceding rule;
but subsequently, upon the exchange, this [present] rule constitutes a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*. For it has been said:

"If one exchanges non-monetary goods while perceiving them as non-monetary, yet they are monetary goods, it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*. By that same [principle], for an article involving an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭavatthu*) with that same allowable article...
For one who causes an exchange, there is likewise no offense at the time of receiving the original item; however, for the subsequent barter, there is an *dukkaṭa* offense. Why?

Because an unallowable thing was caused to be exchanged. But for one who causes an allowable thing to be exchanged for another allowable thing—except with those who share the same Dhamma—at the time of receiving the original item, there is no offense under the preceding training rule;
yet for the subsequent barter, there is an offense under the later training rule concerning buying and selling.

It is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). For one who receives [goods] after having arranged for buying and selling, there is no offense under the subsequent training rule;
however, for one who employs [the goods] for the purpose of profit, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Furthermore, this set of four cases regarding the bowl should be understood as illustrating the gravity of this transaction involving money. Whoever...
For instance, having acquired silver, one causes iron seed to be produced from it; having had that smelted, one has a bowl made from that metal.
This bowl is called "greatly unallowable" (*mahā-akappiya*); it cannot be rendered allowable by any means whatsoever.
For if one destroys it and has a platter made, that too is unallowable. If one has an axe made, even a tooth-stick cut with it is unallowable.
It is not allowable (*akappiya*). To make a fishhook means that even the fish killed by it are not allowable.
Having heated the blade of an axe, one heats water or milk;
that too is indeed not allowable. Furthermore, if someone takes silver and buys a bowl with it, this bowl is also not allowable. "Of the five... [and so forth].
"It is not allowable for those who follow the same Dhamma," as stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. However, it can be made allowable;
for when the root is given to the owners of the root and the bowl is given to the owners of the bowl, it becomes allowable.
Having given an allowable article and received [the item] in exchange, it is permissible to use it.
If someone, having caused silver to be received, goes with a kappiyakāraka (an attendant for allowable goods) to a smith’s workshop and, upon seeing a bowl, says,
"This one pleases me," and the kappiyakāraka gives that silver and instructs the smith—
this bowl, although acquired through a transaction involving allowable goods, is exactly like the second bowl, because the price was accepted.
It is not allowable. Why is it not allowable for the others? Because the root [the money] has not been relinquished.

However, if one who has not accepted the money goes with a kappiyakāraka (an agent for what is allowable) whom he sent, saying, "Buy a bowl for the Elder and give it to him," and having gone to the smith's house and seen the bowl, says, "Take these kahāpaṇas and give this [bowl] to him," and [the kappiyakāraka] takes the kahāpaṇas...

Having been made to give it, he took it; this bowl is not permitted for that very bhikkhu because of his improper conduct, but it is permitted for others because the original owner did not accept it back.
It is said that the preceptor of the Elder Mahāsumana was the Elder named Anuruddha. He [Mahāsumana] had such a bowl as this...
Having filled it with ghee, he offered it to the Saṅgha. The pupil of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga also had such a bowl; the Elder likewise, having filled it with ghee, had it offered to the Saṅgha.
This is the set of four improper bowls.
But if, without accepting the silver himself, he goes with the attendant who was sent with the instruction, "Buy a bowl for the Elder and give it to him," to the smith's house,
and upon seeing the bowl says, "This one pleases me" or "I will take this one," and the attendant gives that silver and instructs the smith— this bowl is entirely allowable.
It is also fit for the use of the Buddhas. 591.

"Perceiving what is not money as money" means perceiving items such as coarse leaves as gold and so forth. "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that if one causes [something] that is not money to be bartered for by that [person], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
This same method applies when one is in doubt. However, for one who perceives what is not money as [money]...
There is no offense even for one who engages in buying and selling with five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, saying, "Take this and give that.

The rest is self-evident. It has six origins; it is an action; it is not characterized by liberation through perception; it is without [wrong] intention; it is an offense of formal rule; it consists of bodily and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness; and it involves three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the bartering of silver is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning buying and selling: 593.
"At that time" refers to the training rule on buying and selling. In this context, *kati hi pi tyāyanti* means "how many are these for you? (or "what do these amount to for you?").
In this context, the syllable *hi* is for the purpose of completing the meter, while *pi* expresses censure; the meaning is: "How many days will this weak outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) last for you?
Alternatively, there is also the reading *katihimpi tyāyanti*. Therein, *katihi* means "how many days," that is, "for how many days.
The rest is exactly as previously explained. *Katihipi myāyanti* is also explained by this same [method].

It should be understood according to this method. Regarding the phrase "a householder [gives] to a householder": here, *naṃ* is a particle used in the sense of a noun; thus, it is said that "a householder [gives] to one called a householder.
(594) "Of various kinds" means manifold, by way of allowable articles such as robes and so forth.
For this very reason, in the word-commentary on this term, only allowable articles—beginning with robes and ending with threads for tassels—are shown.
Indeed, the exchange of unallowable goods does not fall under the category of buying and selling. "Buying and selling" refers to both buying and selling.
For by taking another's allowable goods in such a manner as "Give me this for that," one enters into buying;
and by giving one's own allowable goods, one enters into selling.
595. *Ajjhācarati* means he acts having overcome [the restraint]; the meaning is that he utters words of transgression.

"When there is both buying and selling" means: when there is buying by one who brings another's goods into his own hand, and selling by one who puts his own goods into another's hand, according to the corresponding expressions such as "this for that," and so forth.
However, in the text, one's own goods are shown first.
"It should be relinquished" means that allowable goods received from another by way of purchase must be relinquished.
For this buying and selling, with the exception of the five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, [is forbidden] by all others—both householders and those gone forth—even down to...
It is not permissible even with one’s mother or father.
Herein is the analysis: whether it be cloth for cloth or food for food—whatever is allowable—if one says, "Give this by means of that," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Even if, having spoken thus, one gives one's own goods to one's mother, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one says, "Give this to that person," or says, "Give this to me and I will give that to you," and then takes the goods for oneself even from one's own mother, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
When one's own goods reach another's hand, or when another's goods reach one's own hand, it is an offense involving relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
However, there is no formal request (*viññatti*) when one says to one's mother or father, "Give this."
When one says, “Take this,” there is no misappropriation of what was given in faith. When one says to a stranger, “Give this,” it is a formal request (*viññatti*).
When one says, “Take this,” it is a misappropriation of what was given in faith.

When one engages in buying and selling by saying, “Give this for that,” it is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Therefore, when exchanging allowable goods, even with one’s mother or father...
One may exchange goods for goods with those who are not relatives, provided one avoids the three offenses; herein is the method of exchange:
a monk has rice for his provisions on a journey, and seeing a man with food in hand along the way, he says, "We have rice, but we have no need for this; however, we do need food."
He speaks. A man takes rice and gives a meal; it is permissible. There are no three offenses.
There is not even the slightest act of signaling. Why? Because the root exists. And further, it has already been stated:
"He says, 'This is ours; we have need of this and that. But he who [speaks] thus...
Without having [previously] said, "Give this to that person," one exchanges it; it remains exactly as it was in its original state.
Seeing a scavenger, one says, "Eat this rice, and then bring dye or firewood"; there is an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) for each count of the dye-skins and each count of the firewood.
[One says to] dentists and others, "Having eaten this rice, do such-and-such a thing."
If he has a craftsman fashion various implements such as a bellows, or has a washerman wash a cloth, it is a *yathāvatthuka* offense.
If he has a barber cut his hair, or has a laborer perform new construction work, it is likewise a *yathāvatthuka* offense.
However, if he does not say, "Having eaten this meal, do this," but rather says, "Eat this meal... [the offense is determined by the specific instruction].
If she says, "You have eaten, you will eat, do this," it is permissible. And here,
although there is no such thing as having to hand over one's own property— whether for washing clothes, cutting hair, or new work such as clearing the ground—
it is not possible to reject this [practice], because it was stated emphatically in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Therefore, just as one confesses a *pācittiya* offense when an article subject to forfeiture has been used or lost, so too here it must be confessed.
596. Regarding the phrase "one who perceives a trade as a trade," etc.:
whoever enters into a trade, whether he perceives that trade as such, or is in doubt about it, or does not perceive it as such, there is indeed a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offense.
In the *Cūḷattika*, the meaning should be understood as follows: in two instances, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
597. "He asks the value" means he asks, "What is the value of this bowl of yours?
But when [the other] replies, "It is worth this much," if his allowable goods are of great value, and he responds to him thus: "Lay follower, my..."
"This object is of great value; give your bowl to someone else.
Upon hearing this, the other says, "I will give you another dish as well," and thus it is permissible to take it; this falls under the definition stated as "this belongs to us.
If that bowl is of great value while the monk’s object is of little value, and the owner of the bowl [recognizes] its low value...
If he does not know [the value], the bowl must not be accepted; one should declare, "My property is of little value.
For if one accepts it after knowing its high value or by means of deception, one incurs the obligation to pay for the stolen goods once they have been appraised.
If the owner of the bowl gives it saying, "Very well, venerable sir, let the remainder be my merit," it is permissible.
“He points it out to the kappiyakāraka” means that, setting aside the person from whose hand he takes the goods, he designates another— even if only his own son or brother—
as the kappiyakāraka and says, “Let this one take such-and-such and give it to you.
If that person is clever and repeatedly takes it away or disputes over it, one should remain silent.
If there is no substitute, and he does not know how to take it, the merchant deceives him; he should be told, "Do not take it.
Regarding the phrase "This is ours," etc., he says: "This oil or ghee has been accepted by us and is ours;
we have need of something else that has not been accepted. If, after taking that, he gives him something else, [the first...]
One must not have one’s own oil measured. Why? Because there might be oil remaining in the measuring tube; if one were to measure it later, that which has not been formally accepted would be spoiled.
The rest is self-evident. It is originated by six bases; it is an action;

it is not released through perception; it is without mental consciousness; it is an offense of formal rule; it consists of bodily and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning buying and selling is finished.
The second chapter, the Chapter on Silk, is finished.
3. The Chapter on Alms Bowls.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Alms Bowls (Patta-sikkhāpada) 598. "At that time" refers to the training rule concerning alms bowls.

In this context, "trading in alms bowls" means that while wandering through villages, market towns, and so forth, they will engage in the trade of alms bowls. "Or from a potter's shop": "pots" (āmattāni) are said to be vessels; these...
"Those whose wares they are, those are the potters; the shop of those potters is a 'potter's shop' (*āmattikāpaṇa*), meaning a shop of a merchant who sells the wares of a potter.
(602) "Three sizes for the bowl" means three measurements for the bowl.

"He takes a half-āḷhaka of boiled rice" means he takes boiled rice from two *nāḷis* of husked rice according to the Magadha measure. "The Magadha *nāḷi* is twelve and a half *palas*"—so it is said in the Andhaka Commentary.
It has been stated: "In the island of Siṃhala, the standard *nāḷi* is large; the Tamil *nāḷi* is small; the Magadha *nāḷi* is of the proper measure.
According to that Magadha *nāḷi*, one and a half *nāḷis* make one Siṃhala *nāḷi*"; thus it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
"A fourth part of solid food" (*catubhāgaṃ khādanaṃ*) means a portion of solid food equal to a fourth part of the rice; this refers to a hand-held quantity of bean soup (*muggasūpa*).

It should be understood according to its suitability. "Concomitant sauce" (*tadupiyaṃ byañjanaṃ*) refers to sauces such as fish, meat, vegetables, fruits, or shoots that are appropriate for that rice.

Herein is the detailed explanation: taking two Magadhan *nāḷis* of old, undamaged, well-husked, and purified rice grains, one prepares a porridge from those grains that is free of husks, not watery, not clumped together, very clear, and resembling a heap of jasmine buds.
Having cooked the boiled rice until it has drained and placed it all without remainder into the bowl,
one should add a bean soup made from all its constituent ingredients— measured at a fourth part of that rice, neither too thick nor too thin,
and easy to handle with the hand. Then, one should add condiments such as fish or meat, in portions corresponding to each mouthful, until enough is provided for the final mouthful.
However, substances such as ghee, oil, gruel-water, sour rice-gruel, and so forth, do not count [toward the limit];
for they belong to the same category as boiled rice, and one is unable either to subtract or to add them.
Thus, if all of this that has been placed [in the bowl] remains level with the lower rim of the bowl's mouth, then for one who cuts with a thread or a razor, whether it be the thread or the razor—
If it touches the lower edge, this is called the "superior" bowl.
If it stands piled up, having exceeded that line, this is called the "superior-inferior" bowl.
If it does not reach that line and remains entirely within it, this is called the "superior-superior" bowl.
"Nāḷikodana" means rice cooked with one Magadhan measure of rice-grains. "Patthodana" means half a nāḷi of rice cooked with one Magadhan measure [of rice].
The rest should be understood according to the method already stated. However, this is the distinction in name alone:
if all of it, beginning with nāḷikodana, is poured in and remains level with the lower line according to the stated method, this—
The bowl called "medium" (*majjhima*) is as follows: if, when placed upon a heap of rice, it stands over the middle line, this is the bowl called "medium-small" (*majjhimomaka*).
If it does not reach that middle line but remains entirely within it, this is the bowl called "medium-large" (*majjhimukkaṭṭha*).
If all the food, such as a handful of boiled rice, is poured in and it stands level with the bottom line, this is—
"Small" (*omaka*) refers to a bowl. If it stands beyond that line, piled up like a stupa, this is called the "very small" (*omakomaka*) bowl.
If it does not reach that line but remains within it, this is called the "small-inferior" (*omakukkaṭṭha*) bowl.
Thus, there are these nine bowls. Among them, two are not bowls: the "superior-superior" (*ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭha*) and the "very small" (*omakomaka*). "Superior to that... [and so on].

"Not obtained, inferior, not obtained"—this was said with reference to these two. For here, because it is superior even among the superior, the "superior" is called "not obtained" from that [standard];
and because it is inferior even among the inferior, the "inferior" is called "not obtained" from that [standard].
Therefore, these two may be used by way of being vessels for consumption, but they do not qualify as objects for formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna).
They do not require formal assignment (*vikappa*). However, the other seven types of bowls may be used either by making a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhahitvā*) or by assigning them to another.

If one exceeds ten days without doing so, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya pācittiya*); that is, for one who lets any of those seven kinds of bowls exceed the period of ten days, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

607. Regarding "using a bowl that has not been relinquished": after drinking rice-gruel and washing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); after eating a snack and eating a meal and washing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Thus, for each such act, there is an offense of wrong-doing. 608. Regarding "there is no offense if one resolves or designates it within ten days":

here, it should be understood that even a bowl of the correct measure must be fit for resolution or designation. A metal bowl is fit for resolution if it has undergone five firings; a clay bowl is fit for resolution if it has undergone two firings.

Both [the bowl and the robe] must be given; only when that has been given is it subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). If even one meal’s worth is lacking, or if even a mere *kākaṇika*’s worth of the price has not been paid, it does not become subject to formal determination.
Even if the owner of the bowl says, “When you have the price for it, you may give it then;
in the meantime, determine it and use it,” it still does not become subject to formal determination.

For if the cooking is incomplete, it does not reach the status of "cooked" (patta); and if the root has not been given—whether in its entirety or in part—it does not regain its own nature, but remains the property of another.
Therefore, it only becomes subject to formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) once both the cooking and the root are finished.
That which is subject to determination is also subject to assignment (vikappana); thus, whether it has come into one's hand or not, it must be formally determined.

Or it may be assigned. For if the bowl-maker, having obtained the materials, either wishes to give them himself or says, "Venerable sir, having made a bowl for you, I shall set it aside after firing it on such-and-such a day," and the monk lets ten days pass beyond that appointed date, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). But if...
The bowl-maker says, “I will make a bowl for you, cook it, and send the message,” and does exactly so;

yet the monk sent by him does not inform that monk. However, another person, having seen or heard of it, informs him, saying, “Venerable sir, your bowl is finished. This report is not authoritative. But when—
If he has been sent by that person and announces it, then for one who lets ten days pass from the day the word was heard,
there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). If the bowl-maker says, "I will make a bowl for you, cook it,
and send it in someone's hand," and does exactly so, then the monk who comes having taken the bowl— his own...
If, having placed it in the courtyard, he does not inform anyone, and someone else says, "Venerable sir, is that beautiful bowl you have recently brought back?
[and one asks], "Friend, where is the bowl? [and they reply], "It has been sent into the hands of such-and-such a person"—even the word of this person is not authoritative.
However, when that monk gives away the bowl, from the day it was received, for ten days...

For one who lets it exceed [ten days], there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. Therefore, before ten days have elapsed, it must either be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) or assigned (*vikappetabba*).
In this regard, there are two ways of determining the bowl: one determines it by means of the body, or one determines it by means of speech.
When determining it according to those methods, one should say, "I relinquish this bowl," or "I relinquish that bowl."
Either in the presence of others or behind their backs, having set aside an old bowl or given it to another, one should—
having touched with the hand a new bowl wherever it may be placed—
make a mental application by thinking, "I resolve upon this bowl," and then resolve it either by means of the body through a physical gesture, or by means of speech through vocal expression.
Or it may be determined by means of speech. In this regard, there are two ways of determining:
if it is within arm’s reach, one should break the seal with the words, “I determine this bowl.
But if it is inside a room, on an upper terrace, or in a neighboring monastery, one should observe the place where it is kept and break the seal with the words, “I determine this bowl.”
When performing the formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it is permissible to determine it alone, and it is also permissible to determine it in the presence of another.

This is the benefit of being in the presence of another: if doubt should arise as to whether or not one’s determination has been properly made, the other person will remind one and cut through that doubt. If someone obtains ten bowls and [wishes to] determine them all...
If he wishes to use it for himself alone, he need not resolve upon all of them. Having resolved upon one bowl, on the following day he should relinquish that one and resolve upon another.
By this method, it is possible to maintain [the practice] even for a hundred years.
Could there be a loss of the resolution for a bhikkhu who is thus diligent? There could be. For if he [should lose the bowl]...

Or he gives it to another, or he disrobes, or he renounces the training, or he dies, or his gender changes, or he relinquishes it, or there is a hole in the bowl, or the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is lost. And this has been said:
“Given away, disrobed, renounced, By death, and by the change of gender;”
“By the removal of the *liṅga* (the sign) and by a hole—it becomes [non-robe] with the seventh.
One also abandons it through being stolen by thieves or through taking it on trust. By what size of hole does the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) break?
By one through which a grain of *kaṅgu* rice can both exit and enter. For this is the smallest grain of the seven types of grain.
If it has been restored to its original state by means of iron filings or a peg within ten days, it must be formally resolved upon (adhiṭṭhātabba) again within those same ten days.
This, first of all, is the analysis regarding formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) in the context of the rule: "He resolves or designates (vikappeti) within ten days.
As for designation (vikappana), there are two kinds of designation: face-to-face designation (sammukhā-vikappanā) and behind-the-back designation (parammukhā-vikappanā). How [is this so]?

What is face-to-face assignment (*sammukhā-vikappanā*)? Having ascertained whether the bowls are one or many, and whether they are present or absent, one should say, "This bowl," or "These bowls," or "That bowl," or "Those bowls," and then say, "I assign this to you.
This is one type of face-to-face assignment. Up to this point, it is permissible to store them away or to use them.
It is not permitted to dispose of it or to make a formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) over it.
However, if one says, "Use what belongs to me, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit," then this is called relinquishment (paccuddhāra);
from that point on, its use and so forth are permitted.
Another method: having likewise ascertained whether the bowls are one or many,
and whether they are present or absent, one should say in the presence of that same bhikkhu,
"this bowl" or "these bowls," or "that bowl" or "those bowls," and then state the name of whichever among the five fellow practitioners one prefers.
Having taken it, one should say: “I dedicate this to the monk Tissa,” or “I dedicate this to the nun Tissa, the trainee Tissa, the novice Tissa, or the female novice Tissa.
This is another form of *sammukhā-vikappanā* (dedication in the presence). Up to this point, it is permissible to set it aside;
however, for any of the purposes such as personal use, it is not permissible at all. Then that monk [should say]: “To Tissa...”

When it is said, “Use the property belonging to a bhikkhu… [and so on] … use the property belonging to the novice Tissa, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit,” this is called *paccuddhāra* (renunciation).
From that point onward, even its use and so forth are permissible.
How does renunciation in the absence of the person (*parammukhā-vikappanā*) take place? It is the same as for bowls, whether they be one or many, and whether they be present or absent.
Having recognized [the bowl], one should say, "This bowl" or "These bowls," or "That bowl" or "Those bowls," and then say, "I give this for your formal assignment (vikappana).
He should then ask, "Who is your friend or acquaintance?
Thereupon, the other should reply in the same manner as before: "Three monks... or "...three female novices."
Then that bhikkhu should say, "I give [this] to the bhikkhu Tissa," or... pe... "I give it to the novice nun Tissā.
This is an assignment in the absence (*parammukhā-vikappanā*). To this extent, it is permissible to set it aside;

however, for any purpose such as personal use and so forth, not even one of these is permissible. But by that bhikkhu, in the manner already described for the second assignment in the presence (*dutiyasammukhā-vikappanā*)—

When it is said, “Use what belongs to so-and-so, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit,” this is called *paccuddhāra* (renunciation). From that point on, even using it for one’s own enjoyment and so forth is permissible.

However, the distinction between these two types of *vikappanā* (assignment) and the entire remaining sequence of words, along with their origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors, should be understood according to the method already explained in the commentary on the first *kaṭhina*-training rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning cloths (*patta-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning less than five mends (*ūnapañca-bandhana-sikkhāpada*). 609.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning less than five mends. Regarding this, "he does not get by": it is said that if he...

The noble disciple would not have survived; he would have undergone a change of state, being so tormented by them. However, because he was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), he did not survive by means of his body alone.
Therefore it is said: “He could not sustain himself, and even his wife and children were exhausted.
612–3. Regarding the phrase “with less than five bonds”: here, one who has less than five bonds is called “one with less than five bonds” (*ūnapañcabandhana*).
The meaning is that the five bonds do not fill up for him; thus, it is "by one who has fewer than five bonds. The instrumental case is used here to denote a characteristic of such a person.

In this regard, since even for one who is entirely without bonds (abandhana), the five bonds do not fill up because they are utterly non-existent, the word-commentary states, "or one who is without bonds," and so forth. Furthermore, because it was stated as "by one with fewer than five bonds,"...
For one whose bowl has five binding points, that [bowl] is not a proper bowl; therefore, it is permissible to request another.

Furthermore, since this "binding" occurs only when there is a place for binding and does not occur when there is none, the following was said—"what is called 'without a binding place'"—in order to demonstrate its defining characteristic.
"There is not even a two-finger-width line" means that there is not even a single line measuring two finger-widths below the rim of the mouth.
"He for whom there is a two-finger-width line," however, refers to one who has such a single line;
having pierced it at its lower edge with a needle for leaves, and having cooked it, [he should tie it] with a cord of thread, a cord of hemp, or a cord of tin.
If it must be bound, that binding should be concealed with a triple-layered cloth or some kind of adhesive paste so that food does not stick to it.
That bowl should be used after having performed the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), or it may be bound after making a small hole [in the rim].
However, it is not permitted to bind it with pure substances such as honey, flour, molasses, resin, or lac.
After boiling down the molasses, it is appropriate to bind it with stone powder.
However, when pierced near the rim by a bowl-piercer, the vessel breaks because of the thickness of the rim; therefore, it should be pierced from below.
For one that has two lines, or even one line measuring four finger-breadths, two bindings should be applied. For one that has three [lines], or even one...
If it is six finger-breadths wide, it has three [fingers’ depth]. If it is four [fingers wide] or only one [finger deep], or eight [fingers wide], it has four [fingers’ depth].
If it is five [fingers wide] or only one [finger deep], or ten [fingers wide], it is not yet fit even if bound; it must be requested as something else.
This, then, is the determination regarding the clay bowl.

Regarding an iron bowl, even if it has five or more holes, if those holes have been closed with iron filings, lac, or a metal disk and are smooth, that very bowl may be used; no other should be requested.
However, if even a single hole is large, even if it is closed with a metal disk...
It is not smooth; food sticks to the bowl; it is unallowable; this is an improper bowl. Another one must be requested. 615.
"The Elder should be told" means that after showing the advantages of the bowl, he should be told: "Venerable sir, this bowl is of the right measure, beautiful, and suitable for an elder;
please accept it. "If he does not accept" refers to one who does not accept out of compassion.
An offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, there is no offense for one who, out of contentment, does not accept [the bowl], thinking, "What need have I for another bowl?
"The edge of the bowl" means a bowl that stands at the edge after having been turned over in this manner.
"Not in an improper place" means it must not be placed in an improper location such as on a bed, a chair, under a canopy, or on a door-bolt. Where the former...
If he places a beautiful bowl down, it should be placed in that very spot;
for the place for setting down a bowl has already been stated in the Khandhaka by way of the passage beginning, "I allow you, monks, a bowl-stand.
"Not by non-use" means it should not be used for purposes other than its intended function, such as for boiling gruel, fuel, dye, or cooking. On the way...
However, when illness has arisen and no other vessel is available, it is permissible to coat it with clay and use it to cook rice gruel or heat water.
"It must not be given away" means it must not be handed over to another. But if the *saddhivihārika* or the *antevāsika*...
If one sets aside another excellent bowl and takes it up, thinking, "This is suitable for me; this is for the Elder," it is permissible.
Or, if someone else takes that [bowl] and gives his own bowl, it is permissible. There is no need to say, "Bring my bowl.

Regarding the phrase "when [the Sangha] has finished the invitation" (*pavāritānaṃ*): in a place where the invitation has been performed by way of the Sangha, it is permissible only with a bowl having five joints. By way of an individual...
It is stated in the *Kurundi* that at a place where the formal invitation (*pavāraṇā*) has been performed, it is permissible even with less than five stitches. The rest here is self-evident.

It has six origins, is an action, is not liberated by perception, is without thought, is an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), is bodily and verbal action, involves three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule regarding less than five stitches is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Medicines (Bhesajja-sikkhāpada) 618.

"At that time" refers to the training rule on medicines. Regarding this, "It is well, venerable sir," [the King said] after seeing monks clearing away a mountain slope for the sake of a cave-dwelling for an elder who was sent by him;

wishing to give a monastery attendant, he asked. 619–21. "Separate" means distinct and alone. "Adorned with garlands" means one who has made a garland, a wearer of garlands; "decorated with flower-garlands."
The meaning is as follows. *Tiṇaṇḍupaka* means a grass cushion. *Paṭimuñci* means she placed it [on her head].
"It became a golden garland" means that as soon as it was placed on the girl's head, by the power of the Elder’s resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it became a garland of golden lotuses.
For as soon as that grass cushion was placed on her head, the Elder resolved: "Let this become a golden garland. A second time...
"He approached... [as before]...": he approached on the very second day. "He resolved that it be golden":
he determined, "Let it be made of gold. "Of the five medicinal tonics": of ghee and so forth. "Those who live in abundance":
those practicing for the sake of an abundance of requisites. "In jars and pots": here, "jars" (*kolamba*) refers to large-mouthed vessels.
They are so called. "Adhering and clinging" means they have dripped down from below and from both sides.
"Scattered and strewn" means scattered by those digging the ground with the smell of ghee and other substances, and strewn above by those digging the walls and those walking about.
"With storehouses inside" means having storehouses arranged within.

622. *Paṭisāyanīyāni* means things that should be tasted; the meaning is that they are to be consumed. *Bhesajjāni* (medicines) refers to those things so designated whether or not they perform the function of a medicine.

By first showing what is well-known in the world through terms such as "cow-ghee" (*gosappi*) and so forth, he then includes the ghee of other animals—such as deer, roe deer, and hares—by the phrase "the meat of which is allowable."
For those who have milk, they certainly have ghee as well; whether that be easy to obtain or difficult to obtain, it is mentioned for the sake of avoiding confusion. The same applies to butter.
"They may be used after being stored" means they may be used after having been kept in storage.

How so? Regarding the ghee and other substances mentioned in the Canon: first, as for ghee, having been received before midday, it is permissible to consume it both with food and without food on that same day before midday.
From after midday onwards, it may be consumed without food for seven days.
If the seven-day period has elapsed, if it was kept in a single vessel, there is one *nissaggiya* offense. If...
There are *nissaggiya* offenses according to the number of items. What is received after midday is permitted only for seven days provided it is free from meat.
What has been set aside—whether before or after midday—is not permitted to be consumed;
however, it may be applied as an ointment or for similar purposes. Even if the seven-day limit is exceeded, there is no offense, provided it is not intended for consumption.

Because it is stated [in the Vinaya]: "They are to be exchanged. If one who is not ordained makes ghee out of fresh butter received before midday and gives it, it is permissible to consume it with food before midday.
If he prepares it himself, it is permissible to consume it even for seven days provided it is without food.
However, if ghee is made by anyone out of fresh butter received after midday, [it is permissible for] seven days as well.

Only that which is non-material (nirāmisa) is permitted. The determination regarding what has been prepared using what was received should be understood according to the method of pure ghee explained previously.
Ghee made from milk or curd received before midday—even if prepared by one who is not fully ordained—is permitted on that same day before midday.
That which is made by oneself is permitted only as non-material. Regarding one who is heating butter (navanīta):
For it is not a case of cooking by oneself; however, it is not permissible to have food together with that which has been cooked by oneself.
Furthermore, it is likewise not permissible from after midday onwards. Even if seven days have elapsed, there is no offense, because it was received while still possessing its original substance;
for it is said, "having received those. However, regarding ointments and the like made from things received after midday—
It should be brought [to the monk]. If it was prepared by those who had received it before the meal, there is no offense for either party after seven days have passed.
This same principle applies to unallowable meat-ghee (*akappiyamaṃsasappi*). However, this is the distinction:

where a *nissaggiya* offense occurs due to ghee mentioned in the Canon, here there is a *dukkaṭa* offense. In the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, having stated a semblance of a reason, it refers to human ghee (*manussasappi*).
Butter and fresh butter are prohibited, yet that prohibition is ill-founded because they are permitted in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Furthermore, a detailed explanation regarding them will follow later.
Even fresh butter mentioned in the Canon, if received before midday, is permissible on that same day even when mixed with food.

From the time after the meal onwards, it is purely non-material. If seven days have elapsed, they are subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*): according to the number of vessels when placed in various vessels;
and according to the number of lumps when placed as individual morsels, even if not mixed together in a single vessel.
What is received after the meal is to be understood in the same manner as clarified butter (*sappi*). In this regard, however, even curd-balls and even drops of buttermilk [are included].

"Therefore, it is permissible to eat that [curd] once it has been washed," said the Half-Elder (Upaḍḍhatthera). However, the Elder Mahāsīva said, "From the time it was permitted by the Blessed One, they ate it as soon as it had been removed from the buttermilk.
Therefore, one who consumes butter should wash it and eat it after removing the curd, buttermilk, flies, ants, and so forth.

If one wishes to cook ghee and consume it after making it, it is permissible to cook it even if it has not been washed. The intention here is that whatever curd or buttermilk remains therein will perish;
for to this extent, it is not considered "received with a physical basis" (savatthuka-paṭiggahita).
However, because it has been cooked together with the food offering (āmisa), they feel scruples regarding it as well.
Regarding those who are anxious: now, the entire method for the use or non-use of what is an offense and what is not an offense—

concerning fresh butter kept after having been received, fresh butter made from milk or curd received before the meal, fresh butter made from those received after the meal, fresh butter made from what was already received,
fresh butter made from what was not yet received, and unallowable meat-butter— should be understood according to the same sequence as that stated for ghee.
But for the monks who have entered for alms, they pour even ghee, fresh butter, cooked oil, and uncooked oil right there [into their bowls];
therein are drops of buttermilk and curd, grains of rice, husks of rice, flies, and so forth.
Having been cooked by the sun and strained, what is thus obtained is "seven-day medicine" (*sattāhakālika*).
Having accepted it, it is permissible to cook it together with medicines already kept on hand and even to make a nasal drop (*natthu-pāna*) from it.
If, at the time of the meal, a modest novice (*sāmaṇera*) releases the cooked food containing meat into the fire so that the rice grains and other ingredients that fell there do not burn,
and then filters it and cooks it again before giving it away, it is permissible for seven days according to the same method as before.
Regarding sesame oil: first, that which is received before the meal is permissible even if it contains food; from after the meal onwards, it must be entirely free of food.
However, if seven days elapse, its status as an *nissaggiya* (an offense requiring forfeiture) should be understood according to the number of containers.
That which is received after the meal is permissible for seven days only if it is entirely free of food. This applies to what has been set aside after being formally accepted (*uggahitaka*).
It is not permissible to swallow it; however, it may be applied to the head and so forth, and there is no offense even if seven days have elapsed.
Having accepted sesame seeds before midday, oil produced from them is permissible even if mixed with food before midday;
from after midday onwards, it becomes inedible, though it may be applied to the head and so forth, and there is no offense even if seven days have elapsed.
Having accepted sesame seeds after the meal, the oil produced from them is indeed not fit for consumption because it was accepted with its physical basis (the seeds) still present;

there is no offense even if seven days have elapsed, as it may be applied to the head, for anointing, and so forth. The same rule applies to oil made from sesame seeds that were received either before or after the meal.

If oil has been made by an unordained person before midday—either by splitting sesame seeds that were received before midday, or by steaming sesame flour, or by moistening it with warm water—it is permissible even if it contains food residue (*sāmisam*).

However, oil made by oneself is permissible before midday only when it is free of food residue (*nirāmisam*), because it has been extracted; since it was personally prepared, it is not permissible if it contains food residue.
However, because it has been accepted with a physical basis (a vessel), both [types of oil] are inedible from the time after the meal onwards;
they may be applied to the head and so forth, and there is no offense even if seven days elapse.

If, however, the warm water is only a small amount, sufficient merely for sprinkling, it is not considered a formal offense, as it does not count toward the limit of cooking by oneself. This also applies to mustard seeds, sesame oil, and the like.
Regarding those things accepted without a physical base (*avatthuka*), the legal determination for sesame oil and oil without a base is similar to what has been stated.
However, if it is possible to make oil from the powders of mustard seeds and so forth accepted before midday through cooking in the sun, that is permitted even with food (*sāmiṣa*) before midday;
from after midday onwards, it must be entirely without food (*nirāmiṣa*). Upon the passing of seven days, [it becomes an offense].

It is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). However, since they prepare oil by first steaming mustard seeds, *madhuka* powder, and so forth, and then roasting castor seeds, the oil made by those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) is permissible even with food before the midday meal.
Furthermore, because these substances are lifelong requisites, there is no fault in accepting them along with their base materials. By oneself...

It should be consumed for seven days using only non-material (nirāmisa) enjoyment. Oil made from mustard seeds, madhuka, or castor seeds that have been accepted for the purpose of making oil is "seven-day time-limited" (sattāhakālika);

if it was made from materials already stored, it is not fit to be swallowed but is permitted for external use, and there is no offense even if it exceeds seven days. Oil made from such substances after they have been accepted is valid for seven days.

That which was made on the second day is permissible for six days. That which was made on the third day is permissible for five days. That which was made on the fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day is permissible only for that very day.
If it remains until sunrise, it is subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). That which was made on the eighth day is not fit for consumption;
however, because it is not subject to forfeiture, it is permissible for external use. Even if...
If one does not [use it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for exceeding seven days with mustard seeds and so forth taken for the purpose of oil.
However, there are other oils not mentioned in the *Pāḷi*, such as those from coconut, *nimba*, *kosamba*, *karamanda*, *atasī*, and so on;

for one who accepts these and exceeds seven days, there is an offense of wrong-doing. This is the distinction between them. The rest concerns the category of food to be consumed only during the day (*yāvakālika*).

Having observed the rules regarding lifetime medicines, the entire procedure concerning self-cooked food, food received before the meal, and food received after the meal should be understood according to the method already stated. 623.
Regarding "animal fats and oils": "Monks, I allow animal fats as medicines: bear fat, fish fat..."
“Pig’s fat,” “boar’s fat,” and “donkey’s fat”—this refers to the oil from permitted fats.
And here, by the mention of “bear’s fat,” the fat of all unallowable meats is permitted, with the exception of human fat.
Furthermore, by the inclusion of “fish,” the susukā is also included; however, it is mentioned separately because it is a predatory fish. And by the inclusion of “fish and so forth” here—
The fat of all permissible meats is permitted. Among meats, however, the flesh of humans, elephants, horses, dogs, snakes, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas is impermissible.
Among fats, only human fat is impermissible. Regarding milk and other such liquids, there is nothing that is impermissible.
Fat-oil extracted by those who are not ordained (anupasampanna) and processed by them, if received before midday—even if it contains solid food—is permissible before midday.
It is permissible. From after the meal onwards, it is permissible for seven days provided it is entirely without meat.
However, whatever therein resembles fine dust—whether meat, sinew, bone, or blood—that is not considered an offense (*abbohārika*).
But if, having received fat, one prepares it oneself, having received it before the meal, cooked it, and strained it, it may be used for seven days as a non-meat substance.
It may be consumed. For this was said with reference to non-material consumption:
"What was received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time may be consumed as an oil-consumption.
Even in that case, what is not allowable is indeed not allowable. However, it is certainly not permitted to receive or to prepare [food] after the meal has been finished. For this has been said:
“Monks, if one should consume what was received at an improper time, cooked at an improper time, and mixed together at an improper time, there is an offense of three *dukkaṭas*.

Monks, if one should consume what was received at a proper time, but cooked at an improper time and mixed together at an improper time, there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*. Monks, if [what was] received at a proper time...”
“If one should consume what was received at the proper time, cooked at the improper time, and mixed [with other things], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
But if, monks, it was received at the proper time, cooked at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time, and one should consume it, there is no offense.
Then the resident pupils asked the Elder Upatissa: “Venerable sir, having cooked ghee, fresh butter, and fat together...”
“Are they allowable, or are they not allowable?”—“They are not allowable, friend. It is said that the Elder felt scruples here as if he were stepping on a cake of ghee.

Then they asked him further: “Venerable sir, if there is a lump of curd or a drop of buttermilk in the butter, is that allowable?”—“That too, friend, is not allowable. Then they said to him: “Venerable sir, …”
“By cooking them together, they become blended and potent, and thus they suppress disease,” he said. “Very well, friend,” the Elder accepted.
But the Elder Mahāsumma said, “Permissible meat and fat are allowed for use when there is food; the other is allowed for use when there is no food.
However, the Elder Mahāpaduma, after rejecting it by asking, “What is this? [said], “Are not there monks afflicted by wind-disorders?”

"By adding the five roots, *sāvaya*, *āguya*, clear oil, pork fat, and so forth to the gruel and drinking it, that gruel—being rich in heat (*tejussadattā*)—subdues the disease," he said, and added, "It is permissible.
As for honey (*madhu*), it means the honey of bees; that is, by honey-bees, which are small bees, and by bumblebees.
And honey has been prepared. That which was received before midday may be consumed with meat before midday;
from after midday onwards, it may only be consumed without meat for seven days.
If, upon the lapse of the seven days, the great honey—which resembles molasses—has been kept cut into pieces, or otherwise placed in various vessels, [it remains permissible].
The forfeiture offenses are determined by the number of items. If there is only one piece, or if they are in a single vessel, there is only one offense of forfeiture.
That which has been stored should be understood according to the method already stated; it may be applied to the ointment for wounds and so forth.
If honeycomb or honey-cakes are not smeared with honey and are pure, they are to be kept for life. If they are smeared with honey...
But [this] is indeed of the same category as honey. "Cīrikā" refers to long-winged flies; and those called *tumbala* are black large bees with bony wings.
In their dwellings there is honey resembling resin (*niyyāsa*), which is permissible for life (*yāvajīvika*).
"Phāṇita" is that which is produced from sugarcane, derived from sugarcane juice, whether uncooked or partially cooked (*avatthukapakkā*).

All varieties of sugarcane products, including molasses, should be understood as being without a [fixed] basis. That molasses, if received before midday, is permissible even if it contains solid food;
from after midday onwards, it is permissible for seven days only if it is free from solid food.

If the seven-day period is exceeded, there is an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya) according to the number of bases. Even many lumps, having been ground into powder, may be placed in a single vessel.
If they form a solid mass, it is a single offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*). The method for what has been stored should be understood according to the same procedure already stated;

it may be applied to the fumigation of houses and similar uses. If molasses is made from unstrained sugarcane juice received before midday, and it was prepared by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), it is permissible even if containing food (*sāmiṣa*).
If it was prepared by oneself, it is permissible only if it is free from food (*nirāmiṣa*). After midday...
However, from that point on, because it has been accepted with a physical base (*savatthuka*), it is not fit for consumption; there is no offense even if seven days have passed.
Even if it is prepared after midday using what was accepted without having been strained, it is still not fit for consumption;

there is no offense even if seven days have passed. This same principle applies to molasses made from sugarcane that was accepted [after midday]. But if it is prepared before midday using what was accepted after having been strained—
If it was made by one who is not fully ordained, it is permissible even with meat before the meal;

from after the meal onwards, for seven days, it must be without meat. If it was made by oneself, it must be without meat even before the meal. However, if it was made by one who has received it through a water-strainer after the meal, it is permissible for seven days provided it is without meat.
The same method applies to what was made by one who has memorized the instructions. "Baked sugarcane treacle..."
"Or crushed sugarcane treacle is permissible even before the meal," so it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, after posing the question, "Is this cooked [treacle] with its base (the sugarcane) permissible or not?
it is stated: "There is no such thing as 'not to be used after the meal' regarding sugarcane treacle. That [latter view] is correct. [This applies to] honey-plant flower treacle made with cold water.
Before the meal, it is permissible [to consume] that which contains meat; from after the meal onwards, for seven days, it must be entirely without meat.
If the seven-day period is exceeded, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the number of instances. Honey-syrup made by adding milk is "timely" (*yāvakālika*).
As for sugar and candied sugar, they are purified by removing the milk-impurities; therefore, it is permissible. However, *madhuka* flowers [are permissible] before the meal.
It is permissible [to eat] raw; it is also permissible [to eat] roasted. Having roasted them, it is permissible even if they are ground, whether mixed with sesame seeds and the like or unmixed.
However, if one takes them and uses them for the purpose of making fermented liquor (*meraya*), then once they have been processed, they are not permissible from the moment they become seeds.
This applies to all fruits that are to be consumed within the same day (*yāvakālika*), such as plantains, dates, mangoes, *labuja* nuts, jackfruit, tamarinds, and so forth.
Treacle is indeed to be used only within the time-limited period (*yāvakālika*). When they prepare treacle with black pepper and other ingredients, that is for life-long use (*yāvajīvika*).

Regarding "having accepted them": even if one accepts all of them and places them together in a single jar without separating them, upon the lapse of seven days, there is only one offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
If they have been separated, there are five offenses of relinquishment. However, during the seven days...
Without exceeding the limit, it may be consumed at will—by one who is ill as well as by one who is not—in accordance with the method already stated.

For there are seven kinds of "specified" (odissa) gifts: specified by illness, specified by person, specified by time, specified by occasion, specified by place, specified by dwelling, and specified by medicine.
In this context, "specified for illness" means: "Monks, I allow raw meat and raw blood in the case of a non-human affliction.
Thus it was permitted specifically for that illness; it is allowable only for one who is afflicted by that very ailment, and not for anyone else.
Furthermore, it is indeed allowable at any time—whether during the proper time or the improper time—and whether it is permissible or impermissible.
"Prescribed for a specific individual" (puggalodissa) means: "Monks, I allow the rumination of one who ruminates.

But, monks, it must not be swallowed after having been brought out through the mouth-opening. Thus, what is permitted specifically for a particular individual is allowable only for that person, not for anyone else.
Regarding what is called *kālodissa*: “Monks, I allow you to give four kinds of great filth—excrement, urine, ash, and clay”—this was permitted specifically for the time of being bitten by a snake;
at that very time, it is allowable even if not formally accepted, but not at any other time.

"Designated by occasion" (*samayodissa*) means: those non-offenses permitted with reference to specific occasions in such passages as "except on an occasion, there is no offense for eating in a group"; these are non-offenses only at that particular time, not at other times. "Designated by place" (*desodissa*) means:

ordination and so forth permitted with reference to border regions, such as "I allow you, monks, in such frontier districts to confer ordination by a group of five including one who is an expert in the Vinaya"; these [acts] are [permitted] only in that very place.
They are permissible, but not in the Middle Country.
Regarding "fat" (*vasā*): it is that which was permitted by the Blessed One with the words, "Monks, I allow medicinal fats";
excluding human fat, the oil of all permissible and impermissible fats may be used for those who require it, according to the rules for the use of oil.
It is permissible to consume them.
"Medicines" (bhesajja) refers to those permitted by the name of medicine in the passage:
"I allow you, monks, five medicines"—namely, ghee, butter, oil, honey, and molasses—which are capable of serving as food. These...

Having accepted them, they may be used as one pleases during that same day before the meal; however, from after the meal onwards, provided there is a valid reason, they may be used for seven days in the manner already described.

(624) "If more than seven days have passed and one perceives that they have passed, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). Even if the amount is only the size of a mustard seed, or even if taken once with a finger merely to taste it on the tongue, it must indeed be forfeited and an offense of expiation confessed.
"It should not be used for bodily enjoyment" means that one must not smear the body or the sores on the body with them.
Things smeared by those [sores], such as the saffron robes, walking sticks, sandals, foot-rests, bedsteads, chairs, and so forth, are also unfit for use.
According to the *Mahāpaccarī*, "Even on the door-panels and window-shutters, the places where they are grasped with the hand must not be smeared."
It is said: “But having mixed it with astringent substances, the doors, windows, and door-panels should be smeared with it”—thus it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā.
“There is no offense if one resolves upon it within seven days”: if, within the interval of seven days, one resolves upon ghee, oil, fat, head-oil, or an ointment;
or honey as a salve for wounds; or molasses; or house-smoke—there is no offense.
If one wishes to pour consecrated oil into a vessel containing unconsecrated oil,
and if the vessel has a fine hole such that each drop of oil poured in is submerged by the old oil, it must be consecrated again. However,
if the opening is large and much oil enters at once, submerging the old oil, it need not be consecrated again.
There is no need for a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). For that [object] follows the destiny of what has already been resolved upon.
By this same method, it should also be understood that even if unresoluted oil is poured into a vessel of resoluted oil. 625.
Regarding the phrase "he relinquishes": here, if the property belonging to two people has been accepted by one and remains undivided, [it is not considered relinquished].
If seven days have passed, there is no offense for either of them; however, it is not permitted to consume [the medicine].
If the one who received it says to the other, "Friend, please use this oil for just seven days," and the other does not use it, whose offense is there?
There is no offense for anyone. Why? Because it was relinquished by the one who received it.
Because the other has not accepted it.
"It perishes" means it becomes unfit for use. Regarding the phrases "by what is abandoned," etc.:

that mind by which the medicine is abandoned (*catta*), vomited (*vanta*), or released (*mutta*) is itself called "abandoned, vomited, or released. By that mind, the person is without regard [for the medicine].
It is said: "Thus, having given it to a novice without expectation" is the meaning. Why was this stated? The Elder Mahāsumma said:
"In order to show that there is no offense for one who, having given it within seven days, subsequently receives it back and uses it.
However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "This should not be requested; for regarding what was given within seven days, if it is used again..."
“There is no offense at all. However, this was said for the purpose of showing that there is no offense in using [the medicine] after seven days have passed.

Therefore, if a novice, having prepared or not having prepared it, should give such medicine as has been given to that bhikkhu for the purpose of nasal treatment, he may take it and perform the nasal treatment. If he is a fool...
If he has [the oil] but does not know how to give it, another monk should say to him: "Sāmaṇera, do you have oil?
"Yes, venerable sir, I have it. "Bring it; we shall prepare medicine for the Elder. In this way, too, it is permissible.
The rest is self-evident.

The origin of the offense is by way of the *kathina* (formal robe-making ceremony); it is non-intentional, not associated with liberation through perception, without consciousness, an offense by rule, consisting of bodily and verbal action, associated with three types of consciousness, and associated with three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning medicines is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Rain-Cloak (Vassikasāṭika) 626.

"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning the rain-cloak. Therein, "the rain-cloak was permitted" means it was permitted in the Cīvarakkhandhaka in the context of the story of Visākhā. "Even beforehand" means prior [to the end of the rainy season]. 627.

"One month remains of the summer" means one of the last months of the four summer months remains. "Having made" means by way of the completion of sewing, dyeing, and the formal authorization (*kappa*).
Having finished [the robe]. And while making it, one should determine it as a single [robe] at the proper time; it is not permitted to determine two.
"When more than a month remains of the summer" means when more than a month remains of that which is called the summer season.
Regarding the phrase "having made it when more than half a month remains of the summer, he puts it on," the field for seeking the *vassikasāṭika* (rainy-season robe) is established here.
The field is fourfold: the field of performance, the field of wearing, and the field of determination.
The time is twofold: the time of the belly and the time of the back. One should understand that there are two tetrads: the tetrad of the time of the back and the tetrad of the time of the belly.
In this regard, from the full-moon day of Jeṭṭha-Mūla and the following first-day-of-the-month (pāṭipada) until the Uposatha of the dark fortnight—

This one half-month is both the field for seeking and the field for making. For within this interval, it is permissible to seek and to make up a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) that has not yet been obtained;
however, it is not permissible to wear it or to formally resolve upon its use.
From the last *pāṭipada* day following the observance day (*uposatha*) of the dark fortnight until the full moon of Āsāḷhī, this is one [period].
"Half a month is the period for all three: seeking, making, and wearing.
For within this interval, it is permissible to seek, to make, and to wear; however, it is not permissible to resolve [upon the robe].
From the first day of the fortnight following the full moon of Āsāḷhī until the full moon of Kattika—these four months are the period for seeking, making, wearing, and resolving.
The field of four kinds. For within this interval, it is permissible to seek what has not been obtained, to make use of what has been obtained, to wear it, and to resolve upon it.
This, first of all, is the fourfold field that should be understood.
Furthermore, from the first day following the full moon of Kattika until the full moon of Jeṭṭhamūla—

These seven months are called the "back-season. For, during this interval, if one—having given rise to the thought [of needing] in the manner beginning with, "It is time for a rain-cloak"—causes a rain-cloak robe to be produced from a place where one is not invited by a person unrelated [to oneself], there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) under this training rule.
[This applies when one says: "Give me a rain-cloak robe," and so forth.

For one who causes [the robe] to be produced after making a request according to the prescribed method, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) under the training rule concerning requests from those not related (*aññātakaviññatti-sikkhāpada*).

Likewise, for one who causes it to be produced from a place where one is invited by a relative after having aroused mindfulness in the manner already stated, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture under this very same training rule.
For one who causes it to be produced after making a request, there is an offense under the training rule concerning requests from those not related.
There is no offense. For this has been stated in the Parivāra:
"One may ask one's mother for a robe, even if it has not been assigned to the Saṅgha;
by what would there be an offense for him? There is no offense regarding a relative."
“This question was thought out by the wise.
For this question was spoken with reference to this meaning. Thus should the “Fourfold Set on the Back” be understood.
Furthermore, from the first day of the waning moon following the full moon of Jeṭṭha (Jyeṣṭha) until the full moon of Kattika (Kārttika),...

These five months are called the "period of the womb. For during this interval, if one—having aroused mindfulness in the manner described—procures a *vassikasāṭika* robe from a person who is unknown and has not invited one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the breach of the rule.

However, if those people have given a *vassikasāṭika* robe previously, even if they are currently unknown and have not invited one, there is no breach of the rule; for in their case, it is necessary to arouse mindfulness.

Because it has been permitted: for one who causes [a robe] to be produced after making a request, there is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* offense under the training rule concerning requests from those not related (*aññātakaviññatti-sikkhāpada*).
This, however, applies even to those who normally give rain-cloths (*vassikasāṭika*).

For one who, having aroused mindfulness in the manner already described, causes [the robe] to be produced from a place where relatives have invited [one to accept], there is no offense under this training rule. Regarding the request...
For one who makes [something] and brings it to completion, there is no offense under the training rule concerning requesting from an unrelated person (*aññātakaviññatti*).

The statement, "One should not say, 'Give to me,'" was indeed spoken with reference specifically to the time of seeking when the person is an unrelated one and has not been invited. Thus should the fourfold set regarding the stomach be understood.

Regarding the rule, "If one, being naked, causes the body to be rained upon, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," here the offense is determined not by counting the drops of water, but by way of the conclusion of the bath.

For every instance [of using it], he should be made to undergo an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, there is no offense for one bathing with water fallen from the sky onto an open courtyard;
nor is there an offense for one bathing with water poured from jars in a bathhouse, a pond, or similar places.
Regarding the phrase "the rainy season is postponed": if, when the last month of the hot season has arrived, the *vassikasāṭika* (rainy-season robe) sought out [for that purpose]...
Having spent one month, they further postpone the first month of the rainy season and treat it as the last month of the summer;
the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloak) should then be washed and stored. It may be used for two months without being formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhita*) or assigned to another (*avikappita*).
On the day of entering the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyika*), it must be resolved upon. If, through forgetfulness or because it is insufficient, [it is not resolved upon],...
Or if it has not been made, he receives a privilege for six months—two months of the rainy season and four months [of the dry season].
