However, if the *kaṭhina* is spread in the month of Kattika, he receives another four months; thus, there are ten months.
Beyond that, if one sets aside the basic robe (*mūlacīvara*) with the expectation of receiving more, there is a further one-month [privilege].

In this way, one receives the exemption for eleven months. However, if it has been obtained and completed within the rains-retreat (vassa), from one or two days up until ten days before the commencement of the rains, the commentaries do not discuss when it should be determined (adhiṭṭhātabba).
But if it is completed within ten days starting from the day it was obtained, then it may be determined during that same ten-day period.

It must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*). If ten days have elapsed since its completion, it must be determined on that very day. If ten days have not yet passed, one must not let the robe-season (*cīvarakāla*) expire—this is our own opinion.
Why? Because [the Blessed One] said: "Monks, I allow you to determine the three robes, but not to assign them [to another];
the rain-bathing cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) may be determined for the four months of the rainy season, but after that, it may be assigned."

For it has been said thus. Therefore, there is no offense even if ten days have elapsed prior to the commencement of the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyikā*). And it has been said: "An extra robe may be kept for at most ten days.

Therefore, if a robe is obtained and finished within the rainy season—whether one, two, or more days before the commencement of the rains retreat, up until the tenth day—it must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) within those ten days or on that very day, according to the method already described.
If ten days are not sufficient, one must not let the robe-season pass by.
In this regard, it might be argued that because of the statement, "One may determine [the robe] for four months of the rains," it is permissible to determine it at any time within those four months.
If that were so, then why is it said, "One may determine the itch-covering cloth for as long as the illness lasts"?
It has also been stated that even that [period] might have to be exceeded by ten days. And if that were so, it would contradict the rule: “An extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days.
Therefore, one should accept exactly what was stated above; otherwise, having found another firm reason, one should abandon [this interpretation].
Furthermore, it is said in the *Kurundi* at the conclusion of the section on offenses involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*): “When?”
Should it be determined? Once finished within ten days from the day it was obtained, it must be determined within that same ten-day period.
If one is unable to do so, one receives the privilege [of not determining it] until the full moon of Kattika.
630. Regarding “one whose robe has been stolen”: this was said specifically with reference to the *vassikasāṭikā* (the rainy-season robe). For those who are naked, it is indeed that very robe.

There is no offense in causing rain to fall upon the body. In this context, a "calamity" refers to a danger from thieves that befalls one who is bathing after putting on a costly rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*).
The rest here is self-evident. It arises from six origins; it is an action;

it is not dissociated from perception; it is without mental intention; it is an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*); it consists of bodily and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness; and it involves three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭika*) is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Taking Away a Robe (*cīvaraacchindana-sikkhāpada*) 631.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning taking away a robe. In this context, the phrase "whatever they may say to you" means whatever they may say to you... [text continues].
“I am. It is said that he gave [the items], thinking, “He will set out on the journey with me, carrying my bowl, robes, sandals, and rugs.
Therefore he spoke thus. “Seized” means he took them by force; however, because he took them under the impression that they were his own, there was no *pārājika* offense.
Since he seized them after causing distress, an offense was prescribed.
633. “If one takes [robes] oneself, it is a *nissaggiya pācittiya*”: for one who takes away many robes that are joined together as one, there is a single offense.

For one who takes away many robes that are not joined together and are standing separately, and who causes them to be brought back by saying, “Bring the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), bring the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*),” there are offenses according to the number of items. “Those given by me...”
Even for one who says, "Bring all of them," there are numerous offenses by means of that single utterance.
"If he instructs another, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)": if he instructs, "Take the robe-cloth," it is one offense of wrong-doing.
When the one instructed takes many, it is one offense of expiation (pācittiya), as in the case of one saying with his voice, "Take the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi), take the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga)."
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the speech. For one who says, "Take all that was given by me," there are numerous offenses for a single utterance.
634. "Another requisite" means anything at all, even down to a needle, with the exception of the last robe that is permissible for assignment (vikappanupaga).
Even in the case of needles set aside after being wrapped, there are offenses of wrong-doing according to the number of items. It is the same for those wrapped loosely.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that if they are tied with a tight knot, there is only one *dukkaṭa*. The same principle applies even when they are placed inside a needle-case.
The same principle applies to medicinal substances such as *tikaṭuka* and so forth, whether they have been placed in a bag and tied loosely or tied tightly. 635.
"Or he gives it" means he gives it saying, "Venerable sir, this is suitable for you alone," or alternatively, [he gives it thinking], "He will give it."
“Friend, we gave you this robe thinking, ‘He will perform his duties, he will take formal admission from us, and he will master the Dhamma.
Yet now, you do not perform your duties, you do not take formal admission, and you do not master the Dhamma.
When addressed with such words, [he replied], “Venerable sir, I suppose you speak thus for the sake of a robe.”
If he gives it saying, "This robe is for you," in this way he gives it. Or, if a young monk has gone away in another direction, he says, "Make him turn back.
If he does not turn back, [the teacher] says, "Take the robe and hold him back. If he turns back in this manner, that is well.
If he gives it saying, "I suppose you are speaking for the sake of the bowl and robe; take them," in this way too...
Either he gives it back himself, or seeing that [the student] has disrobed, he says: "We gave you the bowl and robes thinking, 'He will perform the duties for you';

now you have gone away after disrobing. The other replies, "Take back your bowl and robes," and thus he gives it back. Or he says: "I give them only to one who takes the formal support (upajjhāya) from me; to one who takes it elsewhere, I do not."
"I will not give. I give only to one who performs his duties, not to one who does not; I give only to one who masters the Dhamma, not to one who does not;
I give only to one who does not disrobe, not to one who disrobes"—giving in this manner is not permitted;
for one who gives thus, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, it is permitted to have [the robe] brought back. This refers to what was given after having renounced it.
One who takes [the robe] by snatching it away must be dealt with according to the value of the article. The rest here is self-evident.

This [offense] has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (kiriya), released through perception (saññāvimokkha), accompanied by consciousness (sacittaka), a fault censured by the world (lokavajja), consisting of bodily and vocal action, associated with unwholesome consciousness, and characterized by painful feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the snatching away of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Requesting of Thread (Suttaviññatti-sikkhāpada) 636. "At that time" refers to the training rule regarding the requesting of thread.
In this context: *khoma* is thread made from *khoma* fibers; *kappāsika* is that produced from cotton; *koseyya* is thread made by spinning silk threads; *kambala* is... [blank]
The *Eḷakaloma-sutta*. "Sāṇa" means cloth made of hemp. Regarding "bhaṅga," some say it is simply individual bark-fiber thread;
however, it should be understood that cloth made by mixing these five together is called "bhaṅga.
For every instance of having it woven, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If the weaver lacks a distaff, a loom, or other such tools, those [should be obtained] from the forest...
If he sets down an axe or a hatchet, thinking, “I will bring it,” then from that point on,
for every single instance of the weaver’s work— whether for the sake of an accessory or for the purpose of weaving a robe—
the monk incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. When a length of one span has been woven in width and one cubit in breadth, it becomes a *nissaggiya pācittiya* offense.
In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however, it is stated: "For one who has it woven until the end, there is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* for every single piece.
This too should be understood as having been said with reference to this very same measurement;
for only that which reaches the final stage of being formally assigned (*vikappanupaga*) enters into the category of a robe (*cīvara*).
Furthermore, the determination of this matter should be understood as follows: first, a robe that has been personally requested is unallowable;
the rest, obtained through such means as relatives and so forth, is allowable. A weaver who is neither a relative nor one previously invited, if obtained through a formal request, is unallowable;
the rest is allowable. In that regard, for one who has an unallowable robe woven by an unallowable weaver, [the offense] is incurred prior to...
According to the method already stated, it is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*).
However, for one who has a permissible cloth (*kappiyasutta*) woven, just as there was previously an offense of expiation, so too is there an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Likewise, for one who has both a permissible and an impermissible cloth woven, if one section is made entirely of permissible cloth and one section is made entirely of impermissible cloth—thus being like a field divided by boundaries—if [the robe] reaches the measure of a final robe...
It is like a robe: if it consists of unallowable thread, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for each border; in the other case, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If they have fewer borders—even if only as much as the size of the eye-socket—there is an offense of wrong-doing for every border according to the number of borders.
Now, if by means of an intervening thread, or if it is allowable in length but not in width...
If it has been woven after being made unallowable, there is an offense of wrong-doing for each individual warp-board.
Even when having an allowable weaver weave an unallowable thread, there is an offense of wrong-doing just as there was previously a formal act of relinquishment (nissaggiya).

Likewise, when having a weaver weave both allowable and unallowable threads, if the portions consisting of unallowable threads are less than the measure of a subsequent robe, [there is an offense of wrong-doing].
In those cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by way of counting the sections. There is no offense regarding the sections of allowable thread (*kappiya-sutta*).

Now, if it is woven such that there is an allowable [thread] lengthwise and an unallowable [thread] crosswise, either by means of an alternating thread or by making the allowable long and the unallowable across, there is an offense of wrong-doing for every single plank.
However, if there are two weavers—one who is allowable and one who is unallowable—and the thread is unallowable, if they...
They weave by turn: if they weave on an improper loom, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every piece of cloth woven; if it is shorter, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If they weave with another [type of loom], there is an offense of wrong-doing in both cases. If both take up the shuttle and weave together, there is an offense of expiation for every piece of cloth woven.
Now, if the thread is allowable and the robe is limited in size by field-bounds and so forth—
If the weaving is done by an unallowable weaver, there is an offense of wrong-doing for every section woven; if woven by another [allowable weaver], there is no offense.
If both [weavers] take up the loom and weave together, there is an offense of wrong-doing for every section on the loom.

Now, if the thread is both allowable and unallowable, and they weave them alternately, then regarding those robes made of unallowable thread that reach the full measure of the last robe, [there is an offense of wrong-doing for every section woven by the unallowable weaver].
When the sections [of cloth] have been separated, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the count of the separated sections.

In cases where they are fewer than that, or where they are made of allowable thread, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Even if they are made of unallowable thread by a permissible weaver, or if they meet the measurement requirements, or if they are fewer than that, there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing.
However, if they are made of allowable thread, there is no offense.

Now, if one weaves by alternating threads—making the length unallowable and the width allowable—or if both of them take up the loom and weave together, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every individual piece of cloth in a robe that has no fixed dimensions;
if it has fixed dimensions, there are as many offenses of wrong-doing as there are dimensions. However, this meaning is not explicitly stated in the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā).
This is evident in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries; here, however, it is evident in every respect.
If the thread is allowable, and the weaver is either a relative, one who has been invited, or one employed for wages, there is no offense on account of having it woven.
However, for one who wishes to avoid the offense arising from the lapse of ten days, [the cloth] must be at least the size required for assignment (*vikappanupaga*).
When the warp has been removed, it must be resolved upon exactly as it stands. For if it were completed after ten days have elapsed, it would become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
The same principle applies even when relatives and others have set up the warp and offered it, saying, "Venerable sir, please accept this robe-cloth for yourselves."
If a weaver, being thus employed or wishing to give it himself, says, "Venerable sir,
I shall weave this robe-cloth for you and set it aside on such-and-such a day," and the monk lets ten days pass beyond that specified date,
it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
But if a weaver says, "I will weave a robe for you and send word," and does exactly so,
yet the monk sent by him does not inform that monk, but another person— having seen or heard it—
informs him, saying, "Venerable sir, your robe is finished," this report is not authoritative. When...
However, if one who has been sent by him reports [the arrival], and he lets ten days pass from the day he hears that person's words,
it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If the weaver says, "I will weave your robe and send it into the hand of someone,"...
He acts in that same way; however, if the monk who went to fetch the robe places it in his own cell but does not inform the other,
and someone else asks, "Venerable sir, is the robe recently brought back beautiful?", and [the first monk] replies,
"Where is the robe, friend?", and [the other] says, "It was sent into the hands of such-and-such a person," even the word of this person is not authoritative.
But when that bhikkhu gives away the robe-cloth, if he lets ten days pass from the day it was obtained, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
However, if the cost of having it woven has not been paid, he remains protected for as long as even a single kākani-coin’s worth remains unpaid.
640. There is no offense for one who requests thread for the purpose of sewing a robe; there is no offense for one requesting thread for the sake of sewing a robe.

The meaning is as follows. In the phrases beginning with "in connection with" (*āyoge*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause; thus it is said that there is no offense for one who makes himself understood by means of such causes as "connection" and so forth.
The rest here is of plain meaning. It has six origins (*samuṭṭhāna*); it is an action (*kiriya*);

it is not liberated through perception (*nosaññāvimokkha*); it is without [volitional] mind (*acittaka*); it is an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*); it consists of bodily and verbal action (*kāyakamma-vacīkamma*); it involves three types of consciousness (*ticitta*); and it involves three types of feeling (*tivedanā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning weaving is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Great Weaver. 641.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning the great weaver. Therein, "having weighed the thread" means having measured the thread.
Having made a measurement with a palm. *Appitaṃ* means thick. *Suvītaṃ* means well-woven;
it has been woven evenly in all places. *Suppavāyitaṃ* means well-stretched; it has been stretched well upon the loom, made even in all places.
*Suvilekhitaṃ* means well-scratched with a stylus. *Suvitacchitaṃ* means well-carded with a carding comb.
"Thoroughly washed" is the meaning. "Attached" means deficiency. "On the loom" means having brought it onto the loom specifically for the purpose of stretching it out lengthwise.
642. "If that monk there" means where those weavers are—in the village or the town.
"Should undergo alteration" means he should undergo a specific modification or an additional arrangement. However, the manner in which he underwent the alteration is as follows in the Pāḷi:
In order to demonstrate that [which exists], it was said: "This indeed, friends," and so forth.
"He speaks Dhamma" means he delivers a discourse on the Dhamma; by the phrase "by his word, whether long, broad, or compact," it specifically demonstrates the manner of expanding upon the Sutta.
"Previously uninvited" means having been previously uninvited by the owners of the robes. The rest is of plain meaning.

It has chasamutthāna as its origin; it is functional (kiriya); it is not a liberation through perception (no-saññā-vimokkha); it is without consciousness (acittaka); it is an offense by designation (paṇṇatti-vajja); it consists of bodily and verbal action (kāya-kamma-vacī-kamma);
it involves three types of consciousness (ti-citta); and it involves three types of feeling (ti-vedana). The commentary on the Mahāpesakāra Sikkhāpada is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Urgent Robes (Accekacīvarasikkhāpada) 646–9.
“At that time” refers to the training rule on urgent robes. Therein, “not having arrived within ten days” means: ten days is a “ten-day period” (*dasāha*);

not having arrived by that ten-day period is “not having arrived within ten days” (*dasāhānāgata*), which means not having reached the end of the ten days. That is what is meant by “not having arrived within ten days.”
The accusative case is used here in the sense of the locative by way of absolute conjunction;

for this very reason, it is stated in its word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "when ten days have not yet passed. As for the term *pavāraṇāya*, this is an instrumental case used for the purpose of non-confusion, in order to show in its own form that which was previously described as "when ten days have not yet passed."
“On the full moon of the first Kattika month” means the full moon of the first Kattika month.
Here too, because the nominative case is not employed for the first word, the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative, according to the previous method. This is what is meant:
“From the time it is said, ‘The first Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā) is ten days away,’ even if during those days there is an urgent robe-cloth for a bhikkhu...”
"If a monk knows, 'This is urgent,' he may accept even all [the robes].
By this, the time for storing robes that have arisen from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pavāraṇā is shown.
Granted, this is already established by the rule, "An extra robe may be kept for at most ten days," but it is stated here by way of a specific occasion (*atthuppatti*).
However, having shown a meaning as if it were something never before mentioned, the training rule was established.
"Urgent robe" (*accekacīvara*) refers to a robe that is required with urgency; and in order to show its state of urgency, it is said:
"He wishes to go with an army," and so forth. In that context, by the word "faith" (*saddhā*), merely the presence of faith is indicated.
"Confidence" (*pasāda*) here means being well-pleased and possessing strong faith. "This is called an urgent robe" (*accekacīvara*):
by these reasons, a robe that has been announced—either by sending a messenger or by coming in person—with the words, "I shall give a *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) robe," is called an urgent robe.
However, from the sixth [day] onwards, even a robe that has arisen which is not urgent...
Even a robe that has been set aside after being formally relinquished receives this very same exemption.
"Having made a sign, it should be deposited" means it should be placed there having made some kind of mark. Why was this said?
Because if they should divide it before the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he by whom it was taken must not be one whose rains-residence is broken.
If, however, it exists, that robe belongs to the Saṅgha itself. Therefore, having identified it, one may give it away at ease. (Rule 650:
"If there is a robe for which one is in haste, and one perceives it as such," and so forth—this was stated with reference specifically to what has been distributed.
But if it has not been distributed, whether it is in the storehouse of the Saṅgha, there is no offense even when the time for robes has passed.
Thus is the ten-day allowance for an extra robe. For an unmade *vassikasāṭikā* robe, there is a five-month period when the *kathina* has not been spread;
six months when the *vassa* has been extended; and another four months when the *kathina* has been spread.
On the final day of the winter season, by means of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the basic robe, there is yet another month; thus, there are eleven months.
The exemption: it should be understood that for a basic robe (*mūlacīvara*) there is an exemption of one month based on the expectation of its acquisition;

for a hurried robe (*accekacīvara*), if the Kathina has not been spread, there is an exemption of one month plus eleven days; if the Kathina has been spread, there is an exemption of five months plus eleven days;
beyond that, there is no exemption even for a single day.
"In another [robe] similar to an urgent robe" means in something other than an urgent robe. The rest here is of obvious meaning.

The origin of the *kaṭhina* rule: it is of non-action, not involving liberation through insight, without mental concomitants, an offense by formal precept, consisting of bodily and verbal action, associated with three types of consciousness, and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the urgent robe is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Peril (Sāsaṅkasikkhāpada) 652.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning peril. In this context, "those who have completed the rains retreat in forest dwellings" means that they had previously lived only in the forest.
However, because their robes were worn out, they spent the rains retreat in lodgings within a village due to the necessity of those requisites.
Having worn [the robes] and having finished making their robes, thinking, “Now, being free from obstacles, we shall practice the duty of a recluse,” they dwell in forest lodgings.
*Kattikacorakā* means thieves in the month of Kattika. *Paripāpentī* means they cause distress;
running here and there, they terrify and drive people away. *Antaraghare nikkhipituṃ* means to deposit [the goods] within a village.
Since requisites are difficult to obtain through the Dhamma and in accordance with the law, for a bhikkhu who practices effacement (sallekha) is not even able to request them from his own mother,
the Blessed One therefore permitted him to deposit his robe within an inhabited area for the purpose of protecting it.
However, because it was appropriate for bhikkhus, he did not prohibit dwelling in the forest.
653. Regarding the phrase *upavassaṃ kho pana*: here, *upavassa* means "having entered the rains" (*upavassa*); it is equivalent to "having entered the rains" (*upavasitvā*).
For here, as in the case of *upasampajja* and similar forms, the nasalization (*anunāsika*) is to be understood. The meaning is: "having entered upon the rains and having dwelt [there].
And this word is connected with the phrase: "a bhikkhu dwelling in such lodgings. What has been said?
What is it? Having entered the rains residence and dwelt there, from that time until the conclusion of the full moon of the later Kattika month—
whenever a bhikkhu is dwelling in forest lodgings that are considered risky and dangerous—
if he so desires, he may [leave] one of his three robes behind in an inhabited area.

Regarding the phrase "should deposit": since one who has entered the rains residence and remains until the full moon of the first *kattika* month is considered among those who have completed the rains residence (*vuṭṭhavassa*),

this term "those who have completed the rains residence" was stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) solely to show the person eligible to deposit the robe, without engaging in this overly complex analysis of the phrasing.
This also connects with the phrase, "a bhikkhu dwelling in lodgings. For here the meaning is:
"among such bhikkhus as those who have completed the rains-residence and are dwelling in lodgings," it is said that it refers to any one whatsoever among those bhikkhus.
The definition of a forest (*arañña*) has been stated in the commentary on taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). However, this is the distinction: if the monastery is enclosed by a wall...
If [the monastery] is enclosed, it should be measured starting from the gatepost (*indakhīla*) of the enclosed village, or from the place suitable for a boundary in an unenclosed village,
up to the enclosure of the monastery. If the monastery is unenclosed, even if it is far away, it should be measured from the very first dwelling,
or the dining hall, or the place of regular assembly, or the Bodhi tree, or the shrine (*cetiya*).
It is measured from the lodging; one should measure it by establishing that boundary.

Even if there is a village nearby, and the sounds of householders in the houses can be heard by those staying in the monastery, yet because it is obstructed by mountains, rivers, and so forth, it is not possible to go in a straight line—then one must follow whatever is his usual path, even if he has to travel by boat on that route.

One should take a distance of five hundred bow-lengths from a village. Whoever blocks the path here and there for the sake of securing a portion of a nearby village is to be understood as a "thief of the ascetic practice" (*dhutaṅgacora*).

Regarding the phrase "deemed dangerous": they are "deemed" (*sammatāni*) to be "dangerous" (*sāsaṅkā*); the meaning is that they are recognized as such. In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, the passage beginning with "in the monastery or in the vicinity of the monastery" is stated to show the reason why those places are deemed dangerous.

“With fear” means together with dangers; the meaning is that they are accompanied by powerful fears. In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, the phrase “in a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery,” and so forth, is stated to show the reason why those places are dangerous.

“He should deposit it in a village for alms within range” means that he should deposit it in a village for alms—provided it possesses the necessary qualifications—that he himself prefers, located in any direction around the forest dwelling.
Herein, these are the qualifications: having entered the first *rains-residence* (*purimikā*) and being invited at the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*); this is one [qualification].
The factor: if one has arrived during the later period or one’s rains-residence has been interrupted, one is not permitted to deposit [the kathina].
It must be the month of Kattika; this is the second factor. One may not do so after the month of Kattika;
the lodging must be exactly five hundred bow-lengths in size; this is the third factor. Or, in a place less than that measure, within a distance of four hundred bow-lengths...

Or, if it is beyond the proper measure, one does not obtain [the robe]; for that which is intended here is precisely that distance where, having gone for alms, one can return to the monastery again by the time of the meal.
However, if one who has been invited travels even half a *yojana* or a full *yojana* and then returns to stay, this is "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*).
It is only when there is danger and fear that this constitutes the fourth factor.
For even if one is staying in a lodging that possesses the [necessary] factors and is free from fear and danger, one is not permitted to leave one's belongings behind.

"Except by the consent of the monks" means except for that consent granted at Kosambī regarding the *udositaka* training rule; if such consent has been obtained, it is permissible to live apart [from one's robes] for more than six nights.
"Having again entered the village boundary" refers to the case where the lodging is in the eastern direction from the alms-village, and this...

The meaning is that if he has gone toward the western direction and, being unable to reach his lodging before the seventh dawn rises, he may enter the village boundary and stay in an assembly hall or wherever else; having learned the news regarding the robe, it is permissible for him to depart.
If he is unable to do so, he must relinquish [his claim] while remaining right there.
"It will remain as an extra robe. The rest is self-evident. Regarding the origin of the offense (*kathina-samuṭṭhāna*):

it originates from body and speech, and from body, speech, and mind; it is non-action (*akiriya*); it is not a liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*); it is without thought (*acittaka*); it is an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇatti-vajja*); it consists of bodily and verbal action; it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning suspicion (*sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Food Prepared for Others (Pariṇata-sikkhāpada) 657.
"At that time" refers to the training rule concerning food prepared for others. In this context, "of a group" (*pūgassa*) means of a multitude;
the meaning is "of a community. "Prepared" (*paṭiyattaṃ*) means "made ready. "Many meals for the Saṅgha" (*bahū saṅghassa bhattā*) means many meals for the Saṅgha.
They point out that there are many avenues for gain and that there is no loss whatsoever for the Saṅgha. "Oṇojetha" means "give.
But why is it not permissible to speak in this way? Why is it not allowed?

For in the case of alms brought forward (*abhihaṭabhikkhā*)—which have been brought and prepared for the sake of the Saṅgha in a single place—there is no such thing as a "designated speech" (*payuttavācā*) regarding the portions set aside specifically for those who were invited to bring them.
658. *Saṅghikaṃ* means belonging to the Saṅgha. For because it has been dedicated to the Saṅgha, even if it has not yet entered [the Saṅgha’s] hand, it belongs to the Saṅgha in one sense;

however, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), by way of explaining the meaning, *saṅghikaṃ* is shown in its direct sense as: "that which is called *saṅghika* is what has been given to the Saṅgha and relinquished."
"Acquisitions" (*lābha*) refers to the object to be obtained. For this very reason, it is said in its explanation: "even a robe," and so forth.
"Dedicated" (*pariṇata*) means that which stands having been directed toward the Saṅgha, inclined toward the Saṅgha, and leaning toward the Saṅgha.
To show the cause by which it becomes dedicated, the word-commentary states: "the speech [of 'we will give' or 'we will make'] has been broken."
659. *Payoge dukkaṭan* means that for the act of diverting to oneself a gain that has already been dedicated [to the Saṅgha], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);

when it is obtained and comes into one's hand, it is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). However, if it has been given to the Saṅgha, it is not permissible to take it; it must be returned to the Saṅgha itself.
Furthermore, if one eats together with the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*), having had the value of the goods assessed...

[The robe] must be made up. However, if one knows that [an item] has been dedicated to the Saṅgha—whether it was dedicated by fellow practitioners, laypeople, or even by one’s own mother—and having redirected it to oneself, takes it, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If, however, one redirects it to another person, saying, "Give this to such-and-such a bhikkhu," there is a simple offense of expiation (suddhika-pācittiya).
If one dedicates to another one’s own bowl or robe, it is both a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* and a *suddhika-pācittiya*.
This same method applies when there are many items. And this has been said:
"By means of the *nissaggiya*, there is an offense; by means of the *suddhika*, there is a *pācittiya*."
"One might incur [an offense] on one side;
this question was pondered by those skilled in the Dhamma.
This was said with reference to the dedication [of merit]. Also, even at the time of the rainy-season robe, in the mother's house, for the Saṅgha...

If, knowing that a rain-cloak has been assigned [to the Saṅgha], one appropriates it for oneself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). If one appropriates it for another person, it is a simple offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

If people bring ghee, oil, and so forth, intending to provide a meal for the Saṅgha, and a sick monk, knowing that these items have been assigned to the Saṅgha, requests anything from them, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, if he asks, "Do you have ghee and so forth brought for yourselves?
and when told, "Yes, we do," he says, "Give some to me as well," it is permissible.
Furthermore, if the lay followers, seeing him feeling anxious, say, "The Saṅgha receives only what has been given by us; please take it, Venerable Sir," this too is permissible.

660. "Dedicated to the Saṅgha for another Saṅgha" means: having dedicated something to the Saṅgha in one monastery, one redirects it toward another monastery, saying, "Give this to the Saṅgha in such-and-such a great monastery.
"Or for a shrine" means: one redirects it for a shrine, saying, "What is the use of giving to the Saṅgha? Perform an offering for the shrine. Regarding "dedicated to a shrine":
here, having made a restriction, [the offense occurs] when, from a garland or a sapling planted for the sake of one shrine, [one takes it] for another shrine.
It is not even permissible to offer flowers [to a stupa]. However, if one sees a parasol or a banner already offered to one stupa, it is permissible to have the remainder given to another stupa.
Regarding that which has been dedicated to an individual: even if it has been dedicated to something as lowly as a dog, one should say, "Do not give this to the dog."
If he dedicates it to another person by saying, "Give this to him," it is a *dukkaṭa*.
However, if the donors say, "We wish to give food to the Saṅgha, we wish to make an offering to the Cetiya, and we wish to give requisites to a single bhikkhu;
we shall give according to your preference. Speak, to whom shall we give?"—when they have spoken thus, by him...

The monk should say, "Give it wherever you wish. However, if they simply ask, "Where shall we give it?", he should speak according to the method set forth in the Pāḷi. The rest here is of obvious meaning.

It has three origins: it originates from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind; it is an action (kiriya), liberated by perception (saññāvimokkha), associated with consciousness (sacittaka), a worldly offense (lokavajja), bodily and verbal action, unwholesome consciousness, and possesses three feelings.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the bowl, within the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya,
is finished. The third chapter, the Chapter on the Bowl, is completed.
The commentary on the Nissaggiya [offenses] is finished.
The commentary on the Pārājika section is finished.
